The renames preserved meaning across repeated runs. Ten professional developers judged the polished tests in a study. They rated them as readable as hand-written tests. The trick worked regardless of the model used.
arxiv-2412-18943: Milan Damnjanović and Ivanka Milošević present a 2024 arXiv paper cataloging obstructed atomic limits in thread-like materials. An obstructed limit is a topological state whose charge centers sit away from the atoms. Using line group symmetry, the authors revisit the standard theory with its group machinery in the open. They distill it into a theorem that flags every possible case. The survey then runs the test across the families of quasi-one-dimensional systems, arranging results in order with examples.
arxiv-2412-19343:
Atoms lined up along a hair-thin glass fiber can trade light with the fiber far more strongly if their spacing makes their glow add up. Vera and Solano propose two trap designs that hold a one-dimensional atom array at the second-order Bragg spacing, exactly one wavelength apart. At that spacing the atoms' radiation interferes constructively into the fiber, and guided light reflects back coherently.

Both schemes trap with far-off-resonance light to keep scattering and heating low, and both adjust the trap to cancel stray shifts. Their calculations use rubidium-87 atoms, but the authors note the designs carry over to other species. The goal is a platform for collective and nonlinear light effects.
arxiv-2412-19543:
Generative image models are good at common scenes and bad at rare ones. Rare cases sit in thin regions of the data, and mode collapse makes models skip them. Subeen Lee, Jiyeon Han, Soyeon Kim, and Jaesik Choi generate diverse rare samples from pretrained GANs. They optimize latent vectors under several goals at once. A normalizing flow estimates density in feature space, which scores rarity. Controls let a user set rarity, diversity, and closeness to a reference image.

The method needs no retraining of the generator. Tests across datasets and GAN types support the claims, both visually and numerically. The authors aim the tool at fields where unusual examples matter most.
arxiv-2412-19643:
Naoko Nakagawa and co-authors rebuild thermodynamics for fluids that sit in gravity, in a 2024 paper. Textbook free energy ignores the weight of the fluid itself. Their version adds gravity's pull and the column's height as true variables, after fixing a single reference point for height so the math stays consistent.

From this frame they derive how liquid and gas settle together under gravity. Liquid at the bottom is stable, yet liquid floating on top is also locally stable, and flipping between the two counts as a first-order transition. Molecular simulations matched the predictions. The work speaks to anyone modeling tall tanks, atmospheres, or stars.
arxiv-2412-19743:
A large collaboration wrote a perspective paper from 2024 on flavor physics at a planned circular electron-positron collider in China. Flavor physics studies how the heaviest quarks and leptons change into lighter ones, a sensitive probe for new particles. The collider is designed to run in several modes. Its Z-boson mode would make about four trillion Z particles, a sample no past machine can match.

Decays of those Z bosons would give razor-sharp measures of how the Z couples to other particles. They would also yield huge numbers of boosted heavy quarks and leptons in a clean setting. That bounty suits precise tests of rare decays and subtle asymmetries. The paper surveys the landscape of what such a machine could settle in flavor physics. It weighs the program against the design's stated brightness and modes.
arxiv-2412-19843:
Owais Ishtiaq Siddiqui and co-authors tackle a hard sorting task in their 2024 study: telling oil spills from clean sea in satellite data. Spills are rare, so most sets of images hold far more clean shots than spill shots, and plain tools often miss the rare class. The team turns to quantum Bayesian networks, a method that mixes chance-based logic with quantum states.

Their method sorts spill and non-spill zones with a very high score on a standard test of sorting skill. The authors frame the gain as a step toward sharper watch over seas and coasts. They also note that each data set brings its own snags, so more tuning is still needed.
arxiv-2412-19943:
Nicholas Wawrykow wrote a 2024 math paper on how hard it is to program robots moving in a narrow strip. The robots are disks that must fit only a set number across the strip width. They must also make a series of stops along the way. The paper computes a measure of how many cases any such program must handle.

Both a standard version and a spread-out version of that measure get exact values. As long as the disk count tops the strip width, the formula has a clean form. The result shows that non-looping programs face a case load that grows with stops and disks.
arxiv-2412-20043:
Chencheng Zhu, Kazutaka Shimada, Tomoki Taniguchi, and Tomoko Ohkuma present a 2024 method for picking examples to show a language model at work. Models can learn from examples placed in the prompt, which helps for science text extraction where labeled data are scarce and costly. Which examples are picked can change the result a great deal.

Their method, STAYKATE, mixes two ideas. One picks examples that represent the whole pool, borrowed from active learning. The other fetches examples close to the case at hand. Across three science data sets, the hybrid beat both standard trained methods and other selection methods. The gain was largest for entity types that other methods found hard.
arxiv-2501-00143:
Cheng-Hau Yang and three co-authors brought a shifted edge method to heat flows. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with joined flow and heat runs on meshes that do not fit the body's shape. Their build uses an octree mesh, part filled, with the shifted boundary method. A half implicit form of the thermal flow laws keeps runs fast yet true. The method can pin both field and slope terms on cut cells.

That gives true flux reads near hard shapes. Slope terms, the hard case, held exact on their meshes. Runs span flow regimes from slow to swift. Readers in flow sims get a way to keep edge truth with no body fit mesh grind.
arxiv-2501-00443:
Yu Tong and Yongtao Zhan wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four about how fast a quantum system settles into its thermal state. Preparing Gibbs states, the thermal states of quantum matter, is a key task for quantum computers. A recently proposed process, called a Lindbladian, can drive a system toward such a state, but its speed needed proof.

The authors study weakly interacting fermion systems, the setting of models like the Fermi-Hubbard model of electrons in a lattice. They show that, at any temperature, the key spectral gap stays above a fixed constant when the interaction is weak enough. That constant does not shrink as the system grows. Mixing time thus grows at most in step with system size, so the states can be prepared efficiently.
arxiv-2501-00543:
Fabrizio Colombo, Elodie Pozzi, Irene Sabadini, and Brett Wick settle the Corona problem for a class of quaternion-valued functions, in work the text head dates to 2024. The classic Corona problem, solved for one complex variable, asks when functions with no common zero admit a bounded solution to a Bezout-style equation. Its quaternionic version had stayed open, partly because pointwise multiplication misbehaves for these functions.

The authors recast the equation under the multiplication that does work, turning it into a system of equations on the unit disc. They then adapt a classic proof of the one-variable theorem to solve that system. The result extends Corona theory into hypercomplex analysis.
arxiv-2501-00743:
Mengran Li and a team of co-authors repair incomplete graphs in twenty twenty-five. Many real graphs lack attributes for some nodes. Graph neural networks trained on such data produce biased results. Feature propagation is the standard repair, filling gaps from neighbors. It suffers a cold start problem, worst for low-degree nodes and reset attributes.

Their method, AttriReBoost, rethinks how propagation begins. New boundary conditions and added virtual edges improve node connectivity. Propagation then converges more stably and efficiently. The reconstruction needs no gradient computation, so overhead stays low. Readers working with messy real-world graphs get a way to restore missing features without training a heavy imputation model first.
arxiv-2501-00843:
Baisa presents a 2025 computer vision paper on tracking many moving objects in video at once. A tracker must match each new detection to the right track, frame after frame. Strong clues such as motion and looks help, but weaker clues can help too. The study tests four ways to fuse those clues into one matching cost.

The fusion options range from a simple minimum to weighted sums and gated products of the clue costs. Tests ran on three public sets, MOT17, MOT20, and DanceTrack. Results show the choice of fusion method changes tracking quality a great deal. The paper aims to help vision researchers pick the right fusion for this matching step.
arxiv-2501-01543:
Sara Tro, Ian Grooms, and Keith Julien work out approximate formulas for when convection starts in a rotating fluid with gripping walls, in a 2025 paper. No-slip walls stir a secondary flow called Ekman pumping, which shifts the onset of Rayleigh-Bénard convection away from the free-slip case. Guided by numerical solutions, the authors build a reduced model and solve it in closed form for long, slow waves.

Their formulas track the full numerical stability results closely. Different scalings of the wave size are explored in turn. The work gives analysts a quick way to estimate how rotation and wall grip together set the convection threshold.
arxiv-2501-01843:
Yirong Wang and co-authors describe a simpler optical lattice in a 2025 arXiv paper. Optical lattices trap atoms with interfering laser beams for quantum work. Keeping several beams phase-locked is hard, needing delicate optics and electronics.

Their scheme passes a single beam through a prism with symmetric facets and large apex angles. The lattice forms from parts of the same beam, so no moving parts or phase locks are needed. They built both a triangular lattice and a ten-fold quasi-crystal lattice. Stability tests showed the lattice constant changed by barely one percent. Position drift was likewise tiny.
arxiv-2501-01943:
Renato Prisco, Jonathan Ronca, and Francesco Tramontano published a paper in 2025 on a program for loop integrals in particle physics. Such sums come up when teams work out scattering amplitudes at higher orders. The program, called LINE, solves differential equations for the master integrals by series expansion. Boundary values can come from the user or be worked out inside the program by a regions method.

The code is open source, and it brings the steps of the team together in one place. Worked cases show how the runs go in real use. The authors offer the tool to theorists who need reliable numbers for such sums in work that calls for great exactness.
arxiv-2501-02043:
Petr Kisselev and Padmanabhan Seshaiyer model epidemic spread across the United States with a hybrid of classic and neural methods in a 2025 study. A metapopulation design treats each region as its own susceptible-infected-recovered pool, with human mobility carrying infection between pools. Graph neural networks estimate the movement-linked parameters that older fitting handled poorly.

Earlier hybrid versions already beat standard methods on data gathered before the period studied here. The authors extend that comparison for COVID spread across connected regions. Mobility-aware forecasts help officials judge where interventions matter most, since a purely local model misses infections arriving from elsewhere.
arxiv-2501-02143:
Zhaobin Mo, Yunlong Li, and Xuan Di built SafeAug in two thousand twenty-five to grow safety-critical driving scenes out of real road data. Near-crash data are scarce in natural recordings, so teams lean on simulation, whose images look fake beside real ones. Their frame edits real scenes into hazardous ones while keeping the look of real footage.

A detector first finds vehicles, then depth estimation and a three-dimensional shift move a vehicle into a risky proximity. Dynamics data are adjusted to match the staged danger. On a standard driving data set, a self-driving model trained on the augmented data beat rivals trained with resampling tricks, with image realism largely kept.
arxiv-2501-02243:
Density functional theory is the workhorse method for computing how electrons behave in molecules, but its shortcuts fail for some hard cases. Yunzhi Li and Chen Li study those shortcuts in 2025 at an extreme edge: the semiclassical limit, where a key constant of quantum physics is sent toward zero. Exact theory says the energy should stay finite there.

The pair show that mainstream shortcuts instead blow up in that limit, breaking the exact rule. They link the same flaw to the poor energies these methods give for strongly bound metal pairs. The test gives makers of new shortcuts a sharp check to pass. It may point the way to better tools for hard molecules.
arxiv-2501-02343:
Maitri Mandal and co-authors show that a sheared colloidal glass can remember its past, in the manner of the Kovacs effect. Their paper appeared in 2025. The classic effect, seen in glasses after temperature jumps, reveals hidden memory in disordered matter. Whether it survives under shear, which keeps volume fixed, was unknown. The team combined experiments, simulations, and response theory on a dense suspension of tiny spheres.

A two-step shear protocol produced the telltale memory hump. With stronger, nonlinear pushes, the response drifted from the simple theory. That drift tracked microscopic flows in which particles stray from the smooth shear pattern. The authors conclude the memory effect extends to volume-preserving pushes, and that local flow patterns govern how strong the memory is.
arxiv-2501-02443:
Mustafa and Guvendi study a quantum oscillator in a space with spiral flaws. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses the Klein-Gordon equation, the relativistic wave rule for spin-free fields. Two flaw types are in play. One twists a radial line, and the other twists a circle. The authors test each flaw with and without a magnetic field.

The first flaw shifts the energy levels of the oscillator in all cases. The second flaw leaves energies alone unless a magnetic field is on. Wave shapes pick up the flaw's mark in both cases. The team solves the equations exactly in most cases. Some cases need a weaker exact form tied to Heun functions. For the second flaw, the field strength alone sets how fast the oscillator swings.
arxiv-2501-02643:
Tamás Pető, Ferenc Iglói, and István Kovács study a disordered magnet chain buffeted by two kinds of random field at once. The Ising chain carries random bonds, a random transverse field, and a random longitudinal field. Experiments on a lithium holmium yttrium fluoride compound motivate the model. Strong disorder renormalization, which decimates the strongest couplings step by step, reveals its low-energy fate at zero temperature.

Each field alone leads somewhere known: transverse randomness gives ordered and disordered fixed points plus an infinite-disorder critical point; longitudinal randomness gives the classical random-field fixed point. Together, the flows are drawn to one of two disordered fixed points. At the infinite-disorder point, the one relevant direction runs along the separatrix between them. The correlation length diverges there with an exponent near one.
arxiv-2501-03043:
A. Müller and a large team measured hollow-atom resonances in boron ions in 2025, jointly in experiment and theory. Firing photons at helium-like boron ions, they hunted states where both inner-shell electrons are excited at once, leaving a double core hole that quickly decays. The ion beam mixed ground-state and long-lived excited ions, so two resonance series appeared, one from each starting state, across hundreds of electronvolts.

Spectrometers reached resolving power in the tens of thousands, pinning the strongest resonance energies to about a milli-electronvolt. Relativistic many-body calculations, including electron correlation and radiative effects, reproduced the pattern level by level. Such precision benchmarks atomic theory in a regime where several effects compete at once.
arxiv-2501-03143:
Beta Pictoris is a young star with a dusty disk and two known giant planets, still forming worlds. Lacquement, Beust, Faramaz-Gorka, and Duchêne ask in a 2025 study whether one more planet hides past the outer known one. The inner edge of the dust disk sits near 50 units from the star, but two planets should carve it near 28.

The team ran many orbit simulations with one or two added planets in the disk plane. A single added planet, light and on a near-round path, matched the seen edge well. Two lighter planets could also fit the data. Such planets would sit below the reach of current sharp imaging. Better cameras may one day catch one.
arxiv-2501-03743:
Massimo Bernaschi, Pasqua D-Ambra, and co-authors speed a key linear solver on clusters of graphics chips, in a 2025 paper. Such solvers sit at the heart of physics based models and often form the main drag on run time. The method they use cuts sync steps between chips.

Their code groups small steps to use chip speed more well. It also hides data moves behind math work when many chips share one sparse task. Tests on a classic heat spread case show the plan works well. The work points to strong growth on large chip clusters with less talk between nodes.
arxiv-2501-03943:
Eloi Descamps and co-authors wrote a 2025 physics paper that rebuilds the basics of quantum optics around a strict counting rule. The rule, a superselection rule, forbids mixing states with different photon numbers unless a phase reference exists. Standard teaching tools quietly assume such a reference and skip the rule.

The authors adopt a picture of light states that obeys the rule from the start. Within it, they restate key tools: near-classical states, phase-space pictures, and a universal set of gates. The framework keeps the feel of the older picture while matching ideas from spin systems. It gives one shared language for all bosonic codes, from single photons to smooth field states.
arxiv-2501-04043:
Bogdan Dimitrov extends a math route for timing a GPS signal when all six orbit traits can change, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Past work let only the angle along the orbit vary, with relativity effects counted. The full set maps into three space coordinates through a known change of variables.

The travel time is cast as a squared form in the small changes of the six traits. A varied-form method plus a Stokes step needs second derivatives to stay nonzero. In shape terms that need matches the presence of Morse functions. No such function exists for the omega angle, the author shows. Readers get both the wider frame and its hard limit.
arxiv-2501-04343:
Qiang Sun and co-authors build in 2025 a generator of question-answer pairs for knowledge graphs that change over time. Such temporal graphs store facts with dates, and question answering over them is starved of training data. Hand-building custom pairs for each new graph is slow.

Their framework sorts questions by how the question's timeline relates to its context, then generates pairs for any temporal graph fed to it. The generator ships as an open-source Python package. The authors offer it as a universal tool to bootstrap temporal question answering data sets, with the categorization scheme as a guide for coverage.
arxiv-2501-04543:
Christopher Lazik and co-authors ask in 2025 whether language models can craft user personas that designers find as believable as human made ones. Generated personas promise to speed human centered design. Yet they may miss the context and feeling that make a persona true to real users, which threatens quality, above all for beginners.

The team gathered ten personas made by design experts under set attributes from past work. They then generated model made counterparts and had users judge both kinds for credibility. Where the fakes feel thin shows exactly what models still miss about people. The study gives design teams a sober check on when a machine persona can stand in for research, and when it cannot.
arxiv-2501-04643:
Gao and co-authors redesign capsule networks to classify hyperspectral images with far less computing. Such images carry rich spectra for mapping land cover, but capsule networks link their layers so densely that costs explode. Their 2025 method adds a wavelet based downsampling step with attention, so detail is not lost as features shrink.

A multi-scale routing scheme then prunes most capsule links, keeping only the useful ones. A pyramid fusion step merges spectral and spatial patterns at several sizes, and local self attention highlights the meaningful links that remain. The result matches the best accuracy reported for this task while using less time, fewer operations, and fewer parameters. The authors present it as a practical choice for real monitoring systems.
arxiv-2501-05143:
Alexander Borichev, Artur Nicolau, Myriam Ounaies, and Pascal Thomas studied in 2025 when a quotient algebra of bounded analytic functions has a strong invertibility property. In plain terms, the property says a function that stays near full size on an inner function's zero set must be invertible in the quotient, with a controlled inverse.

They prove this property matches the maximal growth of the inner function away from its zeros. It is also described through how narrow the function's low-level sets are, and tied to a weak embedding property from earlier work. Divisors of such inner functions are studied too, with a geometric account of which zero sets keep the property for all divisors.
arxiv-2501-05243:
Chandan Kumar Sheemar, Symeon Chatzinotas, and a team of co-authors argue for merging two satellite jobs into one. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, covers joint communications and sensing for sixth-generation networks. Satellites now carry split gear for talking and for watching Earth. Demand growth makes that split wasteful in cost and spectrum.

A shared payload can do both jobs with less hardware. It also opens services that split gear cannot offer. The authors walk through one test case to show the idea can work. They then list the hard spots: design, signals, and rules. The paper aims to spark work on shared space systems.
arxiv-2501-05343:
Starquakes measured by asteroseismology can reveal a star's inner structure, but one trusted tool breaks down for red giants. Ong and co-authors revisit the small frequency separation between radial and quadrupole vibration modes, long read as a direct probe of the deep interior.

The classic estimator linking that separation to the sound-speed gradient works on main-sequence stars, yet fails badly on red giant models. The authors derive a single expression that reduces to the classic one for young stars while matching the giants' behavior. In giants, the separation turns out to track global traits, scaling with the square of the large separation over the peak frequency, not the interior. They also show that shifts during the move off the main sequence mark where the convective envelope's base sits, which may help pin down mixing at that boundary.
arxiv-2501-05543: Piotr Chruściel and co-authors build a family of black holes with curved rims in high space counts. The work dates to 2025. The holes spin like a known class of holes in a space that curves the other way. Their edge cross-parts are not round, which breaks the usual mold for such holes. The set is free of any sharp tear at its core and works in even counts of space plus time.
arxiv-2501-05643:
Anna Marklová and co-authors ask whether large language models grasp iconicity, the natural link between a word's sound and its sense. Words like cuckoo echo what they mean. Models meet sound only through text, so their grip on such links is in doubt. Their 2025 study has a top model invent fake words in a made-up tongue, built to sound like their meanings.

Hundreds of Czech and German speakers then guessed the fake words' meanings. They beat chance by more than they do for far-off real tongues, so the words do carry the link. Model-based guessers did even better than humans. Extra checks probed how widely the trick works and which cues each side used. The authors say models encode sound-sense links in their own way.
arxiv-2501-05743:
Tianji Cai and co-authors hunt for patterns in scattering data from planar maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. The object in view is the three-gluon form factor of the chiral stress tensor, a close cousin of the Higgs-to-three-gluon amplitude in QCD. A bootstrap program has produced data for this form factor up to eight loops.

In their 2025 paper, the symbol of the form factor is a set of words in six letters, each with an integer weight. The team studies which weights vanish and how the rest relate. Many word families turn out to have closed-form weights, and simple recursions link weights at one loop order to words below. The patterns hint at rules that hold at every loop order.
arxiv-2501-05843:
Andrew Mummery wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on how fast a black hole can spin. As a disc of matter feeds a black hole, it usually spins the hole up, while captured light pushes back and slows it. The balance sets a top spin, long known as the Thorne limit, near 0.998 in the simplest theory.

Mummery asks how that limit shifts when the infalling gas glows brightly just inside the inner edge of the disc. Simulations show magnetic stresses make that plunging region shine, adding to the braking effect. The extra light lowers the top spin to about 0.99 for typical cases. The shift is small, but it matters for reading the spins astronomers measure.
arxiv-2501-05943:
Mayank Singh and co-authors design a controller that uses electrical stimulation to help a weak ankle move. Functional electrical stimulation can fire paretic muscles to lift or point the foot, but ankle motion is nonlinear and hard to steer. Their 2025 paper builds a model predictive controller on Koopman operator theory, which recasts nonlinear motion in a linear form.

Sensors worn on the body feed the model, which predicts how stimulation will move the ankle for both lifting and pointing muscles. The linear form lets the controller plan in real time with more precision. Simulations and lab experiments back the approach. Rehab engineers get a data-driven route to finer stimulation control.
arxiv-2501-06143:
Gerd Kortemeyer and co-authors test in 2025 how a multimodal AI system handles physics concept tests in many languages and subjects. Concept inventories are standard surveys that probe student grasp of ideas in mechanics, electricity, optics, heat, and more advanced fields. Past studies fed the system plain text only.

Here the tests were uploaded as images, as a student would see them on paper, drawn from a public physics teaching site. Scores varied by subject, with laboratory skills the weakest area, and by language, with English and other European languages strongest. Which items were hard barely changed across languages. Against published student data, the system beat average students after teaching in every subject but laboratory skills. Items needing image reading tripped it more than pure text items, a caution for classroom use.
arxiv-2501-06543:
Fucai Li, Jinkai Ni, and Ling-Yun Shou prove that a hard system of equations for magnetized fluids has solutions that last for all time. The equations govern a conducting fluid whose density varies from place to place, even jumping sharply, while it flows and carries a magnetic field. Such rough starting data defeat most methods.

Working in the whole of three-dimensional space, the team shows that small starting flow and field yield one clean solution that lasts forever. They also describe how it settles over time. A special two-dimensional-flavored case even allows part of the data to be large. They also prove uniqueness under very weak assumptions on the density. The results extend a classic line of work on fluids to the magnetic, uneven-density case.
arxiv-2501-07543:
Debabrata Sahoo, Rameswar Sahu, and Kirtiman Ghosh map how hard the future LHC can push the hunt for leptoquarks that decay into a top quark and a tau lepton. Their 2025 paper studies third-generation scalar leptoquarks, particles that would link quarks and leptons. The machine setting is the 14 TeV collider, at two assumed data volumes.

Machine learning taggers spot the fat, boosted tops and the heavy bosons that fake the signal, and a multivariate classifier sorts signal from standard clutter. The team then sets the cross-section limits a null result would imply, at 95 percent confidence. Reach extends well past current mass limits, which they credit to the tagging gains.
arxiv-2501-07843:
Xianghong Jin and co-authors put a candidate quantum material on the stand to prove its unusual magnetic pattern. The cobalt compound Na2Co2TeO6 may host triple-q order, where spins arrange under three wave directions at once, rather than the usual zigzag. Such an order should shrug off weak symmetry-breaking strain, and its swirling spins should twist passing light.

In clean single crystals, squeezing the sample in the plane left the neutron diffraction signals unmoved, just as the triple-q picture predicts. Light sent along the axis showed a strong Faraday rotation in the ordered state, driven by the spin vorticity, and its sign could be flipped by training the crystal's small net moment. Both tests argue the exotic order is real.
arxiv-2501-07943:
Eline Honig and Emiel Lorist bring, in a 2025 paper, the tools of optimization to a corner of harmonic analysis. Their objects are collections of sets with a boundedness property called the Carleson condition, and a related packing property called sparseness. Both matter in the study of wave-like functions and operators. Computing the exact Carleson constant of a collection was previously only approximated.

The authors give an algorithm that computes it exactly and runs in strongly polynomial time. The method rests on minimizing a submodular function. A second method shows any Carleson collection is sparse, with the best possible link between the constants. The key move recasts the duality between the two properties as the classic duality between maximum flow and minimum cut in a network. The paper grew out of the first author's bachelor's thesis.
arxiv-2501-08043:
Marta Andronic, Jiawen Li, and George Constantinides rebuild neural networks out of polynomials so they can think faster on chips. Ultra-low-latency inference, needed for tasks like spotting particle jets at CERN or intrusions on a network, already hides network operations inside the lookup tables of FPGA chips. Their 2025 paper notes those tables can compute far richer functions than the simple steps they usually hold, and puts whole multivariate polynomials inside them.

Polynomial building blocks reach the same accuracy with far fewer layers of logic, cutting both delay and chip area. The catch is table size, which explodes with input count. Their answer is a pruning method guided by a hardware-aware penalty that pushes each neuron toward few inputs in a structured way, rather than relying on preset sparsity and lucky seeds. Tests on intrusion detection, jet identification, and handwritten digits confirm the gains.
arxiv-2501-08443:
Xu Li and co-authors improve how AI models that mix sight and language pick what to look at, in work the head dates to 2024. Such models lean on the last layer of their vision part, which can miss detail held in earlier layers. Past fixes mixed all layers the same way for every task.

The team first tested layer worth across eighteen checks in six task types. Layers proved to help unevenly, and flat mixing gave weak results, they found. Their fix is a module that weighs layers by the words of the user's ask, with no extra sight tokens added. Wide tests showed the guided mix beat past models. The lesson is plain: what a model should look at depends on what it was asked.
arxiv-2501-09843:
Light absorbed by a molecule can spread across a network of neighbors or stay trapped on one, and the network's wiring decides. Gregory Scholes argues for a new wiring in this 2025 paper. Molecular exciton research has leaned on aggregates where only nearest neighbors couple strongly. Denser coupling demands structures chemists have not yet built.

Scholes imports a concept from discrete mathematics: expander graphs, wirings with a spectral gap. Systems with such a gap should shrug off disorder and keep their coherence. The paper reviews the graph theory behind the claim and the reasons excitons localize. Resilient delocalization would serve solar capture and quantum devices alike. The challenge is now synthetic, not conceptual.
arxiv-2501-09943:
Belu Ticona, Fernando Carranza, and Viviana Cotik survey computing resources for Argentina's Indigenous languages in a 2025 paper. The country holds at least forty such languages across seven families, and most face extinction, taking heritage and know how with them.

The survey sizes speaker groups from the latest census and flags why the census likely undercounts them. It then catalogs what language technology exists for each tongue, from word lists to speech data, noting which were built for local varieties. Gaps stand out: a shared map of tools is the first step toward building more.
arxiv-2501-10043:
Hengjia Zhang and Xiaoping Xu compute growth measures for a family of symmetry representations, in a 2025 paper. The representations act on solutions of the Laplace equation. They arise by transforming classic oscillator models of special linear algebras. Earlier work pinned down the varieties tied to these modules. This paper finds the Hilbert polynomial of each variety.

A second polynomial tracks growth relative to any generating subspace. The authors show the variety's polynomial never exceeds the module's for large inputs. They give an exact condition for when the two agree. The leading term of the module polynomial is found explicitly. It does not depend on the chosen generating subspace. Such polynomials encode dimension and degree information. The results complete a picture begun in the pair's earlier studies.
arxiv-2501-10143:
Recommender systems that guess why a user clicked promise better suggestions, but Faisal Shehzad, Maurizio Ferrari Dacrema, and Dietmar Jannach could not make the promise reproduce in a 2025 study. They took five recent intent-aware models from top venues and tried to rerun them as published.

In two cases, even the authors' own code with the reported best settings failed to reach the reported numbers. Worse, every one of the five was beaten by at least one traditional, non-neural model once the baselines were properly tuned. The authors place the failure in a pattern seen across neural recommendation research: weak baselines and loose reporting inflate gains. Their call is for stricter scholarly practice, tuned comparisons and reproducible setups as the price of a claim.
arxiv-2501-10343:
Benjamin Kiefer and co-authors report, in a 2025 paper, the results of the third Maritime Computer Vision workshop challenges. The contests target vision systems for unmanned surface vehicles and underwater craft. Sea settings are hard for cameras: glare, spray, small distant objects, and shifting light. The report gives a full overview of what the competing teams built and how they scored.

More than seven hundred entries came in across the challenges. The authors review the results with both hard numbers and close reading of sample outputs, tracing trends in the methods used. All the data sets, scoring code, and the live leaderboard are public. The report serves as a snapshot of where sea-going machine vision stands and what still trips it up.
arxiv-2501-10743:
Songita Das and Gourab Ghatak analyze the trade-off between fresh data and energy in wireless sensor networks where devices live off harvested power. The devices draw energy from transmitter signals, then spend it sending data packets. The authors split each time slot by a chosen factor: the first part harvests energy, the second sends data. They define a joint success measure: the chance that harvested energy and signal quality both clear their thresholds.

Exact values for that measure are hard, so the paper derives lower and upper bounds. From the same framework they compute the peak age of information, how stale the freshest data can get. Longer harvesting starves transmission time, while shorter harvesting starves energy. Both queuing styles studied share the same best split point. The authors recommend that split for different power levels and deployment sizes.
arxiv-2501-11243:
Chenrui Sun and co-authors cut the energy cost of training drone flight paths in a 2025 paper. Drones can act as flying base stations in future 6G networks, filling gaps that fixed towers cannot. But each new setting demands fresh training of the flight controller, and that training burns power. The team apply transfer learning, where a controller keeps what it learned before and adapts it, instead of starting over.

Their learner pairs a dueling double deep Q network with multi-step learning. In two simulated settings, training energy fell by about thirty-one and fifty-nine percent. Tests on real city maps of Ottawa and Rosslyn cut energy by about forty-five and thirty-seven percent. Ray tracing on true map data grounded the tests.
arxiv-2501-11443:
Edoardo Giovanni Tolotti rebuilds a ladder of plate models for a trickier elastic material in a solo 2025 paper. A classic result sorts thin plate behavior into tiers by how energy scales as thickness shrinks. That proof leans on a stiffness bound that snaps when the material has several rest shapes, as in metals that switch phases.

Following a known patch, Tolotti adds a term that fines jumps between rest shapes, which keeps wild bends in check. In that frame the full tier ladder returns, with each rest shape's mark on the tiers made plain. He then shows energy minimizers settle as they should under outside forces with free edges. A fresh take on best fit rotations carries the proof for that step.
arxiv-2501-12043:
Aitor Brazaola-Vicario and six co-authors present a 2025 design tool for quantum key sharing, a way to swap secret keys with security backed by physics. Real gear for this task costs a great deal, which slows wide use in future 6G networks. The team built a detailed simulator for one scheme, called coherent-one-way, so systems can be planned on a computer first.

The paper lays out how the scheme works, then defines two yardsticks: the rate of errors in the shared key and the rate at which secret key is produced. To check the tool, the team built a real setup and ran tests at three link lengths, both with and without a mock eavesdropper. The test results matched the simulated ones well, which supports using the tool for design work.
arxiv-2501-12143:
Michela Rigoselli reviews what three X-ray observatories reveal about isolated neutron stars in a 2025 paper. These dead stars glow in X-rays two ways: heat leaking from the cooling surface, and non-thermal light from particles whipped around the magnetosphere. Some show hot spots where currents rain back down.

Middle-aged pulsars mix both components, while other classes emit heat alone. A puzzle animates the review: a new class of slow, strongly magnetic pulsars shows no X-rays at all, defying expectations. Rigoselli surveys recent results on named oddballs, from the thermally shining RX J1308.6+2127 and the enigmatic Calvera to fresh candidate stars, using data from XMM-Newton, NICER, and eROSITA.
arxiv-2501-12243:
Yizhou Liu, Ziming Liu, and Jeff Gore propose a new optimizer for training language models, built on a picture of the loss landscape as a narrowing valley. Their 2025 paper starts from the success of Adam and its cousins, then asks why a simpler sign-based method sometimes wins. On synthetic landscapes they find the answer: when gradient noise is high, Adam shrinks its steps too hard and stalls.

Their optimizer, FOCUS, keeps the sign method's bold steps and adds a pull toward a moving average of past weights, which steadies the walk. On GPT-2 training it proved steadier than the sign method and faster than Adam. Better optimizers compound across every model trained after them.
arxiv-2501-12443:
Ayan Chattaraj and three co-authors explore what a future European neutron source could reveal through neutrinos bouncing off atomic nuclei. In this scattering, the neutrino strikes the whole nucleus at once, a process sensitive to both standard physics and new effects. The intense beam planned at the source promises far more events than past setups.

The team forecasts limits on the weak mixing angle and nuclear size within standard physics. Beyond it, they test new neutrino interactions and hidden sterile neutrino ideas, including cases where particles transform mid flight. Statistical analysis across detector options and backgrounds drives the forecasts. The authors argue the source could lead this field and complement other probes.
arxiv-2501-12743:
Castelló, Luna, and Terradas teach neural nets to spot sun filament swings in a 2025 paper. Filaments are cool gas arcs on the sun that sway with set beats. Daily watch of those beats may tell how the arcs grow. Hand reads held the field back. The team first fit the sway spectra with a Bayesian chain method, the gold path. That path is slow, so they trained two nets to match it.

Each pixel of a sun watch cube gets a spectrum read. Noise in the read splits to red and white parts, both fit in the chain. The nets then call real swings at a set trust line. On past known cases the nets found the same events as the gold path. A fresh day with new events tried their reach. Run time fell by a wide span with no loss of trust.
arxiv-2501-13543:
Luca Canali and co-authors describe a modern data platform for the ATLAS particle detector at CERN, in a 2025 paper. ATLAS logs a flood of control data on how its parts run. That data sits in a database built for quick single lookups, not for broad scans across years and thousands of devices. Experts who hunt faults need the broad view.

The new pipeline moves the data onto Apache Spark and CERN's Hadoop service. It links to the SWAN notebook hub, so experts can explore the data in Python with standard tools. The setup scales to long spans and many devices at once. The team proved it on a real fault hunt for data links in the New Small Wheel detector. They argue such platforms let experts find and fix faults far faster.
arxiv-2501-13743:
Te Pei and co-authors present GPT-HTree, a 2025 framework for classification that stays readable to humans. Many accurate models are black boxes, which blocks their use where reasons matter. Their design chains three tools. First, hierarchical clustering groups people by their most telling features. Resampling then balances the classes inside each group. Decision trees finally draw a tailored sorting path for each cluster.

A large language model writes plain language descriptions of each cluster. Those notes bridge the numbers and the actions a user might take. The authors argue the chain keeps the accuracy of modern methods while restoring a clear chain of reasons. Each prediction can be traced through its cluster and its tree path. They present the framework as a template for explainable classification in data rich fields.
arxiv-2501-14143:
Power grids that sense and steer themselves promise cleaner energy, if their many risks can be tamed. Parag Biswas and co-authors survey that field in a 2025 review. Topics span grid parts, gains, and fresh tech lines.

Sun and wind power arrive in gusts, straining balance. Cyber attacks threaten a grid run by data. Fleets of electric cars could swamp local wires. AI and data tools are proposed for forecasting and control. Privacy and safety get their own treatment in the survey. The authors close with gaps and next steps for builders.
arxiv-2501-14243:
Hadi Mehrabpour and Abhisek Saha study flow patterns in collisions of light ions in a 2025 paper. When nuclei collide, the debris flows in patterns that fade along the beam direction, and that fading can reveal the shape of the starting nuclei.

The work covers collisions at two major labs for the first time in this detail. Some measures told apart rival models of the oxygen nucleus, while two models behaved much alike. The team compared several systems, from deuteron gold to oxygen oxygen and neon neon, and found a layered order in the fading. A reshaped measure tamed a skew that comes from lopsided systems. Flow angle patterns also differed by system in clear ways.
arxiv-2501-14343:
Xianqi Tong, Yiling Zhang, Bin Li, and Xiaosen Yang study in 2025 how one way hopping changes where waves settle in a near repeating chain that breaks normal rules. Some systems lose energy, so their math needs new tools. Such chains can trap waves at spots, spread them out, or pile them at an edge.

Using a global theory, the authors drew maps of which phase wins under each setting. Wave spread and trap points lined up with shifts in deeper traits. One way hopping made trapping lopsided. When the hopping itself varied in a pattern, broad phases collapsed into edge piled skin phases.
arxiv-2501-15143:
Kamchatnov reviews a notion called asymptotic integrability for wave systems in this 2025 paper. The idea concerns short wave packets riding on a smooth, large background wave. If their motion keeps an extra conserved quantity, one that ignores the starting state, the system earns the label. That single fact unlocks a chain of results.

It yields a Hamiltonian theory for how narrow solitons move, and a Bohr-Sommerfeld style rule for solitons born from a strong pulse. For systems with two wave variables where the condition holds exactly, the same structure produces Lax pairs for classic solvable equations. The review argues this sheds fresh light on why complete integrability arises in nonlinear wave physics.
arxiv-2501-15243:
Siran Li and Xiangxiang Su studied in 2025 how well fluid flow in a huge space can be mimicked by flow inside a very large box. Their test case was the classic equations of incompressible flow. Engineers and theorists often swap the endless space for a bounded tank, and they need to know what accuracy that swap costs.

Building on known decay rates for gentle flows, the pair derived hard numbers for how fast high order details of speed and pressure converge between the two settings. Their transfer needs mild smallness conditions on the starting flow or on an auxiliary steady problem. The work sharpens two earlier studies that used repeating boundaries or covered only three dimensions.
arxiv-2501-15343:
Nicholas LaHaye, Anistasija Easley, and colleagues teach a model to find smoke and fire in airborne measurements without hand labels in a 2025 study. A major field campaign flew through wildfire and farm fire smoke to study air quality and climate effects, gathering far more data than analysts can annotate. Self-supervised learning lets the model learn structure from the unlabeled flights themselves, then surface smoke plumes and active fire fronts.

Automated spotting turns an archive too big to read into evidence about how fires pollute regions and warm the planet. The same approach suits future campaigns as fire seasons lengthen.
arxiv-2501-15643:
Jordi Lopez-Abad and co-authors study special families of sets in advanced mathematics, in work from 2025. The families are called ideals, and the ones they study can be described by series in Banach spaces, which are complete spaces used in analysis. Recent work had sorted these ideals by how they can be so described.

The team gives clear descriptions of these ideals inside two classic spaces of continuous functions. A space called c0 plays a key role in their work. They also study colouring ideals, built from sets where a two-colouring stays uniform. Among their results, they show one random ideal of this kind is badly behaved, build well-behaved universal ones, and link the two topics. The paper answers a question posed by other researchers in the field.
arxiv-2501-15743:
Hongyan Gu and co-authors show that scanning slides at several depths sharpens AI cancer checks in this 2025 paper. The task is spotting mitosis, cells caught mid-division, in brain tumor tissue. Counting them guides care for meningiomas, but they are tiny and easy to miss on a flat scan.

The team scanned the same twenty-two slides on three scanners, each in flat and layered modes. Three AI pipelines then hunted mitoses in both versions. Layered scans raised the catch rate by about seventeen percent across every scanner and pipeline pairing. False alarms barely moved. The authors say depth scanning gives AI a fairer look at small patterns, with real gains for patient workups.
arxiv-2501-16043:
Michele Della Morte, Benjamin Jager, Sofie Martins, and Tobias Tsang test a spread flow on force fields. The work came out in 2025. They check how the flow reads the field's twist charge on a grid. The stage is a force field whose stuff mimics a super form of Yang-Mills thought. In the end, they want to call out its full scale of bits.

Slope flow smooths the field as it runs. The smoothed field's twist charge should settle to firm marks. The team studies part charges across more than one grid gap. With a boosted force step in the spread core, the charge firms up at mild flow times. With the stock Wilson flow, it does not. The point is of use in real work. The pick of step in the flow rules if the twist charge is read with trust.
arxiv-2501-16443:
Weipu Zhang and co-authors present an object-centric world model for sample-efficient reinforcement learning, in a research paper from 2025. Agents that learn from pixels need many trials, which blocks real-world use. World models cut trials by simulating experience, but pixel-level losses often miss small objects that decide success in busy scenes.

Their framework adds object representations from a pretrained segmentation network to a strong world model. A few annotated frames suffice to teach which objects matter. The model then tracks object dynamics and interactions without extra labels. Tests beat the base model on a classic game benchmark and set top sample efficiency on hard boss fights in a complex game.
arxiv-2501-16643:
Koji Inoue and co-authors benchmark language models on a dialogue task in a 2025 paper. In a conversation among three people, a system must judge who is being addressed to know who should speak next. That judgment, called addressee recognition, is a distinctive challenge of multi-party dialogue.

The team is building a multi modal corpus of three person discussions and annotated part of it with addressee labels. Explicit addressees appeared in only about a fifth of turns, which shows how often the target is implied. They then tested a leading large language model, GPT-4o, on the task. Its accuracy sat only slightly above chance. The authors argue that more work is needed before models can navigate group conversation well.
arxiv-2501-16743:
Lishuo Pan, Yutong Wang, and Nora Ayanian replan flight paths for a large robot swarm in clutter, in real time, in a 2025 paper. When many drones share a tight space, their routes must be redone as conditions change. Naive per-robot planning deadlocks or collides.

Their method works in layers. The workspace is divided into cells, and paths inside each cell are computed in parallel. A shared optimization pass then smooths the result into deadlock-free motion that stays feasible even if a step fails. Simulations ran up to 142 robots, and a live test flew 24 small quadrotors. Mixing central coordination with local freedom lifted task success well above purely decentralized schemes, a design pattern for warehouse and delivery swarms.
arxiv-2501-16943:
Quantum computers come in two broad styles, and the analogue style, which steers a system with smooth controls rather than step-by-step gates, has been the neglected sibling in software. Mateusz Meller, Vendel Szeremi, and Oliver Thomson Brown survey its programming tools in a 2025 review. Their focus is fit with supercomputing centers, where quantum machines will likely live as accelerators.

The authors catalog the tools that can program analogue machines, from Hamiltonian simulators to quantum annealers, and grade each for readiness to plug into high-performance computing workflows. Circuit-based tools have drawn most integration work, leaving analogue gaps in scheduling, data movement, and hybrid control. The review names those gaps and recommends fixes, arguing analogue machines' simpler abstraction could ease the path to large-scale quantum algorithms if the software stack catches up.
arxiv-2501-17043:
Thiago Guerreiro shows that gravity's own self-interaction can entangle gravitational waves and squeeze their quantum states. His 2025 paper works within the effective field theory of general relativity, where waves are treated as quantum excitations on a curved background. The question is whether spacetime ripples can carry truly nonclassical features, not just classical noise.

Working in the geometric optics limit to sidestep deep quantization problems, he finds that nonlinear gravitational processes couple wave modes together. That coupling can generate entanglement and squeezing in the outgoing radiation. The same nonlinearities can also reveal quantum features present in incoming waves, acting as both source and detector. The author draws a parallel with quantum optics, which proved light's quantum nature. The result suggests a fresh observational route to quantum gravity.
arxiv-2501-17143:
Nan Sheng, Xun Tang, Haoxuan Chen, and Lexing Ying tackle the storage of probability distributions that live in hundreds of dimensions. Gibbs distributions arise across physics and statistics, but writing one down normally fails because its normalizing constant cannot be computed. Their pipeline first draws samples and then compresses those samples into a compact tensor form.

For sampling, they use an ensemble form of annealed importance sampling, a population method suited to distributions with many separated peaks. The samples then pass through a functional hierarchical tensor sketching step, which builds the numerical representation. The authors apply the full approach to Ginzburg-Landau models with hundreds of variables, a test bed known for stubborn metastability, where samplers get trapped in one mode. They report that the method handled those hard cases, suggesting a workable route to representing very high-dimensional distributions.
arxiv-2501-17743:
Continelli proves that flocks still form when the agents' communication is delayed and sometimes fails, in a mathematics paper published in 2025. The model she studies is a standard one for flocking: each agent steers toward the group's average motion. Real swarms, robotic or animal, face lag and dropped signals. She allows delays that change over time and windows where agents stop exchanging information entirely.

Under a condition that the group stays excited enough, on average, she proves velocities align exponentially fast. Her decay estimates do not shrink as the flock grows, which matters for giant swarms. A second setting, with delays tied to each pair, yields weaker rates. The results extend flocking theory toward realistic communication. They also reassure engineers of drone swarms that occasional silence is survivable.
arxiv-2501-18143:
Fangyuan Xie, Jinghui Yuan, Feiping Nie, and Xuelong Li recast a graph cutting problem as a bounded transport problem to speed up clustering. Their 2025 paper works on min cut, a classic way to split graphs into groups. Standard solvers run slowly, resist solution, or collapse to trivial splits.

Size limits on groups become upper and lower bounds in the new framing. The result is a double-bounded nonlinear transport problem, handled here for the first time. Their solver builds on the Frank-Wolfe method and reaches a proven shrink rate for smooth convex cases. Applied to size-limited min-cut clustering, it runs on eight benchmark sets. Scores match or beat rival methods on several sets and measures, the authors report.
arxiv-2501-18643:
Pratik Shrestha, Sujan Kapali, Swikar Gautam, Vishal Pokharel, and Santosh Giri build a phone based system that turns shoe photos into 3D models for augmented reality shopping, in work from 2025. Flat photos limit online shoe shopping. A true 3D model lets a buyer inspect a shoe from all sides and place it in their space.

The system uses a fast splatting method to build lifelike models from 2D images. The team made a custom data set of shoe cutouts to train the step that isolates the shoe. The best model scored high on overlap with hand labels. Image quality scores were strong as well. The authors see use across wider fashion goods.
arxiv-2501-18743:
Seyed Mehrinezhad Chobari, Hossein Aghababa, and Mohammadreza Kolahdouz design quantum circuits in a 2025 paper. Their circuits build a special shared state, called a W state, across three or four particles, with any chosen weights and phases. They then teleport such states, sending each particle separately through a shared four-particle channel.

Pre-processing by the sender cuts the resources needed for the sending. The receiver uses extra helper particles to rebuild the final states. Running the protocol both ways at once improves efficiency further, since unknown particles held by users can serve as helpers. Simulations with a public quantum toolkit confirmed the protocol works as designed.
arxiv-2501-18843:
Shreyas Srinivas, Ian Jones, Goran Panic, and Christoph Lenzen redesign a circuit that protects computer chips from sudden voltage dips, in a 2025 paper. When voltage droops, a chip must slow its clock at once or compute garbage. The circuit they rework senses the dip and retunes the clock frequency on the fly.

Their version uses latches instead of flip-flops and drops a timing component the old design needed. It reacts within two clock cycles and halves the synchronizer chain that guards the changeover. A new differential sensor design covers a masking part the earlier work left open. The team also reworked the correctness proofs for the new timing and built the circuit on a real chip process.
arxiv-2501-19043:
Genc Hoxha and co-authors introduce in 2025 a way to search satellite image pairs with plain text, and the other way around. Remote sensing archives hold huge runs of images over time, and past search tools needed a sample image in the same form as the archive. In real work, a user may have only words.

Their self supervised method learns from paired images and sentences without hand labels for the search task. Separate encoders draw strong features from a two time image pair and from text, and projection heads line those features up in a shared space. Two fusion plans merge the time pair: a simple global blend and a transformer based blend that reads change over time. The work opens text driven search of Earth observation archives, useful for tracking land and city change.
arxiv-2501-19143:
Ching-Chun Chang and five co-authors guard AI perception with an imitation game against fake inputs. Fakes come in two kinds: crafted inputs that fool a set model, and trap doors planted in training that fire on a cue. Their 2025 shield sends each input to a generative agent that reads it, takes in its sense, and builds it back clean. The rebuild keeps the sense, not the trap.

The agent works in words and images at once, and thinks in steps as it reads. Simulations ran the shield on white-box and black-box fakes of both kinds. In each case the shield washed the fake out and the model read true. The team frames sense-first rebuilds as one guard for both fake kinds, where past guards split by kind.
arxiv-2502-00143:
Ambre Chabert wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on wave patterns on spinning shapes. The shapes are surfaces of revolution, like a vase profile spun around an axis, and the waves are near-modes called quasimodes.

Chabert studies a projector that picks out waves in a very narrow band of frequencies. She bounds how large those waves can grow, measured by a standard norm, for a wide class of such surfaces. The proof adapts a microlocal method built for wider bands and leans on the special integrable structure of these surfaces. That reduces the work to careful bounds on explicit wavy integrals, for which she builds new tools. Small disks around the poles are left out of the claim. The result is the first sharp bound of its kind for such narrow bands beyond the most symmetric shapes.
arxiv-2502-00243:
Douglas Finkbeiner and co-authors describe a fast way to find rhythms in starlight in a 2025 paper. New sky surveys track billions of objects with a thousand or more readings each, so hunting for periodic brightening and dimming must be both quick and sharp.

Their method, Fast Periodicity Weighting, grows out of Gaussian process math and makes no guess about the shape of the repeating pattern. That matters because real cycles vary wildly, from clean sine waves to eclipses and flares stacked together. The team built the tool for the Zwicky Transient Facility's sample of 1.5 billion objects and released code for both normal and graphics processors. The finder can sweep huge surveys without forcing every star into one mold.
arxiv-2502-00343:
Ahmed Abdelmoniem, Sameh Abdulah, and Walid Atwa build a translator that turns array database queries into big-data jobs, in a 2025 paper. Array databases store data in multi-dimensional grids. Systems like SciDB serve science users well. Their query language is easy to state but the jobs behind it are not. MapReduce, a popular large-scale processing model, demands low-level code. Writing it by hand is slow and error-prone.

The translator focuses on structural aggregations. These include circular, grid, layered, and sliding summaries over arrays. Such summaries have no plain match in classic databases. Users can also add their own summary functions with little effort. Generated code beat short hand-written code by up to about eleven times. The work mirrors earlier translators from standard query languages. It brings the same convenience to array users. Big science datasets stand to gain most.
arxiv-2502-00443:
Cedric Join and co-authors recast model-free predictive control in a 2025 conference paper with plain algebra steps. Predictive control is popular but needs a sound model of the process, which is often missing.

The new view rests on a linear equation with fixed coefficients, drawn from fresh takes on optimal and model-free control. Classic tools like dynamic programming drop out, and computing stays light. Two nonlinear cases, a chemical reactor and a two-tank system, show the method at work. A model-aware rival edges it out only slightly. The authors argue full modeling and heavy learning are not always needed for good control, in engineering or in AI at large.
arxiv-2502-00543:
Mohammad Nazeri, Anuj Pokhrel, and their co-authors built VertiFormer, a 2025 transformer model that helps off road robots move over rough ground. Robots must grasp how wheels and terrain interact on steep, rugged land. Unlike text or image fields, real off road driving data are scarce and costly to gather with physical robots.

VertiFormer learned from only one hour of driving data. A new masked training scheme teaches it to predict the next pose, the next action, and the next patch of terrain at once. That single training supports many tasks at once, including forward and inverse models of how the robot moves. The design targets terrain that is not just rough but sharply vertical in places.
arxiv-2502-01243:
Chengfeng Zhou and co-authors build OphthBench, a 2025 benchmark for testing large language models on eye medicine as practiced in China. Models are being eyed for clinic use, but their real competence and limits in this specialty were unmeasured. The benchmark follows a typical eye clinic's flow and splits it into five scenes: education, triage, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis.

Across those scenes sit nine tasks and five hundred ninety-one questions of varied type. The team then ran thirty-nine popular models through the full set and dissected the results. A clear gap showed between what the models can do and what clinical work demands. The authors publish the framework so developers can see exactly where models fail, in which scene and which task type. They frame the benchmark as a map for closing that gap before any ward deployment.
arxiv-2502-01343:
Roswitha Hofer, writing solo in 2025, gathers shared traits of two famed number grids and their black-and-white forms. One grid stems from Pascal's triangle of counts. The other is built from Catalan numbers, in a stacked form tied to a paper-folding chain. Both show up in the study of even spread and in number theory at large.

Hofer sets out what the pure grids share with their forms cut to just zero and one, all in whole numbers. Such zero-one grids have lately yielded counter cases to a long-standing guess in the field, which she cites as a spur. The note is a survey of known traits, not a report of new tests. It aims to guide work on grids of this kind.
arxiv-2502-01543:
Siphendulwe Zaza and co-authors clean fish tracking data in a 2025 paper. Acoustic tags reveal how aquatic animals move, but sets of millions of pings hide odd, false movements that distort science. Hand checking is slow and leaky. The team works with fifty tagged dusky kob fish tracked for five years in a South African estuary.

Over three million detections feed a full pipeline: cleaning, resampling, labeling, feature building, and model choice. A neural autoencoder wins, catching every true anomaly in their tests with the help of a custom threshold rule. Rival models miss most anomalies. The authors publish detailed guidelines for similar telemetry work.
arxiv-2502-01843:
Sending each new job to the shortest queue is the classic way to balance load, but real networks ration bandwidth and forbid idle servers. Andrea Fox and four co-authors rebuild the problem in 2025 as a constrained decision process, where both actions and states can carry limits. Two new policies grow from the shortest queue idea with safety built in.

Unlike earlier approaches, the policies are provably safe while still chasing low occupancy. Wide numerical tests across settings back the claim. The authors argue constraints should be designed into the policy, not patched around it. A queue, in their account, is a promise the network must be able to keep. Balance and obedience, they show, can coexist.
arxiv-2502-02043:
Gyeongbin Park, Hee-Suk Cho, and Chang-Hwan Lee study in 2025 how finer physics terms sharpen what gravity waves tell us about neutron stars. When two such stars merge, their waves carry marks of how much each star squashes under the other's pull. That squash hints at what the star is made of inside.

The team added correction terms up to a high order in the standard wave model. A fast math method gave error bars without full slow runs. Added terms did not settle in a neat pattern, they found. Error shrank as the pair's net spin rose, and stiffer star stuff gave cleaner reads. Sharper squash reads would help rule star recipes in or out when the next merger sings.
arxiv-2502-02143:
Ruxuan Zhang published this paper in 2025. It advances a conjecture about the hidden symmetries of hyper-Kähler varieties, a prized class of geometric spaces. These spaces generalize the famous K3 surface. Zhang proposes that a twisted version of their derived category, a bookkeeping system for sheaves on the space, is governed by an associated lattice. The lattice in question is the Markman-Mukai lattice, a grid of numbers attached to the variety.

He proves the claim under stated numerical conditions. The proof leans on a special bundle built by Markman and on a recently settled twisted equivalence result. One payoff: two well-behaved moduli spaces of sheaves on a K3 surface share the same derived category whenever their dimensions agree. The paper speaks to the deep dictionary between geometry and algebra.
arxiv-2502-02243:
David Touzeau and three co-authors proposed a new test of how the universe expands, in a 2025 paper. The test uses photos of faint galaxy shapes bent by gravity, a probe of large structure. A known transform can wipe out the effect of nearby lenses from such maps.

That wipe-out rests only on how fast the universe expands, not on how matter is spread. So the test can pull facts about expansion from any scale in the maps. The team built a null test from it and rated how it would fare in next-stage sky surveys. Their forecasts show sharper limits on dark energy, with noise from galaxy shapes, not chance spread, as the main limit ahead.
arxiv-2502-02343:
Tiny crystals of a light-sensitive material change shape when they absorb light, but the change is hard to catch. Zhou Shen and a large team of co-authors report in 2025 that they caught it directly, using very short X-ray flashes. They fired the flashes at single quantum dots of a lead-based crystal, with and without light excitation.

The diffraction patterns showed small shifts that point to a strain field spreading across each dot. Computer models matched the shifts to a paired charge state: one charge spread out, the other pinned in place. The result gives a clear picture of how such pairs warp the crystal, and shows the method can sense tiny strains in very small crystals.
arxiv-2502-02443:
Zi-Qi Yang, Miaomiao Wang, and Mehrdad Kermani make a working robot safer to touch without slowing its job in this 2025 paper. Robots that share space with people must yield softly on contact. Standard soft control covers the tool tip but not the arm's body, and yielding anywhere can wreck the main task.

Their design pairs a reshaped tip controller with a motion generator, so a person can grab the tool, swap it, and let the robot drift back to its task on its own. A second controller works in the arm's spare motion space, the directions that do not affect the tip. That lets the whole body lean away from accidental bumps while the tip stays on course. The team proved the system stays passive, a key safety property, and tested it against rivals on a seven-joint robot arm.
arxiv-2502-03443:
Francisco Arco, Thomas Biekötter, Panagiotis Stylianou, and Georg Weiglein study top quark spin links in two thousand twenty-five. Their case is a heavy new spin zero particle that decays at the LHC. It can split into a Z boson and a lighter spin zero particle. The lighter one then splits into top quark pairs.

Two chains are possible, with odd or even parity roles swapped. Current searches cannot tell the two apart if their rates match. The team shows that spin links in the top quarks can split them. Angles from the leptons in top decay do the work. With high volume LHC data, the split should be clear.
arxiv-2502-04143:
Leon Emmerich and co-authors measure how much sound a porous material soaks up on site, using two microphones and a neural network, in work from 2025. Lab tubes give clean numbers, but real walls and panels are finite and already installed. The classic two-microphone field method suffers from those edges.

A compact network reads the pressure link between the two microphones and predicts the soaking rate of an endless slab. Training used simulated data from a boundary model with a standard foam law. Bench tests on fiber samples of varied size and source height matched tube and theory values well. The method could rate installed materials in place, without cutting samples.
arxiv-2502-04343:
Thomas Bläsius and co-authors turn traffic assignment on its head, studying road networks where sharing makes travel cheaper as more people use a road. Their 2025 paper contrasts this synergistic case with the classic one, where each added car raises costs through congestion. Shared vehicles flip the logic: more users on a road mean more sharing potential and lower cost per rider.

A simple method, best response with all travelers updating at once, settles into equilibrium, unlike the classic case, which needs slow step by step updates. A realistic test on Stuttgart data confirmed fast convergence. As a first use, an equilibrium fed a bus line planner and cut the vehicles it needed sharply.
arxiv-2502-04643:
Brian Formento, Chuan Sheng Foo, and See-Kiong Ng show a new way to attack large language models in a 2025 paper: ask them how confident they are. Modern closed models reveal nothing but their final text, so classic attacks that read internal scores no longer work. Attackers can only see the final label. The team test whether a model's stated confidence can stand in for those hidden scores.

Across current models, the stated confidence proved well calibrated rather than made up. Lowering that confidence by tweaking the input raised the chance of a wrong classification. Their method, which swaps words to push confidence down, beat existing black box attack methods on three data sets and two open models. The work names confidence elicitation as an attack vector that defenders of closed systems should weigh.
arxiv-2502-04743: Jiaqi Xie and Fei Xu give, in 2025 work, an exact test for a seating question in number theory. When can a ring of whole forms, taken from a wide field inside a split number world, be seated in a like ring of the wider world? Their test is one clean rule, checked case by case. Past finds from many hands fall out of it as plain cases. Fresh cases come with it. The rule ties a loose shelf of past work into one frame.
arxiv-2502-04843:
Feifei Li, Qi Song, Chi Zhang, Hui Shuai, and Rui Huang introduced PoI in twenty twenty-five, a filter that makes synthetic views safe for training camera localization systems. Scene coordinate regression predicts a 3D point for every pixel, demanding exact supervision. Rendered views from neural synthesis can augment training, but they blur and distort where the original capture was thin.

Their pipeline renders novel views with 3D Gaussian splatting, then refines them with a one-step diffusion model that invents plausible detail. A progressive filter then keeps only pixels whose reprojection error is small, discarding untrustworthy ones during training. On the 7Scenes and Cambridge Landmarks benchmarks, the method steadily improved localization over strong baselines and reached top performance with competitive training cost.
arxiv-2502-05043:
Yueying Li and co-authors design greener AI serving systems in this 2025 paper. Large language models now run on vast fleets of machines, with high power use and carbon output. The team studies traces from two live services at a major cloud firm to find where the carbon sits.

Their checks hold three surprises. The chips drive running carbon, but the host machines drive the carbon locked in building the gear. Batch jobs done out of rush hours fill much of the fleet's work. Gear and jobs also vary widely in kind. Their design, built on cut, reuse, right-size, and recycle rules, cut modeled carbon by close to half while holding speed goals.
arxiv-2502-05743:
Xiao Li and co-authors study a puzzle from 2025 about diffusion models. These models were built to make images. Yet they also learn useful image features on their own. Feature quality first rises as noise grows. It then falls again at high noise.

The team use the fact that image data sit near a low size shape. On that base, they prove the peak appears when the model truly catches the data shape. Tests on class tasks back the claim. The peak shows when the model makes fresh images. It fades as the model starts to copy its training set.
arxiv-2502-06443:
Elisabetta Cornacchia, Dan Mikulincer, and Elchanan Mossel show in 2025 that hard to learn low dim tasks turn easy when data get a small random shift. Such tasks ask a net to learn a rule that rests on a few hidden inputs. Past work set hard and easy cases apart by set traits of the rule.

A random shift in the mean of the data is the tweak at play. With it, any one index rule on bell shaped data learns as fast as a plain line rule. The claim then spreads to a class of few bit rules as well. Hard cases, the team shows, are rare.
arxiv-2502-06543:
Zhu Chen, Ina Laube, and Johannes Stegmaier present in 2025 an unsupervised method to align developmental stages of zebrafish embryos from 3D point clouds over time. Embryo stages often need synchronization for biomedical analysis. Manual labeling is slow and can carry subjective bias into the results.

An autoencoder learns descriptive features from the point clouds without labels. A deep regression network then aligns embryos in time using those features. Average mismatch was under four minutes over an experiment lasting more than five hours. The fully unsupervised approach scales easily and avoids human annotation effort entirely, they note.
arxiv-2502-06643:
Seokjin Go and Divya Mahajan tackled a speed problem in large models that split work among expert parts, in a 2025 paper. Only a few experts wake for each token, which saves cost. Spread across many graphics chips, though, uneven routing leaves some chips swamped while others wait.

Their system, MoETuner, places experts on chips by solving a planning problem that weighs load, talk between chips, and compute cost. It also uses a pattern in routing: tokens sent to one expert tend to go to a small set next. In tests, end-to-end speed rose by about nine percent on one node and by more across many nodes. The gain came from cutting the long tail of waits.
arxiv-2502-06743:
Saroj Kumar Panda and co-authors propose a fair way for network operators to train shared AI models, in a 2025 paper. In federated learning, each operator trains on its own data and shares only model updates. That protects privacy, but it raises fairness issues. Some operators may feed in skewed data, and predictions may favor some users over others. The team's target task is forecasting traffic and assigning resources in optical networks.

Their framework checks fairness on two levels: accuracy spread across operators, and service quality spread across connections. Tests used real traffic traces shaped into uneven, non-identical data sets. Fairer forecasts across operators led to fairer resource shares across connections, the team reports. The work speaks to settings where rival operators must cooperate without pooling raw data.
arxiv-2502-06943:
Shohini Bhattacharya, Oleksandr Tomalak, and Ivan Vitev make the first calculation of QED effects inside a nucleus at future collider energies, in a 2025 paper. The planned Electron-Ion Collider will smash electrons into heavy nuclei to map their inner structure. Photon-driven effects within the nuclear medium could distort those maps.

Focusing on deep inelastic scattering from a lead nucleus, the team finds corrections that may reach or exceed the planned measurement precision.
