They compare single and multiple re-scattering of particles crossing the nucleus and gauge the main uncertainty by varying how the nuclear charge is screened. The work aims at cleaner extraction of the nucleus's true structure.
arxiv-2502-07043:
Cheeranjeev Purmessur, Kaicheung Chow, Bernard van Heck, and Angela Kou run a quantum bit built on phase slips, not on the stock junction. Stock junctions in quantum chips come from aluminum, and they cap heat and frequency range. A constriction junction from a wide-gap material could lift both caps, yet such junctions have been wild and short-lived. Their 2025 bit uses constriction junctions of titanium nitride.

The bit hums near 17 gigahertz at zero field, set by its coil. Readout and control worked in full, and the bit held its state past 60 microseconds. It also ran at heat past 300 millikelvin, far warm for its kind. The team adds the junction to the chip toolkit and sees new protected bit kinds in it.
arxiv-2502-07543:
Anton Galaev, a solo author, presents a 2025 math paper on holonomy in curved spaces with contact structure. Holonomy tracks how vectors twist when carried around loops. The setting joins sub-Riemannian geometry, where motion is limited to set directions, with a K-contact structure.

Galaev proves a clean split for the horizontal holonomy group. It either matches the holonomy of a related Riemannian space, or it sits inside that group as a subgroup one step down in size. Parallel spinors, examples, and consequences are then discussed. The result gives geometers a tight rule for a class of spaces that mix contact and limited-motion traits.
arxiv-2502-07943:
George Fletcher, Olha Nahurna, Matvii Prytula, and Julia Stoyanovich argued in 2025 that data models deserve the same close reading that literary scholars give texts. Every database, statistical model, and machine learning system rests on an underlying data model, and that model quietly records the material, social, and political conditions that produced the system. Reading it closely can reconnect analysts with a system's origins, craft, and design choices.

Borrowing from literary criticism, where no single correct reading exists, the authors still insist that beginners need systematic guidance, since computing training often teaches students to set social and political questions aside. Their work sets out to fill the gap: a methodology for reading data models closely, aimed especially at readers trained in computing and data science.
arxiv-2502-08143:
Quan Nguyen, Shinji Ito, Junpei Komiyama, and Nishant Mehta sharpen learning bounds for slot machine style problems in a 2025 paper. In such problems a learner picks among arms with unknown payoffs and must keep total loss low. The best bounds adapt to the data seen and hold in both calm and hostile settings, yet past bounds got only part of that wish list at once.

Their method matches a stability score to a penalty in real time inside a known learning frame. The bounds they prove keep the best rate in hostile play and a far leaner rate in calm play. The same bounds bend to sparse or low loss data on their own. The authors pitch the pairing as a route to fresh bounds in online learning.
arxiv-2502-08443:
Quentin Le Coent, Virginie Rondeau, and Catherine Legrand teach how to test a stand in end mark with joint builds that join two past schools, in a paper from 2025. True end marks take years, so trials prize stand ins that can be read fast. One school pools past trials for tie marks, and one reads how much drug force runs through the stand in.

Their join build does both in one frame, for death time ends with time or track stand ins. Two new joint forms fit the two stand in kinds, in a free code pack. Three cancer data sets show the rite at work. The join gives a full sureness read in one run.
arxiv-2502-08543:
Saori Morimoto, Makoto Katori, and Hiraku Nishimori model self propelled camphor disks on water with added randomness, in a 2025 paper. Camphor floats are a handy lab stand in for active matter, since each disk pushes itself along by leaking camphor into the water. Past models paired disk motion equations with a smooth field for the dissolved camphor.

Their new models swap that field for random walks of single camphor molecules, which injects real fluctuation into the system. Simulations then show single disks propelling themselves and disks pushing each other away, as in the bench experiments. The one dimensional versions, where viscosity rules, get close study. Noise, the work shows, belongs inside the model, not outside it.
arxiv-2502-08943:
Wenbo Zhang, Hengrui Cai, and Wenyu Chen argued in a 2025 paper that language model benchmarks should sample many answers, not one. Models are random generators, yet standard scoring uses fixed settings or a single draw, leaving sampling luck inside every published number. Their hierarchical statistical model captures both the benchmark's traits and the model's randomness, giving a truer picture of the test itself.

Multiple generations sharpen score estimates and cut their variance. The samples also yield a per-prompt difficulty score: the share of correct answers across draws. Plotted on a data map with meaning, these scores expose bad or ambiguous items during benchmark building. The authors frame repeated sampling as cheap insurance for the field's main measuring stick.
arxiv-2502-09343:
Ilse Fischer and Hans Höngesberg count patterned number arrays called monotone trapezoids, in a 2025 mathematics paper. These arrays grow out of alternating sign matrices, a classic topic in counting math. Earlier work counted the triangle case and, in doing so, settled a famous count. The trapezoid case fixes the bottom row but leaves the top row free, a new twist for this area.

The authors give a formula built from operators, step-by-step rules that act on other formulas. One key operator stays hidden in the triangle case and only shows itself here, which made it hard to find. Their formula adds a row-strictness rule to a known count for a related array family. They also find a surprise link to a branch of algebra and propose a wider guess.
arxiv-2502-09543:
Noam Soker and Dmitry Shishkin identify the main jet axis of a supernova remnant in a 2025 paper. The remnant, called W49B, holds two ear like bulges on opposite sides with rich heavy elements. The authors argue those bulges were inflated by a pair of jets when the star exploded.

A line through the clumps at the tips of the two ears marks the jet axis, they say. Three arcs around that axis look like parts of full rings that jets carve in other objects. Finding a jet axis rules out one explosion type and leaves two jet based options, the authors argue.
arxiv-2502-09643:
Mathieu Helfter proves a result in the study of fractal size in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. Size for rough sets is often read by two scales, the Hausdorff scale and the packing scale. Each scale uses its own gauge function, a rule that says how size shrinks with width.

Helfter shows that, under mild rules on the gauges, one set can hit two preset scales at once. He builds a compact set in the Baire space whose two measures are both finite and positive, one for each gauge. He then plants that set inside any Banach space with endless dimensions. This gives a yes to a question posed by Fan about spaces with freely chosen scales.
arxiv-2502-09743:
Arne Rubehn and Johann-Mattis List improve how computers map the meaning of concepts across languages. A concept can be stored as a point in a space, so that near points have near meanings. Past maps were built from words that carry two meanings in many languages. Those maps miss cases where only part of a word carries the extra meaning.

The new method adds these partial cases to the network that feeds the map. The maps were tested on word likeness scores, records of meaning change, and word link data. In each test, the partial cases gave better maps of concepts. The authors show the maps can capture distinct kinds of links between meanings, which helps work with sparse data and rare tongues.
arxiv-2502-10043:
Giuseppe Gaetano Luciano and Yassine Sekhmani study how a generalized uncertainty rule can mimic dark energy that changes over time. Their paper from 2025 starts from a quantum gravity trait found in most models: a smallest length at the Planck scale. That rule reshapes the entropy law for black holes.

In the model, the correction acts like a fluid that adds to the fixed cosmic term, shaping the early universe while matching the standard picture today. The team traces how matter clumps grow in this setting with a classic collapse model. Growth runs slower than standard for set values of the new parameter. Wave data from future detectors could cap that parameter more tightly than most past limits.
arxiv-2502-10343:
Alon Hendler Avidor and co-authors study impurity freezing in a quantum magnet in this 2025 paper. Sodium ruthenate hosts restless magnetic moments on a frustrated triangular lattice. Its ground state stays dynamic rather than settling into order.

Swapping some ruthenium for iron plants strong local moments in the lattice. The swap triggers local spin freezing with classic spin glass signs. Bulk magnetism then follows a Curie-Weiss pattern set by the planted moments. The frozen patches look like dynamic host moments pinned around each impurity. The picture matches swiss cheese models known from copper oxide studies. Results show how fragile a quantum disordered state can be.
arxiv-2502-10543:
Assaf Naor and Kevin Ren settle how badly finite sets from Lp spaces distort when placed into Euclidean space. For p above 2, they prove the Euclidean distortion of any n-point subset grows like p cubed times the square root of log n. That beats the general guarantee from Bourgain's embedding theorem for arbitrary metric spaces. The separation modulus of such sets is also pinned down, sharp apart from the dependence on p.

From that modulus result, any 1-Lipschitz map from such a set into a Banach space extends to the whole space with controlled Lipschitz constant. Matching statements hold for doubling subsets of Lp as well.
arxiv-2502-10643:
Savvas Raptis and co-authors argue that shock waves in space can boost electrons to extreme speeds far more easily than long thought, in a 2025 paper. Collisionless shocks ride ahead of exploding stars and solar wind. They rank among nature's strongest particle boosters. The puzzle was the entry step: how plain electrons gain enough speed to join the main boost at all.

The team blends direct satellite reads with fresh theory into a reinforced model. Short-lived structures, wave-particle interplay, and shifting solar wind all team up across scales. Each can nudge electrons past the entry line, which lands in the mild suprathermal range. Since such helpers abound in plasmas, a typical shock can feed electrons to near light speed on a steady basis. The model sharpens ideas on where cosmic ray electrons come from.
arxiv-2502-10743:
Shuqi Liu and colleagues present 1bit-Merging, a method to merge large language models with low storage cost. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses a need created by specialist models. Fine-tuned models excel in narrow areas like chat, math, or code. Classic merging blends them into one static model. That blend often dulls the skill of each specialist.

Routing methods keep accuracy but store much more data. The new framework pairs routing with one-bit quantized task vectors. Different skills live in different layers of a model. Chat skill sits mainly in attention layers, while math and code sit in MLP layers. Targeted compression exploits that split. Tests on two model families matched or beat prior methods. Storage needs fell sharply at the same time.
arxiv-2502-10843:
Peter Holderrieth, Michael Albergo, and Tommi Jaakkola wrote a machine learning paper in two thousand twenty-five about drawing samples from sets of discrete choices. Many tasks need samples from a known but unscaled chance distribution. Their method, named LEAPS, learns the jump rates of a process that moves between choices over time.

The hard part is scoring how good each path is, since standard network designs make that score too costly to compute. The authors build a compact form for the jump rates using networks with a local symmetry property. That design lets them train the system at scale while keeping the scores steady and low in spread.
arxiv-2502-11043:
Min-ho Yu and Hang-Hyun Jo study how events that arrive in bursts leave fingerprints on a standard statistics curve. Many systems, from messages to trades, fire in clusters separated by quiet gaps, and the sizes of back-to-back bursts often correlate. The autocorrelation function, which measures how a series resembles itself over time, is the usual lens for such patterns. The authors build a model series with correlated burst sizes using a coupling technique from statistics.

They then solve exactly for that model's autocorrelation under any distributions of gaps and burst sizes. For a concrete case they plug in exponential distributions for both. The worked example shows how correlation between one burst and the next changes the way the curve decays. The result gives analysts a cleaner way to read burst structure out of recorded time series.
arxiv-2502-11443:
Jing Niu, Peng He, and Tong-Jie Zhang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It pins the Hubble constant with a full covariance matrix built by a neural net, from cosmic clock data.

The cosmic chronometer method reads the universe's growth rate from old galaxies. Past work dropped the off-diagonal terms of the error matrix, or used a short one, which blurs the Hubble value. A net built to keep the matrix well formed grows a small known matrix into a full one. Set by a leave-one-out test, it beats a Gaussian process rival as a maker. With the full matrix in hand, two methods then bound the constant. The center barely moves, but the width of the bound shifts in clear ways.
arxiv-2502-11743:
Real training data is messy: human labelers often give the same example several different labels, only one of them right. Partial-label learning trains a classifier anyway, without hand-cleaning the data, by treating the candidate set as a hint. Tobias Fuchs and Florian Kalinke note that leading methods break easily under heavy label noise, strange examples, and crafted attacks. Their method rests on subjective logic, which keeps uncertainty explicit instead of hiding it in one score.

Their method reads the sizes of the network's class activation values, the internal signals behind each class, and turns them into stated uncertainty. A new rule then redistributes trust among the candidate labels, and the authors prove this rule is optimal. In experiments, the approach kept its accuracy better than rivals when label noise ran high. It also handled out-of-distribution examples better and resisted adversarial tweaks.
arxiv-2502-11843:
Seven researchers test whether chatbots can hold a personality in conversation in a paper from 2025. Two agents were assigned traits from the OCEAN framework, each set high or low. They then talked in pairs on a set topic. Judge agents later tried to infer the assigned traits from the transcripts. The team checked consistency, agreement between models, and match to the assignment.

Models could be steered toward trait-driven talk, but stability varied a lot. Results depended on which models were paired and on the discussion setting. The authors say consistent, readable personality in dialogue remains hard. The study gives a framework for measuring persona drift in deployed agents.
arxiv-2502-11943:
Zheng and a large team studied in twenty twenty-five a light-only way to sense weak fields with flaws in diamond. Those flaws glow in a way that shifts with field strength and line. The light way needs no micro-waves, so kits can be small and plain.

They read glow at low fields in stones rich in such flaws at room warmth. Glow marks matched near-tied states of the flaw's spin parts and their kin in the stone. False runs of the field acts matched the reads in a fair way. Top glow strength rests on flaw count and light strength, they find.
arxiv-2502-12043:
Amir Ziaie and co-authors find new wormhole solutions inside a classic alternative gravity theory, in this 2025 paper. Wormholes are tunnels through spacetime that most theories only allow with exotic matter that breaks energy rules. The Brans-Dicke theory adds a scalar field to gravity, which may relax those demands.

The team assume matter that pushes differently along and across the tunnel, with a simple pressure law. They solve the field equations exactly for two families of tunnels. Energy conditions hold at the throat, and in places throughout, without exotic matter. A curvature check confirms no hidden singularities. Parameter limits for healthy tunnels are spelled out.
arxiv-2502-12143:
Yuetai Li and co-authors find a learnability gap for small language models in a 2025 paper. Large models reason well, and teaching small models from their long chains of thought seemed promising. Yet small models with three billion parameters or fewer do not gain steadily from those long chains. Shorter, simpler reasoning fits their capacity better, the team shows.

Their fix, Mix Distillation, blends long and short chains, or chains from large and small models, in one training mix. That balance lifts small model reasoning well above training on either kind alone, they report. Direct distillation from strong reasoners has clear limits, they argue.
arxiv-2502-12243:
Audrey Lindsay and Fabian Ruehle test how well neural networks learn knot invariants in a 2025 paper. Knots can be described in several ways, and their numerical traits vary in how hard they are to predict. The authors ask which encodings and traits suit machine learning best.

Braid encodings gave the strongest predictions overall in their tests. Traits from hyperbolic geometry and knot diagrams proved easy to learn. Traits from deeper topological data proved harder, and one trait could not be learned from any encoding. Two new scores compare networks trained on related traits, revealing hidden links in how the models work.
arxiv-2502-12443:
Di Liu and six co-authors built a system that helps art therapy clients do homework in a 2025 paper. Between sessions, clients are asked to make art and reflect, but many get stuck without guidance, and therapists cannot easily follow what happened. The team designed two linked apps.

The client app pairs a conversational agent with AI-assisted art-making to scaffold the homework. The therapist app lets practitioners customize the agent's behavior and review an AI-compiled history of each client's work. A thirty-day field study with twenty-four clients and five therapists showed the system supporting reflection in daily life. Therapists bent the agents to their own principles, adding a personal touch. The compiled histories became real material in sessions. The paper draws lessons for designing AI that strengthens, rather than replaces, a human care relationship.
arxiv-2502-12743:
Jiazhou Ji and co-authors test whether large language models can spot text written by models like themselves, in this 2025 paper. Telling human writing from machine writing matters, since the tools can be misused. The team asked six models, both closed and open, to judge texts and explain their calls.

Models did best at spotting their own writing, but even then they were far from reliable. Adding a third choice, undecided, improved both accuracy and the quality of explanations. The team also catalogs why explanations fail: wrong features, made-up claims, and faulty logic. Their dataset of human-checked judgments supports the analysis.
arxiv-2502-12843:
Nastassia Grimm, Camille Bonvin, and Isaac Tutusaus write a 2025 cosmology paper. Dark matter has never been seen directly, so how it falls into gravity wells is an open question. The usual guess is that it falls just like normal matter, ruled by Euler's equation alone.

The team tested that guess with survey data on galaxy motion and gravity wells across deep time. Data fit the standard equation well for the range they probed. A possible extra force on dark matter was capped at a small share of gravity's strength. Forthcoming sky surveys should tighten the cap a lot. The work shows how galaxy data can test basic rules for the unseen bulk of the universe.
arxiv-2502-13143:
Zekun Qi and co-authors teach robots to grasp which way an object faces, in a 2025 paper. A robot that must plug in a cable or lift a cup needs the object's working direction, not just its spot. Old pose codes lean on fixed frames and templates, which break on new things. Their notion, semantic orientation, names the direction by its job, like the plug-in way of a USB stick or the handle side of a cup.

To feed it they built a bank of 300,000 3D objects tagged with such directions, and a model that predicts them for new things. Plugged into a vision-language agent, the sense of facing drives full six-way spatial reasoning and robot acts. Zero-shot, it passed about half of one hard test set and three quarters of a simulated one. The authors pitch language as the bridge from seeing to handling.
arxiv-2502-13343:
Priya Baral and co-authors report an odd sideways voltage in a magnetic metal that works at room heat. Their 2025 paper studies a crystal of iron and gallium with a spiral magnet pattern. Such sideways signals often trace to twisted spin shapes, but a plain spiral should give none.

Beam tests revealed a set of magnet phases in the crystal. In a magnetic field the spiral tilts into a cone shape, and a strong sideways signal appears at and above room heat. The team credits waves of spin motion, not a static twist, for the effect. That route widens the search for materials that mix magnet order with useful electric response.
arxiv-2502-13643:
Yuxin Xia, Iacopo Savelli, and Thomas Morstyn speed up multi level market optimization in a 2025 paper. Sequentially cleared markets stack decisions: an upper level choice must foresee several lower level clearings. Exact multi level models grow past three levels only with difficulty.

Their approach blends ranked optimization with a weighted sum to approximate the stack as one level. A tailored Benders decomposition splits the problem along its levels for speed. The test case schedules power plants across linked electricity, gas, and carbon markets in the northeastern United States. Only profitable gas plants get committed. Computing time fell by about a third on average, and optimality gaps shrank by over ninety percent.
arxiv-2502-14143:
Lewis Hammond and a large team of co-authors map the risks that arise when many advanced AI agents act in the same world, in a 2025 report. Single agents are already hard to steer; crowds of them, each pursuing goals for different owners, create failure modes that single-agent safety work does not cover. The report builds a structured taxonomy of those risks.

Three failure modes anchor the scheme: agents failing to coordinate, agents falling into conflict, and agents colluding against others' interests. Seven risk factors feed those failures, from hidden information and network effects to selection pressure and weak commitment tools. Real cases and experiments illustrate each danger. The authors also point to promising defenses, arguing that governance and safety work must take the multi-agent setting seriously now.
arxiv-2502-14443:
Ketels proposes curing the infinite answers that plague quantum field theory by bending the space of momenta itself. Standard fixes tame runaway high-energy terms but add fake parameters, break symmetries, or rest on arbitrary recipes. His 2025 approach builds the bending into the measure used for integrals, so suppression of high energies comes from geometry alone.

The scheme needs no outside regulators and keeps the equations of motion plus full Lorentz symmetry. Suppression stays as weak as possible while still forcing finite answers, proven for key integrals. Built first in curved geometry language, it extends cleanly to relativistic spacetime. The author suggests wider uses in spectral geometry and quantum gravity. The pitch is an intrinsic fix in place of ad hoc renormalization.
arxiv-2502-14843:
Andriani Keliri and Marco Schiro study a quantum dot joined to two superconductors with a slave spin method, in work from 2025. The dot holds electrons that interact strongly. The setup can switch between two ground states, a paired Kondo state and a lone moment state, which marks a shift in the junction's phase.

At the mean field level, the dot maps to a simpler level model plus a helper spin that tracks dot parity. That picture captures the Kondo phase and its contest with superconductivity when the gap is weak. It fails in the lone moment phase. The authors add fluctuations to describe fast dynamics of the helper spin.
arxiv-2502-15343:
Anna Wegmann, Dong Nguyen, and David Jurgens ask how word splitting affects language models in a 2025 study. Models first cut text into small units, and that step may treat rare spellings or local forms less well. The team test whether the best way to split words depends on the kind of task.

They train base models with a common splitting method and vary the source texts, the first split step, and the size of the word list. The first split step had the largest effect overall. They also offer a new way to judge a splitter by its effect on later tasks, which beats older scores.
arxiv-2502-15643:
Luka Grbcic, Juliane Müller, and Wibe Albert de Jong propose a new design method in a 2025 paper. Inverse design means starting from a wanted result and working back to the settings that give it. Such searches can be slow when the design space is large. Their method pairs paired neural networks with active learning.

Active learning picks the most useful new examples to add, so fewer are needed. The team tested the idea on three tasks: wing shapes, light-handling surfaces, and a heat spread problem. In each case their method beat standard approaches, reaching better accuracy with fewer training samples. That saving matters when each test run costs much time or computing power.
arxiv-2502-15743:
Tillman shows a fresh sieve that yields primes and their part splits with no cuts. Most sieve ways lean on split steps to sift whole counts. His sieve builds both primes and full splits in one pass. The chains it makes are the p-adic worth counts of n. Each such chain proves to be a self-like chain in form. Self-like chains are those that hold their shape at all scales.

Those chains then make shape fractals, like the Levy Dragon form. A link twixt the odd part chain and one more form caps it. That form is the Heighway Dragon in the text of the work. Count math and plane shape meet in that close link. The sieve thus ties prime parts to bent plane art.
arxiv-2502-15943:
Milan Sil and co-authors model a simple ion in a planetary nebula, in a 2025 paper. The ion, HeH+, is destroyed so fast by reactions that its formation and destruction can excite its energy levels, an effect called chemical pumping. Whether that effect matters for this ion had not been tested.

The team model the ion cloud in the nebula NGC 7027 with a photoionisation code and reaction rates, then analyse three emission lines with two codes. One approach adds the reaction rates into the level calculations and samples the fit. Both approaches agree well, and the pumped model reproduces the line fluxes and their ratio within about twenty percent. An extra formation route improves the match. The authors conclude the three lines are not sensitive to pumping, though short-lived levels are overpopulated when pumping is included, and more lines are needed to pin down conditions.
arxiv-2502-16543:
Jiayi Chen, Bangming Deng, and Shiquan Ruan (2025) compute Hall polynomials in a setting where algebra meets geometry: the weighted projective line. Hall polynomials count how objects in a category can be assembled from smaller pieces, and they underpin the theory of quantum groups. The authors' stage is defined by a triangle singularity, a simple equation in three variables with weights. Over it sits the category of coherent sheaves, the geometric objects of the line.

They calculate the polynomials for three families: extension bundles, line bundles, and torsion sheaves. The method uses derived equivalence, a bridge that translates the problem into another category where the answers are easier to reach. As a payoff, their route gives one unified explanation for earlier computations done case by case for tame quivers by Szántó and Szöllősi. A single geometric picture, the paper argues, was behind those scattered results all along.
arxiv-2502-17043:
Rajmadan Lakshmanan and Alois Pichler release a Julia package for decisions under uncertainty, in a 2025 paper. Stochastic dominance ranks risky options by whole outcome spreads, not just averages. Its use stalls because the classic form carries endless constraints.

Recent theory cuts those constraints to a finite set, even at higher orders of the ranking. The package builds on that cut to check and to optimize under dominance terms. It works as a black box that slots into standard solving frames. The authors aim to put a core finance and choice tool within reach of working analysts, as free and open code.
arxiv-2502-17343:
Giulia Ricciardi, Natascia Vignaroli, and Francesco Vissani present a 2025 study of inverse beta decay. That reaction, where an antineutrino strikes a proton and yields a positron and a neutron, has a rate the authors aim to sharpen. The reaction is the workhorse signal for detecting neutrinos from reactors and supernovas. The authors focus on energies from a few to hundreds of MeV, the range those sources cover.

They review updated values and error bars for the reaction rate. They also weigh a subtle correction from so-called second-class currents, an exotic flow pattern in the weak force. Knowing the rate's precision matters now that experiments gather huge data samples. A fuzzy rate would blur what the data say about neutrinos, so tight theory keeps the measurements honest.
arxiv-2502-17543:
Fahim Tajwar and co-authors present Paprika, a 2025 way to train language models to explore and make choices in new settings. Many models do poorly when a task needs step-by-step fact gathering. Paprika trains a model on made-up task chats that call for distinct plans, so it learns broad choice skills.

After training, the model can face a brand new task and adapt from feedback alone, with no new training steps. The team also picks training chats with care, favoring tasks where the model can still learn a lot. That choice makes the training data work harder. Results suggest a path toward models that solve fresh tasks on their own.
arxiv-2502-17843:
Istiaq Ahmed Fahad and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on spotting vehicles on hard roads with a transformer model. Light, road type, and vehicle mix all shift as a car drives. Older vision tools, which mix plain networks with set rules, can strain in such mix. The team is the first to try a detection transformer for this task.

Their training scheme, named Co-DETR, sharpens how the model learns traits and focus. Extra heads in training give more signal and lift the yield of good picks. Tests on a data set of tough road scenes pit their method against transformer and YOLO forms. Their method won on scores. The authors say it is fit for real use in self driving stacks.
arxiv-2502-18043:
Pierre Descouvemont analyzes in a 2025 paper two neutron transfer reactions on halo nuclei with a semi microscopic model. Halo nuclei carry a sparse cloud of neutrons far from a tight core. The model used assumes that cluster form, so the cloud's long tail is rendered faithfully.

Targets are helium 6 and lithium 11, the classic core plus two neutron halos. Overlap integrals and strength factors come out of the cluster math with no fitted knobs. Cross sections for both transfer reactions are then computed in a standard distorted wave frame. One channel to an excited lithium 9 core is added for the lithium case. Match with measured data is fair given the zero adjustment setup, he reports.
arxiv-2502-18343:
Single layers of chromium chloride can be magnetic, and growing them cleanly opens a window on two-dimensional magnetism. Giuseppe Buccoliero and co-authors grew such monolayers in 2025 on gold, nickel, and graphene-coated nickel, all from the same starting powder in high vacuum. They watched the films form with diffraction, tunneling microscopy, and X-ray magnetic measurements.

The surface decides the chemistry: gold and bare nickel yield different compounds, one with three chlorines per chromium, one with two, each with its own magnetism at four kelvin. Graphene lets the richer compound grow on nickel too. Mixed islands showed opposed magnetization in places, a sign of magnetic frustration between neighbors.
arxiv-2502-18443:
Jake Poznanski and co-authors release an open toolkit that turns PDFs into clean training text with a fine tuned vision language model, in work from twenty twenty-five. PDFs hold trillions of quality words for training language models, but messy layouts defeat cheap extractors. Top commercial models cost too much per page or cannot take private files.

Their seven billion parameter model trained on over a quarter million diverse crawled pages. It reads pages into plain text in natural order, keeping tables, lists, and equations. A million pages cost about one hundred seventy-six dollars to convert. A new benchmark of fourteen hundred hard PDFs showed the toolkit beating even the best commercial rivals. All parts are public.
arxiv-2502-18743:
Armin Aminimajd, Joao Maia, and Abhinendra Singh present a 2025 paper on predicting the force network inside thick suspensions. A dense suspension of grains in liquid stiffens sharply near jamming, when grains lock into a load-bearing web of frictional contacts. Measuring or simulating that web near jamming is hard and slow.

A deep graph neural network learned the web from simulation data, treating grains as nodes and contacts as links. Trained on a single flow condition, it still predicted networks across wide ranges of density and flow, from dilute to jammed and from startup to steady flow. The approach offers a cheap stand-in for costly simulations of pastes, slurries, and other dense mixtures.
arxiv-2502-18843:
An-Jun Liu and Bryan Clark make neural-network wavefunctions practical for quantum chemistry in a 2025 paper. Finding a molecule's ground state predicts its properties, and neural quantum states are flexible candidates for the job. Two obstacles stand out: sharply peaked ground states resist sampling, and energy evaluations grow steeply with system size.

The authors add a suite of fixes: compact subspace construction, truncated energy evaluation, better sampling, and physics-informed tweaks. Applied to a backflow model, the upgrades beat classic coupled-cluster methods and rival top-tier techniques on accuracy while scaling better. Ablation studies assign credit to each fix. Performance tracks how spread out the state is, with delocalized states hardest to capture.
arxiv-2502-19243:
Great Britain wants far more solar power by 2035, yet local grid limits and slow hookups hold back new panels. Hussah Alghanem and Alastair Buckley build a model in a 2025 paper that maps how much solar each small region now holds. Their map uses land type and other local traits to explain the spread across areas.

The model explains most of the gap between regions, with small errors on the whole. Built-up land and farm land stood out as the strongest signs of where panels cluster. The tool can split a national target into local shares, rank regions against each other, and sketch where future growth may land. Grid planners can use those maps to plan upgrades, ease hookup queues, and settle land-use fights early.
arxiv-2502-19743:
Chen and a large team report in twenty twenty-five telescope observations of sudden X-ray bursts from a neutron star system. These bursts come from nuclear burning on the star's surface. During bursts, the hot cloud around the star may cool, causing a dip in hard X-rays. That dip had been seen in nine sources, but never in this prolific burster, which cast doubt on the idea.

A Chinese X-ray telescope watched the system in its hard state and caught ten bursts. Two bursts showed a double peak in soft X-rays, hinting at a brief swelling of the star's surface layers. The hard X-ray dip did appear above a set energy, and its depth levelled off partway. The authors read this as proof that only the inner part of the cloud cools.
arxiv-2502-19843:
Hubert Baty, writing alone in 2025, shows how a type of neural network that uses physics rules can solve hard equations when data are sparse or noisy. The method can work from data at the edge of a region or from points inside it.

Baty also uses the networks in reverse, to find unknown values in the equations from the data at hand. The main test case is the solar corona, the hot outer layer of the Sun, where strong magnetic fields shape hot gas. The paper makes the case that this tool suits such plasma problems well.
arxiv-2502-20043:
Amir Mafi, Rando Rasul Qadir, and Hero Saremi present a 2025 result on two neatness traits of monomial ideals in algebra. Such ideals are built from single-term polynomials, and the traits sort how cleanly a ring built from them can be taken apart. The team asks when the two traits amount to the same thing.

For generic monomial ideals, they prove the traits match exactly: the quotient is pretty clean just when it is sequentially Cohen-Macaulay. The match holds for some special ideals too. An example in the paper also breaks a past guess about generic ideals.
arxiv-2502-20143:
Tuomas Uusnäkki and co-authors run a quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits in a 2025 paper. Quantum engines need tight control of heat baths and of the working unit's energy. Superconducting circuits give that control, but no cyclic quantum engine had been built with them. A quantum-circuit refrigerator acts as a tunable heat bath here.

The working unit is a flux-tunable transmon qubit. The team runs a few Otto cycles, with tailored cooling and heating steps split by flux ramps that shift qubit frequency. Single-shot readout tracks the state through each cycle. Output power and efficiency come out positive and match simulations, they report.
arxiv-2502-20443:
Tao Han, Matthew Low, Tong Arthur Wu, and Keping Xie survey what a future muon collider could find in this 2025 paper. Smashing muons at high energy can create heavy new particles directly, up to nearly the full beam energy. The beams also carry a spray of lighter particles that open extra creation paths.

The team tabulates production rates for many colored states, from triplets and sextets to leptoquarks. Direct pair creation is strong, while pairs from the beam spray are far rarer. Single creation drives the reach for some exotic states. Mass estimates suggest a ten-trillion-volt muon collider could pass the big proton machine's reach on several fronts. The results mostly carry over to electron colliders too.
arxiv-2502-20743:
Keiya Ishiguro and co-authors study symmetry rules in a landscape of string theory settings, in a paper from 2025. Their setting is type IIB theory placed on folded torus shapes, where fluxes thread the cycles of the space. The shape data are summed up in period vectors, and the team asks which changes to those vectors leave the physics in a valid form.

Two kinds of symmetry turn out to be needed to fix the basis of cycles in a clear way. One is a broad form of the classic S change, and the other comes from the mass patterns of closed strings. With that basis fixed, the authors trace how fluxes shift under the symmetries and sort the resulting vacua on folded spaces.
arxiv-2502-20943:
Xue Yang and co-authors expose a backdoor attack on reference-based image upscaling in a 2025 paper. Reference-based super resolution uses a second, similar image to recover fine detail. No one had tested how open it is to planted backdoors. Their BadRefSR framework plants one via the reference image.

A trigger pattern is added to reference inputs, and a mixed loss trains the model. Behaving normally on clean pairs, the model swaps in an attacker's chosen image on triggered pairs. Tests across varied attack settings show the trick works reliably. The team post code and warn that reference pipelines need security checks before deployment.
arxiv-2502-21143:
Hyungi Lee, Seungyoo Lee, and Juho Lee shrink the data needed to train uncertainty-aware networks, in a 2025 paper. Bayesian neural networks report not just a guess but how sure the guess is. That honesty costs heavy computing, since the networks carry whole ranges of possible settings.

A pseudo-coreset is a tiny, learned stand-in dataset that mimics the full data. Earlier versions for Bayesian networks ate memory during training and gave weaker results. The new method uses variational inference, a principled shortcut for hard probability math, to learn the stand-in set with less memory and cost. Benchmark tests show better accuracy than the earlier approach. The work makes uncertainty reporting more practical on large datasets.
arxiv-2502-21243:
Barbara Kaltenbacher and William Rundell tackle, in a 2025 math paper, a hard reconstruction problem in slow-spreading systems. Their equation models reaction and subdiffusion, where spread crawls slower than usual. Two hidden traits must be found at once: how the reaction term bends, and how it varies across space. The two are multiplied together, which tangles any attempt to split them.

The pair test several data setups: readings along the edge over time, a snapshot of the inside at the final time, and a mix of both. They build fixed-point schemes and a frozen Newton method to do the rebuild. For final-time data, they prove the scheme converges and that the answer is unique. Computer tests show how the methods perform as the spread order changes.
arxiv-2503-00043:
Nilay Yilmaz and co-authors introduce VOILA, a benchmark that tests multimodal language models on visual analogy problems, published in 2025. These models join vision and text well, but measuring abstract reasoning across several images is hard. The benchmark asks a model to generate an image that completes an analogy between two given image pairs.

The tasks are open-ended and dynamic, with no fixed answer choices. Experiments showed current models struggle: they grasp relations between images poorly and reason weakly at a high level. Accuracy on hard text-answer scenarios stayed low even for the best models, far below human performance. Following a step-by-step prompting strategy, from least to most, improved results. The authors evaluated both open models and GPT-4o, and frame the benchmark as a sharper tool for probing machine reasoning.
arxiv-2503-00143:
Tom Pan and co-authors published a computing paper in 2025 on predicting protein structure from crystal data. Finding a protein's exact atomic shape is a hard problem in biology. The team built a hybrid model that joins test data with learning methods. It reads maps derived from crystal scattering and known fragments of amino acid units.

The model, called RecCrysFormer, directly predicts the electron density maps needed to build atomic models. Training reuses results from earlier rounds and from standard refinement steps as extra inputs. On a test set of synthetic fragments drawn from a public protein bank, the model gave good accuracy. It also held up when crystal size and angle values varied.
arxiv-2503-00543:
Xiaoshan Huang and co-authors published this study in 2025. It asks whether merging black hole pairs could flash light that telescopes might catch. The pairs LIGO hears are born, in this picture, with a leftover gas disk around them. As gravity waves shrink the orbit, tides squeeze the disk. The squeeze raises a two-armed spiral wave that stands still in the pair's rotating frame.

Simulations show the spiral drives gas inward far faster than normal. Even a weakly ionized disk drains away long before the holes merge. With the gas gone, the merger happens in the dark. The authors say this dims hopes for a glowing partner to the gravity wave signal, at least for this kind of system. Disk draining, in short, beats the merger clock.
arxiv-2503-01043:
Doosung Park builds cohomology theories for singular spaces in a solo 2025 paper, the first of a series. Logarithmic schemes keep track of a boundary divisor where geometry degenerates, and the aim is a cohomology that sees both the space and its boundary cleanly.

Park's method works inside logarithmic motivic homotopy theory over a very small base. It recovers the K-theory of the open complement from ordinary K-theory, and a logarithmic version of topological Hochschild homology from the usual one. Among the payoffs, the K-theory of non-regular schemes becomes representable in the log motivic world, and a logarithmic cyclotomic trace appears for the well-behaved cases.
arxiv-2503-01343:
Hui Gao confirms a guess about which graphs push a new degree based index, the complementary second Zagreb index, to its max for a set size. Such indices boil a graph's shape down to one number used in chem-ical graph work. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The index came from a fresh geometric view of graph edges, set out by Furtula and Oz. In that same work, the authors guessed which graphs of a given order reach the top value. Gao proves the guess holds, which pins down the extremal graphs fully. The result closes an open point in the study of these new indices.
arxiv-2503-01643:
Jiayu Wan and Liu Liu wrote a 2025 math paper on neural networks that mimic a key gas flow equation with random inputs. Their networks are built to stay accurate when the gas is close to calm balance, a regime where plain networks often fail. They split the system into large scale and fine parts to build the training loss.

The authors prove two main claims with care. First, good networks of this kind exist when the loss can be driven near zero. Second, as the loss falls, the network answer moves toward the true one, with error shrinking fast over time. The work gives firm ground for using such networks on gas problems with uncertain data.
arxiv-2503-01743:
A large Microsoft team introduces compact language models in a 2025 technical report. The text model holds under four billion parameters yet beats similar-sized open models and matches models twice its size on math and coding tasks. The secret is a curated diet of high-quality web and synthetic data, heavy on math and code. A much larger vocabulary aids many languages, and a grouped attention scheme speeds long outputs.

Its sibling adds vision and speech to the same core. Small adapter modules with routers let the modes combine without interfering. The report details the recipes and benchmarks for both models.
arxiv-2503-01843:
Kalra and co-authors ask when memory-hungry parts of the Adam optimizer can be shrunk without hurting training. Adam, the default trainer for modern models, stores running averages of gradients and squares; that second store is the heavy one. Their tool is a layer-wise signal-to-noise analysis: where the second-moment values in a layer barely vary, the block can be replaced by its mean. The analysis shows how architecture, settings, and data decide where that is safe.

The result is SlimAdam, which compresses second moments only along the dimensions the analysis clears, and leaves the rest untouched. Across varied architectures and training setups, it matched Adam's accuracy and stability while cutting up to 98 percent of the second-moment storage. Code is public. For teams training large models on tight hardware, the paper replaces guesswork about optimizer memory with a measured rule.
arxiv-2503-01943:
Nicolas Underwood and Fabien Paillusson present a 2025 paper on telling apart kinds of non-ergodic behavior from data. Ergodicity, roughly whether long observation of one system matches averages across many, is used inconsistently across fields. The authors first sort out three major meanings of the term and how they relate. They then introduce a spectral method that works on data alone, without knowing the system's equations.

The method can find, measure, and classify non-ergodic subgroups inside a population that is ergodic overall. They demonstrate it on the Kob-Andersen model, a lattice model of glassy slowdown. Because the method needs only data, it applies to simulations and experiments alike. The authors aim to give many disciplines a shared, practical language for a slippery concept.
arxiv-2503-02143:
Jordan Peper and co-authors argue that world models for robots should be built so their inner states mean real physical things, in work from 2025. Such models predict future sensor views for planning and control. Their learned inner codes usually map to nothing a human can name, which limits trust and safety checks.

Four principles are proposed. Organize the inner space by physical intent. Learn codes that respect the symmetries of the physical world. Fuse many kinds and strengths of supervision in one training run. Split the output generation into parts that scale and can be checked. Tests show the principles at work. The shift is from models merely informed by physics to models readable in physical terms.
arxiv-2503-02243: Naokant Deo and Sandeep Kumar build a new family of approximation operators in a 2025 paper. Their sequence ties the construction to a class of polynomials through their generating functions. They compute the operators' moments, including what the central moments settle to as the sequence advances. Then they bound how fast the operators converge, using a standard smoothness measure, and prove further results in a Lipschitz-type space.
arxiv-2503-02743:
Urvisha Shethia, Vedali Inamdar, and Viraj Kulkarni check Eloquent, a digital speech treatment app for stuttering, in a two thousand twenty-five pilot study. Stuttering disrupts speech fluency and brings psychological and social difficulties.

The the research team compared speech samples before and after treatment using the Stuttering Severity Index-4 and the S24 communication attitude scale. Overall severity scores fell by more than half, with gains in reading, speaking, duration, and physical concomitants. Over three quarters of people taking part got better by at least one severity group. Attitude scores also got better, hinting structured app-based treatment can build fluency and confidence.
arxiv-2503-02843:
Maicol Ochoa and co-authors compute how electrons behave around phosphorus atoms in silicon in a 2025 physics paper. Such donor devices are a hopeful base for quantum computers, since each added atom can hold controlled quantum states.

Their method solves the many-electron problem atom by atom, with no shortcuts borrowed from atomic orbit sets. Checked against a trusted method for two electrons on one phosphorus atom, it matched well while needing smaller computing boxes. The team then worked out charging and binding energies for pairs of phosphorus atoms and watched how the electron clouds reshape each other. Precise maps like these help engineers place dopants so future quantum devices act as designed.
arxiv-2503-03043:
Andy Dong, Wei-Ning Chen, and Ayfer Ozgur wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It shows how the random choices already built into model training can be used on purpose to strengthen privacy for the data behind the model.

In many setups, each data sample takes part in only some training rounds, or updates only part of the model. The authors prove that this partial involvement hides each sample's influence more than past analyses credited. They apply the idea to federated learning, where phones or hospitals train a shared model by each updating a random slice of it. That trick, used to save memory, turns out to buy real privacy. They also add a new sampling scheme that gives each sample a fixed number of turns, beating random sampling on privacy.
arxiv-2503-03443:
Isaac Roberts and four co-authors propose a concept based way to explain uncertainty in machine learning models. Models report how confident they are, but explaining where that doubt comes from is hard, above all with rich, high dimensional data. Past explanation tools pin doubt on single features and stay local.

Their method uses concept vectors, directions in the model's inner space tied to human ideas. These vectors yield explanations of doubt for single cases and for the model as a whole. The team shows the explanations are not just descriptive: they can guide tweaks that refine and improve the model. The work targets trust in classification systems.
arxiv-2503-03543:
Dragos Costea, Alina Marcu, and Marius Leordeanu present a method for rebuilding scenes in 3D from drone video, in this 2025 paper. New views far from the filmed path often come out poorly, which limits self-flying drones. Their pipeline loops between a neural renderer, which makes sharp images, and a classic geometry method, which keeps shapes honest.

The loop is self-supervised, so it needs no labeled training data. A transformer-based stage adapts the rendering to new viewpoints on the fly. Tests showed better image views and better mesh models than before, mainly in thinly filmed areas. The team frames the work as a step toward safer flight in complex outdoor settings.
arxiv-2503-03643:
Peter Danchev, Arash Javan, Omid Hasanzadeh, and Ahmad Moussavi study a class of rings in this 2025 algebra paper. A ring is a set where adding and multiplying follow set rules. In the class they name, each member splits into a center part plus a part from a special subset.

The team sharpens recent results on when such rings have clean splitting traits. They show the trait carries over to power series rings, in both directions. They also show that if the trait holds for a polynomial ring, a long-standing open guess in ring theory must hold for the base ring. Related side results round out the picture for close ring families.
arxiv-2503-03843:
Fluids full of tiny spinning rotors can organize themselves in surprising ways. Maji, Padhan, and Pandit study a two-dimensional system of counter-rotating spinners in simulations. At low activity the spinners sort into separate regions, a process called phase separation. As activity rises, the system crosses over into a new turbulent state instead.

In that state, the swirl of the flow turns out to be directly proportional to the field marking which spin type dominates each region. The team explains this neat link in theory and measures the state's fingerprints: power-law spectra for energy and concentration, bursts of intermittency, and flow-topology statistics. The model joins two classic equations, one for phase separation and one for fluid flow. The authors suggest the findings may speak to living systems, where spinning units such as cells and cilia stir their surroundings.
arxiv-2503-03943:
Hafiz Usman Naseer and co-authors simulate in 2025 how bubbles trigger turbulence in a viscoelastic channel flow. Elastic turbulence arises in polymer fluids even at slow speeds. Their interface-resolved simulations cover single and two-phase flows across wide ranges of flow and elasticity numbers.

Injecting bubbles into a smooth flow bends streamlines enough to spark elastic instability. The flow then transitions to a full turbulent state with a characteristic energy spectrum. Once turbulent, drag rises in all cases. At low speeds, bubbles line up in strings at the channel core, with intermittent bursts nearby.
arxiv-2503-04243:
What sets the pace of star birth in a galaxy? Jing Dou, Yingjie Peng, and fourteen co-authors argue the invisible halo of dark matter around it does much of the governing. Working only with central spiral galaxies, they tracked how the balance between molecular and atomic hydrogen, and the efficiency of turning gas into stars, shifts with galaxy and halo properties. Both climbed steeply and steadily with halo mass.

Near a halo mass of a trillion suns, the trend tips over: past that point, galaxies mostly stop forming stars. Disk size, itself set by the halo's mass, spin, and concentration, also shapes how fast atomic gas converts. The team sketches an arc in which halo growth first feeds star formation, then shuts it down, and calls the halo a global regulator earlier work underrated.
arxiv-2503-04443:
Makarov and co-authors ask what deep resting does to the way a metal glass softens into liquid. Metallic glasses are frozen liquids, and long holding just below their softening point lets their inner structure settle. Their 2025 paper studies zirconium-based glasses after such deep relaxation, watching heat flow and stiffness side by side.

Resting produced a strong peak in excess heat capacity, while the stiffness changed only modestly. The authors propose that the high-frequency shear stiffness is the master quantity steering relaxation: the energy barrier for atomic rearrangement scales with it, and its size shifts as defects come and go. Feeding measured stiffness into their theory reproduced the heat data for every glass state. They argue that a deeply rested glass crosses its transition almost like a first-order phase change, sharp and sudden.
arxiv-2503-04843:
Alessandro Pasqui, Hervé Turlier, and a team of co-authors sharpen 3D microscope images along their weak axis. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents ZAugNet. Microscope stacks often have fine detail across a slice but coarse steps between slices. Light damage limits and sample traits cause that gap.

Their method fills in new slices between real ones in a learned, curved way. Each pass doubles the depth detail. A rival-maker network plus a teacher trick keeps it fast and sharp. Tests across imaging types beat rival methods on most scores. A plus version fills gaps at any spacing, which suits uneven real data sets.
arxiv-2503-05143:
Wenhao Wang and colleagues released the first benchmark for training phone agents on scattered user data in a 2025 paper. Mobile agents learn to operate apps for users, but central data collection is costly and hard to scale. Federated learning trains on data that stays on each phone, yet the field had no standard test bed, so results could not be compared fairly.

FedMABench bundles several datasets with many subsets, a range of federated algorithms and base models, and hundreds of apps in a few categories. Experiments found federated methods consistently beat training on one phone alone. Which apps a user has drove much of the difference between users, and even unrelated app categories showed linked patterns during training.
arxiv-2503-05243:
Gianluca Passarelli, Angelo Russomanno, and Procolo Lucignano examine a quantum complexity measure in a boundary time crystal in a 2025 physics study. Time crystals of this kind settle into steady states whose entanglement can change sharply under monitoring. Those transitions were known to depend on how the underlying open-system dynamics is unraveled into individual histories.

The authors instead track nonstabilizerness, sometimes called magic, which measures how far a state lies beyond easy classical simulation. Unlike entanglement, it stays the same across unraveling choices for large systems. Its steady value shows a cusp at the mean-field critical point rather than a full transition.
arxiv-2503-05443:
Sam Bennett and Amihay Hanany wrote a 2025 note in string theory about brane setups and the gauge groups they create. Their systems mix D3, D5, and NS5 branes with O3 orientifold planes. These setups build three-dimensional theories with orthogonal and symplectic gauge groups. A long-standing puzzle is how to tell apart two close forms of the D-type group.

The note gives a partial rule for reading those group nodes in quiver diagrams. The clue is the placement of half D5 branes near the orientifold planes. The authors also propose links between Coulomb branches of related quivers. A further rule covers how half branes act on long chains in the diagram.
arxiv-2503-05743:
Francesca Pelusi and co-authors wrote a 2025 note on momentum balance in a lattice fluid method. The method mimics fluid flow on a grid and can model two phase flows. A key need is a pressure tensor whose flat interface value stays constant, the mark of mechanical balance.

The authors use the lattice momentum balance to build that tensor for a known two phase model with a single range force. Their build holds the constant value to machine precision at each node. They give closed forms for the coexistence curves under varied pseudo potential and forcing choices. The note offers a strict route to control the tensor in wider settings.
arxiv-2503-06143:
Michael Orlitzky and Giovanni Barbarino answer, in a 2025 math paper, a sorting question about a class of cones. A cone's Lyapunov rank is the size of the symmetry algebra tied to it. That rank does not change when a cone is reshaped by a linear map. Yet different cones can share the same rank, so rank alone usually cannot name a cone.

The authors narrow the field to symmetric cones, a well behaved family used in optimization. They ask whether any of those cones can be picked out uniquely by rank alone. For cones that cannot be split into simpler parts, they give a complete answer. For the general case, they make partial progress. The result clarifies what a single number can and cannot tell about shape, in a setting where such invariants guide theory.
arxiv-2503-06243:
Hirschfeld and Thas survey arcs, caps, and their kin in finite space geometry. Arcs and caps are basic point sets with clean rules on how lines meet them. The survey pulls key results into one place for readers who work in this field.

It gives special care to broad forms of ovals and ovoids, the curved like stars of this discrete world. Fresh results sit beside open problems that still lack proof. The piece serves as both a map of what is known and a call for new work on these tidy, strict shapes.
arxiv-2503-06543:
Aritra Banerjee and Abir Ghosh revisit exact solutions for a simple fluid flow model in this 2025 paper. The model treats a perfect fluid moving along one direction, a setting used for matter in high-energy collisions. Known solutions split into two regimes, depending on whether the flow looks the same under boosts.

The authors lay out the full analytic solution space for this system. They build an explicit one-parameter family of flows that interpolates between the two regimes. A single dial at the level of the solutions moves a flow from one regime to the other. They also construct a generalized spread of entropy across rapidity for these flows, working at the level of potentials. The paper firms up the map of what flows this model allows.
arxiv-2503-06643:
Batu Guan and co-authors made code benchmarks that renew themselves in two thousand twenty-five. Models may have memorized public test sets in training. Scores then flatter skill they do not have. The framework mutates test programs while keeping meaning. Syntax changes, semantics stay identical. Fresh-looking tests thus probe true understanding.

Ten popular code models faced the dynamic tests. All scored far worse than on static versions. Some model rankings flipped dramatically. Memorized answers stopped working under mutation. Reasoning about code had to be genuine. The method resists contamination by construction. Benchmark owners can regenerate tests on demand. The authors argue static leaderboards now mislead buyers.
arxiv-2503-06743:
Cheng Huang and co-authors present in 2025 an unsupervised model that maps the main blood vessels in eye scans used to screen for glaucoma. Changes in those vessels signal the start and progress of the disease. Mapping them is vital for modeling but hard to do well, and labeled data are scarce.

Their model first grows a vessel skeleton with a space filling method that also estimates vessel width. A generative network and a statistical model of widths then rebuild the vessels in two and three dimensions. The authors report near perfect marking accuracy without labeled data or heavy computing. Tests suggest the approach beats existing deep learning models on this task.
arxiv-2503-06843:
The T2K team, a large group of physicists, report in 2025 on a hard-to-spot reaction of neutrinos, the tiny particles that pass through matter with ease. They study cases where a neutrino hits a target and makes a single charged pion, without the neutrino itself changing form. The work uses the ND280 detector near the beam source.

The paper explains how the team picks out this faint signal from a sea of other events. It then shows how to work out the rate of the reaction in a way that does not lean on one set model of how neutrinos act. Such rates help test the rules that guide neutrino science. They also help future experiments read their own data with less bias.
arxiv-2503-07443:
Steven de Rooij and co-authors measure stray particles in superconducting circuits in a 2025 paper. Such circuits lose quality when broken pairs of electrons, called quasiparticles, linger. The readout signal itself can create more of them, yet how that happens was not well pinned down.

The team measured particle counts across heat levels, readout power, and circuit sizes. Smaller active volumes held higher particle counts under the same readout push. That effect sets a limit on how sensitive a class of light detectors can be. Known direct absorption models failed to explain the counts, so the authors argue an indirect path must dominate.
arxiv-2503-07543:
Four authors build a new algebraic structure out of the loops on a smooth closed surface or space, using Morse theory, the study of a landscape's peaks and passes. Their object, a based multiloop algebra, generalizes an older braid skein algebra. In the torus case, that older algebra is a known Hecke-type algebra from representation theory.

The multiplication rules mix two ingredients: trees of gradient paths on the loop space, and string-style operations that join and split loops. After a change of base, the authors show their algebra matches a wrapped Heegaard Floer algebra built from cotangent fibers, a bridge between two research areas. They also compute the sphere case in full, where the result can be read as a derived Hecke algebra. The work ties Morse theory, string topology, and Floer theory into one framework.
arxiv-2503-07643:
Aidan Gao and Junhong Lin present, in 2025 work, a tool that groups map data by place with the help of graph networks. Sorting points by area serves fields from crime study to town planning. Old tools, though, ignore what near points say, and they fade as data grow in size and depth.

Their tool, ConstellationNet, joins an image-style net that codes each point, a graph net that pools news from near points, and batch handling for speed. Across data sets it beat top tools at both sorting with labels and grouping without them. It also shrank model size and training time by up to tenfold. The team sees fast use in outbreaks and medical scans, where fresh data must be read at once.
arxiv-2503-07943:
Taoxu Zhao and co-authors fuse text and image to read sentiment more truly. Their 2025 paper deals with multimodal sentiment analysis, where words alone miss what a picture adds. A BERT model pulls features from text, while a vision transformer named DINOv2 pulls features from images. Three fusion designs then blend the two streams, from a basic merge to self and dual attention blends.

Tests run on three sets: a meme bank and two multi-view sentiment sets, in single and multi label forms. The blends proved workable and practical, the team reports. The study backs paired signals over text-only reads.
arxiv-2503-08443:
Alexandru Aleman and Alex Bergman wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on invariant subspaces. An invariant subspace is a part of a space that an operator maps back into itself. The paper studies two linked operators, one that takes derivatives and one, the Volterra operator, that builds up integrals.

The authors use an abstract setup where the two operators undo each other. One is compact and fades to zero with repeats, while the other is unbounded but well behaved. Their results cover many cases, from Schrödinger operators to large classes of systems. A key tool is a model built from spaces of entire functions. The work widens what is known about these classic operators.
arxiv-2503-08543:
Cassandra Overney, Cassandra Moe, and their co-authors describe BoundarEase, a 2025 system built to improve public debate over school attendance boundaries in the United States. Districts draw those boundary lines, and the lines shape who can attend which school. Public processes for changing them are often unclear, hard to follow, and sharply divided.

The team worked with a large district serving nearly 150,000 students. A first study with 16 community members found three frictions: people thought of their own family first, struggled to grasp how changes would hit others, and found impacts hard to understand. The system was designed against those frictions, aiming at debate that weighs the whole community. The paper reports the design and its evaluation with the district.
arxiv-2503-08843:
Rajitha de Silva and five co-authors improve feature matching for farm robots in two thousand twenty-five. Their test ground is vineyards, where rows of vines look much alike. Like looks make image points hard to tell apart. That hurts pose checks and place finding for the robot.

The team adds semantic facts to each key point in the image. Points in regions with meaning get richer codes. That makes twins in looks easier to split apart. Tests span two tasks, pose checks and place finding. Match accuracy rose across all point and code types tried. Gains held over months of hard field work.
arxiv-2503-09543:
Oskar van der Wal and co-authors release, in a 2025 paper, a set of 45 fresh training runs to study how steady language model training is. Small shifts at the start, such as the random seed, can change what a model learns. Yet few shared tools exist to study that spread for text models that write word by word. Their set, PolyPythias, adds nine seeds for each of five sizes of the Pythia suite, from 14 million to 410 million weights. With past runs, the count comes to 50 runs and about 7,000 saved states.

The team reads how the seed shapes final scores, the language traits learned, and the phases of training. Broad scaling trends held firm across seeds and sizes. Some runs stood out as odd ones, and the team marks their traits. The set may help staff foretell a run that will go off track.
arxiv-2503-09743:
Timothy Laurence and seven co-authors present a 2025 paper on spotting food poisoning from online restaurant reviews. Many stomach illnesses never reach a doctor, so official counts miss them. Reviews, though, often describe symptoms and suspect dishes in plain words. The team built an expert-designed labeling scheme for reviews in a public data set, covering illness detection plus symptom and food extraction.

Large language models, guided by prompts alone, scored above ninety percent on all three tasks. They beat smaller models that had been fine-tuned for the job. Extra tests probed the models for bias in detection, with reassuring results. The authors see strong potential for review-based surveillance of gut illness. They caution that review data themselves skew toward certain diners and places, so counts need careful reading.
arxiv-2503-09843:
Gheorghe Craciun, Abhishek Deshpande, and Jiaxin Jin compute a special parameter region for chemical reaction networks, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Reaction models can swing wildly, with multiple steady states or chaos. A lucky few behave like a tame class of systems with very stable dynamics, even when they do not look the part.

Such impostors are called disguised toric systems, and the set of parameters making a network one is its disguised toric locus. Until now, measuring that set was awkward. The authors give a general, efficient method for its dimension. They demo the method on models of biological networks, including a classic oscillator, feedback gene circuits, and circadian clocks.
arxiv-2503-10043:
Wenjie Li and co-authors propose a plug-in that improves image super-resolution at very low extra cost, published in 2025. Super-resolution rebuilds a sharp image from a blurry, low-resolution one. Common building blocks, such as convolutions and window-based Transformers, see only a limited area at once, which limits gains under tight compute budgets.

Their plug-in, FourierSR, uses Fourier tokens instead of those blocks. It relies only on Fourier transforms and multiplication, which cuts complexity while giving a global view of the image. Added to existing efficient methods, it raised a standard quality score by a clear margin on a test set. The added parameters and compute were a tiny fraction of the original models' size, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-10343:
Halil Mutuk reweighs a particle inside nuclear matter in a 2025 paper. The rho meson, a short-lived particle, changes its properties when it sits inside dense matter, and those changes hint at how fundamental symmetries recover at extremes. Standard sum rule methods assume a shape for the particle's spectrum before fitting; Mutuk instead uses an inverse method that rebuilds the spectrum directly from theory.

Applied here to the rho in nuclear matter for the first time, the approach finds a marked drop in the particle's mass, matching earlier predictions. The result leans on how the dense medium suppresses vacuum condensates and strains a common factorization shortcut. Mutuk presents the method as a cleaner benchmark for lattice simulations and heavy-ion experiments.
arxiv-2503-10943:
Marnik Bercx and co-authors present a 2025 paper charting where conventional superconductors hide among materials scientists already know. The hunt ran on a database of experimentally confirmed crystal structures. For 4,533 non-magnetic metals, the team computed an estimated critical temperature from how electrons couple to lattice vibrations, refining the sampling for the best candidates.

Top prospects then got high-grade treatment, with automated tools computing precise coupling maps. The result is a ranked landscape of Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer superconductors, the classic phonon-driven kind, across known compounds. Such a map tells experimentalists which shelf materials deserve a cold test first, instead of blind synthesis of ever stranger crystals.
arxiv-2503-11243:
Nayana Venkatareddy, Partha Sarathi Mondal, Jaydeep Mandal, Shradha Mishra, and Prabal Maiti published this physics paper in 2025. It studies a mixture of hot and cold particles that sorts itself into separate regions. The effect, called two-temperature induced phase separation, appears when the heat gap between the two kinds passes a threshold.

The team attacked the problem at two scales. Atom-level simulations showed the sorting begin at once in dense mixtures, forming woven domains of hot-rich and cold-rich zones. A simpler paired-equation model, which lets the two kinds trade heat, reproduced the same woven pattern. Both routes found domains growing with the same power over time, the classic exponent seen in ordinary mixtures at rest. The match across two and three dimensions suggests universal rules govern even this out-of-balance sorting.
arxiv-2503-11343:
Three researchers present a video prediction method from 2025 that uses motion maps to bend its own filters as it works. Guessing the next frame of a video matters for self-driving systems, video coding, and media tools. Fixed filters struggle when a scene holds many kinds of motion at once, from a panning camera to a small moving object.

Their network first estimates how each pixel moves, then uses that map to steer flexible sampling at several scales. Wide scene shifts and small object moves can thus be handled in one pass. On eight standard test clips, the method beat prior scores by about one unit on a common quality scale. Its speed stayed close to rival methods, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-11543:
Wystan Benbow and colleagues present recent highlights from the VERITAS active galactic nucleus discovery program, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. VERITAS is among the world's most sensitive very-high-energy gamma-ray observatories. About half of its good-weather observing time has targeted active galactic nuclei. Many sessions belong to an ongoing program hunting new gamma-ray nuclei.

When a discovery is made, the collaboration pairs spectral and variability measurements with broadband observations. Together these probe the jet-powered processes inside the nucleus. Recent highlights include four very-high-energy discoveries. They are the objects B2 0912+29, 1ES 1028+511, 1ES 1118+424, and RBS 1366. The report shows how a long-running discovery program keeps expanding the catalog of extreme galactic nuclei.
arxiv-2503-11743:
Tianliang Xu, Eva Maxfield Brown, Dustin Dwyer, and Sabina Tomkins present PublicSpeak, a framework for finding public remarks in local government meetings, in this 2025 paper. Cities make big choices at small meetings, and newsrooms cannot cover them all.

The framework uses meeting structure, domain knowledge, and language cues in a probabilistic model to pick out what residents said. The team tested it on a new dataset of meetings and used it to survey issues raised in seven United States cities. It beat the prior best method by ten percent on average and by up to forty percent in places. The tool could help journalists and watchdogs hear the public at scale.
arxiv-2503-11943:
Patricia Medina sharpens the sorting of 3D laser scan data by adding a new set of shape measures. Her 2025 paper works with LiDAR point clouds, clouds of points that map terrain in three dimensions. Sorting those points into classes like ground, plants, and buildings drives maps for many fields.

Medina defines product coefficients, quantities drawn from measure theory, and computes them for each point's neighborhood. In tests, these values joined the usual shape features taken from principal component analysis. Adding them lifted sorting accuracy within her framework by a clear margin. She presents the coefficients as a general add-on for point cloud tools. The paper gives the formulas in full so others can adopt them.
arxiv-2503-12043:
Ali Raeisdanaei, Juho Kim, and co-authors give a free tool that uses tongue models to run a risk read way, in a 2025 paper. The STPA way maps how safe acts can fail in hard kits. Its full runs eat much staff time in most firms that use it.

Tongue steps fill, sort, and trace STPA sheets in the tool flows. Past real risk sheets built by staff test the tool for truth. Scores show high truth on most STPA tasks in those tests. Staff time saved is the main gain claimed for the tool. Code is shared free for firms to take up.
arxiv-2503-12543:
Andrea Longhin re-analyzed Galileo's observations of Jupiter's moons in twenty twenty-five, comparing each entry of the Sidereus Nuncius against a modern sky simulator. Earlier studies had sampled the record; this one checks every observation. It uses both Galileo's sketches and his written angular measurements.
