Band correlation maps guide random sampling of new traces. Kept samples are those that track the real data most closely. A forest classifier cannot tell fake from real above chance, which signals high fidelity. Spread tests agree, so the method offers a private, scalable data source.
arxiv-2504-16243:
Griffin Smith and co-authors model swarming particles with a continuum equation in a 2025 paper. Janus particles are tiny spheres with two unlike faces. They drift and propel themselves, and experiments show that Brownian jostling plus quorum sensing is enough to make them cluster. Quorum sensing here means slowing or steering by neighbor counts. The team asks whether a partial differential equation can capture that group behavior without tracking every particle.

Their nonlocal advection-diffusion model does reproduce the clustering seen in experiments and in agent-based simulations. It also predicts something the earlier views missed: clusters can take an annular, ring-like structure under the modeled rules. The authors present the equation as both an explanation of the physics and a cheaper design tool for active matter studies.
arxiv-2504-16443:
Duy-Tho Le, Trung Pham, Jianfei Cai, and Hamid Rezatofighi introduced MGIoU in twenty twenty-five, a unifying loss for fitting parametric shapes in computer vision. Overlap, measured by intersection over union, is the canonical score, but optimizing it is messy: regression losses ignore it, direct versions are unstable or shape-limited, and each field handcrafts its own fix.

MGIoU projects convex shapes onto their surface normals and computes a one-dimensional normalized overlap there — simple, fast, and fully differentiable. A plus variant handles unstructured convex shapes, and a minus variant penalizes overlap for tasks like collision-free path prediction. On standard benchmarks the losses beat existing ones while computing ten to forty times faster, and they keep clean metric properties like scale invariance.
arxiv-2504-16643:
Jun He, Xiaosong Peng, and Yi Zhang build the module theory that sits on top of multiple Rota-Baxter algebras. These structures carry several interacting operations of a kind used in combinatorics and mathematical physics. The paper sets up left, right, and two-sided module structures for these algebras and constructs free modules for them, using a mixable tensor product to get the commutative case.

The authors give an exact condition for when a free module can itself carry the free multiple Rota-Baxter structure. They then define the analogues of projective and injective modules. The category, they show, has enough of both to support derived Hom functors, the machinery of homological algebra. A tensor product of multiple Rota-Baxter algebras is introduced, flat modules are defined, and both free and projective modules are proved flat.
arxiv-2504-16843:
Ilyass Taouil, Haizhou Zhao, Angela Dai, and Majid Khadiv use image generation models to guide humanoid robots in a 2025 paper. Their task is loco-manipulation, where a robot must walk and handle objects in a planned sequence. Instead of planning from scratch, they ask a diffusion model to imagine scenes of a person acting with objects.

From those images they extract where contact should occur and what pose the robot should take. Those cues feed a whole body planning method that enforces physical limits, yielding smooth paths the robot can follow. Tests in simulation cover several long horizon tasks and probe each step of the extraction pipeline.
arxiv-2504-16943:
Chiara Fusar Bassini and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on how flexible German gas power plants really are. Models usually guess flexibility from turbine specs, but real plants answer to owners, contracts, and habits. The team compressed five years of hourly output from 49 large gas units into learned profiles and clustered them without supervision.

Four clusters emerged: two of nimble peakers and two of sluggish non-peakers. Half the fleet ramped no better than coal plants. The stiff units, mostly owned by industry and city utilities, kept generating even when prices went negative. The authors warn the renewable transition needs rules that unlock this sleeping flexibility.
arxiv-2504-17043:
Policy choices rest on data that are flawed by error, gaps, and bias, and the way analysts patch those flaws can sway the outcome. Adway Wadekar and co-authors propose a 2025 framework for testing how much a decision should be trusted anyway.

The idea is to define scores and plots that target the final decision, not just the raw estimates. Analysts vary their patching assumptions and watch whether the decision itself would flip. Two worked examples show the method: one weighs measurement error in a model of vote share, the other weighs filled-in values when judging how many children face high lead levels. The framework aims to make confidence in a policy call explicit and checkable.
arxiv-2504-17143:
Bethany Foxon, Sindhu Jammi, and Thomas Fernholz engineer a cleaner microwave transition between trapped atomic states, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The atoms are rubidium eighty-seven dressed by radio-frequency fields, a common setup for cold atom experiments that rely on steady superpositions.

The dressed states shift with the surrounding static magnetic field, and that shift blurs the transition. A single off-resonant microwave field already cancels the part of the shift caused by the nuclear magnetic moment, at least to first order. Adding a second microwave frequency suppresses the field dependence further, as the team demonstrates in the lab. The resulting transition is narrow and far less touchy about field drift. Such a stable link between trappable states is useful across cold atom schemes. It gives experimenters a sharper tool for controlling atoms held in traps.
arxiv-2504-17243:
Xinyu Zhou and co-authors tackle grokking, a training puzzle in which a model masters a task long after it has memorized the training data, in a 2025 paper. Their method, NeuralGrok, learns how to reshape the model's gradients during training. An extra small module adjusts each part of the gradient by how much it helps true learning.

A two level training scheme guides that module. In tests on arithmetic tasks, models using the method generalized much sooner, above all on hard problems. The method also kept training steadier and steadily lowered model complexity. Standard weight decay, by contrast, sometimes caused instability. The authors add a new complexity measure to explain why the reshaping helps.
arxiv-2504-17443:
Gabriele Fici, Giuseppe Romana, Marinella Sciortino, and Cristian Urbina study how word-rewriting rules change a key measure of text repetitiveness, in a 2025 paper. The measure counts runs of equal letters in a famous reordering of a text, the Burrows-Wheeler transform, which underpins modern compressed search. A rewriting rule, a morphism, swaps each letter for a fixed block. The team asks which rules keep the run count nearly steady.

For two-letter alphabets, they pin the safe rules down exactly: they are the rules long known to preserve primitivity, the property of words that are not repeats of a shorter word. They also show that testing a rule for safety runs in fast, polynomial time. Side results probe two related rule classes. The work ties compression to older fields of codes and symbol dynamics.
arxiv-2504-17543:
The classic knapsack problem packs the most value into a limited space. Hubert Villuendas, Mathieu Besançon, and Jérôme Malick study a harder version where chosen items must also sit close together, a need that arises when spotting change points in time series. They attack it with semidefinite programming, a powerful relaxation method.

The team builds several relaxed models, putting the closeness rule either in the constraints or in the goal. They compare how tight and useful each version is. One penalty knob in their models smoothly trades closeness against solution quality. On the hardest test cases, the method gives strong solutions and tight bounds. It beats the existing exact formulation in flexibility. The authors present it as a practical heuristic for a problem that exact solvers handle poorly.
arxiv-2504-17643:
Steve Göring presents a small image search engine that researchers can run themselves, in a 2025 paper. CLIPSE uses the CLIP model to turn both pictures and typed queries into matching numeric codes, so a text phrase can fish out images by meaning rather than by filename. The design prizes plain structure that others can extend.

Two benchmarks cover how fast the engine indexes a collection and answers a query. It handles smaller datasets well on its own. For bigger ones, the paper advises running several copies in parallel. A modest, open tool suits labs that need private, meaning-based search over their own image piles.
arxiv-2504-17743:
Arnaud Casteigts, Michelle Doring, and Nils Morawietz asked in 2025 which degree sequences can be realized as temporally connected graphs. In a temporal graph, edges carry time labels, and a path must respect the order of time. Deciding whether a given graph can be labeled to be temporally connected is known to be hard, so the authors relax the question to degree sequences alone.

Their main result fully characterizes the feasible cases. Recognition runs in linear time for ordinary degree sequences and near-linear time for multigraph ones, and the checks can be made constructive at little cost: an algorithm builds the graph itself. The catalog title appends a conference note; the clean title governs. Readers get a complete answer where the original problem was intractable, by changing what is asked.
arxiv-2504-17843:
Blakesley Burkhart and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper announcing a nearby dark molecular cloud. Theory has long predicted that much molecular gas hides from the usual tracer, carbon monoxide. Such dark gas matters because it is the raw material of stars.

The cloud, named Eos, sits only ninety-four parsecs from the Sun, the closest known of its kind. It is the first molecular cloud found by the ultraviolet glow of hydrogen molecules at its edges. Its rim traces the edge of a large X-ray and radio structure in the northern sky. Distance checks used dust maps, X-ray absorption, and hot gas lines, placing it on the surface of the Local Bubble. Carbon monoxide maps show only a little bright gas, far below the cloud's true mass.
arxiv-2504-17943:
Weighing young calves often enough to track growth is slow work, and their spotted coats make camera-based estimates tricky. Liao and co-authors used depth images to predict calf weight without touching the animals. They trained a deep learning segmentation model to outline each calf in the image and compared it with a simpler threshold method, then fed the body measures into weight models.

The learned model outlined calves far more accurately, with an overlap score of 0.98 against 0.89 for the threshold method. For single weigh-ins, a gradient boosting model predicted weight best, missing by about 4.4 percent on average. A mixed model that used repeated images over time did better still, missing by about 2.4 percent. The authors say the system could automate weight tracking before weaning and ease farm management.
arxiv-2504-18443:
Simon Dold and four colleagues add proof logging to optimal classical planning, the task of finding the cheapest valid plan for a stated problem. A solver's claim that no plan exists, or that its plan is best, is usually taken on trust. Their work lets an outside party check the claim.

The framework issues lower-bound certificates built from pseudo-Boolean constraints. It does not depend on which planning algorithm produced the answer. As a case study, the team adapts the A-star search to log proofs of optimality at modest extra cost. They show the method for two standard heuristics, pattern databases and the h-max rule. Any heuristic whose steps fit the same logic can join in.
arxiv-2504-18543:
Olufemi Oyadare, a solo author, works on harmonic analysis for bundle-valued forms in a 2025 paper. The setting is a homogeneous space, a curved space that looks the same from every point, carrying differential forms whose values live in a vector bundle. The goal is a Fourier transform for such forms, strong enough to anchor a full theory on these spaces.

Starting from a functional equation that the classical transform obeys, Oyadare derives the Helgason Fourier transform for this setting. He gives the transform as an explicit integral formula built from a spherical kernel and a boundary map. A related Poisson transform links the pieces back together. The paper is dense, formula-led work aimed at specialists in analysis on symmetric spaces.
arxiv-2504-18643:
Jaehan Bae and a large team benchmark the computer codes used to model planet-forming disks, in a 2025 paper. Forward modeling is the standard way to read the substructures seen in such disks. For the results to be trusted, the codes in wide use must agree with each other. The team set out to check that agreement in a systematic way.

They simulate one disk with an embedded giant planet using five hydrodynamics codes, four grid-based and one particle-based. They then run two radiative transfer codes to compute disk temperatures and images. Comparing the outputs shows where the codes match and where they diverge. The exercise strengthens confidence in how disk images are read across the field.
arxiv-2504-18743:
Zaiwei Chen and Phalguni Nanda prove the first finite-time guarantees for a workhorse reinforcement learning algorithm in this 2025 paper. The algorithm is average-reward Q-learning, which learns the value of actions when reward is judged by its long-run average. Their version updates entries one at a time, out of sync, with adaptive step sizes that act as a private clock for each pair.

They show the learning sequence closes in on the best action values at a tidy rate, both in a span seminorm and, with a centering step, point by point. Adaptive steps turn out to be required: without them the method can aim at the wrong target. The steps also act like built-in importance sampling that evens out the uneven updates. Because each update depends on the whole history, the proof needs new tools, including a time-varying rewrite and fresh concentration bounds.
arxiv-2504-19043:
Connor Jerzak, Priyanshi Chandra, and Rishi Hazra learn clear voting plans from conjoint data, with honest doubt bounds. Their 2025 paper faults the standard scores, which average over rival traits and hide the clash when both sides pick at once. The team learns them offline from randomized preference data. Each plan is a product of chance picks, one per factor level.

The plans seek the best average case, then extend to a two-player minimax game of rival picks. A closed-form optimizer solves a tractable two-way case, and gradient steps cover richer ones. The Delta method carries the doubt to the plan and its value. Primaries and party divergence enter as measured amounts. On a presidential conjoint, these plans yield vote shares in past ranges. Plain averaging plans miss that range.
arxiv-2504-19343:
Alexis Miller and co-authors study a spread out star group in a 2025 paper. The group, called OCSN-49, holds about two hundred stars spread wide across the sky. Data from the Gaia space craft first brought groups like this to light.

The team took sharp spectra of four stars from across the stream. All four shared sun like metal levels and near same mix of elements. Age checks pointed to a few hundred million years, yet orbit tracing gave a far younger spread age. The gap fits a past event that tore the young cluster apart and left its stars drifting.
arxiv-2504-19443:
Yejin Jeong and Donghun Lee built an AI system that grades knee arthritis from X-rays more consistently than human readers often manage. Doctors grade the disease with the Kellgren and Lawrence scale, but grades vary between observers. Their system adapts CLIP, a model that links images with text, so it learns from both the X-ray and written descriptions at once.

Two added training rules push the model to agree with itself: one checks that a flipped copy of the same knee gets the same grade, and one enforces steady predictions. The system reached about 72 percent accuracy, the best reported for the task, beating plain CLIP by more than two points. The authors argue such consistency checks matter for fine-grained medical diagnosis.
arxiv-2504-19743: Jianjun Jin introduces a wider family of Hilbert matrix operators on weighted sequence spaces. His paper, from twenty twenty-five, builds each operator from a positive measure on the unit interval. He proves an exact test, both needed and enough, for when these operators stay bounded. The result extends a recent theorem in the same line, which Jin cites from a twenty twenty-three journal paper.
arxiv-2504-19943:
İsmail Burak Ateş, Şengül Kuru, and Javier Negro organized light-matter Hamiltonians into supersymmetric families in a 2025 paper. The Jaynes-Cummings model, an atom exchanging energy with a single light mode, is quantum optics' basic building block, and its detuning, the mismatch between atom and light frequencies, tunes its behavior. Supersymmetric quantum mechanics pairs Hamiltonians whose spectra nearly coincide, and the authors wield those transformations as bridges between different detunings.

Pairs of Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonians with different detunings turn out to be supersymmetric partners, and the bridges even reach the anti-Jaynes-Cummings variant with its counter-rotating coupling. Whole hierarchies of models follow, their symmetries exposed, including a shape-invariant chain of near-resonant systems. One solved model now unlocks its relatives.
arxiv-2504-20043:
John Ellis and co-authors test dark matter ideas against new telescope data in this 2025 paper. The James Webb Space Telescope sees galaxies from the first ages of the universe. The team compares how fast stars formed back then under several dark matter models. They use Webb data plus older Hubble records.

The data hint that the first stars were heavier than today's mix. They also suggest that blasts from early stars and black holes slowed star birth less at the earliest times. Fuzzy and warm dark matter still fit, but only above set particle weights. Ideas that add extra small-scale clumping gained no support. Standard cold dark matter remains a good match overall.
arxiv-2504-20343:
Writing a sound report from a medical scan is slow, skilled work, and models that draft it stumble on fine detail. Amaan Izhar, Nurul Japar, Norisma Idris, and Ting Dang built MicarVLMoE in 2025 to do better. Their model pairs a sight encoder that reads body detail at many scales with a bridge that lines sight up with words. A bank of expert word units then takes turns by need, steered by gates.

Where past work stuck to chest X-rays, this one spans CT scans, eye films, MRI, and gross flesh photos. On four known data sets it topped past scores for report quality. Peel-away tests showed each part of the build earns its keep. The team also say the model's inner steps read more clearly than rivals', a plus in the clinic.
arxiv-2504-20643:
Moran Mizrahi and co-authors tackle AI creativity in a 2025 paper. Large language models write fluently, yet their ideas often feel samey and shallow. The team argues that real creative leaps come from reshaping the structure of an idea, not from swapping surface words.

Their system turns ideas into structured forms, mixes those forms in planned ways, and then turns the result back into plain language. They tested the idea in cooking, with a system called DishCOVER that invents recipes. Expert judges found the dishes mostly coherent and workable, and far more novel and varied than those from GPT-4o. The authors hope the same structured mixing can lift creativity in other fields as well.
arxiv-2504-20743:
Topological phases are states of matter armored by global structure, and letting a system leak energy, non-Hermiticity, enriches their zoo. Daichi Nakamura and co-authors classify in 2025 such phases when a nonsymmorphic symmetry joins in, a crystal symmetry that pairs a flip or rotation with a fractional slide. That combination had sat largely unexplored.

Their census finds phases counted by Z2 and Z4 labels with no analogue in either the closed-system crystal families or the open systems lacking this symmetry. The boundary states carry unusual complex-valued energy curves, signatures an experiment could hunt in photonic or acoustic setups.
arxiv-2504-20843:
Mishra and five co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a model of atomic nucleus mass rooted in chiral effective field theory, a step-by-step theory of the strong force. The theory gives a force law with eleven dials, called low-energy constants, to fit. Binding energies test such laws hard, since each nucleus binds its parts by a set total.

The team use a Hartree-Fock method to compute binding energies from the law. Fast emulator models let them tune the eleven constants to the energies of eighteen even-even nuclei. They then test the tuned model on 107 even-even nuclei with mass numbers from 16 to 56. The overall miss runs at 3.5 MeV per nucleus on the scale used. The authors offer the model as a base for mass predictions beyond the test set.
arxiv-2504-20943:
Rudnei Ramos and Gabriel Rodrigues re-examine a minimal model of warm inflation, in a two thousand twenty-five cosmology paper. Warm inflation keeps the early universe warm during its rapid expansion, unlike the standard cold picture. The model studied couples an axion-like inflaton to Standard Model gluons, adding no other new fields.

The original analysis used several approximations. Ramos and Rodrigues redo the calculations with WI2easy, a precision tool for warm inflation dynamics. They scan the full parameter range compatible with observations. The earlier conclusions mostly hold. One important change appears in the weak and strong dissipation regimes, where the precise treatment shifts the results significantly. The paper clarifies how much trust the minimal model deserves.
arxiv-2504-21643:
Luca Marzari, Francesco Trotti, Enrico Marchesini, and Alessandro Farinelli make learning-based robot navigation provably safer with automatically designed barrier functions, in a paper from 2025. Robots in messy real settings cannot rely on a learned policy never straying into danger. A verified safety layer can overrule bad moves.

Their method samples the state space to find unsafe regions, then builds a barrier function that keeps the robot out of them. The safety layer wraps any policy, correcting actions only when needed. Tests ran in simulation and on a real robot, including a fast-changing water monitoring task. Unsafe actions were corrected while navigation stayed efficient.
arxiv-2505-00443:
Language models answer better when they can look things up, but a central library of knowledge raises privacy alarms. Chenhao Xu and co-authors distribute the library instead. Their DRAG framework spreads retrieval across a peer-to-peer network of devices. No single server holds the data, so owners keep control. A topic-aware random walk guides each query: the model extracts the query's topic, and the walk steers toward peers likely to know it.

Across three datasets and several models, the distributed system nearly matched central retrieval quality. It used half as many messages as naive flooding of the network. The design fits places like smart healthcare, where patient data cannot be pooled but knowledge still needs to travel. Privacy and competence, the work argues, can coexist.
arxiv-2505-00943:
Martin Bridson proves fixed point theorems for groups acting on curved spaces known as CAT(0) spaces. Such spaces generalize flat and saddle shaped geometry, and a fixed point is a spot the whole group leaves unmoved. Finding one shows the action is tame in a strong sense.

Bridson builds fixed points step by step, showing larger and larger subgroups each fix some set. Special patterns in the subgroup lattice, paired with intersection theorems of Helly type, force those sets to overlap. The method yields lower bounds on the smallest space dimension in which groups of geometric interest can act without any fixed point. For automorphism groups of free groups, he pins a concrete bound.
arxiv-2505-01143: Rafael López gathers open problems on compact constant mean curvature surfaces with boundary in a 2025 paper. Such surfaces bend by the same mean amount at each point and stop at a rim. The asks are short to state yet stand unsolved. Past work's state gets a sweep for each ask. The note is brief, a map of live ends in surface theory for geometers.
arxiv-2505-01343:
Editing a fact inside a multimodal AI model is tricky: change too little and the fact stays wrong, change too much and unrelated knowledge breaks. Dongliang Guo and co-authors name that tension the generality-locality trade-off. Different facts deserve different blast radii, yet older editors treat them all alike.

Their method, BalancEdit, first probes each fact with positive and negative examples to map its true influence scope. The edit then lands in a small, discrete codebook inside the model's latent space, leaving the base weights untouched. A new dataset, OKEDIT, grades editors on exactly this balance. Tests in 2025 show strong edits with minimal collateral damage.
arxiv-2505-01543:
Masoud Ataei analyzes market efficiency across time scales in a 2025 finance paper. His tool is a Financial Chaos Index built from eigenvalues of realized volatility. Granger causality and network analysis link that index to economic, policy, and news uncertainty measures over thirty four years of daily data.

At daily frequency, the semi strong form of market efficiency was rejected. Price moves responded predictably to lagged news uncertainty. At monthly frequency, that structure largely vanished, supporting efficiency at coarser scales. Fiscal and monetary policy uncertainty sat at the core of the volatility network, with other indices acting as bridges in crises.
arxiv-2505-01843:
Jay Armas and Giorgos Batzios derive a famous quantum anomaly from the spin of black branes, using holography as the bridge. Spin hydrodynamics describes fluids whose particles carry rotation. Spinning black branes in higher dimensions ripple with exactly such a fluid on their surface. Their 2025 paper follows those ripples in a supersymmetric gauge theory's strong-coupling regime.

Viewed from ten dimensions, the spinning fluid's gravitational anomaly becomes, in the four-dimensional mirror, the R-current chiral anomaly. The match gives the anomaly a geometric home. The authors also sort their spin hydrodynamics against the versions built for heavy-ion collisions. Theoretical physicists get a duality that explains an anomaly instead of merely asserting it.
arxiv-2505-02043:
Xinzhu Ma and seven colleagues wrote a 2025 computer vision paper on rebuilding CAD models from point clouds. A point cloud is a spray of dots that traces an object's surface. Turning that spray back into an editable design file is a core task in engineering.

Common methods hide the design inside a smooth field, which blurs sharp edges and makes edits hard. Their system, Point2Primitive, predicts the design's basic shapes directly. A transformer decoder treats the shape set as one prediction task. Each primitive stays exact and parametric, ready for a designer to tweak. Tests judge how close the rebuilt models come to the originals.
arxiv-2505-02543:
Dimitris Kallis, Moysis Symeonides, and Marios Dikaiakos benchmarked the energy appetite of an industrial internet-of-things system in a 2025 paper. Factories are filling with connected devices, robotic arms, conveyors, smart cameras, that automate making. Their energy bills are becoming a real operating cost that physics-based models predict poorly. The authors put forth a benchmarking methodology for measuring and analyzing device and application power demands. Then show it on a teaching-scale cyber-real system: a robotic arm, a conveyor belt, a smart camera, and a work out node.

Micro-benchmarks and an end-to-end application generate a rich data set of speed and power readings. Used to train machine learning models that predict energy use from application and system traits. Data-driven energy models, the authors argue, are the useful path to greener industrial automation.
arxiv-2505-02643:
De Beck and three co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on the dusty shroud of NML Cygni, an extreme red supergiant star. Such stars are the parents of common supernovae, and the density and shape of what they shed shapes the blast. Using a radio interferometer, the team weighed and mapped the star's gas and dust.

Two strong dust components reach far beyond the zone seen in visible light, totaling a few thousandths of a sun's mass in dust alone. Gas readings imply a heavy wind, shedding several ten-thousandths of a sun each year. The outflow is lumpy and one-sided, not a neat shell, and fast gas near the star hints at unseen action. The authors suggest a hidden companion star may be sculpting the flow, a clue for how these giants die.
arxiv-2505-02743:
Real data carry two kinds of doubt: noise in the data itself, and doubt about the model. Jiaxiang Yi and Miguel Bessa propose training two networks together so each handles one kind. A variance network learns the data noise, while a Bayesian network tracks model doubt. Earlier setups forced one network to do both jobs, with awkward fixes.

Trained as partners, the pair pulls the two doubts apart cleanly. Their method also sharpens the main prediction itself. The authors test it on many data sets, including a time-based one they built where the true noise is known. Their 2025 paper reports the approach is simple to add to many model types and scales well.
arxiv-2505-03043:
Kais Ammari and co-authors study a transmission problem in elasticity with a kind of damping in a 2025 paper, with a full numerical study. The work asks how fast the system energy fades over time.

The authors show the system fades at a polynomial rate when the start data are smooth enough. They also prove that rate cannot be improved, so it is sharp. Computer runs back the theory and show the sharpness in practice. Such transmission problems model waves crossing between materials with loss at the join. Readers get both a proof of best decay and clear numerical proof that the bound is real.
arxiv-2505-03443:
Valerio Bellandi presents a 2025 paper on a spread-out document store built for Italy's Ministry of Justice. Central systems are easy to manage but fail at one point; spread systems scale and survive failures but are harder to run. The ministry's design places edge stores across sites, each studying the text and data it holds. The design supports search by meaning rather than keywords alone.

Bellandi reviews the trade-offs that guided the choice and describes how the edge design lifts search capability. Legal archives are huge, sensitive, and scattered across offices, a natural fit for the approach. The paper is a single-author account of the architecture and its rationale. It aims to guide similar public sector builds.
arxiv-2505-03843:
Restaking lets the same staked funds secure several blockchain services at once, but the security can fragment. Abhimanyu Nag, Dhruv Bodani, and Abhishek Kumar study services that draw security from multiple shared security providers at once. Splitting stake across providers creates a weakest link problem: an attacker can attack the service through whichever provider is cheapest to corrupt.

The authors compare two designs with game theory and optimization. In the fragmented design, each provider guards its own slice, and flexibility comes at the cost of inheriting the cheapest attack. In the unified design, one validator set and pooled punishment rules protect the whole stake, giving tighter guarantees. They derive cost conditions and market balance points for both, and sketch future work on moving stake between providers without breaking incentives.
arxiv-2505-04343:
Matthew Roche and co-authors study a 2025 question in planet science: how much air a young planet loses when it is struck by another large body. Such giant impacts end the main phase of planet growth. They can strip away gases that shape what a planet is made of. Yet the loss depends strongly on how the impact happens.

Using a suite of 3D computer models, the team shows that loss is driven in two ways. Plumes of thrown out material act near the impact site. The shock also breaks out on the far side of the planet. They build a scaling rule that predicts loss closely across a wide range of planet sizes and impact setups. Applied to models of solar system growth, the rule suggests that many impacts together can remove a large share of a planet's early air.
arxiv-2505-04543:
Quentin Chuet, Tianjiao Dai, Qiancheng Ouyang, and François Pirot wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a strict form of graph coloring. In a proper coloring, neighbors never share a color. The conflict-free twist adds a demand: near each vertex, at least a set number of colors must appear exactly once among its neighbors.

The authors bound how many colors such a coloring needs, in terms of the graph's maximum degree. For any fixed demand level h, they show that h times the degree, plus a small log term, always suffices. That result widens earlier work and sharpens a recent bound for the simplest case. When the minimum degree is also large, the bound drops further, close to the degree itself. The authors conjecture the true ceiling is h times the degree plus one.
arxiv-2505-04643:
Hannes Waldetoft, Jakob Torgander, and Mans Magnusson estimate hate crimes from text data in 2025. Counting such crimes needs labels for police reports, but hand labeling is slow and costly. Most reports are negative, which makes the counting task highly imbalanced.

Their method feeds a neural network's predictions into classic survey estimators as an aid variable. Three estimators are used to count yearly hate crimes and gauge police under-reporting in Sweden. With labeled training data in hand, the method gave efficient estimates with far less hand work. The paper shows the steps on real Swedish police reports.
arxiv-2505-04843:
Sebastián Castro and co-authors send language models into a simulated cyber battlefield as defenders. Fast incident response decides whether an intrusion spreads, and autonomous defenders promise speed. Reinforcement learning agents can defend but train slowly and explain themselves poorly.

The team plugged language model agents into CybORG's multi-agent CAGE 4 arena, the first such test, with a new protocol letting defenders message each other. Mixed teams of language and learning agents revealed complementary strengths and blind spots on both sides. The authors map where each style shines, aiming at future squads that pair explainable judgment with drilled reflexes for real security work.
arxiv-2505-05143:
Five researchers tackle a puzzle in the lottery ticket hypothesis, the idea that a big neural network hides a small subnetwork that can train just as well. Finding that winning subnetwork is costly, and its pattern of kept weights normally fails when training restarts from a fresh random start. The authors suspect the problem is misalignment: networks trained from different starts land in matching solutions, but with their internal units shuffled.

Their fix is to shuffle the winning pattern of kept weights so it lines up with the new starting point before training begins. Across image datasets and three network designs, this alignment greatly improved how well the sparse network learned from a random start, beating the unshuffled pattern by a clear margin. The work supports the view that network solutions match up to a shuffling of units.
arxiv-2505-05343:
Sooyoung Park, Arda Senocak, and Joon Son Chung teach a vision-language model to find where sounds come from, in a 2025 paper. Their base model, CLIP, was trained to match images with text. The team extends it to audio without giving it any text labels.

Sound clips are first turned into tokens the model's text side can accept, forming audio-based embeddings. These guide a mask that outlines the sounding object in the picture. Image features inside the mask are then pulled toward the audio embedding during training. A second variant learns from a larger model's scene descriptions. Across five tasks the method beat prior leaders and generalized well to new settings. It promises cheaper sound-aware video tools that need no hand labels.
arxiv-2505-05843:
Linda Scheu-Hachtel and Jasmin Zalonis strengthen, in a 2025 paper, a cryptographic tool for learning from private data. Functional encryption lets an analyst compute one approved function of encrypted data and nothing more. A noisy variant also scrambles the answer just enough to guarantee differential privacy. The authors extend the idea to many data holders whose number can change over time, with labels controlling who may run which analysis.

Their concrete scheme, DyNo, covers everything earlier noisy schemes could do. It runs leaner in space and time, and it holds up even when some clients are corrupted, a stronger promise than before. To show the point, they build a privacy-preserving logistic regression protocol on top of it. The paper targets settings like hospitals pooling data, where the math must protect patients while the analysis still gets done.
arxiv-2505-05943:
Maan Alhazmi and Abdulrahman Altahhan add a three way attention block to convolutional networks that read facial expressions, in this 2025 paper. Convolutional designs have retaken ground in image classification, and expression reading is a demanding test. Their block fuses triplet attention, which weighs channels and space jointly, with squeeze and excitation, which reweights channels by importance.

Four variants of the combined block were inserted into three standard backbones. Gains appeared across the board, strongest in the modern ConvNeXt design. Testing spanned four data sets, from small object photos to large expression collections. On the popular FER2013 benchmark, the best model set a record accuracy of about seventy-eight percent. The authors argue the block is a portable upgrade for vision models generally.
arxiv-2505-06443:
Tehreem Zahra, Mubasher Jamil, and Mustapha Azreg-Aïnou calculate how a gyroscope would wobble near a rotating naked singularity, and use real X-ray timing data to constrain the idea, in a 2025 paper. Naked singularities, collapse endpoints without an event horizon, would expose extreme gravity to view. A test gyroscope's spin precession is one fingerprint.

In weak fields their formulas reduce to the familiar black hole answers. But for an equatorial observer, precession can separate a rotating naked singularity from its Kerr cousins. The team ran simulations against quasi-periodic oscillation data from five real sources. For one famous system, the spin estimate disagreed with continuum-fitting values; for two others it clashed with spectral results. The authors present the mismatches as useful tension: precession offers an independent yardstick for compact objects, and it does not always agree with the others.
arxiv-2505-06743:
Marius Baden and co-authors (2025) build a trajectory predictor for self-driving cars that a human can cross-examine. Neural predictors guess where cars, cyclists, and pedestrians will move, but can break physics or read as nonsense. Earlier fixes added prior knowledge, a social force model for how agents interact, or motion models for realism, yet each suited one road-user type. The authors' system, TPK, adds both kinds of priors for all classes.

Class-specific interaction layers let the model treat a truck differently from a child. A rule-based social force model, DG-SFM, makes interaction terms readable rather than buried in weights. Motion constraints keep predicted paths within what wheels and legs can do. The aim is trust: an engineer, or a regulator, can inspect why the car expects a cyclist to swerve, and reject predictions that could never happen.
arxiv-2505-08143:
Jiawei Zhou and co-authors compare how language models and human experts explain COVID-19 health facts, in a 2025 case study. Fact-checking health claims calls for clear words that build trust. The team gathered many false health claims with explanations from trusted checking groups. They then generated model-written versions of the same explanations.

Styles were scored on wording, persuasion tactics, and fit with reader values. Model articles scored lower on persuasion, certainty, and moral framing. Yet blinded readers still preferred the model versions most of the time. They praised the clarity and completeness of the machine-written pieces. The split result raises sharp questions for health communicators about style versus trust.
arxiv-2505-08443:
Carles Falcó, Ruth Baker, and José Carrillo propose in 2025 a local equation model for clustering behavior that is usually described with nonlocal equations. Swarms, cells, and crowds often gather through attraction and repulsion, and the standard models let each point feel distant points directly.

Using cell sorting by differential stickiness as their test case, the authors build a fourth-order local system akin to thin-film equations. In it, sorting emerges from relative surface tension between cell types, a physical picture the nonlocal models blur. Their approach ties a biological pattern to a mechanism that experiments can probe directly.
arxiv-2505-08543:
Francesco De Cosmo and Luca Sgheri present a 2025 study of how limb-scanning instruments locate the points their sight lines graze. Such instruments read the atmosphere's edge, and air bending curves their rays, so the lowest point of each ray, the tangent point, must be computed, not assumed. The authors relate instrument tilt angles, air properties, and tangent point positions for a configuration modeled on the CAIRT instrument.

They pull weather data from reanalysis databases and solve the Eikonal equation numerically to trace the rays. Earth's ellipticity and real air conditions both enter the calibration. The results are compared with an earlier study for the MIPAS instrument, and key differences are drawn out. The work serves designers of atmospheric sounders who need pointing they can trust.
arxiv-2505-08743:
Geoffrey Messier, Sam Elliott, and Dallas Seitz show, in a 2025 paper, how to link records about the same person across a city's housing and homelessness services without exposing private data. One person may touch many agencies, and scattered records hide how the system actually serves them.

The team linked more than 235,000 records using privacy-preserving matching, then compared several matching and grouping methods. Scores came both from standard accuracy checks and from system measures, such as shelter stays and time in the system. Method gaps looked bigger under the system measures. The work proves such linkage is practical for planning better care.
arxiv-2505-08843:
Marco Corrias and a team of co-authors present a way to clean up microscope images, in two thousand twenty-five. Images from microscopes carry noise and other unwanted signals. Those flaws can hide the fine features that scientists need to see.

The workflow rests on a method that splits an image into parts and removes the unwanted ones. The team tested three forms of the method on images from three kinds of microscope. One form proved the most flexible, while another was best for plain noise removal. Their code is shared as part of a public tool, for use during or after image capture.
arxiv-2505-08943:
Philip Ernst and Oleksii Mostovyi studied the value of partial information in pricing in two thousand twenty-five. They look at a pricing rule for income streams and claims, and ask how it changes when an investor gains insider-type knowledge. Their model allows the risky asset to jump suddenly.

They derive the state price density for three kinds of agents. One knows nothing about the jumps, one knows exactly when each jump will occur, and one has partial knowledge of jump sizes. For each, they characterize the pricing rule and give a formula for it. That lets them quantify how much partial information is worth, and how that worth differs across income streams and claims.
arxiv-2505-09243:
Lan Zhang and co-authors weigh and shape the Milky Way's dark matter halo in a 2025 paper. Their tracers are giant stars from Chinese and American sky surveys, plus blue horizontal branch stars, all with fresh motion data from the Gaia mission. Motions across the galaxy's radius and height first mapped how the velocity ellipsoid tilts.

Jeans modeling then turned those motions into a dark matter profile, testing halo shapes that flatten by different rules. Separate fits to each star family agreed within their error bars. The best story lets the flattening vary with distance: the halo squashes inward near the center and rounds out farther away. In that model the halo's edge sits near one hundred ninety kiloparsecs, and the mass inside sixty kiloparsecs is pinned to a tight range.
arxiv-2505-09443:
Kiprian Berbatov and Andrey Jivkov present a 2025 paper on formulating transport laws directly on meshes built from cells. Many materials mix parts of different dimensions: membranes, fibers, and bulk regions in one structure. Smooth math struggles with such hybrids. A discrete calculus that lives on the mesh itself can treat them natively.

The authors extend an existing combinatorial form theory from strict balance laws to full transport formulations. Their framework defines discrete versions of the core operators and needs no smooth embedding or special dual mesh. A mixed version of the formulation yields a neatly blocked matrix, which allows fast local elimination during solving. Comparisons with a rival discrete calculus highlight the differences.
arxiv-2505-09543:
Ram and six colleagues run a learned energy model inside dynamical density theory with no retraining in twenty twenty-five. The theory tracks how particle crowds flow using a free energy rule. Exact rules are out of reach for most real systems. A neural rule learned from still bulk data by pair matching was on hand.

Moved into the moving version, it matched costly particle simulations well. Tests used a three dimensional fluid under tricky outer fields. A flow based extension handled a gas uptake setup drawn from real studies. The route promises cheap, true models of out of balance crowds.
arxiv-2505-10043:
Yifan Wu and co-authors help users find the right chart by typing a plain question, in a paper from 2025. Past test sets were too clean to mimic real business use, where many charts look much alike.

Their new bench holds near twenty two thousand charts and a few hundred real queries, set up as target versus close decoy tasks. Old tools that lean on looks alone scored poorly. The team auto wrote layered notes on each chart, from shape to use, and trained a finder on them. Scores rose by wide margins on both exact and fuzzy queries.
arxiv-2505-10343:
Abril Sahade, Judith Karpen, and Spiro Antiochos report a new kind of solar eruption in twenty twenty-five. Coronal mass ejections and coronal jets are well-studied eruption forms with shared physics. Partial eruptions were known to produce jets. These three events did something different.

The eruptions segmented after they began, and went on to produce coronal mass ejections. Multiwavelength data from three solar observatories let the team rebuild the events in three dimensions. Magnetic field extrapolations showed the filaments lay under pseudostreamer structures. Splitting followed interaction between the filament's flux and external open field at null points. The breakout mechanism seemed to halt the system and split it. Readers meet a hybrid eruption that rewrites what partial eruptions can do.
arxiv-2505-10443:
Pedro Orvalho and Marta Kwiatkowska wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It asks if language models truly reason about code, or guess, by mutating programs in ways that keep their sense but change their dress.

Five such swaps are used: renaming, flipping comparisons, swapping branches, trading loop kinds, and unrolling loops. Nine models, open and closed, are graded on two benchmarks, with experts checking if right calls rest on sound thought. The top closed models lead, but the study finds right calls built on flawed thought in a wide share of cases. Calls flip often under the swaps, with drops that run deep.
arxiv-2505-10943:
Kirill Polovnikov and Mehran Kardar wrote this 2025 physics paper on how parts of a polymer chain wobble over time. A polymer's segments move both by their own internal motion and by the drift of the whole chain's center of mass. The authors show how that shared drift shapes the wobble of each segment.

Because internal forces cancel out, and outside noise is spread evenly, the center of mass tends to spread at a rate that falls as one over the segment length. That law holds no matter the chain's fractal shape, its spring-like traits, or its activity. The drift adds set corrections to measures of segment motion. The team checks the idea with theory, with simulations, and with imaging data on chromatin, the DNA material inside cells. In chromatin, the motion exponent they extract reveals hidden constraints on its packing.
arxiv-2505-11143:
William Denault introduces Nash, a regression method that learns how hard to shrink each predictor from side information about that predictor. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Sparse regression picks a few strong signals from many candidates. Flat penalties treat all candidates alike, which wastes structure like grouping or graph links.

Nash feeds each covariate's side information into a neural network that sets its personal penalty. No cross-validation is needed to tune the shrinkage. A split variational Bayes scheme separates prior learning from inference. That split cuts the heavy step to one batched pass, speeding things up hugely. Tests on real data beat existing methods on accuracy and flexibility. Biomedical data, with its many data types, are a natural home.
arxiv-2505-11243:
Elliot Epstein, Apaar Sadhwani, and Kay Giesecke propose a model for forecasting many related time series at once in a 2025 paper. Loans, stocks, and customers each follow their own history, yet shared forces move them together. Standard sequence models read one series at a time and need hand-built summaries to sense the group.

Their Set-Sequence model adds a set module that summarizes the whole group at each time step. A sequence module then forecasts each unit using its own features plus that summary. The design handles uneven series and changing group sizes, and scales in a straight line with group size. It beat strong baselines on stock portfolios and loan risk tasks.
arxiv-2505-11343:
Rajeeva Laxman Karandikar, Bhamidi Visweswara Rao, and Mathukumalli Vidyasagar offer a new proof route for two workhorse learning algorithms in a 2025 paper. Stochastic approximation and stochastic gradient descent both learn from noisy data step by step. Classic proofs lean on differential equations or on martingale theory. Both routes tie the learner's behavior to the noise in restrictive ways.

Their route rests on a generalized strong law of large numbers, which extends the classic law. That split lets the traits of the target function and the traits of the noise be handled apart. The allowed noise is wider than in either classic route: it need not even have a finite average under the right conditions. They also adapt the proof to a gradient free version that uses only function values. The conditions they reach are the weakest yet, they argue.
arxiv-2505-11443:
Manish Kumar and eight colleagues present a 2025 battery materials study comparing twin crystals that differ by a single element. The pair, VNb9O25 and VTa9O25, share a Wadsley-Roth structure whose channels should shuttle lithium quickly. Niobium and tantalum are chemical siblings with nearly identical size, so the comparison isolates electronic effects from geometric ones.

The niobium version wins on speed: lithium diffuses about ten times faster in experiments, and simulations agree within a factor of six, tracing the gap to lower hopping barriers. Charge analysis shows lithium carries more charge among niobium's more electronegative neighbors, stabilizing its transit. The tantalum twin also needs more charge before turning metallic. The authors say cation choice is a real design dial for fast-charging electrodes.
arxiv-2505-11643:
Xiang Fu, a solo author, tests whether teaching a small language model in easy-to-hard steps can coax out reasoning, in a 2025 paper. The model is a modest GPT-2 with about one hundred twenty-four million parameters, named Cognivolve for the run. Its syllabus climbs four rungs, from matching words up to multi-step symbolic inference. No task-specific tuning follows.

The staged model hit target scores in half the training steps of a one-phase rival. More of its attention heads joined in on reasoning, and those heads sat deeper in the network. Shuffling the order or resetting the trainer killed the gains, which pins them on the ordering itself. One catch stands out: final answer accuracy still trailed a standard run by about thirty percent. Fu lists fixes to try next.
arxiv-2505-11743:
Cloud systems fail in tangled ways, and older alarms struggle to keep up with their scale and speed. Cheng Ji and Huaiying Luo propose in 2025 a framework that uses large language models to spot faults and trigger self-repair. The model reads system logs, error reports, and live data streams with an eye for meaning, not just patterns.

The design layers two kinds of learning: supervised methods sort known faults, while unsupervised methods flag odd behavior. Together they let the system predict some failures before they happen and start healing steps on its own. In tests, the authors report better detection accuracy, less downtime, and faster recovery than traditional tools. They present the approach as a step toward cloud platforms that mind themselves.
arxiv-2505-12143:
Arun Kumar and Paul Schrater ask where stable knowledge sits in a learning system. A model must hold some parts fixed as cases change. But it must not lose the facts that a task still needs. They argue that the fixed parts should be set at the level of relations. At that level, sense-making works through links between things.

The authors build groups by closing paths through an abstract space of relations. These groups form the core where knowledge is stored and where learning takes place. Links between groups then carry the shifts that a task calls for. To ground this view, they set out its math base. That base rests on a closed semiring, a structure from relational algebra.
arxiv-2505-12243:
Ilan Adler, Richard Karp, and Sheldon Ross sharpen classic bounds on the chance that at least some of a set of events will occur, in a 2025 paper. The old bounds come from sums that add and cut terms in turn. They date back to work in the eighteen hundreds by Boole.

The trio pin down the exact flaw in each old sum. From that, they give a plain proof of the best bounds of one form. They also add new bounds that use more of the known joint odds. The new bounds are often tighter than the old ones, while they stay simple to state and use.
arxiv-2505-12843:
Eight researchers in China correct length bias in reward models in a 2025 paper. Models trained on human preferences tend to reward longer answers regardless of quality, and training then hacks that flaw. Earlier fixes either skipped modeling the bias shape or assumed it grows in a straight line.

Their framework, FiMi-RM, works in three stages. A standard reward model trains first, bias included. A small fitting model then learns the true curved link between length and reward. That curve is folded back into the reward model, separating length from preference. The debiased model fed preference training and best of n selection with better length controlled win rates and a fairer score spread.
arxiv-2505-13043:
Hao-Ran Yang, Xiaohui Chen, and Chuan-Xian Ren improve gaze estimation across data sets in a 2025 paper. A model trained to guess where a person looks often fails on new cameras or settings. Past fixes hunt for features that stay the same across domains, which theory now shows is not enough.

Their view adds label shift: the mix of gaze angles itself changes between domains. A correction framework reweights the training data using a bell-shaped curve, sidestepping the trouble that gaze is continuous. A second measure keeps the learned link between features and labels steady. Across standard tasks and model types, the method generalized better than rivals.
arxiv-2505-13443:
Samuel Goldstein and co-authors explored wavy patterns in early space data in a 2025 study. Waves in a three-point pattern from the young cosmos can come from traits of the field that drove early growth, or from heavy fields at play then. These waves offer a rare view into how the cosmos began.

The team ran large computer worlds that start with these waves built in. They found that later growth of clumps in space washes the waves out on small scales, so the signal is mostly lost there by now. A classic math shortcut describes the loss well. Good news came too: a fix-up step can bring much of the wave back, which keeps the search for these clues alive.
arxiv-2505-13543:
Muyang Fan, Songyang Liu, Shuai Li and Weizi Li wrote a 2025 paper on traffic control in cities with mixed human and robot cars. Jams hurt both travel time and quality of life. Most past work used small networks or single crossings. The team studied a large, real network with many signals.

Their method lets each crossing act as its own agent that learns from local data. Signals and robot cars share control of the flow. Tests ran on a real network of more than a dozen crossings in Colorado Springs. The key question was whether control holds up when trip patterns shift over time. Wait time was the main score.
arxiv-2505-13643:
Rajib and co-authors present a method, published in 2025, for keeping shared AI models accurate as the world shifts after training. In federated learning, many clients train one model without pooling raw data. When the model meets new conditions at use time, its accuracy sags. Adapting at test time can fix that, but in federated settings it raises costs, privacy risks, and memory strain. The team's approach lets clients adapt together while keeping their data private.

Their design aims to stay light on computation and memory, so it can run on modest devices. Adaptation is continual: the model keeps adjusting as conditions drift, not just once. Collaboration means one client's adaptation can help the others. The authors frame the method for privacy-sensitive uses like health and finance. It addresses a real weakness of deployed federated systems, which otherwise freeze at their training day.
arxiv-2505-13843:
Yang Xiang and co-authors clean up noisy speech by treating its meaning and its sound as separate jobs. Most speech enhancement systems guess the clean signal directly from a noisy recording, which can blur what was said and hurts later uses such as text-to-speech. Their method works in stages on a factorized code: one layer holds the semantic content, what the words are, and another holds acoustic detail, how they sound.

A diffusion model then rebuilds the fine sound, guided by the recovered meaning. Because content is pinned down first, the system stays robust in messy sound scenes where direct methods degrade. Tests showed cleaner speech than leading baselines on quality measures. The recovered speech also fed speech synthesis better, a practical bonus the authors highlight. They present the hierarchy, meaning first, sound second, as the reason the method holds up when noise gets complicated.
arxiv-2505-14243:
Two parties who share a secret key by quantum means can, in the plain form, be fooled by rigged gear. Syed Arslan and three co-authors survey a stronger form in 2025 that trusts no gear at all. Its proof rests only on what the two ends observe: a breach of a classic bound on linked reads.

The survey walks the base ideas first, from Bell tests to what counts as secure. It then sorts the designs on offer, from schemes built on a named game to broader game frames, with their proofs. Lab builds of the method are weighed as well, from light sources to detectors. Finite-key reads, where the key is short, get their share. The open snags close the tour.
arxiv-2505-14943:
Ross Nordby introduces a way in 2025 to measure how close a language model sits to a target behavior. The method tunes soft prompts — learned input vectors rather than words — until the model shows the behavior. The effort needed to get there becomes a distance score. Nordby aims the tool at safety work, where testers hunt for hidden skills a model might conceal.

The framework is shown on language tasks, chess, and pathfinding. A generalized form helps build new task tests from the same idea. Because the score is a number, it can feed automated red-team suites. It may also give early warning as models grow stronger and harder to probe.
arxiv-2505-15043:
Ze Wang and co-authors present a real-time planner for small flying vehicles in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The planner helps a human operator steer a micro air vehicle through cluttered spaces. It must avoid obstacles without building a full map of the surroundings, and with limited onboard computing.

The method builds a histogram of where obstacles lie around the vehicle and plans a path from that summary. A manager switches planning modes based on obstacle positions. The team validated the system in simulations and indoor flights for a teleoperation task. They also compared it against other planners on a purpose-built simulation platform.
arxiv-2505-15543:
Nonparametric statistics must handle functions of wildly varying smoothness, ideally with one method that adapts on its own. The three authors study a class of heavy-tailed priors on basis coefficients, called oversmoothed heavy-tailed priors, and ask whether their posteriors contract at the right rates. They also examine horseshoe priors in this nonparametric frame for the first time and show they fit the same framework.

For Sobolev-smooth signals under squared error they derive contraction rates, plus a lower bound showing the prior's scaling form is necessary for full adaptation. For the wider Besov setting with general losses they get minimax rates that adapt to smoothness, including the sparse zone. An implementation and a simulation study round out the paper, which offers flexible priors with proven adaptive performance.
arxiv-2505-15643:
Lan V Truong, writing alone, studies how to find the best option among many noisy choices when several options tie for best. The 2025 paper uses the bandit model, where each choice gives random rewards. The goal is to name a best choice with set confidence while using as few trials as possible.

Past work often assumed the number of best options was unknown. Truong takes the case where that number is known ahead of time. A new lower bound shows the least trials any method needs, and it is tighter than older bounds. A revised stopping rule for a known method meets that bound in the long run. The result is the first proof of that kind for this setting, with clear guidance for trial design.
arxiv-2505-16043:
Decoy systems that lure attackers waste the attacker's time, but a defender with few decoys must guess where to plant them while several attackers probe at once. Dongyoung Park and Gaby Dagher model that contest in a 2025 paper as a leader-follower game under uncertainty. Each attacker is given its own prized targets, skills, and costs.

The defender updates its beliefs about each attacker from what alarm systems catch, then moves the decoys to match. In tests the defense shut down attack success within a few rounds. It also stayed fast on networks of hundreds of nodes and well over a thousand links. The frame suits real networks where the defender cannot watch everything and must bet smart with scarce traps.
arxiv-2505-16243:
James Rossmanith and Christine Vaughan present a new way to split the equations that describe a plasma, in a 2025 paper. The Vlasov equations track how charged particles spread through space and velocity when collisions are rare. A classic solver splits the space and velocity parts and handles each in turn, but that split caps the accuracy of key totals like mass and energy.

Their method first replaces the particle spread in each velocity band with a small local fluid model. The split then separates the coupling between bands from the motion inside each band. The local models alone give high accuracy for the global totals, while the coupling terms keep the full distribution consistent. Tests on standard plasma problems confirm the scheme behaves as promised.
arxiv-2505-16343:
Neural field equations model how activity spreads across the cortex, the brain's outer layer. Daniele Avitabile and co-authors study these equations in this 2025 paper when the inputs are not fixed but random. Chance enters the wiring, the firing rules, the incoming signals, and the starting state.

They pin down conditions on the randomness that guarantee a single, well-defined solution, and they link how smooth the solution is to how smooth the inputs are. The results cover both linear and curved versions of the field. The team also treats the grid-based versions used in computing, laying groundwork for methods that track uncertainty in brain simulations.
arxiv-2505-16443:
Daniele Avitabile and three co-authors present 2025 work on math models of how brain tissue responds as a connected field. These models contain random inputs, such as the strength of links between cells and the signal that starts the activity. The team builds computer schemes that estimate the range of likely outcomes instead of a single answer.

Their method pairs a standard spatial grid with a sampling scheme for the random inputs. They prove error bounds for the schemes and give conditions under which the math stays well behaved. Tests on both simple and nonlinear cases matched the rates they predicted, which supports using the schemes for careful forecasts under uncertainty.
arxiv-2505-16543:
Robb Calder and co-authors test whether ozone on Venus could be a false sign of life on Venus-like worlds, in work from twenty twenty-five. On Earth ozone tracks oxygen made by photosynthesis, so it tempts as a life sign. Venus has an ozone layer despite hosting no known life. A photochemical model of the Venus air probes that layer's origin. Day-side oxygen atoms drifting to the night side fall short in the model.

That drift cannot make enough night ozone without excess oxygen gas. Tweaks to lower air chemistry, heat structure, or starlight also fail. An unknown chemical pathway must therefore build the Venus ozone. Rates for that pathway that match the seen ozone are estimated. The same puzzle extends to Venus-like exoplanets in general. Until the pathway is known, ozone stays a shaky life sign there.
arxiv-2505-16743:
Florentin Beck, William Rudman, and Carsten Eickhoff prune language models row by row to reach extreme sparsity without wrecking quality. Pruning removes weights so big models fit smaller hardware, but most methods cut every layer by the same share, which wastes some rows and starves others. Their 2025 method, TRIM, sets a different cut rate for each row of each layer. An iterative loop adjusts the rates, guided by quality scores, putting sparsity where the model tolerates it.

High sparsity is where uniform methods collapse, so the gains matter most there. The approach treats pruning as budgeting: spend cuts where they cost least. The authors frame rows, the output dimensions, as the right unit of choice. Their results target deployment on modest machines. Smarter allocation beats bigger hammers, is the paper's lesson.
arxiv-2505-16843:
Kalle Koskinen and Christof Külske study a classic model of magnetism under disorder in this two thousand twenty-five mathematical physics paper. They examine spherical ferromagnets in several dimensions when random magnetic fields act on the spins. Two versions are compared: one where the random fields grow with volume, and one where they do not. The analysis uses metastate frameworks developed by Aizenman and Wehr and by Newman and Stein.

The authors show that the metastates rest on a continuum of random product states, whose weights they describe. For the volume-scaled model, the overlap distribution shows spin-glass traits, including replica symmetry breaking and non-self-averaging behavior. Their proofs rest on concentration estimates, finite-volume Gibbs measure analysis, and the asymptotics of random walks and their spherical projections.
arxiv-2505-17243:
Yakov Berchenko-Kogan and Evan Gawlik construct finite element spaces in a 2025 paper for a broad family of tensor fields. The fields, called double forms, alternate in two sets of inputs and underlie equations in elasticity and geometry. Computer methods need polynomial pieces that fit these fields' symmetry and joining rules.

The pair build spaces for nearly every natural subspace of double forms, skipping one that admits no constant pieces. Their construction recovers several known element families for symmetric matrices as special cases. It also yields new spaces, including one for tensors with the symmetries of the Riemann curvature tensor. The work unifies scattered constructions under one scheme.
arxiv-2505-17443:
Elfarouk Harb, Yousef Yassin, and Chandra Chekuri published a mathematics and computing paper in 2025 on optimizing the average value of set functions. The problems cover minimizing or maximizing a ratio over non-empty subsets, a frame that includes classic tasks like densest subgraph. The team introduces two broad forms that allow negative and non-monotone functions. They show several named problems are equivalent under fast reductions.

Through one shared lens, two known solvers act as universal tools for all these problems. Tests across hundreds of experiments and seven problem types back the claim. General convex and flow methods beat task-specific baselines, which the authors call a surprise worth noting.
arxiv-2505-17543:
Kaixing Yang and co-authors generate genre-faithful 3D dance from music in this 2025 paper. Older systems treated genre as a minor tag rather than the core driver. That weak use broke music-motion sync and let style drift mid-dance, above all at tricky rhythm changes.

Their system, MEGADance, splits the job in two. First, dance motion is encoded into compact tokens under body physics limits. Then a mixture-of-experts model with a hybrid backbone maps music into those tokens with genre in charge. On two dance benchmarks it topped prior methods in both quality scores and look. Code is public.
arxiv-2505-17643:
Ketabi and Ramachandram presented this paper in twenty twenty-five on joining two kinds of patient data. Hospitals store structured records, such as lab values and codes, plus free-text notes written at discharge. Models that use records alone can miss the context that notes carry. That gap hurts tasks like predicting whether a patient will return to hospital soon.

The authors train a model that pulls matched record-and-note pairs close together and pushes unmatched pairs apart. The record encoder, once trained this way, feeds standard prediction tasks. For predicting return visits within thirty days, it beat a strong standard model by a clear margin. The work shows that clinical notes can teach record-based tools useful context.
arxiv-2505-18343:
Yash Kumar Atri, Ahmed Alaa, and Tom Hartvigsen present a way to update language models without erasing old knowledge, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Models often hold stale or false facts, yet past edit methods overfit or cause forgetting. Their frame stores facts in a graph set in curved space.

Curved space keeps parent and child facts apart, so an edit to one does not spill onto the other. Updates move through the graph in a shape-safe way. Guards mask key settings and reset parts of the graph net on a cycle. Tests on three data sets showed steadier, more exact edits.
arxiv-2505-18443:
Serkan Hosten recalls in 2025 the early years of toric ideals, a now-common tool in algebra. The term entered the field around 1990 through Bernd Sturmfels, the author notes, and the first decade brimmed with new results. Uses spread fast, and Sturmfels promoted the ideas through his own work and that of his students and partners.

Hosten calls the piece a personal and subjective recalling, not a formal history. Its center is the role Sturmfels played in that first decade, when the ideals and their special bases were taking shape. First-person records like this preserve how a field felt while it formed: the bets, the people, and the pace. Later readers get the math from textbooks; they get the story only from witnesses.
arxiv-2505-18643:
Steven Ndung'u and co-authors present a light-weight way to spot odd radio galaxies, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Radio surveys pour out vast data, and labeled odd cases are rare. Their method reads the shapes of radio sources with tunable filters that pick out set patterns.

An outlier tool then flags sources whose shapes stray from the normal run. No odd examples are needed during training, which solves a key snag. On a benchmark set the method scored above a heavy deep-learning system. The team sees promise for next-generation telescopes, where speed and open discovery matter most.
arxiv-2505-18743:
Luca Arpaia and co-authors present a solver for shallow water flow in this 2025 paper. The shallow water equations model coastal seas, floods, and tides. Real seabed shapes are rough, which breaks methods that assume smooth ground.

Their discontinuous finite element method uses high-resolution seabed data with no smoothness demands. Proofs show the method keeps mass, stays well-balanced, and holds water depth positive under mild step limits. It also carries passive tracers in a consistent way. Adaptive meshes refine where the flow needs detail. Tests on ideal and real coastal domains show the method handles rough beds and wet-dry fronts well.
arxiv-2505-19343:
Chun-Sheng Hsueh studies the shapes of spaces through two linked toolkits in this 2025 math paper. One toolkit, open books, describes a space as pages sweeping around a spine, like leaves around a binding. The other, handle decompositions, builds a space by attaching blocks one by one.

Hsueh builds handle layouts that encode a given open book layout. He then shows how sliding one handle past another reveals a fresh open book on the same space. These slides recover known ways of stabilizing open books by adding twists. As a payoff, any open book with trivial twisting can be stabilized until its page is a joined sum of simple sphere bundles.
arxiv-2505-19443:
Ranjan Sapkota, Konstantinos Roumeliotis, and Manoj Karkee compare two styles of AI-assisted coding in a review from two thousand twenty-five. Both lean on large language models, but they split the work between human and machine very differently. Vibe coding keeps the human in a chatty loop; agentic coding hands whole goals to autonomous agents.

The review builds a taxonomy of design, feedback, safety, and debugging across the two styles. Twenty use cases show vibe tools shining in prototypes and teaching, while agents excel at enterprise automation and pipeline work. Hybrid designs that pair chat interfaces with agent back ends are rising. The authors predict success lies in blending both, inside a human-centered process, rather than picking a winner.
arxiv-2505-19943:
Huan Zhang and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on keeping pre-trained models limber as they learn task after task. Most routes freeze the base model and add small plug-ins like prompts. That spares old skill but caps how far the model can bend to new data. Full tuning bends well yet can wreck the base.

Their method, MIST, tunes a sparse slice of the base weights. Picks are guided by a mutual information aim, and random drops thin the flow more. Less than a twentieth of the weights move at all, and far less per step. Added ahead of freeze routes, it lifts scores across many continual tests.
arxiv-2505-20043:
Marcello Cellina, Matteo Corno, and Sergio Savaresi built the tracking system that lets driverless race cars overtake each other at up to 275 kilometers per hour. At those speeds, knowing exactly where rival cars are and how fast they approach is the difference between a bold pass and a crash. Their algorithm fuses laser and radar returns in a Kalman filter that treats each sensor honestly: radar's range-rate goes straight into the measurement model, and the known track layout informs every prediction.

Late measurements, a real hazard when sensors and computers lag, are reprocessed from buffers so no information is thrown away. The system ran on the PoliMOVE team's car through real, fully autonomous overtaking maneuvers against other robots. The authors present the work as a proving ground: tracking that survives racing's extremes builds margin for the gentler chaos of public roads.
arxiv-2505-20243:
Bhawna Piryani and co-authors survey temporal question answering, the field that teaches machines to answer questions involving time. Such questions carry time limits or context, and the source material keeps growing as news, web archives, and knowledge bases add time-stamped content. A system in this field has to spot the time intent in a question, make sense of time expressions, order events, and reason about facts that change.

The survey organizes past work through one shared lens: how the time span of the source texts, the time span of the questions, and the skill of the model interact. That view lets the authors compare data sets, tasks, and methods side by side. They review gains from neural designs, above all transformer models and large language models. They also cover the benchmark data sets and scoring methods used to test whether a system truly handles time well.
arxiv-2505-20343:
Sonal Prabhune, Balaji Padmanabhan, and Kaushik Dutta hunt for a subtle gender bias in chatbots in a 2025 paper. They define entropy bias: a gap in how much information a model gives men versus women answering the same real questions. Their test set draws real user questions from education, jobs, personal finance, and health.

Four popular models were tested, with answers judged by metrics and by another model acting as judge. At the topic level, no clear bias appeared. Question by question, though, most answers differed in quality by gender, with wins scattered on both sides that cancel in averages. For a person asking one question, that scatter is the real risk. The authors offer a simple fix: generate both versions and merge them into one answer. Early tests show the merging trims the gap.
arxiv-2505-20643:
