Bo Pan and Liang Zhao ask in 2025 whether past experience can speed up reasoning in large language models. More compute usually improves model answers but slows them down. Humans, by contrast, get faster and better with practice on similar tasks, which motivates the study.

They formalize the speedup problem by task similarity and compute budget. Their framework, SpeedupLLM, uses adaptive compute allocation and memory mechanisms with theoretical guarantees. Experiments vary similarity, memory, and reasoning methods. Models generally reason faster with past experience, cutting compute cost by up to about half with the right setup, they report.
arxiv-2505-21043:
Sam O'Connor Russell and Naomi Harte show, in a 2025 paper, that adding visual cues improves computer prediction of turn taking in two person conversation. Smooth alternation is what makes talking with a robot or video partner feel natural. Most prediction models listen only to speech, yet human turn taking is richly multimodal.

Their model, MM-VAP, combines voice with facial expression, head pose, and gaze. On videoconference interactions it predicted holds versus shifts at 84 percent accuracy, against 79 for the best audio only rival. Breaking results down by the length of silence between turns showed gains at every duration. Ablation tests found facial expression contributed the most. The authors also checked that automatic speech alignment can train such models from telephone speech. Their working claim: when partners can see each other, a model needs eyes as well as ears.
arxiv-2505-21243:
Some quantum puzzles have no consistent assignment of pre-set answers — a property called contextuality. Colm Kelleher and Frédéric Holweck ran such tests in 2025 on the newest IBM quantum computers and reported clear violations of the classical limits.

Their tests included a Rio Negro inequality and Mermin games, a kind of team riddle no classical strategy can always win. The machines produced the largest Rio Negro violations yet, and the first wins of the full Mermin game on this hardware. Finite geometry shaped the tests, with larger layouts yielding richer data. The results show today's noisy quantum hardware can still display deeply non-classical behavior.
arxiv-2505-21643:
Topçu and co-authors report the first integral-field observations of two gamma-ray burst host galaxies with the Webb telescope in a 2025 paper. Long gamma-ray bursts flag distant galaxies by their bright afterglow, finding galaxies too faint for normal surveys. The hosts sit at cosmic noon, the era when star formation peaked across the universe.

An integral field unit maps spectra at every point of the galaxy image at once, revealing motion and chemistry across the galaxy. Earlier host studies mostly took one combined spectrum. Spatial maps show where stars form and how gas moves where the burst occurred. The work tests whether burst sites are special neighborhoods or typical parts of their galaxies.
arxiv-2505-21743:
Crashes that kill are rare, so records of them are thin, noisy, and often missing. Zihao Li and co-authors argue in 2025 that crash prediction must learn from near misses too. Past models lean on the few crashes on file, and even fine simulations miss the rare setups that end badly. The authors tie their plan to Vision Zero, the goal of ending road deaths.

Their plan builds fake near-miss scenes and explains them with set tools. Crash rates guide scene engines, varied driver models, and cause-based learning. A digital twin links small scenes to broad patterns across a road network. A checker with many goals keeps the fake scenes close to real ones. The aim is to turn sparse crash data into rich signals for safer roads.
arxiv-2505-22243:
Bin Li, Diwei Liu, Zehong Hu, and Jia Jia propose UDuo, a framework for matching users to resources online under budget limits, in a 2025 paper. Classic methods assume users arrive by a fixed random pattern, an assumption that breaks when real traffic shifts over time. UDuo instead tracks a time-stamped profile of arrivals and spending, learns pacing rules that adapt across constraint setups, and forecasts how arrivals will move next.

Tests on real pricing workloads showed faster convergence and better efficiency than the classic stochastic model. The authors also prove that the method stays near optimal while respecting constraints as conditions change. The framework targets ad systems and other allocation problems where demand will not sit still.
arxiv-2505-22543:
Ziheng Jia and co-authors build large training sets to scale up perceptual video quality assessment. Models that judge video quality need vast labeled data, which this field lacks. Human-rated sets have stayed small beside other vision fields.

Their OmniVQA framework builds instruction data with humans in the loop. They scaled it into the largest such set in the field so far. A companion set trains models to give numeric quality scores. The data stress both technical flaws and aesthetic quality. A paired training strategy blends lessons from both sets. The work shows data scaling laws can lift quality models too. It gives the field shared resources for fair progress checks.
arxiv-2505-22643:
Dekai Zhu, Slobodan Ilic, and co-authors make laser scan scenes with labels in one pass, in a 2025 paper. Past range view makers gave bare scans with no labels, then a split tool had to guess them. That split left clashes between shape and sense in the made scenes.

Their maker, Spiral, gives depth, shine, and sense maps at once from a spread based build. Fresh sense keen grades judge how good such made sets are. Tests on two road sets beat past pairs with the least bulk of all. Made scans also cut hand label work for real sort training.
arxiv-2505-22843:
Alexander Herzog, Aliai Eusebi, and Lorenzo Cavallaro argue that malware detectors must prove their confidence, not just their accuracy, in a 2025 paper. Modern tools adapt as malware drifts, and their headline scores look strong. But users act on a model's certainty: unsure cases get human review, while sure ones pass at once.

If certainty does not match real error, budgets burn on useless samples and risky files slip through with high confidence. The authors propose Aurora, a framework that audits a model's confidence for reliability and stability under distribution shift. Its metrics go beyond snapshots to how confidence behaves over time. A detector that cannot say when it is unsure is not trustworthy in use, whatever its score.
arxiv-2505-23243:
Pallis shows how tweaking the kinetic side of a Palatini gravity model rescues simple inflation theories from new data. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Recent measurements from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope tightened the allowed patterns for the early universe's burst of expansion.

Plain power-law inflation models clashed with those results under standard gravity. Adding a non-minimal link between the inflaton field and gravity, plus a matched kinetic mixing, restores the fit. The inflaton stays below the Planck scale, and energies stay within the theory's safe range. The model also embeds into supergravity with two chiral fields and a simple superpotential. A shaped potential term keeps the partner field stable during inflation.
arxiv-2505-23343:
Sixian Wang, Zhiwei Tang, and Tsung-Hui Chang filter bad AI images early in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models make pictures by gradual denoising, and output quality swings with the random path taken. Fixes usually need full generation plus outside reward scores, which costs time.

The team spots a signal inside the path itself: a running gap between guided and unguided scores tracks where good samples cluster. Their plug-in method uses that gap to drop weak samples partway through, with no retraining and no outside scorer. Tests on image benchmarks show gains in human taste scores and prompt-following measures. The authors expect the trick to extend beyond images.
arxiv-2505-23443:
Benyamin Trachtenberg and Nir Rosenfeld study strategic classification with nonlinear models in a 2025 paper. In this setting, users reshape their features at some cost to win a label they want. Most past theory covers linear classifiers, whose straight boundary lines act in ways that are easy to foresee.

Working from the boundary up, the pair show how a curved edge changes the game. Past the linear case, user moves can raise or lower the effective complexity of a model class, and the drop can be without limit. Universal approximators such as neural nets stop being universal once users react to the model. Tests confirm gaps in performance even for model classes with no limits at all. The results reset what learners can promise when people game the classifier.
arxiv-2505-23543:
Jan Ignatowicz and co-authors argue for a new model to enrich records for digital heritage sets, in a 2025 position paper. Libraries hold vast scans of old books and objects, yet thin records make them hard to find and link. The authors propose joining vision models, language models, and knowledge graphs in one frame.

Their model adds a layered vision step that hunts for nested marks, such as text inside seals. They test the idea on early printed books from a digital library in Poland. They also release a hand marked set of one hundred five pages. The paper weighs the real hurdles that museums and libraries face in using such tools.
arxiv-2505-23643:
Manuel Costa and eight co-authors applied in 2025 a classic computer security idea, information-flow control, to autonomous AI agents. Agents that browse, read mail, and run tools can be hijacked by poisoned text in their inputs. The team built a formal model of agent planners and sorted which protections dynamic tagging can truly enforce.

Their planner, Fides, labels data by secrecy and trustworthiness and blocks forbidden flows outright, with tricks for hiding data selectively. In a standard attack arena it finished many tasks while holding its guarantees. Formal leashes may let agents roam more, not less.
arxiv-2505-23743:
Amber Yijia Zheng and co-authors present a 2025 method, DarkDiff, for rescuing photos taken in near darkness. Camera software that cleans raw dark images often smooths detail. Models trained from scratch for the task can miss sharp detail and true color. DarkDiff instead retasks a ready-made image generation model for the camera pipeline. The pre-trained model's sense of what scenes look like guides the clean-up. Noisy raw input goes in, and a cleaner, sharper image comes out.

Tests on three low-light data sets led the field in judged quality. The method kept fine detail that regression-based tools tended to blur. Colors in deep shadow came out closer to the truth. The authors say reuse of a strong general model beats building a narrow one. That lesson may shape how camera software is built next. The work targets the raw stage, before photo processing.
arxiv-2505-23843:
Wenhan Dong and co-authors warn, in a 2025 paper, that current tests of lateral thinking in large language models can fool their own graders. Multi-round tasks with hidden facts are a key test of such thinking. Yet scores from automatic metrics may hide shortcut taking, rigid habits, and giving up too early.

Those hidden flaws make models look stronger than they are and weaken trust in the tests. The authors propose sharper standards for grading. They call for checks on the reasoning path itself, a wider set of scores, and direct comparison with human performance. Better grading, they argue, is needed before test scores can guide real claims about model thinking.
arxiv-2505-24043:
Four mathematicians in Poland and Madagascar proved that a fluid equation shaken by pure jump noise has weak solutions in a 2025 paper. The flow obeys the Navier-Stokes equations, but the random kicks arrive as sudden Levy jumps rather than smooth static. Such models fit fluids with shocks and bursts.

The proof first builds tidy approximations and leans on known energy bounds. A change-of-space theorem then extracts a limit process on a fresh probability space. The second half shows that limit truly solves the equation, by proving a companion process is a pure jump martingale and calling on a representation theorem. The authors offer the route as an alternative to recent methods for random partial differential equations.
arxiv-2505-24243:
Joohwan Ko and Justin Domke present Model Informed Flows for Bayesian inference in this 2025 paper. Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution with a simpler family. Complex layered models create posteriors with awkward shapes that simple families fit poorly. Flow based families and a reparametrization trick each help in part.

The authors prove the two tricks together equal a certain autoregressive flow with an added shift. That insight guides a new architecture. It adds the shift mechanism, prior information, and the model layer order. Tests on layered and flat benchmark models gave tighter posterior fits. Performance matched or beat the best prior methods. The work turns a theoretical link into a practical inference tool.
arxiv-2505-24343:
Chen and Nixon investigate, in a 2025 paper, how to keep artificial viscosity from quietly steering simulations of accretion discs. The smoothed particle method needs some numerical stickiness to handle shocks and keep particles orderly. Too much, though, and the fake friction outruns the physics being studied.

Running steady discs in a standard code, they varied the linear and quadratic viscosity knobs and watched the disc's surface density. The winning settings were those that piled up the most mass for the same inflow, a sign of least fake drag. The code's defaults, above all the quadratic term, ran too sticky for calm discs. Their fix ties the quadratic knob to the linear one's shock switch, so viscosity rises only when a real shock demands it.
arxiv-2505-24543:
Avila and four co-authors retested a basic law of the early universe in this paper from twenty twenty-five. The cosmic microwave background should cool exactly in step with cosmic expansion. The team rebuilt that temperature history from two data sets using Gaussian processes, a flexible statistical method. One set came from galaxy clusters bending the background light.

The reconstruction mostly matched the standard law. At low redshifts, though, hints of deviation reached about two standard deviations. The inferred present-day temperature also sat in mild tension with the precise satellite value. The authors float shifting fundamental constants as one possible cause. They treat the result as a prompt for sharper measurements, not a refutation.
arxiv-2505-24643:
Juan Wisznia and co-authors ask whether classic sorting methods still win when a language model does the pairwise comparisons. Their 2025 paper rethinks ranking tasks where each comparison costs a pricey model call rather than a cheap check. That cost shift, they argue, breaks the old math of which method is best.

The team offers a framework that counts model calls as the real cost. Tricks such as grouping questions into batches and saving past answers change which methods come out ahead. Some methods that are perfect under the old cost rules lose their edge here. The work guides anyone building ranking systems on top of language models.
arxiv-2505-24743:
Manosh Manoharan asks what really lets simple dark energy models ease the Hubble tension, in a paper from 2025. Two no-extra-parameter models seem to favor a faster current expansion, which would calm the clash between early and late universe measures. Suspect priors and dataset choices might be doing the work.

Minimally extended versions of both models actually favor low expansion rates, and the high values trace to prior choices. Dropping certain high-redshift absorption data restores strong tension with local measures. New survey data also sit uneasily with older distance estimates. Reframed as interacting dark sectors, easing the tension demands an odd sign-switching coupling.
arxiv-2506-00343:
Mustafa Chasmai and three co-authors release a sound library of wild species in a 2025 paper. Volunteers around the world record animals and upload the clips. The iNaturalist platform gathers those observations in one place. The team turned its sound records into a research data set.

The set holds about two hundred thirty thousand audio files. They cover more than five thousand five hundred species. Birds, mammals, insects, reptiles, and amphibians all appear. Over twenty seven thousand recordists contributed clips. Each file carries a single species label, though labels can be rough. Tests show the set works well as pretraining for other tasks. The authors hope it powers tools that help track wildlife by ear.
arxiv-2506-00643:
Weijie Xu and five colleagues build a benchmark for a neglected test format: select all that apply. Most model exams ask for one right answer, but real problems in law, medicine, and reading often have several. Models are rarely graded on finding them all.

Their SATA-Bench spans many domains, and they ran twenty-seven leading models through it. The best scored under forty-two percent on exact match. Two flaws explain much of the gap: models favor certain options whatever the content, and they miscount how many answers to give. The team's fix, Choice Funnel, adjusts token bias and sets an adaptive threshold. It raised exact match by up to twenty-nine percent while cutting compute cost by nearly two thirds.
arxiv-2506-00743:
Yeshwanth Venkatesha, Souvik Kundu, and Priyadarshini Panda speed up federated fine-tuning of language models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Federated learning trains across many devices without gathering private data. Devices are weak and their data differ, which makes tuning large models costly.

Their method prunes attention heads inside each client model, guided by a confidence-based importance score. A weighted scheme then merges head updates, favoring crucial ones, and a strategy picks which clients join each round. Tests on four data sets reached ninety percent sparsity with under two percent accuracy loss. Communication needs fell and training operations dropped sharply.
arxiv-2506-00943:
Chanuka Wijayakoon and co-authors test whether large language models can write smart contracts that stay faithful to the law. Smart contracts automate parts of legal deals in code. Checking their legality by hand is slow and needs rare double expertise.

The team scores compliance by modeling both the legal text and the code as processes and comparing their behavior. Four models each drafted contracts from five legal agreements, making twenty in all. Every model produced code that ran without syntax errors. Legal fidelity, though, varied and fell short in notable ways. Running code is not the same as lawful code. The metrics give the field a way to measure that gap.
arxiv-2506-01043:
Yufan Zhou, Yongbo Xiao, and An Liu present a beam design to estimate the uplink channel in a large antenna system, in a paper from 2025. Such systems split beam forming between analog and digital parts, which makes channel reading hard in real settings. Past schemes needed pilots sent over many time slots.

Their design groups the antenna columns and gives each group a narrow beam that covers one slice of vertical angle. That cuts interference from unwanted angles and sharpens vertical estimates. A search method then tunes the grouping for better sideways accuracy. A low cost inference method uses the design to read the channel fast and well. Tests showed clear gains over base methods.
arxiv-2506-01343:
In game theory, a correlated equilibrium tells players how to coordinate their choices using shared signals. Whether such equilibria can be computed quickly depends on properties of the game. Howard Dai studies a max-polymatrix game in 2025, where each player's payoff from many pairwise contests is set by their single best edge result rather than a sum. An open question asked whether known fast methods apply to this variant.

Dai shows the game has the polynomial expectation property, the exact condition that lets the classic results of Papadimitriou and Roughgarden go through. Correlated equilibria for this max variant are therefore computable by those methods. The paper closes with ideas for carrying the argument to other polymatrix variants, and a brief look at whether the property is truly necessary for computing such equilibria.
arxiv-2506-01743:
Wenyuan Jiang and Shuo Guo survey how the world's most frugal radios agree on timing, in a 2025 review. Backscatter tags have no battery-hungry transmitter; they surf on ambient radio waves, reflecting them to send data. Before any of that works, tag and reader must synchronise, and doing so on microwatts is the hard part. The survey reviews recent methods across three host technologies: Bluetooth Low Energy, mobile LTE signals, and WiFi.

Named systems are compared by timing granularity, accuracy, compatibility, and power cost, from PassiveBLE to SyncScatter. The trade-offs are fundamental: finer synchronisation buys throughput but burns the power budget that makes backscatter attractive. The authors map open problems, including security and scale, and sketch where ultra-low-power synchronisation research should head next. It is a field guide for tag designers.
arxiv-2506-01843:
Jonas Eidesen studies quantum error-correcting codes through a new mathematical lens, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Stabilizer codes and Clifford codes protect quantum information from noise. Their structure is usually described case by case.

Eidesen defines projective error models, which let representation theory organize both code families uniformly. He also introduces a third class, called weak stabilizer codes. Relationships among the three classes are worked out. The obstruction to a nontrivial stabilizer code turns out to be a class in group cohomology. Similar obstructions are found for weak stabilizer codes. For nice error bases, he characterizes exactly when a Clifford code is a weak stabilizer code. Two infinite families of non-stabilizer Clifford codes follow.
arxiv-2506-02143:
Fatih Kansoy and Dominykas Stasiulaitis show that green companies respond to central bank moves in their own asymmetric way, in a 2025 paper. Sustainable investing now tops thirty-five trillion dollars, yet how environmental, social, and governance traits alter monetary policy transmission was unknown. The team measured stock reactions in tight windows around one hundred and sixty Federal Reserve announcements over twenty years.

High-ESG firms gained a small shield, about 1.6 basis points of protection, against surprise rate hikes. But they suffered about 2.6 basis points of extra sensitivity to forward guidance, the bank's signals about the future. The Paris Agreement flipped the pattern: before it, green firms were the more vulnerable ones; after it, they gained protection, a swing of 186 basis points. A model of sustainability-minded investors with longer horizons reproduces the asymmetry. The authors call ESG a new dimension of monetary policy's uneven effects.
arxiv-2506-02243:
Tamara Cucumides and Floris Geerts present a 2025 framework that turns tables into graphs shaped by the task at hand. Tables and linked records are the most common data forms in real machine learning. Graph neural networks can mine their links, yet most builds lean on rigid graphs drawn from key fields alone.

Their system, auGraph, upgrades a base graph by lifting select data columns into nodes. A scoring rule picks which columns carry signal for the target prediction. The upgrade keeps the source schema intact while adding task shaped links. In tests, auGraph beat graphs built from schema rules or rough heuristics on linked and plain table tasks.
arxiv-2506-02443:
Hamidou Tembine and a large group of co-authors argue in this 2025 paper that AI is built for the wrong sense. The world holds more than seven thousand languages, yet machine intelligence feeds on written text. That bias locks out over seven hundred million people who take in the world mainly by ear, many in rural and remote regions.

The authors call such people audio-literate: fluent in speech, song, and story, but not in reading. For them, a text-first chatbot is a closed door. The paper presses for systems that start from audio, hearing and speaking in local languages as their native mode. The stakes are access itself: health advice, farming knowledge, and public services ride on these tools. An AI that cannot listen cannot serve most of the world's tongues.
arxiv-2506-02543:
Dinesh Chandra Maurya wrote a 2025 paper on dark energy in a modified theory of gravity. The catalog creator field is empty, but the head names Maurya as the sole author. His model uses a flowing dark energy field called quintessence, inside a gravity theory built on a quantity named Q, with a thick, viscous cosmic fluid.

He solves the field equations for a lopsided expanding universe model and gets a hyperbolic form for its growth. Data from cosmic clocks, sound-wave relics, and supernova catalogs were used to pin the model's settings. He then traces how expansion speed and braking change over time, and runs checks that sort dark energy models into kinds. The work tests whether this richer gravity can match the real sky.
arxiv-2506-02743:
Thi Nhung Dao, Martin Gabelmann, and Margarete Mühlleitner compute corrections, in a 2025 preprint, to how the Higgs boson couples to itself in an extended model. The model is the next-to-minimal supersymmetric one, fitted with an inverse seesaw to give neutrinos their tiny masses. The Higgs self-coupling shapes the Higgs potential and future collider signals. The team adds one-loop corrections plus the biggest two-loop pieces. The treatment is applied to the Higgs mass, so the two stay consistent.

The new neutrino and sneutrino sectors leave marks. Effects reach about ten percent on the self-coupling of the standard-like Higgs. The Higgs mass shifts by up to four and a half percent. These numbers hold at points that pass all current data checks. The corrections also feed into decays of heavy Higgs states to lighter ones. Everything is coded into a public program.
arxiv-2506-02943:
Xu, Wang, Briand, and Liu built a tool in twenty twenty-five that writes code tests on its own with help from smart chat models. Hand-made tests for Java code take much time and care. Old auto tools check code acts but not what the code should do.

Their tool, CANDOR, splits the work among set chat agents that draft full tests as a team. A panel of such models talks through the right test answers to cut false claims. In trials it matched a top old tool on code reach and beat it on fault finds. It also beat a tuned rival on right test answers by a clear gap.
arxiv-2506-03043:
Nikita Puchkin and co-authors bound the sample cost of learning a potential in 2025. The head byline names six authors, though the catalog lists three. Such potentials drive a class of generative models that steer one distribution into another with least effort.

Their study asks how well a fitted potential generalizes from a finite sample. Under mild conditions on the target and the starting process, they bound the error with high probability. The excess risk can fall nearly as fast as one over the sample size, up to log factors. The bound holds even when both distributions stretch without limit.
arxiv-2506-03143:
Qianhui Wu and co-authors presented GUI-Actor in 2025, a way for software agents to find the right spot on a screen. An agent that clicks and types must first ground a plan: pick the patch of screen where the act belongs. Most methods make the model spell out number pairs for the spot, a poor fit for coarse visual features and vague targets.

GUI-Actor skips the numbers. A small added head learns to match a special token against all patches of the screen at once, offering one or more candidate zones in a single pass. A checker then grades the candidates and picks the best. On screen tests, the method beat prior bests and held up on new screen sizes. A small model of theirs even topped a far larger rival, and training just the new head proved enough.
arxiv-2506-03343:
Sam Hopkins and Joel B. Lewis wrote a 2025 math paper on a special class of ordered sets. An ordered set in this class looks the same from any point upward, a trait the authors call upho. Each such lattice holds a smaller core lattice that fixes key counts for the whole set.

Earlier work asked which small lattices can serve as cores. Here the authors ask how many ways one core can occur. When a small lattice has no inner symmetry, it can serve as a core for only finitely many upho lattices. Yet the count of ways can also grow without bound, even for the simplest rank two cores. The paper ends with a sketch of a method to list all such ways.
arxiv-2506-03443:
Ali Salloum and four co-authors study politics and polarization on the social platform Bluesky in a 2025 paper. Political talk now spreads across many fragmented platforms, each with its own users and algorithms. The team collected all platform activity from December 2024 to May 2025 and mapped political topics in English language posts.

About thirteen percent of posts touched politics, led by international conflicts, United States politics, and social technology debates. Structural polarization was high on several topics. Yet the most polarized topics were lopsided: the smaller side held only one to two percent of users. The authors find Bluesky users more politically uniform than on older platforms, even as familiar narratives repeat.
arxiv-2506-03543:
Wanghao Ye and a large team present CogniPair, a platform of digital twins meant to rehearse social encounters before they happen. Ordinary chatbots lack the inner workings of human psychology, so the team built agents on Global Workspace Theory, a model of consciousness. Specialized sub-agents handle emotion, memory, social norms, planning, and goals, coordinated through a shared workspace.

A faithful twin also needs the right personality, so the team designed an adventure-style test that reads character from choices in story scenes rather than from self-descriptions. Twins then meet in simulated dates and job interviews, letting both sides gauge fit. Tests with 551 agents and a university speed-dating dataset showed a 72 percent correlation with human attraction patterns and about 78 percent accuracy at predicting matches.
arxiv-2506-03643:
Lingjun Mao and four co-authors argue that images deserve labels in proportion to what they hold in a 2025 paper. Most vision encoders squeeze every image into the same fixed count of tokens, the chunks a model reads. A cluttered room and a blank wall get the same budget, which wastes effort on simple scenes and starves rich ones.

Their encoder, DOVE, gives each image a variable count of tokens sized to its content. It rebuilt images faithfully while using far fewer tokens on average, and its features beat rival tokenizers on probe tests and mixed media tasks. A second version takes a text query and spends its tokens on the parts the query asks about. Code and trained models are shared openly.
arxiv-2506-03843:
Fatemeh Taherasghari and Clifford Will work out how pairs of compact objects move in an altered theory of gravity, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The theory, Einstein-Aether gravity, adds a fixed time-like vector field to spacetime. The pairs in question are black holes or neutron stars in tight orbits. Such systems lose energy as gravitational waves, which slowly shrinks the orbit.

The authors derive the motion equations to high precision, reaching the order where radiation reaction shows up. They build on field solutions from a companion paper. The method tracks both gravity and the aether field near the pair. Their formulas match the order used for standard gravity tests. Waveform builders can use them to test whether real signals fit this rival theory.
arxiv-2506-03943:
Shiyi Yang, Can Chen, and Didong Li define a 2025 measure of curve for hypergraphs, webs where one link can join many points at once. Curve tools read the shape of plain networks well, but past lifts to hypergraphs were either crude or costly. Their new measure has a closed form, which keeps it both sharp and cheap.

Across fake and real data sets, the measure split links inside groups from those between them. It also bared hidden labels, tracked change over time, and grouped like hypergraphs. A cheap shape tool of this kind can serve many tasks, from spotting odd nodes to sorting whole webs.
arxiv-2506-04043:
Mikel Ngueajio and co-authors grade persona-guided chatbots that answer hate speech in this 2025 paper. Auto-written counter replies can soften online hate, but their tone, clarity, and safety are open questions. The team built a four-part grading frame covering persona, length and reading ease, feeling tone, and ethics.

Three large models were tested under three prompting styles on two hate speech data sets. Replies often ran long and read at college level, shutting out many readers. Prompts that guided feeling gave warmer, clearer replies. Still, safety and real-world effect stayed shaky, the authors warn. They urge care before such tools are let loose.
arxiv-2506-04543:
Riley Hultquist, David Simonne, Sayantan Mondal and Ericmoore Jossou designed a multipurpose cell for watching electrochemical damage as it happens in 2025. The cell holds a sample under precise electrical control while synchrotron X-rays image it in three dimensions.

A key choice separates the reference electrode from the working and counter electrodes, which keeps measurements trustworthy. The modular build adapts to different beamlines and stages. Tests showed the cell supports live measurements of corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement under two imaging modes, coherent diffraction imaging and dark field microscopy. Such in-place watching can reveal exactly when and where materials start to fail in harsh settings.
arxiv-2506-04643:
Ojaswini Sharma and Aradhya Shukla recast the drift of heat goods near a black hole as a twin wave tale, in a paper from 2025. The drift rule that tracks chance paths in bent space time shrinks, in their hands, to a plain wave task with a bowl shaped well. That shape is the stock well of wave math.

Twin wave math then gives a deep link twixt the drift rule and the black hole pull. One bend trick of that math spawns a kin set of wells that share one tone set but wear new wave forms. The kin wells widen the class of heat tales the hole can host. All keeps in pure math, with no new sky data claimed.
arxiv-2506-05043:
Arne Nothdurft and ten co-authors estimated timber measures for Austrian mountain forest stands in a 2025 paper. Managers need stand-level numbers for volume, basal area, tree size, and density across 824 stands in the Brixen im Thale district. Field crews measured 146 plots with a handheld laser scanner.

Airborne laser data supplied the predictors, and a small-area framework turned plot models into stand estimates with uncertainty. The authors compared single- and multi-output models, with and without spatial effects, using blocked cross-checks. Despite hints that complex models should win, simpler spatial models, and sometimes plain ones, performed about as well. The paper gives forest planners a tested recipe and honest error bars.
arxiv-2506-05143:
Scharmer and co-authors recount how tough solar imaging tools get built in a 2025 paper. Their subject is a pair of imaging spectropolarimeters, CRISP and CHROMIS, on the Swedish one meter solar telescope, plus a next model now in build. Both read the Sun in fine color slices and track light polarization.

Each tool pairs a sharp and a soft Fabry Perot etalon with a prefilter to set its band. A lens based telecentric layout, with no fold mirrors, keeps images clean and alignment simple over years. The team covers needs, models, build, calibration, and the polarimeter units. Past tests showed the pair beat plain filters on surface detail.
arxiv-2506-05243:
Language models sometimes state false facts, called hallucinations, and one way to catch them is to check whether a source text supports each claim. Ron Eliav and co-authors proposed a guided reasoning method for that check in 2025, called CLATTER. Instead of asking a model for one quick verdict, the method walks it through three steps in order.

First the text is split into small claims. Then each claim is matched to evidence in the source and classified, and finally the verdicts are combined. Guided this way, models made finer and more accurate calls. The authors also define scores for the quality of each middle step, which backed the gain.
arxiv-2506-05543:
Sethuraman and a team of colleagues introduced FRAME in twenty twenty-five, a video encoder trained to support dense prediction tasks such as tracking objects and labeling each pixel. Image encoders miss how scenes change over time. Existing video models, in turn, often trail image models on fine detail tasks.

FRAME learns by predicting present and future image features from past and present frames. The teacher features come from a strong image model, giving precise, stable targets. The encoder also aligns a summary token with a language-image model, enabling tasks such as video classification. Across six tasks and seven datasets, FRAME beat image encoders and prior video models. It stays compact, the authors note, suiting many downstream uses.
arxiv-2506-05643:
Keaton Holt and co-authors build a unifying framework for how material spreads through dynamic mitochondrial networks. Mitochondria fuse, split, and move, forming temporal networks that range from single fused webs to scattered units with brief contacts. Proteins, lipids, ions, and RNA move within those networks by diffusion and exchange.

The model fills networks with a material made locally and consumed globally. Steady content is set by the balance of encounter rates between clusters, fusion and fission rates, and diffusion inside clusters. As connectivity rises, spread shifts from a social network regime limited by cluster meetings to a physical network regime limited by diffusivity. Parameters from three human cell lines show real cells access both regimes.
arxiv-2506-05743:
Models trained to group similar items learn rich features from data, and those features power many tools. Ruining Sun and six co-authors warn in this 2025 paper that better features can also leak more about the data the model trained on. They study attacks that guess whether a given item was part of the training set, a risk for private records.

Tests across several data sets and model designs show a clear trade: as encoders grow more advanced and extract better features, the leaks grow worse. The team also builds a new attack that reads the size pattern of a feature vector and judges membership from it. Their attack beat older methods, above all when the attacker knew little and could ask few questions. The findings argue for privacy checks alongside accuracy gains.
arxiv-2506-05843:
Myungkyu Koo and five co-authors present in 2025 FontAdapter, a tool that teaches image generators a brand-new font from one sample glyph in seconds. Text-to-image models can blend lettering into scenes, but matching an unseen font normally needs long fine-tuning with a font dictionary. That delay kills real-time design work.

A two-stage curriculum solves it: the model first learns to read font traits from lone glyphs, then to set styled text into natural scenes. Synthetic datasets built from large online font collections feed each stage. The system handles unseen fonts at inference with no retraining, and it also edits text, blends styles, and carries fonts across languages. Fast font matching opens custom lettering to live design tools.
arxiv-2506-05943:
Pawel Kryszkiewicz and Hanna Bogucka tackle garbled radio signals in a 2025 paper. Power amplifiers in transmitters bend multicarrier signals, which wrecks standard receivers, though the bending also spreads useful extra copies of the data.

Most advanced receivers lean on past decisions, so their gains show only when errors are already rare. The authors propose a combiner that works without such help. No formula gives its best weights, so machine learning finds them. Simulations beat both the standard receiver and a leading decision-aided one on error rate. The catch is cost: the work grows fast with the number of carriers, so wideband use needs more study.
arxiv-2506-06043:
Rao and co-authors sharpen fast MRI reconstruction by also policing the maps that say how each coil in the scanner hears the body. Their 2025 paper uses implicit neural representation, a method that fits a small network to one scan at a time, so no library of full scans is needed for training. Speed asks for sparse data, which makes the coil maps hard to pin.

Most such methods only keep the image itself smooth, and let the coil maps drift. Their network, INR-CRISTAL, adds a smoothness rule for the maps, which suits their known soft shape. In tests the maps came out cleaner with fewer ghosts, and the rebuilt images kept fine structure better while shedding artifacts.
arxiv-2506-06143:
Carolin Benjamins and co-authors release a benchmarking framework, in a paper published in 2025, for tuning machine learning models. Tuning means picking settings, like learning rate, that make a model train well. Dozens of tuning tools exist, and testing each on many tasks is slow and messy without shared ground.

Their framework, carps, pairs any number of tuners with any number of tasks through a light interface, and it ships with an analysis pipeline. The first release holds over three thousand tasks from five collections and twenty-eight variants of nine tuner families. It covers plain tuning plus harder kinds with budgets, many goals, or both. To save compute, the team also picked small, diverse starter subsets of ten to thirty tasks per kind.
arxiv-2506-06243:
Benjamin Smith, Jianhui Gao, and Jessica Gronsbell build fairmetrics, a software pack for the R language that grades how fair a learning model is across groups. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A model can be right on the whole yet bent against a group set by race, sex, or age. Such bias can lock in the gaps of the world. The pack grades many group fairness marks at once. They span three views: that outcomes stand apart from the group, that errors match across groups, and that a score means the same in each group. It gives both point marks and ranges, through one plain call, on health data used as a case.
arxiv-2506-06443:
Luis Pinto shows that the middle layers of pre-trained molecule encoders hold richer information than the final layer everyone uses, in a 2025 paper. Encoders that turn molecules into number vectors feed tasks like property prediction, and standard practice reads only the last layer's output. Pinto first traced how information flows through five different encoders.

Middle layers kept broad, general features, while the final layer squeezed information into a narrower shape. Across 22 prediction tasks, frozen middle-layer vectors beat final-layer ones by about five percent on average, and sometimes by far more. Fine-tuning a shortened encoder did even better, gaining about nine percent on average and setting new records on several benchmarks.
arxiv-2506-06643:
Moushumi Medhi and Rajiv Ranjan Sahay estimate scene depth from a single blurred photo. Their paper appeared in 2025. Judging depth from blur usually needs several shots taken with different focus settings. One shot leaves the task underdetermined, so few teams have tried it. The authors add a second clue: the dark channel, a measure of the darkest values in small patches of the image.

Blur softens contrast in a way that depends on distance, and the dark channel captures local contrast and structure. Joining the two cues lets their program infer depth from one image. The program is trained end to end with a rival-network setup. Tests on real photos showed the added cue gives meaningful depth maps. The method could help phones and small cameras that can take only one shot.
arxiv-2506-06743:
Allie Tran and a team of co-authors review in 2025 three years of progress at the ACM Lifelog Search Challenge, a contest where systems race to find moments in vast personal recordings. Lifelogs, years of photos and data from wearable cameras, are only useful if a person can retrieve one remembered moment fast.

The review covers the 2022 to 2024 workshops, comparing systems across tasks such as finding a known item and answering questions about a life. Year by year, the tools grew sharper at search and interaction. The paper charts where lifelog retrieval stands and what still trips it up.
arxiv-2506-06843:
HaoYang Shang and five co-authors borrow a theory of human memory limits to design teams of AI models. Cognitive load theory says working memory is narrow, so teaching must budget it. Their 2025 paper argues that a language model fed giant crafted prompts suffers the same squeeze: attention is finite, and bloated context rots performance. Rather than piling more into one model, systems can split work across agents the way good teaching splits a hard lesson.

The analogy becomes a design lens with rules, not a metaphor for its own sake. Coordination choices, who holds what context, follow from the theory. The authors test whether united agents beat isolated ones on complex tasks. Their claim is that architecture, informed by how minds overload, beats ever-longer prompts. The paper speaks to builders of multi-agent systems.
arxiv-2506-06943:
Forough Shirin Abkenar fine-tunes large language models to sniff out faults in WiFi networks. Pathologies in IEEE 802.11 networks are usually hunted with hand-built rules or classic classifiers. The approach here crafts prompts by hand, then fine-tunes two model families on the task: encoder-only models and decoder-only causal models. Labeled network data trains the detectors.

The sequential encoder model reached high detection accuracy on labeled data. The causal model matched that standard on unlabeled data, where labels are the scarce resource. Abkenar offers language models as a flexible diagnostic layer for wireless operations.
arxiv-2506-07243:
Mohammad Tanver Hossain and seven co-authors measure the tiny forces that build hagfish slime, in a 2025 study. When threatened, a hagfish releases mucus and coiled protein threads that burst into a cohesive net in seawater. How the threads deploy, and how they grip mucus and each other, was poorly measured before.

Using a custom glass-rod force sensor, the team made the first direct in-place measurements. Threads start peeling from their coils once the pull passes about 6.8 nanonewtons. A flow setup found the shear rate at which coils unravel, matching an updated peeling model. Thread-to-mucus grip proved stronger than thread-to-thread grip. Surprisingly, deployed threads added little to the slime's bulk resistance under steady flow. The results clarify how the slime assembles so fast and hint at designs for synthetic fiber gels that deploy on cue.
arxiv-2506-07343:
Yinan Huang, David Gleich, and Pan Li find a hidden pattern in the powers of a matrix built for directed networks. Magnetic graphs encode direction by adding phases to a graph's matrix, a trick borrowed from quantum physics. Past work used the matrix's spectrum to read global traits, but its powers, which capture local behavior over steps, were little explored. Their paper appeared in 2025.

The team shows that the powers count walks on the graph, sorted by how many edges each walk runs against the arrows. Those walk profiles turn out to be a Fourier transform of the matrix powers, so profiles can be rebuilt exactly from powers at a few phase settings. In real networks even fewer settings give a good rebuild, which means the data compress well. They show uses in spotting frustrated directed loops and in predicting missing links.
arxiv-2506-07443:
Predicting court judgments with language models fails when the reasoning wanders, and Weijie Shi and co-authors build a system that checks its own steps. LegalReasoner first finds a case's dispute points, splitting a hard case into smaller questions. It then reasons step by step while a separate verifier grades each step for correctness, progress, and promise.

When the verifier spots an error, expert-designed strategies trace the fault and repair that step. To train the system, the team releases LegalHK, a dataset of 58,130 Hong Kong court cases annotated with dispute points, reasoning chains, and verification labels. On a large open model, agreement with real court decisions rose from about seventy-two to eighty percent.
arxiv-2506-07643:
Jae Sung Park and ten co-authors teach a vision-language model to draw dense scene graphs, in a 2025 study. A scene graph lists objects in an image and how they relate, from left-of to holding. Such graphs power visual reasoning, yet hand labels are scarce. The team built a synthetic data set by asking a teacher model to fill missing relations in old graphs, then sifting the output for quality. Their student model, ROBIN, learned from that data.

A self-edit step, where a stronger model prunes and adds relations, polished the graphs further. The final set holds millions of relations over hundreds of thousands of images. ROBIN beat like-sized rivals trained on a hundred times more data on relation tests. It also set a new best score on a phrase-to-image grounding test. The authors credit the refined data, not raw scale.
arxiv-2506-07743:
Intoccia, Chirico, Pepe, and Cuomo present a 2025 methods paper on solving the Poisson equation with help from quantum computing. That equation shows up in many fields, from heat flow to electric fields. Classic ways to solve it grow slow and costly as the grid of points gets large.

Their hybrid method uses the quantum Fourier transform to find the terms of the solution right inside the quantum step. Tests showed gains in speed, memory use, and accuracy over classic routes. The authors frame the work as an early step, since quantum hardware still has real limits in practice.
arxiv-2506-08043:
Ashkan Shahbazi and co-authors predict soft tissue bends in real time by wedding neural nets to a physics kernel, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Full physics solvers are too slow for live surgery tools. Pure data nets stray into shapes flesh cannot take.

Kelvinlet priors, drawn from classic force math, seed the nets with true bend shapes. Big solver datasets teach the rest, for one or many graspers. Across net builds, truth and bend shape both improved. Tests used standard keyhole grasp tools on hard tasks. Readers get a physics-aware tissue sim fast enough to steer by.
arxiv-2506-08143:
Francesco Tonin, Alex Lambert, Johan Suykens, and Volkan Cevher speed up in 2025 a fair form of spectral clustering, a method that groups data by the shape of its connections. Fair clustering asks that each demographic group appear in every cluster in fair proportion, a requirement that makes the math much heavier.

The authors recast the fair problem inside a difference-of-convex framework and add a variable trick that splits it into easier pieces. An alternating solver then handles each piece, and each one turns out to be cheap. The result is fair grouping that can run at a scale where the older methods stall.
arxiv-2506-08243:
Zhenjiang Mao, Artem Bisliouk, Rohith Reddy Nama, and Ivan Ruchkin grade the confidence of reasoning models over time in a 2025 study. Language models answering math problems step by step often sound sure even when wrong. In classrooms that false confidence is risky, since learners may not spot the error.

Their framework treats confidence at each step as a signal unfolding in time. Rules written in a temporal logic language state what healthy confidence patterns look like. Robustness scores against those rules give structured, readable confidence estimates. Reshaping strategies then push model confidence toward the stated rules during evaluation.
arxiv-2506-08343:
Reasoning models write long chains of thought, and much of that length is filler like the word Wait. Chenlong Wang and co-authors test removing that filler in this 2025 paper. Long chains cost time and money, and the extra loops rarely add new insight. Their method, NoWait, simply blocks the tokens that signal self-reflection while the model writes.

The team tried the method on ten benchmarks spanning text, image, and video reasoning. Five families of reasoning models were tested. Chains shrank by roughly a quarter to a half, depending on the task. Accuracy held steady across the cuts. The trick needs no retraining, so it plugs into existing models. Leaner chains could make advanced reasoning cheaper to run at scale.
arxiv-2506-08743:
Michael Färber, David Lamprecht, and Yuni Susanti wire the web's formal knowledge graphs into neural recommenders. Over a thousand knowledge graphs follow the RDF standard, rich with typed facts about things and their relations. Graph neural networks, meanwhile, had mostly fed on plainer graphs, leaving that semantic wealth untapped.

Their integration uses both halves of an RDF graph: link structure from object properties and content from data values. Experiments sweep several network designs, feature starts, and graph mixes across recommendation tasks on graphs with millions of nodes. Semantic richness lifted recommendation quality throughout. The authors frame the work as groundwork for recommenders over the whole Linked Open Data cloud.
arxiv-2506-09143:
M Siudek led a large team hunting black holes by full-spectrum fitting in a 2025 paper. Active galactic nuclei are usually found by X-rays, radio waves, infrared colors, or emission lines, and each route catches a different subset. Their study fit the whole light distribution of galaxies from a big survey and flagged likely hosts by the active fraction. The method recovered most line-selected and infrared-selected cases.

Adding clean infrared data cut contamination by star-forming galaxies sharply. Half the new candidates escaped all standard methods, yet extra checks classified most of them, often as faint or retired systems. The authors say fitting completes the census.
arxiv-2506-09743:
Nicolas Renaud presents software that lets neural networks help write molecular wavefunctions inside quantum Monte Carlo runs. The package is built on a mainstream deep learning library, so it is built for graphics hardware. Users can slot machine learning parts, such as neural backflow changes and flexible correlation factors, into the trial wavefunction. Links to two known quantum chemistry codes supply starting orbitals and exponents. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Renaud tunes wavefunctions for four small molecules, from hydrogen to carbon monoxide.

Breaking curves and the forces along them were worked out for each one. The results agree well with baselines and recover a large share of the correlation energy. The aim is rapid trials: new wavefunction ideas can be put together, tested, and checked quickly in one place.
arxiv-2506-09843:
Timothy Bastian and co-authors examine this 2025 noise problem unique to radio pictures of the Sun. When a radio telescope array images a very strong source, the source itself becomes the dominant noise, called self-noise. The Sun is always in that regime. A companion paper laid out the theory; this one works through what it means for real solar observing.

The authors walk through classes of science cases for current and planned solar arrays, mostly at decimeter and centimeter wavelengths. Each case gets its self-noise limit spelled out: how faint a feature can be trusted next to the Sun's glare. The results extend to other wavelength regimes too. Observers can use the analysis to design exposures that respect the floor no processing can remove.
arxiv-2506-10343:
Dongwon Jung and co-authors mine running code for trustworthy reasoning lessons for language models in a 2025 paper. Teaching step-by-step thought is hampered by sloppy supervision: human traces cost dearly, and model-written ones drift into error. Programs, by contrast, execute exactly the same way every time.

The team converts execution traces into plain-language chains of thought. Models trained on these grounded traces reason better across varied benchmarks, and the skill transfers between domains. Ablation checks confirm the traces are unusually accurate. A side benefit: trained models think more briefly at test time, skipping the rambling that inflates cost.
arxiv-2506-10543:
Luiz Tizei and eight co-authors measure light absorption in nanowires of an unusual crystal form in a 2025 paper. Silicon and germanium usually crystallize in a cubic pattern, but a hexagonal diamond form could serve future lasers and quantum devices. Its light handling was unexplored, so the team combined electron microscopy, energy loss spectroscopy, and first principles simulation.

The wires, grown as branches inside the microscope, were nearly perfect single crystals, letting the team read their true optical response. Hexagonal silicon absorbed visible light more strongly than the cubic form, with a marked rise above a certain energy. Hexagonal germanium absorbed near one electron volt but showed no clear feature at its direct band edge, matching theory. The work links crystal structure to optical behavior.
arxiv-2506-10743:
Young stars are ringed by disks of gas and dust where planets form, and harsh light from nearby giant stars can strip those disks away. Rossella Anania and a large team of co-authors study that stripping in 2025, in the eighth paper of the AGE-PRO survey of disk evolution.

The team focused on ten disks in the Upper Scorpius region, where outside ultraviolet light is modest but steady. They compared the observed masses and sizes with computer models of slowly draining disks, run with and without the stripping effect. The plain models could not match what the telescopes saw. Adding outside light loss, which eats the disk from the outside in, shrank the model disks toward the observed sizes and masses.
arxiv-2506-10843:
Feline Lindeboom, Martijn Brehm, Davide Grossi, and Pradeep Murukannaiah study how to elect diverse committees when voters' ballots are patchy or noisy, in a 2025 paper. Diversity is measured as coverage: a committee should span as many voters' approvals as possible. Finding the best coverage is provably hard, with a known best approximation. When voters approve only a few candidates, the team ask how many questions must be put to voters to approach that best.

Asking everyone blindly would take a quadratic number of queries. Asking adaptively, guided by earlier answers, cuts that to roughly linear, and their greedy algorithm nearly matches the bound. With noisy answers, the cost rises with the number of voters too. Tests on real discussion data and synthetic ballots showed the algorithms work well even on modest instances. The authors aim at fairer digital democracy tools.
arxiv-2506-10943:
Adam Zweiger and five co-authors let a language model rewrite itself in twenty twenty-five. Language models are powerful but static: their weights never change after training. New tasks and knowledge must be crammed into prompts. Their framework, SEAL, lets a model adapt its own weights instead.

Given a new input, the model generates a self-edit. An edit may restructure the information, set optimization hyperparameters, or call data augmentation tools. Supervised fine-tuning on those edits produces lasting weight updates. A reinforcement learning loop trains the model to make good edits. The reward is the updated model's downstream performance. No separate adaptation module is needed, since the model's own generation steers the change. Readers get a step toward models that learn continually from experience.
arxiv-2506-11243:
Santiago Góngora and a team of co-authors test how far small language models can go in grading tutor responses, in two thousand twenty-five. Their team joined a shared task on evaluating artificial intelligence tutors. They limited themselves to models under one billion parameters, to mirror labs in the Global South where computing power is costly.

Across five tracks, their models stayed within a modest gap of the winning teams. The smallest gap was about six points and the largest about thirteen, on the organizers' strict score. All their models can run on a cheap graphics card or even without one. The authors conclude that small models are competitive for tutor evaluation under tight budgets.
arxiv-2506-11643:
Saswati Roy and co-authors compute how light bends as it passes a rotating, charged black hole, away from the hole's equatorial plane. Treating spacetime itself as a material medium lets them derive a formula for the bending angle. Both spin and charge should leave marks on the path of light.

They find that more charge reduces bending when spin is fixed. More spin raises bending for light moving with the rotation and lowers it against it. Bending is strongest in the equatorial plane and weaker toward the poles. Dragging of spacetime by the spin also shifts in a mixed way as charge and spin interact.
arxiv-2506-11743:
Antonin Joly and co-authors sort the matrices that shrink graphs in a 2025 paper. Graph coarsening merges nodes to make a graph smaller and cheaper to hold. A reduction matrix maps signals down, and a lifting matrix maps them back up.

Most past work ties the two matrices as near inverses and hunts for low loss. The authors note the pair is not in fact even handed. Rules on the lifting matrix alone can keep key graph traits alive. They build a family tree of valid reduction types and tell which have closed forms. The tree frees designers to pick pairs past the old tie.
arxiv-2506-11943:
Amy Wayland, David Alonso, and Matteo Zennaro forecast how outside data can rescue cosmic shear measurements in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Weak lensing surveys map dark matter, but gas physics muddies the small-scale signal. Tracers of hot gas around clusters could calibrate that muddiness.

Using mock data for a future flagship survey, the authors ask how tightly the gas model must be pinned down. Key parameters need ten to twenty percent precision to keep lensing results intact. X-ray data from about five thousand clusters should reach that bar for hot gas content. The harder part, tracking ejected gas, needs sensitive microwave background data from a next-generation experiment. The forecast maps a route to self-calibrated lensing cosmology.
arxiv-2506-12143:
Two plastics that mix fully still move at split speeds inside, and Shannon Zhang and Michael Webb simulate why, in work from twenty twenty-five. Local makeup maps were built across all blend ratios and heats. Entropy gauges tied the patchiness to each plastic's mobility.

The stiff partner's wiggles matched its lone form at like softness. The loose partner sped up, fed by extra free room and varied neighborhoods. Chain-mode reads show the stiff one's speedup spreads evenly, as if the loose partner's help leaks past its own zone. Blend design gains a nano-scale rule book.
arxiv-2506-12243:
Lobo and co-authors ask whether a quantum clock can tell rival theories of gravity apart in two thousand twenty-five. Metric theories differ in set constants that tweak how mass bends space and time. A quantum clock that moves slowly through a weak field ends in a state shaped by those constants.

Quantum state tests can then sort the theories. The authors show that a single detection can rule out one named theory, and can split two theories with certainty. Success odds hinge on four factors: the gap in proper time between the two states, the clock's energy gap, path length, and speed. Long-lived nuclei such as thorium look best as clocks, and using many clocks at once lifts the odds further.
arxiv-2506-12343:
Martínez-Martínez and Méndez-Bermúdez read the edge states of chance graphs by their wave marks, in a 2025 paper. Two graph kinds serve: link by luck and link by near place. Their link mats are thin kin of a stock chance mat clan.

As mean links grow, the graphs shift from lone to shared state rule. Top wave marks drift to a famed curve form at high link loads. Gaps twixt top marks and state spread shares trace the same shift. Edge marks thus flag the shift sans the full wave list. Graph growth can be read off edge states lone.
arxiv-2506-12543:
Teodora Srećković, Jonas Geiping, and Antonio Orvieto wrote a 2025 paper on a puzzle in training language models. A training method called Adam far outperforms the older SGD method on such models, and many explanations have been offered. The team reran the contest with great care, tuning both methods fully and varying batch size, momentum, and safeguards.

With small batches and correct tuning, SGD with momentum matched Adam. That result undercuts several popular explanations for the gap. Using models borrowed from physics, the team trace much of the gap to batch size itself. Knowing which knob truly matters can save large sums, since training runs are costly and tuning is often guesswork.
arxiv-2506-12643:
Prachnachai Meakpaiboonwattana and eight co-authors published a study in 2025 on whether posting an AI project on Hacker News actually grows it. The forum is a prime launchpad for programmers, and open-source teams increasingly promote there, but measured evidence on the payoff was thin.

The team analyzed 2,195 stories and their comments over two years, then tracked the 1,814 linked GitHub repositories. At least nineteen percent of the AI developers had promoted their own projects. After a story appeared, forks, stars, and contributors on the linked projects rose significantly, and community engagement skewed positive. Promotion on the forum, the authors conclude, is a real growth channel rather than vanity noise. The finding gives small teams a reason to launch in public.
arxiv-2506-12743:
Pavlina Jordanova and Evelina Veleva present a 2025 statistics paper on estimating the shape of a skewed distribution. Their tool family, the IAPO estimators, grows from probabilities of values that fall outside asymmetric fences. Those fences mark unusually high or low draws, with the asymmetry of the data taken into account. Earlier cousins of the method ignored that asymmetry.

Here the estimators are worked out for the exponentiated Fréchet distribution, a model for heavy-tailed data. The link between the target parameters and the outside probabilities solves more easily in this form. Simulated data test how fast the estimates settle. Against the older IPO variants, the new estimators read the right tail's heaviness index more accurately. Convergence rates close the study.
arxiv-2506-12843:
Natesh Reddy and Mark Stamp study how to rewrite machine-made text so it reads as human in a 2025 paper. Detectors can now spot text written by large language models with fair reliability. The authors test whether a second model can edit such text enough to fool those detectors.

Two sequence models, T5-small and BART, were used to rework sentences from a chatbot, adding traits more typical of human writing. Detectors trained on plain machine text lost much of their accuracy on the edited text. But when detectors were retrained with edited examples, they again spotted machine text with high accuracy. The work shows both an attack and a defense, and deepens what is known about text rewriting.
arxiv-2506-12943:
Alon and Cederbaum solve exactly a trap full of mixed boson clouds. Three species of bosons, each with its own mass and count, share one harmonic trap and push on each other with spring like forces. Because every interaction is harmonic, the whole many body problem yields closed forms for the ground state and its energy.

The team then asks how each species fragments, splitting across several states rather than one. New effects appear that one or two species cannot show. A third species can serve as a bath that tunes the others' fragmentation. Even two species that never touch can steer a third through a shared partner. The paper maps these control tricks.
arxiv-2506-13143:
Siqi Ouyang, Xi Xu, and Lei Li describe a speech translation system built at Carnegie Mellon University for a 2025 shared task. The system turns live English speech into Chinese and German text as the words arrive, without waiting for full sentences. Such streaming translation is hard because speech comes in a flow with no clear breaks.

The system pairs a speech encoder that works chunk by chunk with a large language model that writes the translation. Training ran in two stages on robust speech clips drawn from three public data sets. A dial lets users trade speed against accuracy by changing how long the system waits. On the test set, the system scored well on both language pairs, with delays of only a few seconds.
arxiv-2506-13243:
Chuanhong Liu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on semantic communication for tasks. Semantic systems send meaning, not raw bits, to save bandwidth. Large AI models boost meaning extraction but cost heavy compute. That cost clashes with real-time links. The team uses knowledge distillation to shrink the big model into a light one. Standard shrinking is slow and blind to channel state, which hurts it here.

Their fast method stores compressed knowledge ahead of time. That pre-storage skips long inference during shrinking. The design also fits task-oriented goals, where only task-relevant meaning matters. Wireless teams get a light sender that still thinks with big-model knowledge. Drones, cars, and field sensors all need meaning at low power. The paper speaks to that gap between smart models and weak devices.
arxiv-2506-13543: Ofer Gabber and Shizhang Li proved a result in 2025 for families of varieties over a p-adic ring of integers. For a smooth proper family, they show the crystalline torsion in its cohomology can be controlled using its étale torsion. The control also draws on the cohomological degree and the ramification. The technical heart is a boundedness theorem for annihilator ideals of a certain torsion in Breuil-Kisin prismatic cohomology. The authors note that this result may be of independent interest.
arxiv-2506-13643:
Sheron Blair and co-authors chase fault-tolerant quantum computing with continuous-variable gates in a 2025 paper. Machines that encode information in oscillators scale attractively and suit bosonic error correction. A known finite gate set is universal, but nobody had shown those gates alone could build encoded, protected states.

Working with the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill encoding, the team numerically optimized circuits made only of the universal gates to prepare the needed grid states from empty modes. The states came out clean enough that their error rates fell below the threshold for a fault-tolerant memory when combined with stabilizer codes. The gap between universality and fault tolerance narrows.
arxiv-2506-13943:
Andy López-Oquendo, Joseph Hora, David Trilling, and Howard Smith commission an upgraded infrared camera on near-Earth asteroids in two thousand twenty-five. Heat glow reads an asteroid's size and reflectivity well, but ground infrared tools have thinned as upkeep grew hard. The MIRSI camera at the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility was rebuilt to help fill the gap.

First science runs reached out to twelve and a half microns. Forty-two looks at thirty-one near-Earth objects yielded sizes and albedos, with a paired optical camera fixing brightness at the same moment. The team also sized debris from the Didymos impact hours and days after the DART strike. A coming flyby target of Japan's Hayabusa2 mission got its measures too.
arxiv-2506-14043:
Nathaniel Hermann and Shane Hutson present analytic solutions for anomalous diffusion problems, in a two thousand twenty-five physics paper. Diffusion is the spread of mass from place to place. It shows up all through physics and engineering. In many real materials that spread is anomalous. It obeys fractional rules, not the plain rules of the old books.

Past work leaned on computer runs or on hard special functions. Hermann and Hutson give closed-form solutions for the time-fractional cases that come up most. Their answers use Mittag-Leffler and M-Wright functions. They also use generalized fractional error functions that they work out in the paper. They show this kind of spread can be seen as a two-parameter stretched-time process. A hands-on method then turns classic Fickian solutions into anomalous ones. The paper is the first in a planned series.
arxiv-2506-14343:
Titova, Korolkov, and Izmodenov model ripples that can grow along the heliopause, the boundary where the solar wind meets the gas between the stars. Where two flows slide past each other, waves can build in a pattern called the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. Whether that happens at the Sun's boundary affects how the two regions mix.

Their two-dimensional model adds neutral hydrogen atoms, which swap charges with ions as they cross the boundary. That swapping turns out to calm the ripples strongly. As the settings move toward more swapping, the flow changes from unstable to smooth. The flanks of the heliopause are the test ground in their simulations. The results matter for reading data from probes near that frontier.
arxiv-2506-14543:
Bosco Garcia-Archilla, Alicia Garcia-Mascaraque, and Julia Novo wrote this numerical analysis paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on speeding up simulations of spread-and-react processes. Full simulations of such partial differential equations can be huge, so engineers compress them with reduced order models built from snapshots.

Most past error work assumed the simplest time stepping, implicit Euler. This paper studies backward differentiation formulas of orders one through five as the time engine for the reduced model. The authors prove the error shrinks at the matching optimal rate in time. Their snapshots come from finite element runs and are fed in as first-order difference quotients, a choice that is key to pointwise error bounds. The result widens the menu of proven time steppers for reduced models.
arxiv-2506-14743:
Supercomputers waste resources when jobs hold a fixed number of processors while their needs rise and fall. The authors extend a framework for dynamic resource management that lets running MPI jobs grow or shrink. Building on their earlier runtime, they add methods from a second framework: new ways to spawn processes and move data during reconfiguration. Two strategies stand out, merging communicators and reconfiguring without stopping the job, both aimed at cutting memory overhead.

The team tests the enhanced system on a world-class supercomputer with changing workloads. Against static allocation, dynamic management cuts total completion time by 40 percent and raises resource use by over 20 percent. The authors note that such malleability is still rare in production systems because of gaps in standards and ease of use. Their modular design is meant to close those gaps.
arxiv-2506-14843:
Luca Gherardini and co-authors test in 2025 CACTUS, a tool for early staging of a common eye disease of old age. The disease harms the center of the retina and hits millions of older adults. No cure can undo its harm, so early calls count a lot.

Care data are often scant or patchy, which drags model scores down. CACTUS was built to stay clear and open, so users can see why it calls a stage. It weighs gene, food, clinic, and person traits in one frame. The team reports it beat plain models and named key traits that match known medical facts.
arxiv-2506-15343:
Víctor Mayoral-Vilches argues in his 2025 thesis that the best way to guard robots is to attack them first, in a planned and lawful way. He draws on ten years of work with robots. The thesis uses machine learning and game theory to speed up the search for weak points in a robot and the steps used to exploit them.

A core claim is that a robot's design and its safety are two sides of one coin. The same layout that sets what a robot can do also sets where it can be attacked. By mapping that link, defenders can fix weak points before real attackers find them. The work sets out tools and steps for this attack first approach. It is aimed at robot builders and safety teams who want proof, not guesses, about how secure a robot is.
arxiv-2506-15543:
Hristo Papazov and Nicolas Flammarion wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It extends a classic theory of learning in the limit, asking what a learner can grasp when it can also watch how a program runs, not just what it prints.

Gold's framework asks which function classes a learner can pin down from endless examples. Plain input-output views cannot crack the class of all computable functions. The authors add time-bound views and views of an agent's action path. With cost caps, or rough time bounds, the wall falls. Learning from action paths turns out to match learning rational functions from inputs and outputs. A hard note closes the work: no neat test sets exist for fast functions, even with path views.
arxiv-2506-15643:
Xin Chen and co-authors revisit randomness in greedy model building in a 2025 paper. Random forests sample a subset of features at each step, a trick long treated as mere variance control, like shrinkage. That story rests on smooth fitting methods. The team instead studies greedy forward selection, which acts more like a decision tree's adaptive search.

Under a clean design, they prove sampling features can cut both bias and variance at once. Training error and model size can even move non-monotonically as the sampling rate changes, breaking the shrinkage analogy. In the limit, the method reweights least-squares coefficients by rank, with weights following a logistic curve. Randomness inside a greedy search, it turns out, does different work than in smooth fitting.
arxiv-2506-15943:
Bruce Huang and three co-authors present a 2025 paper on how a team of decision-makers can learn together without wasting trials. In bandit problems, an agent picks actions and learns from noisy rewards tied to an unknown rule. Many real settings hold many agents at once, each with a slightly different rule. Working alone ignores the chance to pool lessons. The authors ask what the best possible total regret is when agents collaborate.

They derive a hard lower bound linking regret to the number of agents, rounds, and how much their rules differ. They then give a two-stage algorithm that reaches that bound, using a layered Bayesian model of the differences. The math shows exactly when teamwork pays and how much. The results guide the design of shared learning in settings like personalized medicine and recommendation.
arxiv-2506-16343:
Cedric Moller and Ricardo Usbeck analyze how knowledge graph facts affect relation extraction in a 2025 paper. Relation extraction pulls typed links between entities from text, and graph position may hint at the right link.

The team tests many data sets that vary in relation count, training size, and graph source. Adding graph features lifts scores across the board. Gains are largest when training examples are lopsided across relations. Graph-aware neural methods supply the features, tested in supervised and zero-shot modes. Both modes improve with graph help. The work backs graph context as a cheap boost for text extraction systems.
arxiv-2506-16543:
