Primož Kajdič, Manuela Temmer, and Xochitl Blanco-Cano study how single eruptions from the Sun change the space that later eruptions must cross, in this 2025 arXiv paper. An eruption that sweeps through the space between the planets can clear the path, letting a follower travel faster and keep more of its energy. That clearing is called preconditioning.

The team picked a set of isolated eruptions and compared the solar wind and magnetic field for two days before and after each one. Behind an eruption, the wind was thinner and its pressure lower, while its speed rose and the field grew stronger and more radial. Even slow eruptions reshaped their wake in this way. The results feed better models of space weather.
arxiv-2506-16943:
Botta-Cantcheff, Cruz, and Martinez revisit the birth of the universe in de Sitter holography in a 2025 paper. The famous no-boundary proposal says the cosmos began as a smooth rounding-off, with no past edge. In the better-known anti-de Sitter frame, excited states are easy to build by setting edge terms. De Sitter space has no such natural edge.

The authors ask whether an added boundary can define a family of excited states for the de Sitter ground state. They trace how the Hartle-Hawking recipe fixes the ground state, then test the added-boundary route against holography rules. The work probes the state's family tree.
arxiv-2506-17743:
Julian Golak and co-authors weigh simple lock schedules for canal traffic in a 2025 paper. Water locks pace inland shipping, and tangled schedules breed delay and error. Periodic schedules, repeating on a fixed cycle, are easy to run and predict. Their cost is waiting time when boats arrive off rhythm. The team set out to price that cost.

They first fit a periodic arrival pattern that mimics a real record of irregular traffic. Against that record they judge how well cycle schedules serve the boats. The answer helps lock keepers choose between simplicity and speed with numbers in hand. Predictability itself has value for crews planning long hauls.
arxiv-2506-17843:
Sidhant Kumar Suar and Sarah C. Millholland study planet tilt in a 2025 paper. Tilt shapes a planet's air and its chance to host life. They ask how a young star's own change can push a planet's tilt to large values early on.

A young star is wide and spins fast, so its gravity tugs the planet's orbit in a slow drift. As the star shrinks and slows, that drift rate falls and can meet the planet's spin drift. When the two meet, the planet can be caught and its tilt grows. Planets within one AU are most at risk, though disks, other planets, and tides can shift the outcome.
arxiv-2506-17943:
Counting principles that look identical for real finite sets can come apart inside weak arithmetic, shows Wei Wang in a 2025 arXiv paper. When maps are only definable by formulas of a set complexity, the pigeonhole and Ramsey principles split into a strict ladder of strengths.

Wang places the general pigeonhole principle strictly between a counting principle and its weak sibling, for maps of the stated complexity. He also shows the finite Ramsey theorem for such maps does not yield the weak pigeonhole principle. The results map the fine structure of what weak systems can prove about finite combinatorics.
arxiv-2506-18143:
Lancelot Blanchard, Cameron Holt, and Joseph A. Paradiso present a music system from 2025 that adds harmony to a solo voice. Older tools often need the singer to set a key or play notes on a keyboard. Their system works without that input. It listens to a melody and builds a four-part harmony on its own.

The system joins pitch finding and voice models with trained music models. Together they turn one vocal line into a rich choral sound. The authors set out their methods and share the code online. They also look at uses in live shows and in writing music, and they note that the tool now works offline. Future work aims at real-time use.
arxiv-2506-18543:
Xiaodong Wu and co-authors run a broad security test of large language models in a 2025 paper. Jailbreak attacks craft inputs that trick a model into unsafe output. The team gives the first full test of the DeepSeek family, set against two GPT models on a standard harm benchmark with hundreds of bad requests.

Seven attack styles were tried. DeepSeek resisted some automated optimization attacks but fell more often to hand-crafted and prompt-based tricks, with uneven refusals. The top GPT model held a steadier line, which the authors credit to stronger safety tuning. Readers get a clear trade-off between open model efficiency and safety depth.
arxiv-2506-18643:
Gregory Kehne, Ulrike Schmidt-Kraepelin, and Krzysztof Sornat study in 2025 how to elect committees by approval votes with an eye on the candidates' side. Most work asks whether voters are fairly represented. They ask instead whether like minded candidates get like shares of seats, while keeping voter fairness.

Fixed rules cannot hit that ideal, so they build random rules that stay neutral, reward support, and shift smoothly as votes change. One rule adapts a greedy method with soft random picks and runs fast. It keeps strong fairness after the draw and barely wobbles under small vote changes. Deeper methods in the paper push stability further.
arxiv-2506-18943:
Andrew Kiruluta and Priscilla Burity rebuild vision-language models without two costly parts, in work from 2025. Most such models lean on convolutions to read images and on self-attention to fuse words and images, both heavy at scale. Their model swaps in a spectral dictionary mixer, which codes each patch or word bit as a sparse mix of wave atoms.

The billion-scale test model scored near top marks on image caption tests and fair marks on visual questions. It closed most of the gap to a strong rival while using far fewer weights, less memory, and faster runs. The shared wave code also makes word-image links clear to inspect.
arxiv-2506-19043:
Biao Ma and Lamine Messaci prove a rigidity law for symmetries acting on a class of tree-like spaces, in a 2025 paper. The spaces are median spaces of finite rank, a geometry that blends graph and cube traits. A cocycle twists a group's action by a rule; superrigidity says such twists are far less free than they look. The pair take a dynamical road to the result.

For a product of well-behaved groups, every cocycle into the space's own symmetry group proves rigid. The same holds for Kazhdan groups, whose actions are famously stiff. When the actors are lattices, grids of the product groups, the method yields a fresh proof that their maps into such symmetries are rigid too. The authors present the dynamical route as the engine, reusable past this case. It ties the shape of the space to the shape of the group.
arxiv-2506-19143:
Paul Bogdan and co-authors hunted in 2025 for the sentences that steer a language model's chain of thought. Top models now reason in long written chains, but standard probes read single passes, not unfolding steps. Their black-box method swaps one sentence at a time for a fresh, unlike one, then reruns the chain and scores how much the final answers shift.

Some sentences swayed the whole path far beyond others. The team names these thought anchors; they tend to plan ahead or handle doubt. Set attention heads kept looking back at them from later steps. Links between sentences also foretold task hardness. A deep case study on a hard math problem showed the toolkit in action, and the tool is shared in public.
arxiv-2506-19243:
Yixuan Wang and co-authors train physics-guided networks to high precision in a 2025 paper. Such networks solve equations by folding the physics into their loss. On endless domains, and near blow-up points, plain training lacks the needed sharpness.

Their modular plan weighs net shape, sample spots, and optimizer choice one by one. Paired with proof tools and classic analysis, sharp network solutions can probe whether equations blow up. For a one-dimensional flow case, the frame hits very high precision. For a two-dimensional case tied to famous open problems, loss fell far below prior work with fewer steps. The path points toward machine-level precision.
arxiv-2506-19443:
Jian-Rong Li and Ayush Kumar Tewari connect two areas of algebra and geometry in this two thousand twenty-five paper. On one side stands the Grassmannian cluster algebra, with a prized basis called the dual canonical basis. Its elements match certain tables of numbers, called Young tableaux. On the other side stands a geometric shape, the hypersimplex, which can be cut into pieces in patterned ways. A map from earlier work links the two sides.

The authors show that each tableau induces one of these patterned cuts. For the smallest case, they prove the link is exact: certain prime tableaux match the coarsest cuts. Computer evidence extends the pattern to larger cases. They also guess a formula for counting the finest cuts. The paper deepens the tie between algebra and polyhedral geometry.
arxiv-2506-19743:
Shenbin Qian and co-authors shrink product search embeddings by nesting them, so stores can search huge catalogs faster. Their 2025 paper names the twin demands on shopping search: understand messy user queries and still answer in real time across millions of items. Large embeddings help accuracy but slow every lookup.

Their nested design lets one trained model serve at several embedding sizes, with the smallest running far more cheaply at query time. Training cost stays unchanged, and accuracy improved across several transformer encoders in their tests. The team checked the method under two training losses and on four test sets with hard cases like short, vague queries. Efficiency without an accuracy tax is rare in retrieval, and shops feel both sides daily.
arxiv-2506-20043:
Ahmet Sarigun, Bora Uyar, Vedran Franke, and Altuna Akalin present PocketVina, a docking tool that finds how drug-like molecules fit into protein pockets, in a paper from 2025. Docking must sample poses that are physically valid, a hard task for new or varied targets. Learning-based tools can produce poses that break basic physics.

PocketVina pairs pocket prediction with a search across many pockets at once. On four standard benchmarks, it led in poses that were both close to the true pose and physically valid. It also sorted active from inactive targets in a new set of over 500,000 protein-ligand pairs. The tool needs no task-specific training and uses far less GPU memory than a deep learning rival.
arxiv-2506-20543:
Sanne van Kempen, Jaron Sanders, Fiona Sloothaak, and Maarten Wolf test a learning method for routing work in skill-based queues. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Such queues run call centers, data centers, and cloud services. Each job needs a server with the right skill. A recent reinforcement learning algorithm promised near-optimal routing, but only in theory so far.

The team runs the method on a real-world dataset as a case study. It learns fast and adapts when conditions change. It also beats fixed benchmark rules. A new heuristic rule added by the authors cuts delays further. The method can balance several goals at once, such as profit, fair server load, and shorter waits. The results suggest it could run live.
arxiv-2506-20643:
Gustav Mogull, Jan Plefka, and Kathrin Stoldt compute how much angular momentum two spinning black holes shed as they fly past each other. Such scattering events radiate gravitational waves that carry spin away. Their 2025 study uses worldline quantum field theory, treating each hole as a moving line with quantum fields around it. Paths are solved to second order in the spins. Leading results come in the time domain, the next order in frequency terms.

A fresh family of loop integrals enters the craft. The radiated angular momentum matches known results at the checked order. The framework is built to climb higher. Sharper scattering math feeds the waveform models that observatories match against real signals.
arxiv-2506-20743:
Minh-Hao Van and co-authors survey, in a 2025 paper, how artificial intelligence is reshaping materials science. Foundation models, trained once and adapted widely, promise a break from narrow tools built for one task each. Materials work suits them well, since it spans many data types and scales. The survey covers the models, the AI agents built on them, and the data sets and tools that feed the field.

The authors sort uses into six areas, from mining papers and answering questions to designing new materials and planning processes. They review both single-mode and mixed-mode models, plus robot-run labs that test ideas on their own. Early wins come with clear limits: shaky generalization, murky reasoning, skewed data, and safety worries. The survey ends with directions for growth, including steady learning and better data governance.
arxiv-2506-20843:
Dogon and Vigdorovich present a 2025 mathematics paper linking stability, hyperlinearity, and spectral gap for higher rank lattices. The core claim runs one way: if a certain matrix group is flexibly stable in a Hilbert-Schmidt sense, then it has a non-hyperlinear finite extension. A yes to a sharper question about maps that almost agree would thus give an explicit non-hyperlinear group.

The pair then widen the lens to far-out maps of lattices with strong rigidity traits. There, they prove character rigidity equals a weak form of stability. Spectral gap measures how maps resist drift toward trivial ones. The paper ties three research threads into one frame for group theorists.
arxiv-2506-21243:
Daniel Peralta-Salas, David Perrella, and David Pfefferle disprove a folk belief in a 2025 math paper on curl eigenfields. Woltjer's principle picks field shapes that minimize energy under a twist constraint. Many assumed the lowest such field in a round domain must share that round symmetry.

The team build ring shaped domains with full rotational symmetry in space. In some of them, the first curl eigenfield is indeed symmetric as expected. In others, no first eigenfield is symmetric at all, a sharp split. That means energy minimizers need not inherit the symmetry of their domain. The result settles a long held guess in plasma and fluid math against the folk view.
arxiv-2506-21443:
Fraudsters change their scripts as platforms evolve, and that drift in language, called concept drift, can hide attacks in plain conversation. Şenol, Agrawal, and Liu build a detection system that pairs large language models with structured domain knowledge. Three parts work in sequence: one model flags deceptive conversations, a drift unit checks whether the topic or style has shifted, and a second model judges the shift as harmless or fraudulent.

Tested first on fake reviews and then on a multi-turn dialogue set seeded with fraud and spam, the system reached ninety-eight percent accuracy with a LLaMA-based build. It beat plain zero-shot models clearly. The authors say the domain knowledge cures much of the ambiguity and invention that plague bare models in risky settings. They aim the design at high-stakes monitoring where explanations matter.
arxiv-2506-21543:
Chatterjee and co-authors study a harder version of the hidden clique problem, where a hidden group hides inside a graph whose edges carry real number weights. In the classic problem, the task is to tell a purely random graph from one with a planted tight knit group. Their 2025 paper sets the test as a choice between two hypotheses about how the weights were drawn.

Inside the hidden group, edge weights follow one distribution, and all other edges follow another. The team finds limits on group size for when the two cases can and cannot be told apart, when both distributions are known. With only partial knowledge, they still bound the best possible error. Fast spectral tests succeed once the group is large enough.
arxiv-2506-21743:
Jinpai Zhao and co-authors taught in 2025 a neural network to forecast storm surge by painting it in color. Surge flooding is a coastal killer, yet earlier machine learning forecasts were coarse, station-bound, or brittle in new places. Their method projects messy water-height fields onto structured images, encoding height in red-green-blue values. A convolutional memory network then predicts the movie of the flood.

Real wind fields drive the model as time-varying input, and the shape of the seafloor enters as a fixed map. Training used a large set of synthetic storms in the Gulf of Mexico. Forecasts stayed robust a full forty-eight hours out along the Texas coast. The model also carried to other coastal regions without retraining. The authors pitch the color trick as a bridge between physics data and image-based AI.
arxiv-2506-22043:
Yun-Peng Li and co-authors let a gamma-ray burst's jet wobble at a pace set by its own feeding. Jets from these explosions can precess like a slowing top, stamping pulses on the light curve. Earlier studies fixed the wobble period by hand. Here the period grows out of fallback matter raining onto the black hole and the disk that rain builds.

In the model, the period first drops fast during the early fallback rush, then lengthens almost linearly as the disk settles. Thick, sticky disks and slow black hole spin stretch the period further. Fitted to real multi-pulse bursts, the model naturally yields pulses that spread apart and widen with time, in both long and short bursts. Geometry tunes how tall each pulse stands.
arxiv-2506-22143:
Muhammad Umar Farooq and Oscar Saz improve speech recognition for mixed Arabic and English in this 2025 paper. Speakers often switch tongues mid-sentence, and training data for such speech is scarce. Self-taught speech models also vary a lot across Arabic dialects.

Their fix splices real audio clips into fake mixed speech, a dataset they call SAGE. Fine-tuning with that data cut word errors by 7.8 points on mixed benchmarks. A replay trick kept the model from forgetting older skills. Adding a simple word model cut mean errors further. The work shows fake data can stand in for scarce real speech.
arxiv-2506-22743:
Chenyang Wang and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on materials whose behavior depends on the shape of the sample itself. In non-Hermitian lattices, energy can leak, and the spectrum under open edges can change with the sample's geometry even for huge samples. Why this happens had no general answer.

The catalog record carries the title above, while the paper's own head names it General theory for geometry-dependent non-Hermitian bands. The authors build a band theory for higher dimensions based on strip Brillouin zones, which track the spectrum as the lattice grows axis by axis. Shape dependence, they show, comes from those zones disagreeing with each other. A crisp test follows: geometry matters exactly when the complex spectrum covers nonzero area. The criterion opens a path into shape-aware physics.
arxiv-2506-22943:
Siyun Liang and six co-authors raised the rate of a meaning-compressed transmission through a fluid antenna, in a paper published in 2025. Meaning-based sends ship the gist of data, not each bit, to save bandwidth. Their base station holds still antennas; the user holds one whose ports can switch on in a grid, near the base. Three dials must be tuned as one: the beam shape, the compression rate, and the port choices.

Their alternating method tunes each in turn. At each step the best compression rate falls out in closed form. Simulation runs support the gains of the method under a set power limit. The team presents fluid antennas as a gain for gist sends in tight near fields.
arxiv-2506-23343:
Mu-Chun Chen, Xueqi Li, Xiang-Gan Liu, and Michael Ratz investigated in 2025 how fermion mass hierarchies can arise in models with modular flavor symmetries. Why particle masses span such wide ranges is a long-standing puzzle. Their key tool is that mass matrix determinants transform as one-dimensional vector-valued modular forms.

Under fairly general assumptions, they show that getting strongly ranked masses forces the modulus value to sit near one of three critical points. They revisit the universal behavior near those points and classify the hierarchies that arise at two of them. The classic Froggatt-Nielsen mechanism is compared with its modular form, and limits on expansion coefficients prove key to predictive power.
arxiv-2506-23543:
Hui Li and co-authors speed up image generation by changing how it is chopped into tokens as it is cleaned from noise. Diffusion transformers split the image into patches, and the patch size sets how many tokens the model must process. The design uses one patch size throughout. Their method, PPFlow, uses large patches early, when the image is noisy, and small patches late, when detail forms. A separate learned projection handles each patch size.

The approach works on the full image representation and needs no re-noising. Trained from scratch, it ran about one and a half to two times faster than a comparable model at similar image quality. Starting from a pre-trained model did even better with little extra training. The authors release code and a trained checkpoint. The savings matter because these models are slow and costly to run.
arxiv-2506-23843:
Joris Bekkers presents a 2025 paper on reading team formations in soccer from player tracking data. Coaches and analysts want to know which shape a team is using and which role each player fills. The method he describes, called EFPI, answers both questions by matching players to set formation templates.

EFPI scales the real player positions to match each template, then finds the match that keeps total distance lowest. The template with the lowest cost is picked as the formation for that moment. The same approach works on one frame or on longer stretches, such as a full period or a short spell of play. An optional setting stops the label from flipping when two shapes score almost the same. The code is shared openly in a Python package.
arxiv-2507-00743:
An Le and co-authors classify eye surgery type from post operative scans with a neural network in a 2025 paper, based on the head byline. The task is to tell whether an epiretinal membrane operation also removed the inner limiting membrane, or the membrane alone. Their model builds on a standard image network and reads center scans from optical coherence tomography.

Cleaning steps such as energy cropping and wavelet denoising lifted accuracy from the raw scans. Two tunable wavelet unit designs were then built into the network, letting filter values adjust during training. One design pushed accuracy higher still. The units sat in downsampling, strided convolution, and pooling layers.
arxiv-2507-01043:
Szymon Świderski and Agnieszka Jastrzębska present a way to build a neural network that grows and shrinks as it trains, rather than keeping a fixed shape set by hand. The shape of a network matters as much as its weights, yet most work fixes the shape in advance.

A search method drawn from game play tries out changes to the shape and picks the best. It can change each input stream on its own, which helps with data that have many streams over time. Tests on image and time based tasks gave strong results. Code is shared so others can repeat the work.
arxiv-2507-01143:
Reza Jalayer and co-authors review in 2025 how robots can locate where a sound comes from, with a focus on deep learning methods. Knowing a sound's origin helps a robot navigate, talk with people, and watch the health of machines. Older surveys covered sound work in general, not the limits robots face on small bodies with few microphones.

The review first covers classic methods that use arrival time gaps, beam steering, and signal subspace tricks. It then turns to learned methods, from plain neural networks to layered and attention based designs. Data sets and training plans get their own deep look, since they anchor learned performance. Studies are sorted by robot type and use case. Open problems named include noise robustness, many sources at once, and the tight size and power limits of real robots.
arxiv-2507-01443: Schmidt and Umeda check how grid Dirac math tools near their smooth kin in this twenty twenty-five paper. The grid tools live on cube nets in three-space, while the smooth kin rule free mote flow in the same frame. They prove the grid tools do draw close to the smooth ones in the strong sense, yet not in the stricter norm sense.
arxiv-2507-01943:
Ethan Silver and co-authors use machine learning and a space telescope to find very small gravitational lenses in 2025. A lens bends light from a far galaxy around a near mass. Small lenses probe low mass halos that test dark matter models. Past searches miss them since their rings are tiny.

Forecasts use a fake lens catalog and deep source lists. A neural net trained on simulations finds near all standard lenses. A second model pinpoints the tiny ones that humans cannot see. Rates suggest the telescope can find many per square degree. Tests on older telescope images found two missed candidates. The work shows machine aid can beat human search here.
arxiv-2507-02643:
Diego Corrêa da Silva and Dietmar Jannach survey a decade of work on calibrated recommendations, in a 2025 paper. A recommender is calibrated when the mix of items it suggests matches the mix of tastes in a user's own history. Without calibration, systems drift toward a narrow slice of what a person likes. Researchers have lately used calibration to fight sameness, bias, and unfairness in suggestions.

The survey reviews the technical recipes for achieving calibration, from post-processing suggestion lists to training with calibration in mind. It also gathers the evidence on whether calibration helps in practice, and for which goals. A closing section lists the limits and snags that builders meet when shipping calibration in real products. The paper serves as a map for a fast-growing corner of recommender research.
arxiv-2507-02743:
Five authors, Mélanie Gaillochet, Mehrdad Noori, Sahar Dastani, Christian Desrosiers, and Hervé Lombaert, wrote this 2025 paper on cheaper training for medical image segmentation. Tracing organs pixel by pixel takes expert time and costs a lot. Box outlines around a target are far quicker to draw, so methods that learn from boxes are in demand.

Vision foundation models can segment well when a user gives a prompt, such as a point or a box. Prompt learning adapts such models to a task and cuts user input. Past prompt learning, though, still needs full pixel masks for training. The new frame joins the two ideas: it learns to make its own prompts for a foundation model using only box outlines as training labels. That pairing could bring strong segmentation to clinics that cannot afford dense annotation.
arxiv-2507-03243:
Zifei Wang and co-authors read driver reviews to learn what makes a charge stop good or bad, in a study from 2025. Charge stops shape how it feels to own an electric car, and poor stops slow the shift to clean cars. The team mined near 17,000 Google Maps reviews of stops.

A chat model sorted each review by topic and tone. Twelve topics came out, from access and uptime to price and snacks near the stop. Two score models then guessed star marks, one for each driver and one for each stop as a whole. A game-based tool ranked the weight of each topic. Warm words on place and perks lifted marks most, while sour words on breaks and upkeep sank them. The map gives stop owners a clear fix list.
arxiv-2507-03443:
Hui-Min Wang works the paths and slow turns of balls round a spin hole in a bent gravity tale. The work dates to 2025. The tale adds a field part to the stock hole form, with a dial for its strength. Round-ish paths that tilt off the flat plane frame the test.

A path math form gives the kept counts for such paths. The last firm path of each tilt shifts with the dial and the hole's spin. Two turn rates are worked out: the plane's slow swing and the path's own creep. The swing grows with spin and dial, while the creep trades the two off. A spin-top probe adds a third read of the dial.
arxiv-2507-03543:
Boyang Wang and co-authors introduce H2HTalk in a 2025 paper on judging chatbots that act as emotional companions. More people turn to large language models for comfort and support, yet tests of how safe and caring these systems are have lagged behind the models. The benchmark looks at both personality growth and warm, understanding replies.

The test set holds more than four thousand crafted scenes, spanning chats, memory of past talks, and planning tasks that mirror real support talks. A safety module based on attachment theory aims to keep exchanges healthy. The team ran fifty models through the same protocol. Long-term planning and memory stood out as weak points, mostly when user needs were unstated or shifted mid-chat. All materials are released for others to use.
arxiv-2507-03643:
Jackson and five co-authors wrote this paper in twenty twenty-five on dust devils. These spinning dust columns occur on both Earth and Mars. A devil's width sets how much dust it lifts into the air. Yet what fixes a devil's width, and how widths are spread across a population, has stayed unclear.

The authors propose that widths follow a power law tied to a simple physical picture. Fits to several published Mars datasets support that form. They also model devils as heat engines. From that model, the number of devils per unit area scales with their efficiency and the heat flowing from the ground. The results help estimate how much dust devils add to the air of both planets.
arxiv-2507-03743:
Marcus Högås and Edvard Mörtsell test a modified theory of gravity against new cosmic data in a 2025 paper. The data combine galaxy distance measures, the faint glow left from the early universe, and exploding stars used as distance markers. A live question is whether dark energy changes over time.

One common model lets dark energy vary, and it fits the data somewhat better than a fixed value. But that model worsens the clash between two measures of how fast the universe expands. The authors' bimetric gravity, which uses two linked measures of space, fits better and eases that clash at the same time. The paper makes a case for taking the modified theory seriously as data sharpen.
arxiv-2507-03843:
Hospital cost models must stay readable, accurate, and stable year to year, but fine-grained diagnosis codes sabotage stability: thousands of ICD-10 codes appear so rarely that their fitted costs swing wildly. Chi-Ken Lu, David Alonge, Nicole Richardson, and Bruno Richard show in 2025 that the fix can be simple — merge codes by truncating them.

Cutting codes from seven characters to six or fewer shrinks the regression while keeping every diagnostic family represented. Unlike ridge penalties, nothing gets discarded. The authors prove why it works: merging predictors raises the trace of the Hessian matrix, which directly lowers the variance of the estimates. The result also explains, they note, why health systems already favor broad groupings like DRGs over raw codes in real-world risk adjustment.
arxiv-2507-04043:
Kai Deng tests how the style of an AI helper changes how well students solve simple coding tasks, in a 2025 study. Chatbots now sit inside many school tools, yet little is known about how they should talk with learners. Deng compares three styles of the same model: passive, which answers only when asked; proactive, which offers tips on its own; and collaborative, which trades ideas back and forth.

Fifteen high school students each solved three problems, one under each style. Students finished fastest with the collaborative helper, and they rated it highest for satisfaction and felt help. The passive and proactive styles trailed on both counts. How an AI speaks, Deng argues, matters as much as what it knows, above all for beginners.
arxiv-2507-04143:
A lone stranger atom in a cold atom cloud dresses itself in the cloud's waves and walks as one heavy guest, till the grip grows strong and the guest falls apart. The authors, a five-name team writing in 2025, build a spare tale of that fall. Their guest is allowed one cloud partner in its dress, the part lab probes see best. The dress can rot into states with more partners, priced by a ghost term in the grip.

The spare tale was first checked against a richer one that allows two partners, and it held. It then matched two fresh lab studies, one on the guest's glow and one on its wild swings out of balance. The team offer the frame as a fast lens for lab data on a hard many-body guest.
arxiv-2507-04343:
Tudor Octavian Pocola and co-authors present an energy systems paper, published in 2025, on sharing a large grid battery with a local energy community. Big batteries earn money by stacking several services for the power grid, while communities of homes with their own solar panels also need storage for flexibility. The paper studies a rental model where the community buys capacity from the battery operator.

The authors give a method to size and price the rented share so both sides gain. They test flat and dynamic tariffs and rival grid uses, and they review linear optimization models for running the battery day by day. Older daily window methods are shown to have practical limits that their analysis helps planners avoid.
arxiv-2507-04543:
Hsuan-Wei Lee and co-authors show in 2025 that smarter, context aware punishment can hold cooperation at lower cost than flat fines. In public goods games, uniform fines do stop cheating, but enforcers pay heavily, and that cost invites a second round of free riding on the enforcers themselves. A harsher stick is not the fix, they argue.

Their spatial game adds norm responsive punishers next to standard ones. These fine at double rate, at double cost, only when at least half the local group already cooperates. Large simulations on grids found full removal of defectors at fine levels below what uniform enforcement needs. The gain comes from saving effort inside cheater zones and striking hard at the borders where cooperation meets defection. Those borders then grow like fronts, spreading prosocial play across the grid.
arxiv-2507-04643:
Oleg Titov estimates the instantaneous Earth rotation velocity direct in two thousand twenty-five. Very long baseline interferometry tracks Earth with distant radio sources. Its standard reads are group delay and fringe frequency. Group delay serves most geodesy work, while fringe frequency sits ignored.

Titov shows fringe frequency can gauge spin speed on its own. Thirty years of routine data feed daily estimates from it. Two pole angles come out day by day with tiny formal error. Plain least squares does the analysis on the big network data. The series can track spin wobble beside classic length of day values.
arxiv-2507-04743:
Manuel de León and Rubén Izquierdo-López extend a classic tool of physics. Poisson brackets describe how quantities change in mechanics, and they sit at the heart of field theories as well. The authors build a theory of extensions for graded versions of these brackets, set inside graded Dirac manifolds, a layered geometric frame that mixes smooth structure with algebra.

They then show what the extension buys. The field equations of a chosen theory fall out of the bracket setup, and so does the time behavior of forms of any order built on the field. The result mirrors the role plain brackets play in mechanics, where one bracket generates the motion of the whole system. The paper is pure theory, aimed at giving field theory a cleaner geometric base.
arxiv-2507-04843:
Francesco Giorgino and co-authors wrote a 2025 physics paper on bursts of many photons from a quantum dot. Shining a tuned light on an atom, real or made, is a prime way to make non-classic light. Most work chases single photons, yet bursts of more are always there in the glow.

Their atom is a semiconductor dot set in a tiny pillar cavity, pumped by short light pulses. By counting matches up to fourth order, they caught up to four photons from a single pulse. Fine time reads tracked how the bursts unfold. They also give a time gate trick that purifies a single photon source while keeping its yield high. The work sharpens the map of photon emission in driven systems.
arxiv-2507-05143:
Mingtao Xia and Qijing Shen offer a new way to train neural networks that mimic random fields in a 2025 paper. Random fields model things that vary by chance across space, from soil traits to weather. Rebuilding such a model from data is a core task in uncertainty work.

Their method rests on a broadened distance measure that handles mixed data, both smooth values and fixed categories at once. They prove the network can match target fields under mild conditions. Training uses a local form of the loss that keeps computation light. Tests on several uncertainty tasks show the approach works in practice. Engineers get a faster route to simulators that respect both kinds of data.
arxiv-2507-05443:
Ashwin Rao, Sze Yuh Nina Wang, and Kristina Lerman study gender gaps in online talk about reproductive rights. Their 2025 paper draws on millions of posts on a major social platform after a landmark United States court ruling on abortion in 2022. The ideological split on abortion is well known, but how gender and place interact was less clear.

Using inferred traits of posters, they find gender shapes attitudes and emotional tone beyond ideology alone. The gap between men and women grew wider in conservative regions. A leaked draft of the ruling spurred a surge in posting, led by pro-abortion women in places where access was under threat. The study shows public talk in a crisis is structured by identity and place, not party lines alone.
arxiv-2507-05643:
Huzaifa Unjhawala and co-authors present a physics-based simulator for vehicles and tools moving through soil, built into the Chrono engine. Older terramechanics formulas are semi-empirical and fail on digging, grading, or wheels with complex lugs. Their model, Chrono CRM, treats soil as a continuum of interacting particles using smoothed particle hydrodynamics.

The terrain can push back on rigid and flexible machines alike inside the same simulation. The team validates the model against three physical tests, including one with NASA's MGRU3 rover. Benchmarks against a high-fidelity discrete method check its speed. Engineers gain a versatile sandbox for designing off-road robots and planetary rovers.
arxiv-2507-05843:
Yue Peng and co-authors present an AI method that fakes a lab stain on tissue images, in a 2025 paper. Pathologists stain tissue to reveal key proteins, but the process is slow and costly. Virtual staining aims to turn a standard image into the stained one. When the paired images come from nearby slices, their shapes differ, which breaks simple mapping.

Their method, USIGAN, moves features between image types without needing exact position matches. It draws out the overall shape meaning of the tissue first. That avoids forced one-to-many links between slices. The result should keep the medical meaning of the real stain. Faster, cheaper virtual stains could widen access to advanced tissue tests.
arxiv-2507-05943:
Krainov and co-authors examine a burst of light from a quantum dot in a 2025 physics paper. The dot, a tiny charged speck in an optical cavity, was driven by laser pulses of a set size. The light it gives off forms groups of several photons at once, and the team asked what those groups are made of.

Tests varying pulse length and cavity tuning show the burst mixes two kinds of photons. Some are emitted by the dot itself, and others are laser photons scattered off it, combined in a coherent way. Their model, which includes both scattering and re-excitation of the dot, matches the measured statistics of the bursts. The work clarifies a source of multi-photon states for quantum optics.
arxiv-2507-06143:
Sheldon Dantas and co-authors prove that the Daugavet property and its polynomial form are the same for Banach spaces. This property governs how operators nearly reach their norm. A long-standing open problem asked if the polynomial version is stronger.

Their proof leans on a geometric picture of the property. That picture was first stated with the weak topology. It stays valid when the weaker polynomial topology replaces it. The same trick shows linear centers are polynomial centers too. A weak operator version also implies its polynomial twin. New examples follow for tensor products of spaces. Those products now gain the property in fresh cases. The note closes a chapter in Banach space theory.
arxiv-2507-06243:
Md Nahid Hasan, Md Monzur Murshed, Md Mahadi Hasan, and Faysal Ahmed Chowdhury build machine learning models that predict which breast cancer treatment a patient is likely to get. Choice of treatment is made hard by the varied nature of the disease. Choices rest on many factors tied to each patient. The study uses The Cancer Genome Atlas breast cancer clinical data set.

The models predict the chance of chemotherapy or hormonal therapy. They are trained with five-fold cross-validation. They are gauged on accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, sensitivity, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating curve. Bootstrap methods gauge model doubt, while SHAP values aid reading by naming key predictors. Among the models tested, gradient boosting hit the highest stable scores. It beat two other boosting methods.
arxiv-2507-06743: Dorin Popescu gives a short account of a special case of Zariski's uniformization theorem in prime characteristic, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The note is mainly an exposition. It treats extensions of valuation rings seen as a filtered union of smooth algebras. That view is the core of the uniformization claim in this setting.
arxiv-2507-06843:
Neeraj Kumar Tomar and co-authors add new separation axioms to topology. Topology studies spaces through their open sets, and separation axioms say how well points and sets can be told apart. The authors build two new families from special kinds of open sets. One family rests on sets they call SC-star open, and the other on H-star open sets.

The first family holds four kinds of spaces, in strong and weak forms. The second family holds three kinds, marked with subscripts from the classic scale. The authors prove basic traits of each new kind and show how they relate. Such sorting helps map the fine ladder of space types that pure math uses.
arxiv-2507-07043:
Haris Khan and co-authors review smart hearing aids in a 2025 paper. Older aids mostly made all sound louder, which left speech hard to follow in noise. New aids use deep learning to cut noise in a selective way and keep the voice a user wants.

The review sums up model types, chip and hardware choices, clinic tests, and user needs. Recent models scored large gains on noisy tests and some now run in real time with low delay. Gaps remain in power use, changing rooms and streets, and fitting each user. The authors call for lighter models, steady learning on the device, and shared test rules before wider clinic use.
arxiv-2507-07143:
Karthik Pappu and co-authors model how computer worms spread using scientific machine learning in this 2025 paper. Classic epidemic-style equations miss the feedback loops of real networks, while pure neural models hide their reasoning. The team compared three approaches on data from the famous Code Red worm outbreak.

A hybrid method, which embeds a small neural network inside the classic equations, cut prediction error by nearly half against both rivals. The team then translated the learned feedback into plain formulas. Those formulas revealed brakes on spread, such as network saturation, security response, and worm mutation. The authors say hybrid models can sharpen early warning and response planning.
arxiv-2507-07243:
Kyle Celano leads a team of seven on this combinatorics paper from two thousand twenty-five. It counts parking functions where each car stops at most a fixed steps past its wished-for spot.

A parking function's displacement counts how far each car must drive on. The team sorts these ℓ-interval functions by inversion, displacement, and major index. For the tightest case they find a cyclic sieving effect at fixed displacement. Closed forms count that case by inversion count. They also show a classic map of Foata keeps the set intact just at the extremes of ℓ. There, inversion and major index turn out to be spread alike.
arxiv-2507-07543:
Chen Amiraz and four co-authors study why retrieval-augmented generation systems falter when a user's question and the document that answers it are written in different languages. Their paper came out in 2025. The test setting pairs Arabic and English, using real corporate documents rather than the open web.

Every combination of question language and document language was tried. Performance dropped substantially whenever the two languages differed. The failure sits in the retrieval step itself: the retriever ranks foreign-language documents badly, so the generator never sees the right page. Two simple fixes helped a lot: force equal retrieval from both languages, or translate the question first. The authors say cross-language retrieval deserves direct attention in practical systems.
arxiv-2507-08143:
Vivek Chari and Benjamin Van Durme present a 2025 method to shrink the memory cache of a large language model with little loss. Models now take in very long texts, and the cache that stores past word states grows huge. Cutting that cache in a smart way is key to running such models at low cost.

Their method scores each past word by its weight for future words and keeps the top ones, with no training and no need to know the next query. It matched rival methods while keeping a fifth fewer words. A tuning step finds how far a given text can be squeezed before quality drops. With that step, the cache fell by 68 in 100 on a long-text test set with no loss. Tests span 27 tasks and two model families.
arxiv-2507-08243:
Chandra Sekhar Mukherjee, Joonyoung Bae, and Jiapeng Zhang present CoreSPECT, a framework that boosts clustering methods. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a pattern in real data. Density and geometry often correlate in layered ways. Ground-truth groups tend to sit inside a multi-layered manifold structure. Standard clustering tools often miss that structure.

CoreSPECT runs a base clustering method on chosen core regions first. It then extends the partial grouping to the full dataset. A neighborhood graph carries labels outward layer by layer. Early theory supports the design under the authors' model. Large tests covered nineteen datasets, from images to genomics. The framework lifted scores for methods like K-Means. It offers a general add-on rather than a single new algorithm.
arxiv-2507-08443:
Georgios Balanos and three colleagues present KGRAG-Ex, a system that makes retrieval-augmented generation easier to explain. Such systems ground language model answers in outside sources, but readers cannot see why a source was picked. Knowledge graphs offer a fix, since their entities and links form clear paths.

The system builds a domain knowledge graph by prompting models to extract facts. For each query, it finds key entities and paths, then turns them into short plain-language passages that steer retrieval. Perturbation tests then check which graph parts most shaped the answer. Experiments probe how sensitive these explanations are and how graph position relates to influence.
arxiv-2507-08543:
Jianhao He and John Lui give quantum algorithms for sparse optimization in twenty twenty-five. The problem is projection-free convex optimization with sparsity constraints. It covers many tasks in machine learning and data science. The authors treat both vector and matrix domains.

For vectors, two quantum algorithms find near-optimal solutions with fewer queries than the best classical method. The savings reach a factor tied to the square root of the dimension, or even the full dimension. For matrices under nuclear norm constraints, two more algorithms speed up the update step. Their gains also scale with dimension. Sparsity here means most entries stay zero, which keeps solutions simple. Readers get quantum speedups for a workhorse optimization family.
arxiv-2507-08843:
Arpita Soni and co-authors propose a way to predict where a person will go next without taking their data off their device. Their 2025 paper joins federated learning, which trains models locally, with large language models. Location data is deeply personal, so central storage is a privacy risk.

Their system keeps user data on the device and uses a compact product trick to tap language model skill. It was tested on four public movement data sets drawn from location-sharing services. Scores led the field on each set, the authors report. The system also cut model size and memory use by large shares. The work speaks to app builders who want useful forecasts for maps and transport without pooling raw traces.
arxiv-2507-08943:
Pedro Lopes, Paola Accioly, Paulo Borba, and Vitor Menezes compare two ways teams use Git, the code tracking tool, to build software. One way keeps many side branches with set roles, while the other sends all changes to one shared branch. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Branch based flow, with GitFlow as the best known case, moves code from lone branches toward the main branch as it matures. Trunk based flow skips those steps. The authors gather proof on how developers in Brazil work with each flow and what helps or blocks each one. Their aim is to guide teams that must trade speed against code quality.
arxiv-2507-09343:
Charles Cadieux and co-authors finish mapping a nearby planetary system in a 2025 astronomy paper. Around a small red star, the space telescope TESS found three transiting planets on tight orbits, and ground spectrographs added a fourth; the worlds span Earth-like to possibly water-rich.

Sixteen fresh sectors of telescope data plus reprocessed precision velocity measurements, cleaned of the star's own activity, sharpened every planet's size. Transit timing wobbles pinned down masses and orbit shapes. A fifth planet emerged from the analysis, sitting in the star's habitable zone. The system becomes a prime target for atmospheric study with the largest telescopes.
arxiv-2507-09443:
A nuclear fuel rod's inner heat and stress cannot be measured directly while a reactor runs, yet knowing them could prevent failures. Luiz Aldeia Machado and co-authors build a machine learning route to that knowledge in this 2025 paper. Simulations from two established fuel codes generated the training data, spanning eleven runs at varied power levels.

A convolutional network learned to infer the rod's full temperature field from a few readings on the cladding surface. It trained for over a thousand rounds without overfitting and predicted temperatures with high accuracy. Those temperatures then fed a mechanics model that computed stress and strain. The authors aim at real-time monitoring tools for predictive maintenance in power plants.
arxiv-2507-09743:
Riano Giribaldi and five co-authors ask how evenly the early Milky Way was enriched with new elements. Their twenty twenty-five paper looks at the oldest, most metal-poor stars in the galaxy's halo. Stars born then carry the chemical marks of the first rounds of star death.

Many past charts show wide scatter in the ratio of magnesium to iron for these stars. That scatter was read as proof that early enrichment was patchy. With sharper measures of the stars and modern 3D models, the team finds the spread is narrow in a key range. Their read: the early enrichment in magnesium was more uniform than thought.
arxiv-2507-09943:
Chemical reaction networks, where many species react in shared steps, are awkward to model as ordinary graphs. Shesha Gopal Marehalli Srinivas and co-authors build a random network model that keeps the true structure, called a hypergraph, in this 2025 paper. Their model also tracks the atoms inside each species, so the networks stay chemically sensible.

The paper splits connectedness into two senses that match for graphs but part ways for hypergraphs. One sense governs what an open network can keep making at steady state. The other governs what can be built from a starting set in a closed network. Both senses switch on sharply, like a phase change, as networks grow. The results argue for modeling reactions on their own terms.
arxiv-2507-10143:
David Calhas and Arlindo Oliveira add deep recurrence to dynamical segmentation models. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes a gap between brains and neural networks. Brains refine perception over time through feedback loops. Most networks, by contrast, process input in one static pass. A predictive coding inspired loop is proposed to close that gap.

The loop runs from output back to input inside a U-Net. Two biology-inspired operations keep the feedback stable. Softmax projection and exponential decay serve that steadying role. Tests used a controlled synthetic segmentation task. The feedback model beat its feedforward twin under noise. It also learned from far fewer examples in trials. Findings support feedback for robustness and data efficiency.
arxiv-2507-10243:
Hao Zhou, Si-Qiang Luo and Xiang Liu revisit the spectra of triply heavy baryons, particles made of three heavy quarks, in 2025. Working in the nonrelativistic quark model, they use the Gaussian expansion method to compute masses up to D-wave states with full angular momentum mixing.

Their masses for the lowest states agree well with lattice QCD calculations, while excited states come out systematically lighter than lattice values. From the wave functions they also estimate radiative decay widths, which differ notably from earlier theory. Along the way they correct several misconceptions in past work about symmetry rules and wave function construction. The results give experimental searches a sharper map of where these rare particles should appear.
arxiv-2507-10843:
Motoki Omura and co-authors keep a learning agent from wandering away from its training data. In offline reinforcement learning, the agent must improve using only past records, since fresh trials may be costly, as in robotics. If its choices drift outside the records, its guesses turn unreliable. Many methods penalize that drift by comparing action frequencies, a measure that can misread actions never seen before.

Their method instead measures drift as a distance between action distributions, using transport maps built from special neural networks, which avoids the instability of adversarial training. On a standard benchmark suite it matched or beat widely used rivals. Code is public.
arxiv-2507-11143:
Lam Pham and eight co-authors build a neural network that spots and outlines landslides in satellite imagery. Landslides are growing more frequent with extreme weather and land misuse, yet watching for them over huge, rugged areas is hard for people. An automatic system could scan remote sensing images as they arrive.

Their architecture, RMAU-NET, adds residual blocks and multi-head attention to a U-Net design. It handles both detection and pixel-level segmentation in one model. On three benchmark datasets the system posted strong F1 and overlap scores. The authors present it as an end-to-end tool for monitoring landslide events over large terrain.
arxiv-2507-11343:
Farhan Shah and a large team analyze light pollution across the northern Netherlands in this two thousand twenty-five report. They draw on a network of sky quality meters that track night sky brightness. Data span from two thousand twenty to two thousand twenty-three. The team joined the ground readings with satellite cloud data. Their region also covers part of the German Wadden Coast.

They ranked yearly brightness changes at twenty-seven sites. In the darkest areas, sky glow is growing by roughly three to seven percent per year. Clouds matter, since they bounce city light back down and brighten the sky. The report tracks this indirect form of light pollution in detail. Its findings can guide local policy to protect dark skies and the species that need them.
arxiv-2507-11543:
Iman Reihanian, Yunfei Hou, Yu Chen, and Yifei Zheng review how tools that make text and code are used in teaching computer science. Their review, from two thousand twenty-five, centers on truth, real work, and fair tests.

The tools speed work and aid fresh ideas by students. Yet they can state false things with ease, spread errors, hold bias, and blur the line between a student's work and the tool's. The authors stress that human eyes must stay in the loop. The works they read urge mixed tests that join tool and human marks, tools to spot bias, and skill in the use of such tools for both students and staff.
arxiv-2507-12143:
Pavel Šindelář and Ondřej Bojar report in 2025 on a shared task that casts language models as teacher, student, and examiner in turn. The Sensemaking task asks models to make sense of a text in three exam like steps: write questions, answer them, and score the answers. All steps must stick to given source materials.

Seven sources fed the 2025 round, from fact check analyses to lecture transcripts, in four languages. Four teams entered, and shop bought models served as baselines. A fully automatic grading scheme was checked against a light human one. Odd gaps in what automatic grades reward are among the findings.
arxiv-2507-12243:
Aznabayev and co-authors compute the spectra of the last unstudied hydrogen molecular ions in a 2025 physics paper. The ions, DT+ and T2+, contain heavy forms of hydrogen. Fine work for them had not been done, unlike for their lighter cousins, so this gap had stayed open for years.

The team solved the Schroedinger equation in a variational way for a wide range of states of vibration and rotation. They reached the highest such state that can exist, with spectroscopic precision. They also computed transition strengths, relativistic corrections, and hyperfine structure constants. Such values guide lab work on rare tritium-bearing molecules and test quantum theory at high accuracy.
arxiv-2507-12343:
M Rybakov and M Shcherbakov measure the cost of reasoning in modal logics with a convergence rule in this 2025 paper. Many modal and intuitionistic logics are already hard with few variables in play. Adding an axiom that forces paths to converge shifts that cost in unclear ways.

The pair study four logics built by adding the convergence axiom to standard bases. Two of them stay fully hard even with just two variables allowed. Two others reach the same hardness with a single variable. The results stretch to wide families of related logics as well. Knowing these bounds tells tool builders how much reasoning power a tiny language can still demand.
arxiv-2507-12443:
Rajdeep Mondal and co-authors flag a quiet flaw in AI-built network settings in a 2025 paper. Language models can draft route maps and access lists, the rule sets that steer network traffic. Made-up facts get the blame for bad drafts, yet a deep snag is vague user intent. Rule sets overlap in the traffic they cover, so which rule wins is a choice no model can guess. Counts from a large cloud show rule sets with hundreds of such overlaps.

Their test system, Clarify, adds a part that asks the user sharp questions. Once the user clears the fog, the system builds the rules step by step and checks them. The authors say the fog-clear step fits far past networks. Any task where parts can join in more than one sound way needs it.
arxiv-2507-12543:
Amir Raz and Merna Youssef present a 2025 paper on a late-time pattern in a toy model of quantum chaos. The model, a scaled SYK setup, can be drawn as chord webs, and its energy level stats show a slow ramp at late times. The team works the ramp out by hand from those webs.

A double-trace link is first split into single-trace pairs over a base of operators. The right operators behind the ramp are named, first in the plain limit, then at full strength. The late-time form checks out, and a trumpet-shaped count falls out as a bonus.
arxiv-2507-13143:
The tools that make measurements deserve a place in the record of science, argue Muhammad Haris, Sören Auer, and Markus Stocker in a 2025 paper. Details about research instruments, their settings, calibrations, and uses, are scattered across sources or missing entirely, which weakens how data get read.

The team proposes a scholarly knowledge graph that gathers instrument descriptions from many sources and links them to the papers, data sets, and facilities they touch. With those links in place, researchers can trace which instrument produced which result and plan new experiments on firmer ground. The graph also opens a way to measure how much a given instrument shapes a field, a kind of credit that catalogs rarely assign.
arxiv-2507-13243:
Swapping one element for another inside a crystal can retune its magnetism, sometimes with surgical precision. Jacob Fritsky and co-authors grew a samarium skutterudite crystal and replaced tin with germanium step by step. The crystal offers two distinct tin seats, and germanium showed a strong preference for one of them, filling it entirely by the second substitution step. X-ray and spectroscopic checks confirmed the seating chart.

The parent compound orders antiferromagnetically at about seven kelvin. Each germanium dose pushed that ordering colder and smeared its signature, signs of growing magnetic frustration, which the authors blame on extra germanium electronic states at the key energy level. Site-selective alloying thus becomes a fine dial for magnetic behaviour, a design lesson for quantum materials.
arxiv-2507-13343:
Yushu Wu and a team of co-authors make mobile video generation practical in twenty twenty-five. Diffusion transformers make strong videos, but they cost too much computing for a phone. On-device generation is even harder than running such models on big machines. The team offers a chain of optimizations to close that gap.

First, a highly compressed autoencoder shrinks the input data without hurting visual quality. Second, a pruning strategy guided by knowledge distillation cuts the model to mobile size. It is careful to spare the parts that matter most. Third, a step distillation method tailored to these transformers cuts the steps needed. Readers get a path to real-time video generation in seconds on a handset.
arxiv-2507-13443:
Raniere de Menezes and five co-authors introduce a free Python package for cleaning up telescope spectra, in this 2025 paper. Spectroscopy splits light into a rainbow that reveals what stars and galaxies are made of and how fast they move away. Reduction software is often tied to one instrument or built on aging tools that resist scripting.

Their package, easyspec, handles long-slit spectra from any telescope that saves standard FITS files. It reworks trusted routines from the classic IRAF suite in modern Python and adds fitting methods based on Monte Carlo sampling. To prove it, the team reduced data on an active galaxy taken with an Italian national telescope camera. They measured its redshift and weighed its central black hole, matching an earlier IRAF study. The authors offer the tool for custom pipelines.
arxiv-2507-13843:
Xiaochun Huang and co-authors scan in 2025 the cold skin of a rare metal mix for the true marks of its odd superconduct state. Scope shots had shown a gap on the skin's arc states alone, with a knot form. What the gap looks like in real space was not known.

A probe scope reads a wide, even gap on clean flats of the stuff. In the gap sit spread skin states with a fine grain wave. Those states read best as bound pair states in the gap. A hand built model fits their prints with a swirl pair form. The skin states tie straight to the gap.
arxiv-2507-14443:
Ueda and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy study of the dust disk around the young star HL Tau. Such disks are where planets form, and dust traits decide how growth proceeds. The team modeled the disk's glow at six wavelengths, from under a millimeter to near eight. Fine images let them fit temperature, density, and grain size across the disk.

Fits favor dust rich in organics with loose, porous grains in the outer disk. Solid carbon-rich dust fits less well once light scattering data join in. If grains are porous and organic-rich, they can clump fast enough for pebble accretion to build planets. The study ties disk chemistry to planet birth rates.
arxiv-2507-14543:
Sharanya Mukherjee, Md Hishaam Akhtar, and Kannadasan propose live captions for sign language inside video meetings. Deaf signers often prefer signing to typing on calls, yet few hearing colleagues know sign. Computer vision that turns signs into subtitles could close that gap.

The team builds a browser extension that watches the camera feed and posts translated captions for everyone on the call. Training leans on a large public data set of word-level American Sign Language clips, over two thousand videos from more than one hundred signers. The paper frames the tool as an accessibility layer for the meeting software people already use daily.
arxiv-2507-14643:
Jifeng Shen and five co-authors fuse camera types for object detection in a 2025 paper. Pairing visible light with heat vision helps spot objects at night. Fusion methods often chase local detail and miss shared meaning. They also trade off view size against computing cost.

Their frame, MS2Fusion, runs two interaction paths inside a state space model. One path mines what each camera type adds to the other. The second aligns the two views into a shared semantic space. Joint training lets both paths feed one detection output. Tests on three standard benchmarks beat rival fusion methods. Gains held across varied scenes and lighting in their trials. The authors pitch the design for surveillance, driving, and rescue work.
arxiv-2507-14743:
Traffic cameras hold rich facts, but models that answer questions about traffic video stumble on busy scenes. Joseph Raj Vishal and co-authors built a test set to push those models harder, in work from twenty twenty-five. Hours of real traffic film from many crossings were cut into short clips.

More than twenty-five thousand question-answer pairs cover motion over time and space, car interplay, and crash spotting. Top current models were tried on the set and showed clear weak spots on fine motion links. Extra training on the set lifted their scores by a solid margin. The set is public, and the team hopes it helps build traffic watchers fit for real streets.
arxiv-2507-14843:
Fang Wu and co-authors argue that a popular way of training language models may mostly reshuffle what the base model already knows, in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has boosted reasoning scores. Whether it truly widens the reasoning frontier is disputed. Average accuracy can hide what changes underneath.

Their framework tracks support for verified solutions question by question. It measures where access grows, shrinks, or stays put across training. Across models and tasks, shrinkage outweighed expansion in aggregate. More questions lost their verified solutions than gained new ones. The finding tempers hype around the method. Labs gain a finer lens for judging training runs. Better recipes may need to protect old skills while adding new ones.
arxiv-2507-15043:
Chris McDaniel links the shape of a two-variable polynomial to the sign pattern of a family of Toeplitz matrices. A Toeplitz matrix holds the same value along each diagonal. Total nonnegativity means every minor of the matrix is zero or more. His 2025 paper builds helper polynomials called higher Hessians from the starting form.

Good sign traits in those helpers force the Toeplitz matrices to be totally nonnegative. One main result turns out to match a special case of a deep Hodge theory theorem by Cattani. McDaniel gives a fresh proof of that case through the Hessian route. The other result leans on newer work by Karp and Purbhoo from real Schubert calculus. The paper ties algebra, geometry, and matrix theory into one frame.
arxiv-2507-15443:
Adrien Coppens and Valérie Maquil present a way to measure joint attention during mixed-presence collaboration around wall-sized displays, in a 2025 paper. When some partners stand in the room and others join remotely, knowing whether everyone is really looking at the same thing matters. The measurement must fit a room-sized setup without getting in the way.

Their approach uses head gaze data to judge shared attention. They built it for a user study with two wall-sized displays and describe how the system ran in practice. Early lessons come from one session's data in particular. The authors offer the method as a step toward judging the quality of mixed-presence teamwork more rigorously.
arxiv-2507-15543:
Alessandro Calamai, Matteo Franca, and Michal Pospisil restore chaos to a class of systems where a geometric quirk had banned it, in a 2025 paper. Their systems are piecewise smooth: the rules change abruptly across a curve. A small periodic push perturbs a system that, unperturbed, loops back to its rest point along a homoclinic path. In smooth systems the classic Melnikov test then guarantees chaos. The team had earlier found an obstruction, impossible in the smooth case, that blocks chaos here when the push is periodic.

This paper shows that once the obstruction is removed, chaos returns as in the smooth case. The proof builds the chaotic set in a new way. Examples illustrate the mechanism. The work completes a small saga in nonsmooth dynamics: persistence of the homoclinic loop, an obstruction, and now the condition under which the full chaotic picture survives.
arxiv-2507-15843:
Beniamino Accattoli and co-authors study a compiler step called closure conversion in a 2025 paper on programming language theory. Compilers for languages with nested functions use the step to turn inner functions into top-level ones. Each converted function is paired with the values it needs from its surroundings, and that pair is called a closure.

The paper compares that method with the closures used inside abstract machines, the simple models that show how programs run step by step. The authors give a new proof that the conversion is correct, plus a cleaner way to handle the saved values, plus a cost study. Their cost study shows the conversion lowers some running costs while making the starting code larger, leaving total cost about the same.
arxiv-2507-16343:
Pengfei Cai and co-authors build a sound detector that can find events named in words or shown by example clips, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Most detectors know only a fixed list of sounds. Their model, DASM, treats detection as matching sound frames against query vectors from text or audio prompts.

One decoder branch decides which events are present, while a context branch pins down when each event runs. A masking trick at test time uses kinship between known and new classes to boost new-class skill. Scores beat language-based rivals on a strong public set and topped a trained baseline on a second set. Readers get open-list sound search that still times events well.
arxiv-2507-16443:
Kai Deng and co-authors stretch a leading 3D vision model from room-scale scenes to kilometer-long outdoor drives. Their 2025 paper starts from the wall such models hit: memory caps the length of the image stream they can rebuild in one go. Their system, VGGT-Long, needs no camera calibration, depth supervision, or retraining.

The stream is cut into chunks, each rebuilt on its own. Overlapping parts are then aligned, and a light loop-closure step ties the path shut when the route revisits a place. On three driving data sets the system ran where the base model failed outright. Its paths and geometry matched classic methods, which the authors pitch as a route to scalable one-camera 3D mapping.
arxiv-2507-16543:
Tom Krueger and Wolfgang Mauerer present a 2025 way to track a hidden fuel of quantum computing called non-stabiliserness. Some quantum states can be faked by a normal computer, and the extra kind is what gives quantum methods their edge. Knowing where a method spends that fuel can guide better design.

Their approach pairs a resource theory of such states with the shape of how states move as a method runs. New distance tools reveal waste that older checks hid. Neat, structured methods spent the fuel well, while looser ones wasted it. The work gives builders a sharper lens on quantum advantage.
arxiv-2507-16743:
Keneni Tesema and co-authors build a network that cleans and fills 3D point clouds at once in a 2025 paper. Self driving cars, robots, and headsets need full point clouds, but real scans come back patchy and noisy. Most past fill tools train on clean fake data and stumble on real flaws.

The team made a test set with many stacked flaws to show those limits. Their network, DWCNet, adds a noise control block that uses contrast based learning and self attention to hush noise while it fills gaps. It topped rivals on clean and flawed sets, both fake and real. Code and data will be shared in public.
arxiv-2507-16943:
Eric Bergshoeff, Giacomo Giorgi, Jan Rosseel, and Patricio Salgado-Rebolledo take a first step toward broad matter links for Aristotelian gravity, in work from twenty twenty-five. Aristotelian gravity drops the usual boost rules of space and time. Matter can sit on stacked sheets called brane foliations of any size. The goal is a clean recipe that builds many such links at once.

The team enlarges the core algebra into two conformal algebras joined as a sum. One part acts along the sheets, and the other acts across them. A leaner version with a single uneven stretch rule suffices in some cases. With that frame, they build electric and magnetic forms of the theory. None of the forms keep Galilean or Carrollian boost rules. They then add matter links for both mild and stronger models tied to fracton studies.
arxiv-2507-17143:
Laura Bernard and three co-authors build a dictionary for testing Einstein's gravity with gravitational waves in this 2025 paper. When two black holes spiral together, their waves should match general relativity. New theories bend that signal in patterned ways. The dictionary assumes any bend comes from a local effective theory built from curvature terms, maybe with extra fields. It then states how each bend scales with the two masses and at what order it enters the wave's phase.

Observers can run the dictionary backward: a measured bend points to a family of theories. It also helps separate real new physics from instrument or modeling error. The results plug into nearly all existing inspiral tests. Data from many events can be combined more efficiently with the scaling rules in hand. The authors frame the work as a bridge from observation to interpretation.
arxiv-2507-17443:
Astero Provata, Georgios Boulougouris, and Johanne Hizanidis study sync shifts in spiking networks with adaptive links, in a 2025 paper. The head expands initials from the catalog. In brain like networks, link strengths change over time based on the firing of the cells they join, a rule first set out by Hebb.

Their network is a ring of leaky integrate and fire neurons linked at a distance. Without adaptivity it shows mixed states such as chimeras, where part of the ring is in sync and part is not. With fast adaptive links and negative coupling, the network moves through chimera forms of unlike multiplicity. The size of the synced and unsynced zones tracks the mean link strength.
arxiv-2507-17543:
Xue Wen Tan, Kenneth See, and Stanley Kok build a scam guard that plays the crook first, in a study from 2025. Chat scams grow fast and cost dear. A guard that waits for the trap is late; one that dreams the crook's next line can warn in time.

Their frame, ASR, runs three beats: dream the crook's path, play it out, and reason on the play in plain words for the user. A tuned tongue model, ScamGPT-J, learned from a fresh bank of scam chats cross kinds. Tests show the frame lifts catch, most in job scams. A sad twist: the most at-risk souls trust the aid least, so the build must court them first.
arxiv-2507-17643: Song, Xie, and Yang study maps of projective varieties and the orbits of points under them. They prove that the arithmetic degree of a point with a dense orbit must be a cohomological Lyapunov multiplier of the system. They then apply that result to draw a consequence for the dynamical Mordell-Lang conjecture.
arxiv-2507-17843:
Bruno Marques da Silva, Larissa Ferreira Rodrigues Moreira, and co-authors work in a 2025 paper on edge gaming over future mobile networks. Games need low delay, and operators must prove they meet service promises to players. The network part that carries user data lacks a clean way to gauge player delay.

Their design loops an analytics function with an upgraded data plane in the core. An AI model inside the analytics unit sorts games by type from traffic traits. Delay estimates flow back so the control plane can act with delay in mind. The loop runs without probing the player's device, a stated aim of the design. Results open fresh paths for edge gaming research, the authors say.
arxiv-2507-18143:
Gonzalo Cardenal-Antolin and five co-authors benchmark large language models for HIV medical decision support, in work from 2025. HIV care is complex, with many drug options, other illnesses and adherence problems. Their benchmark, HIVMedQA, holds curated open-ended questions built with an infectious disease physician, graded for understanding, reasoning, recall, bias, harm and accuracy.

Seven general and three medical models were tested, with prompt methods used to lift scores. One leading proprietary model topped most measures, and two of the top three were proprietary. Scores fell as questions grew harder, medical fine-tuning did not always help, and size alone did not predict success. Reasoning proved harder than factual recall.
arxiv-2507-18343:
Ariana Sahitaj and co-authors built in 2025 a hybrid annotation framework for detecting propaganda in social media text. Labeling propaganda is subtle, and even trained humans agree poorly on fine-grained technique labels. Large language models can pre-label at scale, but their labels need human checking.

The team organized fourteen propaganda techniques into three broad groups and ran a human labeling study that confirmed low agreement on the fine labels. Their pipeline has a large model extract suspect spans, explain them, and assign labels. Human verification then raised both agreement and speed. Finally, they trained smaller models on the large model's high-quality labels rather than on the noisy human ones.
arxiv-2507-18643:
Syeda Tasnim Fabiha, Rubaiyat Jahan Mumu, Farzana Aktar, and Mainul Hossain model share prices on the Dhaka Stock Exchange, starting from what drives market liquidity. Investors favor liquid shares, and liquidity hangs on average share price. The authors ask which factors move that price, and how well simple models capture it.

A thorough linear regression analysis came first, with each factor's individual contribution to price variability identified and explained. A random forest model then outperformed the linear model on the comparison metrics they used. One negative finding stands out: the time series data alone could not support a predictive linear model. The paper separates explanation from forecasting in the Bangladeshi market.
arxiv-2507-19743:
Zhuolin Xu and co-authors define what it would mean for AI code generation to be ethically sourced.
