Puskás and a large team of co-authors ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether galaxy mergers in the early universe lit a fire under star formation and black hole growth. Mergers are credited with both at later times, but evidence at high redshift is thin. Using JADES survey data, the team assembled a mass-complete sample of 2,095 young galaxies and identified major merger pairs probabilistically.

They built a control sample of non-merging galaxies matched in redshift, mass, isolation, and environment. Pairs closer than about twenty kiloparsecs showed a modest boost in specific star formation rate, about twelve percent above the controls, fading by fifty kiloparsecs. Averaged histories split pairs into two families: systems still approaching, with rising star formation, and systems past closest pass, which peaked earlier. Surprisingly, pairs showed no significant excess of active galactic nuclei, so encounters alone do not seem to switch black holes on.
arxiv-2510-14843:
Zahr and Liva analyze, in a 2025 arXiv paper, error-correcting codes designed to work at any rate while staying close to the theoretical limit. MacKay-Neal codes are a flexible family whose rate can be adapted, and spatial coupling, linking many small code blocks into a chain, is known to push decoding thresholds toward capacity. The authors combine the two: the inner code is a protograph-based spatially coupled low-density parity-check code.

Using density evolution, the standard tool for tracking decoding messages over iterations, they compute the ensembles' asymptotic thresholds. A specially defined parallel channel model makes the analysis tractable. The thresholds land within 0.15 decibels of capacity for the binary-input white Gaussian noise channel, across the full rate range from zero to one. One code family can thus serve slow, ultra-reliable links and fast ones almost equally well.
arxiv-2510-14943:
Yang and co-authors simplify how a language model can grade its reasoning, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Training with verifiable rewards teaches models to solve problems, but at test time no verifier is present, so they learn to self-verify. Earlier approaches made the model generate a solution, then a separate verification, using two prompt templates. The routine is slow.

The authors prove a shortcut. The true reward of a solution equals a score readable from one number. That number is the model's next-token log-probability for a chosen token at the solution's last token, adjusted by a constant and the KL coefficient. Their algorithm, LaSeR, adds a loss term aligning this last-token score with the verifier's reward, jointly improving reasoning and self-grading. At use time the score costs one extra token of inference. Experiments show better reasoning and stronger inference-time scaling from the self-reward.
arxiv-2510-15043:
Dufresne-Piché and Nadarajah generalize, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a family of high-order simulation schemes prized for running stably on unstructured grids. Energy stable flux reconstruction methods form a family of linearly stable variants, and each can be rewritten as a filtered discontinuous Galerkin scheme. That filtered viewpoint is the lever the authors use to widen the family.

They introduce Sobolev Stable discontinuous Galerkin schemes, a conservative, linearly stable generalization built through the filter framework, and review how generalizations relate to it. Von Neumann analysis compares the schemes with the extended variant. The two families behave differently in dispersion and dissipation, yet both raise the time step, the CFL limit, by a similar amount, with similar spectral accuracy. The edge goes to the new schemes: the parameter range over which they enlarge the time-stepping limit is larger, giving practitioners more room to tune.
arxiv-2510-15143:
Victor Gitton and Renato Renner settle an eight-year-old conjecture about quantum correlations in a small network, in this 2025 arXiv paper. When three parties share quantum systems from three separate sources, their measurement results can show non-classical patterns that no classical setup can reproduce. The triangle network is the simplest case with this feature, but its math is non-convex and hard, so general proof methods have been missing.

One test case is the Elegant Joint Measurement distribution, a tidy, highly symmetric pattern that quantum systems can produce in the triangle network and that many suspected no classical system could match. Gitton and Renner now prove that suspicion correct. They combined inflation, a causal inference technique, with symmetry reductions and a large-scale optimization algorithm to keep the computation feasible. Their computer-assisted proof runs in exact arithmetic, giving a firm certificate rather than a numerical hint.
arxiv-2510-15343:
Raghvender and six colleagues simulate a family of tellurite glasses at the atomic level to explain their prized optical behavior. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies glasses built from tellurium oxide mixed with thallium oxide and titanium oxide. Such glasses are strong nonlinear optical materials, useful for switching and amplifying light, but their performance depends on atomic structure that is hard to see directly.

Using first-principles molecular dynamics, the team built large models of the glasses and checked them against measured x-ray data. Adding thallium oxide broke the tellurium-oxygen network apart, lowering coordination and creating loose oxygen atoms. Adding titanium oxide did the opposite, stitching the network back together with small titanium-bearing rings. Their computed vibration spectra matched measured trends as the mix changed. A small share of titanium oxide kept the tellurite network's strong optical nonlinearity while restoring its connectivity, a useful recipe for glass designers.
arxiv-2510-16043:
Jordan Stone, Youssef Saleh, Darryl Wright, and Jess Riedel survey physics experts on whether our vacuum could decay and whether technology could trigger that decay. Vacuum decay would replace the present vacuum with a lower-energy one, and the new region would spread near light speed, rewriting physical law everywhere it reached. The stakes make expert judgement worth recording carefully.

Twenty experts answered what the authors believe is the first structured survey on both questions. Average replies put the chance that our vacuum is metastable below half, and the chance that arbitrarily advanced technology could induce decay, if decay is possible at all, lower still. Disagreement was wide on both points. Participants said progress hinges on theories beyond the standard model, and even believers in decay expected artificial induction to challenge a civilisation with galactic resources.
arxiv-2510-16243:
Lanke Fu and four co-authors attack a stellarator design trap: optimizing the plasma first and the coils second can yield beautiful physics wrapped in impossible magnets. Their remedy folds a fast coil model directly into the plasma optimization, a quasi-single-stage approach.

The proxy rests on QUADCOIL, a differentiable coil optimization code that scores realistic metrics like forces and permanent-magnet layouts at speeds earlier tools could not match. In one study the method redesigns the MUSE stellarator's permanent magnets with twenty-nine percent fewer magnets than the previous solution. In another, coils for the ARIES-CS concept cut both peak and average electromagnetic forces by twenty-seven percent. Designers can now balance plasma quality against coil cost inside one loop.
arxiv-2510-16443:
In a paired 2025 report, Dimitris Stefanopoulos and Andreas Voskou share their win in a defence contest. The task was to train a model that stays right on clean data and on attacked data. Attacks came from a shuffle trick that swaps values to break patterns. The event was part of the same ECML-PKDD 2025 physics challenge as their attack win.

First, the pair made 15 million fake training samples with that same shuffle trick. Then they trained a model with a shared-weight block plus a fusion tail. It scored 80 percent on mixed clean and attacked data. That beat the next team by two points and took first place.
arxiv-2510-16543:
Lasha Berezhiani, Gia Dvali, and Otari Sakhelashvili work out a time result in quantum gravity in 2025. Quantum gravity seeks one frame for gravity and quantum rules. They use a strict method, called BRST, that keeps the maths gauge-clean. A gauge is a free choice in how fields are drawn. Their aim is to state how the total energy driver acts in that frame.

They derive an exact identity for that driver in the bulk of space. Up to an edge term, it is a paired product of two BRST parts. That form shows time flow acts as a re-timing on true degrees of freedom. Yet they show this does not make time flow trivial. Backgrounds, bulk links, and scatter results still shift in real ways.
arxiv-2510-16643:
Aaron Ray leads five co-authors in a 2025 study on robots that grasp words about place. A 3D scene graph maps a room as objects linked by spatial ties. Language models can reason over such maps, but full maps swamp their text window. Their fix stores the graph in a graph database, not in the prompt. The model then pulls just the parts it needs per task.

A query tongue called Cypher is the model's tool for those pulls. Tests cover task steps and questions about scenes. Cypher pulls beat both full-window dumps and code-writing pulls by a lot. Wins hold for small local models and big cloud ones. Token use for scene facts drops sharply at the same time.
arxiv-2510-17043:
Md Ahmed Al Muzaddid and William J. Beksi improve person matching across cameras in a 2025 paper. Person re-identification links images of the same person across views. Systems describe each person with a feature summary. One summary per identity class acts as its representative.

Earlier work mostly used the plain average of a class's summaries. A few studies tried other representatives only during retrieval. The authors show those choices give weaker matching results. Their method picks generalized representatives beyond simple class averages. The number of representatives per class can be tuned per application. Applied over several existing embeddings, the method improved results substantially. Better representatives, they argue, are an overlooked lever in re-identification.
arxiv-2510-17143:
Shantnav Agarwal, Javier Alonso-Mora, and Sihao Sun teach drone teams to haul loads with no central boss in this 2025 paper. Loads hang from cables below two or more drones in flight. Past methods need one central planner or steady radio links. The team drops both needs so each drone plans on its own.

Each drone learns by copying a central planner that sees the full scene. Smooth path nets keep moves tied to true motion laws. Each drone can train in under two hours on a plain laptop. Tests in sim and real flights match central plans on hard paths. The work suits teams that fly where links are weak or lost.
arxiv-2510-17743:
Alexandr Grebennikov and Matthew Kwan solve a grid puzzle about points and lines. How many points can sit in a square grid with few on any line? Each straight line may hold at most k points, where k is fixed. Earlier work settled the question only for much larger k values.

For large constant k, the pair proves the best count is exactly k times n. Here n is the side length of the square grid. Their proof builds on recent work by three other researchers. It also borrows ideas from Jain and Pham. The same approach gives new bounds for higher-dimensional versions.
arxiv-2510-18043:
Joong Ho Choi, with seven co-authors, shrinks the prompts and files that agent workflows feed to language models. Long chained prompts and rich data streams make such work slow and costly. CompactPrompt cuts low-value tokens from prompts and groups linked phrases so meaning survives the trim.

Attached documents are compressed in parallel, with repeated patterns shortened and numeric columns quantized. On finance question benchmarks, total token use fell by up to about three fifths, while answer quality dipped only slightly for the strong models tested. Teams running agents at scale get a pipeline that lowers bills without gutting results.
arxiv-2510-18143:
Huan Song, with eight co-authors, grows training data for small language models by studying how they fail. Small models are cheap and fast but trail big ones on hard, specialized tasks. Fine-tuning helps, yet preparing data by hand is slow. Their PaDA-Agent reads validation results to find failure patterns first.

Augmentation plans are then drafted to shrink the generalization gap directly, not just to fix single wrong answers. Experiments beat strong model-based augmentation baselines on the tasks tried. Teams deploying small models get an evaluation-driven loop that turns weak spots into fresh, targeted practice data.
arxiv-2510-18343:
Emily L Hunt, with Tristan Cantat-Gaudin and five co-authors, measures completeness of a star cluster census in 2025. Open clusters are loose groups of stars born together, useful tracers of Milky Way structure. Nobody knew how many clusters the Gaia DR3 census missed, or why.

The team simulated clusters and ran over eighty thousand injection-and-retrieval tests against the census method. A simple logistic model, fitted to those tests, predicts detectability from star count, parallax error, and data density. Parallax error means uncertainty in a star's measured distance. The model proved highly accurate and revealed surprises, like faster-moving clusters being easier to detect.
arxiv-2510-18743:
Kasun Wijewardhana and his five co-authors propose feeding a new kind of antenna system wirelessly. Pinching-antenna systems run signals through waveguides and pinch the guide at chosen points to radiate, creating clear line-of-sight links that fight the heavy losses of millimeter-wave and terahertz signals. But wired feeding ties installation to spots near the base station, leaving distant users poorly served.

Their wireless-fed version powers the waveguides without cables, extending coverage beyond the base station's neighborhood at lower cost. Indoor and outdoor scenarios in the article show advantages over the wired design. Numerical results add that the wireless-fed systems deliver higher data rates than conventional fixed antennas. The authors close with research directions needed to bring the concept into next-generation networks.
arxiv-2510-18943:
Reinaldo Francener, Victor P Goncalves, and Gabriel Rabelo-Soares study the muon trident process. They look at far-forward detectors at the Large Hadron Collider. In this process, a muon hits an ion. It then makes a pair of charged leptons.

The team works out cross sections for two routes of the process. They also predict event rates for muon and tungsten hits. The rates suggest the process can be seen at FASER. Tau pairs from muon hits may show up there for the first time. Bound states from quantum electrodynamics may show up too.
arxiv-2510-19043:
Jiaxing Ma and three co-authors show that measurement back-action creates linked thermal noise across many vibration modes in modern mechanical sensors. Sensors now resolve the basic thermal noise floor over a wide band, not just near resonance, which speeds data taking and reveals brief signals once hidden.

Stronger measurement, though, pushes back on the device. The authors find that this back-action correlates noise from modes far apart in frequency, so measured spectra depart from standard single-mode and independent multimode predictions. Sensor designers must account for that coupling to read broadband data correctly.
arxiv-2510-19443:
Adithya Nandakumar, Ricarda S Beckmann, and Vid Irsic explore how bursts of accretion change the long-term spin of massive black holes when superradiance is also at work. Superradiance lets an axion cloud drain spin from a rapidly rotating black hole, while infalling gas adds spin back, and real feeding arrives in uneven episodes rather than a steady stream.

Simulations show the contest between angular momentum gained from accretion and lost to the axion cloud decides the outcome. Boosts that arrive before the main spin-down phase matter most, because they can delay or reshape that drop. The results refine predictions linking black hole spins to ultralight particles.
arxiv-2510-19643:
Konstantin Hess and three co-authors tackle a statistical problem in estimating how treatments affect different patients over time. When treatment sequences stretch over long horizons, few patients in the data follow any given sequence, so overlap between groups collapses and ordinary estimators become unstable. Their answer is an overlap-weighted orthogonal meta-learner that concentrates on the regions where the data actually support the intervention.

Built on a new Neyman-orthogonal risk function, the method stays robust when its helper models are misspecified, and it can wrap around any machine learning model. Experiments with both transformer and recurrent network backbones showed more reliable effect estimates than existing meta-learners. The approach targets personalized medicine, where treatment paths are long and data are thin.
arxiv-2510-19943:
Denis Sedov and Mathias S. Scheurer show that quantum geometry can decide how fragile a superconductor is to impurities when time-reversal symmetry is broken. The shape side of Bloch states is already known to affect flow stiffness and pairing. Here the authors derive a general formula for how the critical temperature responds to disorder. It is built from weighted commutator terms linking the order parameter to how impurities act.

The formula picks out a quantum geometric pair-breaking effect. Without time-reversal symmetry, even non-magnetic impurities can suppress the state. With kinetic pair breaking present, dirt can instead enhance pairing. The critical temperature then rises and falls in a jagged way as impurity load grows. The analysis applies directly to rhombohedral graphene, twisted molybdenum ditelluride, and superconducting altermagnets. It also addresses finite-momentum pairing.
arxiv-2510-20543:
Sangmitra Madhusudan, Kaige Chen, and Ali Emami test if language models parse clause shape or just lean on sense cues. Their set, CenterBench, holds 9,720 asks on center-embedded lines, where a clause nests in a clause. Each line with sound sense has a twin with the same shape but odd sense, such as a postman who gives drugs. Six asks per line probe plain sense, clause links, and cause chains.

Six models face the set. The gap from sound to odd twins grows in a steady way as nest depth grows, with mid gaps near 27 points. Sense pull even harms asks on end acts, where cause links count most. Thought-heavy models score more, yet their traces show cue use, long loops, and skips.
arxiv-2510-20843:
Gourav Banerjee, working alone, seeks a clean necessary and sufficient test for when a function is absolutely continuous on the whole real line or another unbounded interval. The classic fundamental theorem gives such a test on closed bounded intervals through the derivative lying in a local integrable class.

No matching derivative test was known for unbounded intervals, where behavior far out can break naive extensions. Banerjee investigates the gap and states a condition that is both necessary and sufficient in the unbounded case, building on the known local condition. The result completes a basic piece of real analysis that textbooks leave open beyond bounded intervals.
arxiv-2510-20943:
Srivathsan Badrinarayanan leads five co-authors on meta learning for predicting how protein mutations change measured properties across different tasks. Mutation effects drive drug discovery and protein design, yet models fine tuned per data set transfer poorly when lab conditions differ and target data are scarce.

Two ideas anchor the work, the first use of model agnostic meta learning for this problem, and a mutation encoding that inserts separator tokens so the mutation sits inside the sequence context. Built on transformer backbones, the method trains for fast adaptation to new assays. Better cross task transfer could cut the lab work needed to screen promising protein variants.
arxiv-2510-21343:
Mai Ye and fifteen co-authors squeeze a copper-oxide superconductor and watch its atomic structure respond. They use synchrotron X-ray diffraction paired with simulations. The material is an underdoped mercury barium copper oxide. It serves as a model system for high-temperature superconductivity. Strain offers a clean knob for probing its inner order.

Pressing along one crystal direction expands the other two only slightly. Yet the copper-oxygen distance along the third direction grows by nearly one percent. That is a surprisingly large move. The strain also creates a new diffuse scattering signal. The signal reflects a short-range charge pattern repeating about every two unit cells. Its order extends roughly four cells. The signal ignores the onset of superconductivity. It matches a charge pattern predicted for a spin-liquid model on a square lattice.
arxiv-2510-21643:
Gabriele Fiore and Ciaran Williams compute a small but nagging correction to a Higgs factory background process. Two gluons fusing into two photons, with electroweak effects from the first two generations of quarks included. At the precision the Large Hadron Collider now reaches, percent-level effects matter for reading data correctly.

The two-loop amplitude is organized through projection operators into scalar form factors, and the hard integrals behind it are handled with generalized polylogarithms and iterated integrals. A fitted semi-numerical scheme speeds the heaviest pieces enough for practical use inside a Monte Carlo event generator, where the results now live. For collider energies, the electroweak correction lands around a couple of percent of the leading result, small but well within the accuracy modern analyses must track.
arxiv-2510-21743:
Roman Ya. Kezerashvili surveys ways a spacecraft could travel without carrying propellant, drawing instead on natural forces or energy from outside the craft. The review weighs each option for long interstellar journeys, where hauling fuel becomes the central obstacle.

Gravity assists borrow speed from planets but only when alignments cooperate. Solar sails ride pressure from sunlight and can gain extra push from heat-driven surface effects, though their huge reflective sheets degrade over time. Magnetic sails push against the solar wind with superconducting loops, while electric sails use long charged wires to repel solar wind particles and can accelerate harder. A final section considers quantum vacuum effects, such as the Casimir force, as a speculative route that remains unproven.
arxiv-2510-21843:
Anand Bhardwaj and Samer Faraj report an inside look at building an artificial intelligence tool for scheduling operating rooms at a Canadian hospital. Their focus is not the software's accuracy but the quiet choices made early on about which parts of the work the system would represent and which parts it would leave out.

Scheduling as the designers imagined it was rule-bound, predictable, and centered on surgeons. Scheduling as staff actually practice it is fluid, patient-facing work full of ethical judgment calls. Because the early framing shut those human dimensions out, the authors describe a case of epistemic foreclosure, where key moral concerns never entered the design at all. The study warns that abstraction choices in high-stakes settings carry real moral weight.
arxiv-2510-21943:
Ruaridh Macdonald and six co-authors, Filippo Pecci, Luca Bonaldo, Jun Wen Law, Yu Weng, Dharik Mallapragada, and Jesse Jenkins, introduce MacroEnergy.jl, an open-source toolkit for planning whole energy systems. Big transition questions span electricity, fuels, steel, chemicals, and more at once, and models that treat each sector separately miss how they trade resources.

Written in the Julia language, the framework builds systems from a small set of sector-neutral parts that snap together into flexible networks and connect to many standard solvers. Companion packages add advanced methods such as decomposition, letting users keep fine detail across time and place without the model collapsing under its own size. The authors pitch the tool at researchers and policy analysts who need capacity plans at national scale and modern detail.
arxiv-2510-22543:
A correct final answer can still hide sloppy reasoning, such as guessing or skipping steps. Yuyang Ding, Chi Zhang, Juntao Li, Haibin Lin, and Min Zhang study those flawed but rewarded training runs in a 2025 paper on language model reasoning.

Such runs help models improve quickly at first, then cap later progress by reinforcing unreliable habits. Their method, FAPO, adds a penalty for flawed positive runs without new parameters. The penalty lets models use shortcuts early, then pushes them toward sound reasoning later. A generative reward model detects the flawed runs by checking the reasoning process itself.
arxiv-2510-22643:
Graph networks can sort whole graphs with great skill. But a small attack can trick them. Sofiane Ennadir wrote a 2025 paper on one weak step in those networks. His co-authors are Oleg Smirnov and Yassine Abbahaddou. Lele Cao and Johannes F Lutzeyer are co-authors too. The weak step is pooling, which squeezes node data into one sum.

The team bound the risk of sum, mean, and max pooling. Each of those forms fails in its own way. Their new form uses a top singular vector. That vector is the lead pattern in the node data. Tests on real sets show more strength than the old forms. The new step fits many types of graph models.
arxiv-2510-22843:
A software package can turn abstract poset theory into tools. Penelope Beall, Nikola Kuzmanovski, Yu Oliver Li, and Alexandra Seceleanu present one in 2025. It is called MacaulayPosets. It runs inside Macaulay2, a computational algebra system. Posets are sets with a partial order.

The package uses a poset data type from a prior package. It studies the Macaulay property for posets. Such posets arise from monomials in commutative rings. A Macaulay poset has ranked levels. Its total order fits the partial order well. That fit yields bounds on subset sizes. Bounds apply inside order ideals of a given rank.
arxiv-2510-23343:
Yossi Oren, Viraj Pandya, Rachel S Somerville, Shy Genel, Osase Omoruyi, and Amiel Sternberg trace the cosmic baryon cycle in the IllustrisTNG100 simulation. Gas flows into galaxies, forms stars, and is blown back out, carrying energy and metals. They measure inflows and outflows through the interstellar and circumgalactic media.

By binning galaxies by halo mass and redshift, they identify which feedback dominates: supernovae, or the kinetic and thermal modes of black hole feedback. Flows are measured at the halo edge and at the galaxy interface. The accounting shows how feedback regulates galaxy growth across cosmic time.
arxiv-2510-23443:
Chiara Bonfanti, Alessandro Druetto, Cataldo Basile, Tharindu Ranasinghe, and Marcos Zampieri propose a neuro-symbolic multi-agent approach to joining legal and cybersecurity knowledge. Law and cyber security meet in a complex space of cases, statutes, and technical flaws. Standard legal research tools struggle with the nuanced links between them, hindering collaboration between lawyers and security experts.

Their system aims to navigate the cyber-legal domain, combining neural methods with symbolic structure and multiple agents. First results on multilingual tasks are promising. Better integration could speed incident response where legal duties and technical facts collide.
arxiv-2510-23543:
Benjamin Girard and Sofia Zotova work in additive combinatorics, the study of patterns forced to appear inside sets of numbers. They focus on the Erdős-Ginzburg-Ziv constant of certain groups, which measures how large a multiset must be before it must contain a fixed-size subfamily summing to zero. Their groups are p-groups shaped much like rank-two groups, plus products with cyclic groups of coprime order.

Adapting Reiher's proof of Kemnitz's conjecture, the authors sharpen an earlier theorem of Schmid and Zhuang. They obtain better upper bounds for the constant across these group families. For one new infinite family of groups, whose rank can grow without limit, they pin down the exact value of the constant. That exact case also confirms a conjecture made by Gao about how the constant behaves.
arxiv-2510-23943:
Diana Aldana and six co-authors present AIRe, a training scheme that reshapes an implicit neural representation while it learns, instead of fixing the architecture in advance. Such representations encode signals like images as neural networks fed with sinusoidally encoded coordinates, and they capture detail well. The catch is choosing input frequencies and network size up front, amid redundancy, usually by tedious tuning.

AIRe alternates two moves. Pruning finds the least useful neurons, shifts their knowledge to the survivors through targeted weight decay, and then removes them in a structured way. Densification adds fresh input frequencies where the signal is being underfit, widening the basis where it counts. On image and signed-distance-field tests, the method shrank models while holding or improving reconstruction quality. The authors plan to release code and pretrained models, pitching the scheme as a cleaner trade between size and fidelity for implicit representations.
arxiv-2510-24343:
Maciej Wilczynski and four co-authors simulate how mechanical strain changes radiation damage in nickel crystals. Using molecular dynamics, they bombard strained and unstrained single crystals with repeated overlapping collision cascades of five kiloelectron volt impacts at room temperature. Strain alters how defects form, move, and recombine during each cascade.

Tensile strain promotes stress assisted defect motion and helps more defects survive than in the unstrained case. The heat spike from each impact grows shorter and weaker as strain rises, signaling faster energy spread and changed recombination. Shockley type partial dislocations dominate the resulting structure, and the analysis tracks how the dislocation network evolves under strain.
arxiv-2510-24443:
Tom Ó Nualláin writes alone on forecasting stock market swings. Realised volatility measures how much prices moved over a past span. His model, GNAR-HARX, blends two known tools for this task. One tool reads links between markets as a network of nodes. The other splits past swings into daily, weekly, and monthly parts.

He adds outside signals too, such as prices of option contracts. The test covers ten world stock indices over about sixteen years. Daily forecasts roll forward across the years two thousand five to twenty. Local and standard forms of the model gave the best scores. Fully linked networks beat networks learned from the data itself. All his forms beat single-market rivals, often with fewer inputs.
arxiv-2510-24643:
Yujun Kim, Chaewon Moon, and Chulhee Yun study how many weights a net needs to learn a data set in a safe way. Safe here means the net keeps its call for points near each training point, not just at the point. They track how that need grows with a ratio of two gaps.

The pair of gaps sets how wide the safe zone is next to the gap between unlike labels. For small ratios, the count matches the plain learn case. As the ratio grows, the count grows too. Their new bounds are tight across the full range and beat past bounds.
arxiv-2510-25043:
Karthekeyan Chandrasekaran, Chandra Chekuri, Weihang Wang, and Weihao Zhu study hedgegraphs, a step past hypergraphs where edges are grouped by color. Such groups can show how edges lean on each other, which plain graphs can not. But the group form breaks a key tool: its cut count lacks a neat math trait that fast plans rely on.

The team brings in a polymatroid, a broad math frame tied to the hedgegraph, as a new lens. With it, they get fresh plans that run well for some link tasks. Old graph and hypergraph claims also grow into new forms through this lens. The lens opens paths past the old cut block.
arxiv-2510-25343:
Hadi Aghaee, Christian Deppe, and Holger Boche study oblivious transfer. Their 2025 paper uses noisy broadcast channels for it. Oblivious transfer is a basic cryptographic building block. One sender communicates with two receivers here. The channel is discrete and memoryless in type. Receivers may be honest but curious about data.

They analyze non-colluding and colluding receiver models separately. For each case, they derive general upper bounds. Those bounds limit achievable oblivious transfer capacity. They also propose two explicit transfer protocols. The first uses binary erasure broadcast channels. It ensures correctness and privacy for independent receivers. The second protocol stays secure under receiver collusion. It adds entropy sharing and privacy amplification steps. For non-colluding receivers, bounds coincide exactly. That gives a complete characterization of achievable rates.
arxiv-2510-25543:
Manuel Rieger led nine co-authors on diamond color centers. Nori N Chavira Leal, Rubek Poudel, and Tobias Waldmann helped. Lina M Todenhagen, Stefan Kresta, and Viviana Villafane joined. Martin S Brandt, Kai Muller, and Jonathan J Finley joined. Their 2025 paper tunes silicon vacancy centers electrically. Those centers show excellent spin coherence and optics.

Negatively charged silicon vacancy centers suit quantum technologies. Electrical tuning uses in-plane contacts applying moderate fields. Second-order Stark shifts exceeding ten gigahertz are showed. That matches the inhomogeneous distribution scale in nanostructures. Single centers show great variation in polarizabilities. Local strain strongly affects polarizability values there. Observed polarizabilities exceed tin vacancy centers largely. Optical linewidths increase moderately with applied field. Large Stark shifts can overcome frequency inhomogeneity. Scalable quantum repeaters may benefit from this tuning.
arxiv-2510-25643:
Karl Welzel, Yang Liu, Raphael A Hauser, and Coralia Cartis study tensor method convergence. Their 2025 paper studies adaptively regularized tuning methods. Tensor methods use derivatives beyond second order. They minimize regularized Taylor expansions at each step. Optimal global hardness improves as order increases. Local convergence was studied by Doikov and Nesterov.

They extend local results to locally uniformly convex functions. Fully changing methods need no Lipschitz constant knowledge. That gives first sharp local rates for such methods. Non-unique model minimizers complicate changing convergence study. Choosing the right local minimizer preserves convergence order. Otherwise superlinear rates can degrade in limit. Changing higher-order methods reach superlinear convergence for degeneracies. Sharp bounds quantify expected convergence order there. Tuning scholars gain precise guidance on minimizer choice.
arxiv-2510-26143:
Bo Pang, Deqian Kong, Silvio Savarese, Caiming Xiong, and Yingbo Zhou propose a two stage curriculum to spread reasoning skills from mathematics to other domains. Reinforcement learning can draw out strong reasoning in language models, but most open work concentrates on math and code. Their Reasoning Curriculum first elicits reasoning in pre training aligned domains such as math, then adapts those skills elsewhere through joint reinforcement learning.

Stage one uses a brief cold start and math only training with verifiable rewards, where answers can be checked exactly. Stage two trains on mixed domain data to transfer and consolidate the skills. Tests on two model families gave consistent gains, and ablations show both stages are needed for the full effect.
arxiv-2510-26243:
Hieu M. Vu and Tan M. Nguyen introduce a geometric method to steer the behavior of a large language model without retraining it. Steering methods adjust internal activations, the numeric patterns that represent a prompt inside the model, to raise or lower a behavior such as refusal. Prior methods add a vector or delete a direction inside a two dimensional subspace, which makes them sensitive to settings and prone to side effects on unrelated traits.

Angular Steering instead rotates activations within a fixed two dimensional plane, toward or away from a target behavior direction, giving continuous, fine grained control. An adaptive variant rotates only activations that align with the target feature, which improves stability. Refusal and emotion steering serve as test cases.
arxiv-2510-26343:
Nicolas Arancibia Robert, working alone, extends a classic result about generic representations in packets of representations of a real group. For a real group, an L-packet is a finite set of representations tied to one L-parameter, a homomorphisms based label from the Langlands program. Work of Kostant and Vogan says the packet contains a generic representation, one with a Whittaker model, exactly when a related orbit of geometric parameters is open.

Arancibia Robert proves the same equivalence holds when the L-packet is replaced by the micro packet attached to the parameter by Adams, Barbasch, and Vogan. As a corollary, he deduces the enhanced Shahidi conjecture for real groups. The Arthur packet for a parameter contains a generic representation exactly when the parameter is trivial on the SL2 factor.
arxiv-2510-26443:
Rhodri Guerrier, Adam W Harley, and Dima Damen adapt big 3D reconstruction models to track points through video. Models such as DUSt3R and MASt3R can match points between views of a still scene. Tracking moving points is harder, and most trackers lean on time flow across many frames.

Guerrier and his two co-authors first show these models already track still points well, beating a leading tracker by a wide margin on one benchmark. They then fine-tune MASt3R with a mix of still and moving point pairs, plus a head that flags whether a point is visible. Their PointSt3R uses only pairs of frames, with no time context. It matched or beat rivals on four data sets, with strong gains on two, and the paper adds three-dimensional tracking results and tests of its design choices.
arxiv-2510-26643:
Emmanouil Sylligardos, with four co-authors, studies how to pick the right anomaly detector for each time series. Anomaly detection flags odd points in data over time, and recent benchmarks show no single method wins across mixed collections. Picking a method per series, based on its traits, is the scalable route.

Sylligardos and the team evaluate two hundred thirty-four model configurations, built from sixteen base classifiers, across more than one thousand nine hundred eighty time series. The classifiers act as selectors, choosing which detector to run. Their selection methods beat every single anomaly detector, while taking about the same running time. The study, a preprint of a VLDB Journal article, is presented as a strong baseline for the selection step in automated pipelines.
arxiv-2510-26943:
Drake Osaben, Jiong Qiu, and Dana W Longcope track how solar flare loops relax after magnetic reconnection. A flare releases energy as field lines reconnect across a current sheet and settle to a lower energy state. Observers often measure progress by the shear angle of the new loops, but that angle is an imperfect gauge of relaxation.

Osaben and his two co-authors develop a technique to infer the three-dimensional structure of post-reconnection field lines, including their local twist, which vanishes for a current-free field. Their method fits loops in extreme ultraviolet images to extrapolations whose feet must match observed flare ribbons. Applied to an eruptive two-ribbon flare from December 2014, the twist fell as the flare progressed. The field proved neither potential nor linear force-free, and the method gives the first time history of a flare's energetic relaxation.
arxiv-2510-27343:
Ali Norouzifar and Wil van der Aalst sort business traces into good and bad runs in this 2025 paper. Firms log each case as an event log, a list of steps taken. Some runs end well; others waste time or break rules. A single map of the process blurs that split and hides what drives each outcome.

Their method learns plain rules from flow traits, like which steps came in which order. Runs with like outcome profiles are grouped, and a process map is built for each group. The maps stay small and readable, and they show what sets good runs apart from bad ones. The tool is public, and tests on real logs from several firms back the approach.
arxiv-2510-27443:
Meenu Ravi, Shailik Sarkar, and three other co-authors forecast how much green a wildfire will strip away, in a 2025 paper. Knowing the loss county by county helps crews target recovery work. Past models missed some drivers and could not say how sure they were. Their system, MVeLMA, reads many data kinds at once.

Satellite views, weather, land traits, and fire records feed a stacked ensemble, a team of models whose outputs a final model blends. A probabilistic layer adds uncertainty ranges to each forecast. In broad tests the system beat strong baselines at predicting post-fire vegetation loss. Its confidence maps flag the counties at highest risk. Planners can use those maps to send aid where the land will heal slowest.
arxiv-2510-27543:
Malik H. Altakrori and nine co-authors present DialectalArabicMMLU in 2025, a test of how well large language models handle Arabic as people speak it each day. Most past tests use Modern Standard Arabic, the formal written form. Spoken forms differ by place, and they are used far more in daily life than formal text.

Test items were hand-translated into five spoken forms: Syrian, Egyptian, Emirati, Saudi, and Moroccan. The set holds fifteen thousand question pairs across thirty-two school and work fields, plus more in English and standard Arabic. Nineteen open models were tested, and scores varied a lot by dialect. The gap shows that skill in formal Arabic does not ensure skill in its spoken forms.
arxiv-2511-00243:
Gavin Crowder, Lora Ramunno, and Stephen Hughes compare ways to prepare a quantum dot that emits one photon at a time, a key part for quantum light sources. The standard method excites the dot head-on, but then a filter must remove the pump light, which wastes half the signal. Newer schemes use pulses tuned away from the dot's own color to skip that filter.

The team tests three such pulse schemes head to head. A two-color pulse loses ground because strong pulses stir lattice vibrations that blur the emission. The other two schemes stay clean, though one is sensitive to pulse errors and the other is harder to build. The study maps which trade-offs matter most.
arxiv-2511-00443:
Ruthwik Reddy Doodipala, Pankaj Pandey, Carolina Torres Rojas, Manob Jyoti Saikia, and Ranganatha Sitaram explore how to pretrain a foundation model for resting-state brain scans. Masked reconstruction, hiding part of the input and asking the model to rebuild it, is a strong self-supervised recipe. Most work hides random regions, but the authors instead mask whole anatomical regions, chosen with a standard brain atlas, applied directly to full four-dimensional scan volumes.

On the ADHD-200 dataset, with nine hundred seventy-three subjects, region-guided masking beat random masking at telling healthy controls from people with ADHD, lifting accuracy by over four percent. Attribution analysis found the limbic region and cerebellum contributed most to faithful reconstruction. The authors argue anatomical masking yields representations that are both stronger and easier to interpret.
arxiv-2511-00843:
Xinsong Li, Ning Jiang, and Jay Selvaraj present the Portal UX Agent, a system that turns plain language requests into working user interfaces. Free form code generation is flexible but often breaks reliability, security, and design rules. Fully fixed interfaces are safe but cannot adapt.

Their middle path lets a language model plan the interface at a high level, while a deterministic renderer assembles it from approved components and layout templates under a strict schema. That keeps output auditable and reusable. The team also builds an evaluation framework mixing automatic checks on coverage, layout, and accessibility with a model judge for meaning and polish. In multi domain portal tests, the agent reliably produced coherent, usable interfaces.
arxiv-2511-01343:
Alvaro Vazquez Rodriguez, Manuel Fernandez-Veiga, and Carlos Giraldo-Rodriguez place cloud native network functions across the cloud continuum. That is the chain of computing sites from core data centers to the network edge that 5G and future 6G services run on. Interdependent tasks form service function chains, and placements must respect resource, bandwidth, connectivity, and latency limits at once.

Classical optimization, heuristics, and reinforcement learning all struggle with scale or with new network conditions. Their alternative treats placement as generation: each scenario becomes a heterogeneous graph. A graph neural network denoiser, trained with constraint aware penalties, iteratively refines a noisy assignment of functions to cloud sites. At run time many candidate placements are sampled and the best feasible one is kept.
arxiv-2511-01443:
Chaoqun Fei and colleagues give graph neural networks a cheaper sense of edge bending. The curvature of a graph's edges tells a network how information can flow, and the classic Ollivier-Ricci version is meaningful but far too expensive to compute on large graphs.

Their stand-in, effective resistance curvature, measures how easily messages pass along an edge using the electrical resistance between its endpoints instead of an optimal transport distance. They prove the new measure's low computing cost and that it can stand in for the Ollivier-Ricci version. Across diverse graph learning tasks, networks using effective resistance curvature matched the results of the classical measure while sharply cutting the computing overhead, making geometric priors usable at scale.
arxiv-2511-01643:
Riccardo Campi and five colleagues answer energy-efficiency questions with a language model grounded in a knowledge graph. Regulations and guidance documents in the energy field are dense and scattered. So the system first extracts a knowledge graph from them automatically. It then navigates and reasons over the graph, to answer users in several languages.

Validation used a dataset of 101 expert-checked question-answer pairs and the RAGAs evaluation framework. The system answered about three quarters of questions correctly, about 75 percent overall, and rose to about 81 percent on general energy-efficiency questions. Multilingual ability looked promising, with translation costing only about 4.4 percentage points of accuracy. The authors report both the architecture's strengths and where it still fails.
arxiv-2511-01743:
Song Gao and six colleagues move mixture-of-experts models, the architecture behind many large AI systems, onto mobile edge networks. In their Networked Mixture-of-Experts system, no single device holds the whole model. Clients answer inference requests collaboratively. They route each task to neighbors whose expertise fits, then aggregate the replies.

Training such a scattered system is the hard part, since edge devices are short on storage, compute, and shareable data. The authors propose a federated learning framework that mixes supervised and self-supervised learning to balance personalization with generalization while keeping communication efficient and data private. Extensive experiments demonstrate the system's effectiveness. They also give practical guidance on how the training algorithms behave. This is a step toward running large-model inference across the devices people actually carry.
arxiv-2511-02243:
Zhuoran Zhang and six co-authors study what happens inside a multimodal language model when its eyes and its reading disagree. Given contradictory visual and textual information, the model must follow one modality, and earlier work measured this only with coarse, dataset-level statistics. The authors decompose the behaviour into two factors: the gap in confidence between the model's visual-only and text-only reasoning on each case. The model's built-in preference when that confidence is evenly matched.

A controlled dataset that varies the difficulty of each input type let them trace a clean law: the more relatively uncertain a modality is, the less the model follows it, monotonically. Probing predictions layer by layer showed the model oscillating between modalities in ambiguous cases, which explains the indecision seen from outside. The balance point between the two becomes a practical measure of inherent modality bias.
arxiv-2511-02443:
Pinku Routaray calculates how a neutron star would vibrate if some of its matter were dark. The study is relativistic. It focuses on the fundamental, or f-mode, oscillation, whose frequency and damping time are targets for gravitational-wave astronomy. Usual matter in the star is described by a relativistic mean field model. The dark matter is a fermionic component, bound by gravity and spread non-uniformly, as a Higgs-portal interaction would capture.

Two parameters steer the dark component: one combining concentration and particle mass, and one setting how steeply the density falls off. Adding the dark matter shifts the f-mode frequency and strengthens the damping, signalling tighter coupling between matter and spacetime ripples. The author maps correlations among the dark parameters, star observables, and mode properties. He calibrates fitting formulas, using the GW170817 merger event to bound the oscillation behaviour of a dark-matter-admixed star.
arxiv-2511-02643:
Planets around pairs of stars are often left out of planet counts, even though half of all stars sit in such systems. Kendall Sullivan, Anne Dattilo, and Natalie Batalha fixed that gap in a 2025 study using data from the Kepler mission. They built a large sample of close binary stars and counted planets orbiting one star of each pair.

Close binaries hosted far fewer planets than single stars. In the core range they had 58 percent fewer planets per system, a gap far too large to be chance. Across the wider range the shortfall was 50 percent. Planet sizes also fell off smoothly, with no valley seen in single-star data. Formation and survival of planets look harder around two suns.
arxiv-2511-02743:
Fedor Ryabinin, Alexey Gotsman, and Pierre Sutra revisit Egalitarian Paxos, a protocol that lets computer replicas agree on an order for commands without a leader. Classic Paxos leans on one leader, which can fail or slow distant clients. The egalitarian design spreads the work, but its spec is tangled, vague, and known to hide subtle bugs.

Their 2025 paper presents EPaxos*, a simpler and provably correct variant. The main advance is a cleaner failure-recovery method, backed by a rigorous proof. The protocol also widens the range of crash counts it can tolerate, up to limits the authors show are optimal. Since many later protocols build on Egalitarian Paxos, a sound base has value beyond this one system.
arxiv-2511-02843:
Luc Ramses Talla Waffo surveys what is known about two families of ratios built from famous functions. One uses the Riemann zeta function at odd integers. The other uses the Dirichlet beta function at even integers, each scaled by matching powers of pi. Whether these numbers are irrational is unknown, and the 2025 paper gathers several distinct analytic frameworks that converge on their values, giving a unified view of the evidence.

The formulas point toward linear independence conjectures about these constants. If those conjectures were proved, the irrationality of the ratios would follow at once. The paper is thus a map of a long-standing open area: it shows how separate lines of analysis meet at the same numbers, and what a proof would unlock.
arxiv-2511-03143:
Erfan Shayegani and four colleagues teach chatbots to show the right kind of empathy for the task at hand. Generic warmth misses what users expect in a medical chat versus a booking chat. Their 2025 paper first studies 672 real multi-turn conversations across eight tasks, measuring the gap between the empathy users hoped for and what they felt they got, before and after each chat.

To close that gap, they generate synthetic conversations steered toward task-matched empathy patterns, then train small expert adapters, one style per context. The trained system cut the empathy gap by about 73 percent, and empathy scores more than doubled on their metrics. Adapters also held their tone across long chats, where plain system prompts faded fast.
arxiv-2511-03343:
Daniel Walsken, Pavel Petrov, and Matthias Ehrhardt speed up a standard method for tracing guided sound waves through the ocean. Their split-step approach usually leans on grid differences to handle depth, which caps accuracy on coarse grids and wastes parallel hardware on fine ones. The team swaps that part for a spectral treatment built on a sine transform.

With steady sound speed, the depth part comes out exact under matching edge rules. Shifts in sound speed are handled as a series of small corrections. Tests show strong accuracy across ranges while running in a form that parallel machines like. Better wave tracing helps sonar, ocean sensing, and any task that reads sound bent by water layers.
arxiv-2511-03543:
Bratati Bhat, Ankan Das, Prasanta Gorai, and Dipen Sahu model why two infant stars born together show different chemical fingerprints. The pair, IRAS 4A1 and 4A2, sits in one low-mass proto-binary system yet differs in physical and chemical traits. Using a radiative transfer code, the team models the warm inner envelope, called a hot corino, around each star.

Methanol and formaldehyde lines are the main probes, since the same transitions look different toward each twin. A simple spherical infalling envelope with a narrow outflow anchors the model. Fresh high-resolution views from a major interferometer frame the puzzle the model must match. Sorting dust glow from absorption helps explain how two siblings diverged so early.
arxiv-2511-03843:
Ira Wolfson, writing alone under the title Quantum Inaccessibility, revisits Loschmidt's paradox: why does the world move one way in time when microscopic laws work equally well backwards? Evidence fields in the catalog carried a different title, but the arXiv record governs here, and Wolfson argues the answer lies in access, not dynamics.

Chaotic motion, he argues, pushes phase-space structure below the quantum resolution scale at a critical time. After that point the reversed state still solves the equations, yet no physically allowed operation can select it. Predictions include a sigmoid drop in fidelity and logarithmic scaling of that critical time, matching decades of Loschmidt echo experiments and a stadium-billiard simulation.
arxiv-2511-04343:
Hitting times measure how long a random walk takes to travel between two nodes. Themistoklis Haris, Fabian Spaeh, Spyros Dragazis, and Charalampos Tsourakakis build local methods to estimate them at scale. Older methods need the full graph, which fails on very large networks.

One method stops the walk estimate when two walks, started from each end, first meet. The team supports it with analysis using product graphs and Markov chain bounds. A second method extends earlier work by Peng and others from 2021. Local estimates like these serve network ranking, recommendation systems, and models of how diseases spread.
arxiv-2511-04443:
Sergey Vinogradov, writing alone, models the first flash events inside silicon photomultipliers. These sensors count single photons, but they also fire extra pulses called afterpulsing and crosstalk. Telling the first true event from that noise sets the timing quality of the detector.

Vinogradov applies order statistics, a classic tool from scintillation detector timing, to the arrival times. Crosstalk is treated as a branching Poisson process and extended to afterpulsing. Seeds, free charges able to trigger new avalanches, anchor the model. It predicts that the first-arrival spread narrows as more events occur, a guide for sensor design.
arxiv-2511-04643:
Alamgir Munir Qazi and two colleagues show retrieval can beat generation for fake news detection. Many top systems use large language models to write explanatory rationales. Those systems cost heavy compute and can hallucinate in real deployments.

Their framework, DeReC, pairs dense retrieval with a specialized classifier instead. General-purpose text embeddings do the heavy lifting, with no generated rationale at all. On the RAWFC dataset, runtime fell by ninety-five percent, from twenty-three minutes to far less. Accuracy also improved over the explanation-writing models, a rare win on both speed and quality.
arxiv-2511-04943:
Shalmali Bandyopadhyay and co-authors study positive solutions of elliptic systems whose boundary terms grow faster than linear. A scale factor in the system acts as a knob, and the team asks how solution branches form as that knob moves.

By mixing a rescaling trick with degree theory and regularity results, they prove a connected branch of positive weak solutions that splits off from infinity as the factor nears zero. With extra terms near zero, a branch from zero also forms. They then count how many positive solutions occur for each factor value.
arxiv-2511-06343:
Shen Bian finds the dividing line between calm spread and collapse in a two-species chemotaxis model. Chemotaxis describes creatures or cells drifting toward chemical signals, here with two species attracting each other through a power-law force. Diffusion follows a porous medium style, tuned so the system's free energy keeps a conformal symmetry.

Special steady states, symmetric and spread out rather than compact, set the threshold. When both species start below the steady states in the stated norms, solutions exist for all time. When both start above them, solutions blow up in finite time. The result gives a clean critical test for global existence in three or more dimensions.
arxiv-2511-06943:
Ayushi Sharma and sixteen co-authors turn citizen science photographs into global maps of plant traits. Traits such as plant height, leaf area, and leaf nitrogen content drive ecosystem processes, but field readings are costly and sparse. Over fifty million geotagged plant photographs worldwide capture morphology and physiology that current trait maps ignore.

Their system, PlantTraitNet, is a multimodal, multitask deep learning system that predicts four key traits from photos under weak supervision, while reporting its own uncertainty. Aggregating predictions across space yields global trait maps. Validated against independent vegetation survey data and benchmarked against leading products, the maps proved consistently more accurate for every trait tested. The result shows that computer vision over citizen imagery can scale global ecological mapping.
arxiv-2511-07043:
Songmei Qin and eight co-authors catalog blue straggler stars in Milky Way open clusters using Gaia's third data release. Blue stragglers look younger and bluer than their cluster siblings, and finding them clarifies how stars interact and evolve in clusters. Starting from published cluster catalogs, the team inspected each cluster's color-magnitude diagram for candidates, then redid membership with the pyUPMASK algorithm and fitted isochrones to derive age, distance, reddening, and metallicity.

Stragglers were identified by their positions relative to the fitted isochrone, the zero-age main sequence, and the equal-mass binary sequence. The catalog adds 272 new stragglers in 99 clusters: 153 blue stragglers, 98 probable blue stragglers, and 21 yellow stragglers. That grows the number of Milky Way open clusters known to host stragglers by about twenty-two percent.
arxiv-2511-07343:
Zeman Li and seven co-authors remove the training bottleneck of recurrent language models with deep test-time memory, such as Titans and TTT. These models scale linearly with sequence length, unlike transformers, but train painfully slowly because a chunk-size compromise rules everything: big chunks are fast but inaccurate, small chunks accurate but slow. Their scheme, TNT, decouples the two stages.

Stage one pre-trains efficiently with a hierarchical memory: a global module digests large hardware-friendly chunks while parallel local modules handle detail, with periodic memory resets breaking sequential dependencies for massive parallelization. Stage two briefly fine-tunes only the local modules at a small, high-resolution chunk size. On Titans and TTT, TNT trained up to seventeen times faster than the most accurate baseline configuration while together improving accuracy.
arxiv-2511-07543:
Zewei Wu, Andrey Kravtsov, and Harley Katz model how the early universe became transparent. Young galaxies leaked ultraviolet light that ionized hydrogen between them, ending the cosmic dark ages. How much light escaped faint galaxies strongly steers that history, yet escape fractions stay poorly measured.

A galaxy formation model matched to local dwarfs and to distant galaxy counts supplies star formation histories. Varying escape assumptions shows how much faint galaxies, down to very dim limits, drive ionization timing. Including them changes the predicted ionized fraction across redshift. The results guide telescope searches for the tiny galaxies that likely reionized the cosmos.
arxiv-2511-07743:
Yuezhe Yang, Qingqing Ruan, and Wenjie Cai synthesize new ultrasound views in real time. Ultrasound is safe and common, but its narrow field of view limits three-dimensional understanding. Gaussian splatting renders novel views for ordinary photos, not for echo physics and free-moving probes.

UltraGS adapts splatting with depth-aware primitives that carry learnable fields of view, keeping geometry steady under loose probe motion. A differentiable acoustic renderer mixes simple wave effects to form intensities efficiently. A clinical dataset supports evaluation. Freehand ultrasound that can be re-viewed afterward could help training, planning, and review without rescanning patients.
arxiv-2511-07843:
Jay Chooi, Kevin Cong, and Russell Li bring a favorite optimizer into private training. Differential privacy protects people inside datasets, but private optimizers often lag in accuracy. AdamW trains modern models well in public settings, so a private version is worth building carefully.

DP-AdamW adds privacy noise to decoupled weight decay training. A bias-corrected variant, DP-AdamW-BC, repairs the second-moment estimate that noise distorts. Theory and experiments check whether performance survives the privacy budget. Hospitals, banks, and platforms all need models trained on sensitive data; optimizers that keep both accuracy and formal privacy widen what can be learned safely.
arxiv-2511-08143:
Qiankun Pi, Yepeng Sun, Jicang Lu, and Qinlong Fan propose RelPrior for extracting relations from whole documents with language models. Document level extraction must find which entity pairs truly relate, beyond single sentences. The usual extract then predict pipeline floods the model with unrelated pairs, and labels outside a fixed set get counted as errors even when associations were found.

RelPrior first uses a binary relation check as a prior to filter unrelated pairs. It then uses the predefined relation set to match entities for triple extraction instead of predicting labels directly. On two benchmarks, this reorder beats existing language model methods and reaches top performance.
arxiv-2511-08543:
Soumik Ghosh and three co-authors ask whether measuring part of a quantum system can leave the rest more random than the whole. The effect, called deep thermalization, turns the unmeasured part into a set of states that mimics fully random states, known as a quantum state design.

The team proves a tight limit: starting from a global design of one strength, the leftover part can reach at most half that strength in general. They show the bound cannot be improved by building a case that hides a sign pattern in higher moments. Chaotic motion changes the picture, though. Under chaotic dynamics the leftover ensemble becomes fully random in the large-system limit, even from a weak global design.
arxiv-2511-08643:
Anna Van Boven and Kyri Baker look for a cleaner way to check whether market power schedules can actually run on the grid. Wholesale markets use linear approximations, but the full AC power flow check often breaks bounds on reactive power, voltage, or line heat limits.

Their augmented method adds two bus types to the usual setup. At a troubled bus it gives up the generator voltage setpoint and instead fixes voltage at a load bus, moving a degree of freedom across the network. On the IEEE fourteen, fifty-seven, and three hundred bus test systems, switching bus types cuts total violations. The authors present the approach as a streamlined route to feasible setpoints that respect every bound.
arxiv-2511-09043:
Farjana Yesmin builds a federated learning system for hospitals that keeps patient data private, cuts network traffic drastically, and runs on modest hardware. Medical institutions cannot pool records, yet models improve when they train together, so MedHE combines adaptive gradient sparsification with CKKS homomorphic encryption, letting a server aggregate updates it cannot read.

A dynamic threshold with error compensation selects the top gradient entries each round, shrinking communication by ninety-seven point five percent, from over twelve hundred megabytes to thirty-two megabytes per round. Formal analysis grounds security in the ring learning with errors problem, and differential privacy holds with epsilon at most one. Across five trials accuracy reaches about eighty-nine point five percent, statistically indistinguishable from ordinary federated learning. The design targets HIPAA compliance and scales past one hundred institutions.
arxiv-2511-09243:
Helena Bordini de Lucas and six co-authors map how brain activity changes across sleep stages, using recordings from inside the human skull. Intracranial data from 106 patients offer unmatched detail in space and time for studying neural dynamics. The team compares wakefulness with the N2 and N3 sleep stages and REM sleep.

They summarize each signal by weighted permutation entropy and a statistical complexity measure, placing stages on a complexity-entropy plane. Each stage occupies its own region, giving it a distinct dynamic signature. A whole-brain computer model of adaptive spiking neurons reproduces the pattern by adjusting one adaptation parameter. A support vector machine then separates the cortical states with high accuracy, suggesting medical and research value.
arxiv-2511-09443:
Hongchao Shu and eight co-authors improve how a bronchoscope's position is tracked inside a patient's airways during procedures. Respiratory motion and anatomy differences shift the live endoscopic view away from the preoperative CT scan. Earlier vision methods often failed to generalize across patients, leaving alignment errors.

Their system registers each endoscopic frame against CT-rendered depth maps using a fine-tuned encoder that ignores modality and domain gaps. A differentiable rendering loop then refines the camera pose through depth consistency. Trained only on synthetic data, the system localized with an average position error of 2.65 millimetres and small rotational error on their benchmark. They also release the first public synthetic benchmark data set for bronchoscopy navigation.
arxiv-2511-09843:
Daniela Martin and six co-authors adapt a solar physics foundation model to classify structures in the solar wind. Space weather driven by solar activity threatens satellites and ground infrastructure, and streams such as coronal mass ejections vary in density, speed, temperature, and magnetic field. Their model turns features from a model pretrained on Solar Dynamics Observatory images toward in-situ plasma readings instead.

These features are combined with spacecraft position and solar magnetic connectivity, encoded with Fourier features, to form a neural field model. Fine-tuning uses labels derived from Parker Solar Probe readings. Overall accuracy was modest, which the authors attribute to coarse labels, class imbalance, and limited transfer from the pretrained model, but the study establishes feasibility and shares its code publicly.
arxiv-2511-10343:
Alistair O'Brien, Didier Rémy, and Gabriel Scherer work on type systems, the rules programming languages use to catch errors before programs run. They study the ML family of languages, whose type inference finds the most general type for each expression. Popular extensions of ML can break that property, making inference unpredictable and sometimes fragile.

Existing fixes force type information to flow in one fixed order, which rejects some correct programs. The authors let information flow in any order, pausing a check when it needs facts that are not known yet and resuming later. They show the method restores principal inference for two difficult OCaml features, record label overloading and first-class polymorphism.
arxiv-2511-10543:
Igor Rivin describes an automated system that reads mathematics papers, hunts for errors, and writes full referee reports with journal recommendations. He reports applying it to more than 37,000 papers from the arXiv repository across several fields of mathematics.

According to Rivin's analysis, the system found errors at notable rates, about one paper in ten in numerical analysis and somewhat fewer in geometric topology. It found none in a small category theory sample. He reports it flagged errors even in historical works by Euler and Dirichlet and in papers by living Fields medalists. The system also sorted papers by journal suitability. Rivin argues the method could extend to physics and computer science, making automated peer review at scale feasible.
arxiv-2511-10743:
Lena Komarova leads an 18-author team measuring how well twelve bright galaxies in the reionization era produced ionizing photons, a key input for understanding how the early universe became transparent. The galaxies come from the REBELS survey, observed with JWST's NIRSpec instrument in integral-field mode.

Whole-galaxy scores cluster near the canonical value used in reionization models. Zooming into 25 individual star-forming clumps reveals a much wider spread, with the top clumps showing strong hydrogen emission consistent with very young stars. The score correlates with specific star formation rate, star formation surface density, and stellar mass. From earlier data, the team estimates only about two percent of hydrogen-ionizing light escapes these galaxies, implying ionized bubbles around them of roughly a million parsecs.
arxiv-2511-10843:
Alexander W. Goodall, Edwin Hamel-De le Court, and Francesco Belardinelli bring a surprising result from off-policy evaluation into the heart of reinforcement learning. Recent work showed that data collected by a well-designed behavior policy can yield return estimates with provably lower variance than data collected by the policy being improved. On-policy collection, it turns out, is not variance-optimal after all.

The authors extend that insight to the fully online setting, where evaluation and improvement interleave and a single worker's behavior policy gathers the experience. This differs from distributed setups such as IMPALA, which mainly correct mismatches between many workers and a changing learner. Extending two policy-gradient methods with the new regime, they report better sample efficiency and performance across a diverse set of environments.
arxiv-2511-10943:
Jialin Wu, Jian Yang, and their colleagues offer a direct way to merge expert models so users can steer the trade-offs between tasks. Older merging tools first run a costly search that grows fast as tasks are added, then build models on demand. That search stage is the main bottleneck the authors set out to remove.

Instead of tuning raw weights, they fix the merged model's final output layer with a single linear step that has a closed-form answer. User choices feed straight into that step, so a balanced model can be built at once. Tests show a better spread of trade-offs, closer matches to user choices, and far lower cost.
arxiv-2511-11043:
Asen Nachkov, Jan-Nico Zaech, and their colleagues present DSS, a planning method that lets a self-driving system search for better actions inside a simulator before it moves. Safe driving in dense traffic needs that kind of look-ahead, but search is hard when the policy, the world model, and the scoring rule all must be learned. DSS leans on a simulator whose physics are built in.

The simulator predicts the next state and also scores it, and its smooth math lets the agent improve actions by gradient steps over imagined futures. It mixes that search with random sampling. Tests show clear gains in tracking and path accuracy over learning-only and other planning methods.
arxiv-2511-11243:
Jitesh Chavan, Rohit Lal, and their colleagues present Arcee, a state-chain design that improves Mamba state-space models for vision tasks. Mamba scans inputs in order with a selective step that keeps a running state, which suits sequences but fits images awkwardly. Standard Mamba restarts each block's state from zero, throwing away what the prior block had built up.

Arcee instead hands each block's final state to the next block as its starting point. The handoff is built as a smooth boundary map, so gradients flow across blocks end to end. The design is parameter-free, costs almost nothing, and works with all prior vision Mamba variants, treating the passed state as a mild directional prior.
arxiv-2511-11343:
Ibrahima Bah, Shlomo Razamat, and their colleagues study a clash in quantum field theory. The clash is between locality and unitarity for symmetries. It grows sharp for a new kind of symmetry. In that kind, symmetry actions often cannot be undone like group actions can.

Locality says far-apart actions do not affect each other. The authors argue it still forces clear patterns. Those patterns govern how symmetry actions work on the state space. From them, the team builds a test value. The value gauges how non-local a symmetry action is. In a class of cases, it encodes data from the fusion rules. Those rules say how symmetries combine.
arxiv-2511-11543:
Edward Chernysh proves that sign-changing solutions defined on all of space exist for weighted critical p-Laplace equations of Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg type. Such entire nodal solutions cross zero, so they capture behavior that one-signed solutions cannot.

Classes of symmetry are examined to show which patterns a solution can be forced to respect. For suitable symmetry setups, a nontrivial sign-changing solution with exactly that symmetry exists, while other symmetry types are shown to clash with each other. Infinitely many distinct symmetry types turn out to admit nodal solutions. Results of this kind guide the study of weighted elliptic equations where weights and critical growth make compactness delicate.
arxiv-2511-11843:
Yiwei Zhao and seven co-authors introduce TD-Orch, a framework that decides where small tasks and their data should meet inside a distributed system. Each task in a batch needs one data item, and moving tasks, moving data, or both can bring them together, so orchestration decides both speed and network load.

A distributed push-pull technique balances work across machines even when access patterns are heavily skewed, while keeping the programming interface simple. On key-value store workloads the system reaches up to two point eight times speedups, and graph processing serves as the flagship application. Lambda-style task systems gain a principled way to fight hotspots without burying developers in placement logic.
arxiv-2511-11943:
The Euclid Collaboration reports a hunt for very massive galaxies shining less than a billion years after the Big Bang, in the first quick data release from the Euclid space telescope. Galaxies above a high mass threshold at redshifts five to seven stress formation models, which must assemble them implausibly fast.

Across about twenty-three square degrees in two deep fields, Euclid photometry is combined with Spitzer infrared and ground-based optical data for energy distribution fitting. Rigorous cuts leave a conservative sample of one hundred forty-five massive galaxy candidates. Each confirmed system at that epoch is a datapoint galaxy formation theory must absorb, and Euclid's wide fields will multiply them.
arxiv-2511-12043:
Hao Li and five co-authors uncover a new privacy risk in retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, systems that answer questions using private text collections. Attackers can try to tell whether a given text was in that collection. Older attacks work poorly here because the system is a black box and gives weak signals.

The team names the leak BudgetLeak. It varies the generation budget, the cap on how long a reply can be, and watches how answer quality changes. Texts in the collection gain quality faster as the budget grows. Tests on four datasets beat prior baselines, which points to a need for new defenses.
arxiv-2511-12143:
Jialiang Wang and six co-authors tackle learning from noisy labels, where some training examples are tagged wrong. Robust loss functions are a common defense, because they limit how much a wrong label can pull the model off course. The team looks for a property that predicts when a loss will stay robust.

They introduce the variation ratio and build a family of losses whose ratio stays bounded. Theory shows a smaller ratio should mean better robustness, and it also gives simpler ways to meet known conditions for sound losses. They recast several common losses in this bounded form, and tests on varied datasets show gains and flexibility.
arxiv-2511-13143:
Gorka Abad and nine co-authors audit how the security community evaluates defenses against backdoor attacks. A backdoored model behaves normally until a trigger input activates hidden misbehavior, and dozens of defenses claim to stop it. The authors reviewed one hundred eighty-three defense papers from 2018 to 2025 and found the testing a patchwork: inconsistent setups, metrics, and threat-model assumptions that make defenses impossible to compare fairly.

They then ran over three thousand experiments themselves, crossing three datasets, four architectures, sixteen representative defenses, and five attacks, showing that a defense's measured strength swings a lot with the setup. Gaps they name include unreported overhead, untested behavior on benign inputs, and biased tuning choices. The paper closes with concrete recommendations to standardize testing. Its message to users is blunt: a defense is only as proven as the protocol that tested it.
arxiv-2511-13243:
Xiaoqi Han and 6 co-authors examine how editing multimodal models can quietly break their use of images. Editing aims to fix wrong facts, but older tests use random or weakly matched images and can overstate success. The authors build a fuller locality test with three image settings and seven data types.

Their dynamic test, De-VQA, reveals a flaw they call transient blindness, where an edited model leans on text and ignores the picture.
