Confinement is the effect that keeps quarks bound inside particles, and Polyakov gave a classic account of it in lower dimensions. Whether a similar story works in our four dimensional world is the open question here.

Bolognesi shows that a generalized Polyakov mechanism can lead to confinement at weak coupling when the theory sits in a spatially varying magnetic field. At a threshold field strength, monopole loops gain an almost flat direction. In that regime confinement works much like the lower dimensional case, with monopoles replaced by deconfined bits of a loop.
arxiv-2512-15843:
Reinis Irmejs and J. Ignacio Cirac improve the simulation of sparse, non local fermion models on qubit hardware in a 2025 paper. Interacting fermion systems are a prime target for quantum computers, but encoding fermionic operators on qubits adds heavy overhead. The team studies models where each of N fermionic modes joins only a constant number of interactions.

Their encoding adds a few auxiliary fermions per mode, which removes the long Jordan Wigner strings that inflate circuits. Preparing the auxiliary state costs once, and it stays fixed during evolution. Long time Trotter evolution then reaches asymptotically optimal circuit depth, turning a multiplicative logarithmic overhead into an additive one. About order d times N extra qubits are needed.
arxiv-2512-15943:
Researchers show that a fine tuned small language model can beat large models at agentic tool calling in a 2025 paper. Large models are costly for routine enterprise work, which motivates targeted small models. The team fine tunes the OPT-350M model, released by Meta AI in 2022, with supervised fine tuning for tool use tasks.

After one epoch of training, the small model reaches a 77.55 percent pass rate on the ToolBench evaluation. That score far exceeds ChatGPT with chain of thought at 26.00 percent, ToolLLaMA DFS at 30.18 percent, and ToolLLaMA CoT at 16.27 percent in their comparison. The authors argue thoughtful targeted training lowers adoption barriers for production generative AI.
arxiv-2512-16043:
Yilda Boukhtouchen and three co-authors study a new way to spot dark matter in their arXiv paper, posted in 2025. Some theories say dark matter comes in loosely bound clumps rather than single particles. When such a clump crosses Earth, collisions with ordinary nuclei can knock pieces loose, so the clump breaks apart into a cascade as it travels.

The authors trace how the freed pieces scatter and spread through the planet. They identify signs that underground detectors could catch, including several scatters that do not line up, distinctive timing gaps between hits, and matching signals in distant laboratories. These fingerprints depend on the clump's makeup, so a detection could reveal what the composite is. The work targets weakly interacting dark matter at the TeV scale.
arxiv-2512-16343:
Kai Hong Law reports particle physics results in a short 2025 conference paper from arXiv, given at the 32nd International Symposium on Lepton Photon Interactions. It presents selected new findings from the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, all searching for particles in the dark sector, the hypothesized family that may include dark matter.

The searches use data from the collider's Run 2 and Run 3 periods. Dedicated data streams were used to open up the low-mass range, where ordinary recording triggers would miss faint signals. Machine learning methods separate possible signals from background noise. The seven-page contribution is a compact status report for specialists tracking what CMS has and has not found.
arxiv-2512-16643:
Leena Diehl and a large CMS team study how neutron damage in silicon sensors heals over time, a process called annealing. The sensors, made on 8-inch p-type wafers for the future High-Granularity Calorimeter at the High-Luminosity LHC, must survive very high radiation doses.

Small test diodes were exposed to reactor neutrons in Ljubljana, then held at steady heat levels from 5.5 to 60 degrees while the team tracked charge and current. From the data they pull out healing time scales within the Hamburg model frame. The values will help predict how sensors act during yearly stops and long shutdowns, and improve models for other projects at like doses.
arxiv-2512-16943:
Tariq Ahmad Mir and Marcel Ausloos ask whether delayed recognition, the fate of papers ignored for years before citations burst, struck the very man who first studied it. Eugene Garfield wrote on the pattern from 1970 to 2004, long before van Raan named such papers Sleeping Beauties in 2004.

The pair trace citations of the Garfield 1980 paper that first hit the pattern head on. It drew a mere 10 citations up to 2004, then woke weakly in 2007 with 20 more by 2010, after a 28-year sleep. That even Garfields own paper on the theme suffered the theme is, the authors note, a rich irony.
arxiv-2512-17143:
Sandeep Mishra and a large team present Pro-Pose. It is a method that turns a casual full-body photo into a clean, reposable portrait avatar. Pro photos offer fine light and flattering poses. Self-taken shots come with clutter, occlusion, and harsh settings instead.

A paired data set of the same person in many outfits and poses does not exist. The team thus works in canonical UV space. That is a flattened body map that splits pose from appearance. A novel reposing step models occlusions and makes new views. Multi-image fine-tuning locks identity under extreme pose shifts. Output portraits score strongly on real imagery. They give virtual try-on a cleaner biometric base.
arxiv-2512-17243:
Paul X McCarthy, Xian Gong, Marian-Andrei Rizoiu, and Paolo Boldi map how aid money really moves around the world. Aid is often told as a story of country giving to country, which hides the groups the cash passes through. Using 10.9 million records, they trace over one million payments worth about one trillion US dollars among 22,773 organisations.

Size, they find, is not the same as power in the network. Big donors such as USAID rank only as central as their partner counts suggest. Foundations, research groups, and delivery firms sit in the most central spots. Nearly every group links into one web, yet money flows down long one-way chains. Losing one major funder could strand many groups below it.
arxiv-2512-17543:
Davide Giovagnoli, Enzo Maria Merlino, and Diego Moreira sharpen a boundary rule for a hard class of equations. The Hopf-Oleinik lemma says a solution that peaks inside a region must lift off the border at least linearly, like a ramp. Their version covers degenerate, fully nonlinear operators, where the equation's strength fades with the gradient, and it pins the ramp's steepness to constants set only by the equation's structure.

A counterexample marks the rule's edge: for equations that only act at large gradients, the ramp can fail entirely. The team then applies the rule to free boundary problems, where the border itself is unknown, proving tidy Lipschitz control for a Bernoulli problem and for a flame spread model. Such bounds keep simulated flames honest.
arxiv-2512-17843:
Yueru Yan and four coauthors built ShareChat, a large collection of real chatbot conversations gathered from links that users shared in public. The corpus holds 142,808 conversations and over 660,000 turns from five platforms: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, and Grok. Unlike older datasets, it keeps each platform's own features, such as citations and code.

Three case studies show what the data can reveal. One compares how fully each platform meets user intent, another compares how search based systems cite sources, and a third tracks how reply speed changed over time. The set covers 95 languages from April 2023 to October 2025 and is open to other researchers.
arxiv-2512-18143:
Konstantin Larin and Daniel R. Kowal fix a quiet flaw in studies linking air pollution to health. Exposure for each county is itself a model's guess, then fed into a health model. Two common shortcuts, using one best guess value or borrowing the first model's spread with no feedback, both bend the final doubt ranges out of shape.

Their algorithms run both stages as one Bayesian whole, passing news both ways. Applied to fine particle pollution and county death rates in the South-Central United States, the joint method gave sharper estimates with honest ranges. Sound doubt matters here, since such studies guide clean air rules worth billions.
arxiv-2512-18643:
Sergey V. Berezin studies a generalized root called the ultra-radical in this 2025 mathematics paper. The ultra-radical is the multi-valued solution of an equation linking two exponents, and inside its convergence radius each branch is given by a Master-J power series. Beyond that radius, analytic continuation requires switching to one of two conjugate series, and picking the wrong one breaks the branch.

Berezin gives a fixed geometric rule that selects the correct series for every branch index, removing trial and error. His key finding is that only the principal branch stays continuous as the parameters vary smoothly, even in limits leading to an exponential equation or an ordinary binomial root. Other branches oscillate wildly or lose their identity, which matters for systems whose exponents change with state.
arxiv-2512-18743:
Justine Fasquel and Shigenori Nakatsuka work on W-algebras, structures in algebra built by shrinking a Lie algebra's symmetry through quantum Hamiltonian reduction. When two W-algebras are linked by such a reduction, results can transfer between them. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, gives a general test for when that link exists.

The test concerns good pairs: a nilpotent orbit with an even good grading in a simple Lie algebra. When the pair passes, a quantum Hamiltonian reduction between the linked affine W-algebras must exist. For type A, any two W-algebras from adjacent nilpotent orbits are related this way, in general. The result organizes a large family of algebras used in conformal field theory and mathematical physics.
arxiv-2512-19443:
Evelyn Zhang, Fufu Yu, Aoqi Wu, and Zichen Wen prune visual tokens for multimodal language models without wrecking fine detail. Long image token streams make these models slow. Older pruning either trusts importance scores warped by position bias, or enforces diversity while ignoring the user's prompt and the image layout.

D2Pruner first locks in a core of pivot tokens by a debiased attention score. The rest are placed on a graph linking near and similar tokens, and a maximal independent set picks the survivors. Importance and structure are both honored. The authors report that localization tasks, where earlier methods failed badly, hold up far better.
arxiv-2512-19643:
Rajyasri Roy, Dibyajyoti Nayak, and Somdatta Goswami address the way neural operator surrogates drift off course during long simulations. Neural operators mimic expensive partial differential equation solvers at a fraction of the cost, but step-by-step rollout errors compound, and average accuracy scores give no promise for any single run. Their framework, ANCHOR, keeps a trusted classical solver on standby inside the loop.

ANCHOR watches a smoothed average of the equation's residual, a physics-based error signal needing no ground truth, and calls in the classical solver only when drift grows. The error signal tracks true relative error closely in tests on six standard equations, from Burgers' and Allen-Cahn to Navier-Stokes and three-dimensional heat flow. Long rollouts stay bounded and steadier than a standalone operator, at far less cost than full simulation.
arxiv-2512-19843:
Philipp Ketz, Adam McCloskey, and Jan Scherer ask how to tell if a hand-built stats test is a good one. In odd settings, researchers craft tests with the right size by wit. But their power against other cases stays unknown. The paper builds a number-based frame around weighted average power. That rule trades off the odds of catching each rival case.

A nested search finds the weights that bring a given test closest to the best test of that kind. A surprise shows up. The best test's reject odds form a near power envelope for the hand-built one. That gives a yardstick for optimality, with proof that the search converges. The method is applied to two known tests. One is for weak instruments. The other is for a parameter near its edge.
arxiv-2512-19943:
Haoyi Zhong and three co-authors build SE360, an editing system for panoramic photos. Text-guided editing works well on plain images. But 360-degree panoramas wrap around the viewer. Naive methods then give results that look wrong. They look wrong in the flat wrapped form and in perspective views alike. SE360 rests on training data made with no human labelers.

A coarse-to-fine pipeline makes the data on its own. It uses a vision-language model with adaptive projection tweaks. It segments objects with their physical context in view. The pairs it yields are sound in meaning and in geometry, even from unlabeled panoramas. A two-stage polish then boosts realism. It also guards against the model learning to lean on erasure marks. On that data, the team trains a transformer-based diffusion editor. It takes text, mask, or guide-image input.
arxiv-2512-20243:
Thomas Attema and co-authors test what happens when the 5G core network swaps its cryptography for post-quantum methods. Quantum computers would break today's standard schemes, so mobile networks must eventually migrate. The question is whether the larger keys and heavier math of post-quantum methods slow the network down.

In a simulation environment, the team modelled registration and deregistration of varying numbers of user devices. They measured bandwidth use and latency under the new methods. Performance did shift measurably, but the extra computation and message size caused no real harm to network functions. The results support earlier findings that the 5G core can absorb post-quantum cryptography without inherent problems.
arxiv-2512-20443:
Alexandros Kanargias and co-authors compute how a strongly coupled quantum fluid resists shearing, at temperatures far below its chemical potential. Holography translates the hard problem into gravity: black branes in four-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, within Einstein-Maxwell theory. The team calculates retarded Green's functions at low frequency and temperature.

A new energy scale appears when the transverse space has finite volume, set by nearly gapless Schwarzian modes. Below it, quantum-gravitational corrections change the Green's functions, and the authors track them across regimes. Shear viscosity rises above its semiclassical value as temperature drops. The famous viscosity-to-entropy ratio dips below the semiclassical bound in one window, then turns around and finally diverges at the lowest temperatures.
arxiv-2512-20643:
Suriya R S and co-authors forecast colliding gravitating bodies with physics-aware machine learning. The n-body problem is fundamental to astrophysics, but purely data-driven predictors ignore the laws they should obey and demand huge data sets. Scientific machine learning embeds the known physics directly into the model.

Working in Julia, the team compares neural ordinary differential equations against universal differential equations, which keep part of the true equations inside the learner. Noisy synthetic data stand in for imperfect observations. The key measurement is the forecasting breakdown point, the least training data from which accurate prediction of unseen futures remains possible. The universal model needs only a fifth of the data; the neural model needs almost all of it. Physics, supplied generously, pays for data.
arxiv-2512-20743:
Yao Lu and fifteen co-authors give engineers a better way to model superconducting quantum circuits while microwaves are driving them. Josephson circuits form the hardware of many quantum computers, and accurate models guide precise control. Older tools handle still circuits well but miss effects from drives, noise, and energy loss through microwave ports.

Their techniques start from classical microwave simulations run in standard finite-element software. From those, they build the full time-dependent Hamiltonian for circuits of any shape, under charge, flux, or mixed control signals. Tests on realistic devices captured driven behavior plus drive-caused relaxation and dephasing. The toolbox should help designers tune circuits before building them.
arxiv-2512-21243:
Anatoly Onishchenko, Alexey Kovalev, and Aleksandr Panov fix a blind spot in robot planning: the map goes stale. Language-model planners for household robots typically consult a scene graph built before the task begins, assuming every object stays where the graph recorded it. LookPlanGraph starts from static assets and object priors, then keeps revising the graph while the plan runs. A vision-language model reads the robot's camera view to verify expected objects and register new ones.

In VirtualHome and OmniGibson simulations with moved objects, the updating planner beats static-graph rivals, and real-world trials confirm the approach works off-screen too. The team releases GraSIF, a dataset of 514 instruction-following tasks with an automated validation framework, assembled from SayPlan Office, BEHAVIOR-1K, and VirtualHome sources. Robots that look while they act, rather than trusting yesterday's map, fail less in homes that refuse to sit still.
arxiv-2512-21343:
A home energy system must juggle goals that pull against each other: lower bills, lower emissions, and rooms that stay comfortable. John Boik, Kobus Esterhuysen, Jacqueline Hynes, and five co-authors present EcoNet, a Bayesian controller built on active inference. It plans for households and whole neighborhoods while forecasts of weather and solar output remain uncertain.

Active inference lets each agent weigh conditional, conflicting preferences instead of chasing one fixed target. The system schedules devices and resources across homes, coordinating use rather than optimizing each house in isolation. Simulations accompany the design. The approach speaks to anyone building home energy management that must act sensibly when the future is only partly known.
arxiv-2512-21443:
S. M. Mallikarjunaiah presents a computational framework for simulating cracks in materials whose density varies by position. Predicting how a crack behaves inside such uneven material is hard, because the governing equations become nonlinear and the fields change sharply near the crack tip.

The method is an hp-adaptive finite element scheme, which automatically refines the simulation mesh where needed and raises the polynomial order where the solution is smooth. One error indicator, based on jumps across element edges, decides where to shrink elements. A second, based on how fast expansion coefficients decay, decides where to raise the order. Mallikarjunaiah tests the framework under three loading regimes: pure tension, pure shear, and mixed loading. The simulations resolve the interaction between the crack-tip process zone and the material's uneven density. He also analyzes how density-dependent material laws change stress and strain near the tip.
arxiv-2512-21843:
Gregory Berkolaiko, Jacob Shapiro, and Beyer Chase White revisit the spectral localizer, a tool that reads the topological nature of a quantum system from a finite matrix. Topological invariants usually live on infinite grids, which are out of reach. The localizer, created by Loring and developed with Schulz-Baldes, packs the invariant into a single count, positive minus negative eigenvalues, of one finite matrix built from position and Hamiltonian data.

The authors give a direct, simple proof from spectral theory that treats the one- and two-dimensional cases in one way. Their argument avoids heavier tools used in earlier proofs. They also recast the localizer through the bulk-edge correspondence, viewing it as a higher-dimensional topological insulator. The paper repairs a foundation: the localizer was already used, and now its proof is simpler.
arxiv-2512-22243:
Alan Inglis leads a fifteen-author team predicting mycotoxin contamination in Irish oat crops, where fungal toxins threaten food safety and farm income. Their dataset mixes environmental, farm-practice, and geographic information for oat samples collected across Ireland. The team compares five modeling approaches on the multi-response task, from a plain multilayer perceptron to three transfer learning models: TabPFN, TabNet, and FT-Transformer.

TabPFN, a transfer learning approach, performed best overall, followed by the baseline network. Judging used regression and classification scores reported for each toxin and on average. A permutation analysis of variable importance found that weather patterns across the ninety days before harvest mattered most, together with seed moisture content. Such forecasts could support earlier intervention on risky crops.
arxiv-2512-22343:
Salvador Centelles Chuliá and Ranjeet Kumar build a neutrino model built to be testable. Their flavor model pairs an A4 symmetry with a type-II seesaw mechanism for making neutrino masses. The resulting mass matrix obeys a sum rule which, combined with measured mass-squared differences, fixes the full neutrino mass spectrum with no free wiggle room.

Applying the measured mixing data forces inverted ordering of the masses and restricts the Majorana phases. The model predicts a neutrinoless double beta decay rate near its maximum allowed value for inverted ordering, putting it within lab reach. In the charged lepton sector, a rough triality symmetry suppresses muon flavor violation while letting only certain tau decay channels through, giving labs a sharp checklist.
arxiv-2512-22443:
Jie Zhou, Xin Chen, Jie Zhang, and Zhe Li define and measure accounting reasoning, the domain-specific thinking language models need before enterprises can trust them with accounting work. Models are reshaping research and business practice, yet their fit for professional fields stays unclear. Grounding their criteria in the training data characteristics of the GLM model series, the authors build an evaluation system for accounting-oriented reasoning.

They test GLM-6B, GLM-130B, GLM-4, and GPT-4 across a range of accounting reasoning tasks. Prompt engineering improved every model to varying degrees, and GPT-4 showed the strongest overall accounting reasoning. Still, the results say current models fall short of real-world accounting needs, and enterprise-grade deployment will require much more optimization.
arxiv-2512-22543:
Tsuyoshi Yoneda studies how vortex rings deform in smooth, incompressible 3D flow governed by the Euler equations. The ring carries Kelvin waves and undergoes radially expanding Lagrangian transport. Yoneda builds a geometric Lagrangian system to expose the methods behind these deformations. It avoids singular integral representations of the pressure. It also yields a new wave equation for the swirling particles' axis.

Inside that system, the paper identifies intrinsic nonlinear methods driving the deformations. A machine-learning-flavored analysis supports the picture: a hybrid optimizer pairs Bayesian global exploration with adjoint-based local refinement. The adjoint method alone cannot escape local minima in the highly non-convex loss landscape, which is exactly why the hybrid design is needed.
arxiv-2512-22943:
Alexey Remizov presents the Legendre transformation, the classical device that swaps a function's variables for its slopes, from a geometric angle. Instead of the usual formula-first treatment, the note builds the transformation through a Legendrian lift, viewing curves together with their tangent directions in a larger contact space. That viewpoint makes otherwise puzzling features feel inevitable.

Chief among them is why dual curves develop singularities. Points where the original curve bends the wrong way project to cusps in the dual picture, and the lift shows exactly where they come from. The note then applies the transformation to the Clairaut differential equation, a classical setting where straight-line solutions and a curved singular solution meet. It closes with remarks on contact transformations in general, exhibiting an infinite family of them that differ from the Legendre transformation itself.
arxiv-2512-23043:
Muhammad Haseeb and co-authors investigate why federated averaging loses accuracy when each client's data look different from the others. In federated learning, phones or hospitals train locally and share only model updates, and skewed local data are the norm. The open question is whether averaging erases what clients learned internally, or merely misaligns the final classifier with representations that survive intact.

Working with sparse client-trained vision models plus dense controls, the team combines circuit discovery, linear probing of frozen features, head-only fine-tuning, and sparse feature dictionaries. On CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST, severe label skew drove some class accuracies near zero even though class-specific structure stayed recoverable inside the network. Probes on the frozen representations far outperformed the averaged classifier, and retraining only the head recovered much of the loss. The evidence points to preserved but misaligned representations rather than outright erasure.
arxiv-2512-23143:
C. Evans Hedges offers a short, playful piece of exposition connecting number theory to video games. The cultural hook is the spectacle of irrational numbers, most famously pi, being fed as controller input to play Pokémon. Behind the joke sits a real question about disjunctive numbers, numbers whose digits eventually contain every finite string, and what such a number can achieve when its digits drive a game.

The write-up shows that for any finite state game, a disjunctive number, used as the input stream, will eventually win that game. Hedges is frank that the proof techniques are well known and that the result follows immediately from folklore in graph theory and cellular automata. The paper's purpose is to collect the argument in one place with the game as motivation. It doubles as a gentle entry point into normality, digit expansions, and reachability in finite systems.
arxiv-2512-23643:
Konstantin Yakovlev and Nikita Puchkin develop theory for one of the core objects in modern generative modeling: the score function, the gradient of the log-density of data, and its derivatives. Diffusion models live or die by how well neural networks approximate the score. Real data usually sit near low-dimensional structures inside high-dimensional spaces and may have unbounded support, two features that break many existing guarantees.

The authors prove approximation error bounds for the score and its derivatives simultaneously, matching known results while dropping the usual bounded-support assumption. The bounds avoid the curse of dimensionality, so they do not explode as the ambient dimension grows, as long as the data's intrinsic structure stays simple. Guarantees cover derivatives of any prescribed order, extending far beyond the first-order estimates the literature usually settles for.
arxiv-2512-23743:
Yunguo Yu tackles automated assignment of ICD-10 diagnosis codes to clinical notes, a job where an invented code is not a harmless error but a safety and billing risk. Neural coders are accurate yet hallucinate unsupported codes; rule-based coders never hallucinate but need hand-built knowledge bases that do not scale. Hybrid-Code v2, in this substantially extended second version, aims for both safety and coverage.

A neural stage proposes candidate codes, and a symbolic layer verifies them through checks on format, supporting evidence, negation, timing. Exclusion rules; an automated mechanism also grows the knowledge base from unlabeled clinical text. Yu reports that on five thousand cases the system reached high coverage and precision with zero Type-I hallucination by construction, and claims a formal guarantee for that property. The arXiv record's fuller title governs over the catalog entry.
arxiv-2512-23843:
Manish Krishan Lal analyzes the Reflect-Reflect-Relax algorithm, an iterative scheme for finding points that satisfy two constraint sets at once, in the regime of tiny steps. Taking the small-step limit turns the iteration into a continuous flow, whose behavior can be studied with dynamical systems tools. The question is whether the algorithm settles reliably or wanders.

In the smooth transversal setting, the transverse dynamics form a hyperbolic sink, so a natural gap measure decays exponentially. On a tubular neighborhood of the feasible manifold, the squared gap is a strict Lyapunov function, which rules out cycles and chaos inside that basin. In discrete steps, the flow is piecewise constant and can slide along boundaries, capturing solutions in finite time; the small-step algorithm is exactly a forward-Euler discretization of this flow. A percolation-based heuristic then organizes how performance degrades toward the Douglas-Rachford limit.
arxiv-2512-23943:
Chris Hays, Ben Laufer, Solon Barocas, and Manish Raghavan formalize a legal duty that machine learning has made practical to test. American discrimination law can hold a firm liable for skipping a less discriminatory alternative: a model that does the same job with less disparate impact. Because retraining with a new random seed yields models of similar accuracy but different impact, firms can search for such alternatives, and regulators increasingly expect a good-faith search.

The hard question is when to stop. The authors cast the search as an optimal stopping problem and give an adaptive stopping algorithm that bounds, with high probability, how much improvement continued retraining could still bring. That bound lets a developer certify, even to a court, that further search is unlikely to help. Stronger assumptions tighten the bounds, and the method is validated on real credit and housing data.
arxiv-2512-24043:
Sergey Sergeev, writing alone, studies a lattice of quantum oscillators. The lattice follows the Kagomé pattern, a two-dimensional arrangement. An operator moves the system forward step by step in time. Sergeev builds that operator from a solution of the tetrahedron equation. That equation is a three-dimensional cousin of relations behind many solvable models.

The paper focuses on the case where the motion fits ordinary quantum mechanics. Sergeev sets out algebraic equations for the operator's eigenvalues and eigenstates. The guess rests on a lattice version of the Bethe ansatz. That is a classic stepwise method for solving such systems. The note is compact and technical. Still, it links several branches of mathematical physics in one short argument. Later work can test the formulas, extend them, or use them to compute spectra for this class of lattice models.
arxiv-2512-24243:
Fuqiang Gu and five colleagues fuse two kinds of camera data for scene segmentation. Ordinary cameras fail in hard conditions. Fast motion, low light, and strong contrast defeat them. Event cameras handle those conditions well. They report changes with fine timing and low latency. But they lack color and texture. Neither sensor suffices alone.

Their framework, MambaSeg, runs two branches in parallel. Mamba encoders process the image stream and the event stream. An interaction module then fuses the two. It works along the spatial dimension and the temporal dimension at once. That joint fusion reduces cross-modal ambiguity. It also aligns the modalities more finely. Two driving datasets hosted the experiments. The method reached state-of-the-art segmentation scores there. It did so at significantly lower computational cost.
arxiv-2512-25043:
Alice Moayyedi proves that verifying whether a given spanning tree is thin is coNP-complete, a hardness result about checking a property tied to the Thin Tree Conjecture. A thin tree uses only a small proportion of edges across every cut of a graph. Efficient thin tree construction would yield a constant-factor approximation for the asymmetric traveling salesman problem.

Even verification, easier than construction, turns out to be computationally hard in the worst case. Complexity theory readers get a barrier result clarifying why thin tree algorithms are elusive. The finding redirects hope toward construction methods that do not rely on verifying arbitrary candidate trees.
arxiv-2601-00043:
Hollis Williams, writing alone, examines acoustic levitation, where sound waves hold droplets in midair without contact, and asks where the standard theory of that trapping stops being accurate. His 2026 paper starts from the Gor'kov description, obtained by averaging the acoustic field over time. That averaged picture is widely used, yet it has lacked a quantitative test for when it can be trusted.

Williams derives Gor'kov theory as the leading slow-time limit of the instant radiation force, then computes the first correction for finite inertia. The correction weakens the trapping drift and predicts fast oscillations with an amplitude tied to the sound wavelength, reaching hundreds of microns in typical ultrasonic setups. From this he extracts a simple breakdown parameter. The result is a universal rule of thumb for designing acoustic traps, and a clear marker for where time-averaged force models begin to fail.
arxiv-2601-00143:
Gang Qu, Guanghao Li, and Zhongming Zhao build a deep learning system to detect Alzheimer disease from DNA methylation. Their 2026 model reads methylation profiles from brain and blood style tissues. Such marks are stable but change with disease. They may serve as early, noninvasive signs. The catch is that marks vary a lot across tissues and studies.

The model mixes a per site linear step with convolution and self attention layers. Subject data and tissue labels help it split shared from local effects. Tests span six public datasets and one separate cohort. It beats standard machine learning methods on accuracy and generalization. Reading tools then flag patterns tied to known disease pathways. These cover immune signaling, sugar coating of proteins, fat metabolism, and cell membrane systems. The work aims at markers that repeat across tissues.
arxiv-2601-00543:
Chung-Wei Victor Yuan tackles a quiet failure of small language models: their internal embedding space loses its shape. When capacity is tight or the training data spans several languages, the geometry that organizes meaning can collapse, and later tasks built on those embeddings suffer. Standard compression methods match the big model's outputs but not that underlying structure, so the small model drifts in meaning.

Yuan's framework, Embedding Consistency Regulation, first extracts semantic anchors from the teacher model's embeddings, computed once in advance. The compact model then learns to keep consistent geometry around those anchors, without imitating the teacher's scores or inner features. Only a small projection is added when the model runs, offering a light way to protect meaning during compression.
arxiv-2601-00643:
Francesco Bonacci and colleagues study elastic filaments that are sheared back and forth, a system ranging from biological fibers to soft materials. Working with microfluidic experiments on actin filaments and matching simulations of a fluctuating elastic rod in viscous fluid, they watch how the filaments behave over many cycles of strong oscillatory shear.

As the oscillation period grows, thermal noise and flow-induced bending combine to make the motion irreversible, breaking away from tidy reversible dynamics. Filaments settle into a cycle, nearly straight and aligned with the flow at full periods and buckled at half periods. A time-glide symmetry produces two such attracting states. The findings clarify how chaos and attractors can arise in a deceptively simple soft-matter setup.
arxiv-2601-00743:
Aliakbar Nafar, Chetan Chigurupati, Danial Kamali, Hamid Karimian, and Parisa Kordjamshidi lower the barrier to neuro-symbolic programming, where neural networks are combined with explicit logical rules. Such programs are more robust and interpretable, but building them in frameworks like DomiKnowS demands fluency in a specialized syntax, which keeps many users out.

Their system, AgenticDomiKnowS, turns a free-form task description into a complete program through an agentic workflow that builds and tests each component separately. Users who do know the framework can intervene mid-process to refine intermediate outputs. Both experienced users and newcomers produced complete neuro-symbolic programs in ten to fifteen minutes, work that previously took far longer by hand.
arxiv-2601-01043:
Jose Alves, Manfred Lindner, Farinaldo Queiroz, and Manoel Vasconcelos propose a new hunting ground for dark matter: single molecule magnets. These are molecules that act like tiny magnets. In a strong field they sit in a tense, unstable state. A small deposit of energy can tip one molecule over, and the released energy then spreads to its neighbors in a chain.

That chain, a magnetic avalanche, records how much energy the first hit delivered, which makes the setup a detector. The authors work through molecules based on dysprosium and on manganese. They estimate gains of more than ten times in sensitivity over current searches for two kinds of dark particles, axions and dark photons. The idea links chemistry, materials science, and particle physics in one device.
arxiv-2601-01143:
Peng Chen proposes KOS-TL, a logic system meant to give self-running knowledge systems a firm formal base. Chen argues that older ways of storing knowledge keep symbols still, while real systems must act and change over time, leaving a gap the new framework tries to close.

KOS-TL has three layers. One sets basic types, one tracks change through events, and one links real signals to logical evidence. Chen defines how the system works and proves it cannot get stuck during change. Each update carries proof that it is valid. Examples cover tracing goods in industry and checking rules for payments across borders.
arxiv-2601-01243:
Alejandro Toral-Lopez, Damiano Marian, and Gianluca Fiori model how charge hops between trapped states in disordered materials such as organic semiconductors and perovskites. At low temperatures, charges take long hops to far but favorable sites; when warmer, they hop only to nearest neighbors. Experiments see a switch between these regimes, but models of the switch have lagged behind.

The team built a Monte Carlo simulator based on a random resistor network that captures both regimes in one framework. They show how traits like the reach of each trapped state and the spread of site positions and energies decide which regime rules. The simulator matches experimental data closely, reproducing the regime switch and hopping behavior in one, two, and three dimensions. It serves both as a lens for reading experiments and as a design tool for materials where hopping carries the current.
arxiv-2601-01343:
Zhong and 5 co-authors address a stubborn choice in signal analysis: how many basic waves hide inside a mixed signal. A common method splits signals into modes, but users usually pick the count by trial and error. Wrong picks add fake modes or lose real parts of the signal.

Their idea draws a cutting curve under the signal's spectrum. Peaks rising above the curve count as modes, while noise fragments stay below it. A math framework then improves the curve, and the authors prove their method always settles. Tests on made-up signals, real signals, and heart data gave sound counts and center values without waste.
arxiv-2601-01443:
Jie Yang and Wei Tan model why silicon particles crack inside lithium-ion batteries. Silicon stores much more lithium than graphite, but it swells hugely as it charges, and the swelling splits the particles. Their model couples four processes at once: lithium transport, deformation, a phase-field description of cracks, and fatigue damage over repeated cycles.

Simulations of single charge cycles and many-cycle fatigue show clear trends. Bigger particles, faster charging, and longer pre-existing notches all speed cracking and shorten life. The team turns those runs into a validated map of fracture behavior that designers can read directly. They also test a remedy: drilling nanopores into the particle. Pores cut expansion, soak up tensile stress, and force cracks onto longer paths. The framework links stress-diffusion theory to particle failure and guides the design of silicon anodes that survive real battery duty.
arxiv-2601-01743:
AI agents pair a foundation model with reasoning, planning, memory, and tools, turning plain-language requests into real computation. Bin Xu surveys this fast-moving field, organizing agent designs into a single taxonomy covering how agents deliberate, plan, call tools, and interact with their environments.

The survey maps components such as memory, world models, planners, and critics, plus coordination patterns from lone agents to decentralized multi-agent teams. The survey weighs trade-offs. Speed trades against accuracy. Autonomy trades against control. Capability trades against reliability. It also explains why evaluation is hard. Agents are non-deterministic. Credit for success spreads over long task chains. Hidden costs like retries pile up. Open problems include verifying tool actions, scaling memory, and making results reproducible.
arxiv-2601-01843:
UTe2 is a heavy-fermion material and a leading candidate for spin-triplet superconductivity, but the symmetry of its pairing has been hard to pin down, especially under pressure. Shuo Zou, Fengrui Shi, and twenty-four co-authors probe pressurized UTe2 with point-contact spectroscopy on one crystal face.

Signatures of Andreev bound states point to a component of the order parameter that is odd along the crystal's vertical axis, for both ambient and pressurized samples. A single quantity, the relative weight of that component against the in-plane components, distinguishes the multiple superconducting phases pressure creates. The measurements place strict constraints on pairing symmetry and give spectroscopists a fingerprint for telling the phases apart.
arxiv-2601-02243:
Ahmed S. Alahmed, Audun Botterud, and Saurabh Amin study how a desalination plant that makes fresh water can also help run an electric power grid. Their plant joins heat based generation, membrane units that can be turned up or down, and renewable power. The plant sells water to a utility and can buy or sell electricity as its own needs change.

Inside, the authors build a math model for scheduling the plant to earn the most profit while respecting how the machines and markets work. They find a simple threshold rule, worked out in near closed form, that tells the plant when to switch modes. Tests in simulation show clear gains over simpler methods and show how prices and technology choices change profit.
arxiv-2601-02543:
Linfeng Ye, Zhixiang Chi, Konstantinos N. Plataniotis, and En-hui Yang propose a new training loss for image classifiers, to replace the standard cross entropy loss used almost everywhere. Their loss is built from normalized conditional mutual information, a quantity from information theory. And they first observe that it moves in the opposite direction to accuracy, so lowering the loss should raise accuracy. An alternating algorithm makes the loss practical to minimize during training.

On image recognition and on whole slide medical image subtyping, models trained with the new loss beat the strongest existing losses by substantial margins. At about the same computing cost as cross entropy. On ImageNet the top one accuracy gain with a standard ResNet-50 was close to three percentage points. And on a cancer slide benchmark the macro F1 gain over the best baseline was larger still. Gains held across architectures and batch sizes.
arxiv-2601-03243:
Daniel Grier, Jackson Morris, and Kewen Wu prove new results about QAC0, the class of constant-depth quantum circuits built from single-qubit gates and generalized Toffoli gates. It is arguably the smallest natural class of constant-depth quantum computation, and nobody had shown it computing any nontrivial Boolean function. Repeated attempts to carry classical circuit lower bounds over to it had failed, and the authors offer an explanation: these quantum circuits are stronger than they look.

They prove an unconditional separation, showing QAC0 is not contained in the classical class AC0 with mod-p gates. Given many copies of the input, QAC0 circuits can even compute everything in TC0, the class of threshold circuits. A new amplitude amplification technique, which makes approximate constructions exact, drives several of the results.
arxiv-2601-03643:
Zeev Nutov, writing alone, answers an open question about how much memory a connectivity oracle must use. An oracle is a compact data structure that can quickly say whether two points in a network are joined by many disjoint paths. In 2022, Pettie, Saranurak, and Yin proved that such oracles for undirected graphs need a large amount of space, growing with both the connectivity level and the network size.

They asked whether that lower bound still holds when the graph itself is already highly connected. Nutov shows, by a very simple proof, that it does. The bound cannot be dodged by assuming a well-connected network. For algorithm designers, the result closes a loophole: there is no cheap shortcut for storing many-path connectivity, even in favorable graphs.
arxiv-2601-03743:
Yi Yao and fourteen co-authors present O-Researcher, a training framework for open-ended deep research models built from cooperating agents. The performance gap between closed and open language models, they argue, comes largely from unequal access to high-quality training data. Their answer is to synthesize research-grade instructional data automatically, using a multi-agent workflow that simulates tool-integrated reasoning end to end.

Training then proceeds in two stages, supervised fine-tuning followed by a new reinforcement learning method tuned for alignment and capability. Across model scales, the framework pushed open-source models to new state-of-the-art results on a major deep research benchmark. The broader claim is significant: carefully synthesized data from agent teams may let open models chase frontier research skills without proprietary datasets.
arxiv-2601-04143: Thierry Coquand, writing alone, gives a constructive version of the proof for the local structure of étale algebras. Étale algebras are a central class in algebra, valued because their local behaviour can be described in a standard form. A constructive proof, unlike a classical one, builds its objects and avoids steps that rely on pure existence claims.
arxiv-2601-04343:
Yongyi Zang and seven co-authors cover the first Music Source Restoration Challenge in a 2026 arXiv paper. Restoration is harder than ordinary source separation: the goal is to recover clean, unprocessed instrument stems from professional mixes that also carry real-world damage, undoing both studio effects and degradation. Five teams entered the inaugural contest.

Systems were scored objectively on studio-made mixtures with three automatic metrics, and subjectively on genuinely degraded recordings. The winning system beat the runner-up by wide margins on both objective quality and listener ratings. Breaking results down by instrument shows restoration difficulty varies sharply: bass stems came back fairly well across teams, while percussion resisted almost everyone. The organizers release the dataset, evaluation rules, and baselines so the contest can run again.
arxiv-2601-04443:
Ahmad Mohammad Saber and five co-authors set language models to guard power transformers, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Current differential relays protect transformers by comparing currents, and cyberattacks that fake those measurements can trip a healthy transformer or mask a real fault. Their idea is to translate the multiphase current readings into structured natural-language prompts that compact language models can read.

Three small, locally deployable models are finetuned on those prompts, including one with a lightweight adapter, and tested against a broad field of conventional machine and deep learning detectors. The language model detectors matched or beat the baselines under ordinary conditions, complex attack scenarios, and measurement noise; the best caught nearly ninety-eight percent of attacks while never missing a genuine fault. The models' attention patterns also point at the time and phase regions that drove each alarm, giving operators an explanation, not just a verdict.
arxiv-2601-04543:
Venkat Abhignan and three co-authors squeeze more secret key out of quantum hardware limited by its detectors, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum key distribution lets two parties share a secret key with security rooted in physics, and the coherent-one-way protocol is a practical favourite. In real setups the single-photon detectors at the receiver are the bottleneck: slow and inefficient, they cap the key rate.

The team shows experimentally that merging time-bin information from two such detectors on the receiver's data line raises the key rate with only a minimal rise in errors. They then extend the protocol from a pair to a point-to-multipoint network, adding a second receiver so three users share key material for one-time-pad encryption. Improving the combined rates inside the security margins takes parameter tuning, but the techniques apply to any coherent-one-way installation.
arxiv-2601-04943:
Yunlong Xue, Zhengyang Bai, and Yu-Qiang Ma propose using a dissipative time crystal as an ultra-sensitive microwave sensor in a 2026 paper. A time crystal here is a driven quantum system whose oscillations persist and break time-translation symmetry on their own. The authors study a driven Rydberg atom system that loses energy to its surroundings, mapping its monostable, bistable, and oscillatory phases under mean-field coupling.

Near a phase transition, the oscillatory phase reacts with critical sensitivity to a microwave field. Unlike single-particle detection, where the signal fades in a simple way, the collective crystal response can amplify weak fields. Such sensing could sharpen measurements for radar, communications testing, and searches for faint electromagnetic signals.
arxiv-2601-05243:
Xingyi He and 6 co-authors teach a robot hand to grip tools in the right way from one human show in a 2026 paper. A good grip on a tool is a grip that lets the tool be used, not just held. That skill is key to robot tool work. Work on it has been held back by a lack of big data sets, and by models that miss the sense of a grip, its shape, or both.

Their frame, CorDex, grows its training stock out of fake runs in a sim, all sprung from that one human show. A match-based engine lays the one grip over new tools and new scenes to make a rich, clean stock. A hand that learns a grip from one show could be taught a new chore in the home, the shop, or the lab with no weeks of data work first.
arxiv-2601-05343:
Ryan Cooke, Nao Suzuki, and J. Xavier Prochaska name a world net of plain stars to set the scale for the next breed of scopes in a 2026 paper. To set the light scale of a sky survey now hits a wall: a flaw of a few parts in a hun-dred, worse near hydrogen's Balmer lines. The next huge scopes need a far more keen scale than that.

The team found a net of bright white dwarf stars round the sky. A white dwarf is the dense core a star leaves when it dies. These ones shine with a form close to a pure black-body arc, from the near shades past sight to the warm shades past red. A star whose true form is set by plain physics, not by a guess, makes a near-flawless scale mark for the new scopes.
arxiv-2601-05443:
Oana Vesa and 2 co-authors examine, in a 2026 solar physics paper, how equatorial Rossby waves tilt with depth inside the Sun. Rossby waves are large, slow waves shaped by rotation, and on the Sun they may reveal interior dynamics. The team used about fourteen and a half years of helioseismology data from the SDO/HMI instrument.

Two methods, ring-diagram and time-distance analysis, gave consistent depth-dependent phase patterns. Deeper layers led in phase over shallower ones, implying a stable backward tilt against solar rotation. That tilt showed no clear link to the solar cycle, while wave power did rise and fall with the cycle. Such tilts can affect how angular momentum and energy move through the solar interior.
arxiv-2601-05543:
Chaoren Wang and 6 co-authors tackle, in a 2026 paper, the gap between how speech language models reason from speech and from text. Given the same content as text, these models usually reason better. The authors link that gap to hidden representations drifting apart across layers and to behavior wandering during long reasoning chains.

Their framework, TARS, trains models with reinforcement learning and two alignment rewards. One reward measures how similar hidden states stay between speech-based and text-based runs. The other checks whether outputs stay semantically consistent with reference text completions. On the MMSU and OBQA benchmarks, the method narrowed the gap and reached leading results among speech models of its size class.
arxiv-2601-05843:
Ivo Düntsch and Ewa Orlowska present, in a 2026 book section, discrete dualities for algebras arising from rough set theory. Rough sets approximate a concept from below and above when information is incomplete. A discrete duality pairs classes of algebras with classes of relational systems, yielding representation theorems that translate between the two views.

The section recalls such dualities for several algebra types from the rough set literature. It builds on early work by Jonsson and Tarski, Kripke, and van Benthem, who established the broader duality tradition in logic. The piece recalls and synthesizes established results rather than offering a new test or proof program. It therefore serves readers as a compact reference map of how rough-set algebras are represented relationally.
arxiv-2601-06643:
Michael Ganzburg studies asymptotics of certain B-splines in 2026. He examines the Mellin transform of associated B-splines with special knots. The results are expressed in terms of theta-like functions, he reports.

The proof rests on polynomial interpolation of power functions mainly. Properties of certain theta-like functions complete the argument, he explains. B-splines underpin curve design, approximation, and numerical analysis everywhere. Their Mellin transforms connect them to number-theoretic functions like theta series. Finding asymptotics clarifies how these splines behave at extremes. Approximation theorists get exact limiting forms for a special family. Such results often unlock error estimates for practical spline methods. The paper is a careful piece of classical analysis with modern tools.
arxiv-2601-06843: Research by Junyan Lin and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with speak while watching. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance across many tasks. Yet most systems remain limited to offline inference, requiring complete inputs before generating outputs. Recent streaming methods reduce latency by interleaving perception and generation, but still enforce a sequential perception–generation cycle, limiting real-time interaction. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07543:
M Silvestrini and a large team from many lands introduce CASCO, a project linking galaxy simulations with real observations. Small mismatches on galaxy scales have pushed cosmologists to test alternatives to cold dark matter. Warm dark matter is one such option. CASCO asks how strongly galaxy scaling relations can pin down cosmological and astrophysical parameters, including warm dark matter ones. The work appears as a 2026 preprint.

The team combines multi-resolution hydrodynamic simulations with data from real sightings in one joint analysis. Scaling relations connect observable galaxy traits like size, mass, and rotation speed. Because such models can be rerun under changed rules, they show which relations carry real weight. The project aims at sharper tests of dark matter using galaxies astronomers already observe. All of this rests on facts that teams can check with their own eyes and tools.
arxiv-2601-07743:
Pelle Brooke Borgeke goes on with a study of how small terms can unseat a spectrum, in a 2026 analysis preprint. The paper is part two of a series on subprincipal controlled quasimodes. Quasimodes are approximate solutions to an operator equation. Here they hinge on the subprincipal symbol, a lower term often seen as minor. The notation follows semiclassical analysis, with a small parameter h.

Such weak stability means tiny shifts can move eigenvalues far more than one would guess. Quasimodes built from subprincipal data show where that sensitivity comes from. A grasp of it matters for operators from quantum theory and wave physics. The paper is dense and aimed at microlocal analysis experts. It extends part one's analysis of the same construction. Readers get a deeper account of how lower-order terms control approximate solutions. It builds step by step on part one.
arxiv-2601-07943:
Francesco Coghi, Amarjit Budhiraja, and Juan P Garrahan tackle large deviations for systems whose rules rest on their own past. They take on the broad task of writing such large deviations for non-Markovian systems in closed form. Their systems are self-interacting jump processes. The rules rest on the past through a functional of a state based measured mean. A clear split of timescales drives their solution. Their 2026 preprint derives the exact level 2.5 result.

Level 2.5 tracks swings in both filled states and flows at once. Exact formulas there are rare for history-dependent systems. Bounds that follow can limit how exact such currents can be. Self-interacting processes model reinforced walks, learning, and acts that adapt. The paper serves statistical physicists working on fluctuation theory. It extends a powerful framework to systems with memory. Systems with a past show up in walks, in learning, and in live cells.
arxiv-2601-08843:
Haotian Deng and three co-authors test chat models as graders of short student replies. A teacher gives a rubric, a list that says what earns full or part marks. Student words vary a lot, so part marks are hard to set fair. Chat models look like a cheap fix, but their marks must match the rubric, not their own taste.

The team runs a broad check of model graders on rubric tasks. They look at how close marks sit to human marks, how sure the model is, and how marks hold up when replies are tweaked. A reader who runs a class or a test firm gets facts on trust. The work shows where a model grader can help, and where a human must still check.
arxiv-2601-08943:
Axel de la Macorra and Jose Agustin Lozano Torres test a dark energy model next to new sky data. Dark energy is the name for what speeds the growth of space. Their model ties dark energy to a bound state, with its own clear past. They check it next to a cold dark stuff model in the same frame.

They fit both to fresh range marks from the DESI survey. They add old space light data and star burst range marks from three sets. A good fit must please all sets at once. A reader in cosmos work gets a strict test of a less known model. It shows if bound dark energy can stand with the best data we have.
arxiv-2601-09043:
Nick Polson and Vadim Sokolov give a Bayes frame for nets that pick one expert from a pool for each input. Such nets are called mixtures of experts. One expert may suit math asks, a next may suit code. The pool can grow vast, so most experts should sit out most asks. A firm prior can force that thrift in a smart way.

They use the horseshoe prior, which shrinks weak signs hard but lets strong signs stand. Gates that pick experts learn from data as they go. Their learn rule tracks just key sums as new data flows in. A reader who builds large nets gets a sparse pick plan with doubt built in.
arxiv-2601-09343:
Prateek Dwivedi, Benedikt Pago, and Tim Seppelt attack one of the oldest open problems in algebraic complexity theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper seeks lower bounds using symmetry and homomorphism polynomials. At stake is Valiant's 1979 conjecture, which claims the classes VP and VNP are distinct.

In plain terms, the conjecture says the permanent needs far larger algebraic circuits than the determinant. A full split of the two classes has resisted proof for decades, as in many parts of complexity theory. The authors look for new leverage from symmetry, hoping structured polynomials can force the lower bounds that direct methods have missed.
arxiv-2601-09543:
Jason Carpenter, Faaiq Bilal, Eman Ramadan, and Zhi-Li Zhang test a simple idea for cutting web pages into blocks. Their 2026 arXiv paper examines how well DOM coordinates work for page segmentation. Web pages are a vast store of data for people and, now, for language-model systems.

That data is huge and unstructured, so automated extraction must be robust. Segmentation, splitting a page into its meaningful regions, is a first step for extraction and retrieval. The authors check whether the coordinates already present in a page's document tree are enough to guide it. A cheap signal that works would simplify many scraping pipelines.
arxiv-2601-09743:
Jianhua Yang and four co-authors widen the range of a resonance trick used to pull signals from noise. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies vibrational resonance in coupled Duffing oscillators that learn. Each oscillator adjusts its natural frequency under a learning rule as the input changes.

That self-learning gives the array frequency-adaptive response. The adaptive rule greatly extends the frequency range over which resonance boosts the signal. The target use is processing weak, noisy radio frequency signals. A self-tuning resonator array could find faint signals on its own, without any manual retuning by an operator.
arxiv-2601-09843:
Simon Portegies Zwart, Arjen Doelman, and Jelmer Sein hunt for the birth stories of braided three-star systems. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies periodic three-body orbits, called braids, in Newtonian gravity. Braids look special and unique, repeating the same woven pattern forever.

The authors suspect braids instead arise from ordinary encounters between four bodies. They reverse-engineer the encounters that could have formed them. The aim is to learn how often braids exist in the Galaxy. If common collisions make braids, then these elegant orbits are a normal product of crowded star clusters.
arxiv-2601-10143:
Haochong Xia and co authors build fake market data that tracks a live market. Models trained on past data oft fail in real trade. Markets drift. The past stops being a good guide. A model then fits old noise and fails on new days.

The team argues that past data alone is not enough. Their rig adapts as it makes new data. It is a data flow rig, not a fixed set. It aims to make spans that act like the live market now. Such spans can train trade models that hold up when the market shifts.
arxiv-2601-10443:
Roberto Ricci retells umbral theory as an algebra of formal power series. Umbral math began as a trick with marks that act like powers. Roman and Rota gave it a firm modern form. Dattoli and kin later made it a work tool for special functions.

Ricci sets that tool in series form. A formal power series is a sum with no need to settle. In that tongue, umbral steps read as algebra moves. The paper lays out the main acts in that form. It aims to make the tool clear to those who know series work well.
arxiv-2601-10743:
Ayesh Abu Lehyeh, Anastassia Gharib, Tian Xia, Dryver Huston, and Safwan Wshah present UBiGTLoc, a system that locates sensor nodes in wireless IoT networks. Knowing where each node sits is key for smart cities, smart farms, and other sensor-driven work. Most current methods lean on anchor nodes whose positions are known from GPS.

Anchors are costly and cannot cover every setting, such as indoors. UBiGTLoc blends a BiLSTM network with a graph transformer in one framework. Sequence learning and graph structure each carry clues about position. Joining them aims at accurate location with fewer anchors. The work serves network designers who need maps of their own sensors.
arxiv-2601-11943:
Loren I. Matilsky, Lydia Korre, and Nicholas H. Brummell propose a dynamo story for a thin layer in the Sun. The tachocline is a narrow shear layer at the base of the Sun's outer zone. Above it, spin varies with latitude, and below it, spin is near rigid.

The layer's thinness is a long puzzle. Inward flow should have spread it over time, in a process called radiative spreading. A dynamo-held layer could stay thin in spite of that flow. Their story also bears on how the Sun's spin slows with age.
arxiv-2601-12143:
Devin Hunter and Chinwendu Enyioha build a reactive controller for self-driving race cars. Attention-based neural models now lead in real-time nonlinear control. As such models enter safety-critical work, their calls need firm statistical grounds.

Their frame uses an Attentive Neural Process for gap-based driving choices. A physics-informed form adds known motion laws to the model. The pair aim for fast calls that still hold safety bounds. Race tracks give a hard, fast test bed for such control.  Race data give fast, hard tests for the control frame.  Gap choice is a hard case for safe, fast driving in a race.
arxiv-2601-12243:
Shreya Rajpal, Michal Golovanevsky, and Carsten Eickhoff sum long procedural videos with help from labels. Summaries turn long videos into short, clear forms for review and records. The need is high in fields such as surgical training, where video is long and stakes are high.

Past tools used basic visual traits, then vision-language models that grasp sense and time flow. Their label-guided method uses known step labels to pick key parts. A guided summary can keep the steps that matter for teaching. The work tests that guide on such videos.
arxiv-2601-12743:
Debobrata Rajak and nine co authors study how twisted light interacts with solids. Intense ultrashort pulses can carry orbital angular momentum, a twist in the light wavefront. Little is known about how such pulses drive high harmonic generation in solid state platforms. For conventional light, electron dynamics can often be confined to a single Brillouin zone.

The dipole approximation also describes many standard interactions well. Twisted light may break those simple pictures, and that is the gap the team probe. Their title names the transfer of orbital angular momentum in the harmonic process. New harmonics carrying a twist could serve optics and materials probes. The work opens a fresh corner of strong field physics.
arxiv-2601-12943:
Han Xu and Di Wang bring dependent types to automated amortized resource analysis. Static resource analysis determines how much a program consumes, like time, without running it. Affine type systems have been a dominant approach to this problem. They fall short on precise resource behavior of higher order programs, though. Partial applications are a noted hard case.

Their dependently typed approach takes a non affine route. Higher order programs pass functions as values, which breaks simple counting. Dependent types can track resource use inside the type itself. Precise static bounds help compilers and users trust performance. The work serves programming language theory and verified software.
arxiv-2601-13143:
Chaeyoung Jung, Youngjoon Jang, Seungwoo Lee, and Joon Son Chung speed up models that read both sound and sight. Such audio visual models join a large language core with ears and eyes. The join makes their token load swell, so runs cost more time and power.

Token prune work has cut load for plain text and for sight plus text models. It had not been fit to audio visual models. Their method, FastAV, is the first prune frame built for that case. It drops the least need tokens while it keeps the key sound and sight clues. For live apps such as video chat aids, cuts like this can make big models fit to run.
arxiv-2601-13543:
S. M. Troshin and N. E. Tyurin back a guess form for elastic scatter based on the rule of its imaginary part. In such scatter, two bits graze and part with no break. The scatter size is a complex count with a real and an imaginary part.

Marks at the Large Hadron Collider at 13 TeV hint at a shift in the clash zone. The zone that makes new bits may turn from a black disk to a black ring with a bright core. Troshin and Tyurin argue the imaginary part rules the size. A guess built on that rule may then track the real part with less free play. Such a form aids reads of total clash rates.
arxiv-2601-13943:
Zhiyuan Peng and a large team build a benchmark for making whole software services from scratch in 2026. Language models and agents have made remarkable progress in code generation. Past benchmarks test single functions, single classes, or edits to existing code. They neglect complete microservice repository generation, the real zero-to-one workflow.

Their RepoGenesis starts from a readme file and asks for a full repository. That task spans design, many files, and working links between parts. A firm benchmark shows if agents can build services end to end. Firms could then judge agent tools on work that mirrors real projects.
arxiv-2601-14243:
Haocheng Xi and a team from NVIDIA, MIT, UC Berkeley, and other labs present Jet-RL in this 2026 paper. Their topic is training large language models with reinforcement learning, the trial-and-error method that builds reasoning skills. Such training is slow and costly. The rollout phase, where the model drafts many trial replies, takes over 70 percent of the total time.

Jet-RL tries to cut that cost with FP8, a compact number format that uses eight bits per value. The team built one shared flow for training and rollout, so both phases use the same low precision. The goal is on-policy learning that runs faster without a new split between the two phases.
arxiv-2601-14543:
Zhuofan Jia and Jian Pei extend a fairness concept to messy data in this 2026 paper. The Shapley value provides a principled framework for fairly distributing rewards among participants according to their individual contributions. Prior work applied it to data valuation in machine learning. In that use, each participant's data are scored for how much they help a model.

Existing formulations overwhelmingly assume each participant contributes a fixed, deterministic dataset. Real data are rarely so clean: values arrive with uncertainty attached. The authors study the Shapley value on uncertain data. Readers get a fairness calculus that still works when the contributions themselves are not known exactly.
arxiv-2601-14843:
Endre Sørmo Rundsveen writes a short note on a new kind of module category in algebra. His 2026 arXiv paper builds on work by Gupta and Zhou, who set up these extended module categories. The note deals with Nakayama algebras, a well-studied family of algebras.

Rundsveen shows that a certain part of the category, called a postprojective component, exists for some algebras. He also gives a knitting method to build it step by step. The method works through number vectors that track cohomology, the algebra's own way of counting holes and gaps.
arxiv-2601-15243:
Adam LaClair, Matthew Mastroeni, Jason McCullough, and Irena Peeva ask when a graph's edge ideal gives a Koszul algebra. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with binomial edge ideals. Each edge of a graph gives one quadratic polynomial, and together they generate the ideal.

Koszul algebras have a tidy, linear form of resolution that algebraists prize. Many authors have studied when these ideals define one, ever since the class was first set out. The authors take up that question for binomial edge ideals. Their work sorts out which graphs pass the test.
arxiv-2601-15343:
Jingxu Wu and Jie Shi build a rigorous frame for slow escapes from a metastable state. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with gradient systems of Landau type, inspired by QCD phenomenology. A free-energy-like functional drives the system, with a field, a stiffness term, and a potential.

A control parameter tunes the whole landscape smoothly. The authors study rare transitions between the wells of that landscape. They use Eyring-Kramers asymptotics, formulas for how long a state lasts. Gamma convergence ties the finite models to their limit, so the transition rates stand on firm ground.
arxiv-2601-15543:
Jun-Yong Park works on height zeta functions for elliptic surfaces in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting uses a perfect field whose characteristic is not two or three. Over the function field in one variable, he studies a moduli stack of minimal elliptic curves. The stack sorts curves by Faltings height, a measure of arithmetic size. It comes from a recent height-moduli framework.

The paper's claim is in its title: a certain zeta function is rational. The function is weighted by the trivial lattice rank of the surfaces. Rationality is a strong structural fact for such a generating series. It means the series can be written as a ratio of polynomials. Arithmetic geometers use such results to count curves by height. The abstract is dense and formula-led, aimed at specialists.
arxiv-2601-16043:
Nam Van Tran builds a flow method for a class of hard maths tasks. His 2026 preprint deals with tasks that mix inverse maps and mixed bounds. Such tasks show up in game and trade maths. He sets up a flow that shifts with time and uses casts to stay in bounds. The flow is of second order, so past speed shapes its path.

Under set terms, Tran proves the flow has one path. He also proves that path moves fast toward the sole true answer. He then turns the flow into steps a code can run. The step form keeps a push from past steps. The work gives both proof and a usable method in one place.
arxiv-2601-16143:
Kryzhniy gives a broad scheme to solve sums and growth tasks with high grade curve fits. His 2026 preprint joins many task types in one frame. The types span sum tasks, mixed sum and growth tasks, and plain growth tasks. Both start point and edge point tasks fit the frame. The scheme can also fit ill posed tasks, where small shifts cause big swings.

The core is a fit built from pieces of high grade curves. High grade fits can track hard shapes with few pieces. One scheme for many types cuts the need for case by case code. The work aims at trust and ease of use. It serves teams with mixed maths task loads.
arxiv-2601-16243:
Niccolò Castronuovo, Alberto Dennunzio and Luciano Margara show a key trait of group cell grids can be checked. Their 2026 preprint deals with cell grids whose rules rest on group maths. The trait is top spread, where a start state can reach near any state. For plain cell grids, that trait can not be checked by code. No code can settle it in all cases.

For group grids, the pair plus one show a code can settle it. That split marks group grids as far more tame. Tame traits let teams trust grid based tools and codes. The proof draws a sharp line in grid theory. It guides which grid types suit safe use.
arxiv-2601-16343:
Fionnuala Curran sums how much true chance a quantum state can give. Her 2026 preprint deals with chance born when a state is read. A read in a base where the state is not flat gives true chance. A spy tied to the state may try to guess the read. Guess odds set how much clean chance the read can yield.

Curran asks what if the spy is held back in a set way. Held spies change the clean chance count in clear terms. Clean chance feeds keys and draws in quantum tech. Firm counts tell teams how much chance a state earns. The work is a pure sum study of chance.
arxiv-2601-16443:
Kanishk Gandhi and three coauthors grow end less shell task worlds for agent train. Their 2026 preprint deals with tools that act in a text shell. Past task sets were built to test agents, not to train them. Train by trial needs a scale path, not a fixed set. The team builds a full auto path that makes new tasks on its own.

Each new task comes with checks that can grade the agent. Fresh tasks stop agents from rote learn of a fixed set. Scale of fresh tasks lets trial learn run long and wide. That breadth is what self growth needs most. The work, named Endless Terminals, feeds that need.
arxiv-2601-16843:
Marta Fernández-Lomana and a team of five co-authors probe a superconductor with a needle tip. The crystal LaRu2P2 turns lossless below a cold mark. A scan tool drags a sharp tip across its face. The tip reads how electrons pair and flow. Their 2026 preprint reports those reads at near-zero cold.

The reads show a single gap in the pair states. That gap fits the classic BCS tale of pairing. Vortex swirls in a magnet field form a neat grid. Such maps test if this crystal pairs in the plain way. They also guide hunts for odd pairing in kin crystals.
arxiv-2601-17243:
Rain and heat extremes put lives and farms at risk, yet they are hard to pin down. A study with no named author in the record builds a tool for honest doubt ranges. The tool is a quantile neural network with a new loss design. Its full name is the ReLU-bias loss quantile neural network. Two tweaks shape how it learns.

One tweak keeps quantile skill even across the full range. The other stops the output spread from collapsing to a false point. Good doubt ranges matter as much as best guesses. They tell planners how bad an event could get. The frame can serve climate risk work where ranges guide real choices.
arxiv-2601-17543:
Yi Lyu, Luke Dotson, Nic Draves, and Andy Zhang review Capture the Flag games in cybersecurity teaching. CTF games let students attack and defend real systems in play form. The authors sort them into four types. The types are attack-based, defense-based, jeopardy, and gamified wargames. Each type trains a unlike mix of skills.

They sum up the traits of each type in turn. That map helps teachers pick games that fit their goals. Hands-on play builds skills lectures cannot. It also shows who thrives under time pressure. Security courses need grads who can act, not just recall. A clear taxonomy helps schools design play with purpose. The review serves new and veteran teachers alike.
arxiv-2601-17743:
Jun Zhu and five co-authors compress video with a hierarchical temporal neural representation. Implicit representations model videos as continuous functions. They offer compact storage and flexible rebuilds. Most past methods treat time as one more input. That limits how well they capture complex time patterns. The team's design builds time in a hierarchy instead.

Layered time structure can hold both fast motion and slow trends. Classic codecs split time in like ways by design. Neural methods must learn that lesson to compete. Better time models raise quality at low bit rates. Streaming and storage both gain from that. The work pairs with the team's frequency study. Time and frequency are the two axes of video.
arxiv-2601-17843: Jesse Hoekstra and Frank Windmeijer work on sharper tests for part of a model in instrumental variable studies. Their 2026 preprint deals with the subvector Anderson-Rubin test, used when instruments may be weak.
