Stefan Schwaiger and four co-authors push X-ray microscopy past detector limits with patterned light. Their 2026 paper tackles a concrete need: imaging centimeter-scale battery cells at sub-micrometer detail, where current methods stall near ten micrometers, limited by detector blur and pixel size. The team encodes fine sample detail into structured illumination.

A math framework decodes that encoded high-frequency information from several acquisitions at different illumination phase shifts, producing a super-resolved image. Lab tests first confirm the encoded detail exists, then quantify it on a resolution chart, showing a factor of two point two improvement. The method extends to X-ray microtomography and, since acquisition is inherently multimodal, also yields phase-contrast and dark-field images. Battery and biomedical imaging both gain from the pixel-size escape.
arxiv-2602-18543:
Martin Podhorský and seven co-authors build buried stressors for precisely placed dots. Their 2026 paper reports two-step growth of InGaAs dots via the buried stressor method with varying density. High fabrication accuracy keeps buried apertures about seventeen nanometers from centers.

The team provides a luminescence study of dots and calculations on the aperture's effect on emission and density. Results show reproducible nucleation for same-size apertures and precisely placed low- and high-density nucleation in one step. The work shows potential of the buried stressor concept for single chips, combining single-photon sources and microlasers with varied densities of controlled dots. That paves the way for functional modules.
arxiv-2602-18643:
Richik Chakraborty validates wearable health alerts before users see them. His 2026 paper notes wearable health prediction systems have accelerated, yet generate alerts under uncertainty without principled tools. While large language models increasingly serve healthcare, existing work focuses on diagnosis and risk prediction rather than post-prediction checks.

He introduces Project Hermes, a model-agnostic validation layer for signal confirmation as a sequential task. Hermes operates downstream of upstream predictors, using language-model-generated queries to elicit user feedback and Bayesian confidence updates to separate true positives from false alarms. In a sixty-day migraine case study, Hermes cut the false positive rate by thirty-four percent, from sixty-one point seven percent to twelve point five percent. It maintained eighty-nine percent sensitivity, with mean lead time of four point two hours. Hermes performs no diagnosis and makes no novel predictions; it validates whether upstream signals are meaningful for individuals.
arxiv-2602-18843:
Can a model reason about exceptions to a rule, and do it sparsely? Serafim Batzoglou, writing alone in 2026, introduces ABD, a benchmark for default-exception abduction over finite first-order settings. A model gets a theory with an abnormality marker and several relational structures. It must write a formula in first-order logic. That formula picks out the exceptions. The exceptions must make the theory satisfiable again. They must also stay few.

Three observation regimes are formalised, with exact SMT verification. Ten frontier language models are tested on six hundred instances. The best models reach high validity, but parsimony gaps remain. Holdout tests reveal distinct generalisation failure modes across regimes. ABD thus offers a precise, checkable way to probe a kind of reasoning that everyday rule systems constantly need.
arxiv-2602-19043:
Editing a language model with messy real-world text often fails in a subtle way. Zisheng Zhou, with six co-authors, names that failure Context Reliance in 2026. Knowledge learned from edited text sticks to its preceding context. When that context vanishes at inference time, recall fails. Prepending context restores recall, confirming the diagnosis.

The authors show the flaw is built into gradient-based training. It binds new knowledge to one aggregated context view. Their fix is COIN, a context-independent editing frame. It pushes the model to focus on knowledge in local scope, not on context patterns. Tests show COIN cuts Context Reliance sharply. It also beats strong baselines by a wide margin on editing success. Mitigating Context Reliance thus matters for robust editing.
arxiv-2602-19543:
Knowledge hypergraphs beat binary knowledge graphs by holding complex n-ary facts, but building high-quality ones is hard. Rizhuo Huang and seven co-authors point to a scenario gap. Generic tools struggle across domains with niche jargon, and existing methods fail to balance bare-bones frames against fine-grained details. Their framework, Hyper-KGGen, recasts fact-pulling as a dynamic skill-evolving process.

A coarse-to-fine method breaks texts down step by step, covering everything from binary links to complex hyperedges. A skill-learning module distills field know-how into a shared Global Skill Library through a steady feedback loop. Readers get a skill-driven tool built for high-quality hypergraph making across varied domains.
arxiv-2602-19643:
Large language models write smooth, convincing prose, yet fluency is not truth: answers often hide quiet hallucinations. Alex Robertson and four co-authors present KGHaluBench, a knowledge-graph hallucination benchmark that tests models across knowledge breadth and depth. It builds hard, many-sided questions from the graph on the fly, sizing difficulty with statistics to fight popularity bias.

An automated check pipeline spots abstentions and grades answers at both concept and correctness levels, sorting hallucination types. Trials on 25 frontier models with new accuracy and hallucination metrics show which knowledge factors drive hallucinations across model sizes. Readers get a public benchmark built for fairer, fuller truthfulness testing and future mitigation work.
arxiv-2602-20143:
Take two sets of words, all of the same length, over a finite alphabet. Suppose no suffix of a word in the first set matches a prefix of a word in the second set. How large can the two sets both be? A 2026 arXiv paper by Dmitrii Zakharov, working alone, answers with an isoperimetric inequality for word overlap.

The paper shows the product of the two sets' densities is upper bounded by about one over e times n, where n is the word length, with a small vanishing correction. The bound is asymptotically sharp, meaning no substantially stronger universal bound of this form is possible. Readers gain a clean quantitative limit on how much two word sets can overlap in this suffix-prefix sense, and a proof that the limit cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2602-20243:
Calculations of dark-matter binding by radiated energy have a flaw: in the slow-moving regime, they badly break the rule that probabilities must sum to one. Recent work showed the rule is restored once the effects of binding on the incoming particles themselves are added up rightly. A 2026 arXiv paper by Marcos M. Flores and Kalliopi Petraki makes that diagnosis precise and general.

First, the authors derive Kramers-like formulas wave by wave, showing current binding calculations break the rule badly. Then they show how the fix works. Add up the absorptive parts of the incoming state's self-energy, those parts coming from binding processes, while respecting their structure in the complex momentum plane. The results apply across many theories and feed into practical studies of dark-matter freeze-out, indirect searches, and self-interactions. Readers gain both a sharp diagnosis and the resummation that cures it.
arxiv-2602-20343:
C. Daoutis and four co-authors build an auto tool that sorts galaxy activity from optical spectra. Reliable activity tests matter for understanding galaxy evolution, but old methods need heavy prep work, including starlight subtraction and emission-line splitting, which can bias results. The new tool tells apart star-forming, active galactic nucleus, LINER, composite, and passive galaxies using a support vector machine trained on line ratios and color rules.

Key signs are the equivalent widths of chosen lines, and active nuclei split into broad- and narrow-line types. Overall accuracy reaches eighty-three percent, with recall from seventy-seven percent for composite galaxies to ninety-six percent for passive galaxies. The tool beats old tests by cutting prep work and line fitting, covering all activity classes in one scheme, and working across a wide redshift range thanks to a narrow wavelength need. Skipping starlight subtraction barely lowers scores.
arxiv-2602-20443:
Breaking a stressed solid apart involves stored elastic energy, traveling stress waves, and unstable cracks. Vineet Dawara and Koushik Viswanathan study fracture in chemically toughened glass through high-speed projectile impacts and a new micromechanical network model. Residual stress enters their lattice model as a prescribed inelastic strain distribution, recast as equivalent body and surface forces so fracture paths do not depend on the mesh.

Experiments and simulations show fracture patterns shifting from coarse to fine as impact energy rises, while the cumulative fragment-size distribution always decays exponentially. Fragment-size distributions from varied loads and stress profiles collapse onto one master curve scaled by mean fragment area. Fragment size depends on residual stress size and gradient steepness. At small scales, bonds breaking out of order ahead of the crack tip create apparent crack speeds above the Rayleigh wave speed, explaining tongue-like features and hackle zones.
arxiv-2602-20643:
Movement records help explain urban dynamics and guide urban planning, yet privacy concerns often block access to such data. Jiawei Wang and eight co-authors introduce TrajGPT-R, a system for generating large-scale urban movement trips with a transformer model pre-trained and fine-tuned in two phases. Trip generation is first framed as an offline reinforcement learning problem, with a large cut in vocabulary size achieved during tokenization.

Inverse reinforcement learning then captures trip-wise reward signals, using historical data to infer individual movement preferences. The pre-trained model is fine-tuned with the built reward model, easing classic problems of reward-based autoregressive methods such as long-term credit assignment and sparse rewards. Broad evaluations on many data sets show the system markedly beats existing models in reliability and diversity, with implications for traffic management and urban development planning. Code is public.
arxiv-2602-20743:
Gabriel Loiseau and four co-authors tackle a context-sensitive problem: the right balance between privacy protection and utility preservation shifts with domain, privacy goals, and downstream use. Current methods rely on static, manually designed plans lacking flexibility for diverse needs and often failing across domains.

They introduce adaptive text anonymization, a task where plans adapt to privacy-utility needs. Their system uses task prompt tuning building masking instructions for language models, allowing adaptation to privacy goals, domains, and downstream usage patterns. A benchmark spanning five data sets with diverse domains, privacy constraints, and utility aims tests the approach. Across settings, the system consistently achieves a better privacy-utility trade-off than current baselines. It remains lean and effective on open-source language models, with performance comparable to larger closed-source models. It also discovers novel masking plans exploring other points on the privacy-utility trade-off frontier.
arxiv-2602-20943:
Rebuilding long driving scenes in three dimensions is essential for autonomous-vehicle simulation, but feed-forward methods choke on long sequences. Kaiyuan Tan and seven co-authors propose UFO in this 2026 arXiv paper, a recurrent approach that unifies feed-forward speed with optimization-based quality. A four-dimensional scene representation is refined as each new observation arrives.

Visibility-based filtering picks informative scene tokens for efficient long-sequence processing, and pose-guided modeling tracks dynamic objects over time. Tests on the Waymo Open Dataset show the method beating both per-scene optimization and existing feed-forward methods across sequence lengths. It rebuilds sixteen-second driving logs in half a second, with strong visual and geometric quality.
arxiv-2602-21143:
Language-model agents increasingly tackle research-like tasks, but benchmarks rarely test synthesis across sources. Debjit Paul and sixteen co-authors introduce such a benchmark in this 2026 arXiv paper: DEEPSYNTH, with one hundred twenty tasks across seven domains covering sixty-seven countries. Annotators gathered official sources, formed hypotheses, analyzed manually, and designed tasks with verifiable answers.

Eleven leading models and deep-research agents score at most just under nine on F1 and seventeen and a half on a judge metric, showing how hard synthesis remains. Agents struggle with hallucinations and reasoning over large information spaces. The benchmark gives the field a realistic yardstick for guiding research beyond simple fact retrieval.
arxiv-2602-21343:
Decentralized federated learning removes the central aggregator, but peer-to-peer exchange still leaks network traces: who talks, when fragments move, and which packets correlate across rounds. Chao Feng and six co-authors study sender-message linkability in this 2026 arXiv paper and present UnlinkableDFL, a framework where every participant is both learner and mix relay. Model states split into uniform, onion-encrypted fragments over a peer-run mixnet.

Cover traffic, randomized delays, and independently sampled multi-hop paths carry the fragments, and nodes aggregate locally and remotely without sender identities. Analysis puts a limit on how likely sender-linking is, using uncertain routes and shuffled relays, and characterizes when fragmented aggregation preserves standard federated averaging behavior. A prototype with modern transport and packet formats sustains learning under sparse deployment and churn, though payload fingerprints mark the guarantee's boundary.
arxiv-2602-21643:
Xi Luo and one co-author study skyrmion phases and non-Fermi liquid behavior in nonsymmorphic ReAlX Weyl semimetals. Re is a rare earth element and X is silicon or germanium. They show a skyrmion lattice can alter Weyl fermion behavior, driving it into a non-Fermi liquid state with sign-tunable Hall responses.

A lattice model couples Weyl fermions to localized magnetic moments via Kondo interaction. A multi-Q cycloid setup evolving into a skyrmion lattice under an in-plane Zeeman field shapes band structure through zone folding. With the Kubo formula, the team studies transport in the limit. The skyrmion lattice shifts longitudinal and Hall conductivities markedly. Resistivity deviates from Fermi-liquid behavior, where it scales with temperature squared. It follows a non-Fermi liquid power law with temperature to a power between 3 and 5. The work unifies multi-Q textures, skyrmion physics, and transport.
arxiv-2602-22443:
Markov chains model user behavior everywhere, but building them needs substantial user data, and sharing them can leak private information. Alexander Benvenuti and six co-authors develop a method for protecting the user data behind a Markov chain model. They start by privatizing database queries whose outputs are probability vectors, proving the method differentially private.

Accuracy is quantified by bounding the expected divergence between private and non-private queries. The method extends to stochastic matrices, whose rows are simplex-valued queries, covering data-driven Markov models. The team further bounds changes in stationary distribution and convergence rate between private and non-private chains. Simulations under typical privacy settings confirm the theory holds in practice.
arxiv-2602-22643:
Lei Jin and one co-author revisit a 1980 theory by Ohno on topological entropy of weakly equivalent flows, replacing his measure-theoretic route with a more direct, elementary approach. Their novelty is a unified treatment: entropy and mean dimension, two measures of dynamical complexity, are handled together rather than separately.

For flows without fixed points, the team recovers Ohno's entropy theorem by a substantially different method and extends the analogue to mean dimension. For flows with fixed points, they refine Ohno's construction and strengthen his example toward topological complexity. The engine is a small twist. A modified entropy definition relates a spanning set inside the state space to a finite set outside it. It is shown to yield the same value while adapting cleanly to mean dimension.
arxiv-2602-23443:
Pei-Ming Ho and two co-authors study actions for extended objects like strings, with focus on volume-preserving maps. Actions are treated as functions of the worldsheet or worldvolume metric and the induced metric for objects in spacetime as Riemannian, areal-metric, or volume-metric shapes. For strings in Riemannian spacetime, they weigh actions respecting volume-preserving, general, and Weyl-symmetric maps.

The known Schild, Nambu-Goto, and Polyakov actions appear as special cases, and two main findings follow. First, when actions depend on both metrics, all nontrivial self-consistent actions match classically. Second, volume-preserving map symmetry matches full map symmetry for the classical action. The study also covers strings in areal- or volume-metric spacetimes and higher objects. It shows broad Schild actions match the broad Nambu-Goto action, with one caveat: the Polyakov action with an areal-metric tweak cannot describe critical strings without added terms.
arxiv-2602-23543:
Ziqi Gao and 12 co-authors introduce Synthetic Visual Genome 2, a large-scale panoptic video scene graph dataset. It holds over 636,000 videos, six point six million objects, 52 million attributes, and six point seven million relations. That is an order-of-magnitude jump over prior spatio-temporal scene graph datasets.

A fully automated pipeline builds it from multi-scale panoptic segmentation, online-offline path tracking with automatic new-object discovery, per-path meaning parsing, and GPT-5-based relation inference. Human checks confirm annotation accuracy of ninety-three point eight percent for objects, eighty-eight point three percent for attributes, and eighty-five point four percent for relations. Their TRaSER model adds path-aligned tokens to vision-language models. It improves relation detection by 15 to 20 percent across PVSG, VIPSeg, VidOR, and SVG2 test sets.
arxiv-2602-23643:
Judah Goldfeder and three co-authors argue AI must embrace focus through Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence, rather than chase artificial general intelligence. All from bosses and scholars to doomsayers, leaders, and voices discusses AGI, yet they rarely agree on its exact meaning.

One common meaning, an AI doing all a human can do, prompts a question: are humans truly general? The paper probes what is wrong with our idea of AGI. It asks why even its most sound version is flawed for framing AI's future, and whether agreed meanings are plausible, useful, and truly general. It argues AI should focus rather than strive for breadth, and in focus strive for superhuman scores. SAI means intelligence that learns to beat humans at any key task we can do and fills skill gaps where humans are unable, clearing a talk blurred by AGI's packed meaning.
arxiv-2602-23743:
Yves Kini and 15 co-authors present a NICER view of PSR J0030+0451, with six years of observations. Pulse-profile modeling of NICER-targeted millisecond pulsars has enabled mass-radius constraints. For PSR J0030+0451, hot-spot models yielded different mass-radius constraints, with the preferred model showing mild tension with PSR J0437-4715, PSR J0614-3329, and GW170817.

 The team presents a pulse-profile analysis of NICER observations from 2017 July to 2023 January, raising X-ray counts 50 percent. NICER data are jointly analyzed with archival XMM-Newton observations to constrain spectrum and background. The new analysis reduces the discrepancy between hot spot models. Mass is one point four three solar masses, plus zero point two zero, minus zero point one seven. Radius is twelve point six eight kilometers, plus one point three one, minus one point zero four. Both use sixty-eight percent credible intervals.  Hot spot configurations suggest intra-spot temperature gradients.
arxiv-2602-24043:
Yingxuan You and five co-authors present a unified framework for reconstructing three-dimensional garments from single images and videos, including loose-fitting clothing. The 2026 paper notes that body recovery has advanced, but garment geometry, especially for flowing clothes, remains hard, with uses in virtual try-on, avatars, and mixed reality.

The method joins implicit sewing patterns with a generative diffusion model that learns garment shape priors in two-dimensional pattern space. A mapping model links image pixels, pattern coordinates, and three-dimensional geometry for accurate single-image reconstruction. For video, a spatio-temporal diffusion scheme with test-time guidance enforces long-range temporal consistency, while analytic projection constraints preserve visible geometry and complete occluded regions coherently. Trained only on simulated cloth, the system generalizes to real images and beats existing methods on tight and loose garments alike.
arxiv-2603-00143: Öğüt and colleagues present GrapHist, a graph-based self-supervised framework for histopathology that models tissues as cell graphs rather than generic transformer designs. It combines masked autoencoders with heterophilic graph neural networks. These are built to capture tumour microenvironment heterogeneity. Pre-trained on 11 million cell graphs from breast tissue, it matches vision-based rivals on slide-, region- and cell-level tasks with fourfold fewer parameters. It also far outperforms supervised graph models on cancer subtyping. The team also releases five graph-based pathology datasets as a benchmark.
arxiv-2603-00243: Lee and colleagues measure dwarf galaxy WLM's star formation history from near-infrared imaging of bright giant branch stars across about four half-light radii. From a colour-magnitude diagram of 825 stars, their recovered history matches literature JWST histories in shape and in the 50% and 90% mass-formation timescales. Their AGB times run slightly later than JWST values, with coarser precision from few stars. They also derive a similar age-metallicity relation, and spot a stellar over-density in WLM's outer disk suggestive of an accreted dwarf galaxy.
arxiv-2603-00443: Zhao, Kong, Yang, Wei, Hui, and Rao improve synthetic hand images for three dimensional hand reconstruction, where game engine pictures lack texture variety, arms, and interacting objects. Their SesaHand method draws human behaviour meaning from captions through chain of thought inference, keeping human centred context while dropping stray scenery. Hierarchical fusion then aligns hand and body structure across scales, with extra attention on hand regions. These images beat prior work and also lift reconstruction accuracy.
arxiv-2603-00843: Pan, Ouyang, and He tackle high-dimensional integration for gauging uncertainty, where inputs can run to hundreds or thousands. They reshape integrands with boundary-damping importance sampling so ready-made scrambled nets work where inputs have no bounds. Analysis gives a convergence rate that does not depend on dimension for elliptic equations, and tests with many inputs confirm the method's strength.
arxiv-2603-01043: Mishra tests torsion-based teleparallel gravity as a rival to Einstein's gravity. Einstein's theory faces breakdowns, a quantum clash, and dark-sector puzzles. Torsion changes late-time growth and matter clumping in ways that ease the H0 and S8 tensions. Tests against cosmic clocks, supernovae, DESI, and gravity-wave sirens use Monte Carlo fits. Some models beat the standard cosmos model on recent data, and torsion gravity also matches the seen baryon asymmetry, linking early and late cosmos physics.
arxiv-2603-01343: Zhao and fifteen colleagues build PanCanBench, a benchmark testing language models in pancreatic cancer care beyond general medical knowledge. A human-in-the-loop workflow creates expert rubrics for patient questions stripped of identifiers from the Pancreatic Cancer Action Network, yielding 3,130 question-specific checks across 282 real patient questions. The team evaluates 22 closed and open-source models with an LLM-as-a-judge setup, measuring care coverage, factual truth, and web-search use. Models vary a lot in rubric-based coverage.
arxiv-2603-01743:
Tsung-Ming Tai, Sofia Casarin, Andrea Pilzer, and colleagues predict the next human action in a video before it happens. Their 2026 work faces a core snag: past frames show what was done, not what a person plans next. Pixel-based attention often latches onto clear visual cues and misses the hidden intent.

Their method, Action-Guided Attention, uses predicted action sequences as the guides for attention itself. Those guides push the model to stress past moments that matter for the coming act. A gating step blends that guided view with the current frame traits. Tests on a large kitchen-activity benchmark show strong carry-over from known to unseen cases. After training, the team can inspect which action links the model learned, which makes its forecasts easier to explain.
arxiv-2603-02543:
Evan Angelone and Egon Schulte build chiral polyhedra from affine groups in this 2026 mathematics paper. Chiral polyhedra are highly symmetric shapes whose mirror images cannot be rotated into alignment. Their construction starts from subgroups of the general affine group over a finite field. The prime power setting gives rich arithmetic structure to exploit.

The full affine group appears as the symmetry group of a chiral polyhedron. Its face type depends on the prime power modulo four, with genus computed in each case. Negative results bound the construction's reach just as sharply. No subgroup of these affine groups can fully govern regular polytopes of rank three or more. Chiral polytopes of rank four or more are excluded too. The construction thus captures everything this group family can yield.
arxiv-2603-02643:
Daniel Vaz, Jarle Brinchmann, Sebastian Kamann, and colleagues report the first count of double stars in the tiny galaxy Leo T. This 2026 paper comes from the MUSE-Faint survey, which took repeated spectra of the galaxy's stars. Leo T is the faintest galaxy known with recent star birth, and dark matter seems to dominate its mass.

The team modeled how binary stars shift measured speeds, then estimated pair rates for young and old stars apart. About half the stars appear to be in pairs, with a lower share among the older group. Binary motion did not inflate the galaxy's measured speed spread. That supports earlier claims that Leo T truly is dark-matter heavy.
arxiv-2603-03143:
Jiyuan Wang, Chunyu Lin, Lei Sun, and colleagues edit three-dimensional scenes so every viewpoint agrees. Borrowing two-dimensional diffusion editors for 3D work is tempting, but edits often drift between camera angles, and paired 3D training data barely exist. Their 2026 insight is that checking consistency is far easier than generating it.

That asymmetry suits reinforcement learning. Their system, RL3DEdit, edits in one pass while a large 3D foundation model grades the result: its confidence maps and pose errors become the reward signal. The editor is thus pulled toward outputs that stay coherent in 3D. Tests show stable multi-view consistency and better editing quality than leading methods, at high efficiency. Code and the model are slated for release.
arxiv-2603-03243:
Xiaomeng Xu, Jisang Park, Han Zhang, and colleagues teach mobile robots whole-body skills by watching people, with no robot in the loop. Their 2026 framework, HoMMI, collects demonstrations through handheld interfaces augmented with head-worn sensing. That extra viewpoint captures the global context mobile manipulation needs, making data collection portable and scalable.

The catch is a wider gap between human and robot in both what is seen and how motion maps over. Three design choices bridge it: a body-neutral visual representation, a relaxed encoding of head motion, and a whole-body controller that turns hand-eye paths into coordinated robot movement within physical limits. The system enables long tasks mixing two arms, navigation, and active looking.
arxiv-2603-03443:
Licia Verde questions how standard cosmology's standard ruler really is. Baryon acoustic oscillations leave a characteristic scale in how galaxies cluster, set by the sound horizon of the early universe. Analyses fit templates to extract that scale and convert it into distances. Her 2026 paper flags a subtle mismatch: the textbook sound horizon, computed from sound speed, differs slightly from the scale actually imprinted in clustered matter.

Extended to a broader family of cosmological models, that mismatch biases inferred parameters. For surveys with DESI-like precision, and even more for a forecast fifth-year dataset, the bias becomes a significant fraction of the statistical uncertainty once the true cosmos strays from the assumed one. Verde proposes several corrections suited to different uses. Analysts working in those regimes should apply them or budget the effect as a systematic error.
arxiv-2603-03543:
Project Polyglot, led by Nicholas Kluge Corrêa and Aniket Sen, releases Tucano 2, a fully open family of Portuguese language models. Progress in language models has flowed unevenly across languages, and open Portuguese models lagged behind. Their 2026 suite spans from half a billion to under four billion parameters and opens everything: recipes, logs, and code, so the work can be reproduced and extended.

The training data grows on several fronts at once. A larger, cleaner corpus is joined by a synthetic set filling its gaps, plus post-training sets for instruction following and preferences. Those support skills like retrieval-augmented generation, coding, tool use, and step-by-step reasoning. Extensive ablation studies shape both first training and continued training recipes across base, instruct, and thinking variants. The suite reaches state-of-the-art results on several Portuguese benchmarks, backed by a refined evaluation harness.
arxiv-2603-03943: Ramachandran Anantharaman and others address when nonlinear acyclic networks in steady time can be identified, with motion on edges and all nodes excited. Measuring all sinks proves necessary and sufficient to spot any tree when edge motion are analytic and satisfy a stated condition, analogous to the discrete-time case. The result extends to general directed acyclic graphs, where measuring all sinks is necessary and sufficient when motion are not linear, a condition relaxable for trees. They also give identification methods using higher-order derivatives and parallel paths.
arxiv-2603-04243: He and others present a unified method for joint finding of lacunes and enlarged perivascular spaces. Standard segmentation networks contend with feature interference and severe class imbalance when handling these divergent targets at once. Also, biological and topological consistency are kept through a mixed-control plan mixing Mutual Exclusion and Centerline Dice losses.
arxiv-2603-04543: Wills and colleagues construct linear time quantum codes. Quantum LDPC, locally testable, and transversal gate codes grew rapidly, yet fast codes lagged despite old study. In the channel setting, noise sits between encoding and decoding, key to links between fault safe quantum computers. Their asymptotically good codes encode and unencode with log depth circuits and a linear gate count. Classical reading also runs in log depth with O(n log n) gates, or linear gates at higher depth. Explicit codes use linear gates throughout at log depth.
arxiv-2603-04943: Yun Liu and team handle target speaker extraction, isolating one voice from multi-speaker mixtures where interacting factors degrade real-world scores. Earlier curriculum methods handle factors apart, so the team jointly schedules speaker counts, overlap ratios, SNR thresholds, and synthetic-real proportions for progressive learning. They add TSE-Datamap, a visualization method that bases curriculum choices on training dynamics seen through confidence and variability across epochs. The analysis reveals easy, ambiguous, and hard data regions, and the methods beat random sampling, in hard multi-speaker cases.
arxiv-2603-05243: Josu Aurrekoetxea and colleagues combine analysis and numerics on cosmic strings of field theory in the flat-space Abelian-Higgs model. From soliton theory, they derive the low-energy effective action and find no nontrivial curvature corrections for translational Goldstone modes alone. Higher-energy soliton-profile fluctuations become massive worldsheet modes, and the leading curvature contribution enters only through coupling to the worldsheet Ricci scalar. Lattice simulations with adaptive mesh refinement confirm the effective dynamics and reveal a parametric instability moving energy from massive excitations into the Goldstone sector.
arxiv-2603-05443: István Tomon proves the Karzanov-Lomonosov conjecture. Two subsets A and B of X cross if A minus B, B minus A, A intersect B, and X minus A union B are nonempty. Karzanov and Lomonosov conjectured almost fifty years ago that every subset family of an n-element set with no k-pairwise crossings is O(kn). The author proves O_k(n), settling the main problem. The author proves every k-wise laminar family is linear. K-wise laminar means no k-antichain with nonempty common intersection.
arxiv-2603-06143: Biello and colleagues study Higgs boson production with a top quark pair at hadron colliders, matching next to next to leading order QCD corrections to parton showers. For the two loop amplitude they use soft Higgs boson and high energy approximations, building the latter in full colour and combining both pointwise across phase space. All remaining ingredients enter exactly, with a conservative uncertainty below perturbative uncertainties. Validated fiducial predictions cover Higgs decay into photons with off shell top decays, and the generator is released in the POWHEG framework.
arxiv-2603-06443: Nguyen and colleagues approximate every definable inner-metric Lipschitz mapping in an o-minimal structure by smooth mappings with arbitrarily close derivative bounds. When the structure admits smooth cell decomposition, the approximants can be chosen smooth, and the result extends to outer Lipschitz mappings. The proof builds partitions of unity with sharp derivative bounds, a tool potentially useful for other approximation problems.
arxiv-2603-06543: Shahbazi and team bring SurgFormer, a gated transformer for soft tissue simulation on 3D meshes, trained with solver-made data for guessing node displacement fields quickly. Many-branch blocks combine local message passing, global self-attention, and forward updates, fused through learned gates per node and channel, mixing local and long-range information at scale. Resection information enters as a cut code, joining deformation prediction and shape cases. Two surgical datasets under an XFEM-watch protocol cover cholecystectomy cuts and appendectomy handling, with cut cases.
arxiv-2603-06643: Chakraborty takes general forms of the Quantum Hamilton-Jacobi Equation for the non-Hermitian effective-mass Swanson model and for bits of constant and position-dependent mass. The author shows these equations can be recast as Cayley-Klein Riccati equations with a Lie-Hamilton shape. Possible expressions of Lie symmetry and the Lie integral are also checked. The paper thus places the three kinds within a common Lie frame, with the mirror and sum lines finishing the geometric picture.
arxiv-2603-06943: Iorio and colleagues study how flexible work schedules affect transformer capacity for electric vehicles. Uncoordinated charging shifts home loads and pushes distribution transformers past their limits. Flexible schedules, hybrid, remote, or in-person, plus rooftop solar, can offset that strain, yet the effect was little explored. They build weekly schedule-aware robust and chance-constrained models for charging coordination to find hosting capacity. Tests on a home feeder in Arizona show smartly combining schedule flexibility with solar helps utilities manage changing grid demands.
arxiv-2603-07343: De Santis and colleagues build concept bottleneck models from concepts a black-box model learned on its own, instead of hand-picked lists. Sparse autoencoders pull the concepts out, and a multimodal model then names and labels them on chosen images. The resulting M-CBM stays easy to read while closing much of the usual gap to black-box scores. A new per-decision count of contributing concepts keeps comparisons fair about leakage.
arxiv-2603-07843: Zhang and colleagues watch how children play without words with lifelike figures on a screen, comparing typical children and autistic children. In a staged study with six figures, they logged hundreds of wordless acts, with many repeats, and set the patterns beside those seen before in adults. They also note repeated face and hand moves, which makers of such figures should keep in mind. The work points to what robots should learn to read when no speech is given.
arxiv-2603-08343: Aggarwal and colleagues rethink attention output projection with structured Hadamard transforms for fast models. The dense output map in multi-head models scales fast with model size, adding heavily to parameter count, memory footprint, and runtime cost. The authors replace this map with a fixed, cost-free WHT followed by an affine map. This eliminates about 25 percent of block weights while keeping global cross-head mixing through a norm-preserving map. Transform models show steeper test loss curves per training FLOPs.
arxiv-2603-08643: Giataganas and colleagues show that black hole mergers scramble light rings faster than any other setup. Mapping two spinless holes in a near-circular pair onto one effective Kerr hole, they find the remnant sits where light paths go unstable at the top possible rate. That tie, they suggest, links merger leftovers to their unstable light orbits in a deep way.
arxiv-2603-08743: Mengqi Liao and colleagues squeeze language-model reasoning onto busy servers by compressing paged attention. KV cache memory chokes decoding concurrency, and most eviction fixes fall short for industrial use. Their Zipage engine pairs token-wise eviction with paged attention, schedules fully with prefix caching and async compression, and keeps about 95 percent of full-cache quality at over twice the speed.
arxiv-2603-08843: Marco Manno and colleagues trace neutrino flavor conversion in collapsing stars. Matter resonance flips flavors, and magnetic moments add chirality-flipping turns, mixing neutrinos with antineutrinos for Majorana kinds. The awaited sky signal leans on viewing angle and conversion case, running largest head-on to the jet and peaking a few hundred ms after bounce.
arxiv-2603-09043: Elija Perrier and Michael Timothy Bennett separate talking like a stable self from being one. Machine consciousness tests mostly see behavior, and language plus tool use lets an agent claim the right self even when key constraints are not jointly present at decision time. Applying Stack Theory's temporal gap to scaffold trajectories, they derive two persistence scores from traces, link them to five identity metrics, and map scaffolds into an identity morphospace.
arxiv-2603-09343: A. M. Kamchatnov studies how instability fronts spread in conservative nonlinear wave systems using the Whitham method. He solves the modulation equations Whitham gives for periodic waves of a generalized Klein-Gordon equation, in the limit of large times. By then the disturbed region far outgrows the initial localized disturbance, and the motion settles into a self-similar form. Two typical choices of the nonlinearity illustrate the general case, and in both the fronts travel at the maximal group velocity.
arxiv-2603-09443: Sophie Kollatzsch overviews McMule, a Monte Carlo framework giving QED corrections for low-energy leptonic scattering and decay, and its two newest extensions. One adds electroweak effects at low energies inside the low-energy effective field theory. The other, called disperon QED, folds in pion form factors and hadronic vacuum polarization using OpenLoops with effective theory methods. Kollatzsch illustrates the impact of gamma-Z mixing models for the MOLLER experiment and the care needed to align the pieces consistently.
arxiv-2603-09643: Anupam Purwar and Aditya Choudhary propose MM-tau-p2, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLM agents in dual-control settings where the user's persona is visible. Existing frameworks test text chat agents in user-agnostic settings, yet in customer experience work an agent's behavior evolves as it learns the user's personality. Their metrics cover multimodal robustness and turn overhead when multimodality is added. Even frontier models such as GPT-5 face extra considerations here, and twelve novel metrics give a holistic automated evaluation.
arxiv-2603-09943: Jinyue Li and coauthors present PathMem, a memory based framework that helps multimodal models reason about pathology slides. Diagnosis needs both visual pattern reading and formal knowledge such as taxonomy and grading rules, which current models apply unevenly. PathMem stores that structured knowledge as long term memory. A memory transformer then moves selected parts into working memory, grounded by the case at hand, lifting report scores.
arxiv-2603-10043: Yunsheng Wang and coauthors propose a graph network for recognising emotion in multimodal dialogue. Text, speech and vision cues must be fused while tracking how feelings evolve within and across speakers. Their design builds a subgraph per modality with self and cross speaker links, then applies differential graph attention to filter noise. An adaptive balance step stops dominant modalities from drowning out speech and vision.
arxiv-2603-10543: A Vicente Arévalo and co-authors map a sunspot from photosphere to chromosphere using Stokes inversions. Sunspots are places where strong magnetism shapes hot gas, from the stable lower layer to the shock filled upper layer. Their method joins a magnetic balance rule with a non local heat rule, applied to CRISP data. The maps show the Evershed flow reversing into an inflow higher up, while the moat flow keeps moving outward. An umbral flash showed supersonic upflows and shock like conditions.
arxiv-2603-10643: Teodora Mihailescu and co-authors use Hinode EIS observations to track plasma composition and cooling in the loops of a solar flare. Composition in flaring regions varies in space and time, and how that feeds back on loop dynamics is not fully understood. For an M-class flare they measured cooling rates and FIP bias at loop apex and footpoint. The footpoint cooled more slowly with a weaker bias; the apex cooled faster with a stronger one. Simulations suggest higher bias speeds radiative cooling.
arxiv-2603-10843: Zitai Xu and Guoding Liu propose a way to purify entangled pairs by letting a quantum system evolve under its own natural Hamiltonian, rather than through carefully compiled digital circuits. Their protocol ties the fidelity of the output pairs to out-of-time-order correlators, so systems that scramble information well also distill well. Simulations on Rydberg-atom and trapped-ion setups suggest strong results with short-range interactions and short evolution times.
arxiv-2603-10943: Tim Schneemann and coauthors report the first axion search results from a prototype of SUPAX, a haloscope planned to hunt axion-like particles as dark matter candidates. The prototype ran a copper cavity at 2 K inside a 12 T magnetic field, probing axion masses around 34 micro-electronvolts. The data exclude axion-photon couplings above a stated limit near that mass and also rule out dark photons with kinetic mixing above a second stated limit.
arxiv-2603-11043: Valentas Kurauskas proves, in an asymptotic form, a 2023 conjecture of Juškevičius. It asks how concentrated the sum of independent integer random variables can be at a single point. The concentration function gives the largest probability any one value carries. The conjecture says sums built from minimal-variance variables with matching concentration bounds are the most concentrated of all. His proof leans on an inverse Littlewood-Offord theorem. It also leans on matching lattice sums to a discretized Gaussian in total variation distance.
arxiv-2603-11243: George Saon and coauthors speed up speech recognition by letting a CTC encoder draft for the autoregressive language model that normally writes the transcript token by token. Their three-step scheme accepts the greedy CTC transcript outright when frame entropies fall below a threshold. Otherwise it verifies the draft in one language-model pass under a relaxed likelihood criterion, and resumes autoregressive decoding from the accepted prefix if verification fails. Across nine corpora and five languages the method cuts word error rates while accelerating decoding several-fold.
arxiv-2603-11443: Jakhar and Ray study how the shapes of totally real multiquadratic number fields are spread out. A field's shape is the class of its integer lattice under rotations, reflections, and scaling. These shapes live in a shape space that carries a natural measure from Haar measure. The pair look at fields of degree a power of two where two stays unramified. They show the spread is ruled by that measure cut down to one torus orbit. The result settles a conjecture of Haidar.
arxiv-2603-11543: Huang and co-authors present Mango-GS, a node-guided method for 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes. Per-frame fitting can chase each instant and lose the true motion underneath. Mango-GS instead models motion links across a short frame window with a Transformer. That modeling sits on a sparse set of control nodes. Each node pairs a fixed canonical position with a latent code, anchoring motion and blocking drift. Masking and two multi-frame losses add robustness, with top quality at real-time speed in tests.
arxiv-2603-12243: Xie, Qi, and Sadigh teach a robot to play piano with both hands through fast adaptation. Dexterous tasks need millimeter care, and sim-trained policies often miss that bar on real hardware. HandelBot starts from a simulation policy, then refines it in two stages. A structured stage fixes spatial alignment by tuning lateral finger joints from physical rollouts. Residual reinforcement learning then learns fine corrective moves on its own. Across five songs the robot played with clear gains over direct sim use, from just 30 minutes of real data.
arxiv-2603-12443: Yeung and co-authors couple III-V nanowire quantum dots to photonic circuits with a curved waveguide bridge. A dot inside a nanowire spans a gap in the waveguide, which is not continuous across the device. Evanescent coupling between the photonic parts recovers photons emitted from both outputs. Auto- and cross-correlation tests ran on distinct output facets of the device. Single-photon emission came from both ends for neutral and charged exciton complexes. Cascaded emission was also shown, with each complex collected from a distinct facet.
arxiv-2603-12543: Purves and Lio' introduce CALF, a framework that trains distributed reinforcement learning policies under realistic network conditions. Deployed policies face delays, jitter, and packet loss across edge devices and cloud servers. Standard training assumes zero-latency contact, so performance drops sharply on real networks. CALF instead trains policies inside simulation with explicit network models. Experiments show network-aware training shrinks the deployment gap against network-agnostic baselines. Tests on mixed hardware confirm robust execution, marking the network itself as a key axis of sim-to-real transfer.
arxiv-2603-12743: Chenyang Zhu and co-authors define a new task: binding rich textual knowledge to a visual concept, not just a rare token. Rare tokens are scarce in pretraining data, so older customization methods prove unstable. Their MoKus rests on cross-modal transfer, where text-side knowledge shifts carry into images. First, an anchor stores the visual concept. Then knowledge answers are updated toward that anchor. A new benchmark, KnowCusBench, tests the task, and MoKus beat prior methods.
arxiv-2603-12843: Mitsuki Nagai and Keisuke Yano clarify the geometry of Stein's method of moments for parameter estimation. The method builds estimators that need no normalizing constant. They give a canonical decomposition of such an estimator after centering the score matching one. That split shows score matching sits at the core of the frame. From it, they build an estimator with lower asymptotic variance. Links to Wasserstein geometry explain the gap to maximum likelihood.
arxiv-2603-13143: Sajal Mukherjee and co-authors prove an effective version of the Mayer-Vietoris theorem through discrete Morse theory. The classic theorem gives a long exact sequence, yet no explicit way to compute homology. Their setup splits a simplicial complex into two subcomplexes with gradient vector fields on each part. The fields need not agree on the overlap region. Trajectories of those fields then yield the homology of the whole complex directly. Wise splits can cut the work a great deal.
arxiv-2603-13343: Kushal Khemani and Anjum Nazir Qureshi build an AI system for predictive maintenance in connected vehicles. Most such systems use only internal diagnostic signals and test on simulated or lab data. Their framework fuses vehicle sensor streams with road quality, weather, traffic, and driver data via V2X and APIs. Tests run at the vehicle edge across four layers of checks. Context features raised F1 scores on synthetic data, and LightGBM scored high on the AI4I 2020 benchmark. Field data from five vehicles in three countries backed the lab results.
arxiv-2603-13443: Xin Guan, Yunshan Li, and Ze Wang present NormCode Canvas, a system for sustainable LLM agentic workflows. It realizes Case-Based Reasoning at two levels for multi-step workflows. The base is NormCode, a semi-formal planning language whose scope rule makes each checkpoint a self-contained case. Level 1 treats checkpoints as concrete cases that can be forked, reused, or revised. Level 2 treats each compiled plan as an abstract case, and the compiler pipeline is itself a NormCode plan. Four deployed plans form the evidence.
arxiv-2603-13643: C. M. F. Mingarelli and co-authors review pulsar timing arrays and the new gravitational-wave landscape. PTA experiments now have evidence for a nanoHertz gravitational wave background. The review sets out how detection works, with noise models and cross-correlation methods that isolate the Hellings-Downs curve. It argues that tension with standard merger models is largely resolved by new views of supermassive black hole binary populations. Continuous wave searches, cosmic strings, and ultralight dark matter are also covered.
arxiv-2603-13943: Komurcu and Petkevicius mix two tools to predict how satellite images will look next. Plain regression blurs fine detail. Pure image generators can invent false structures. Their system, Sat-JEPA-Diff, first predicts stable scene features with an I-JEPA module. Those features then guide a frozen Stable Diffusion model through a small adapter. On a global Sentinel-2 dataset, the method keeps sharp edges and land borders clear. It beats plain baselines on scores that track how real the images look.
arxiv-2603-14443: Shahnazari, Ayyoubzadeh and Keshtparvar measure sound patterns in Persian poetry across centuries. Their corpus holds over 1.1 million lines from nearly 32,000 poems by 83 poets. They limit the set to five classic meters for fair comparison. Each line is turned into phonemes and scored on six traits. These traits cover hardness, sonority, sibilance, vowel share, entropy and consonant clusters. The authors find that poets keep distinct sound profiles even after meter and form are controlled. Sound shifts over time track genre and performance shifts, not sharp breaks.
arxiv-2603-14543: Balzer and Benlahlou bring gradient boosting to spatial panel data models. Urban and regional data show patterns across space and time. Standard likelihood or moment methods can fail to give unique answers in high dimensions. Their model-based boosting fits low- and high-dimensional cases with clear output. Random and fixed effects both fit the frame. Built-in selection picks models and variables from the data. Simulations back the method, and real cases cover Italian insurance and Indonesian rice farms.
arxiv-2603-14643: Dejl, Williams and Toni extend argumentation-based support for language model decisions with ArgEval. High-stakes use suffers from opaque, erratic model outputs. Older tools explain single cases but leave the core logic fixed. ArgEval maps the full decision space for a task first. Option ontologies and shared argument frameworks follow for each choice. Cases then draw explainable advice from those shared frames. Users can contest the shared logic itself, not just one output. A glioblastoma treatment study tests the approach.
arxiv-2603-14843: Kang and co-authors keep toxic-post detectors current as disguise tricks evolve with ContiGuard. Toxic posts get reworded to slip past static detectors. Detectors frozen in time decay as tricks change. Updating on disguised text is hard, since warping bends both meaning and key cues. A language-model step first restores warped content to clearer form. Guard parts then shield core feature learning from the noise. The frame is the first built for this rolling detection task, they state.
arxiv-2603-14943: Papadopoulos and co-authors fence radio signals in space with reconfigurable surfaces in RF-Fencing. Programmable wireless settings promise control over how waves spread. RF-Fencing shields some zones while feeding legitimate users nearby. SHIELD, their algorithm, runs many surface units from precompiled codebooks. Light real-time tuning joins the codebook playback. Far-field beam control and near-field quiet zones both emerge in tests. Wide frequency and layout scans back the claims. Covert communication gains a proactive spatial tool, they argue.
arxiv-2603-15543: Mendes Araujo and co-authors study the Drazin inverse of adjacency matrices for oriented Dutch windmill graphs. Walks of set lengths, plus the minimal polynomial of the matrix, drive the analysis. They obtain explicit formulas for the Drazin inverse and pin down its index. The characterization extends known results for paths, cycles, and bipartite graphs. It also offers a constructive route to symbolic generalized inverses in structured networks with cyclic feedback.
arxiv-2603-15643: Wang tackles a knowledge gap in green stormwater infrastructure work. Facts on rain gardens, permeable pavement, and bioretention sit scattered across manuals and forms. General language models often guess wrong on such expert tasks. His GSI Agent mixes three fixes in one framework. It fine-tunes on a curated GSI instruction set. It retrieves from a knowledge base built from city documents. An agent pipeline then joins retrieval with structured answers. BLEU-4 rose from 0.090 to 0.307 on GSI tests.
arxiv-2603-15943: Micluta-Campeanu and co-authors patch failing physics models with learned symbolic terms. Digital twins of HVAC gear can miss real physics and fail calibration. Their Dyad Model Discovery flow augments model equations from telemetry data. Symbolic expressions, fitted to the data, fill the missing pieces. A test case covers a transport refrigeration unit twin. The workflow keeps an engineer in the loop throughout. Suggestions arrive for the engineer to accept or reject. The team calls it a first AI-assisted design flow of its kind.
arxiv-2603-16743: Aliaj, Dian, and Papathanasiou derive new symbol letters for five- and six-point QCD processes. Cluster algebra predicts alphabets for nine-point amplitudes in super Yang-Mills theory. Breaking dual conformal symmetry maps those letters to QCD kinematics. For six-point processes with one massive leg, nested square roots appear. Their letters contain all one-loop integral alphabets for these setups. The massless limit matches known two-loop results, plus 162 new letters. Five-point two-mass candidates show a nontrivial overlap with the literature.
arxiv-2603-17043: Pandey and co-authors present OpenQlaw, an agentic AI assistant for analyzing 2D quantum materials. A physics aware vision model inspects microscope images of material flakes and lists candidate observations. Downstream work then needs exact counts and measurements over those outputs. The team shows that counts in free form summaries can drift from the observations returned. Their state grounded variant turns outputs into image scoped records. Deterministic tools then act on records, with refusal when data is missing. In trials, delegation returned the exact requested count every time.
arxiv-2603-17143: Sambataro and Tezaur study how to speed up the non overlapping Schwarz method used in domain decomposition coupling. They recast the Schwarz scheme as a fixed point iteration. They then test two speedups: Aitken acceleration and Anderson acceleration. They also derive an adaptive Anderson variant with memory adaptation. For two subdomain problems, the Aitken version proved best in efficiency and robustness. For larger multi domain settings, the Anderson version was the method of choice.
arxiv-2603-17243: Ogunsola and co-authors fill in missing theory for the New Transmuted Logistic-exponential distribution, a lifetime model. Its maximum likelihood fit has no closed form, and its consistency had not been checked. The authors derive many properties at once. These include Shannon entropy, stochastic ordering, the mode, and stress strength reliability. They compare ten estimation methods in Monte Carlo tests, scored by bias and error size. On infectious disease mortality data, the new distribution fit better than its base distributions.
arxiv-2603-17543: Strycharczuk and Kirkham outline AURORA, a model that predicts tongue shape from vowel formants. It reads the first two formant values and outputs tongue displacement and shape. Training draws on ultrasound tongue images and speech data from 40 native English speakers. They present AURORA as a teaching aid for phonetics students. Two tools, a Shiny app and a biofeedback prototype, open it to clinics. Speech therapists and their clients are target users.
arxiv-2603-17643: Cheng and Houben ask whose insights steer AI-assisted sensemaking. Groups making sense of big information sets move from vague views toward clear ones. Early outside insights can lock attention onto one frame before checks happen. AI tools tend to offer such insights too soon, they argue. Three open questions follow for teams that plan to use AI this way. They also weigh why users may accept the AI frame too fast.
arxiv-2603-17943: Bajnok, Boldis, and le Plat give the full strong-coupling expansion of the cusp anomalous dimension. The setting is N=4 super Yang-Mills theory at large coupling. The quantity splits into a ratio of two determinants with simple expansions. Nonperturbative terms sort by partitions into distinct odd integers, they show. Stokes constants then follow by an iterative rule. They also fix the O(6) mass gap series and its exact link to the cusp.
arxiv-2603-18043: Prakash shows a provenance paradox in multi-agent LLM routing based on self-reported quality scores. When delegates can inflate their scores, quality-based routing picks the worst ones, below random choice. He extends the LLM Delegate Protocol with contracts that bound goals, budgets, and failure rules. A claimed-versus-attested identity model splits reported scores from verified ones. In tests with simulated and real Claude models, attested routing came close to optimal.
arxiv-2603-18543: Arthur and Machado build a way to track ESG risk as it spreads through supply networks. Ratings can hide poor practice when a firm trades with badly rated partners. Their framework extends PageRank and alpha centrality, with tuning that resists greenwashing. The scores update a firm's own rating and flag influential neighbours. They also show how exposed a firm is to bad conduct upstream. Tests run on synthetic networks, a real firm network, and world trade data.
arxiv-2603-18643: Brüser disproves a long-standing conjecture about polycons, shapes bounded by conic arcs. Wachspress proposed polycons in 1975 for finite element work. Each polycon has an adjoint curve that vanishes on its residual arrangement. Wachspress guessed this curve stays nonzero inside the shape under mild conditions. Brüser gives a polycon bounded by three conics where the curve does vanish inside. Swapping one conic side for a line makes the new adjoint touch the old one. Determinantal forms then describe all adjoints for three-conic polycons.
arxiv-2603-19143: Chiani and co-authors ask what it would cost to scale direct air capture of carbon dioxide. They run a full uncertainty study of this tech in a detailed climate and economy model. Most runs show only modest uptake by mid-century. A small share, four to six percent, reach gigaton scale. That scale needs aid above 200 to 330 dollars per ton for decades. The total public cost could reach 900 to 3,000 billion dollars.
arxiv-2603-19343: Mantovanelli unifies several classic Fibonacci and Lucas identities under one algebraic trick. Take an element whose square is a linear mix of itself and the unit. Then each power of it shrinks to a first-degree form with set coefficients. Those coefficients are the generic Lucas sequence, also known as Dickson polynomials. The same rule, via Cayley-Hamilton, gives power formulas for two-by-two matrices. Applying test functionals to the Fibonacci matrix yields multi-index identities in one sweep. The note is expository and stresses the shared mechanism.
arxiv-2603-19743: Rękas and co-authors study spin motion in a perturbed infinite-U Hubbard chain. Charge moves like free spinless fermions in this limit. The spin order stays frozen, which splits the state space into fragments. The team adds perturbations that break integrability but keep the fragmentation. They find spin motion that ranges from ballistic to anomalous diffusion. Under the perturbations it slows from diffusion to subdiffusion. The subdiffusion route differs from that in disordered systems.
arxiv-2603-20043: Baran, Tarasewicz, and Rżysko simulate how ethane wets different surfaces. On uniform surfaces, tuning the surface potential moves the system from incomplete to complete wetting. The layering transition temperatures match experiments on ethane over graphite well. Patterned surfaces behave in a richer way. Every striped substrate they tried showed a prewetting transition. Yet the path of adsorption depends strongly on the stripe width. The work links surface design to how the first ethane layers build up.
arxiv-2603-20343: Hamis and co-authors give a hands-on guide to fitting ODE models in Stan for biology. Matching dynamic models to time series data is central to mathematical biology. Stan is a free tool that estimates model parameters with Bayesian methods. It has built-in support for ordinary differential equation models. Worked examples move from simple teaching models to real data sets. The guide also explains the core statistical ideas behind Stan. Readers can follow each step and reuse the code.
arxiv-2603-20443: Carmichael and Skinner present TRGS-SLAM, a mapping system for thermal cameras on mobile robots. Thermal images work in darkness and through fog, dust, and smoke. Cheap thermal sensors, though, suffer blur, rolling shutter, and fixed noise. Their system builds on 3D Gaussian splatting with inertial aiding. A model-aware rendering method handles the thermal degradations directly. B-spline trajectory fitting and drift correction add stability. On fast, noisy real-world runs, rival SLAM methods all failed. Their system kept tracking accurately through those same runs.
arxiv-2603-20643: Chen and Xi study the centralizer algebra of a single matrix and its singularity category. Any finite algebra over a field can be seen as the centralizer of two matrices. The one matrix case is thus a key first step. They give a direct and explicit account of singular equivalences for these algebras. The Auslander-Reiten conjecture holds here, as does the Cartan determinant one. In fact all the classic homological conjectures hold for this class. They also track which invariants a singular equivalence keeps.
arxiv-2603-20743: Chen and co-authors study gender bias in instruction text to speech systems. Most past tests vary one cue at a time. Real prompts mix social status, career cues, and persona traits at once. The team models prompts as blends of these three cue types. Strong interaction effects showed up in open source models. Bias tied back to text encoder priors and skewed training data. Plain diversity prompts failed to break these patterns. They argue bias checks must test cue blends, not single cues.
arxiv-2603-20843: Zeng and co-authors propose HiCI, a hierarchical attention module for long context language models. Most tools treat long context as a pure scaling problem. HiCI borrows from theories of how readers build discourse meaning. It first builds representations for text segments. It then merges them into a shared global context. Both levels feed back to guide attention inside each segment. Added to LLaMA-2 with few extra parameters, it stretched context to 100K tokens. Gains held across modeling, retrieval, and instruction tests.
arxiv-2603-20943: Schibler, Xue, and Zhu study how well the convex hull of a hidden point set can be estimated through range queries. The only access to the points is a range emptiness oracle. Algorithms are judged by query count and by the volume error of the output shape. For orthogonal queries, they prove tight error bounds that differ for non adaptive and adaptive plans. In two dimensions the error shrinks with the query count, faster for adaptive plans. Halfplane queries get their own bounds.
arxiv-2603-21243: Liu and co-authors present LSA, a transformer that models long and short term aspect interests for recommendation. Aspect based methods mine review terms, such as price, to learn fine-grained user tastes. User interests shift over time, though, and static graph methods miss brief new focuses. LSA models short term interest from recent aspect interactions and long term interest from global patterns. On four real data sets, it cuts mean squared error by about two and a half percent over the best baseline.
arxiv-2603-21443: Farahat builds a practical method for detecting livelocks in self-disabling unidirectional ring protocols of any size. Earlier work placed this problem at a high level of undecidability. Farahat lifts the analysis to pairs of transitions and witnesses, where hidden structure appears. A product graph built from those pairs captures all livelocks and can be pruned in polynomial time. A backtracking phase then confirms or rules out each cycle. Across 4,349 tested protocols, the method always gave a conclusive answer with no errors.
arxiv-2603-21643: Tsai and co-authors give neutral atom arrays tools to fight atom loss and heating. The tools use helper atoms, called ancilla atoms, plus strong Rydberg gates. Repeated ancilla readout raised detection fidelity over rounds while barely touching data atoms. The team also moved quantum data from electronic states into motional states of strontium atoms. That step allows loss checks mid-circuit that keep coherence intact. A cooling routine then shifts motional heat from data atoms onto ancilla atoms, and the data atoms' temperature dropped clearly.
arxiv-2603-22143: Ackelsberg and Bergelson revisit polynomial equidistribution and recurrence over function fields. Their note fixes two small errors in a 2016 paper by Bergelson and Leibman. That paper proved a Weyl-type equidistribution theorem in finite characteristic. The authors set the fixes inside the wider field of number theory and additive combinatorics in function fields. They also prove new results on intersective polynomials in finite characteristic. Those results describe them through algebraic, combinatorial, and dynamic traits.
arxiv-2603-22343: Qiao and co-authors forecast solar power with a cloud-edge team of models. Edge grids need forecasts that stay right under sudden weather shifts and tight time limits. Cloud-only large models add harmful communication delays. Their framework, CAPE, splits the work three ways. A site expert handles routine calls, and a light edge model sharpens local inference. A cloud retrieval model supplies past cases when the call is hard. A screening module weighs uncertainty and model disagreement to route each case. Final forecasts fuse the chosen outputs.
arxiv-2603-22643: Sirker revisits the origin of the non-Hermitian skin effect. In this effect, many eigenstates pile up at the edge of an open system. It is often blamed on point-gap topology of the Bloch Hamiltonian. Using a Hatano-Nelson ladder, Sirker varies winding and non-normality apart. The skin effect can appear with no winding, and winding can persist with no skin effect. He argues the link holds only for one-band systems. Stable topology instead shows in the singular-value spectrum and in boundary kernel modes.
arxiv-2603-22843: Jimbo and Matsui study how to approximate the Shapley value in minimum cost spanning tree games. Exact computation is hard, so they turn to a related saving game. Recasting the game this way reveals structure that supports relative-error estimates. On that base, they build a Monte Carlo approximation scheme. The scheme is fully polynomial-time and randomized. It gives a principled route to fair cost sharing in network building games.
arxiv-2603-23043: Navarro and co-authors test climate foundation models under no-analog shifts. Future climate states may fall outside all training data. Many models train on data that already include future scenes, hiding true weakness. The team trains three models on historical data only, from 1850 to 2014. Tests cover recent years and cross-scenario forcing shifts. The ClimaX foundation model has the lowest raw error. Yet its error shifts most under strong forcing, with rain errors rising notably. Scenario-aware training is needed, they conclude.
arxiv-2603-23343: Taylor and four co-authors test whether an AI chip can run classic science computing kernels. Tenstorrent's Wormhole is a spatial platform built to speed neural networks. The team ports three numerical kernels to it and composes them into a conjugate gradient solver. They tune the code for the chip's layout and compare it with Nvidia GPUs. The work exposes both porting pains and real openings. They conclude that AI accelerators deserve a serious look for CPU and GPU workloads. More effort should go into making them usable for scientists.
arxiv-2603-23443: Haroon, Khan, and Gulzar test whether language models truly reason when they write unit tests. The team tracks generated tests across 22,374 changed program versions and eight models. On clean code, models hit 79% line coverage with fully passing suites. After meaning-changing edits, new tests pass only 66% of the time. Over 99% of those failures pass on the old code while running the changed region. Meaning-preserving edits also hurt, which hints at surface cue reliance. The authors say today's test generators lack regression awareness.
arxiv-2603-23643: Cahill and three co-authors pin down near-best embeddings for three classic orbit spaces. Bilipschitz theory seeks maps of orbit spaces into flat space with low distortion. Exact best maps were known only for planar rotations, phase retrieval, and reflection groups. The team show a max filter bank plus a linear map nearly hits that best in all three. Their proof first reduces the claim to an inclusion of Lipschitz spaces. Each case then needs its own route, which hints no unified proof comes cheap.
arxiv-2603-23743: Pal asks why sub-sevenfold symmetries seem absent from stacked-ring scaffolds in light-harvesting complexes. These LH2 complexes sit in purple photosynthetic bacteria and help capture light. Pal studies the question with a closed quantum optical coupled-dipole model. The model gives a physics-based view of how the ring parts interact. Her work seeks a reason for the missing symmetry patterns in these natural light-harvesting structures.
arxiv-2603-23943: Nguyen and co-authors present ChargeFlow, a model that refines electron density estimates for charged materials. Density functional theory gives accurate densities, but it costs too much for large screening jobs. ChargeFlow starts from a simple sum of atomic densities and reshapes it with flow matching. A 3D U-Net drives the change on the real-space grid. Trained on 9,502 calculations, it does best where charge shifts are nonlocal. Its densities still support Bader analysis and clean electrostatic potentials on 1,671 test structures.
arxiv-2603-24043: He and co-authors present HAM, a training-free style transfer method for diffusion models. Many methods add control paths that impose style, but they can blur the identity of the content image. HAM starts from style noise and modulates attention during diffusion. Global attention regulation captures broad style. Local attention transplantation keeps fine content details. In qualitative and quantitative tests, the method reaches state-of-the-art scores on multiple metrics, they report. It aims to hold both complex style references and content identity at once.
arxiv-2603-24343: Li and co-authors grow the size of audio deepfake detectors without full retraining. Big models detect fakes better, but stacking layers is costly and needs retraining from scratch. Inspired by brain plasticity, their dropin method adjusts neuron counts in some layers on the fly. A further plasticity step extends the idea. They test on ResNet, gated recurrent networks, and Wav2Vec models. On ASVSpoof2019 and FakeorReal data, dropin improves efficiency, while error rates fall by up to 39 and 66 percent in relative terms.
arxiv-2603-24543: Li and co-authors audit the safety risks of activation steering in large language models. Steering vectors, often built by contrastive activation addition, shape model behaviour without changing weights, but their safety effects are little studied. Using JailbreakBench under one protocol, they find steering reliably shifts jailbreak success rates. Depending on direction, attack success can rise by up to 57 percent or fall by up to 50 percent. They trace this to overlap between steering vectors and the latent directions of refusal behaviour, exposing a control-versus-safety trade-off.
arxiv-2603-25143: Raman and co-authors study swirls in exciton-polariton condensates, fluids of light and matter in a leaky cavity. The system follows an open Gross-Pitaevskii equation with two-body and three-body forces. Dark solitons can snake and break into vortex pairs, and the team derives where that instability starts. A repulsive three-body force, joined with the pair force, holds vortex pairs stable. An attractive three-body force does the reverse and tears vortices apart at the edges. Edge effects from the reservoir hit the attractive case hardest.
arxiv-2603-25343: Shi and co-authors link rare Fibonacci-type primes to the weights of cyclic codes. Their primes generalize Wall-Sun-Sun primes to second-order recurrences tied to quadratic fields. For such a prime, they study codes over two rings whose check polynomial mirrors the recurrence. The weight lists of those codes are the prize. Some codes come out MDS, the best possible spread, when the polynomial splits. Others land near that bar. The work ties a number theory curiosity to code design.
arxiv-2603-25743: Wang and co-authors present RefAlign, a training method for reference-to-video generation. Such systems build videos from text plus reference images. Added features can cause copy-paste artifacts and subject mix-ups. RefAlign adds a loss that aligns the generator's reference features with a visual foundation model. Features of the same subject are pulled together. Features of different subjects are pushed apart. The loss applies only in training, so inference costs nothing extra. On the OpenS2V-Eval benchmark, the authors report the best total score so far.
arxiv-2603-26143: Bouziane and Arslan design pilot patterns that let OFDM systems sense radar targets without grating lobes. Regular pilot spacing creates false echoes in the delay domain. Their two-stage method picks a non-periodic pattern that lowers the peak sidelobe level. Communication anchor rules are enforced throughout. A hybrid greedy and stochastic search solves the hard combinatorial problem cheaply. The design breaks the cycles that cause the lobes. System tests show better range accuracy with no loss in communication error rate, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-26243: Svanberg, Voigt, and Adya model the noise that limits waveguide-based squeezed light sources. Such sources promise strong squeezing without the optical cavities used in older designs. The team studies phase noise, several loss paths, and light that leaks in and seeds the device. They also test a cascaded design where a second waveguide acts as an amplifier to offset losses. They propose these sources for cutting quantum noise in future gravitational wave detectors.
arxiv-2603-26343: Hasan and co-authors propose Hermes Seal, a zero-knowledge framework for messages between self-driving vehicles. Vehicles must prove claims about their sensing and choices without leaking private models or sensor data. The framework uses zk-SNARK proofs for car-to-car and car-to-infrastructure links. In one case study, proofs take 8 milliseconds to make and 1 millisecond to check on a GPU. A second study covers a full perception stack, proving its work while keeping its details hidden.
arxiv-2603-26443: Arends, Peterson, and Weich start a study of resonances on finite-type graphs of groups. The work mirrors spectral theory for finite-type hyperbolic surfaces and manifolds. They look at regular graphs built from groups and study the resolvent of the adjacency operator. They prove the resolvent extends in a meromorphic way and describe the resonant states in geometric terms. Unlike the surface case, these graphs hold only finitely many resonances, and they can be computed in closed form. Examples from curves over finite fields show the same traits.
arxiv-2603-26643: Lin, Liu, Lee, and Jia propose a boundary neuron method for solving partial differential equations. The unknown boundary function is fitted by a shallow network inside a boundary integral form. Hidden parameters are drawn at random and frozen, so the task shrinks to a linear least squares solve. That design keeps the dimension cut of boundary methods and skips nonconvex gradient training. For elliptic problems they prove convergence and error bounds for both boundary and interior values. Tests on Laplace and Helmholtz cases rival the boundary element method.
