Personalisation should adapt to each client, but local gradients are noisy from small, varied data sets, and averaging across clients can distort a client's own direction.

pFLAlign acts at both stages. Locally, it adjusts gradient directions to cut variance during client training. At aggregation, it realigns the global model with each client's personal direction. The design is derived from a PAC Bayesian analysis that shows how alignment preserves client-specific information. Experiments and ablations report steady gains.
arxiv-2605-02543:
Achintya Raya Polavarapu presents a claimed proof of a 1983 conjecture by Thomassen in graph theory. The question concerns graphs with very high chromatic number, meaning many colors are needed to color them so linked nodes differ. Thomassen asked whether such graphs must contain a highly connected subgraph that still needs many colors, within a stated bound.

Polavarapu defines a threshold function for the smallest color level that forces such a subgraph. The paper argues for an upper bound on that threshold for all settings, which would settle the special case Thomassen posed in 1983. The key new step, in the author's account, is a Hall-type feasibility argument that replaces the final counting step in Nguyen's earlier proof. Readers should treat the result as the author's presented proof.
arxiv-2605-02843:
Atal Agrawal presents a fast algorithm for finding bursts of high activity in unevenly sampled time series, aimed at astronomy. Wide-field surveys produce light curves with thousands of irregular points, and upcoming surveys will produce far more. A standard segmentation method paired with hill climbing finds such bursts well, but its quadratic cost does not scale to that volume.

The new method runs in linear time. It seeds candidate regions at strong local peaks, grows them with a gradient-aware search from several sources at once, merges regions at saddle points, and filters spurious finds with a median rule. As a preprocessing stage it hands candidate events to deeper analysis. On quasar and active galaxy light curves from two survey archives, its regions matched the standard method's at far lower cost.
arxiv-2605-03043:
Maksymilian Kliczkowski, Jarosław Pawłowski, and Masudul Haque ask how much a single eigenstate reveals about the Hamiltonian that produced it. They call this learnability and measure it by how well a learning model can rebuild the Hamiltonian from a few eigenstates.

Training an encoder-decoder network on a non-integrable spin chain, they find a sharp split across the spectrum. States near the edges are structured and low in entanglement, so they allow accurate rebuilds from few examples. Mid-spectrum states are near-random and far less informative. The result offers a fresh view of spectral structure.
arxiv-2605-03243:
Sheikh Md. Mushfiqur Rahman, Gregory R. Watson, and Nasir U. Eisty ask what code and test metrics reveal about the long-term health of scientific open-source software. Such software underpins much research, yet whether projects stay maintainable over time is rarely studied directly.

Studying projects in the CASS portfolio, they classed each project by sustainability and compared code structure, test coverage, and code-test links. Sustainable projects showed higher, steadier coverage and clearer code-test ties, while coverage overall stayed low and tangled, highly coupled code proved harder to test. The result is a practical, data-led health check for scientific software.
arxiv-2605-03443:
Uliano Wilyam Purba, Andre Hadiman Rotua Parhusip, Sahid Maulana, Luluk Muthoharoh, Ardika Satria, and Martin C. T. Manullang benchmark sentiment methods on Indonesian Spotify reviews, a three-class task over one hundred thousand scraped comments. After cleaning, about seventy thousand samples remained for comparing classic models with a two-layer bidirectional LSTM under one shared preprocessing pipeline.

The decision tree led the classic models, while the BiLSTM earned the best weighted F1 overall yet failed on the small neutral class. Oversampling with SMOTE gave the classic route more balanced three-class behavior. The authors conclude each approach wins on a different criterion.
arxiv-2605-03543:
Ludovica Falsi, Giuseppe Agostino, Alberto Villois, Francesco Coppini, Paolo M. Santini, Miguel Onorato, Aharon J. Agranat, Stefano Trillo, and Eugenio DelRe study pseudovorticity in 2D optical solitons. True vorticity in a light field lives only at phase singularities. Yet local rotational flow can exist in smooth regions too. That subtler structure had not been mapped in solitons.

Experiments and simulations on photorefractive solitons reveal a dipole inside bright solitons. Quadrupoles appear when solitons fuse. Geometry explains the pattern. Stable high-dimensional solitons, the authors suggest, naturally carry a hierarchy of such multipoles in their phase and amplitude. The work adds a new lens for how light can swirl as it moves.
arxiv-2605-03643:
E. H. Saidi and R. Sammani give new algebraic constructions for the lattices behind code conformal field theories that realize Narain theories. Three lattices matter here: an even lattice, its dual, and an even self-dual lattice sitting between them. Their inclusion chain is governed by a cyclic discriminant group.

The authors describe the structure and representations of all three lattices and build them explicitly, first for the smallest rank case and then for higher-dimensional Lie algebras. More structural features are discussed as well. The work tightens the algebraic foundation for a construction that links error-correcting codes to conformal field theory in two dimensions.
arxiv-2605-03843:
Stephen M. de Bruyn Kops, Peter N. Blossey, and James J. Riley simulate how passive scalars mix in stratified and unstratified turbulence. They use high-resolution large-eddy simulations of decaying flows. Two passive scalar mixing layers, one vertical and one transverse, model a plume much larger than the flow's length scale. Stable layering should suppress vertical mixing, and the simulations quantify that effect.

In the transverse direction, stratified and unstratified evolution are broadly similar, though the scalar spreads slightly faster and fluctuates more strongly when stratified, with a more broken-up interface. In the vertical direction, the stratified layer barely mixes: it grows early until its width tracks the horizontal velocity's vertical integral length, then nearly stops spreading.
arxiv-2605-04143:
Giacomo Cacciapaglia and seven co-authors study heavy partner particles of the top quark. These partners are predicted by theories in which the Higgs particle is made of smaller parts. Most past work looked at partners in smaller colour groups, so the team focuses on a larger six-part colour form.

They build the low-energy rules for these states and map how they decay, mostly into top-rich final states through coloured partner particles. By re-reading ATLAS and CMS searches, they find current collider data rule out many such states below about two to two and a half trillion electron volts.
arxiv-2605-04243:
Tran Quang Liem challenges a common view about why large language models fail hard questions about time. The usual claim is that the models reason badly about order and duration, but Liem argues the real failure comes earlier, when messy text is turned into events.

His framework lifts text into explicit event graphs with time limits, then hands those to a separate symbolic reasoner, keeping extraction apart from deduction. A signal that mixes symbolic ranges with neural uncertainty flags broken structures. With correct structures supplied, the system's checked proof traces answered all four thousand test cases correctly.
arxiv-2605-04643:
Yifei Yuan and three co-authors improve estimates of the political ideology of members of parliament by giving a language model access to a political knowledge graph. Ideology estimates help researchers explain voting behaviour and party alignment. Language models alone already do reasonably well. But they ignore the web of relations among politicians and bodies.

Their retrieval pipeline first queries the graph. It then feeds the structured results into the model's context, alongside text. That captures both what politicians say and how they connect to each other. The team tests the approach on a Swiss parliamentary data set. They compare it against text-only baselines. The question is whether link information sharpens ideology prediction.
arxiv-2605-04843:
Monika Eisenmann and Eskil Hansen prove that Schwarz-like methods converge for a hard class of diffusion equations. These equations can become degenerate, losing their usual smoothing behaviour in parts of the domain. Schwarz methods split the space-time domain into overlapping pieces, which allows the pieces to be solved in parallel.

Their approach adds a false time direction and steps splitting methods toward infinity, an idea related to waveform relaxation. Unlike many such schemes, theirs can be proved to work for nonlinear and even degenerate problems. The proof rests on monotone operator theory together with known results on when solutions to these equations exist.
arxiv-2605-04943:
Anju Rani, Daniel Ortiz-Arroyo, and Petar Durdevic introduce DART, a vision-language model for judging the condition of synthetic fibre ropes from a single inspection photo. Such ropes serve offshore, maritime, and industrial work, where inspectors need more than a label. They need severity scores, repair advice, anomaly flags, timelines, and reports.

DART joins a large vision transformer with a Llama language model through a severity-aware fusion module. Damage-focused masking, per-class severity gates, and a special training loss teach it both damage type and ordering. Trained once on thousands of images across fourteen damage classes, it then supports many inspection tasks without further fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-05043:
Yuji Nakatsukasa and Zheng Tang revisit extracting accurate eigenvalues from a subspace that nearly captures a matrix's leading directions, for positive semi-definite matrices. The Rayleigh-Ritz method is the standard tool and is optimal in several senses for general symmetric matrices. The authors show the positive case allows something better at the same main cost.

They advocate Nyström's method, proving its eigenvalue estimates are always more accurate than Rayleigh-Ritz here, sometimes by an arbitrarily large margin. The gain is biggest when the spectrum decays fast, and similar gains appear numerically for eigenvectors. For trailing eigenvalues the picture reverses, and the authors suggest a remedy for that case.
arxiv-2605-05443:
Watermarking language model text usually bends word choices, and readers pay for detection with worse text. Fabrice Harel-Canada and Amit Sahai present SLAM, a watermark that works differently. Instead of touching word frequencies, it writes the mark into the model's internal geometry at generation time.

Sparse autoencoders find internal directions tied to features like voice, tense, and clause order. Steering those directions leaves meaning and word sampling free. On two Gemma-2 models, detection was perfect, and the quality cost was far smaller than that of leading token-based watermarks, though paraphrasing that reshapes syntax can still erase the mark.
arxiv-2605-05643:
Retrieval systems that search plain text often fetch passages that look relevant but reason nowhere. Jiarui Zhong and Hong Cai Chen propose TGS-RAG, which makes text and knowledge graphs verify each other. Graph-based retrieval has the opposite flaw: pruning at search time can discard valid reasoning paths.

Their framework runs two channels in both directions. A graph-to-text channel uses global voting to check textual evidence against structured facts, while a text-to-graph channel completes the graph from passages. The aim is to close the information islands that form when the two evidence types reason separately.
arxiv-2605-05943:
Luis Solá Conde and Gianluca Occhetta propose a two step approach to Chow quotients in algebraic geometry. A Chow quotient records how a projective variety breaks up under the action of a complex torus. Even for simple varieties, such as rational homogeneous ones, its geometry can be very complicated.

The authors show the quotient's geometry can be encoded in a projective toric variety plus a finite group of its birational symmetries. That encoding turns a hard object into parts that are easier to handle. They then show how to apply the strategy to some particular rational homogeneous varieties. The paper gives geometers a new route into a class of spaces long known for resisting direct study.
arxiv-2605-06043:
Dat Nguyen and Duc-Duy Nguyen propose an image classification system built on compositional relations that stay stable across domains. Photos from new settings differ in color, texture, and style, yet the structural relations among parts of an object often persist. Most domain generalization methods adjust training or align features, leaving that shared structure implicit.

CRISP factors recognition into visual primitives and their relational composition. Soft predicates over primitive locations and appearance give differentiable measures of spatial and visual fit, learned end to end. A backbone, a concept bottleneck layer, and a structural scoring layer work together to reach each class decision. The authors test the system on five real world data sets from the DomainBed suite.
arxiv-2605-06543:
Aaron Beyen, Francesco Casini, and Christian Maes adapt Rayleigh's test for heat-driven sound instability to chemo-mechanical systems. Such surges can destroy control, yet they also create rich behavior and may drive living systems. The authors ask when chemical driving can set a slow mechanical probe into lasting rotation or active motion.

The probe follows Newton's laws while the chemical processes are modeled as Markov jumps. Their Rayleigh-like rules depend on the phase relation between entropic and frenetic, meaning activity-related, contributions. That gives a clear condition for when chemical energy converts into steady mechanical activity, offering a design rule for active matter and tiny machines.
arxiv-2605-06643:
Hao Dong and five co-authors benchmark multimodal domain generalization, where models must work in new domains using several input types at once. Reported gains in this growing field may reflect inconsistent evaluation rather than real progress, since studies vary in datasets, modality mixes, and settings, and mostly test action recognition alone.

Their MMDG-Bench standardizes six datasets across action recognition, fault diagnosis, and sentiment analysis, training over seven thousand networks. Findings are sobering: recent specialized methods barely beat a plain baseline, no method wins consistently, three modalities do not reliably beat two, and corruption or missing modalities degrade every method. A large gap to the upper bound remains.
arxiv-2605-06943:
Steven Song and three co-authors introduce ProtoSSL, a way to pretrain interpretable prototype models without labels. Prototype networks explain predictions by comparing new cases with representative examples, which suits fields like medicine. Earlier versions needed labeled data, tying the learned examples to one task.

ProtoSSL first learns a bank of prototypes from unlabeled data, then assigns them to a downstream task with an efficient procedure. Across six heart-signal datasets, it beats supervised prototype methods when labels are scarce, and also after fine-tuning at full scale. Human judges preferred its explanations, and the framework also extends to audio classification.
arxiv-2605-07043:
Howen Chuah and Monica Torres study the boundary between separated populations in a mathematical model with long-range effects. A system of elliptic equations, tied to a small parameter, models populations that spread and segregate. Earlier work by other researchers settled the boundary's regularity in two dimensions; this paper takes up higher dimensions.

Chuah and Torres extend ideas of angles and cones to higher dimensions, then describe regular and singular boundary points through density and angles. Under stated conditions, the regular part is locally a smooth surface of one lower dimension. When population regions are convex, they prove those regions must be convex polytopes.
arxiv-2605-07243:
Weijie Shi and eleven co-authors speed up language model replies with a block-wise speculative drafter. Speculative decoding drafts many candidate continuations and verifies them in one pass, but existing drafters either call the drafter too often or predict positions blindly. SpecBlock predicts several dependent positions in each forward pass, growing the draft tree block by block.

Hidden states carry path information within and across blocks, and a trained ranking head spends verification effort where acceptance is likely. A cost-aware bandit at deployment updates the drafter only when the expected gain justifies it. Experiments show better speedups than a leading drafter at roughly half its drafting cost.
arxiv-2605-07643:
Emily Darwin and five co-authors report a materials advance for spintronics: tiny magnetic whirlpools called skyrmions, held stable in synthetic antiferromagnets at room temperature with no magnetic field applied. Such textures are protected by topology and avoid the sideways drift that plagues ordinary skyrmions, but keeping them stable at zero field has been hard.

The team built an SAF bias system that sets skyrmion polarity through layer design and a setup field cycle. Using sensitive magnetic force microscopy and computer modeling, they showed reliable zero-field formation. They saw SAF skyrmions under twenty nanometers across, the smallest reported so far. The balanced bias design also holds back stray domains. It offers a scalable route for future skyrmion devices.
arxiv-2605-07843:
Catrin Mair builds the notion of shape for condensed anima, objects in the condensed setting that generalize ordinary spaces. Shape is meant to capture a space's homotopy-theoretic outline, and the question is whether this definition agrees with the standard one where both apply.

Mair proves it does: for all paracompact compactly generated spaces and all locally contractible spaces, this notion recovers the classical shape. Those recovery results imply and extend earlier results on sheaf and condensed cohomology by Clausen, Scholze, and Haine. A second thread describes the basic topological group functor on condensed groups through quasi-topological groups, connecting to the homotopy groups of these anima.
arxiv-2605-07943:
Giacomo Spigler supplies the missing scoreboard for active vision in robot imitation learning. Several systems now let a policy steer its own gaze during manipulation, by moving a neck camera or wrist cameras, and report benefits. But with no shared benchmark nobody could say what active vision contributes, on which tasks, or under what conditions.

TAVIS offers two task suites on two humanoid torsos, one for global search through pan-tilt necks and one for local occlusion through wrist cameras. Its tools include a paired protocol comparing gaze control against fixed cameras on identical demonstrations. They also include a metric for anticipatory gaze: whether the learned policy looks at the right object before acting, as humans do. Baselines show active vision helps, but conditionally, and imitation alone produced human-like anticipatory gaze.
arxiv-2605-08143:
Yuan Fang, Yi Xie, and Xuming Ran improve lifelong editing of large language models, where single facts are patched after deployment without retraining. Existing editors fade as edits pile up and often fail when a question is reworded, so a fix that works once may not stick.

HoReN wraps one MLP layer with a discrete codebook memory that leaves the model's weights untouched. Each entry acts as both a knowledge key and a Hopfield pattern, and edits are retrieved by angle on a sphere, then refined by damped Hopfield dynamics. Paraphrases settle into the right memory basin while unrelated inputs stay stable, and results hold across editing benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-08243:
Gabriel Bathie, Baptiste Mouillon, and Nathanaël Fijalkow speed up the synthesis of mixed-boolean-arithmetic expressions. Those tangled formulas hide program logic. Recovering a clean form from input-output examples serves deobfuscation and compiler work. It also serves reverse engineering and cryptanalysis. CPU tools scale poorly, though. Recent GPU methods lean on caches that break down for bitvector outputs.

Their SIMBA synthesizer enumerates expressions bottom-up on the GPU. It uses no language cache at all. Work stays local and highly parallel. In experiments, SIMBA ran much faster than earlier MBA tools. It also handled larger specifications. Cache-free enumeration fits graphics hardware better than expected.
arxiv-2605-08443:
Linh Tran, Ana Milanova, and Stacy Patterson repair a clash between privacy noise and low-rank fine-tuning in federated learning. LoRA adapters make cross-silo training cheap, but averaging mismatched low-rank factors adds error, and differential privacy noise injected into a narrow subspace can swamp the true update.

Their FedPower framework moves the delicate step to the server. Client updates are reconstructed in full rank and clipped to bound sensitivity, privacy noise is applied there, and the exact aggregated update is then projected back into a low-rank form for distribution. The refactorization keeps the privacy guarantee while sparing accuracy that the usual perturb-then-average pipeline throws away.
arxiv-2605-08643:
Mohammad Yahyavi and five coauthors uncover a hidden link between two light driven electric currents in solids. Injection and shift currents were long treated as separate effects with separate origins. The team shows both trace back to dipoles built from Berry curvature and quantum metric, the geometric traits of electron wave states.

Where electron energy grows nearly in a straight line near the Fermi level and light energy stays low, the two currents become governed by one shared geometric dipole. Dirac and Weyl semimetals plus strained graphene sit naturally in this regime. Nonlinear optics gains a unifying frame where paired measurements probe one geometric property instead of two unrelated processes.
arxiv-2605-08843:
Yuan Mei, Xingyu Song, Xiaowen Song, and Naoya Takeishi fix a hidden bias in training neural surrogates for physical simulations: the training points themselves are unevenly spread. Simulations are sampled on grids that cluster points in some regions, so the model over learns crowded areas and under learns sparse ones, warping physical fidelity. Their M-cubed framework rebalances supervision by partitioning space according to physical variation and spreading training weight across scales.

On three industrial scale datasets, predictions in the continuous domain improve markedly, with errors several times lower in large volumetric cases. Gains survive aggressive subsampling, with models trained on far fewer points beating rivals trained on denser data. Operator learning learns that where points sit matters as much as how many there are.
arxiv-2605-09043:
Napassorn Litchiowong, writing alone, studies how conversations between partners can break down even when both use the same words. One person says a word meaning closure; the other hears surrender. The paper gives this gap a formal measure based on how far apart the two sides' emotional readings of shared anchor words sit.

From speech-act theory and game theory, the author derives a model in which repair efforts can collapse suddenly once the gap passes a threshold, and the collapse is hard to reverse. In a dataset of online talks that went off the rails, warning signs of slowing recovery appeared before the break. A second dataset gave mixed but broadly matching support for the pattern.
arxiv-2605-09243:
Lewis and three colleagues ask how much brain data is worth for machine learning. If a person can solve a task, do brain measurements ease training a model for that task? Recent NeuroAI work suggests adding neural recordings to task training can improve performance and robustness, but when to expect a benefit, or how large, is unclear.

They formulate the question mathematically with a simple linear Gaussian model of task goals and recordings. For an estimator trained on brain data and task labels, they derive scaling laws linking performance to counts. From these laws come value and exchange rates between brain and task samples. Those rates quantify what extra task samples neural data is worth, given alignment, noise, dimension, and sample size. They also analyse test distribution shift, where brain-regularised learning gains robustness through invariances. Under a fixed budget, they characterise when brain data is worth collecting.
arxiv-2605-09343:
Li and a colleague build SKG-VLA for multimodal complaint decision making, treating each case as a structured complaint scene, not a shallow classification task. A Scene Knowledge Graph puts complaint entities, evidence items, policy clauses, time-ordered events, transactional states, and relations tied to actions, into one unified graph.

From that graph, the team builds a data pipeline that makes complaint scene descriptions, rule-consistent graph generalisations, question-answer supervision, and decision recommendations. They also build a large-scale complaint scene dataset with text-only and multimodal in-domain benchmarks. Training runs in three stages — pre-training tuned to the domain, instruction fine-tuning aimed at tasks, and end-to-end multimodal alignment — to give a multimodal decision model structured scene priors. In tests, SKG-VLA lifts policy-grounded reasoning, decision accuracy on complaints, long-tail generalisation, and robustness under incomplete evidence.
arxiv-2605-09543:
Vicente Arévalo and two colleagues speed up three dimensional synthesis for solar spectra where heat balance fails. Reading chromospheric lines needs atomic level counts worked out with the light field. Old codes use one and a half dimensional short cuts that drop sideways light travel. That travel matters near magnetic knots. Their graph neural net treats the solar air as a graph. Nodes hold local physics, and edges hold gaps between points.

Trained on a Bifrost sun simulation with calcium ion counts as truth, the net predicts five level counts plus continuum. Match is near perfect low down and in the mid chromosphere. Errors grow higher up, where far off effects rule, but stay fair on average. Inference runs about a million times faster than step by step solvers. Made line shapes match the full solution within about 2 percent, clearing the way for routine three dimensional fits.
arxiv-2605-09743: Mintu Karmakar surveys systems of self-driving particles, natural and artificial, that spend energy to move or push. He explains flocking, where groups align like birds or fish, and motility-induced phase separation, where particles sort by how fast they move. He also covers crowding, disorder, jamming, kinetic arrest and phase change, asking how noise, speed and outside fields shape group behaviour.
arxiv-2605-10043:
Ma and five colleagues personalise language models from simple yes-or-no feedback, aiming at each user's own tastes rather than one average taste. Most methods study one user's history alone and ignore how users differ from each other. Their framework, C-BPO, treats the target user's data as positive signals and other users' data as implicit negative signals, so differences between users come into focus.

A snag follows: shared task knowledge can look like a personal quirk and get wrongly punished. The authors handle it with an objective drawn from positive-unlabelled learning theory, which strips a positive bias from the negative signals. That keeps alignment to true quirks without harming general helpfulness. Tests across personalization tasks and several base models show C-BPO beating baselines time and again.
arxiv-2605-10143:
Shiga, writing alone, places Thompson's groups inside Teichmüller theory. Thompson's groups F, T and V, introduced by Richard Thompson, touch many areas of mathematics. The paper places them as subgroups of Teichmüller modular groups acting on Teichmüller spaces of generalised Cantor sets. This extends earlier work by de Faria, Gardiner and Harvey on group F and asymptotic Teichmüller spaces.

A sharper distinction follows: groups F and T act with proper discontinuity on such Teichmüller spaces, while group V does not. The paper also shows Thompson's groups act on infinitely many Teichmüller spaces of generalised Cantor sets. Proper discontinuity means the action is discrete and well-separated, a strong geometric property. The F and T results give these groups a cleaner geometric home than V enjoys.
arxiv-2605-10243:
Felicia Volle, writing for the LHCb Collaboration, surveys recent particle-physics results from the LHCb experiment at CERN. This 2026 proceeding covers two fronts: precise measurements in the electroweak sector, which governs the weak force and electromagnetism, and direct hunts for particles beyond the Standard Model.

New first measurements include W-boson and top-quark production rates and charge asymmetries from proton-proton collisions. Because LHCb looks forward rather than centrally, its results probe parton distribution functions, the momentum maps inside protons, in ranges other detectors miss. The proceeding also reports searches for axion-like particles and heavy neutral leptons, candidate messengers between visible matter and a dark sector.
arxiv-2605-10643:
Zanmin Wang asks how far a shallow recurrent layer can go on language modeling. Language models scale depth by stacking layers. His 2026 paper proposes Grounded Prediction Networks, or GPN. A GPN reuses a single state vector at each step through a recurrent block. The block holds one feedforward network and shared matrix memory.

At 130M, a 1-layer GPN with memory reaches perplexity 18.06 on FineWeb-Edu. Within 13 percent of a 12-layer Transformer++ and 18 percent of a 10-layer Gated DeltaNet. A 2-layer variant closes the gap to 6 percent and 11 percent. The shallow model does not match deep baselines. Because the context is a single vector, its geometry can be inspected. Inspection reveals a default-token direction, a horizon of tens of tokens, and memory heads splitting into fast and slow pools.
arxiv-2605-10843:
Dao Sy Duy Minh and seven colleagues align language models to diverse cultures without any training, weight access, or per-country data. Models tend to answer moral questions with a Western outlook, yet a 40-million-judgment study across 233 countries shows moral preferences vary systematically by culture.

Their training-free method steers with disagreement, not consensus: when culturally grounded personas within a country disagree, that spread becomes the signal that moves the model. The approach needs only inference-time prompting, so it works through black-box APIs that hide internals. Deployers get a scalable route to cultural alignment that neither imposes one society's intuitions nor demands a reward model per country.
arxiv-2605-11043:
Dario Izzo and four colleagues give a practical guide to zero-order-hold transcriptions for spacecraft route planning. Their design principles hold across dynamical settings without per-problem tuning. Zero-order-hold methods hold control constant in steps and resolve states by shooting, integrating the equations of motion.

The guide offers a forward-backward shooting construction and a redundant four-dimensional throttle setup that removes a singularity along ballistic arcs. It also offers a softmax time-grid encoding that avoids ordering constraints while keeping the problem smooth, plus the TOPS benchmark of 28 problems across four dynamical models. Mission designers get robust, reusable transcription practice plus a benchmark built to grow.
arxiv-2605-11143:
Alex Stinard presents ClinicalBench, a stress test for assertion-aware retrieval in clinical question answering across admissions, built on MIMIC-IV. Reasoning benchmarks use clean inputs, but the step before reasoning, retrieval over real notes, can flip answers through negation, time tags, and family-versus-patient attribution.

EpiKG tags each fact in a patient knowledge graph with an assertion label and a time tag, and routes retrieval by question intent. ClinicalBench runs 400 questions over 43 patients across nine assertion-sensitive categories, with a seven-condition ablation across six language models and blind physician review. Author-blind paired testing shows a 22-percentage-point gain for intent-aware knowledge-graph retrieval over dense retrieval. Clinical AI teams get a retrieval benchmark that measures the errors reasoning benchmarks miss.
arxiv-2605-11543: Gupta, Sahayanathan, Shanu and Nath test whether single-zone emission models can explain two gamma-ray bursts, GRB 220426A and GRB 230812B. Gamma-ray bursts are the most energetic events known, lasting milliseconds to seconds, yet their emission mechanism stays contested. Some models invoke a thermal blast of hot plasma, others synchrotron emission from rapidly accelerated particles. Both predict the spectral width shrinking over time, but for these two bursts it grows. That growth points instead to several emission zones whose relative shares change over time.
arxiv-2605-11743: Jin and Jeong propose WorldComp2D, space-meaning codes from local views. Latent codes holding meaning and spatial detail drive space-meaning thinking. Yet many methods rely on hidden shapes with dense feature maps or task heads. WorldComp2D forms latent shape by ID and nearness using local fields. It mixes a nearness encoder mapping views into latent space with a finder guessing spots. On facial landmarks it cuts knobs up to 4 point 0 times and FLOPs up to 2 point 2 times versus lightweight rivals, keeping CPU speed.
arxiv-2605-11943: Maryam Jahangiri studies the asymptotic behavior of Bass numbers for graded components of local cohomology modules. For a standard graded ring and a finitely generated graded module, she tracks Bass numbers at a prime of the degree-zero part across three cases. The cases are low cohomological index, regular base with top cohomological dimension, and relative Cohen-Macaulay modules. The work pins down how these invariants evolve as the graded degree grows.
arxiv-2605-12443: Gupta presents a Docker workflow that makes one space simulation framework easy to rerun anywhere. Basilisk is open source software for spacecraft guidance, navigation and control work. Yet setting it up varies with machine, system and settings, since parts and options differ. The workflow packs the whole build setup, parts and simulation tools into one portable container image. It is shown through tasks of rising difficulty, from simple orbit scripts to attitude control with Monte Carlo checks. The paper also covers BSKSim classes, dynamics models and flight software.
arxiv-2605-12643: Yamamoto and four colleagues co-design justice measures for machine systems with the people hit by them. Fairness in machine learning is often framed tightly around shares, yet parties raise a wider range of value concerns. Using workplace justice as a broader frame, the team studies tailored picks at Kiva Microfunds, a charity micro-lender growing money access for poorly served groups. Workshops with Kiva staff from varied teams reveal how roles shape which value concerns staff put first, and how design trade-offs play out among rival goals.
arxiv-2605-12743: Ju and eight colleagues turn view changes into an attack tool against vision-based self-driving. Old real attacks induce shifting seeing errors through patches that drift spotting boxes or change errors over time, treating varying views as a challenge. In contrast, the team shows view change itself can drive the attack. A static, passive hostile camo mounted on a vehicle changes look as it moves, inducing steady path steering in victim seeing without active or changing patches.
arxiv-2605-12843: Li and three colleagues propose ReForge, a method for merging several task-specific expert models into one without retraining them together. It refines the merged model module by module, using Bayesian regression anchored on the strong merged model, and tunes its settings by Bayesian optimisation. A data-free variant swaps in task-vector statistics instead of calibration examples. Across benchmarks, ReForge beats prior plug-and-play merging baselines.
arxiv-2605-12943: Wang, Liu and Ding present MANGO, a framework that organises multi-agent collaboration as a flow network built from past successful workflows. It combines reinforcement learning with textual gradients to jointly tune workflow paths and agent behaviour, while a skipping mechanism spares well-tuned agents from redundant updates. On seven benchmarks it improves over state-of-the-art baselines by up to 12.8% and boosts efficiency by 47.4%, generalising to unseen domains.
arxiv-2605-13043: Lee, Kim and Han defend diffusion language models, whose iterative denoising lets harmful content appear at any spot and persist. Their run-time defence pairs adaptive safety steering, which tunes steering strength from the current denoising state, with safety-aware remasking of unsafe content. A light detector after the first generation block spots unsafe trajectories early and triggers targeted remasking plus regeneration under steering. On LLaDA and Dream it lifts jailbreak defence while keeping benign quality and general capability.
arxiv-2605-13443: Xibo Wang and eight colleagues propose a numerical method for reducing speckle in optical coherence tomography. That technique images tissue with light, and speckle is the grainy pattern that limits its resolution. Their method uses a new image form called real-SCCP, built from a shifted complex conjugate product. In this form, speckle can be modulated after acquisition. Averaging several SCCP images with different speckle patterns therefore suppresses the grain. It reveals structures clearly in tumour spheroids and zebrafish eyes, beating conventional frame averaging.
arxiv-2605-13643: Kaiyuan Liu and five colleagues study local teachability collapse in strong-to-weak on-policy distillation. Supervision should focus where teacher feedback stays discriminative, not uniformly across the whole response. Their trajectory-specific release rule tracks teacher margin over the student's top-K candidates. It aggregates that margin across sentence segments and truncates dense supervision at a BIC-style downward change point. Across five in-domain benchmarks with Qwen3 students, the rule beats standard full-trajectory distillation and better preserves out-of-domain capabilities.
arxiv-2605-13743: Yifan Duan and four colleagues offer GHGbench, an open data set and benchmark covering company- and building-level carbon guesses. The building track merges 491,591 building-year records from 13 sources into one schema across 26 city areas, with climate factors and multi-sense remote-sensing codes. Three findings emerge: building outputs are by design harder than company outputs. The in-to-out gap dwarfs within-model gaps, and multi-sense codes help exactly where tabular carry-over breaks.
arxiv-2605-13943: Vock, Duchesnay and Dufumier read weighted contrastive learning goals as distance geometry puzzles, where the weight plan fixes the goal shape of the learned codes. That view pins down exact best codes for sundry supervised and weakly supervised goals. In sorting tasks, SupCon and Soft SupCon both crush each class to one model code. Yet while fair SupCon regains the classic regular simplex shape, lopsided classes break that shape.
arxiv-2605-14043: Hoshino, Mantani and Furutani tackle the best size for solar-battery hybrid resources that sell into several markets at once. Such hybrids join solar generation with battery storage in one market player, earning from several streams at once. Yet limited power and energy must be split across energy and ancillary-service markets, which muddies profit estimates. Weather and price swings add more doubt, so the paper seeks designs that stay sound under uncertain operating conditions.
arxiv-2605-14143: Nandi and eight co-authors trace a rash of glitches at LIGO Livingston during its fourth observing run to scattered light. Scattered light ranks among the most common noise sources in gravitational-wave detectors, and its non-linear action lifts low-frequency motion into a higher-frequency noise band. From the run's start, many glitches crowded the 10 to 40 hertz band, with shapes pointing to scattered light. Analysis splits them into two populations, and the higher-signal group tracks microseismic ground motion alone.
arxiv-2605-14243: Hyodo and Torii re-examine the fate of V-shaped collision debris, with Saturn's rings as motive. Catastrophic collisions between proto-satellites are put forward as a possible ring origin, a case resting on the equivalent circular orbit. The paper tracks debris spread across a broad V-shaped region in the semi-major axis-eccentricity plane, where each arm holds particles sharing a collision radius. Particles on the two arms carry distinct angular momenta, so inter-arm collisions dominate evolution, breaking the simple circularization the equivalent circular orbit assumes.
arxiv-2605-14343: Gao, Hou and Lin ask whether dependence between samples changes the size of nearest-neighbour regions in machine learning. Working with strongly mixing observations, a form of dependence that fades over time, they prove distribution-free convergence under polynomial mixing. They also prove sharp moment bounds under geometric mixing. The bounds hinge on local intrinsic dimension, the effective dimension near the data, rather than the full ambient dimension. Synthetic tests and real time-series benchmarks support the theory, suggesting neighbour geometry stays informative under dependence.
arxiv-2605-14443: Sayana, Todi and Jash propose reinforcement learning for prompting policies for frozen, black-box language models by distillation of experience. A lightweight prompter maximises task rewards for a frozen worker model, using a buffer coupling scalar rewards with dense textual critiques. Iterative prompt refinement is amortised into single-shot policy weights. On Big Bench Extra Hard and Tau-bench, performance rises from 55 percent to 90 percent in logic reasoning and from 74 percent to 91 percent in tool use. The policy discovers algorithmic heuristics, and iterative distillation beats GEPA with higher sample efficiency.
arxiv-2605-14543: Chen, Jiang, Wang, Wu, Shi, Zhang and Kwok present RxEval, a benchmark testing whether language models can prescribe like clinicians at each time point, not just once per admission. Each of its 1,547 questions gives a patient profile and time-ordered trajectory and asks for a specific medication, dose and route among real prescriptions and perturbed distractors. Sixteen models scored modestly, with the best exact-match rate claimed at only about forty-six percent.
arxiv-2605-14843: Jain, Patel, Unmesh and Ramani introduce MechVerse, a benchmark for physical motion consistency in video generation models. Generated videos often look plausible while violating mechanism constraints, such as spinning a part that should translate or breaking coupling between parts. MechVerse holds over twenty-one thousand synthetic clips from more than one thousand three hundred mechanical assemblies across one hundred and forty-one categories. Three tiers of rising kinematic complexity cover independent articulation, pairwise coupling, plus densely coupled multi-part systems, each clip paired with a structured prompt.
arxiv-2605-14943: Timo Kuosmanen and three others smooth isotonic regression, a tuning-free way to fit rising curves that otherwise comes out as a step function. Steps give no useful marginal values, such as shadow prices or elasticities. Their bilevel optimization fits a continuous, monotonic, piecewise-linear curve to the step estimates, even where the shape is not convex. Simulations show better accuracy in convex and non-convex cases, and a Finnish municipal study shows the payoff.
arxiv-2605-15243: Ziyu Xu and six others frame transcriptome-based drug design as a generative inverse problem: design compounds that drive desired shifts between cellular states, read from gene-expression perturbations. The task is ill-posed, split by a biology-chem domain gap and sparse signals. Their cell response engine distills function-aimed nudge embeddings, aligns them to dual chemical views, and pools well across noisy data. Tests on standard and out-of-distribution rules show consistent gains over old methods.
arxiv-2605-15443: Pierluigi Morra, Brett Tillman, Stuart Laurence, and Tamer A. Zaki feed wall-pressure readings from a Mach 6 cone-flare experiment into direct simulations of the flow. Using only sensors ahead of the separation zone fails to predict what happens downstream, but assimilating all seven sensors captures the onset of separation and the downstream pressure pattern. The simulations also predict disturbance growth beneath the separation shock, where no measurements exist, and show why later predictions stay uncertain.
arxiv-2605-15543: Juho Kim and Tuomas Sandholm propose a domain-independent way to shrink huge games for analysis, borrowing word embeddings from language processing. Treating each game action as a word and gameplay records as text, they train vectors for actions and cluster them to form abstractions. Experiments show the approach works, though it does not beat specialized algorithms tuned to particular games like poker.
arxiv-2605-15943: Marchis and three colleagues study community recovery in stochastic block models under node differential privacy, where algorithms must stay stable when one node's links change. Naive private methods force the privacy parameter to grow fast for consistent estimation. Their new methods sample from an exponential mechanism with a Lipschitz extension and build smooth projections onto bounded-degree graphs. All run in polynomial time, and the authors also prove lower bounds on how fast the privacy parameter must grow.
arxiv-2605-16043: Wigginghaus and four colleagues tackle two-handed rope handling, where a robot must untangle knots despite ropes that bend freely and hide from cameras. They train two policies on the same teleoperation data: one sees wrist-camera video, the other uses the rope's 3D particle state. On an unseen rope setup, the state-based policy beat the visual one by about thirty-one percent on the first grasp-and-pull prediction.
arxiv-2605-16143: Ye and eight colleagues argue that language-model agents fail in new settings because they exploit prior knowledge before exploring enough. They formalize autonomous exploration with Exploration Checkpoint Coverage, a metric for how broadly an agent finds key states, objects, and affordances. Standard task-oriented reinforcement learning yields narrow, repetitive behaviour. Interleaving task and exploration rollouts, then letting agents explore before acting, builds more general and real-world-ready agents.
arxiv-2605-16343: Fang and three colleagues measure LoopQ against the strongest static post-training quantization baseline per comparison. Under W4A4 quantization it lifts five-task mean accuracy by 67.8 percent across four backbones. It cuts average relative perplexity by a conservative 75.2 percent across eight backbone-dataset pairs. They trace the damage to shifting distributions as blocks change roles, states across loop transitions, and errors piling up recursively. LoopQ answers with loop-aware activation scaling, cross-loop state alignment, and trajectory-aware calibration, keeping a shared quantized backbone with adaptations.
arxiv-2605-16643: Murray and colleagues detail the EDGES analysis pipeline for the sky-averaged 21-cm signal from Cosmic Dawn, the era of the first compact objects. They lay out the precise calibration and analysis methods behind earlier EDGES releases, within a new open-source end-to-end package for global-signal experiments. The package formalizes those methods and offers general tools for the wider community. Raw data from earlier EDGES papers are released publicly for extended scrutiny.
arxiv-2605-16743: Jang and colleagues propose LACE, a framework that bridges the visual gap between human and robot hands for learning from human demonstrations. Self-supervised backbones encode rich object semantics but fail to match human and robot hands. LACE aligns human and robot representations in latent space using shared body-part correspondences as sparse supervision, from forward kinematics. One robot demo suffices for training. In zero-shot transfer, LACE-DINO beats DINO by a large margin, about 65%, with gains when data is scarce and in new settings.
arxiv-2605-16943: Jiang, Du and Yu propose one-way impurity scattering as a probe of pairing symmetry in kagome superconductors. A single magnetic impurity gives nearly identical spectra for conventional s-wave and time-reversal-breaking d-wave pairing, so it cannot tell them apart. Two impurities behave differently: for s-wave, time-reversal symmetry forces forward and backward scattering to match, erasing a Yu-Shiba-Rusinov state pair between them, while for d-wave the erasure holds only for inversion-symmetric layouts. The contrast is resolvable in scanning tunnelling microscopy.
arxiv-2605-17043: Giacomelli tests the folklore that Briscola victory depends almost entirely on cards dealt. He pits two rule tweaks of the naive greedy policy, a hoarding policy and a counter policy, against the greedy baseline despite trump luck. A round-robin Monte Carlo contest of one million games across nine pairings keeps about 108 thousand tied-free games each. Wilson intervals, a Bonferroni-corrected binomial test, and a logistic regression on strategy pair and briscola imbalance quantify strategy and trump luck contributions. An appendix makes the simulation, seed, and script fully deterministic.
arxiv-2605-18143: Lihi Idan's 2026 study runs a controlled trial of generative AI help for early-career knowledge work, and finds the gains split very unevenly. Mean scores rise with AI access, yet neither grades nor prior knowledge predict who gains most. What predicts gains is AI interaction skill: the knack of drawing out, sifting, and checking model output. High-skill users gain a lot, low-skill users gain little or even lose ground, but simple concept maps cut the spread.
arxiv-2605-18343: In a 2026 paper, Fabien Le Floc'h gives two direct formulas for Bachelier, or normal, implied volatility in option pricing. Each formula takes price, forward, strike, and expiry as inputs and returns volatility without iteration. One version stresses accuracy in the far tail, while the other splits the near-the-money branch for speed. Tests in double precision keep both close to machine accuracy.
arxiv-2605-18443: Riccardo Ramaschi, Mario Paolone, and Sonia Leva propose a hybrid, lightweight method in a 2026 paper to predict EV charging profiles before and during charging, at both single-charger and fleet levels. Single-charger curves remain little studied, yet battery-aware planning could use them to refine fleet forecasts and departure-time guesses. Tested on multiple cars from a public dataset, the method also gauges how varying data access shifts the time-shifted charging curve.
arxiv-2605-18543: Ammar Waheed and two co-authors present, in a 2026 paper, a per-surface neural network surrogate for real-time hydrodynamics estimation of autonomous ground vehicles in water. Trained only on high-fidelity CFD data from two vehicles, it predicts geometry-resolved forces at under 0.9 milliseconds per sample. Held-out tests give longitudinal-force error of 13 percent and vertical-force error of 3 to 12 percent. Water wading trials confirm predicted drag follows quadratic speed scaling and buoyancy intercepts scale linearly with depth.
arxiv-2605-18643: Xingtai Lv and fourteen co-authors present ZEDA, a 2026 low-cost system turning post-trained static mixture-of-experts models dynamic. Parameter-free zero-output experts enter each MoE layer, and two-stage self-distillation adapts the augmented model against the frozen original as teacher with a group-level balancing loss. On Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM-4.7-Flash across eleven benchmarks, ZEDA eliminates over 50 percent of expert FLOPs at marginal accuracy loss. It beats the strongest dynamic baseline by 6.1 and 4.0 points and delivers about 1.20-fold end-to-end speedup.
arxiv-2605-19143: Serban Cicortas proves weak cosmic censorship for a circularly symmetric Einstein-scalar system in two space dimensions plus time. With a negative cosmological constant, he shows that generic smooth initial data never develop naked singularities in their full evolution. The key step establishes a mass gap, which forces any would-be naked singularity to carry infinite blueshift. That extreme blueshift supplies the instability that rules such singularities out, closing the case for this class of spacetimes.
arxiv-2605-19343: Jiang and colleagues tackle a blind spot in predicting how single cells react to genetic changes. Gene readings are swamped by stable background signals, while change-specific signals are thin, so models mix the two or drop the useful part. Their PerturbedVAE framework pulls the change-specific signal apart from the background and rebuilds causal patterns for prediction. Benchmark tests beat prior methods, most clearly on new combined changes.
arxiv-2605-19443: Rapoport and Wang extend Kudla, Rapoport and Zink's work on p-adic uniformization of Shimura curves for binary unitary similitudes. Their unitary group variant rests on an integral local Shimura variety for an anisotropic unitary group acting over a local p-adic field. Their RSZ variant allows any level maximal at one specially chosen p-adic place, a place where the group is anisotropic.
arxiv-2605-19543: Long proves the quantum homomorphism quasi-order of finite directed graphs is countably universal, so quantum relaxation does not collapse antichains. Finite planar graphs of degree at most seven share the same universality, and the result carries over to undirected graphs and quotient partial orders. The proof is constructive: any finite poset gets explicit planar graphs of degree at most seven matching its order. Directed cases use unions of clockwise cycles, where quantum and classical homomorphisms agree, while undirected cases use an ordered indicator with quantum endpoint forcing.
arxiv-2605-19643: Vianello, Bardin and Salasnich derive quantum-thermal shifts to semiclassical motion of a system using the quantum working action in Schwinger-Keldysh. They discuss the Ehrenfest link and, in the local energy guess, obtain shifts in closed form for any heat and damping, crossing from quantum to thermal as heat rises. At low heat and weak damping shifts follow zero-point jitter energy at the damped rate, matching the loss-free case, opening slope growth. Applied to super Josephson junctions and a long boson junction, shifts reach percent level.
arxiv-2605-19943: Sghaier and colleagues add chance to a tiny loop model to slip out of poor fixed points. The model refines a hidden state in loops, but its fixed path can stall at weak answers. Their method shakes each loop step with noise and runs many paths at once. It picks with the model's stop score, lifting puzzle scores sharply at tiny cost.
arxiv-2605-20443: Lohmiller and Slotine defend a classical-action account of quantum waves against a recent critique. They argue the critic no longer disputes the Feynman kernel method that makes the Bohm-like quantum potential vanish in the first work. The reply also rejects the critic's view of a semiclassical Van Vleck propagator as needing at most quadratic Hamiltonians. It further faults leaving out complex or quaternion positions, multi-valued action branches, and quantization of classical action.
arxiv-2605-20943: Willow Scott, Eugenio Valdano, and Charles Assaad study missing data and cluster graphs, contrasting cluster-level and variable-level missingness. Missing data is pervasive in public health, environmental science, and social sciences. Recoverability is usually studied with fully specified variable-level models, despite applications often offering only coarse structural information, for instance when variables group into clusters for limited knowledge or interpretability reasons. The authors introduce two cluster-based missingness graph classes, m-C-DMG and cm-C-DMG, formalizing compatibility between abstract graphs and underlying variable-level models.
arxiv-2605-21243: Gregory D. Scholes offers a new account of how quantum superpositions give definite outcomes. He derives state vectors for measurements on split parts of an entangled state. One wavefunction, he shows, encodes a special set of statistical outcomes. That explains definite results on each part and links between parts, with no nonlinear terms or ad hoc claims. Nonlocal links, on this view, need no interaction between the split parts.
arxiv-2605-21743: Michelle Yin and Burhan Ogut show platform-derived scores of occupational AI exposure mix task-level AI applicability with the platform's makeup. Swapping the platform input, with the design fixed, shifts the post-ChatGPT employment coefficient by one point nine times. Consumer and enterprise channels from one vendor disagree in sign. The authors formalize the non-classical measurement error, split it into between- and within-occupation selection, and build reweighted bounds. Reweighting to Bureau of Labor Statistics shares shrinks estimates by forty-two to ninety-three percent.
arxiv-2605-21843: Debojjal Bagchi and Stephen Boyles analyze the logit-mapping Jacobian for stochastic equilibrium, building two path methods. The Jacobian splits into a matrix zeroing feasible path-flow gaps and another with non-positive eigenvalues, given monotone link costs. From this, averaging with a step hits rate one minus s, and a flexible constant step rule keeps convergence. A Newton root-finding reformulation exploits Jacobian structure without surface tuning, showing superlinear gains and the first runtimes on Chicago Regional and Philadelphia networks.
arxiv-2605-22143: Yun and Lee investigate holographic dark energy with the Hubble radius as infrared cutoff in Einstein-Cartan gravity. They derive Einstein-Cartan equations via the action principle and Friedmann-like equations by introducing a torsion scalar. Using a Weyssenhoff spin fluid, they find torsion scaling as Phi proportional to a to the minus 3, without an ad hoc ansatz. The redshift-scale relation is preserved, while the torsion deviation parameter is set by an integral over emission to observation time. Their results support the model and prepare likelihood analyses.
arxiv-2605-22443: Wang and colleagues propose a terminal-constraint model predictive control framework for image-based visual servoing of drones. Standard visual servoing loses stability near the target under input and state limits. It also fails when moment-based visual features drop out during aggressive motion. Their framework adds terminal constraints and a terminal cost to the error dynamics, for feasibility, better convergence and stability. A Kalman filter predicts image moments during short visual dropouts, keeping control continuous. Live drone servoing tests confirm the approach.
arxiv-2605-22643: Bisconti and others build Boiling the Frog, a benchmark that tests whether tool using AI agents in office settings fall for slow incremental attacks. Each scenario starts with harmless workspace edits and later slips in a risk bearing request, scoring whether the final workspace state turns unsafe. Across a nine model panel, the strict attack success rate averages about 44 percent. It ranges from about 21 percent for Claude Haiku to about 93 percent for Gemini Flash Lite. Loss of control scenarios fare worst, with category success reaching about 93 percent.
arxiv-2605-22743: Parsa and four colleagues offer SeqLoRA, a method for teaching image generators many personal concepts, such as objects, people, or styles, without them bleeding into each other. It trains each new low-rank adapter orthogonally to earlier ones, using a two-level optimization that keeps both adapter factors free. Tests with up to 101 concepts on Stable Diffusion improved identity preservation and cut cross-concept leakage, with no separate fusion step.
arxiv-2605-22843: Qiu and Chen build a knowledge-aware framework for turning plain-language questions into SQL database queries when annotated examples are scarce. It assembles a knowledge base of schema meanings, abbreviations, business logic, and query patterns, then uses it both to synthesize grounded training data and to guide retrieval at query time. Across seven general and domain benchmarks it lifted open and closed language models, most clearly in low-resource specialist settings.
arxiv-2605-23243: Dahiya and four coauthors test frontier language models for cyber defense with a dual benchmark. White-box flaw spotting runs across C, Java, and Python. Black-box testing runs on five live apps with 118 flaws across 20-plus CWE families. Every frontier model shows 10 to 50 percent false alarm rates, over-guessing flaws. Black-box coverage reaches only 4 to 8 percent, rising to just 10 to 19 percent with outside tools. Set testing method in niche agents lifts per-family spotting above 50 percent.
arxiv-2605-23443: Masajada, Philip, and Streltsov pin down when quantum entanglement can survive long repeater chains with local processing. Entanglement survives at long range exactly when the channel admits a correctable subspace; without one, the transmitted state collapses exponentially fast toward separable states, and standard filtering cannot rescue it. Running parallel channels per link can fight the decay, but the count per link must grow at least logarithmically with station count. For depolarizing noise below threshold, that logarithmic bound is reachable.
arxiv-2605-23543: Schiavio and Binder present JEDI, a benchmark suite for the Java Stream API, which lets developers write computations in an easy-to-read declarative style and simplifies parallel computing. No dedicated stream benchmarks existed, leaving library developers without a way to optimize streams or to advise users on efficient code. JEDI is auto-generated by converting SQL benchmarks into Java benchmarks, covering both stream-based and imperative versions of each query. The suite spotlights inefficient code structures and better alternatives, with a focus on parallelization strategies matched to data traits.
arxiv-2605-24043: Kabra and four co-authors close the loop on discovery, pairing idea generation with test selection. Their system, LLM-AutoSciLab, offers ideas, picks telling tests to split or refine them, and updates its state from the evidence, rather than fitting fixed data sets. To test live work they build ActiveSciBench, with 57 enzyme tasks and 45 gene-network tasks under test budgets. Across NewtonBench and both ActiveSciBench sets, it beats prior methods, and guided tests prove two to five times more sample-thrifty than the rivals.
arxiv-2605-24243: Lavado, Micheletti, and Soares offer GIBLy, a lightweight geometric bias layer for 3D semantic segmentation. Deep models usually need large size and long training to capture basic geometric structures in 3D data, and existing methods lack direct ways to inject geometric knowledge such as simple shapes. GIBLy adds geometric priors into task pipelines, lifting MLP, conv, and transformer designs with features aligned to simple shapes, which stay readable. Across benchmarks it gives steady gains, with about 11 percent higher mean IoU on TS40K using PTV3, adding only 58 thousand weights.
arxiv-2605-24343: Ahmad, Nakisa, and Rastgoo propose Intrinsic Action Disentanglement, a layered learning frame for human-AI teamwork. Team agents must adapt to diverse partner conduct and skill levels, but older methods collapse to one style. Intrinsic Action Disentanglement learns distinct, partner-aware action sequences tied to latent skills. An inner reward pushes split action patterns across skills, giving a clear map from choices to replies. Catching long play runs, it adapts freely to mixed partner shifts. In Overcooked-AI across layouts and partner settings, it beats strong rivals.
arxiv-2605-24443: Ammari and Figalli prove global Lipschitz bounds for Brenier maps between chance measures with weights from a knob family ranging from the size to endless. Source and target may use mixed knobs, with the source no larger than the target. Their global bound stays even in size and both knobs, and for matching finite knobs it removes the fast size link of prior bounds. Local bounds inside fixed balls stay stable as the knobs tend to endless, and they regain Caffarelli's shrink rule with sharp constants.
arxiv-2605-24743: Shresth Verma and others improve multi-turn training by reweighting synthetic trajectories. Single-turn generation shines, but multi-turn interaction lags. Their BOOST framework nests two levels. The inner level trains the model on reweighted data. The outer level trains a light reweighting head on held-out real tasks, assigning continuous weights. A PAC-Bayesian bound exposes a three-way trade among diversity, task shift, and effective sample size. Tests consistently beat baselines, upweighting trajectories that match real data and show higher merit.
arxiv-2605-24843: Ligong Bi and co-authors offer AID-VAR, a plug-and-play fix for cascading errors in visual autoregressive generation. Small early mispredictions amplify and distort the final image. AID-VAR adds error correction inspired by GAN adversarial feedback: a discriminator diagnoses fidelity gaps at each scale change, plus a lightweight guidance injector. The module acts as a non-invasive adapter refining the backbone, steering generation toward real images without destabilizing the latent space. Tests show sharper details and fewer distortions, with 16 percent better FID for 3 percent more parameters.
arxiv-2605-25043: Jiangyan Zhao, Xian Shi, and Jin Xu propose the shared Keyboard design, a Bayesian phase I design that borrows information across doses. Standard Keyboard decisions use only the current dose, missing neighbor signals and risking needless dose changes. The shared design replaces beta-binomial updating with a borrowing Beta kernel posterior using kernel-weighted pseudo-counts. Extensions cover dose insertion, time-to-event outcomes, and a kernel weighting higher-dose toxicities more during escalation. Simulations show accuracy and safety gains for maximum tolerated dose identification.
arxiv-2605-25143: Dao Tran and colleagues improve test-time reasoning by letting a language model revisit earlier partial solutions instead of only extending its current best guesses. Earlier methods prune away the rest, which can discard paths that would still reach a correct answer and collapse diversity. Their approach keeps a persistent pool of prefixes. It selects within random subpools and resamples with a sequential Monte Carlo scheme, reaching higher accuracy per token on mathematics benchmarks across model sizes.
arxiv-2605-25343: Siyu An and colleagues map the road from bolted-together systems toward native modeling, where modalities fuse rather than through own encoders and frozen backbones. The paper defines architectural nativity, separating mid-fusion and early-fusion designs from non-native ones. It sorts native models into text-output comprehension, target generation, and unified modeling. Beyond labels, the roadmap unpacks the work from architecture and data curation through training, use, and evaluation. The goal is a unified model in which understanding and generation coexist.
arxiv-2605-25643: Qin and colleagues offer WeeCare, a handheld pad with fabric electrodes that senses bladder fullness on demand for people who cannot feel it. It uses electrical impedance tomography, a method that maps the body's inside from surface measurements. Because taking the pad off and putting it back shifts placement and contact, they test layout and noise response in simulation. They vary salinity and fill in phantom trials. They track voiding in eight volunteers, finding early evidence that the approach works in these tests.
arxiv-2605-25743: Riener and Shapiro ask whether derivative discriminants of real-rooted polynomials can be certified algebraically in root differences. They compare sums of squares, combinations in squared root differences, and Hermite-matrix factorizations. Where the derivative degree stays fixed while the polynomial degree grows, they put cubic-derivative discriminants in the square-graph cone at every degree. For quartic derivatives the cones separate: square-graph membership holds for degrees 4 through 22, but sums of squares hold from degree 4 up. That refutes the square-graph conjecture at degree 23.
arxiv-2605-26243: Zhishuai Guo and five colleagues' 2026 framework, CE-FedGNN, learns graph neural networks over graphs split across groups that cannot share raw data. It shares neither raw data nor per-round embeddings, exchanging aggregated node representations only occasionally. A moving-average estimator tracks those representations across rounds, handling cross-client links and staleness. Metric differential privacy, which gauges privacy by distance in embedding space, gives meaningful guarantees where standard privacy turns overly cautious. Tests on synthetic banking and citation networks show strong performance with far less communication.
arxiv-2605-26743: Romadani and four colleagues study how heat changes the Casimir force, a quantum vacuum effect, for a field trapped between two plates in a wormhole spacetime. They compute the free energy in the comoving frame under fixed boundary values. Its heat correction fades as temperature rises and stops depending on the background shape, while entropy, internal energy, and heat capacity each follow their own temperature curve.
arxiv-2605-26843: Colombara and three colleagues build a Bayesian warning system for metabolic syndrome risk among blood donors at pre-donation screening. The model jointly tracks the five diagnostic components over repeat visits, accounting for within-donor dependence, and yields a traffic-light rating of low, intermediate, or high risk. Tested on longitudinal data from AVIS Milan, it aims to flag at-risk donors early and support targeted prevention during routine assessment.
arxiv-2605-27043: Felekis and three co-authors tackle distribution shift in recommender systems with causal representation learning. Models trained on logs confounded by the deployed policy, past behavior, and platform filtering face a different candidate distribution at serving time, making offline metrics poor guides to online performance. Their information-theoretic disentanglement criterion depends only on causal components, with a tractable variational lower bound for finite data. A Spotify A/B test with millions of users shows online engagement gains at offline parity, matched on KuaiRand and synthetic benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-27343: Nithesh Chandher Karthikeyan, Jonas Unger, and Gabriel Eilertsen guide image diffusion models with features from a self-taught model. The trick lifts image quality with no text prompt and opens a feature space for steering what comes out. Moving through that space is smooth and disentangled, keeping traits apart and giving finer control of image making without labeled data.
arxiv-2605-27443: Ibrahim Ulgen, Hasan Ozgur Cildiroglu, and Oguz Yayla build a quantum circuit for the GFSPX cipher and test it with Grover cryptanalysis. Their design uses a four-branch generalized Feistel structure mixing ARX and SPN parts, fitting in 209 qubits. The key-recovery attack cost falls below the NIST level 1 threshold, though the hybrid design resists better than other lightweight ciphers.
arxiv-2605-27743: Loay Abdelrazek, Sultan Ertas, and Andrey Silva specify a standardized ontology for intent-based security management in autonomous networks. The TM Forum security ontology, version 4, extends the Intent Common Model to decouple high-level security goals from technical controls, mapping resource costs to protect service agreements. A formal walkthrough of distributed denial-of-service mitigation on a disaggregated radio slice shows constraint conflicts resolving without human intervention.
arxiv-2605-27843: Joao B. Florindo, Lucas O. Lyra, and Antonio E. Fabris tackle texture recognition where training images are scarce. Noting that texture clues cluster near each pixel, they skip heavy attention-based models and pretrain a convolutional autoencoder, pairing deep filters with Fisher vector pooling to summarize patterns. Tests on several texture collections show stronger accuracy without a large added compute cost.
arxiv-2605-27943: Yan Wang and Rong Wu settle a remaining case of a graph-coloring conjecture. Graphs with girth eight and no longer even holes were conjectured to need only three colors, a claim already shown for larger girths. The pair proves every such graph with girth exactly eight is three-colorable, closing the gap left by earlier work.
arxiv-2605-28043: Yao and colleagues compare two newborn planetary disks orbiting a wide binary pair, using them as a natural control experiment. JWST spectra show strikingly similar warm molecular emission, but the companion disk holds far more cold water vapor. The team traces the excess to its smooth dust disk, which lets icy pebbles drift inward across the snow line.
arxiv-2605-28243: Frédéric Faure links geodesic flow on closed hyperbolic surfaces to wave dynamics with an explicit Hilbert-space model. He constructs adapted spaces where the geodesic generator acts as a normal operator with discrete spectrum, except for possible Jordan blocks at one threshold. In this model the flow splits into a damped oscillator part and a shifted wave part. The split yields a dynamical Selberg trace formula and explains the long-time shape of spherical mean operators.
arxiv-2605-28543: Avrile Floro and Luca Benedetto locate the attention heads behind cultural binding in language models: linking a cultural item to its identity. With interpretability tools and a factorial design on an appropriation benchmark, they find two or three mid-layer heads per model supporting binding across eight models. Knocking out identity-to-item links on those heads cuts binding strength by roughly a tenth to a quarter. The heads transfer from instruct to base models, pointing to pre-training origins, and steering lifts differentiation scores while leaving neutral reasoning intact.
arxiv-2605-28643: Gaspard Michel and four colleagues draw novels as dynamic heterogeneous character networks, matching figures with their textual contexts over time. From Project Gutenberg they extract around 20,000 such networks, then train GraphLit, a self-taught method based on a masked graph autoencoder. Across twelve figure tasks, GraphLit beats text-only, graph-only, and prior hybrid rivals. Grounding figures in context drives the gains, while story order and figure ties help task by task, and a final study links story jumps to dynamic social traits.
arxiv-2605-29243: Laerdon Kim and Vivian Nguyen propose a way to cut false alarms when forecasting whether a conversation will derail into personal attacks. Existing models trigger an alert from the estimated risk alone, treating the future as fixed and ignoring the chance that tension may ease. The authors add a deferral step: forward-looking simulations check whether a tense moment still admits plausible paths back to calm. Added to a leading forecasting model, this step sharply reduced false positives without giving up accuracy.
arxiv-2605-29343: Haodi Lei and colleagues present Draft-OPD, an on-policy distillation method. A target model pairs with a draft model checked at once, but fine-tuning on target-made trajectories plateaus: accept rate stops improving. Cause: a mismatch. The drafter learns from fixed runs but is judged on its own blocks. Draft-OPD uses target-aided rollout and replays drafting from check-exposed error positions, so the drafter learns from feedback on accepted and rejected drafts. Tests show more than five times lossless speedup.
arxiv-2605-29643: Yilun Qiu and six colleagues present AgentCVR, a multi-agent framework treating cross-video reasoning as active evidence acquisition. Current models encode multiple videos into one shared context in a single pass, which can hide rare but critical evidence. A Master Agent coordinates dedicated Visual and Audio Agents for focused evidence extraction. Training uses Script-Simulated reinforcement learning, optimizing policy with generated scripts and a text simulator, avoiding costly inference. On a cross-video benchmark, AgentCVR beats single-pass baselines and matches closed-source systems in alignment.
arxiv-2605-29743: Benaoumeur Bakhti derives an exact density-functional account of a flat, angle-stepped wormlike chain under pull. The core is a bond-local closure tying neighbour-pair spreads to single-site angle spreads through a simple exponential link. That link lets the entropy term integrate exactly, and variational steps yield linked equations for one-site and two-site spreads, solved by repeated refinement. The account matches the exact transfer-matrix solution to machine precision on angle spreads and force-stretch curves.
arxiv-2605-29843: Artur Zagitov, Gleb Molodtsov, and Aleksandr Beznosikov push post-training quantization down to low bit widths. Such quantization stays open to activation outliers and lopsided curvature, and fixed Hadamard transforms cannot adapt the basis to layer, calibration data, or quantizer. Their processor, HARP, learns a shaped two-sided orthogonal rotation as sparse butterfly stages, handling non-power-of-two sizes. Fitted on calibration data, it adapts the basis per layer and backend. It improves perplexity across two- to four-bit settings, with best zero-shot gains at two bits.
arxiv-2605-29943: Dekka Muni Kumar, Dhruba Jyoti Kalita, and Yogesh Kumar Meena pick EEG channel sets for motor-imagery links. Their multi-goal search balances channel place, via a Gaussian kernel, against task split, judged by task-linked desynchronization inside trials. Three methods — genetic, swarm, and decomposition searches — hunt together for compact sets near sensorimotor cortex. On four sets it scores high eighties on the best set and mid sixties on the hardest, beating single-goal and fixed-set rivals. Compact sets cut compute load, suiting wearable and live brain-computer use.
arxiv-2605-30043: Sophie Rosu and 16 colleagues trace the outer rings of Supernova 1987A from 1994 to 2024, using Hubble, VLT and JWST data from optical to mid-infrared light. These rings left the star some twenty thousand years before the explosion, yet few studies had examined them. Their brightness has faded for three decades as the blast's first ultraviolet flash dies away, with no sign of the debris hitting the rings. Decay times, temperatures and densities differ between the northern and southern rings, whose spectra stand apart from the equatorial ring's.
