Tongyan Fang and colleagues fine-tune robot policies from sparse success signals in a 2026 robotics paper. A vision-language-action model finishes a whole episode and learns only one bit: success or failure. Yet training needs credit assigned to individual actions, and one scalar reward blurs two goals, staying viable and finishing efficiently.

Their method, HABC, trains separate critic heads for viability and efficiency on different data subsets. A state-adaptive gate blends their advantages, favoring viability while success is uncertain and shifting to efficiency once success is reliable. The blended signal becomes per-action weights on a behavior-cloning loss. Credit assignment is also made intervention-aware: outcome labels apply only to segments the policy itself executed, not to human corrections. On three contact-rich two-armed tasks with a real robot, success rates jump from low baselines to high ones, more than doubling on the hardest task.
arxiv-2606-17143:
Collander and Lee show that a common modeling shortcut distorts young exoplanets in a 2026 planetary science paper. Models of how planets shrink over time describe the envelope with an adiabatic index, gamma, often fixed at the value fitting billion-year-old planets. Thermodynamics says young planets should sit near the lower end instead, which redistributes their interior mass.

The authors vary gamma across the plausible range and track radius over time. Envelopes with larger gamma start puffier, then contract faster and lose mass more quickly. With thin envelopes, high-gamma planets end up more compact within tens of millions of years; with thick ones, radii converge after a billion years. The warning is sharp: assuming the old-planet value overestimates how strongly mass loss sculpts the population, especially for young worlds. Initial thermal state deserves the same care as the physics that follows it.
arxiv-2606-17343:
Eldaly, Figini, and Alexander present a 2026 arXiv paper on MRI reconstruction that reports not just an image but a map of how unsure the image is. Faster scans sample less of the measurement space, so reconstruction must fill gaps using prior assumptions about image structure. The authors assume the image is sparse in some transform domain and build a Bayesian framework that works with any sparsifying transform the user chooses for the task.

Inference runs through a split-and-augmented Gibbs sampler, with a proximal Markov chain method handling the awkward non-smooth conditional distributions. Two transforms are demonstrated, one based on image gradients and one on wavelets, across single-coil and multi-coil data. The Bayesian methods beat their optimisation-based counterparts on image quality while also delivering uncertainty maps. Those maps track true reconstruction errors closely and beat deep learning uncertainty estimates.
arxiv-2606-17443:
Chu and Hou present a 2026 arXiv paper on how large language models, now a major channel for product advice, may tilt markets toward famous brands. Skincare is the test category, since buyers cannot judge quality before purchase and lean on reputation instead. Three commercial models were probed in three experiments, with a robustness check on search goods where quality is easier to verify before buying, to see whether the pattern survives a friendlier setting.

When rival products shared identical specifications, famous brands were recommended essentially every time, a conditional monopoly in the authors' terms. A tiny rating edge for a competitor erased that dominance at once in the tests run. Authority-style marketing language, even with fabricated clinical claims, also broke the monopoly, worth a measurable fraction of a rating point. When all brands optimised alike, individual gains collapsed and non-participants vanished from recommendations.
arxiv-2606-17743:
Charalambous and colleagues present a 2026 theory paper on systems that must be controlled while their true state stays partly hidden. Such systems are modeled as partially observable Markov decision processes, where a controller sees only noisy observations. The authors ask how control actions can also carry signals, and they frame that dual task in information theory terms.

They build a new dynamic programming method whose state lives on spaces of probability distributions. Two linked information states, a posterior over the system state and a distribution over such posteriors, are shown to follow Markov recursions and to suffice for optimal control. The team proves matching necessary and sufficient conditions for optimality, and shows the method reduces to standard POMDP equations when no signalling is present.
arxiv-2606-18343:
Knorr derives an analytical approximation for the graviton propagator within Asymptotic Safety, a candidate theory of quantum gravity built around an interacting renormalization group fixed point, in a 2026 physics paper. Whether that approach stays unitary and causal, without inventing extra particles, has been a central open check on its credibility.

Earlier studies answered numerically, finding only the familiar massless pole and a healthy spectral function. Knorr's analytical treatment reaches the same verdict in the spin-two sector: no extra poles appear, and there are no signs of unitarity or causality violations. He also explains why derivative expansions sometimes fake such poles, showing that their residues shrink toward zero as the expansion order grows. The result strengthens the case that Asymptotic Safety propagates exactly the field content of general relativity, no more and no less. It also gives theorists a transparent formula where before they had mainly computation.
arxiv-2606-18543:
Chen, Narasimhan, and Liu at Princeton introduce CEO-Bench, a benchmark that tests whether language model agents can run a company for the long haul, in a 2026 artificial intelligence paper. Agents now handle short tasks well, but real leadership demands planning over long horizons, gathering information in noisy settings, adapting as conditions change, and coordinating many moving parts at once.

The benchmark simulates operating a startup for five hundred days through a programmable interface, with the agent managing the company against a partially observable market. The strongest agents wrote sophisticated code, simulating customer cohorts to forecast cash and mining negotiation history for hidden preferences. Even so, most leading models went bankrupt or stalled, and only two finished above the starting cash balance, neither profiting consistently. The authors present the gap between plausible day-to-day actions and sustained strategy as the capability future agents must close.
arxiv-2606-18743:
Roy and the team ask how much a quantum network's value for teleportation depends on the entanglement distribution scheme deployed on it, in a 2026 quantum information paper. Teleportation across a future quantum internet will move through networks of entangled links. Two plans compete: swapping entanglement along a single source-to-target path, or purifying entanglement gathered over multiple paths.

The authors measure a network's value by a metric averaging the maximum teleportation fidelity over source-target pairs. They present algorithms to estimate it under path-ordering constraints. For regular topologies, rings, complete graphs, triangular and square lattices, and random Erdős-Rényi networks, they show the metric is sensitive to the distribution protocol. Multipath purification raises average fidelity by much. Using the shortest path last beats using it first. And purification lets lattice networks reach quantum advantage at lower link quality than single-path schemes require.
arxiv-2606-18843:
Vanderpijpen and Goetghebeur improve predictions for the patients most likely to do badly, within models that jointly track repeated readings and survival. The work is a 2026 biostatistics paper. Mixed and joint models predict per-person outcomes. But when the goal is flagging extreme or poor outcomes, standard random-effects predictions shrink toward the average, and miss the tail.

Building on optimally weighted random-effect estimators offered for mixed models, the authors define poor outcome as death, or substandard repeated measures. They estimate random effects by minimizing weighted squared prediction errors, with weights that punish tail errors more. They call the resulting tools WRaPs. They derive closed-form answers from the usual joint model inputs. For complex settings, they give computed answers through Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo. Sim runs map the finite-sample behavior. A use case predicts single outcomes and survival in a randomized glioblastoma study.
arxiv-2606-18943:
Rädsch and colleagues audit the Physics-IQ benchmark in 2026, a test that judges whether video generation models understand real physical behavior. The benchmark compares generated videos against filmed physical experiments, so flaws in prompts or ground-truth clips can distort scores. The authors carry out a systematic check of the samples and scoring rules to see how reliable the signal really is.

Their revised version, Physics-IQ Verified, improves prompt and ground-truth quality and introduces sample-level scoring that weights each sample and metric equally. More than half of all samples are refined, and over a third of prompts are improved in the process. Comparing six image-to-video models then produces moderate but meaningful ranking changes compared with the original benchmark. The authors offer the cleaned benchmark and code so future work on physical understanding in video models can rest on a steadier measurement base.
arxiv-2606-19043:
Galal and colleagues present ultra-precise multi-fiber optical connectors for astronomy in 2026. Modern instruments need fiber links that stay stable across repeated mating and lose very little light. Standard telecom connectors add loss, reflections, and alignment drift that hurt throughput and calibration. The team set out to build connectors made for observatory use, with far tighter tolerances than commercial parts can offer for this task.

The new connectors are made by femtosecond-laser three-dimensional printing, which yields sub-micron ferrule tolerances. Early metrology shows strong hole alignment and roundness across the parts. First throughput tests with three fibers linked at once show losses close to the low target the design aims for. More work on throughput and focal ratio loss is planned to test efficiency and stability under observatory conditions. If those tests hold up, such connectors could help large fiber instruments keep more light and steadier calibration.
arxiv-2606-19243:
Williams and colleagues present a multi-thermal version of ALMANAC in 2026 for detecting coronal mass ejection origins. Reliable spotting of low-coronal eruption starts is a key limit in space weather forecasts, since standard scopes do not directly resolve low-coronal signs. ALMANAC detects eruptive signs in UV images from the SDO satellite, closer to where eruptions begin.

The reworked framework runs across several wavelengths at once, so temperature responses guard against projection effects and artefacts. A clustering scheme merges hits across channels, cutting event splitting while parallel computing keeps near-real-time speed. Benchmarking against twenty halo events shows clearer splitting of eruptions and steadier onset locations than standard estimates. The system also senses precursor low-coronal activity that white-light catalogues miss, a gain for early warning of space weather.
arxiv-2606-19343:
Kostić and colleagues present new results on multiparameter C-semigroups and C-cosine functions in 2026. Multiparameter semigroups, introduced by Hille in 1944, extend semigroup theory from one time variable to several. C-classes generalize further, allowing a regularizing operator. Such sets govern abstract Cauchy problems with several parameters at once.

These C-cosine functions, the second-order counterparts of semigroups, are introduced and analyzed. Several new results describe their generators, kernels, and links to the semigroup case. Uses treat abstract Cauchy problems of first and second order in locally convex spaces. The authors also study forced extensions, asking when such sets extend from smaller to larger parameter domains by force. Extending the one-parameter theory is not routine, since such families can misbehave along different axes. A systematic account of cosine functions and extensions gives analysts firmer ground for multi-time equations.
arxiv-2606-19543:
Aristizabal and four colleagues show in 2026 how to read the spin of a dark sector mediator from its decay pattern. Dark sectors may hide light, long-lived particles that travel before decaying in view of a detector. If such a particle appears, the next task is to pin down its quantum numbers, spin among them.

The team define an angular observable built only from the decay products' four-momenta. Vector bosons born in light meson decays spread through that observable unevenly. Scalars, by contrast, spread evenly in every direction. That contrast separates spin one from spin zero with no extra detector input. Planned searches at DUNE, SHiP, and FASER2 could apply the test across wide untested regions. The regions lie in parameter space that current bounds leave open. A future discovery could thus come with its spin read off from decay angles alone.
arxiv-2606-19643:
Julie Fendler and four colleagues fit Bayesian mixture models to health data that cannot be pooled in 2026. Federated settings split sensitive records across sites that may not share them. Mixture models cluster patients, but standard fitting wants all data in one place.

Their pipeline runs Markov chain Monte Carlo separately inside each data silo. Local posterior samples then merge to approximate the full-data posterior, the Consensus Monte Carlo idea. A variational framing of that merger extends to over-fitted mixtures that infer cluster counts themselves. New cluster-matching algorithms handle clusters missing from some sites. Several aggregation strategies suit different federation constraints, with guidelines for choosing among them. Simulations validate the approach against leading federated rivals. On British geriatric health records, the method recovers multi-morbidity patterns, sometimes finding small clusters better than pooled sampling.
arxiv-2606-19943:
Jingdong Shen and six colleagues build SIMBA in 2026, a two-way model linking satellite infrared spectra to profiles of the air for weather forecasting. Hyperspectral sounders such as FY-4A/GIIRS reveal the vertical structure of temperature and humidity, but most learning methods only retrieve profiles from spectra. The reverse trip, simulating spectra from a state, and the agreement between the two directions are usually ignored. SIMBA performs both jobs in one framework.

A cycle rule ties the two directions together, and a two-way Mamba module tracks long-range links across pressure levels. Trained on matched satellite observations and ERA5 reanalysis, SIMBA beats leading baselines on temperature and humidity retrieval and on rebuilding the spectra. Ablations credit the two-way design and the cycle constraint. Consistent state-to-spectrum modelling could feed directly into forecast systems.
arxiv-2606-20043:
Lihua Feng, Zejun Huang, Qifan Wang, and Yongjiang Wu prove a sharper bound in extremal combinatorics, the study of how large a structured family of sets can be. Their 2026 paper concerns intersecting families, collections where every two sets share at least one element. For such a family they study its symmetric differences, the sets of elements lying in exactly one of two members. They also take up a 2023 conjecture by Frankl, Kiselev, and Kupavskii about how many such differences can arise.

The team settles the conjecture when the ground set is large relative to the set size, for sets of size at least fifty under a mild growth condition. They also pin down the extremal families exactly: a certain class of stars, families built around one fixed element. A concentration inequality, which bounds how far a random quantity strays from its mean, does the heavy lifting in the proof.
arxiv-2606-20243:
Kipngeno Koech and colleagues present Phoenix, a multi-agent system that resolves GitHub issues from triage to pull request with safety controls at every step. Their 2026 paper splits the work among six agents: planner, reproducer, coder, tester, failure analyst, and a pull-request agent, coordinated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Every change is checked against a baseline test run before any pull request opens.

On a twenty-four-instance slice of SWE-bench Lite, Phoenix oracle-resolved seventy-five percent of cases with no regressions on successful runs. A pilot on forty-two real issues across fourteen repositories preserved correctness fully. Manual inspection found about half the pull requests were well-targeted fixes. The other half placed code at wrong paths, a planner weakness the team is addressing with retrieval.
arxiv-2606-20443:
Angan Mukherjee, Tyler Soderstrom, Michael Kurtz, and Victor Zavala monitor industrial processes by watching the shape of their data. Their 2026 paper combines topological data analysis with machine learning for high-dimensional time series. Real-time monitoring needs methods that pull actionable signals out of many simultaneous sensor streams.

Multivariate time series are represented as manifolds, and topological descriptors summarize their structure. A neural ordinary differential equation then learns how that topological structure evolves over time. Tested on real data from an industrial process, the trajectory-based approach detects events from the motion of the shape itself. Shape-based monitoring can flag abnormal behavior that point-by-point alarms in the plant miss.
arxiv-2606-20543:
Shilong Xiang, Zirui Zhang, Lijun Yu, and Chengzhi Mao speed up autoregressive image generation by predicting in two dimensions at once. Their 2026 paper notes that these models flatten images into 1D token sequences, much like language modeling. The flattening throws away the 2D spatial locality of visual signals and creates severe inference bottlenecks.

Spatially Speculative Decoding predicts not only the immediate next token but also the adjacent horizontal token and the one directly below it. Using 2D spatial correlation this way attacks the memory wall in visual inference. Each accepted speculation advances the image by more than one token per step. Aligning the goal with image geometry turns wasted structure into speed.
arxiv-2606-20643:
Mushtari Sadia and five colleagues present Sparc in 2026, a multi-agent system that answers questions about electrical circuit diagrams. Circuit questions need careful math and physics, which remains hard for multimodal language models that read images and text together. Sparc grounds its reasoning in executable simulations instead of asking a model to guess from the diagram alone. Language model agents write, run, and analyze simulation programs based on physical laws.

That design lifts accuracy to 83 percent, with gains of up to 58 percentage points over baseline systems. Because each answer rests on a program that can be rerun, errors can be traced to a step. Datasets and code are public. Sparc matters where a wrong circuit answer is worse than a checked one.
arxiv-2606-20743:
Maruthi Vemula tests whether massive activations in transformers are a removable artifact in a solo 2026 study. Trained transformers develop a few hidden dimensions with values far above the median. These outliers cluster on the first token of a sequence. One view says they exist because the residual stream must serve as both scratchpad and final answer. Vemula builds an architecture, Ledger Residuals, to test that claim directly.

Ledger Residuals splits the stream into two parts. A mutable scratch stream can be overwritten during computation. A protected commitment stream holds only the readout representation. If overload caused the outliers, a dedicated answer channel should remove them. It does not. At two model scales with matched loss, the model rebuilds the same outlier inside the protected channel, though smaller. The result suggests massive activations play a functional role, not merely a defect of shared storage.
arxiv-2606-21043:
Libby Hemphill and three colleagues test bystander bots in 2026 that reply to personal insults on Reddit to reduce further insults. Prior work studied strategies for cutting conflict in online communities. Their randomized controlled trial compares responses drawn from five deescalation strategies. Replies are posted by an automated procedure to insulting comments. The rate at which users post new insults is then measured.

Automated replies can reduce the insult rate effectively. An appreciation strategy performs best. Not all strategies perform well, a finding reported plainly. The authors discuss utility and limits of such tools. Bystander intervention is known to help in physical settings. A bot that thanks or appreciates a user at the right moment could scale that social effect, though automated moderation raises its own risks of misreading context or chilling legitimate heated speech.
arxiv-2606-21343:
Ariadna Sanchez and five colleagues propose a new evaluation framework in 2026 for voice reconstruction, which builds a personal text-to-speech voice for people whose speech is disordered. The goal is a voice that sounds like the person yet is easier to understand. Studies usually grade naturalness and similarity with mean opinion scores, a blunt tool with weak sensitivity and reliability for this task.

The framework pairs subjective tests, using best-worst scaling with situational framing to judge intelligibility and identity, with objective measures. Standard objective scores fail for highly unintelligible speakers, so the team adds a dual-reference distributional measure of the identity-intelligibility trade-off. Applied to seventeen zero-shot systems and 193 speakers, the framework gives a more reliable, task-aligned verdict on reconstruction quality.
arxiv-2606-21443:
Haojie Dong and fifteen colleagues report in 2026 on testing the light sensors of JUNO, the giant underground neutrino observatory in Jiangmen, China, while they were being installed. JUNO's 20-kiloton liquid scintillator detector needs energy resolution of three percent at one MeV, which rests on more than 20,000 large photomultiplier tubes plus tens of thousands of small ones. Catching dead or weak tubes before the detector sealed was essential.

Seven test campaigns ran during installation from October 2022 to December 2024, measuring dark count rate, gain, waveform, and charge spectrum for the 20-inch tubes. The report describes how the tests were implemented on site and what they found across the full production run. The checks validated the tube fleet that now watches for neutrino interactions 700 meters underground.
arxiv-2606-21743:
Finn H. O'Shea and Maria Elena Monzani introduce Cohort Organized Learning, CoOL, in 2026, a clustering method that never computes a distance. Every clustering method, deep ones included, leans on some notion of distance between samples. CoOL replaces it with agreement: several differentiable observers, neural networks, must reconcile their cluster assignments for each sample, learning from one another through an EM loop until the cohort concurs.

The article derives the training gradients, shows how to watch convergence, and how to grade the clusters when done. Examples span vector data and images, since anything a network can ingest can be clustered this way. Limitations and future prospects get an honest discussion. For the label-starved, high-dimensional data of modern physics instruments, tokamaks, dark matter detectors, colliders, agreement-based clustering offers a genuinely different organizing principle.
arxiv-2606-21843:
Tanner proposes, in 2026, a geometric way to measure whether an artificial intelligence agent keeps its assigned identity over long conversations. Agents drift toward generic behaviour as context piles up, but current checks notice only after quality visibly degrades. His framework treats identity as structure inside a geometric space, with drift defined as that structure relaxing toward its simplest form.

Tests on a persistent agent found two conditioning mechanisms behind identity. In one cluster the identity specification fills a behavioural void, and in another it pushes the model away from its post-training defaults. A probe test counted 55 unique response patterns from the specified identity against just one from the base model. Tanner also reports that an apparent drift effect under context pressure turned out to be an artifact of repetitive padding. With varied padding, no deformation appeared through 150,000 tokens of context, and the framework's full diagnostic promise remains unconfirmed.
arxiv-2606-21943:
Yang and colleagues survey, in 2026, how reinforcement learning is used to train large language models, organizing the field by design choices rather than by brand-name algorithms. Two methods, PPO and GRPO, dominate current pipelines, but they cover only a narrow slice of what reinforcement learning offers. The survey rebuilds the topic from three stages of algorithm construction, starting with how the decision problem itself is defined.

Later stages cover exploration, from temperature sampling to tree search and curricula, and learning, split along classic axes such as model-free versus model-based. Mapping the literature onto this grid exposes a lopsided pattern. Monte Carlo credit assignment and critic-free policy gradients are crowded with work. For language models, bootstrapping-based credit assignment, value-based methods, and off-policy actor-critic training remain largely unexplored. The authors present those gaps as concrete chances to import proven classical techniques.
arxiv-2606-23243:
Ran Piao and colleagues teach audio-language models to diagnose from a few examples across hospitals in a 2026 paper. Clinical audio diagnosis in low-resource settings must spot conditions from minimal examples, since large labeled sound collections are scarce. Their framework, Federated Self-Contextualization, learns in-context diagnosis without pooling hospital data centrally. It builds practice episodes by clustering audio representations without labels, creating pseudo-labels that stand in for scarce real diagnoses. Support and query pairs then teach the model to reason from examples.

Piao and colleagues run a three-stage pipeline. Caption-based pretraining aligns audio embeddings with the language model first. Federated training across hospital clients then adapts the model for episodic inference. At test time, a small labeled support set guides diagnosis of an unseen case. On held-out respiratory and cardiac conditions, the method beat audio-language baselines clearly in few-shot tests.
arxiv-2606-23443:
Christian Kenneth and colleagues open up a chemical language model to see what it knows about molecules in a 2026 paper. Such models read molecules as strings and are widely assumed to learn surface syntax only, not real chemical meaning. The team applies sparse autoencoders to MolFormer, an encoder-only model. Sparse autoencoders split internal activity into interpretable features. Layer by layer, they trace how the model builds its picture of a molecule from the string.

Kenneth and colleagues find a division of labor across depth. Early layers rely on position-tracking features to parse the molecular grammar. Later layers encode atoms inside substructures and features tied to drug-like behavior. Oddly spelled but valid molecule strings disrupt the representations more than outright invalid strings, because the position features break and the damage propagates. An interactive visualizer, InterMol, ships with the work.
arxiv-2606-23543:
Li and colleagues tackle a trust problem in training vision models on mathematics problems, in a 2026 paper on multimodal reasoning. Reinforcement learning can teach models to solve diagram-based mathematics, but only if the training answers are actually correct. Pipelines that generate ever harder questions often trust their own labels, so wrong answers quietly poison the rewards that steer learning.

Their framework, VeriEvol, separates two jobs before any training update: making questions harder, and proving answers reliable. Type-aware rewriting turns easy image-question seeds into harder grounded prompts, while a verifier agent accepts an answer only after failing to refute it with counter-evidence from several sources. Scaling the evolved training data from ten thousand to two hundred fifty thousand examples lifts mean accuracy across five benchmarks from about thirty-five to about fifty-five percent. Verified reinforcement data then adds nearly four more points over a plain baseline.
arxiv-2606-23643:
Zhou and colleagues generate personalized multimedia content for each user instead of only recommending existing posts, in a 2026 paper on recommender systems. Platforms depend on user generated content, which may be missing, late, or costly for fresh topics. Generators can synthesize content on demand, but turning sparse user histories into clear instructions remains open.

Their system, TailorMind, links preference modeling with controllable generation. A hypergraph method, which groups users and items in shared clusters, enriches thin histories with patterns from similar users. Textual profiles of taste are then refined using ranking error feedback. Retrieved real posts guide the style, and a reflection step checks that text and images still agree in meaning. On a new benchmark, TailorBench, built from three mainstream platforms, the system matches or beats real user content on coherence and improves novelty and aesthetic scores over generation baselines.
arxiv-2606-23843:
Le and colleagues rebuild the geometry of vision language models so the models stop ignoring the word not, in a 2026 paper on machine learning. Models like CLIP match images with text, yet they handle negation badly, relying on shallow word co occurrence. Fine tuning on negation data helps but damages earlier skills. HANCLIP instead restructures the embedding space itself, so each image is encoded by what it is not, alongside what it is.

Training uses only twenty thousand image text quadruplets. A hyperbolic formulation captures hierarchical relations, while an angular triplet objective pushes negated descriptions away from their positive counterparts. Pretrained knowledge largely survives. On the NegBench benchmark HANCLIP gains consistently, and it stays competitive on standard benchmarks. The method plugs into several existing models.
arxiv-2606-23943:
Contreras argues that the standard score for judging how AI tokenizers chop up text is misleading. Her target is languages that build words from long suffix chains, in a 2026 paper on natural language processing. A tokenizer splits text into units a language model can digest. The usual metric, fertility rate, counts pieces per word, and lower looks better. For Southern Quechua, one word can pack a root plus tense, person, case, and evidence markers. A tokenizer memorizing whole forms scores low fertility while slicing through every meaningful boundary.

Contreras benchmarks four tokenizers on a two hundred thousand sentence corpus, checking cuts against a morphological analyzer. A new metric, morphological boundary accuracy, scores whether splits land on true boundaries. BPE wins on fertility yet scores under seven percent boundary accuracy. A morphology aware rival, PRPE, tops eighty three percent. Fertility alone cannot certify a tokenizer for agglutinative languages.
arxiv-2606-24043:
Mihaila and Seguin compute how a nonlocal measure of size changes when the object it measures is deformed a little. The fractional perimeter gauges a set's boundary through long-range interactions, not local smoothness. Their 2026 work generalises it to a fractional measure for submanifolds of any dimension, surfaces and curves included. A parameter between zero and one governs it. The first variation is the linear response of that measure to a small wiggle.

The computation yields a formula for the variation in full generality. Mihaila and Seguin use it to define a nonlocal mean-curvature vector for embedded submanifolds. That extends the classic notion of how a surface bends at each point. A consistency check anchors the definition. When the submanifold has codimension one, the new vector agrees with the nonlocal mean curvature already widely studied for hypersurfaces. Fractional geometry thus gains a curvature tool matched to its measure.
arxiv-2606-25243:
Stars ring like bells, and the tones reveal what lies inside them, but reading those tones for stars unlike the Sun has been awkward. Joel Ong, Sarbani Basu, Willem Hoogendam, and Vincent Vanlaer show in 2026 that the inversion step works better in coordinates shaped by the star itself. Instead of measuring depth by physical radius, they use an acoustic radius tied to sound travel time, or a buoyancy radius tied to gravity waves. They derive the maths for reshaping the inversion kernels into these coordinates.

Working in the buoyancy coordinate lets researchers compare stars whose inner zones differ in size, a case where standard inversions fail. In the acoustic coordinate, pressure mode inversions no longer need the true star's mass and radius known beforehand. A fast public implementation accompanies the derivation.
arxiv-2606-25443:
Only the Sun lets astronomers watch a star's active regions up close and sample its eruptions directly. Vladimir Airapetian's 2026 review chapter uses that privilege to set a benchmark for activity across cool main sequence stars, from F type down to M dwarfs. Whole disk solar observations, treated as if the Sun were a distant star, define diagnostics for flares, mass ejections, and particle storms. Those same diagnostics can then be carried over to unresolved stellar data.

Radio observations earn special attention because they trace particle acceleration and escaping material. The coming Square Kilometre Array telescopes promise sub second imaging of the solar corona over a wide band, plus the sensitivity to catch quiet and flaring emission from nearby stars. Airapetian maps research directions where such Sun as a star tools sharpen models of stellar space weather.
arxiv-2606-25743:
A foundation model can be queried but not opened, and its predictions are biased by an unknown amount. Yan Zhou studies that bargain in 2026 as black box assisted regression. A learner holds few labelled samples, may call the fixed predictor freely, and knows only that the true function lies within some unknown distance of it. A sharp phase transition governs the problem.

Below a critical distance, trusting the black box is nearly free. Above it, the learner pays the usual nonparametric price. The best achievable risk is the smaller of the two costs. Zhou's safe residual estimator learns only the correction, starting from zero so it begins as the black box itself. Holdout validation reverts to the raw predictor when the correction lacks support, preventing negative transfer. Synthetic experiments confirm the transition. Trials with CLIP on images and a Qwen model on news text show the same tradeoff in practice.
arxiv-2606-25943:
Yorick Fuhrmann works at the meeting point of homotopy theory and algebraic geometry. Part one revisits Borel complete equivariant spectra for finite groups. The classic description comes from Mathew, Naumann, and Noel. Fuhrmann adds a version with coefficients. Attention then shifts to profinite groups, which are limits of finite ones. Two notions of Borel completeness appear there, and they generally differ. One is levelwise, and the other is its hypercompletion.

Part two studies smooth Artin motives. These are motive categories steered by the étale fundamental group of a base scheme. In the Nisnevich setting, Fuhrmann extends a theorem of Voevodsky. Smooth Artin motives become modules over a Bredon cohomology spectrum for the profinite group. In the étale setting, the gap between the two completeness notions matches a known gap. It is exactly how étale sheaves differ from hypersheaves on finite étale schemes.
arxiv-2606-26443:
Baiqi Li and six colleagues argue that robots working beside people need to know what those people just did, not only what a command says. Their benchmark, WatchAct, pairs real videos of human actions with matching simulator scenes and executable robot tasks. Systems can thus be scored on behaviour they watched, not on a single snapshot of the scene.

WatchAct holds three thousand long tasks across fourteen activities. The tasks test reading events, recovering step order, inferring unstated intent, and tracking how a scene changed. Scores separate planning from execution. One grade covers turning video into a plan, another covers carrying out a perfect plan, and a third covers the full pipeline. Even the best system finished only about one task in six in simulation, and fewer on a real Franka robot arm. People scored near perfectly at planning.
arxiv-2606-26543:
Tarikul Islam and Mahbub A.H.M. Latif propose a unified weighting framework for causal questions in case-control studies. Such studies compare people with a disease against people without it. They are efficient when outcomes are rare. Their backward sampling, though, distorts the outcome distribution. Most fixes need the true population prevalence, the share of people with the outcome, or estimate only total effects.

Their three-stage approach estimates prevalence first. A density-ratio method combined with outside covariate information does that job. Stage two rebuilds the target population with design weights. Stage three applies stabilised causal and mediation weights inside a marginal structural model. Mediation analysis separates an effect that flows through an intermediate factor from one that acts directly. The framework estimates total and pathway-specific effects without knowing prevalence in advance.
arxiv-2606-26743:
Amjad Hussain and six colleagues improve millimetre-wave radar point clouds by fusing them with camera images. Radar point clouds are sparse, noisy, and structurally incomplete. Yet downstream tasks like object detection and tracking depend on their quality. Images carry rich semantic information about what objects are present. The authors use that information to constrain and align radar output.

Their method aligns radar points with image meaning in depth and semantics. A sparse completion strategy then raises point density and restores missing structure. The enhanced clouds were tested in detection and tracking tasks. Accuracy and robustness improved in complex environments. The work targets driver assistance systems, where radar's reliability in bad weather is valuable but its sparseness limits perception.
arxiv-2606-26843:
Martin Bauer and Levin Maier prove that closed shortest-path loops exist on a class of endless-dimension groups. A geodesic is a shortest path; a periodic one closes into a loop. Half-Lie groups are such groups where combining elements is smooth only on one side. They model shape change and fluid motion. Classic theorems guarantee closed geodesics on finite spaces with rich loop structure.

Building on recent completeness results for these groups, the authors prove two results. Every loop family that cannot be shrunk away contains such a closed loop, when the group's loop structure is rich enough. A second result, in the style of Lyusternik and Fet, gives a nonconstant loop that can be shrunk to a point, under a compactness condition and richer loop structure. A reduction to finite subspaces yields uses for groups of smooth shape maps with strong distance rules.
arxiv-2606-26943:
Pablo Concha-Vega, Antonin Loubière, and Kévin Perrot study crossing gates in two-dimensional sandpiles, a step toward a decades-old complexity question. Predicting a sandpile's future is known to be hard in three dimensions, where Boolean circuits can be encoded into the piles. In two dimensions, wires cannot cross without interacting, which blocked the same proof. Whether prediction is easy or hard in two dimensions remains open.

The authors allow non-uniform and weighted grids, where cells hold different thresholds. They prove an equivalence between uniform weighted crossings and a simple class of non-uniform crossings they call primal. One exhibited gate inherently needs more than one crossing point, unlike standard designs. In richer settings, though, the equivalence breaks down. The results map where circuit encoding might still succeed.
arxiv-2606-27043:
Yang and colleagues build a light-based platform for studying open quantum systems, which leak phase information to their surroundings. In such systems a neat wave picture fails, and a density-matrix picture governed by the Liouvillian is needed instead. Their setup is a quantum walk, where light steps through a mesh of linked paths. Controlled phase noise lets them dial random phase loss up or down. Uneven gain and loss add a separate non-Hermitian drive, where energy is not conserved.

Tracking how the light cloud drifts lets the team probe the non-Hermitian skin effect, a piling up of states at an edge. As settings vary, drift crosses over from being boosted by coherence to being boosted by its loss. Those shifts match computer simulations based on quantum channels closely. Random phase loss thus actively reshapes sideways transport, not just weakens it.
arxiv-2606-27243:
Liu and colleagues present NOVA, an agent harness that evolves recommender system architectures inside a live industrial advertising platform. AutoML mostly tunes settings, while generic coding agents produce runnable code that may still fail silently as an architecture. In 2026, NOVA guides edits with an architecture gradient, a non-numeric update signal blending past modifications, verification diagnostics, metric feedback, and trajectory memory.

A verification cascade checks structure, local execution, offline quality, and online impact, blocking bad candidates early. Failure patterns are logged as forbidden directions for later rounds. Four control levels match automation to task risk, routing dangerous work to human-supervised copilot mode. NOVA posts the best effective pass rates on mid-level scaling and literature-to-production tasks. One such cycle shrinks human-attended time more than thirteenfold. Online tests show revenue gains with sharply reduced prediction bias.
arxiv-2606-27443:
Keluskar, Bhattacharjee, and Liu test whether the traits assigned to language model agents change how well a team performs, not just how it talks. Prior work showed low-agreeableness prompts turn agents adversarial and high-agreeableness prompts turn them cooperative. The team varies team makeup across frontier models in three domains: structured coding, open-ended research collaboration, and competitive bargaining. Style and outcomes are measured separately, so talk and results cannot be confused, in a multi-agent study appearing in 2026.

Personality effects hinge on task structure. In coding, low agreeableness shifts tone dramatically yet milestone completion barely moves. In open-ended collaboration and bargaining, the same tweak badly degrades performance. Designers of agent teams therefore cannot treat makeup as cosmetic everywhere. Where work is loosely structured, team makeup is a performance lever; where goals are explicit, it mostly changes tone. The limits of such tuning are mapped alongside its power.
arxiv-2606-27743:
Language models are usually served as if computing resources never change. Real cloud settings fluctuate. Spot instances vanish, and service tiers demand different speeds. Yuhang Chen and thirteen colleagues propose Learning to Allocate, or L2A, in 2026. L2A makes inference adapt to the live resource budget. Gating networks sit inside the model and condition on both the input and the budget.

Training optimises task quality, consistency, and resource cost. Three levers match how pressure appears in deployment. Layers can be skipped under memory pressure. Attention heads can be pruned under throughput contention. Reasoning tokens can be cut when latency tightens. One model then traces the accuracy-versus-compute frontier. On Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B, up to thirty-four percent of layers could be skipped. Accuracy on GSM8K stayed within six tenths of a percent of the dense baseline. The same small gap held on unseen tasks.
arxiv-2606-27943:
A remote point hides in the Stone–Čech compactification of a space. It avoids the closure of every nowhere dense subset. Serhii Bardyla and Jaroslav Šupina develop new approaches to such points in 2026. The spaces considered are Tychonoff spaces. Three lenses characterise when remote points exist. They are topological ultrafilters, measures, and compact-like properties, all tied to the ideal of nowhere dense sets.

Two structural results follow. The space of remote points is homeomorphic to part of a Stone space. That space is built from the smallest Boolean algebra containing all open sets and all nowhere dense sets. For the real line, the space of remote points is proved omega-bounded. Remote points are delicate objects. Their existence often depends on set-theoretic assumptions. Characterisations in terms of ultrafilters and measures give new tools for deciding when they can occur.
arxiv-2606-28343:
Shwan Ashrafi and Dan Roth show how retrieval systems can quietly push minority interests aside, with no one intending it. Retrieval-augmented agents fetch documents from a shared embedding space, where each document sits at a point. Serving a majority taste can pack that neighborhood so densely that a similar minority taste gets crowded out of the top results.

Ashrafi and Roth build a mean-field framework, which tracks the crowd as a whole rather than document by document. In a fixed space they find a phase transition: past a critical majority density, minority performance collapses. Letting embeddings update to maximize accuracy makes things worse, since the dynamics drive the system toward serving only the majority. Relevance-chasing alone, they prove, manufactures this exclusion.
arxiv-2606-28843:
Hawkins and ten colleagues run the first broad study of how fine-tuning language models in many languages affects their safety. Fine-tuning means extra training on a chosen dataset, often harmless material, yet earlier work showed it can make models more willing to answer dangerous prompts. The team fine-tuned Llama, Qwen and Gemma models on benign data translated into nine languages, then tested them across languages as well.

Safety outcomes swung widely with both the training language and the test language. In some settings, compliance with hostile prompts rose fourfold. The drift did not track general ability scores. It differed sharply between languages and models. Training outside English often moved the model's inner representations less, yet pushed it toward either too much compliance or too much refusal. Checking safety only in English, they conclude, gives weak assurance. They release their dataset and test suite for others.
arxiv-2606-28943:
Li, Zhang, Wang and Chen introduce A3M, a learning framework for bidding in repeated auctions where feedback is limited to outcomes. Bidders must learn while rivals change tactics. Existing methods often follow rigid explore-then-exploit schedules, assume rivals stay fixed, and chase bidder profit alone, which limits adaptability and robustness.

A3M combines three ingredients. An actor-critic deep reinforcement learning core balances exploration and exploitation dynamically as results arrive. An opponent model enables fictitious play, planning against imagined rivals, to handle adversaries whose strategies shift over time. A composite reward jointly pursues bidder utility, auctioneer revenue and fairness, with tunable trade-offs. In tests on both discriminatory and uniform price auctions, A3M cut final regret by thirty to forty percent in standard settings. It stayed robust when rivals shifted strategy and scaled well as units grew. Ablations confirmed each component was necessary.
arxiv-2606-29043:
Cheng, Zhang, Huang and Wang test how much of a neural network's generalisation, its success on unseen data, can be explained by two ideas together: sharpness and complexity. Sharpness measures how quickly the loss worsens when weights are nudged; complexity measures how rich the model's behaviour can be. Past quantitative studies mostly scored each measure alone, leaving their joint power unexplored.

Using linear regression and a Pareto-based analysis, which tracks the best trade-offs between the two factors, the team score their combined explanatory power. They also propose new versions of both quantities defined in function space, describing what the network computes rather than its raw parameters. Those function-oriented definitions explain more than existing parameter-level metrics. The two-factor view thus looks like an informative lens across settings. Failures remain, though, so whether the pair can form a complete theory of generalisation stays open.
arxiv-2606-29443:
Esposito, Viscardi, and Hamma examine stabilizer entropy, a measure of how far a quantum state sits from the easy to simulate stabilizer family. That distance, called non-stabilizerness or magic, is a resource for quantum computing. For mixed states, states that blend several possibilities, computing a strict measure is provably intractable. Any exact monotone, a measure that never grows under free operations, needs more than exponential time.

The authors defend a simpler linear version of stabilizer entropy. They show it behaves as a proper monotone with overwhelming probability for flat mixed stabilizer states under non-adaptive Clifford channels. The chance of a violation shrinks exponentially as the system grows. Tests cover Haar-random states, Clifford orbits, and random matrix product states. They also prove safety for certain many-body systems under partial measurements. Their verdict: the linear measure is trustworthy in practice.
arxiv-2606-29743:
Bose, Maheshwari, Miraftab, and Otachi study packings of three-vertex patterns inside plane triangulations, maximal planar graphs where every face is a triangle. They consider three patterns: the three-vertex path, the triangle, and an edge plus an isolated vertex.

For path packings, they prove every triangulation on a given number of vertices contains at least a stated fraction of disjoint paths, and the bound is asymptotically tight. Triangle packings receive lower bounds in terms of maximum degree and the degree sequence. For the induced edge-plus-vertex pattern, every plane triangulation holds a large packing, findable in polynomial time.
arxiv-2606-30643:
Maria Aslanidou, Manan Agarwal and Jacco Vink measure how fast a young supernova remnant is expanding. The remnant, G292.0+1.8, is the oxygen-rich debris of an exploded star in our galaxy, still holding a fast-moving pulsar at its heart. Expansion speed reveals the remnant's age and how its ejecta, the blown-out star material, plough into surrounding gas.

The trio used deep X-ray images from the Chandra observatory taken ten years apart, in 2006 and 2016. They split the forward shock into nineteen pie-shaped sectors and measured profile shifts in each. The average expansion rate came out near zero point zero one six percent per year. That implies an age of roughly twenty-five hundred years in a uniform medium, or about forty-one hundred years under a wind-blown density profile. Heavier elements expanded more slowly than lighter ones, matching their origin in deeper star layers.
arxiv-2606-30743:
P. Figueira and ten colleagues survey how astronomers observe star-planet interactions, the ways a star and its close planet affect each other. Such interactions can brighten patches of the star, change how fast the planet's atmosphere escapes, and distort the spectra taken during transits. The hard part is telling planet-induced signals apart from the star's own restless variability. This chapter reviews the observational toolkit.

Radial-velocity tests track the star's wobble while correcting for line distortions and colour-dependent noise. Precision photometry hunts for variability locked to the planet's orbit, flares modulated by the planet, and active regions the planet crosses. Chromospheric lines, formed at different heights, trace magnetic activity that may carry interaction signatures. Transmission spectroscopy and radio observations add probes of the planet's escaping gas and magnetic coupling. The authors stress that detections need coherent evidence across timescales and diagnostics, not one periodic signal.
arxiv-2606-30843:
Prasoon Raghuwanshi and four colleagues survey TinyML, machine learning squeezed onto microcontrollers, for wireless networks. Next-generation networks want intelligence at the device and edge for real-time, adaptive operation, but moving data costs energy and models age as conditions shift. That ageing, called concept drift, quietly degrades tiny models running on end devices.

The survey maps where TinyML is and is not yet deployed across wireless problems, and catalogues frameworks for designing tiny algorithms. Its main proposal is a federated learning update procedure to fight drift: devices train locally and share only model updates, keeping data on site. The procedure covers both battery-powered and batteryless devices. For batteryless hardware, which loses power unpredictably, the authors discuss update-aware checkpointing, a fault-tolerant bootloader, and an intermittent-aware modify operation. Together these mechanisms aim to keep edge intelligence current without draining the devices that host it.
arxiv-2606-31243:
Trinh studies how much Bell state a separable noise state can absorb before quantum advantages switch on. Mixing a fixed Bell reference with a separable two-qubit noise state traces a line of states. Along that line sit two crossings: the mix becomes entangled, and later it beats classical teleportation limits.

Trinh packages each crossing as a capacity of the noise state, found from one Möbius map. The entanglement absorption capacity depends, for product noise, only on local marginal purities. The fidelity capacity also depends on how the noise aligns with the entangled reference. Closed forms cover product noise and separable complex X states in all four Bell frames. Three extensions push the same capacity idea further, giving noise a single score for two distinct quantum thresholds.
arxiv-2606-31643:
Kumar and Majdoub study when solutions of an inhomogeneous semilinear heat equation, a diffusion equation with a power-law reaction and an added forcing term, must blow up in finite time. Classical Fujita theory gives a threshold exponent for the unforced case. Forced versions usually assume the forcing is integrable, which excludes many growing or uneven forcings.

Replacing integrability with regular variation, a precise way to describe how the forcing mass grows with radius, the pair derive sharp nonexistence results. The critical exponent now depends on the variation index of the spatial mass. They also handle the critical case, sign-changing forcings, space-time forcings and a fractional Laplacian version, giving one unified picture of blow-up thresholds.
arxiv-2608-00143:
Varunsegar studies symbolic attack chain generation from Atomic Red Team techniques. Building attack chains by hand fails to scale as adversary behaviours expand. Classical planning in PDDL can automate the task. It needs techniques translated faithfully into symbolic predicates, though. AURORA, a leading system, sorts actions into nine categories. Whether that fine split is needed was untested.

Her pipeline pairs a language model translator with the Fast Downward planner. She compares the nine-category scheme with a leaner five-category one. The five came from Atomic Red Team run evidence. Both schemes give the same plan validity and cost by design. The real test is predicate category resolution. One case split holding admin rights from using them over a network logon. True resolution gains were confined to one of sixteen techniques. Finer categories mostly sharpen a plan's internal justification, she finds.
arxiv-2608-00243:
Ji tests whether multi-agent debate improves groundedness judgements by LLM judges. Panels of agents are often assumed to judge better after trading critiques. Groundedness verification asks if a claim is supported by supplied evidence. Ji evaluates a homogeneous three-agent panel on six public benchmarks. Those benchmarks cover fact verification and hallucination detection.

Against a fixed single-agent reference, panel accuracy shifts ranged widely. Differences ran from plus 8.5 to minus 4.4 percentage points. Two data sets showed reliable gains, and one a reliable loss. Three were statistically inconclusive. Panel and reference used different model variants, Ji notes. The gaps thus describe complete systems, not a pure debate effect. More debate with the same evidence has structural limits, the results suggest.
arxiv-2608-00443:
Arulandu, Martyn, and Chuang improve ground state preparation by trading imaginary time for randomness. Imaginary-time evolution is a foundational route to ground states on quantum computers. It is non-unitary, so implementations pay exponential cost in the target time. The state also converges slower than the energy, raising observable costs further. Their twirled version pairs imaginary-time steps with random real-time ones.

The real-time duration is drawn from a carefully designed distribution. Randomization quadratically suppresses trace distance to the ground state, they prove. Observable errors fall with it. About half the imaginary time can thus be swapped for unitary real-time evolution. Any black-box ITE method gains a quadratic cost cut. Noisy circuit simulations on an Ising chain show large gains over standard ITE.
blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volume-53:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine opens its fifty-third volume with this January 1843 number. A survey of Great Britain at the commencement of the year leads, claiming for her a position of grandeur and responsibility unparalleled in ancient or modern history. Lesurques, the victim of judicial error, follows; Caleb Stukely reaches part ten; Landor contributes an imaginary conversation; and B. Simmons signs the Curse of Glencoe.

The World of London begins its second series inside, anatomising fashionable society. A sort of hero-worship, as Mr. Carlyle would term it, attaches to the most absurd doings of people who might be fashionable. A counter-jumper or tailor's apprentice adores the memory of the late marquis and counts the Haymarket pavement classic ground. Tasso and Cornelia, a dream of Lord Nithsdale, and an essay on taste and music in England complete a strong Maga number.

March 1843 in Blackwood's belongs first to the Caucasus. Ammalát Bek, a true tale of the Caucasus from the Russian of Marlinski, appears in Thomas B. Shaw's translation, with a preface mocking the English mania for travelling. Schiller's poems reach number six, Caleb Stukely part twelve, and Landor imagines Sandt and Kotzebue, the assassin and his victim, in conversation.

A Tale of a Tub supplies the comedy: an additional chapter on how Jack ran mad a second time. Squire Bull, honest gentleman, has indulged Jack's strange new zeal and even sent lists of usherships with polite notes. He begins to find the humours whimsical and preposterous. The Jeweller's Wife follows El Empecinado's career in Spain, Paul de Kockneyisms amuses the Cockney reader, and the World of London runs its third part under Delta's lost lamb.

April 1843 in Blackwood's mixes husbandry with empires. The Practice of Agriculture leads; Schiller's ballads reach number seven; Charles Mackay sings the Founding of the Bell; and Ammalát Bek advances to chapter three. An imaginary conversation between Landor and the editor of Blackwood's itself turns the magazine's wit inward, and Lord Ellenborough and the Whigs closes the politics.

The Occupation of Aden takes the imperial measure. Wellsted is quoted on the site's natural advantages: happily selected, its imposing appearance displaying splendour while uniting strength with ornament. Aden stood as the port and bulwark of Arabia Felix, its isthmus a disputed two hundred — perhaps twelve hundred — yards in breadth. Caleb Stukley, meanwhile, reaches part thirteen of his dogged serial career, shepherds sing their last, and Dundee gets a burial march.

May 1843 in Blackwood's sends Dumas travelling: France has lately sent forth her poets in great force, and the number reviews Alexandre Dumas's Souvenirs de Voyage in Italy. Dramatist, plot-builder, and admirable storyteller, Dumas has travelled quite in character. Ammalát Bek reaches chapter six, Reynolds's Discourses their conclusion, and Caleb Stukely, at last, part the last.

London's streets supply the surprise subject: the Battle of the Blocks, the paving question. Wood pavement laid by the Metropolitan Company now covers three-fourths of all such pavement introduced, some forty thousand yards laid in 1842 alone — St. Giles, Jermyn Street, the Old Bailey, Piccadilly. A natural history of salmon and sea-trout, a leap-year tale, Schiller's eighth number, and Spain's commercial policy round out the miscellany in proper Maga fashion.

June 1843 in Blackwood's opens a new serial: Marston, or the Memoirs of a Statesman, part one, under Shakespeare's lions and artillery for epigraph. A translation of the Vigil of Venus follows, then chapters of Turkish history on the rise of the Kiuprili family and the siege of Candia in its ninth part. Ignacio Guerra and El Sangrador carry a tale of civil war in Spain.

Ammalát Bek concludes in the Caucasus fighting. A rider falls with the blood-stained corpse dragged by a stirrup, and Hit — killed! is shouted from all the trenches. A young artillery officer crosses himself, jumps down from the battery, and catches the slain Circassian's horse by the reins. The Vicar of Wakefield illustrated by Mulready, a memorandum of a month's tour in Sicily, and commercial policy toward Russia close the volume's first half-year.
blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volume-54:
July 1843 opens Blackwood's fifty-fourth volume with Marston's second part, the statesman still quoting Shakespeare over his memoirs. English music and English musicians get their survey; a prairie and swamp adventure comes from Louisiana; the aristocracy of England is weighed; and Carlyle's Past and Present is reviewed. Heliodorus's Ethiopics represents the early Greek romances, and Charles Edward waits at Versailles.

Sport fills the middle pages. Scrope on salmon fishing for the anglers, and Jack Stuart's bet on the Derby for the rest. Jack's dingy room holds a dinner of soused salmon, perigord pie, iced champagne, and maraschino on the day of the Oaks. Almonds, raisins, and cool claret follow the cloth, and Jack begins on the grey mare: never was there such a jumper. Reginald Heber's Whippiad whips the satire in verse.
braid-neurypnology-1843:
James Braid, a Manchester surgeon, founded the study of hypnotism in Neurypnology, printed in 1843. Watching a mesmerist's show, he saw the trance came from the subject's own nervous state. Braid coined the words neurypnology and hypnotism for the new science. The subtitle ties nervous sleep to the claims of animal magnetism.

He explains trance as a state raised by fixed gaze and strained attention. No magnetic fluid passes from operator to subject, he argues. Cases from his practice show the state used in treatment. The book broke mesmerism away from fluid theory for good. Every history of hypnosis starts with Braid. His terms are still in daily use.
carlyle-past-present-1843:
Thomas Carlyle published Past and Present in 1843, a fierce work of social criticism. Carlyle contrasts a well-run medieval abbey with industrial England in his own day. The past, in his telling, had faith, order, and real leadership. The present has the cash nexus: money as the sole bond between people.

He attacks laissez-faire policy and the misery of factory workers. Captains of industry is his call for a new, responsible ruling class. The book founded a line of Victorian social critique that Ruskin and others followed. Its prose burns with prophetic anger. Historians still cite it on the condition of England question.
cia-0000009043:
Soviet activities around the world, with special attention to the Far East, fill a CIA survey from March 1951. The Korean War was then in its first year, and Moscow's hand in Asia drew sharp American focus. The paper scans Soviet moves across regions before narrowing eastward.

Global surveys helped leaders judge whether Soviet steps formed one design or many local plays. In 1951, with China newly communist, the Far East section carried special weight. The file shows the early CIA thinking in worldwide terms. It also records how completely the Soviet Union dominated the agency's first agenda.
cia-0000009143:
Quynh Luu district, in Nghe An province, is the scene of a November 1972 report on a downed American pilot sighted there. Nghe An stretches along North Vietnam's coast, under routes struck throughout the bombing years. Late 1972 brought the war's final, heaviest air campaign weeks later.

A pilot down in a coastal district faced capture by local militia within hours. Reports from such districts let officials plot a man's likely path into the prison system. Few could be verified on the spot. This file preserves the sighting as filed, one point in a province crossed by many losses.
cia-0000009443:
American journalists held captive by Viet Cong and North Vietnamese forces in Kompong Cham province fill a September 1971 report. Kompong Cham lies in Cambodia, where the war had spread the year before. Correspondents covering that fighting faced capture alongside soldiers' risks.

The report records what was known of the newsmen's capture and condition. Journalists were valuable prisoners: known names with employers and families pressing for news. Their cases drew attention that anonymous captives rarely got. The file documents that attention at the agency level, tracking reporters who had gone to cover the war and became its story.
cia-0000011843:
American troops had landed in the Dominican Republic in 1965 to stop a civil war, and in May 1966 the CIA reported on security conditions there. The intervention had ended the fighting but left the island's politics in a tangle. Elections were near, and the question was whether order would hold once the troops went home.

The report weighs the armed forces, the rival parties, and the risk of fresh violence. It treats the calm as real but fragile, built on an outside presence. For readers, it shows the morning after an intervention, when Washington tried to judge what its landing had bought.
cia-0000012243:
Indonesia and Malaysia were locked in an undeclared war called Confrontation when the CIA weighed both countries' prospects in June 1965. President Sukarno had vowed to crush the new Malaysian federation, which he called a British puppet. Indonesian raids and British-led defenses ground on across Borneo while Sukarno's rule weakened at home.

The paper weighs the fight's course and the future of Sukarno's guided democracy. It also judges what Malaysia could withstand and what Jakarta might do next. Written months before Indonesia's violent upheaval that fall, it shows analysts reading a region on the edge.
cia-0000013143:
General Vang Pao, the Hmong commander of America's secret army in Laos, speaks in a statement recorded in January 1974. His subject is the missing: men held, or said to be held, in North Vietnam after the war's formal end. The Paris accords were a year old, the prisoners were supposed to be home, and the accounting was already failing.

The statement preserves the general's claims in his own voice. His words carried weight with Americans who had fought beside his men in the hills. For readers, it is a Laotian witness speaking into the war's longest argument.
cia-0000013243:
Rules for allied prisoners in Viet Cong Military Region IV are set out in a CIA item from September 1967. Region IV covered the Mekong Delta, the war's watery south. The item shows how the rules changed from place to place. Each zone's chief ran his camps in his own way, under the same flag but with different habits, rations, and degrees of mercy.

The zone-by-zone view is the item's value to the accounting. The same war produced different rules for the jailed in different country. For readers, the page shows a system that was one system on paper only.
cia-0000015243: Davidson wanted a word for word translation of a space message, in a CIA file dated November 3, 1957. Leon Davidson was a keen amateur who pressed agencies on saucer lore. A claimed message from space was just the sort of item he chased. The file shows officials fielding requests that mixed hope, hoax, and hard curiosity.
cia-0000015443: Der Flieger, a German sports magazine, drew CIA notice in an untitled item dated July 5, 1952. The item gives information on the magazine and an article connected with it. That a sports paper earned a file shows how wide the agency's reading ran in the early Cold War. Even small foreign items were clipped, judged, and kept for later use.
cia-0000020343: An alleged attempt on the life of Castillo Armas is reported in a CIA record dated in 1955. The word alleged does the honest work here, since the title claims no proof. Leaders who took power by force often faced plots, real and rumored alike. The agency logged this one as part of its watch on the safety of Guatemala's ruler.
cia-0000023243: The Peronist Armed Forces, and possible involvement by a deleted party in an assassination the clipped title cuts short, fill a redacted CIA record dated in 1973. Peronism was the movement of Juan Peron, then returning to power in Argentina. Armed groups and political killing marked that year in Buenos Aires. Heavy deletions leave the topic clear and the actors hidden from the reader.
cia-0000027943: Conditions and trends in tropical Africa are surveyed in a CIA paper dated in 1956. Tropical Africa was then mostly under European rule, with freedom movements rising in colony after colony. Ghana's independence came the next year and opened a flood. A 1956 survey catches the continent on the edge of a change that redrew its map within a decade.
cia-0000036843:
Two American pilots shot down over North Vietnam were interviewed, and a CIA record dated October 5, 1967 keeps the account. The file names McCain and Flynn in connection with the interview. Prisoner interviews were staged by Hanoi and watched closely by the United States.

Inside are the pilots' words as they were reported, spoken under captivity's hard limits. Such interviews served Hanoi as propaganda, yet they also proved the men were alive. Families scanned every line for news, and officials filed each word for the record. Two voices in one interview also let analysts compare the men's condition and treatment side by side.
cia-0000044043:
The funeral of the slain Jesuits began amid tight security, a CIA record dated October 1, 1989 in the catalog reports. A funeral under heavy guard tells its own story about a country. The mourners gathered to bury priests killed in their own home.

Inside, the scene at the funeral is recorded as it unfolded. Security forces watched a rite of grief as if it were a threat. That watchfulness said much about the fear running through the capital. The file preserves the burial's tense public face, in a war where even mourning had become a political act in the streets.
cia-0000049043: A Newsweek article about Ambassador Deane Hinton is preserved in a CIA item from 1982, filed with the Truth Commission records. Hinton was Washington's envoy to El Salvador in the war's hardest years, a figure praised and blamed in equal measure. Magazine portraits like this one fixed how the American public saw the man running the policy.
cia-0000049143: The Catholic archbishop of Guatemala asked organized labor for support in 1989, and a CIA item preserves the request. Church and labor were the two great networks of ordinary people in Central America, and an archbishop's appeal joined them. The item sits in the Truth Commission file series, a reminder the war's politics crossed every border.
cia-0000049243: Intelligence documents relating to death squad activity in El Salvador are gathered in a CIA item from 1984. The item is a file about files: papers collected because together they built the picture of the squads. It survives in the Truth Commission records, where that picture became charges and findings in time.
cia-0000049343: Salvadoran National Guardsmen linked to murders is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000049343, dated April 3, 1981. Marked for the Truth Commission, the item connects members of the National Guard to killings in El Salvador. It is a short declassified record whose title carries its main claim, preserved among the agency's files on violence in the country.
cia-0000075243: Results of photo comparison in case number 12473 are reported in declassified CIA document 0000075243, dated January 2, 1971. Unlike the Salvadoran papers around it, the file concerns a numbered photo comparison case. Readers find a brief declassified result item whose heading gives only the case number and the comparison's purpose, with no person named in the record.
cia-0000095043: Comments by UAR President Nasir on topics related to the recent hostilities are recorded in declassified CIA document 0000095043, dated June 1, 1967. The heading is cut short in the catalog after the word And. The brief file preserves reported remarks by Egypt's president, a dated record of a leader's comments rather than agency analysis.
cia-0000096943: Internal routing and record sheet for a document titled Proposed CIA Response, with the rest cut short, is declassified CIA document 0000096943, dated February 3, 1973. Internal is misspelled in the original heading. Readers get the paperwork that moved another document, a routing sheet preserved as its own record rather than the response it carried.
cia-0000107443: Communists and the Palestine Question: Missions to Russia: New Head of Armenian is the heading, cut off mid-item, on declassified CIA document 0000107443, dated January 1, 1947. The title bundles three items, joined by colons in the heading. The third item breaks off after the word Armenian in the release. The brief record is a bundled news item from the first day of 1947.
cia-0000112343: Strip Mining Pollutes Dalnegorsk, Martime Kray is the heading, with Maritime misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000112343, dated October 1, 1991. The title ties strip mining to pollution in one named town, Dalnegorsk. The region is named too, in the heading's misspelled form. The brief record preserves the misspelling exactly as released in the files from that autumn there.
cia-0000119743: Timed to 4 p.m. Washington time on October 30, 1956, this CIA situation report covers Hungary seven days into the revolution. The timestamp shows the tempo of crisis reporting, and the paper gives the view from the capital at a turning hour. Marking the hour in Washington time rather than Budapest time shows the report's audience: officials working an ocean away from the streets in question.
cia-0000126943: Dated around April 1986, this CIA Terrorism Review covers an attack on the American chancery in La Paz, Bolivia, the heading breaking off. An assault on the embassy struck directly at the United States presence in the country. The review sets out the incident and its setting. Chancery attacks drew full reviews because the chancery housed the working embassy, and a strike there tested both local guards and American building standards abroad.
cia-0000132143: Dated August 1988, this CIA European Brief for August 18 covers Pakistan. Its subject is the crash that killed the Pakistani president and the American ambassador, with Pakistan misspelled in the heading. It stands as companion to the Middle East Brief on the same day's crisis. Two briefs on one crash show how regional desks divided the world: the same deaths in Pakistan reached European readers as a neighboring desk's crisis.
cia-0000132643:
Relations between Venezuela and Cuba going downhill fill a CIA paper dated May 5, 1960. Caracas had moved from sympathy to suspicion in the space of a single year. The Betancourt government saw Havana's hand behind its own guerrilla troubles at home, and said so in public.

The paper charts that decline step by step, meeting by meeting. A full break in ties would come in 1961, and this report catches the slide well before it. For readers, the entry shows a friendship curdling in dated stages. It also shows how one government's fears about rebels at home reshaped its foreign policy abroad in a single season.
cia-0000132743: Cuba and Central America are treated together in a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. Guatemala, Nicaragua, and El Salvador stood among the neighbors in Havana's sights. The isthmus would become the next great battleground of the Cold War in the years ahead. The short paper surveys the region in that light, country by country.
cia-0000135643: A document in Spanish dated 5 February 1961, filed with the declassified papers of Brigade 2506. The brigade, made up of exiles opposed to Fidel Castro, was training under CIA direction for the invasion of Cuba. The record for this item names no topic or writer. Its value is as a primary source in the brigade's own language, dated to the final training weeks. The text itself, available here in full, is the evidence for anything more specific.
cia-0000135743: This Spanish-language record, dated 2 March 1961, comes from the declassified document set of Brigade 2506, the CIA-trained Cuban exile force. Early March was planning and training time, six weeks before the landing. The catalog title offers no subject for the item. It stands in the original Spanish as a dated fragment of the brigade's paperwork, released through the CIA Reading Room for direct reading.
cia-0000135943: One CIA cable dated 1 January 1954 handles the identification of a contact, a name put to a face and reported by the Lincoln station. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136243: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 5 May 1954, long since declassified, on stated opposition to the bomb drop instructions, a pushback against the bombing plan. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136343: A message from the Guatemala station, relayed to CADICK in this 29 June 1954 cable, reports a junta figure seeking a cease-fire.
