Forti edited Isaac Abravanel's work on salvation at Ferrara in 1551. His preface to it gives Abravanel's life. He also printed another scholar's strictures on a book of the articles of faith in 1556. Later he supplied an alphabetical index to the Mishneh Torah, printed at Venice in 1586. Four short source lines close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-furth-meyer-b-e: Meyer ben Elhanan Furth, a German writer and teacher, stood apart from the Meassefim circle as a conservative voice. He wrote against Reform and its backers. His books include a first guide to algebra from 1806-08 and a plan for a lasting calendar from 1810. He glossed older works on the calendar and on the soul. Several tracts defend older practice against Reform books of his day. His last named work, from 1820-21, treats Maimonides rules on the new moon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ge-harashim-a-v: Ge-harashim means the valley of craftsmen. The entry ties the name to two towns. One was founded by Joab of the tribe of Judah, in First Chronicles iv. 14. The other was held by Benjamites, in Nehemiah xi. 35. In that passage Ge-harashim is named with Lod and Ono. A Jerusalem Talmud note treats those two towns as part of Ge-harashim itself. No size, events, or later history are given in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-get-bill-of-div:
The get is the Jewish bill of divorce. Deuteronomy xxiv speaks of it as a thing well known, though its first use cannot be fixed. In Mishnah times its form stayed plain. It needed the date, the place, the names, and the phrase that the wife is free to any man. Babylonian schools later fixed its full form and wording.

The husband must order the scribe in person. The bill may be written on most materials with lasting ink. It must be made for the pair at hand, never filled in from a blank form. Set words free the wife to marry any man she wishes. Names must be spelled with great care, and witnesses must sign the same day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grace-at-meals-:
Grace at meals means the blessings said before and after eating. The duty of grace after a meal comes from Deuteronomy viii. 10. Eat, be sated, and bless, the verse runs. Only bread of wheat or barley earns the full blessing. Other foods of the land's seven kinds get a shortened form. When three or more men eat together, one leads the grace aloud.

The entry prints the calls and answers of that rite. With ten men, God's name enters the formula. The grace itself has three old blessings, the entry says. A fourth was added after the Bethar massacre. It thanks God "who is good and doeth good." Grace before bread is also quoted. Prayer-books of both rites run past 350 Hebrew words for the full text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gunsburg-karl-s:
Karl Siegfried Günsburg was a German author and preacher. He was born on Dec. 9, 1784, at Lissa. He died at Breslau on Jan. 23, 1860. He studied philology and philosophy at Berlin. With Ed. Kley he published a book of devotions in 1813-14. He preached for some years in Berlin's Jacobson Temple. In 1819 he settled at Breslau and took an active part in its community.

In 1859 he gave his library to the Lehr- und Leseverein, which Abraham Geiger had founded in 1842. His "Parabeln" ran to two volumes in 1820 and three in 1826. He also wrote "Der Geist des Orients" in 1830. With Kley he published a German prayer-book in 1817-18.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hagiz-moses-704:
Moses Ḥagiz, born at Jerusalem in 1671, was a Palestinian rabbi and author who died at Safed after 1750. His father Jacob died in his childhood, so his grandfather Moses Galante raised him. When support from Leghorn stopped in 1689, he fell into hard times and made bitter foes at Safed.

Funds meant for a study house vanished amid slander from his foes. He wandered Italy, then lived by teaching at Amsterdam. There he helped Ẓebi Ashkenazi expose the impostor Nehemiah Ḥayyun, a stand that drove him from the city in 1714. He lived at Altona until 1738, then went home to Palestine. His many books include "Leḳeṭ ha-Ḳemaḥ," "Eleh ha-Miẓwot" on the 613 commandments, and "Sheber Posh'im" against Ḥayyun.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hammath-hot-spr: Hammath was one of the fortified cities of Naphtali, named at Joshua xix. 35. The entry is short. It holds that Hammath is likely the same as Hammoth-dor, a town given to the Levites in Naphtali at Joshua xxi. 32. In the matching list at I Chronicles vi. 76 that town is called Hammon. For the place's position the reader is sent to the Emmaus article, and nothing more is said here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haran-road-comp:
Haran is the city Terah reached from Ur of the Chaldees and died in, set in Aram-naharaim, or Padan-aram. Because Nahor alone of Terah's sons settled there, it was called the city of Nahor. Rebekah was born there; Abraham's servant met her there; and Jacob fled there, married Laban's daughters, and grew rich. Later the Assyrian kings took it, and Tyre traded with it.

Assyrian inscriptions mention Haran often: Assurbanipal was crowned there, and Nabunaid restored the temple of Sin there. The general opinion identifies it with Carrhae in Mesopotamia, famed for Crassus's defeat by the Parthians. Joseph Halévy dissented, placing it in Syria near Damascus, but the Arabian geographers side with Carrhae, a day's journey southeast of Edessa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-havilah-lit-the:
Havilah, a name meaning the sandy land, marks a district or districts in Arabia. Saul struck the Amalekites from Havilah toward Shur, near Egypt. Genesis also lists a Havilah among the sons of Joktan, linked with Sheba and Ophir. A third Havilah, ringed by the river Pison, was famed for gold and precious stones.

Scholars cited here place the land in the north, the south, or the center of Arabia. One view ties it to Yemen, a source of gold in old times. Another looks across the sea to Africa. The entry leaves the question open. It weighs inscription evidence and the views of many named writers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hurewitz-israel: Israel Hurewitz, who wrote as Z. Libin, was a Russian-American playwright born in December 1872 at Gorki. From 1885 to 1888 his brother gave him some secular schooling. He worked at a trade, moved to London in 1892, and reached the United States nine months later. His Yidishe Sketches of 1902 drew Russian-Jewish life in New York with care. From 1898 he wrote plays for the New York Judeo-German stage. Four titles are listed, ending with Gebrochene Hertzer in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-zabarra-jud: Judah ibn Zabarra was a poet and theologian of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, probably a native of Spain. He studied under Aaron ha-Levi, who died in 1293 or 1294, and under Meir Abulafia. He seems to have spent some time at Montpellier. His treatise on resurrection was printed at Constantinople in 1569. Only one of his poems survives. It celebrates the works of Menahem Meiri of Perpignan, and it is known from the preface to an edition of Meiri's introduction.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ireland-8143:
Ireland's first authentic mention of Jews dates to 1079, when five Jews came over the sea bearing gifts to King Fairdelbach and were sent back over the sea. Nearly a century passes before Henry II.'s reign, when Strongbow's forbidden expedition was financed, the record suggests, by Josce Jew of Gloucester, fined 100 shillings in 1170 for the loan.

By July 28, 1232, Henry III. had granted Peter de Rivall custody of the king's Judaism in Ireland, so a community existed, probably near Dublin. The record then falls silent after about 1286; the expulsion of 1290 presumably took the Irish Jews too. Settlement resumed under Cromwell, and Dublin's congregation, reorganized about 1822, built its present synagogue in Adelaide road.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaiah-ben-mali:
Isaiah ben Mali di Trani the Elder, known as the RiD, was a leading Italian Talmudist born about 1180 who died about 1250. He came from Trani, an old seat of Jewish learning, and probably lived in Venice. He exchanged letters with Simhah of Speyer and with Isaac ben Moses of Vienna. He left a learned son and a daughter, whose own son was Isaiah the Younger, often confused with him.

His writing was vast: glosses on Rashi's Pentateuch notes, tosafot on nearly the whole Talmud, sets of decisions, and a work on ninety-two legal topics. The entry praises his clarity: he could lay out the hardest topics with ease. He judged Rashi, Alfasi, and Jacob Tam as sharply as he judged himself when he changed his mind. Güdemann held that for Italy he held the place Maimonides held for the Orient.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ishak-ben-ya-ku:
Ishak ben Ya'kub Obadiah Abu Isa al-Isfahani was a Persian founder of a Jewish sect who lived under the calif Abd al-Malik (684-705). The entry calls him a plain tailor who could neither read nor write, yet, his followers said, wrote books unaided. He claimed to be the last of five messengers sent before the Messiah, his herald and prophet. Some accounts say he later claimed to be the Messiah himself.

He raised a revolt against the calif, and the decisive battle was fought at Rai. One account has him killed there; another says he hid in a cave and his fate stayed unknown. His followers, the Isawites, kept his rules after him. They gave up wine and meat, barred divorce, and prayed seven times a day. They also honored Jesus and Mohammed as prophets sent to their own nations, and they kept the Rabbinite calendar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-napht:
Jacob ben Naphtali was a Talmudist of Gnesen who worked about 1650. His father had been clerk of the Jewry in Great Poland and died in 1646. A fire took Jacob's fortune and his books, and he had to wander with no clear aim. At Amsterdam in 1652 he published "Nahalat Ya'akob: Melizot," a book of poems.

The poems include a dialogue between the body and the soul, hymns for the dedication of a Torah scroll, and elegies on the Cossack massacre of 1648. Jacob also worked as a corrector, overseeing the printing of Nathan Hanover's "Yewen Mezulah" at Venice in 1653. In 1654 he planned to go to Rome to win the pope a letter of protection against the blood charge. Moses Zacuto recommended him warmly to the Italian communities for that errand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jamaica-13943:
Jamaica is the largest island in the British West Indies, with a total population counted in 1901 as 644,841, of whom about 2,400 were Jews. When England took the island in 1655, many Jewish residents were found there. They were known as Portugals, a name Sephardic Jews used to hide their faith from Spanish persecution.

Because the Columbus family's rights kept the Inquisition out, Jews had lived on the island in fair safety under Spanish rule. After the conquest they built much of its trade, and settlers came from England, Curaçao, and Germany. The entry notes that vanilla, sugar, and most foreign trade sat largely in Jewish hands in the early seventeen hundreds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jehoiachin-8543:
Jehoiachin was a king of Judah, son and heir of Jehoiakim, who ruled a little over three months. Jerusalem came under siege by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon almost at once. Unable to resist, the young king gave himself up with his mother, servants, and officers, and all were sent captive to Babylon with the palace wealth and Temple vessels.

For thirty-six years he stayed in prison at Babylon. When Nebuchadnezzar died, his son freed Jehoiachin and gave him an honored seat at the royal table. Rabbinic tales in the entry tell of Temple keys thrown to heaven and of a king changed and pardoned through sorrow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-ledger-t: Jewish Ledger was a weekly journal founded in New Orleans on Jan. 4, 1895, by A. Steeg, who still published it in 1904. Alexander Harris was its first editor. Maurice Switzer followed him, and Max Heller edited the paper in 1896 and 1897. Its editor at the time of the entry was M. J. Lehman, who had earlier run the Jewish Times. The entry ends with the paper's lean: its tendency is toward moderate Reform. No word is given on its size or reach.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joigny-8743: Joigny is the chief town of its district in the Yonne region of France, set on the River Yonne. It held a weighty Jewish community that did best in the twelfth century. The town's leading men are named in an old prayer book. Its rabbis ranked among the most important in France. Two are named here: Menahem ben Perez, who died late in the twelfth century, and Yom-Tob ben Isaac, called the Holy, the martyr, who died at York in England in 1190.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-abba-ben-h:
Jose, called Abba Jose ben Hanin, was a Palestinian teacher of the last decades before the Temple fell. He appears in a law debate beside Eliezer ben Jacob and Hanina ben Antigonus. His name also runs in several other forms, among them Abba Joseph and Abba Issi. That spread adds some muddle to his record. He passed on teachings from two older men.

His fame rests on one burning sentence against the priestly houses of his day. Woe to me, he cried, for the house of Baithus and its rods. Woe for the house of Hanin and its whispering lies. Woe for the house of Katros and its pens. Woe for the house of Ishmael ben Phabi and its fists. The entry closes with a scholar's doubt over who truly spoke those words.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-isaa: Joseph ben Isaac ha-Levi was a Lithuanian thinker of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Well read in philosophy, he was asked while in Prague to explain Maimonides' Guide to Yom-Tob Lipman Heller. Out of that teaching came his book Gib'at ha-Moreh, printed at Prague in 1611 with Heller's notes. Its three parts test Maimonides' proofs for the being of God, his denial that God has human traits, and his proofs for God's unity. A second book set out the Guide's main ideas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaufman-illario:
Illarion Ignatyevich Kaufman was a Russian student of money and state finance. He was born at Odessa in 1847. He finished his studies at the University of Kharkof. He entered state service in 1870. His writing deals most with currency and loans. State debts drew his closest study.

With the central panel on statistics, Kaufman printed key studies of Russian finance. One covers the years 1862 to 1884. Others treat bank notes, bank figures, and exchange rates over fifty years. Since 1893 he has taught statistics at the University of St. Petersburg. He sat for fifteen years on the board of the Landowners' Bank. At the time of the entry he sat on the board of the Imperial Bank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kirjathaim-r-v-: Kirjathaim, "two cities," is the name of two places in this entry. The first is a city on the Moabite plateau. Moses assigned it to the tribe of Reuben. Mesha's inscription says he had built or fortified it. The plain of Shaveh Kiriathaim took its name from this town. Many scholars identify it with ruins now called Ḳariyah. The second Kirjathaim was a city in Naphtali. It was assigned to the Gershonite Levites. In Joshua's parallel list it is called Kartan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kol-nidre-all-v:
Kol Nidre, meaning all vows, opens the evening service on the Day of Atonement, taking its name from its first words. Before sunset the Ark is opened and two Torah scrolls are taken out. The cantor then chants the Aramaic prayer three times, rising from very soft to full voice. The words ask that vows made from one Day of Atonement to the next be forgiven and annulled.

A long and stormy history fills most of the entry. Geonim opposed the prayer, later scholars rewrote its tense, and many western communities dropped it in the nineteenth century. The entry also answers the charge that the prayer frees Jews from oaths to others, stressing that it covers only vows a person takes on alone before God. Its famous melody gets a full section of its own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kuhn-abraham-95: Abraham Kuhn, a German physician born at Bissersheim in Alsace on Jan. 28, 1838, died at Strasburg on Sept. 15, 1900. He studied at five universities and took his medical degree in 1863. At Strasburg he gained a second diploma in 1865 and began lecturing. In 1873 he became assistant professor and head of the clinic for throat and nose diseases. His essays ran in French and German medical journals. His books study the inner ear of fish, amphibians, reptiles, and birds, dated from 1878 to 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-l-arronge-adolf:
Adolf L'Arronge, a German dramatist and theater manager born in Hamburg on March 8, 1838, trained as a musician at Leipsic. Work as an orchestra conductor in several cities came first. In 1866 he took over an opera house in Berlin and began writing farces. His play Mein Leopold, staged in 1873, made his name at once.

Stage hits and theater building fill the rest. Hasemann's Töchter and Doktor Klaus, both from his Breslau years, ran long and still play. In 1883 he reopened a Berlin house as the Deutsche Theater and led it until 1894. New plays kept coming through 1896, alongside a book on the German theater itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-liverpool-10043:
Liverpool, chief seaport in northwest England on the Mersey, had an early Jewish settlement about 1750 that later died out. Tombstones with Hebrew writing were found in an old part of the city. A synagogue marked on a map from 1796 had vanished by 1803.

Jews gathered again about 1780, many of them dealers from Germany, Poland, and London. The town gave them sites for worship and burial over the years. A breakaway group formed in 1838 and built its own synagogue in 1857. Liverpool also saw sermons in English as early as 1806 and the first British group tied to a world Jewish alliance in 1868.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowe-moses-samu:
Moses Samuel Löwe, also known as Johann Michael Siegfried Löwe, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a German painter and engraver born at Königsberg, Prussia, on June 24, 1756. Helped by the Friedländer family, he built such a reputation that Catherine II of Russia commissioned her portrait from him by 1780. He died at Königsberg in 1831.

The entry presents him as one of the foremost miniaturists and pastel painters of his time. His pictures ranked among the most popular at German exhibitions. It also notes that he was a master chess player. His 1806 book of portraits of living Berlin scholars, with their own life stories, drew praise from Goethe. The article is a compact record of a Jewish artist who reached the top of German portrait painting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machir-10243:
Machir, a Babylonian scholar who settled in Narbonne, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. He arrived in France at the end of the eighth century. For generations his descendants led the important community of Narbonne. Tradition in Ibn Daud's Sefer ha-Kabbalah makes him a descendant of the house of David.

The article tells the famous story with care. The calif Harun al-Rashid is said to have sent Machir west at Charlemagne's request. The emperor supposedly honored him with the title king of the Jews and a section of the city. The entry calls this relation probably legendary. Yet it confirms that the family held real privileges for centuries and bore the title nasi, or prince. Benjamin of Tudela saw their high standing in 1165. Machir also founded a Talmud school that rivaled Babylonia's and drew pupils from afar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manasseh-10343:
Manasseh, the tribe that settled on both sides of the Jordan, is traced in a multi-author Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. The eastern part, won after the conquest of Gilead, suited cattle grazing. It ran from the Jabbok up toward Mount Hermon. Western Manasseh stretched from Ephraim to the slopes of Mount Carmel.

The article judges the tribe's later record uneven. It never fully drove out the native peoples of its western land. At David's rise it sent large forces to Hebron, the east sending far more than the west. Both halves appear again under Asa, Hezekiah, and Josiah in reforms and Temple repairs. Yet the eastern tribes finally lost their identity, blending with the peoples around them. Chronicles charges them with chasing the gods of the land. The entry also reaches the second Manasseh, the boy king of Judah whose fifty-three years formed Judah's longest reign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mediator-greek-:
Mediator, an intercessor standing between God and man, is a role Judaism in principle refuses, and a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Kaufmann Kohler works through the tension. Its proof texts are blunt: "The Lord alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him." When offered an angel as guide instead of God's own presence, Moses answers, "If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence."

Yet the article admits the distance between God and frail people felt too wide, and Scripture itself supplies intercessors. Abraham prays for Abimelech, Moses for Pharaoh and for Israel, Samuel and Jeremiah for their generations, and Noah, Daniel, and Job save others by their righteousness. In the later apocryphal and Hellenistic books the idea grows stronger: angels carry men's prayers to the throne, and Jeremiah is pictured praying much for the people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-sar:
Menahem ben Saruk was a tenth-century Spanish philologist. He compiled the first great Hebrew dictionary. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a native of Tortosa. At Cordova he found a patron in Isaac ibn Shaprut. He mourned Isaac in synagogue inscription and elegy. Isaac's son Hasdai recalled him. Hasdai was the great statesman. Menahem was to finish his dictionary for Hasdai. He was also to draft the famous letter to the king of the Khazars.

Patronage then turned cruel. Dunash ben Labrat attacked the dictionary. Slanderers inflamed Hasdai against him. Menahem was beaten by his protector's order. His house was destroyed too. His pleading letter to Hasdai survives. His pupils answered Dunash in a refutation. It was so exact that one pupil stands out. That pupil, Judah Hayyuj, went on to found scientific Hebrew grammar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mond-ludwig-109:
Ludwig Mond was born at Cassel on March 7, 1839. He was the German chemist who built England's alkali industry. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Trained at Cassel, Marburg, and Heidelberg, he crossed to England in 1862. He entered the Le Blanc soda trade. There he introduced a way to recover sulfur from alkali waste.

In 1873, with Brunner, he set up at Winnington in Cheshire. They made ammonia soda by the Solvay process, which he perfected. The works became the largest alkali establishment in the world. Patents multiplied. In 1896 he founded and endowed the Davy-Faraday Research Laboratory at the Royal Institution. The entry lists his presidencies and fellowships. They are the honors of industrial chemistry's first rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-sason-mor:
Sason Mordecai Moses was a Turkish cabalist and Talmudist who lived at Bagdad. Joseph Jacobs and N. E. B. Ezra wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1747, he died at Bagdad in 1831. His books were printed long after his death, at Leghorn and at Bagdad itself.

His Kol Sason treats ethics, and his Dabar be-Itto comments on the Pentateuch and the Talmud in two volumes. He also wrote on ritual in Mizmor le-Asaf and on ethics again in Imre Sason. A fire in his house in 1853 destroyed a large number of his manuscripts. The entry shows how much of a Bagdad sage's work could vanish at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mussafia-adolf-:
Adolf Mussafia was an Austrian Romance philologist born at Spalato in Dalmatia on February 15, 1835. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Meant at first for medicine, he became an instructor in Italian at Vienna in 1855. By 1867 he was a full professor of Romance philology there.

Mussafia made his specialty the early Italian dialects, publishing the Monumenti Antichi in 1864. He also issued a Catalan version, in verse, of the Seven Wise Masters. His Italian grammar was so popular that it reached a twenty-fourth edition by 1895. The entry notes that he converted to Christianity and sat in the Austrian House of Lords.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-the-give:
Nathan was a prophet in the reign of King David. Emil G. Hirsch and Edward N. Calisch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name Nathan means the given one. He appears three times as the king's adviser. Each time his words shape the royal house.

First, Nathan blessed David's plan to build the Temple. That night God said David's son would build it instead. God also promised David a lasting dynasty. Next, Nathan rebuked David over Bath-sheba with a parable. A rich man had seized a poor man's only lamb. David condemned the man, and Nathan answered, Thou art the man. Last, Nathan helped secure the throne for Solomon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nepi-neppi-graz:
Graziadio Nepi was an Italian rabbi and physician. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Ferrara in 1759. He studied there twelve years under Rabbi Jacob Moses. He taught many pupils in his native city himself.

Nepi's Talmud learning sent him to Paris in 1806. He was deputy to Napoleon's Assembly of Jewish Notables. On his return, Cento called him as its rabbi. He held that post until his death in 1836. Italian rabbis sought his advice on hard problems. His books gather his responsa and his sermons. His sketches of rabbis sought to complete Azulai's work. Ghirondi finished and published that last book in 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppert-ernst-ja:
Ernst Jacob Oppert was a German merchant and far traveler. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hamburg on December 5, 1832. He died on September 19, in the year 1903. He was a brother of Jules Oppert, the scholar.

Ernst chose a life in trade while still a youth. In 1851 he went far off to Hong Kong. Later he founded a trade house at Shanghai, in China. In 1866 and 1868 he made trips through Korea. He then went home to Hamburg to live as a merchant. He wrote a book on his trips in Korea. Its title calls Korea a forbidden land to the world. It drew on his own notes and a priest's notes. He wrote books on East Asia and Japan as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-padua-11843:
Padua is a city of upper Italy, west of Venice. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands on the Bacchiglione, a small stream there. Its Jewish flock was one of the great ones of Italy. Synagogue and grave yard stood there as early as 1300.

The first Jew of Padua known by name was a doctor. Jacob Bonacosa put a great work into new speech there. He did that work of Averroes in the year 1255. Midway through the next age, Jews came in throngs to Padua. They came from Rome, Pisa, Bologna, and the Marches. The town's laws for them were free and mild in tone. Its folk bore them with good will, the piece notes. They were let in with no checks on their trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perpignan-hebre:
Perpignan was the old capital of Roussillon, in France. Joseph Jacobs and S. Kahn wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there by the late twelfth century. The kings of Aragon ruled the city back then.

Royal favor and royal limits came in turns. James the First freed Jewish land from tolls and dues. Later laws barred Christian servants in Jewish homes. In 1314 Jews were forced to wear a round badge. In 1415 Ferdinand ordered them to hear conversion sermons. Alphonse later let them drop the badge again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ra-is-12543: Ra'is was the title of the head of a Jewish community in Egypt. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The title held until the days of Mahmud the Second. Each town of Jews in Egypt had its own ra'is. The calif knew him and backed his rule. He held both prayer and court powers in his hands. Jews called the same man by the title nagid. He drew a fixed pay from his community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reggio-isaac-sa:
Isaac Samuel Reggio was an Austro-Italian scholar and rabbi born on August 15, 1784. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Göritz in Illyria. He died there on August 29, 1855.

The article says his father Abraham taught him Hebrew and rabbinics. School also gave him science and several languages. At fourteen he wrote a dirge in meter. Math became his favorite field for clear thinking. In 1802 he solved a hard math problem in print. He also found a new proof of the Pythagorean theorem. Cauchy, the French mathematician, praised that proof. Later he helped found a rabbinic seminary at Padua. The entry shows a mind at home in faith and number.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-richman-julia-1:
Julia Richman was an American educator born on October 12, 1855. Cyrus Adler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. She was born in New York City. She studied in its public schools and Normal College.

The article says she led public school No. 77 from 1884 to 1903. In 1903 she became a district superintendent. She was the first woman chosen for that office in New York. She pioneered special training for children with mental weakness. Her articles appeared in leading education journals. She also held many posts in Jewish communal life. She led charitable and educational groups for decades. She founded and edited a paper called Helpful Thoughts. The entry joins school reform with community service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rott-rosenberg-:
Moritz Rott, born Rosenberg, was an Austrian actor born at Prague on September 17, 1797. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A nephew of the composer Moscheles, he was meant for commerce, not the stage.

Rott debuted at Vienna in 1817 as Karl Moor in Schiller's Die Räuber. His success was instant, and city after city repeated it. From 1821 he led the Theater-an-der-Wien company for eight years. In 1832 he began a life engagement at Berlin's Hoftheater. There he became the favorite of the Prussian public and the king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salt-13043:
Salt is a condiment the Israelites found indispensable for flavoring food from earliest times. Emil G. Hirsch, Immanuel Benzinger, Cyrus Adler, and M. Seligsohn wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Palestine held a copious supply at home.

The Dead Sea, called the Salt Sea in Genesis, brims with salt. After floods, coarse salt crusts the pools and ditches along its shores. The hill Jebel Usdum, ten miles long, is almost pure rock salt. To eat a man's salt meant living on his pay, the entry notes. Our word salary itself descends from that salt money idea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-sir-saul:
Goodman Lipkind and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Sir Saul Samuel. He was an Australian statesman, born in London on November 2, 1820. In 1832 he emigrated to New South Wales with relatives. He died in London on August 29, 1900. His public career began in 1846, as a magistrate.

Samuel entered the New South Wales assembly in 1856. He joined the ministry in 1859. He served often as minister for finance and trade. He was postmaster-general three times as well. In 1880 he became the colony's agent-general in London. There he raised loans of some fifty million pounds. He wrote the Government Savings Bank Act and the Navigation Act. He also worked early for Australian federation. Honors followed, including a knighthood in 1882.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scala-nova-turk:
Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Galante wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Scala Nova. The Anatolian port, called Kuch Adassi in Turkish, faces the island of Samos. It served as the seaport of Ephesus. The oldest stone in its Jewish cemetery is dated 1682. Yet Jews likely lived there in the thirteenth century.

In 1307 a group of Jews left Scala Nova for Smyrna. After the expulsion from Spain, 250 Jewish families settled in the town. Many local family names are still Spanish. Plague in 1720 cut the families to sixty. By 1905 only thirty-three families remained. The synagogue, built in 1772, was rebuilt in 1900. The article also notes a false ritual-murder charge in the mid-nineteenth century. Anti-Jewish feeling tended to flare each Easter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwarz-peter-p:
Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Peter Schwarz. He was a German Dominican preacher and anti-Jewish writer. Schwarz worked in the fifteenth century. John Eck claimed he was a Jewish convert, but no proof exists. He took a bachelor's degree in theology. Then he turned to Hebrew language and literature.

At Salamanca, Schwarz secretly sat with Jewish children at rabbis' lectures. He wanted to perfect his Hebrew. He then won an imperial edict forcing Jews to hear his sermons. In 1474 he preached at Frankfort, Ratisbon, and Worms. He challenged each town's rabbis to dispute, and they declined. Enraged, he wrote two attacks on the Jews and Talmud. He called the Talmud infamous and fit to burn. His books carry Hebrew alphabets and grammar rules. They rank among Germany's earliest Hebrew-type printings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shem-tob-ben-ab:
Shem-Tob ben Abraham ibn Gaon was a Spanish Talmudist and cabalist born at Soria in 1283. Kaufmann Kohler and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied Talmud under Solomon ben Adret in Spain. For Cabala his teacher was Isaac ben Todros.

Hoping the Holy Land would suit deep meditation, Shem-Tob emigrated. He stayed a while in Jerusalem, then settled at Safed. At Safed he wrote the works listed in the entry. Only the first two of them reached print. Scholars still debate his family name Gaon. Some read it as a place name, Jaen, instead. He died in Palestine after 1330, a mystic far from his Spanish home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siegfried-karl-:
Karl Siegfried was a German Protestant theologian born at Magdeburg in 1830. Crawford Howell Toy and Frederick T. Haneman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. In 1875 he became professor of theology at Jena. In 1892 the church gave him a privy councilor's title.

Several Siegfried works matter specially to Jewish readers, the entry says. His Spinoza book treated that thinker as Bible critic and interpreter. His Philo of Alexandria volume became a standard work. It also traced the Haggadah's influence on Philo's thought. With Strack he wrote a textbook of later Hebrew language. He supplied its grammar part, the entry notes. He co-wrote a Hebrew dictionary of the Old Testament. He died at Jena in 1903, a Christian scholar deep in Jewish texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-joseph-13:
Joseph Simon was an American lawyer and politician born in Hesse in 1851. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His parents brought him to Portland, Oregon, in 1857. He was schooled there and admitted to the bar in 1872. He soon entered city and state politics.

Simon sat on the Portland city council from 1877. He chaired the Republican state committee three times. He served twenty years in the Oregon state senate. Five times his fellow senators chose him as their president. In 1898 he was elected to the United States Senate. His term ran until March 3, 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-seal-of:
Solomon's seal was a ring said to bear the name of God. Joseph Jacobs and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Legend says Solomon ruled demons by means of that ring. The Talmud tells the tale at length in Gittin. Arabic writers developed the legend still further in their works.

They said the ring was part brass and part iron. With brass he signed commands to good genii. With iron he signed commands to evil genii, or devils. Asmodeus once stole the ring and threw it into the sea. Solomon lost his power until he found it inside a fish. Arabs later gave the name to the six-pointed star figure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sterner-albert-:
Albert Edward Sterner was an English artist born in London on March 8, 1863. Joseph Jacobs and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied art in Paris at two noted schools. In 1881 he emigrated to the United States. He worked in Chicago before settling in New York.

In Chicago, Sterner did lithographic work and painted stage scenery. From 1885 he lived in New York City. He drew illustrations for Harper's, Century, and Scribner's magazines. His art for Prue and I made his name in black and white. He illustrated editions of Poe and of Mrs. Humphry Ward. His oil painting The Bachelor won a bronze medal in Paris in 1900. The entry follows an illustrator's transatlantic career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanya-14243:
Tanya is a collection of ritual laws and customs. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. It was first published at Mantua in 1514. A Cremona edition followed in 1565. Two more editions appeared after those.

The Mantua title page hints at an older name, Minhag Abot. One reading dates the work to 1314. Buber showed that date is a misprint for 1514. The book follows the plan of Shibbole ha-Leket. It quotes that work and its author Zedekiah often. Its writer cites Benjamin and Judah as teachers. Some pages speak in the voice of Jehiel the scribe. Scholars dispute who truly authored the collection. Candidates include Judah ben Benjamin and his pupil. The entry follows a customs book with a blurred byline.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tur-naphtali-wo: Naphtali Wolf Tur was a Russian Hebraist and poet born at Wilna. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He settled in Warsaw, teaching Hebrew and several modern languages. Sources disagree on whether he died in 1885 or 1884. He was a talented poet, the entry says. Early death left most of his work unpublished. His long poem Ha-Yobel honored Moses Montefiore's centenary. It appeared in the journal Ha-Asif. Other poems ran in Gottlober's Ha-Boker Or.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-van-straalen-sa:
Samuel Van Straalen was an English Hebraist and librarian. He was born at Gouda, Holland, in 1845 and died in London in 1902. Joseph Jacobs and Victor Rousseau Emanuel wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1873 Van Straalen became Hebrew librarian at the British Museum.

Van Straalen translated many Dutch, German, and Hebrew books. His best known work is a catalogue of the museum's Hebrew books. It appeared in London in 1894. The catalogue supplements the older one by Zedner. It also adds an index that covers both volumes. He prepared a subject catalogue too, but that one stayed unpublished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wachnacht-14743:
Wachnacht is the night before a boy's circumcision. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word is Judaeo German for watch night. Family, the mohel, and the sandik spend it in feasting. They recite hymns and prayers through the night.

The stated aim is to guard the child. Evil spirits, above all Lilith, were said to threaten him. The entry gives other, plainer reasons as well. The watch checked on the mother's health. It also readied the rite for the next day. Under past bans on circumcision, families met in secret. Closed doors and lamp light marked those risky nights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-winnipeg-14943:
Winnipeg is the capital of Manitoba, in Canada. Joseph Jacobs and Clarence I. de Sola wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands where the Assiniboine meets the Red River. The first lasting Jewish settlers arrived about 1878. Russian pogroms of 1881 sent three hundred more. Most of them built the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Later waves came from Rumania and Russia. By 1905 the community numbered near three thousand. The city's total population was about eighty thousand. Jews shared fully in trade, industry, and the professions. They hold much of the city's real estate. In 1904 Moses Finkelstein won election as alderman. Some families founded a farm colony at Oxbow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ximenes-sir-mor:
Morris Ximenes (born about 1762) was a London money man who left the Jewish fold. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He made a large fortune on the London Exchange. In 1802 his synagogue chose him as a warden of it.

He said no to that post of honor. The synagogue fined him for the refusal then. He quit the group and took the Christian faith. Later he took up a soldier's life in Kent. Men knew him then as Captain Ximenes on the road. He was made a knight for his service there. He served as high sheriff of Kent as well. His son held no tie to the Jewish group at all. The short entry rests on a book of Anglo-Jewish tales.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zephaniah-ben-m:
Zephaniah ben Mordecai Troki was a Karaite scholar and author. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the late part of the sixteenth century. He was the brother of Joseph ben Mordecai Troki.

His chief work treats the year count and the leap month. Its name joins the new moon rite with the leap year key. He wrote court replies on the laws of rite slaughter as well. Both works are named in a book by Simhah Luzki. That book is a guide to the ways of the just. The entry rests on a past of the Karaite sect in three books. It rests on a list of Hebrew books as well in brief. No facts of his birth or death are given in the piece.
liebig-familiar-letters-chemistry-1843:
Justus von Liebig published Familiar Letters on Chemistry in 1843, a popular book grown from letters on science for a general audience. Liebig wrote to show lay readers that chemistry touches their daily bread, farms, and health. The letters avoid formulas and argue in clear prose.

Liebig explained how chemistry serves agriculture and physiology, the themes of his two great technical books of 1842. He attacked the old idea that living things obey wholly separate laws, and he praised experiment over authority. The letters sold widely and were often reprinted and expanded. They made Liebig a public figure and stand as a model of how a working scientist can address the whole reading public.
matter-histoire-critique-du-gnosticisme-:
Jacques Matter's Histoire critique du Gnosticisme, published in French in 1843, was the first great documentary history of Gnosticism. Earlier writers had treated the subject in fragments; Matter assembled the scattered ancient evidence into one coherent story. His two-part study also traced the movement's influence on later religious sects.

Working through the church fathers and the sects' own traces, he built the field's first real archive. Modern study of early Christian heresy effectively begins with his volumes. The French text demands effort from English readers, but historians still respect its groundwork. Matter founded a discipline almost single-handedly. Anyone tracing how Gnosticism became a subject of scholarship should know his name.
mill-system-logic-vol-1-1843:
John Stuart Mill's System of Logic, Volume 1, appears here in a separate entry for the 1843 first edition's first volume. Mill's full title adds Ratiocinative and Inductive, naming the two kinds of reasoning he treated. Volume 1 covers names, propositions, and the start of induction.

Mill defined the words and statements logic works on, then asked how we prove anything at all. His answer gave pride of place to induction, learning general laws from observed cases. That focus made the book the founding text of the philosophy of science in English. Readers who use this entry get the original 1843 wording of the opening books, before Mill's many later revisions.
mill-system-logic-vol-2-1843:
John Stuart Mill's System of Logic, Volume 2, completes the 1843 first edition in this entry. The second volume carries induction forward and then turns to error and to the study of society. Mill wrote it as the payoff of the whole system.

Chapters finish the methods of causal proof, catalogue the fallacies that spoil argument, and defend a logic for the moral sciences. Mill claimed that history, politics, and the mind could be sciences, though softer ones than physics. That claim shaped how universities later built social science. Together with Volume 1, this entry preserves the complete first edition of a founding work.
mill-system-of-logic-1843:
John Stuart Mill published A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive in 1843. Mill, then in his thirties, set out the rules of proof for both math-like reasoning and the sciences of observation. The book made him a leading thinker of the Victorian age.

Mill defined terms, tested syllogisms, and then built his famous methods for finding causes by experiment and comparison. He argued that even the laws of nature rest on induction, reasoning from cases seen to cases unseen. Later parts applied logic to the study of society. Generations of students learned scientific method from Mill, and his methods are still taught by name.
mill-system-of-logic-vol-1-1843:
John Stuart Mill published Volume 1 of A System of Logic in 1843, the first half of his treatise on reasoning. This entry holds the first edition's first volume, Books 1 to 3 in part. Mill set out to ground all proof, including science, in experience.

Book 1 treats names and propositions, and Book 2 tests the syllogism and its limits. Book 3 begins induction, Mill's central subject, with his methods for finding causes. He held that logic is the science of evidence itself. The volume founded the modern study of inductive logic, and its account of how we learn from cases shaped the philosophy of science.
mill-system-of-logic-vol-2-1843:
Volume 2 of Mill's System of Logic, first edition of 1843, completes the work begun in Volume 1. John Stuart Mill carried induction through its harder cases and then turned to error and to society. Books 3 through 6 fill this second half.

Mill finished his account of causal proof, then catalogued fallacies, the stock errors of reasoning he thought corrupted debate. The last book treats the logic of the moral sciences, arguing that history and society can be studied scientifically. That defense of social science as science drew wide notice. The two volumes together formed the founding text of inductive logic in English.
moneta-adversus-catharos-1743:
Moneta of Cremona, a Dominican friar, finished his Adversus Catharos et Valdenses, Against the Cathars and Waldensians, around 1241. It is the great scholastic summa of the anti-heresy war in five books. Tommaso Agostino Ricchini edited the Latin text at Rome in 1743. Moneta wrote in Lombardy, where the Cathar churches stood strongest in Italy.

Book by book he states the heretics' claims on God, matter, marriage, and the church, then answers them from scripture and reason. His reports of Cathar teaching are full enough that scholars mine the attack as a source for the attacked. The work shows the schools of Paris turned into weapons. It is the high medieval counter-offensive in full armor.
openalex-w1995770643:
Michael Sweet, Nigel Kirkham, Mark Bendall and colleagues reported skin cancer in wild sea fish in PLoS ONE in 2012. They studied coral trout on the Great Barrier Reef in Australia. Skin cancer had been seen more often in people. It had not been reported in wild fish before.

The team found dark skin growths and melanoma in coral trout at two offshore sites. About fifteen in a hundred fish showed the condition. No germ cause was found in the fish. The growths looked like sun-linked melanomas seen in lab fish. The authors concluded that sun ultraviolet light was the likely cause. They called for wider surveys to map how far the condition spreads.
openalex-w2054012543:
Carla Schommer, Javier Palatnik, Pooja Aggarwal and colleagues found a new role for a small plant RNA. Their paper appeared in PLoS Biology in 2008. The RNA, called miR319, controls a family of gene switches. Those switches shape plant development. What the switches do next was largely unknown.

The team traced the chain from RNA to hormone. The switch genes control production of jasmonic acid. That hormone helps plants respond to stress and ageing. The switches also affect when leaves grow old. They slow leaf growth early in development. Later they speed up leaf ageing. So one RNA pathway coordinates two life stages. The finding links gene control to hormone balance.
openalex-w2135168743:
Jianbing Yan, Trushar Shah, Marilyn Warburton, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2009. They characterized a global collection of maize using SNP markers, single-letter DNA differences. The collection held hundreds of inbred lines from temperate, tropical, and subtropical breeding programs around the world.

A new assay tested over fifteen hundred markers across the lines. The team measured genetic diversity, population structure, and family relatedness among the lines. Tropical and temperate subgroups stood out, with complex family ties inside the collection. They also measured linkage disequilibrium, the distance over which DNA variants travel together. That distance varied by chromosome and grew when rare variants or small samples were used.
openalex-w2136669243:
Tim McClanahan, Simon Donner, Jeffrey Maynard, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2012. They tackle a management problem: coral reefs need plans that build resilience to climate change, but the science behind common advice is uneven. Managers need to know which signs of reef health matter most when choosing where to act.

The authors asked experts and reviewed the scientific literature together. They weighed the many physical and biological factors thought to shape how reefs withstand warming. Some widely used ideas lacked firm support in the evidence. The goal is a ranked, evidence-based set of indicators. With it, managers can identify priority reefs with less guesswork.
openalex-w2140214243:
María Dolores Bargues, Débora Klisiowicz, Fernando González-Candelas, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2008. They mapped the genetic geography of Triatoma dimidiata, the main insect vector of Chagas disease in Central America. The bug shows wide variety in looks, genes, and behavior across wild, yard, and home habitats.

The team combined DNA sequence analysis, family tree building, and variation measures. Their aim was to place this species inside its large genus and reveal its population structure. Wild populations that live outside homes matter because they can reinfest houses after spraying. Understanding this diversity helps control teams target the vector where it actually lives.
openalex-w2474124643:
Bruno Leite Sampaio, RuAngelie Edrada-Ebel, and Fernando B. Da Costa studied how weather and place change the chemistry of Tithonia diversifolia. Their 2016 paper appeared in Scientific Reports. The plant, called tree marigold or Mexican sunflower, is a fast-growing tropical weed. The team wanted a model for environmental metabolomics, the study of how conditions shape the small molecules a plant makes.

They sampled leaves, stems, roots, and flowers from two Brazilian states across twenty-four months. Chemical fingerprints came from liquid chromatography, mass spectrometry, and NMR, matched against monthly weather records. Sugars, sesquiterpene lactones, and phenolics in leaves and stems followed a seasonal pattern. That pattern tracked rainfall amounts and temperature changes. The study shows plant chemistry is not fixed; it shifts with the seasons and the local environment.
openalex-w2542984143:
Daniel Malko, Anthony R. Kucernak, and Thiago Lopes published this 2016 paper in Nature Communications. It tackles cheap catalysts for low-temperature fuel cells. Materials made of iron, nitrogen, and carbon could replace costly precious metals at the oxygen electrode. Their activity and durability, though, still fall short of what fuel cells need.

Improving them requires knowing how many active sites they hold and how fast each site works. Standard tools like Mössbauer and X-ray spectroscopy cannot measure those values at the working surface directly. The authors present an in situ electrochemical method to count active sites while the catalyst operates. Counting sites lets researchers link structure to activity in a rational way. That should guide designs with more sites, faster sites, or both.
openalex-w2616925143:
Joshua Quick, Nathan D. Grubaugh, and Steven T. Pullan, with a large team, present this 2017 protocol in Nature Protocols. It explains how to sequence virus genomes straight from patient samples. Fast sequencing during outbreaks reveals how a virus spreads and evolves. The method was sharpened during the Ebola epidemic and the Zika emergency.

The protocol uses multiplex PCR to copy a virus genome in many small overlapping pieces. Those pieces are then sequenced on portable MinION devices or Illumina machines. Working directly from clinical samples skips slow virus culture in the lab. The approach served genomic surveillance during recent epidemics, guiding outbreak investigations in near real time. Detailed steps let other laboratories repeat the workflow anywhere. That portability matters most where outbreaks start and lab infrastructure is thin.
openalex-w2947890843:
Purna Mukherjee, Zachary Augur, Mingyi Li, and colleagues published this study in Communications Biology in 2019. It tests a diet-based approach against glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor that has resisted treatment for decades. The work was done in mice with late-stage tumors.

Glioblastoma cells feed mainly on glucose and glutamine and cannot easily switch fuels, unlike healthy brain cells. The team combined a calorie-restricted ketogenic diet, which cuts glucose, with a treatment that targets glutamine. Starving the tumor of both fuels at once is the core idea. The authors report a therapeutic benefit from the combined approach in their mouse models, pointing to metabolism as a treatment angle.
openalex-w3036495543:
Maciel Queiroz, Dmitry Ivanov, Alexandre Dolgui, and Samuel Fosso Wamba published this review online in Annals of Operations Research in 2020. It maps research on how epidemic outbreaks hit supply chains, written as COVID-19 was disrupting trade worldwide. Prior work leaned on humanitarian logistics, leaving commercial supply chains understudied.

Through a structured review of the literature, the authors chart what had been studied and what had not. Influenza was the outbreak most often covered, and smarter allocation of scarce resources was the most popular topic. They propose a framework with six lenses: adaptation, digitalization, preparedness, recovery, ripple effects, and sustainability. From the gaps they draw a set of open research questions.
openalex-w3109379743:
Jaime Ramirez, Francisco Guarner, Luis Bustos Fernández, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2020. It casts antibiotics as major disruptors of the gut microbiota, the community of microbes living in the human intestine. Those microbes are now known to be required for the body to work at its best.

Most gut microbes cannot be grown in the lab, so they stayed unexplored until gene-based tools arrived. As early as 1885, Louis Pasteur guessed that animals raised without microbes could not survive. The review gathers what antibiotics do to this inner ecosystem: which groups they wipe out, how long recovery takes, and what harms follow. It makes the case for treating the microbiota as an organ worth protecting.
openalex-w3111605943:
Fotios Petropoulos, Daniele Apiletti, Vassilios Assimakopoulos, and colleagues wrote this review in the International Journal of Forecasting in 2022. Titled simply Forecasting: theory and practice, it is a vast survey of how predictions are made and judged. The author list spans dozens of specialists across the field's branches.

The review runs from forecasting theory through data preparation, methods, and evaluation. It treats classic statistical tools alongside newer machine learning approaches. Practical questions, such as cleaning data and spotting anomalies, sit beside deep questions about uncertainty. At well over one hundred fifty pages, it serves as a handbook for students and a map for researchers. Few single works attempt the whole field at once.
openalex-w3113178943:
Gregory Roth, George Mensah, Catherine Johnson, and colleagues published this state-of-the-art review in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology in 2020. It updates the global burden of cardiovascular diseases and their risk factors from 1990 to 2019. Heart and vessel diseases remain the leading cause of death worldwide.

Drawing on the Global Burden of Disease 2019 study, the authors cover thirteen causes of cardiovascular death and nine related risk factors. The collaboration pools all population-level data to give comparable estimates for two hundred four countries and territories. Total cases of cardiovascular disease nearly doubled over the three decades, reaching over five hundred million. Ischemic heart disease and stroke drive most of that burden and the disability it brings.
openalex-w3215126343:
Ronald van Vollenhoven, George Bertsias, Andrea Doria, and colleagues present a task force definition of remission in lupus. Their recommendations appeared in Lupus Science and Medicine in 2021. Lupus, shortened to SLE, is a long-term autoimmune disease with flares and quiet periods. Remission is the stated goal of care, yet doctors lacked one agreed meaning for it. An earlier task force framework had stopped short of a final definition.

The group ran systematic literature reviews and tested questions in chosen data sets. Members then debated the findings, rewrote them as recommendations, and voted. Patients sat on the task force alongside specialists from many countries. A single shared definition lets trials and clinics judge success the same way.
openalex-w4318071643:
Ditte Demontis, G. Bragi Walters, Georgios Athanasiadis, and colleagues present a genome-wide study of ADHD in Nature Genetics in 2023. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is a common brain development disorder with a strong genetic part. The team combined genetic data from nearly thirty-nine thousand people with ADHD and far more controls. They searched the whole genome for variants that raise the odds of the disorder.

The search found twenty-seven significant loci, pointing to seventy-six possible risk genes. These genes are active above all in early brain development and in certain neuron types, including midbrain dopamine neurons. Most ADHD-linked variants are shared with other psychiatric disorders. Genetic risk also tracked with weaker verbal reasoning and executive functions, such as attention itself.
openalex-w7133357343:
Takehito Shukuya of Juntendo University in Tokyo wrote a 2026 review of drug treatment for cancers of the chest, above all lung cancer. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer worldwide. The review covers how gene testing now lets doctors match drugs to the exact changes driving each tumor.

Successive generations of targeted pills for tumors with EGFR or ALK changes have lengthened disease control, including in the brain. Antibody-drug conjugates add another option for some patients. Immune therapy now sits at the center of care for both main lung cancer types. Shukuya also reports a Japanese trial in rare thymic cancer and a new immune drug that improved survival in relapsed small cell lung cancer.
openalex-w7204169643:
Ingrid Prado Souto led a Portuguese-language practice report, in Brazil in 2026, on health schooling in a quilombola community in southwestern Bahia. Quilombola communities descend from settlements of escaped enslaved people and often face social vulnerability. Medical students ran an outreach project on stopping mosquito-borne diseases and viral hepatitis, planned with a participatory rapid diagnosis adapted to an online interview because access to the community was difficult.

Activities reached sixty-two people and included playful school sessions, a myths-and-truths game, a mosquito hunt activity, and home visits with demonstrations about hepatitis. The team reports strong participation, wider knowledge of transmission and stopping, and stronger self-care. They present outreach as a bridge between university and community that also shapes students' training.
openalex-w7204566843:
Rafael Marques Braga led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on fluorescence angiography with indocyanine green in colorectal surgery. When surgeons join two ends of bowel, the connection can leak, and anastomotic leakage remains one of the operation's main problems. Inadequate tissue perfusion is one of its potentially modifiable causes. The dye technique lets the surgeon see blood flow in the tissue in real time, before deciding exactly where to cut and join.

The review examines the technique's impact on reducing leakage and on intraoperative choice-making, since seeing perfusion can change the surgical plan on the spot. For colorectal teams, the practical question is whether a visualization tool reliably identifies poorly perfused tissue early enough to act on it.
openalex-w7204757643:
Shoei Kawasoe and co-authors in Japan released an English-language supplies study in 2026 on iodate compounds made from earth-abundant elements as antiviral supplies. The team wanted inorganic antivirals that do not rely on rare earths. They synthesized iodates of aluminum, copper, manganese, and, for comparison, yttrium, confirmed each was a single phase with some water solubility. Tested antiviral activity against enveloped and non-enveloped viruses under global standard protocols.

All samples showed high activity against enveloped viruses. The copper and yttrium compounds also worked strongly against non-enveloped viruses, an effect the authors attribute to the iodate ions' oxidative power joined with the metal cations' actions at the viral surface. All supplies showed low cytotoxicity. Coating cotton fibers with the released ions kept antiviral results comparable to the powders, marking these supplies, mainly the copper iodate, as promising.
openalex-w7212262743:
Erlani Diogo de Jesus, Hellinton Staevie dos Santos, and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva audit access at the Federal University of Amazonas in Brazil. Access, here, has three faces. One is the built space: ramps, lifts, and halls. One is how facts reach all, in sign tongue and more. The third is stance: how staff treat those who need aid. The team read past theses, laws, and the state norm for built access.

Some ground has been won, they find, in plans and in help at the desk. Two gaps stand out. Staff lack steady training in Libras, the sign tongue of Brazil. The halls also lack fixed, built change that lasts. Full access, they close, takes all arms at once: chiefs, desk staff, tech aids, and the halls themselves. A right on paper must be a ramp in fact.
openalex-w7214216543:
Maguinolia Bueno Maia led a team of Brazilian researchers in a 2026 article on teaching ethnic and racial relations through history classes. The authors connect three themes: the school curriculum, collective memory, and resistance. They ask how history lessons can challenge prejudice and show the many groups that formed Brazilian society.

Their main tool is the editorial cartoon, read as both image and text. Cartoons, they argue, can do more than illustrate a lesson; they can open discussion of power, stereotypes, and acts of resistance in a given time. Used that way, history teaching becomes more critical and grounded in students' real context, while honoring different memories and identities.
openalex-w7214802243:
Breno Márcio Bottino de Melo Silva, Bruna Tainá Maria Ferreira de Matos, and José Carlos Souza reviewed burnout syndrome after the COVID-19 pandemic in a 2026 narrative review. Burnout is the physical and mental exhaustion that grows out of chronic work stress. Searching medical and academic databases, they focused on how new ways of working and studying, from home office to virtual learning, affected workers and students.

The literature they read ties remote and hybrid work, virtual classes, social isolation, task overload, and blurred borders between personal life and work to intensified exhaustion. The pandemic widened burnout's reach, they conclude, and strengthened the case for prevention strategies, mental health support, and healthier, more collaborative, and more balanced work and study environments. Their review speaks to employers and educators redesigning routines after the emergency years.
openalex-w7215085943:
Rafaela Carolina Oliveira da Silva Campos, Josiane Junia Facundo de Almeida, and Juliana Irani Villanueva dos Reis wrote a 2026 qualitative study on Brazilian Sign Language, Libras. It concerns science teaching for deaf students. Reflecting on bilingual and visual teaching materials, they reviewed earlier studies and teaching resources on bilingual education and asked what makes science classes accessible in fact rather than merely translated.

Bilingual resources that join Libras, Portuguese, and visual language widen access to scientific knowledge and support fairer, richer learning, the authors find. Visual experience is central to how deaf students build knowledge, so teaching should rest on visual teaching and respect for deaf culture. Teachers also need training for bilingual practice and image-based resources. Making and using such materials, the authors conclude, strengthens inclusive education that treats Libras as a language of teaching.
openalex-w7215820643:
Ana Lúcia de Souza Almeida wrote a 2026 systematic-style review in English and Portuguese on playfulness in teaching children with ADHD. The disorder affects school results, attention control, and social life. Her review rests on five key studies from 2021 to 2026, on teacher views in public schools, games in math teaching, behavioral strategies, and wider surveys of research on it.

Bringing playful tools into teaching reduced motor inattention, raised intrinsic motivation, and lifted classroom climate in the reviewed evidence. Large structural barriers and gaps in teachers' further training persist, however. Play should not be treated as mere pastime, the author concludes, but as a core neuropedagogical tool for making school inclusion real for children whose minds attend differently.
openalex-w7221131343:
Daiane de Lourdes Alves Velho and five co-authors studied inclusive schooling inside ordinary Brazilian schools in 2026. Inclusion, they argue, means more than a student's presence. It takes real taking part, learning, and belonging in the shared classroom.

Four elements form their network. Teacher training comes first. Expert support in the classroom comes next. Support staff and the shaping of the study plan complete it. Expert help must add to regular schooling, not run beside it as a second track. Support staff should join the shared work without replacing the teacher. The study plan should bend to widen access, not shut the student apart. Moving from presence to taking part, they conclude, takes joint planning and shared duty.
openalex-w7221162543:
Giovanna Azevedo Rodrigues and Marcelo Caixeta continued rebuilding the theory of knowledge around process in a 2026 article. A companion work starts from the concept. This one follows logos, concept, word, statement, and truth. The path runs from Plato through Kant to analytic philosophy.

Frege turned Kant's analytic into a matter of logical deduction. Carnap tied it to language frameworks instead. Quine rejected the notion outright. Yet all three, the authors argue, treat the finished statement as knowledge's basic unit. Their process account starts earlier. It begins in the bond between organism and world. Then it climbs through practice, concept forming, and viewpoint. Only then do word and statement appear. Truth splits into three kinds on their scheme: objectual, formal, and process-based.
phreno-magnet-and-mirror-of-nature-a-rec: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the digitization notice and title page of the Phreno-Magnet and Mirror of Nature, volume 1, dated 1843 in the catalogue record. The title describes a record of facts, experiments, and discoveries in phrenology, magnetism, and related subjects. The title page names Spencer T. Hall as editor, a lecturer on phrenopathy, with Simpkin, Marshall of London and J. H. Greaves of Sheffield as publishers.
plos-pbio-0020243:
Anne E. Bygrave, Kirsten L. Rose, Josefina Cortes-Hernandez, and their team raised a caution about mouse research in PLOS Biology in 2004. Two common lab mouse strains, called 129 and C57BL/6, can develop signs of autoimmune disease on their own as they age. Autoimmunity means the immune system attacks the body itself.

That background noise can confuse studies of gene-targeted mice. If a normal mouse of the same strain shows the same signs, a removed gene may not be the cause. The authors urge care in picking control mice and in reading results. Their warning helps labs avoid false claims about which genes cause lupus-like disease in mice.
plos-pone-0000043:
Olivier Neyrolles, Rogelio Hernández-Pando, France Pietri-Rouxel, and co-authors asked a pointed question in 2006: does tuberculosis hide in fat? Mycobacterium tuberculosis can sleep inside the body for years before waking to cause disease. Its hiding places were thought to be mainly in the lungs and immune cells.

The team tested adipose tissue, body fat, as a place of persistence. Fat is plentiful, long-lived, and laced with immune cells, which makes it a plausible bunker. If the germ truly shelters there, treatment must reach it there too, and relapse after cure becomes easier to explain. The question opened a line of research into fat as an overlooked reservoir in chronic infection.
plos-pone-0000143:
Peter Caley, Niels G. Becker, and David J. Philp published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks a pointed question for pandemic planning: once influenza erupts in one country, how long is the waiting time before it spreads to others? The authors build a model of that inter-country spread.

The answer shapes how much time health agencies have to react with travel measures, vaccines, or alerts. The authors weigh factors that shorten or lengthen the delay. Their work belongs to the planning literature that tries to turn the chaos of the last pandemic into numbers the next response can use.
plos-pone-0000243:
Margarita Gutova, Joseph Najbauer, Anna Gevorgyan, and colleagues published this lung cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Small cell lung cancer is aggressive and often resists chemotherapy. The authors identify a set of tumor cells marked by the protein uPAR that survive chemotherapy, chemoresistant cells that can regrow the cancer.

Finding the cells that outlast treatment is the key to stopping relapse. The authors show these uPAR-positive cells carry that resistant role. The marker gives drug developers a defined target: kill this subpopulation, and the tumor's comeback route may close.
plos-pone-0000343:
Olivia Carter and Patrick Cavanagh published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2007. When two different images are shown to the two eyes, perception rivals: one image wins, then the other. The authors study onset rivalry, the contest at the very start of viewing. They show that a brief presentation isolates an early, independent phase of that perceptual competition.

Isolating the opening phase lets researchers study competition before slower influences pile on. The authors use very short displays to catch it. The result sharpens the picture of how the brain chooses what we see when the eyes disagree.
plos-pone-0000443:
Alexander Maye and colleagues searched for order in behavior with no instructions, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. When animals or people act spontaneously, their choices look random at first glance. The team analyzed spontaneous behavior for hidden structure, patterns that would show the behavior is organized rather than coin-flip random.

Finding order in spontaneity matters for how scientists interpret free behavior in experiments, from flies in a chamber to people at rest. Structured spontaneous behavior suggests the brain generates patterned activity on its own, rather than merely reacting. The paper joins a growing challenge to the idea that unprompted behavior is noise.
plos-pone-0000543:
John R. Talbott argued that the scale of sex work shapes the global AIDS pandemic, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper titled Size Matters. His analysis linked the number of prostitutes in a population to the spread of HIV/AIDS across countries. Commercial sex networks can carry the virus efficiently between high-risk and general populations.

The claim directs policy toward the structure of epidemics, not only individual behavior. Where sex work is extensive, targeted prevention may decide a country's trajectory. Such ecological analyses are debated because country-level patterns can mislead, but they force attention on drivers that clinic-based studies overlook.
plos-pone-0000643:
Timothy H.-C. Hsiau, Claudiu Diaconu, Connie A. Myers and colleagues mapped the control logic of the eye's light-sensing cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Photoreceptors, the retina cells that catch light, carry more genetic diseases than any other cell type. Most of the more than 120 cloned human blindness genes are highly expressed in photoreceptors.

The team studied the cis-regulatory logic, the DNA switches near genes, that runs the photoreceptor gene network. Their aim was an integrative framework, one map joining the switches to the genes they control. Such a map helps explain how photoreceptors become what they are, and why so many mutations blind.
plos-pone-0000743:
Garret Suen, Barry S. Goldman and Roy D. Welch worked on predicting where a bacterium lives from its genome alone. When they wrote in 2007, automated sequencing was so fast that analysis had become the rate-limiting step. Hundreds of prokaryotic genomes were publicly available, with new ones arriving at roughly 20 per month. Each genome is a parts list without an address.

An ecological niche describes the environment an organism occupies and the life it leads there. If gene content predicts the niche, researchers can infer lifestyle for microbes never cultured in a lab. Most microbes refuse culturing, so genome-based prediction opens the majority of bacterial life to study.
plos-pone-0000843:
Yossi Buskila, Yasmin Abu-Ghanem, Yifat Levi and colleagues reported brain support cells making a signaling gas in a mutant mouse, for PLOS ONE in 2007. It was well accepted that glial cells in the central nervous system produce nitric oxide through the enzyme NOS2 only in response to various insults. The team had recently described rapid astroglial, NOS2-dependent nitric oxide production under other conditions, challenging that rule.

In a NOS2 mutant mouse, they report enhanced astrocytic nitric oxide production and neuronal modifications in the neocortex. Astrocytes are the brain's housekeeper cells, and nitric oxide is both messenger and potential toxin. Rewriting when this gas is made changes accounts of brain inflammation and injury.
plos-pone-0000943:
Konrad Kording, Ulrik Beierholm, Wei Ji Ma and colleagues framed perception as the brain drawing conclusions about causes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A sensation matters to an animal because of what it says about the world. Smells, sounds and sights are clues, and the brain must infer what caused them.

The authors apply that idea to multisensory perception, where several senses report at once. The brain has to decide whether two clues share one cause or come from separate events. That decision shapes whether we merge the clues or keep them apart. Their causal inference view gives a single logic for many puzzling perception results.
plos-pone-0001043:
Sherine Abboud, Pekka Karhunen, Dieter Lutjohann and colleagues linked a cholesterol gene to a major stroke type, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene PCSK9 helps set blood levels of LDL cholesterol, the harmful kind. Its variants were already tied to cholesterol levels and coronary heart disease severity.

The team asked whether PCSK9 also raises the risk of large vessel atherosclerosis stroke, the kind caused by clogged big arteries. A gene that links cholesterol to stroke as well as heart disease widens the case for targeting it. Drugs against PCSK9 were a live idea at the time. Genetic evidence from patients helps judge that idea.
plos-pone-0001143:
Long-term cocaine use is known to impair a person's ability to stop a behavior once started. Lorenza Colzato, Wery van den Wildenberg, and Bernhard Hommel asked whether casual users show the same problem, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Recreational users are a growing group, and findings from heavy users may not apply to them.

The study compared recreational cocaine users with non-users on tasks that require inhibiting and executing responses. Their title states the result: inhibitory control is impaired in the recreational users tested. That finding extends concern about cocaine's effects on self-control beyond chronic addiction.
plos-pone-0001243:
Insecticide-treated bed nets and sprays are mainstays of malaria control, but mosquitoes evolve resistance. João Pinto and colleagues studied knockdown resistance mutations in Anopheles gambiae, the chief African malaria mosquito, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. How often such mutations arise in wild mosquito populations is a basic question for resistance research.

The authors report multiple origins of the knockdown resistance mutations in this mosquito across the Afrotropics. Resistance did not spread from a single source; it evolved repeatedly. That changes how control programs should expect resistance to emerge and spread.
plos-pone-0001343:
Thiacetazone is an old antitubercular drug whose precise action was unclear. Anuradha Alahari and colleagues report how it works against mycobacteria, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The mycobacterial cell wall is rich in mycolic acids, complex branched fatty acids that make the wall highly hydrophobic and hard for drugs to cross.

Pathogenic mycobacteria carry mycolic acid subtypes containing cyclopropane rings. The authors show that thiacetazone inhibits the cyclopropanation of these cell wall mycolic acids. Weakening the wall's chemistry explains the drug's effect and suggests related targets for new TB drugs.
plos-pone-0001443:
Cecilia Poderoso and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how cells make steroid hormones. A signal chain known as ERK helps drive hormone based steroid making, but its exact role was vague. Both the signal and steroid making can be sparked by a cell messenger. The team traced a protein complex inside the cell power units.

They show this complex is vital for the chain to tag a key control protein. That tag is a step the cell needs to make steroids. The finding places part of the control inside the power units themselves. It refines the map that drug and hormone research relies on.
plos-pone-0001543:
