By three months after the intervention, all three malnutrition rates had fallen, and they fell further by six months. Growth scores improved clearly from baseline. Children with high pressure in the lung arteries and those corrected at older ages were more likely to stay underweight or wasted. The authors conclude that malnutrition is very common in these children, and that timely correction brings real, quick nutritional gains.
pmc-10713443:
Jihye Kim and co-authors measure how common hepatitis C infection is among people who inject drugs in South Korea, and how few of them get treated. Data for this group were scarce. The team reviewed records from three hospitals that care for most known injecting drug users in the country, covering a decade of testing.

Nearly forty percent of injecting users carried hepatitis C antibodies, far above non-injecting users. Older age, being tested at the prison hospital, and earlier test years were each tied to a positive result. Rates fell over the decade. Yet among those who tested positive, only about seven percent received treatment. The authors call for active testing and treatment programs aimed at this population.
pmc-10713643:
Ajay Ramalingam and co-authors report a 2023 pilot study in sorghum genetics. Sorghum is a hardy grain for dry lands. The team ran a genome-wide scan on a diverse set of lines. A subset of 96 lines was drawn from a larger pool of 219. The scan hunted gene spots tied to yield traits, root form, and leaf pore traits. More than forty thousand clean markers showed rich diversity across the lines.

Two sorghum races split apart clearly in the population structure. Marker linkage faded fast with distance, which sharpens gene hunting. Three scan methods found 42 strong marker-trait links in all. Breeders get new loci to test in crossing programs. Root and pore traits matter for drought, where sorghum earns its place. A pilot scale keeps the claims modest, but the marker set and race split give larger studies a firm base.
pmc-10714443:
Akkoca and three co-authors test whether swaddling calms newborns who receive breathing support through the nose. Their study followed 40 newborns in a neonatal intensive care unit in Turkey during 2022. Each baby was scored on a newborn stress scale, and saliva samples were taken before and after swaddling.

Stress scores fell sharply after swaddling, from about 10 points to about 3.5. Saliva cortisol, heart rate, and breathing rate also dropped, while oxygen levels stayed the same. The authors conclude that swaddling lowers stress in these babies. They recommend larger trials that assign babies to swaddling or usual care by chance.
pmc-10714643:
Zhen Yuan and a large team of co-authors measured in 2023 how well a city-wide bowel cancer screening program in Tianjin, China, found early growths. Since 2012 the program has offered a risk questionnaire and a stool blood test to residents aged forty to seventy-four. Those flagged as high risk were offered a free scope exam of the bowel.

Over four million people completed both first steps, and about five percent were flagged high risk. Flag rates rose with age and were higher in women. Among those scoped, the team reports detection rates by age and sex and the factors tied to finding growths. The data guide how to aim screening at those most likely to benefit.
pmc-10715943:
Letizia Bertoldi and a team of co-authors review care for cardiogenic shock, a state where the heart fails to pump enough blood, in two thousand twenty-three. The condition carries a high risk of death. New temporary support devices that help the heart pump have changed treatment in recent years, alongside long-standing drug care.

The review sets out how to choose among drug-only care, one device, or several devices, by shock severity and cause. It describes the main device types and how each is used. It also covers best practice for putting devices in, since bleeding and access-site harm can erase their benefit. Careful technique is presented as part of the therapy itself.
pmc-10716143:
Jianhai Yu and co-authors published a 2023 study of the first local mpox outbreak in Guangdong Province, China. Case tracing alone could not quickly find the outbreak's source. The team sequenced ten monkeypox virus genomes from the June 2023 cluster and compared them with genomes from elsewhere. The analysis traced the family tree of the virus and its pattern of change over time.

All ten genomes fell in one lineage that also appeared in Portugal and other parts of China at the same time, pointing to quiet spread before detection. The lineage kept gaining mutations at a steady clip. Its change pattern matches an editing system in human cells that can speed viral evolution. The authors say genome tracking can reveal hidden transmission chains and guide joint control efforts.
pmc-10716243:
Jörn Helbert and co-authors report that Venus's upper air has barely changed in four decades, in a 2023 study. The data came from a Mercury probe, BepiColombo, swinging past Venus on its long road out. Its heat eye, built for Mercury, read the planet's mid-infrared glow during the second flyby. From that glow the team pulled temperature profiles and cloud traits for the layer sixty to seventy-five kilometers up.

Those values match the last such reads, taken by a Soviet probe in 1983. The match says the mesosphere, the middle sky above the thick clouds, holds steady over decades. That steadiness sharpens the puzzle of why Earth and Venus, once alike, took such split paths. The authors also note the feat itself: an instrument used far off its design target still gave sound science. The flyby reads join the thin stock of Venus data.
pmc-10716643:
Marco Graziano and co-authors report a 2023 study of how warmth before fertilization shapes salmon breeding success. Eggs and sperm were kept overnight in cold or warm water, then crossed in all pairings. Half of each clutch then grew in cold water and half in warm, to split male and female effects.

Warmth helped eggs but harmed sperm, which cut hatching success. When sperm and embryo warmth matched, hatching came earlier and in tighter step. On the whole, the gametes' shift to warmth did not shield the young, and sperm stood out as the more heat-frail side.
pmc-10717943:
Chunmei Chen, Pu Zheng, Pengcheng Chen, and Dan Wu published this study in 2023. It builds gene editing tools for a bacterium prized for making succinic acid, a building block chemical now drawn from oil. The bacterium, Actinobacillus succinogenes, lacked precise editing tools, which held back strain improvement.

The team fused a nicking version of Cas9 with enzymes that swap single DNA letters. Four editor types emerged; two of them rewrote letters with up to one hundred percent success at target sites. A combined editor changed six sites at once in one design. They then used the tools to switch off sugar and acid transporters. Killing one sugar transporter raised acid output, while killing two acid transporters cut it. The kit opens this industrial microbe to systematic tuning.
pmc-10718943:
Manabu Yamada, Takeshi Okamoto, and Naoki Sasahira report removal of a moved bile duct stent with a new sheath tool in a 2023 case paper. Plastic stents placed to drain the bile duct move out of place in a share of patients. In this case a woman aged fifty eight, treated for pancreatic cancer blockage, came in with fever and yellow skin after her stent moved upward.

Scans confirmed the move. A first try with biopsy forceps failed to pull the stent out. The new sheath was then passed into the duct over a wire. Forceps sent through the sheath grasped and removed the stent, as the title records. The sheath was first designed for targeted bile duct biopsies.
pmc-10719243:
Ünal Üstündağ and four co-authors test a garden herb against metal poisoning in onion plants in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Manganese in excess damages cells and chromosomes. Lemon balm extract is rich in antioxidants, but its shield against metal stress was little tested. The team exposed onion roots to manganese chloride, with and without the extract. They tracked rooting, growth, and weight alongside cell division rates.

Manganese alone cut growth and raised chromosome damage and cell death signs. The extract eased many of these harms. Its own chemistry was profiled to name the likely protective compounds. Onion assays are a cheap early screen for plant protection ideas. The work serves plant toxicologists and natural product researchers.
pmc-10720243:
Madhura More and co-authors study a water toxin in young mice in a 2023 paper. Microcystin-LR, made by algae blooms, harms the liver and poses a special risk to children. The team asked how gut microbes and their products shape that harm early in life.

Young mice exposed to the toxin lost gut bacteria that make acetate, a helpful short acid. With acetate low, the gut barrier weakened and a liver alarm system switched on, driving inflammation. Adding acetate back blocked that alarm and calmed the liver. A cell receptor for acetate proved key, since it lowered the alarm protein through cell disposal routes. The authors name gut care as a target against toxin liver harm.
pmc-10720843:
Xufei Luo, Janne Estill, and Yaolong Chen ask whether medical research that uses ChatGPT needs its own reporting rules. Their short paper, published in 2023, looks at how researchers had begun using the chatbot to help draft scientific papers in fields such as surgery and radiology.

The authors grant that the tool can speed up writing, but they point to real risks. The data behind the model can be out of date, so its output may be wrong or stale. Small changes in a prompt can also produce very different answers, which makes results hard to repeat. To deal with these problems, the team proposes a draft checklist for authors to report how such tools were used. They plan to form an expert group to turn the draft into a full standard, named CHEER. The aim is more openness about chatbot use in medical writing.
pmc-10721343:
Elsiofy and four colleagues report a clinical trial from twenty twenty-three on a hip operation for teens. The work treats a slipped growth plate at the top of the thigh bone. The team tested a method that cuts and resets the bone after a safe hip dislocation.

The trial covered twenty-four hips, split evenly by sex, with a mean age near thirteen years. Most cases were classed as hard or very hard, and three quarters were stable. After about one year, scores for pain, movement, and leg length got much better. Bone death arose in four hips, and all four were unstable cases. The team still calls the method safe and useful for hard cases.
pmc-10721443:
Miranda Smit, Josiane Panisson, and Denise Beaulieu feed growing pigs hybrid rye in place of wheat and ask if extra energy rescues growth. Their twenty twenty-three trial ran one hundred sixty pigs in thirty-two pens. Earlier work saw rye cut appetite and slow gains.

Diets swapped in forty percent rye at low or high energy levels across two growth phases. Intake, weight, energy use, and gut lesion scores were logged. The bet was that richer feed offsets the rye drag. Feed is the top cost in pork; a hardy local grain that holds growth with an energy tweak would widen ration choices when wheat runs dear.
pmc-10722543:
Yolanda Manzanares-Negro and co-authors test how a two-dimensional material holds up under repeated stress, in this 2023 study. The material, MoS2, is a semiconductor sheet one atom thick, eyed for tiny moving devices. Repeated bending can crack such sheets, and missing atoms can seed the cracks, so the team added vacancies in controlled amounts and cycled the sheets.

Clean, high-quality sheets endured a billion stress cycles at eighty percent of their breaking strength, beating steel and nearing graphene. Adding the level of vacancies that large-scale making usually leaves cut the safe strength to about half the breaking point. The team also spotted a sudden reshuffle of defects just before total failure, which they name as the main wear path. The results guide how pure the sheets must be for lasting devices.
pmc-10725643:
Hao Chen and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three study of nanoparticles for gentler cancer heat therapy. Heating tumours with light can kill them, but excess heat harms healthy tissue. Heat also triggers protective proteins that blunt later treatment.

The particles pair a copper-doped core with a coating made from platelet membrane. The core converts a common body chemical into damaging radicals, lowering those protective proteins. Under low-power laser light it also warms the tumour mildly. Cell and animal tests cleared most tumour growth with good safety. The design combines chemical attack with low-temperature heating in one disguised package.
pmc-10725943:
Min Jiang, Changyin Fang, and Yongping Ma map rules for how virus parts and antibodies interact in a 2023 paper. Viruses change their surface parts to escape immune attack. That drift is a core problem for vaccine design. The team asked what amino acid swaps let a virus slip past antibodies.

They used simple protein tags as a stand-in for virus targets. Swaps fell into four classes, from escape to no effect. Most swaps had no effect or an equal effect on binding. Swaps to ring-shaped amino acids often caused escape. Swaps to like chemicals often did nothing at all. The rules may guide vaccine updates and antibody rescue work.
pmc-10727543:
Zhang and Jiang ask whether active middle-aged and older adults in China suffer fewer strokes, once other factors are held equal. Stroke has grown common in China and drags down life quality and family finances. Their 2023 study uses a national aging survey from 2018, covering 5,070 adults over fifty with full data on activity, stroke, health, and habits.

High physical activity tied clearly to lower stroke rates. The link survived layer after layer of controls, for background, health state, and lifestyle alike. The authors conclude that staying highly active lowers stroke risk in this age group. They urge health management and healthy habits alongside activity in prevention work.
pmc-10728043:
Young Yool Chung, Sung Nyun Baek, Tae Gyu Park, and Min Young Kim study hip fracture recovery across the COVID-19 years in 2023. Full bans on family visits in nursing hospitals may have slowed gains. Walk scores at six months cover 81 patients from before the ban era and 103 from the ban era.

Scores ran lower after the ban era began, and the drop was sharpest for nursing hospital patients. The share whose walk grade fell rose by about twelve points across eras. Home-treated patients showed no like split, which keys the harm to sealed wards.
pmc-10728243:
Patrick Gahr and co-authors wrote a study from 2023 on how people fare after surgery for a broken knee plateau. The plateau is the flat top of the shin bone, and a break there can hobble walking for years. The team called back adults treated at one center over five years, sent a joint health survey, and invited each to a check with a sole sensor test of walking.

Fifty-eight of one hundred and thirty-two patients took part, about three years after the break. Most felt fine on pain, daily tasks, and movement. The clear gaps were in sports and in quality of life. Load on the once-broken leg had shifted most on stairs and outdoor walks. Results tracked neither the type nor the weight of the break. Walking tests on varied tasks, the team says, show loss that a flat-ground check can miss.
pmc-10729143:
Ashenafi Woretaw and co-authors survey Ethiopian nurses on keeping surgical patients warm, in a 2023 study. Letting body temperature slip during surgery lengthens stays, invites infection, and raises deaths. Nurses carry the main duty of prevention. Over four hundred nurses in five referral hospitals in the northwest Amhara region answered knowledge and practice questions.

About three in five nurses showed good knowledge of temperature protection. Only about half showed good day-to-day practice. Training and workplace factors separated the strong performers from the rest. The gap between knowing and doing is the practical problem. Hospitals gain a concrete case for refresher training and better warming equipment in operating rooms.
pmc-10729243:
Chronic diseases travel in packs, and knowing which ones cluster could sharpen prevention. Jennifer Ferris and co-authors lay out a plan for finding those clusters in this 2023 study protocol. Rather than running a new trial, they will gather published studies that already grouped diseases by data patterns and combine them anew.

Their method treats the published clusters as a network and meta-clusters across them, testing whether the same disease bundles recur from study to study. A set list of priority chronic diseases anchors the work. No ethics approval is needed, since only published work is used. Findings will be published and shared with health system planners. The protocol is registered in a public database.
pmc-10730343:
Carine Foz and four co-authors study cardiac arrest around surgery in children in this 2023 paper. They used a large United States surgical database from 2019 and 2020, covering more than 260,000 young patients. Only noncardiac operations were included. The team searched for traits that raise the risk of arrest, and for what happens to children after one.

Arrest was rare, at about one case in a thousand, split between the operation itself and the two days after. Risk ran higher for infants under one year, for sicker children, and for those admitted as inpatients or through emergency care. Heart disease, impaired thinking, and long anesthesia time also raised risk. Children who had an arrest stayed longer in hospital and died more often within thirty days. Arrests after surgery proved deadlier than arrests during it.
pmc-10730443:
Adriana Neag and Eric Becker review, in twenty twenty-three, aluminium alloys for thixoforging, a way to shape metal in a semi-solid state. The process has drawn interest for making parts with good properties. Choosing an alloy needs two things: the expected mechanical properties of the part, and the alloy's semi-solid temperature window. The review summarizes wrought and foundry aluminium alloys in depth. It describes methods to evaluate how sensitive each alloy is to heating temperature. For industrial use, the reheating strategy is crucial and should be analyzed systematically.

The reheated microstructure governs how the semi-solid metal flows and how the final part performs. The authors say a future process model should integrate microstructure conditioning during reheating. That would link feedstock preparation to final mechanical properties.
pmc-10730943:
Technologies that remove greenhouse gases or dim the sun are little known to the public, yet opinion about them is already forming online. Finn Müller-Hansen and co-authors mined 1.5 million tweets in 2023, covering sixteen such technologies across fifteen years. Deep learning models scored each post for attention, sentiment, and emotion.

Attention has shifted from geoengineering in general toward specific removal methods, while sunlight-dimming ideas draw little notice and often travel with conspiracy talk. Removal methods framed as natural drew warmer feelings; the same methods soured when labeled geoengineering. The authors argue that social media gives a window on public reaction that surveys, hampered by low awareness, cannot.
pmc-10733943:
Qiangguo Zhou and co-authors design in 2023 a terahertz device that flips light polarization across a very wide band, then add light based switching to it. Terahertz waves sit between microwaves and infrared, and steering them fast is a growing need. Their converter uses a two layer patterned surface that turns incoming linear polarization by a right angle with near perfect purity over its band.

Current and field maps explain how the flip works, and the team charts how each shape choice moves performance. They then build silicon into two new designs so a light pump can switch the conversion on and off. Simulations put the switching time well under two nanoseconds for both forms. The work answers a known weakness of fixed patterned converters: they cannot be retuned once made, while these can, at ultrafast speed.
pmc-10734243:
Marta Acampora and co-authors uncover doctors' perceived barriers and aids to good antibiotic prescribing. Their 2023 qualitative study uses the Theoretical Domains Framework, a tool built to analyze what drives human behavior.

Finding these determinants is crucial for promoting responsible, evidence-based antibiotic use and for fighting resistance. Semi-structured interviews were held with health care professionals. The analysis sorted what doctors said into the framework's domains, to map which factors block change and which support it. Such a map can guide the design of interventions that target the real reasons behind prescribing habits, rather than guessing at them.
pmc-10735643:
Joseph Gaugler and five co-authors synthesize research on how social conditions shape family care for people living with dementia. Family caregivers of relatives with Alzheimer disease and related dementias often suffer harm to their own health. Their burden overlaps with housing, income, and neighborhood factors that drive health gaps.

The authors outline public health actions that could help. These include better tracking and identification of caregivers, stronger community partnerships, and payment incentives for dementia capable care. Cutting the stigma of dementia and caregiving also features. The piece argues that public health tools, aimed at those most at risk, can ease the emotional, social, and financial strain on families.
pmc-10735743:
Danielle McDuffie studies whether gratitude softens the harm of hard life events for grieving Black adults. Her paper appeared in two thousand twenty-three. Black adults face loss more often than other groups, along with racial trauma and childhood hardship. Faith is a common source of strength, and gratitude shares much with that outlook. Yet gratitude had not been tested in this group.

McDuffie surveyed just over one hundred Black adults aged forty-five and up who had lost someone. Both racial trauma and childhood hardship linked to more depression. Gratitude changed that link, with depression differing across levels of hardship and thanks. She argues that care built on strengths and gratitude may help grieving Black adults. More work on trauma and policy could build on these results.
pmc-10735843:
Igor Akushevich, Arseniy Yashkin, Vinit Nalawade, and Julia Kravchenko examine dementia risk after cancer in this two thousand twenty-three study. They used SEER-Medicare data on Americans aged sixty-five and older. The cancer cohort covered more than two million people diagnosed with one of nine slow-progressing cancers, including breast, colorectal, and prostate cancers. A matched non-cancer comparison group of over one million people completed the design.

The team compared Alzheimer's disease and related dementia risk across many age-specific groups for each cancer type. Cancer patients diagnosed between sixty-five and seventy-five showed higher dementia risk than the comparison group. That pattern weakened with older age at diagnosis and eventually turned protective at advanced ages. The authors discuss treatment effects, genetics, and diagnostic practices as possible explanations.
pmc-10736143:
Sangha Jeon, Nicholas Turiano, and Susan Charles link varied social life to longer life in a 2023 paper. Social activity is known to track with better health. Less is known about whether the range of activities matters. The team counted how many distinct social activity types people took part in.

They used data from a large United States aging study. The sample held 5,559 adults first surveyed in 2008. Death records were checked again in 2019, eleven years later. People with more varied social lives were more likely to survive. The link held after checks for health and non-social variety. It showed in all age groups and was strongest in older adults.
pmc-10736243:
Drug options for sharpening thinking in old age are scarce, so training games draw interest, though results vary. Ashley Curtis and seven co-authors build COGMUSE, a homemade brain-training package for older adults with insomnia, so that every feature can be tested and tuned. It holds two games aimed at spatial attention, processing speed, inhibition, and motor skill.

Ten adults with insomnia, averaging about 69 years, played for twenty minutes and rated the experience. Scores ranged from middling enjoyment to strong personal satisfaction, and spoken feedback was largely positive: clear instructions, pleasant graphics, easy use. Complaints targeted fast movement, weak story elements, and missing practice rounds. The authors plan revisions and then a test of whether the training improves thinking and sleep. The evaluation appears in 2023.
pmc-10736343:
Health in later life is rarely a solo affair: spouses and family caregivers share the strain and the coping. Karen Lyons and Kalisha Bonds Johnson introduced in 2023 a conference session on programs that treat the older adult and care partner as a pair.

Four projects anchor the session. One adapts a remote exercise rehab program for rural pairs facing memory loss, using focus groups. Another pilots sleep training for impaired adults and their partners. A third supports dementia pairs in planning future care, and a fourth tests communication training for couples living with heart failure. Across them, recruitment and retention proved stubborn, and speakers shared hard-won design lessons.
pmc-10736743:
Martha Abshire Saylor and co-authors interview everyone touched by a program that helps primary care patients plan ahead for serious illness. Advance care planning interventions reliably raise paperwork completion yet rarely improve the outcomes patients actually feel, perhaps because they tackle too little of the system. The SHARING Choices program was built broader. Their 2023 paper gathers the implementers' own accounts of running it.

Forty people spoke: all nine embedded facilitators, eleven patients and family members, and twenty clinicians and practice managers across two health systems. Tailored interview guides probed how the program landed, what helped, what hindered, and what had to change mid-flight. Thematic analysis sorts their answers into shared themes and points where the groups' experiences diverge. The authors offer the map to any team wondering why a well-designed planning program thrives in one practice and stalls in another.
pmc-10737043:
Galina Gorbunova and five co-authors warn about bias in studies built on Medicare data, in this 2023 paper. Medicare covers nearly all older Americans, but full care records exist mainly for those in traditional Medicare. People in private Medicare Advantage plans leave thin records, so studies based on the data may mislead.

Using a long-running retirement survey from 1998 to 2015, the team compared the two groups across three policy eras. Advantage members were more diverse, less schooled, and poorer, with worse health habits, though their illness levels started low and later converged. People who switched into Advantage plans carried the highest illness and death risk of any group. Findings for Hispanic members lost the most ground, since the two Hispanic groups differ. The authors urge care in study design, above all for ethnic comparisons.
pmc-10737143:
Jeffrey Stokes, Danielle Waldron, Jacquelin Sauer, and Emily Hartford study in 2023 how adults aging with intellectual and developmental disabilities use health care. People in this group now live longer than ever, a credit to better medicine, yet they face steep barriers to care, above all the preventive care aimed at midlife and later years.

Using repeated national survey data, the team tracked what goes with using two preventive services meant for older adults. Their findings show where access breaks down for a population that health systems were not built around. The study gives planners evidence for closing a quiet but wide gap.
pmc-10737343:
Mohammad Hossain and Natalie Pope use a life-story method to explore how culture and age shape views of aging and care. Their 2023 presentation grows from oral history talks with Virginia Bell, a social worker who built a famed friend-based model of dementia care. Bell, at ninety-eight, recalled the people and events that formed her approach.

A mid-forties interviewer helped interpret the story as it was told. Later, a first-year graduate student from Bangladesh joined the analysis, adding a third voice. His reactions are set against Bell's own, within past writing on aging. The project shows how self-story methods can place one life inside a wider social frame, the authors argue.
pmc-10737643:
Angela Curl and Amy Roberts study older adults whose daily care needs went unmet during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2023 paper. The work draws on a large national survey of aging from 2020. Their sample held 685 people over fifty who had trouble with basic tasks such as eating, bathing, or dressing. An unmet need meant having that trouble but getting no help with the task.

Women were less likely than men to report an unmet need. Married or partnered respondents were also less likely to lack help. In a surprise twist, people with stronger thinking scores were more likely to report unmet needs. The authors suggest such people may find workarounds, yet may also be seen by others as needing less help. They urge outreach teams to target groups at greatest risk of going without care.
pmc-10737743:
Matthew Lee and Ellen Yeung trace hard drinking across the life span in a 2023 study of land-wide United States data. A shared tale says such drinking crests in young adult years and then ebbs for good. The crest is well shown, but the long ebb rests mostly on one-time polls.

The team set two waves of a tracked poll side by side, to split age tales in two kinds. One kind reads across folk of each age at one time; the next reads within one life as years pass. Spiked charts show both at once. Drink lore gains a test of which ebb is real and which is a trick of the poll.
pmc-10737843:
Tracie Harrison and Corey Nagel introduce a symposium on how biological, psychological, and social forces shape disability as women age, published in 2023. A growing literature calls for care tailored to culture for people with disabilities, and for accommodations in places not built for them. The symposium asks how far psychosocial programs can promote healthy aging for women with emotional, mobility, and sensory limits.

Sessions move across settings and groups. One examines aging into mobility limits in Mexico, where accommodations are scarce, and compares men's and women's risks. Another studies women with schizophrenia in acute and long-term care, where stigma and neglect block healthy aging. A third links sleep quality to depression and fatigue in sensory loss. A final one addresses building social participation across diverse groups.
pmc-10737943:
A 2023 study validates AnthropoAge, a biological age score built from simple body measurements, across United States and Mexican cohorts. Biological age aims to capture functional decline better than birthdays do. The score predicted death risk well in both countries. It also tracked disease counts and disability beyond chronological age. Prediction was strongest in adults from fifty to seventy-five.

Patterns of aging acceleration differed between the countries, with a marked interaction for Mexican ethnicity. The authors call the measure robust and reproducible. They also say more work is needed to explain why body-based aging varies across populations.
pmc-10738243:
Jana Nikitin, Fabio Selovin, and Fiona Rupprecht ask whether the quality of everyday activities with a romantic partner shapes how lonely a person feels. Past work shows loneliness runs higher in poor-quality relationships, but little is known about its daily sources inside a couple. The team analyzed diary data from seventy-two adults who reported shared activities with their partners over seven straight days, giving five hundred seventy-six reports in all.

People who rated their shared activities lower reported more daily loneliness, and the link was strong. On days when a person's activities were worse than usual for them, loneliness rose as well. Those lonelier across the week gained less relief even from good activities with their partner. Age and gender did not change the pattern. The authors conclude loneliness both grows out of daily couple life and colors how it is experienced.
pmc-10738343:
Farima Sadeqi and Ryan Best test a mental pathway in 2023 between exercise and thinking in old age. Movement is known to buffer decline in memory and thought, mostly through body-based routes. The pair asked whether a sense of purpose in life carries part of that benefit.

They used a national study of adults aged twenty-five to seventy-four. People who moved more reported more purpose, and purpose in turn predicted better thinking scores. The indirect path was small but real at light, moderate, and strong activity levels. Light activity showed a slightly stronger indirect effect than the harder levels, a result the authors discuss with care.
pmc-10738443:
Hospice care eases the end of life, yet Black families in the rural South use it far less than White families. Ellen Csikai and Hee Yun Lee ask what shapes the wish to use hospice for a family member in a 2023 study. They survey older Black adults in Alabama's Black Belt towns.

Among non-caregivers who knew of hospice, schooling, friend gatherings, and mood scores shaped intent. Among caregivers, sex and health literacy joined that list. National data in the study show hospice use at 35.5 percent for Black deaths against 50.8 percent for White ones. The authors urge hospice teaching placed where people gather, like social clubs.
pmc-10738543:
Jungjoo Lee and co-authors sort older adults' free time into three kinds and grade each against the mind. From the twenty twenty Health and Retirement Study they drew about thirty-eight hundred elders and measured memory, working memory, and processing speed with standard tests. Leisure came in physical, intellectual, and community flavors.

All three leisure types were tied to better memory. Intellectual activity alone also tracked with stronger working memory and faster attention and processing. The authors draw a practical line for therapists and healthcare providers. A varied leisure prescription beats a single hobby. But if the goal is the sharpest cognitive toolkit, the book club earns its place next to the walking group.
pmc-10738643:
Helena Swanson, writing alone in 2023, audits how partners join Florida's age-friendly town plans. Her poster study reviews thirteen action plans across the state. Age-friendly change depends on teamwork across a whole community. The study asks who actually sits at the table.

Plans were coded against the World Health Organization's four-step cycle. Partners sorted into government, business, nonprofit, community, and other camps. On average, sixteen partners appeared in each plan. Towns ranged from rural to urban, small to large. The audit shows how broad the coalitions really run. It also names which partner types tend to show up, and where gaps may hide.
pmc-10738743:
Fumihiko Yokota and colleagues interviewed older adults in Japan about social life after retirement during the COVID pandemic. Little was known about how retired Japanese elders kept contact in that period. Writing in twenty twenty-three, the team held face-to-face interviews in two prefectures in early twenty twenty-one with people over sixty-five who had retired around age sixty. Nearly all still worked part time. Transcripts were translated and coded for patterns in contact and in the forces shaping it.

Everyone said contact grew distant after retirement and was disrupted further by the pandemic. Even so, people stayed in touch online and in person with neighbors and volunteer groups, former coworkers, old school friends, children and grandchildren, and hobby friends. Health policy, pensions, income, and family living arrangements all shaped how much contact people kept.
pmc-10738943:
Yuan Fang and co-authors model how thinking skills change with age in the long-running Framingham Heart Study. Their 2023 study uses repeated scores for memory, executive function, and language from 2,339 people over sixty who were free of dementia at the start. Just over half were women, and most had attended college. Healthy ageing is the backdrop, since people differ widely in how fast their minds decline.

Statistical models that sort people into hidden groups were fitted to find distinct paths of change in each domain. Flexible curve shapes let the paths bend with age. The aim is a clearer picture of who declines fast, who holds steady, and when dementia tends to begin.
pmc-10739043:
Hui-chuan Hsu, writing alone in 2023, asks whether the way older people in Taiwan live over many years shapes how their minds work later. The study draws on five waves of a national aging survey run from 1999 to 2015. Hsu tracked nineteen habits, from gardening and reading to volunteering and group activities, and grouped people by the paths those habits took over time.

The analysis covered 1,314 people who finished the last wave. Habits that held up best over the years predicted better thinking scores later on. High levels of gardening, chess, and reading stood out, as did taking part in group activities and keeping stress low. Younger age, fewer limits on daily physical tasks, and fewer depressive symptoms also helped. Hsu concludes that long-run patterns of social activity, mental pastimes, and low stress protect the aging mind.
pmc-10739143:
Ebba Hillstedt and four co-authors map the literature on epigenetic clock age next to frailty in older adults. Epigenetic clocks read age from DNA marks, while frailty scores take time to run in clinic. Their 2023 sweep found 37 works, of which 15 set the two side by side head-on. Most readings ran on whole blood, and frailty came by one of two stock scores in most.

Findings split down the middle: seven works showed moderate to strong ties, eight showed weak or none. Ties, when seen, came with clocks built to predict death or body state, not plain years. The Grim and Pheno clocks led that set. The tie is thus clock-bound, not a flat law. More work is called for before clocks can grade risk at the bedside.
pmc-10739343:
Carleara Weiss and Rebecca Lorenz review high-intensity interval training, sleep and cognition in older adults, in this 2023 systematic review. Poor sleep is tied to cognitive and physical decline in aging, and intense interval exercise might reset sleep-wake cycles. Reviews tying the three together were missing.

Following standard reporting guidelines, they searched three databases and found six papers covering four randomized trials with about one hundred sixty participants, mostly women around age seventy. Training lasted twelve weeks in all trials. Interval training cut the time to fall asleep and time awake overnight versus inactivity, but matched gentler exercise on sleep quality. One trial found better memory and cognition.
pmc-10740843:
Salvatore Chirumbolo and co-authors present, in a 2023 paper, two clinical studies of oxygen-ozone therapy run under an Italian society's protocols. Ozone is a reactive form of oxygen. Mixed with a patient's own blood outside the body, then returned, it is said to be tamed by the blood's own antioxidant shields, and to wake immune pathways. The team applied that method in two settings.

In six patients, treated blood plus topical ozone shrank hard post-surgical wound infections from drug-resistant bacteria, and cut inflammation markers sharply. In two hundred fifty patients with knee arthritis, smaller-scale blood treatment eased pain and function scores by a wide margin. The authors credit ozone's tuning of the innate immune response. The paper sets out their protocols as a model for wider use.
pmc-10740943:
Zhang and co-authors compare the microbes that pull carbon from the air in three wetland types around Qinghai Lake, on the high Tibetan plateau. Wetland soils store large amounts of carbon, and microbes drive much of that storage. Their 2023 study samples a marsh, a river source wetland, and a lakeside wetland, reading a key gene that marks carbon-fixing microbes.

The marsh held the richest and most varied community, and the lakeside the poorest. Different lead groups ruled each site, with one group on top in the marsh and river source and blue-green bacteria on top at the lakeside. Soil heat, moisture, and carbon content shaped the communities most. The authors conclude that the marsh stores the most carbon of the three.
pmc-10741043:
Ki Bum Um, Soyoung Kwak, Sun-Ha Cheon, JuHyun Kim, and Su-Kyeong Hwang published a 2023 mouse study of an autism treatment candidate called AST-001. Autism's core social symptoms are tied to weak dopamine signaling in reward circuits of the brain. The candidate's active ingredient is L-serine, an amino acid, and it is already in late stage human trials.

The team used mice exposed before birth to valproate, a widely used general model of autism. The drug is thought to work by blocking small potassium channels that brake dopamine neuron firing. Treated mice showed improved social behavior. Recordings showed dopamine neuron activity restored toward normal in the reward pathway. The study supports the mechanism claimed for the candidate and its path toward patients.
pmc-10741743:
Susana Cedres and co-authors review current therapy for malignant pleural mesothelioma, a fast-growing cancer tied to asbestos. With no treatment, patients often live only a few months. Standard care long rested on platinum chemotherapy with an antifolate drug, and adding bevacizumab stretched survival by a short margin.

A first-line immunotherapy pairing then changed the field: nivolumab plus ipilimumab beat the older chemotherapy on overall survival in a major trial. Regulators in the United States and Europe approved the pairing. The pairing is now a standard first treatment in many countries. Not every patient gains from it, though. The review covers biomarkers that may flag likely responders and notes that the cancer has low mutation load, which makes it hard to predict who will respond.
pmc-10741843:
Vanessa Souza and co-authors review how microbes in the lungs shape the start and spread of the most common lung cancer type, in work published in 2023. Tumors are often seen as masses of human cells, yet microbe cells also live in and around them. Gut microbes are known to affect lung cancer care, and lung microbes now draw growing interest.

The review covers traits of the lung microbe mix and how it may drive cancer growth. It also covers microbes inside tumors and the chemicals they make, which can feed cancer spread. The authors discuss whether tuning the microbe mix could help prevent this cancer or improve its treatment. They frame the field as complex and fast moving.
pmc-10742043:
Zi-Long Lu and co-authors tested whether a fruit acid can protect mouse lungs from the injury that follows a cut and return of blood flow, in a 2023 study. This injury strikes in many lung diseases and surgeries and can lead to low blood oxygen and organ failure. The acid, drawn from the peel of a fruit, is known to fight inflammation and oxidation.

Mice got low or high doses of the acid around the injury, and human vessel cells were put through a matching low-oxygen test. Treated lungs showed less damage, swelling, and inflammation. Markers of oxidative harm and iron-driven cell death fell, while a protective enzyme rose. The effect ran through a known oxygen-sensing pathway.
pmc-10742543:
Vlad Braicu and co-authors track how rectal cancer care changed in Romania during and after the pandemic. Their 2023 study covers patients who had surgery from 2019 to 2022. The year 2019 served as a pre pandemic control. In all, the database work is set against a sharp fall in surgical work versus that control year. Yearly counts then rose by about ten percent a year.

Keyhole surgery doubled as a share, from twenty five percent in 2020 to 47.5 percent in 2022. Planned surgery rose to 79.7 percent in the last year, as emergency cases fell. Use of treatment before surgery also rose. Yet stage at diagnosis grew worse over time. The share of stage four cases doubled, from 12.5 to 25.4 percent. Blood protein levels and fitness scores also differed by year.
pmc-10742743:
Chin-Ling Hsieh and Pa-Fan Hsiao review leprosy care at a Taiwan hospital during the COVID-19 years. Their twenty twenty-three study covers cases from twenty oh nine to late twenty twenty-two. Leprosy was thought gone from Taiwan, yet a few new cases appear each year.

More than half the patients were Indonesian, and borderline lepromatous disease was the most common type. Rare forms, like histoid leprosy, also showed up. Gene tests found a small share of drug-resistant cases, including one resistant to dapsone. Odd skin signs and immune reactions had delayed many diagnoses. The authors judge control to be good, but warn that rare, resistant cases need sharp eyes.
pmc-10742943:
Katsunori Yanai and co-authors searched, in a 2023 mouse study, for messenger RNA signatures of kidneys that fail with age. Aging kidneys lose function across whole populations, yet the molecules driving the slide were unknown. The team used a mouse strain bred to age fast in the kidney, against a slow-aging cousin.

Chip screening compared old and young kidneys of both strains. Follow-up precision tests confirmed five messenger RNAs whose levels rose clearly in the fast-aging old kidneys and set them apart from every control group. Each of the five climbed with the impairment itself. The authors offer the five as candidate drivers and possible drug targets for age-linked kidney decline. Human checks come next.
pmc-10743043:
Lorena Lugo and co-authors check whether cleaned water is truly safe in a 2023 study. Chemical treatment can destroy a drug or weedkiller in wastewater, yet the half-broken leftovers may still poison stream life. Cleanup is only proven when the treated water passes living tests.

Their plant used iron- or copper-loaded layered catalysts to attack amoxicillin and glyphosate. The team then exposed water fleas, algae, and lettuce seeds to the outflow, and ran a bacteria test for mutation risk. Even treated water stunted lettuce roots at low doses and slowed algae at far lower ones. The verdict: breakdown products still bite, so treatment plants need living checks.
pmc-10743243:
Xianshu Fu and co-authors present a 2023 review of methods for detecting the H5N1 bird flu virus. The strain is highly dangerous to poultry and can infect people, and it has recently shown signs of spreading among mammals. Fast, early detection is the main tool for stopping outbreaks before they grow.

The review walks through five families of tests. Blood-based and immune-based assays look for the body's response or viral proteins. Genetic methods copy and read the virus's own code. Newer biosensors aim for quick answers in the field. For each family, the authors compare speed, accuracy, cost, and ease of use. Their recommendations aim to guide labs and farms choosing a detection strategy.
pmc-10743443:
Zhaoyu Chen and co-authors wrote this 2023 review on how plant hormones and weather jointly govern bud dormancy in woody plants. A bud's sleep and waking set the rhythm of a tree's year, and the timing must match the seasons to survive frost and catch spring. The review maps the control system.

Growth hormones do not act alone: they trade signals in a web, with some enforcing sleep and others calling for release. Light and temperature feed into that web by tilting hormone levels, and sugars add a nutrient vote. The authors trace each hormone's role in setting, holding, and breaking dormancy, then show where the environment plugs in. The synthesis aims to help orchard and forest science as climates shift.
pmc-10743543:
Lipedema makes fat pile up symmetrically on women's legs, and it is often mistaken for plain obesity. Sally Kempa and co-authors profiled blood metabolites in 2023, hunting for chemical signs that separate lipedema from weight alone.

Twenty-five patients were compared with lean and obese control groups of the same size, matched for age. Patients showed lower histidine and phenylalanine and higher pyruvic acid than controls. Among women of similar body mass, those gaps persisted, which ties them to the disease rather than to size. Pyruvic acid separated patients from obese controls with near-perfect accuracy in their tests. The authors offer the three markers as leads toward a blood test for early diagnosis.
pmc-10743643:
Jeremy Marks and Michael Schreiber report a trial of inhaled nitric oxide in premature babies in this 2023 paper. The gas can ease lung disease in early-born infants, who face death and lasting lung damage. Past reviews hinted that benefit depends on dose and on the mother's racial background.

Babies born very early and small were assigned to a short course of the gas or a long course lasting weeks. The long course raised the combined rate of death or lung disease overall, driven by one weight group. Among the smallest babies, though, the long course lowered the chance of death. The long course harmed non-Black infants but showed no such effect in Black infants. The authors link the split to maternal racial identity.
pmc-10743743:
Chang Wang and co-authors show how a toxic metal harms the livers of ducks in a 2023 study. Hexavalent chromium is a hazardous pollutant from industry. Forty-eight young ducks were fed graded doses of it for forty-nine days, from none to a high dose. The team then checked liver shape, blood markers, and the cell pathways that manage energy and cell death.

Damage rose with dose. Liver tissue broke down in disorder, and blood harm markers climbed. The birds' antioxidant defenses fell while damage products rose. Energy-making steps in mitochondria faltered, tied to a drop in a master energy pathway. The balance of mitochondrial fusion and splitting tipped toward splitting. Death signals in liver cells rose while survival signals fell. The authors lay out a chain from oxidative stress to energy failure to cell death.
pmc-10744343:
Bander Albogami tests quercetin and chitosan, alone and combined, against Giardia gut infection in a 2023 rat study. Standard drugs against parasites carry side effects and sometimes fail. Natural compounds might treat infection while sparing the liver and intestine.

Fifty male rats were split into control, infected, and three infected-plus-treatment groups. Quercetin is a plant flavonoid and chitosan a shell-derived fibre, both with antioxidant names. Results covered parasite clearance, liver protection, antioxidant markers, and intestinal muscle structure. The study tests whether the pairing beats either agent alone as a gentler giardiasis therapy.
pmc-10744443:
Chadd Kraus and co-authors report, in a 2023 study, how wildly clinicians disagree when judging sepsis risk, and whether a new host response test could steady triage. Sepsis patients flood emergency departments with vague symptoms, and the cost of missing one is death. Historically, sorting them has leaned on individual judgment.

Twenty six specialists took part in a structured consensus exercise built around tricky case vignettes. Their risk estimates for the same cases ranged from 10 to 90 percent, with poor agreement. When the group worked through what actions a test result should trigger, agreement on next steps improved. The spread is the story: two good clinicians can look at one patient and see different emergencies. A test that reads the patient's own immune response could anchor those judgments. The study quantifies the dilemma such technology must solve.
pmc-10744843:
Emily Castillo-García and co-authors test maqui berry in a metabolic syndrome rat model in a 2023 paper. The dark berry is rich in anthocyanins, plant pigments tied to health gains. Rats on a syndrome inducing diet get the berry for fourteen days. Computer docking studies run alongside to find likely molecular targets.

Treated rats gain less weight and show lower blood sugar, cholesterol, and triglycerides, they report. Insulin resistance and blood pressure problems also ease. Blood markers of oxidative damage improve in both sexes. Docking suggests the berry pigments can bind enzymes and receptors tied to metabolism. Even low blood levels may act on several targets at once.
pmc-10744943:
Aneta Yacheva and co-authors test a scan measure in rectal cancer care in this 2023 study. Diffusion-weighted MRI yields a number, called ADC, that reflects how water moves in tissue. Treatment plans hinge on MRI findings, so the team checked what that number adds across care stages.

Cancer tissue showed far lower values than healthy rectums in their patient set. Deeper tumors and vessel invasion both tied to lower values. After chemoradiation, values rose, and tumors starting lowest rose most. The authors say the measure can help forecast treatment response and sharpen planning.
pmc-10745443:
Yordan Kalchev and co-authors report in a 2023 case study a seventy-four-year-old man whose blood grew a foodborne germ that tied into a burst belly aorta. The germ, Yersinia enterocolitica, usually causes gut illness: diarrhea, gut inflammation, and swollen glands. Blood invasion is rare in healthy people but known in weakened hosts.

His strain, serogroup O:3, reached the blood and coincided with rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, a lethal event. With a literature review, the authors press the link between this bacteremia and aneurysm rupture. Better surveillance, they argue, would sharpen the counts of such rare, deadly pairings.
pmc-10747043:
Bangxiong Liu and six co-authors simulate low-speed impacts on stitched carbon-fiber panels to learn how thickness and stitch density change the damage. Their 2023 study builds a progressive damage model in a standard engineering code. Stitching threads through a laminate is meant to hold its layers together when struck, a known weak point of layered composites.

The model uses established failure rules for fibers and matrix, plus a glue-layer rule for splitting between layers, with stiffness fading as damage grows. Its forecasts matched lab impact tests well. The main harms were matrix cracking under tension and layer splitting. Stitching curbed the splitting and shrank its area, more so at higher stitch density. Thin panels cracked more from bending, while thick ones split more. The results guide impact-tough designs.
pmc-10747343:
Konstantinos Stamatopoulos and co-authors build a body-based computer model for a gut drug that barely enters the blood. The drug, tenapanor, blocks a sodium swap channel in the gut and treats constipation tied to irritable bowel syndrome. Less sodium uptake leaves more water in the gut, which speeds waste along.

The model treats food sodium as the party acted on, and the drug as the actor that cuts its uptake. Meals were built in, since eating wakes the same channel. The model matched sodium in stool and urine of healthy users within a tight range. It also helped explain why dose timing against meals matters, and compared two forms of the drug.
pmc-10747543:
Yong Yang and co-authors study an iron-storage gene from peach trees in this 2023 paper. Ferritin proteins store iron safely and support plant growth, yet their roles in fruit trees were barely known. The team isolated three ferritin genes from a peach cultivar and mapped where each is active. One gene, PpFer1, stood out as the most active across all tissues tested.

Its activity rose sharply when seedlings faced excess iron or peroxide stress, above all in leaves. The team then placed the gene into a model plant lacking its own copy. The rescued plants grew better roots and leaves, held more chlorophyll, and photosynthesized faster than the mutants. Tissue iron rose too. The study explains how a fruit tree gene guards iron balance under stress.
pmc-10747743:
Yang Xu leads a team on sugar genes in the tomato plant. Their study from twenty twenty-three traces genes after genome tripling. Sugar is the main carbon form moved in higher plants.

Gene counts were tallied for grape and tomato in seven gene groups. Group sizes varied a lot from one group to the next. Duplication and loss took distinct paths in the tomato. Tandem copies drove growth of two of the gene groups. Most tomato genes lined up with grape kin genes. All groups were under a weeding form of selection.
pmc-10747843:
Lab-grown body tissue needs a scaffold, a small frame that cells can live on and shape. Rosalia and nine co-authors build scaffolds from two body-safe plastics, PCL and PLGA, mixed in varying shares. They make the frames two ways: by spinning fine fibers, and by casting with salt-like grains that leave bubble-shaped pores. They then measure fiber size, stiffness, wetting, and water uptake.

Fiber spinning gave steady control: more PCL made thicker fibers and softer frames. Cast frames wet better and held stem cells alive well over five days. Spun frames soaked up ten times more water but their cast rivals were less even in quality, since the mix tended to separate. Both kinds let special stem cells keep their flexible, undifferentiated state. The authors weigh the trade-offs for growing tissue in the lab.
pmc-10749443:
Solmaz Valizadeh and co-authors compare two tools for finding tooth decay in a 2023 study. Decay between back teeth is hard to spot early by eye alone. One tool is the standard bitewing X ray, and the other is an infrared camera. Cut teeth under a microscope served as the truth standard for the test.

Forty pulled back teeth without open cavities were examined by both tools. The X ray was better at clearing sound teeth correctly in the results. The camera caught far more true decay, especially shallow enamel decay. The authors suggest the camera as a partner to X rays rather than a replacement.
pmc-10751343:
Xunbo Zheng and co-authors study a gene called TICRR in lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer. The gene helps start DNA copying in cells and has been linked to tumor growth. The team measured the gene in tumor and nearby normal tissue. They also mined large cancer data sets to link its levels to stage, survival, and cell traits.

The gene was far more active in tumors than in normal tissue, and high levels tracked with worse survival. Its levels rose with tumor stage and with heavy smoking and high counts of gene changes. Lab work that silenced the gene shifted cell growth and immune signals. A risk score built on the gene sorted patients well, so the authors propose it as a marker and drug target.
pmc-10753343:
Igor Kovalchuk reviews how plants pass stress shields to their offspring. Most plants tune to their world over generations through gene and tag based change. A shield gained in one life can last into the next crop, then fade if stress stops.

When the shield fades in one step, it counts as a between generation effect. When it lasts past that, it counts as a cross generation effect. The review sums body and tag marks for both, their inner paths, and what they mean for wild life and evolution. Breeders may use such memory.
pmc-10753543:
Hernández-Giottonini and co-authors test, in a 2023 study, whether packaging an antibiotic inside tiny biodegradable spheres beats the plain drug against a stubborn bacterial infection in mice. The bacterium, Brucella canis, hides inside cells where drugs reach poorly. Long treatments and relapses follow.

The spheres measured about 138 nanometers and released their rifampicin load in a burst, then slowly. Infected mice received the packaged or plain drug for comparison. Particle charge and size spread indicated a stable, uniform product. Better delivery to the bacterium's hiding places could shorten therapy for a disease that also threatens the people and dogs around patients.
pmc-10753743:
Mi Tian, Wenjun Gan, and Eun-Suok Oh present, in a 2023 materials paper, a new glue for silicon battery anodes that fights their tendency to fall apart. Silicon stores far more charge than graphite but swells hugely as it charges. That swelling isolates particles electrically and drains capacity fast.

Their binder mixes a conductive clay-like material with hollow core-shell polymer spheres. It forms in place during a water-based process, avoiding harsh solvents. The clay carries electrons while the hollow shells ease ion flow and give swelling room. Together they aim to keep the electrode connected through many cycles. Better binders are a quiet prerequisite for the high-capacity batteries vehicle makers want.
pmc-10754543:
Weijuan Yang and co-authors test a nursing style built on action research for breast cancer patients at risk of arm swelling. After surgery that clears lymph nodes under the arm, fluid can build up and stiffen the limb. The team compared eighty-eight patients across one year: the first half got standard care, the second half got care shaped by cycles of planning, acting, and review.

Swelling struck about two in five of the standard-care group but only about one in five of the action-research group. Daily living scores climbed in both groups and climbed higher with the new approach. Anxiety and depression eased in both groups by the end as well. The authors credit the loop of feedback and adjustment for the gains.
pmc-10755743:
Xichao Zhang and co-authors watch a lone magnetic whirlpool wander near a flower-shaped obstacle. The whirlpool is a skyrmion, a tiny twisted knot of magnetism in a thin ferromagnetic film. The flower shares its handed twist. Heat alone sets the skyrmion drifting at random, with no push from current or a slope in temperature.

As the skyrmion roams, its dance couples to the chiral flower in ways set by their shared topology. The pair can steer where the skyrmion settles and how skyrmions spread out. The effect counts as order arising from disorder at a small scale, found only in ferro- and ferrimagnetic systems. The authors suggest the coupling could sort skyrmions in future devices without any driving force at all.
pmc-10760443:
Felipe Marques da Costa, Augusto Kreling Medeiros, and Marcos Aurélio Fonseca Magalhães report, in 2023 work, a scan trap in a woman with spread lung cancer. Her breath grew short over four weeks while on a aimed drug. A glow scan showed fresh bright uptake in her right breath sheet, a sign that oft reads as the cancer's march.

The true tale ran the other way. Tumour growth in her neck had crushed the nerve to her left breath sheet, stilling it. Her right sheet then worked twice as hard, and hard work alone lit the scan. Chest scans showed the left sheet raised, with no growth in the right. The team warns that not all new glow is spread.
pmc-10770643:
Riitta Freese and Vegard Lysne reviewed niacin for the Nordic Nutrition Recommendations in a 2023 paper. Niacin, known as vitamin B3, feeds the making of two carrier molecules that cells use to move energy. Needs are counted in niacin equivalents, since the body can also build it from an amino acid in food.

Interest in the past decade has centered on large doses used as a drug to lower blood fats. Newer NAD boosters also draw study as ways to raise cell energy stores. The review weighs intake needs, food sources, and the safety of high doses. It feeds into shared food guidance for the Nordic lands.
pmc-10771943:
Hyemin Jung and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three nationwide study of heart attacks in Koreans with HIV who take their treatment faithfully. Modern therapy suppresses the virus in most patients. Heart outcomes in this well-treated group were little studied.

Insurance claims identified thousands of people with strong treatment adherence over a decade. Heart events occurred more often than in the general population. Traditional risks like blood pressure and diabetes still drove many events. Deaths after heart events were counted separately for heart attack cases. The findings argue for heart prevention even when HIV is fully controlled.
pmc-10774043:
Jiahui He and co-authors count heart deaths among breast cancer patients in a United States registry. Their twenty twenty-three study draws near four hundred thousand patients diagnosed from twenty ten to twenty eighteen. Heart disease is the top non-cancer killer in this group.

About seven thousand patients died of cardiovascular causes. Their death rate ran well above the general population rate. Competing risk models sort which traits predict a heart death while cancer risk runs in parallel. Survivorship care often watches the cancer alone; these numbers argue the heart needs equal billing in follow-up plans, from blood pressure checks to drug side-effect review.
pmc-10800443:
Motoko Watanabe and nine co-authors report a woman whose mouth pain came before a form of dementia. Their case report, from twenty twenty-four, begins with burning mouth syndrome. That is a lasting burn in the mouth with no visible cause. The patient, aged seventy-four, ate less as the pain grew.

Two drugs eased the burn and her eating came back. The pain flared again when her and her husband's health worsened. New drugs helped once more over time. Later she grew anxious and at times failed to know her husband. Tests then pointed to dementia with Lewy bodies. The case shows mouth pain care and brain care can cross.
pmc-10806143:
Sophie Irwin and co-authors test a live bacterial therapy, ADS024, against ulcerative colitis in work dated two thousand twenty-three. The gut lining in that disease loses cells and turns leaky. ADS024 is one strain of Bacillus velezensis, a microbe being readied as a drug.

A sterile brew of the strain's secretions shielded colon tissue from colitis patients and human gut cells in the lab. It cut cell death and swelling signals, and blunted death caused by patient serum particles. It also eased a plunge in barrier strength from two swelling chemicals and kept a key seal protein at normal levels. Fed to mice with colon injury, the live strain cut weight loss and tissue damage.
pmc-10808143:
Yu Dgebuadze and five co-authors show that grass snakes carry key fats from water to land, in a 2023 study. Two fatty acids matter for animal health but are scarce on land. The team analyzed fats in grass snakes and in their prey. Prey were young frogs and toads leaving the water.

Snakes carried high levels of both acids in their body mass. Their prey carried them as well. Land food offers no source of one of the acids. So its high level in young frogs and in snakes must come from building blocks of water origin. The finding is presented as a first for this snake species. It marks snakes as a bridge moving water-made nutrients onto land. Such links matter for food webs around ponds and wetlands, the authors suggest.
pmc-10822943:
Naoki Shingai and co-authors report a case where immune pressure let faulty stem cell clones swell fast in a rare blood disease. Their case report was published in 2023, per the head. The disease, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, brings red cell breakdown, clots, and marrow failure, and springs from stem cells that lost a gene called PIGA.

The patient was a woman aged twenty six with low counts across blood lines. About seventy two percent of her white cells lacked the surface anchors the gene supports. Gene reading of those cells found three unlike PIGA faults and no others. She got a shielding drug plus an immune calming drug for six rounds. Her breakdown mark fell, but she still needed transfusions, and the case tracks what drove clone growth.
pmc-10824843:
Xin Du, Xue Ma, and Yang Gao review the natural compound squalene and its uses in animal farming in this paper, published in 2023. Squalene is an oily substance found in shark liver and in many plant seeds. It is known for calming swelling and for fighting harmful oxygen forms in the body. The review pulls together what is known about those body effects. It then asks how the compound could serve in feed for farm animals.

Uses in livestock and poultry are the practical focus of the piece. The authors weigh the evidence for health gains in those settings. They also note where the proof is still thin. The goal is to give a base for deeper work on squalene in husbandry. Reviews like this help feed makers judge a trendy additive. The paper covers sources, body roles, and farm prospects in turn.
pmc-10830643:
Junzhu Xu and co-authors report a lung cancer case with a strong response to a targeted drug, in a paper published in 2023. The patient was a man of fifty-eight who did not smoke. His cancer carried a rare change in the HER2 gene, a type with few good drug options. Many rounds of treatment had already been tried, including chemotherapy and earlier HER2 drugs.

A newer drug, trastuzumab deruxtecan, shrank both the lung tumor and spread in the brain. The man's strength improved a great deal, and he stayed on the drug for almost nine months. A side effect on his blood counts was brought under control. The case suggests the drug can help even after a close cousin drug has failed.
pmc-10839043:
Chengjian Wei and co-authors study how soil microbes respond when a wilt germ attacks tobacco roots. The germ spreads through soil and wilts many crops, yet healthy root zones often hold it back. Comparing soil around healthy and diseased plants, the team combined gene sequencing with chemical profiling of small molecules. Diseased soil held fewer kinds of bacteria and a thinner web of links between them, while several bacterial groups thrived only around healthy roots.

Eight soil traits, among them acidity, phosphorus, and magnesium, shaped which microbes lived where, and the wilt germ disliked acidic, magnesium-rich soil. Healthy soil was rich in chemical pathways that build antibacterial compounds, and four bacterial groups tracked with making them. The paper, published in 2023, argues that farming the right microbial community could become a way to suppress the disease. The authors offer their findings as a base for such strategies.
pmc-10847843:
Ameneh Jafari and five co-authors review the hunt for protein fingerprints that could catch cervical cancer earlier and less invasively. Screening has cut deaths, but compliance stays low and a blood-based test could reach women whom Pap programs miss. Proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins, has begun naming candidate markers and drug targets.

The review also takes up cervical cancer stem cells, the stubborn subpopulation blamed for tumor growth and resistance to therapy. Targeting those cells may matter as much as finding the cancer early. The authors concede practical challenges remain before proteomic tests reach clinics. They argue the approach could still reshape how this cancer is detected and treated.
pmc-10864443:
Ying Wang and co-authors test body and lipid measures as predictors of type 2 diabetes in this study, published in 2024. Diabetes is a major public health concern, and rates in older adults have risen fast. Simple measures that flag risk early could help target prevention.

Data came from a national Chinese study of ageing and retirement. Nearly eight thousand adults aged forty-five and over were included. The team weighed several obesity and blood-fat indices against later diabetes. They checked which indices predicted new cases best. Cheap measures from routine checks would suit wide screening. The results can help clinics pick the most useful index for older adults.
pmc-10866143:
Research on Indigenous land in Canada has often folded Indigenous Peoples into Western ways of knowing, even when ethics rules claim to protect them. Four authors review Canadian material in a 2023 paper on wellness, mental health, and substance use research. International declarations now affirm Indigenous rights, they note, yet policy still treats colonization as finished history. Against that backdrop the authors define research sovereignty: autonomous control over studies on Indigenous territory or involving Indigenous Peoples.

The review gathers key guidelines and principles from Canada and compares them with work abroad. It offers a practice-based tool to help institutions share control. The authors warn that any compilation is only a start; honoring sovereignty in the end requires a shift in how research itself is framed.
pmc-10875043:
H Branch Coslett and four co-authors introduce a quick imagination task that may help measure chronic back pain, in this 2023 paper. The idea rests on how imagining a movement draws on what the body expects it to feel like, pain included. If pain warps that inner simulation, the warp itself becomes a signal.

Eighty-five people with back pain and forty-five matched controls saw pairs of body part names and judged whether they could move so the parts touched. Patients said yes less often than controls, but only for moves needing the lower back or legs. The gap grew with pain severity, and pain ratings tracked the lower body shortfall closely. The authors note the task is fast, needs no equipment, and never asks patients to rate pain directly.
pmc-10876443:
You-Jung Choi, Won Young Wi, Geum Joon Cho, and Jin Oh Na link pre-pregnancy heart rhythm disorders to gestational diabetes in Korea, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Arrhythmias are more common in people with diabetes. Whether they also precede diabetes in pregnancy was unknown. The team used national health insurance records for over a million births.

After exclusions, about three hundred sixty-six thousand singleton pregnancies without prior diabetes were analyzed. Under one percent of the women had cardiac arrhythmias before pregnancy. Gestational diabetes occurred in about nine percent overall, but nearly fifteen percent among women with arrhythmia. Adjusted analysis kept the association significant, with odds roughly seventy-eight percent higher. The link held across age, body size, and blood pressure subgroups. The authors argue arrhythmia history flags pregnancies needing closer glucose watch.
pmc-10925643:
Gene Chatman Clark and co-authors offer a 2023 review on a vitamin-like cofactor and nitric oxide in cancer. The cofactor powers an enzyme that makes nitric oxide, a vessel signal. When the cofactor runs low, as in tumors and chronic inflammation, the enzyme misfires. It then makes radicals that attack the cofactor itself.

That loop locks in low cofactor levels. Nitric oxide signaling warps, killer immune cells are held back, and vessel inflammation grinds on inside the tumor. The review gathers proof for this switch across tumor growth and treatment response. Animal work hints that topping up the cofactor could boost immunotherapy and radiation. Safety questions remain open. The authors frame the loop as an overlooked drug target.
pmc-10936143:
Alberto Dionigi, Mirko Duradoni, and Laura Vagnoli study how different styles of humor relate to depression, anxiety, and stress, published in 2023. Interest in humor and mental distress has grown, but past work rarely split humor into specific styles. Nor did it tie those styles to specific negative states.

A large sample of Italian adults completed an online survey covering eight comic styles. Regression analysis then linked each style to the three distress measures. Benign humor acted as a protective factor for all three. Irony tracked with higher anxiety and stress, and sarcasm with higher depression. Wit was protective for anxiety. The other styles showed no firm links in their analysis. The authors discuss the pattern against prior literature on humor and health.
pmc-11199443:
Lünnemann and three co-authors studied romantic relationships of youth exposed to family violence in twenty twenty-three. Growing up with violence at home can shape later relationships, but the authors wanted a fuller picture, including strengths. They interviewed eighteen young people aged sixteen to twenty who had been reported to child protection services.

The young people described struggles with support, connection, trust, setting boundaries, handling emotions, and resolving conflict. The authors link these patterns to learning by watching others and to attachment theory. Yet many also described good experiences and learning better ways from a partner. With the right social or professional support, the authors argue, these youth can overcome many of the challenges they face.
pmc-11225443:
Ghaffarian Jafarzade Sara and co-authors tie spouse force to women's self sense in bed life in a 2023 study. Sex force is a world health ill with grave, wide harm to its prey in all lands. The work asks how such force maps to how women hold their bed self in mind each day.

Near three hundred wed women of birth age in one town's health hubs form the herd for the work. Set forms log traits, force tales, and self sense grades for each case in the pool. Two thirds of the herd told of force by their mates in the past forms.
pmc-11230143:
Azam Moslemi and co-authors studied yeast infection in foot sores among people with diabetes at a large hospital. The study ran from late 2019 to late 2020 in northern Iran and covered 100 patients. The team recorded patient facts and wound grades, then checked samples with a scope and by growing the fungus in the lab.

Lab tests named the kind of yeast in each sore, using gene-based methods to sort the strains. Foot sores that let fungus in can grow worse and heal more slowly, so clear naming of the cause matters for care. The study gives doctors a picture of how often this yeast shows up in such wounds and which kinds are most common.
pmc-11438943:
Tsvetelina Velikova, Stavros Gerasoudis, and Hristiana Batselova review vaccine advice for people who live with a transplanted organ, in work from 2024. Drugs that guard the graft also blunt the immune system. Shots remain a key shield, but timing and type need care in this group.

The review gathers current guidance and evidence on how well vaccines work after transplant and how safe they are. Routine shots and COVID shots both get attention. Live vaccines raise special caution. The authors stress plans tuned to each patient's drugs, graft, and history. They call for better strategies so recipients gain full protection with the least risk. Gaps in evidence are flagged for study.
pmc-11530743:
Douglas Boyes, Clare Boyes, and the Darwin Tree of Life teams present the genome of the case-bearing clothes moth in a 2024 genome note. The moth's larvae feed on fabrics and carry a small case. A single female specimen from Wytham Woods provides the DNA. The work belongs to a national effort to sequence British species.

The assembly spans 245.3 megabases, they report. Most of it sits in thirty chromosome-like scaffolds, including the Z sex chromosome. The mitochondrial genome is also complete at 25.86 kilobases. Annotation finds 13,811 protein coding genes. The sequence gives a reference for studying this household pest and its tineid relatives.
pmc-11532543:
Mahnaz Mirheidari, Ali Kareem Abbas, and Javad Safaei-Ghomi published a chemistry paper in 2024 on a new reusable catalyst built on layered porous microspheres.
