Porous silica supports speed many reactions. The team coated a magnetic core-shell support with the amino acid phenylalanine and mapped the product with a battery of imaging and analysis tools.

The catalyst was then used to build two families of fused ring compounds from simple starting materials in one pot. The route gave high yields in short times with little catalyst, under green conditions. The authors present the material as a practical, eco-friendly platform for making these drug-like ring systems.
pmc-11536543:
Kyoungwon Jung and five colleagues compare, published in 2024, three ways of pushing the stomach bacterium Helicobacter pylori into its round resting form. The spiral bacterium rounds up under stress, keeping its virulence genes, so the round form still matters for disease. Labs need reliable ways to make it. The team used starvation, the antibiotic amoxicillin, and the liquid left over from growing a mouth bacterium. They checked shape, aliveness, and whether cells could still grow colonies, and read protein profiles of each round form.

Starved cells stopped forming colonies within a week yet stayed alive and round. Amoxicillin drove cells fastest into a living but non-growing state. The mouth bacterium's broth kept cells growing longest, hinting it holds something that preserves the spiral. Protein sets differed by method, with some shared changes across all. The authors say the making method must be reported, since it shapes the cells.
pmc-11538243:
Assi and four colleagues test a gel plus stem cell broth for arthritic jaw joints in rats in twenty twenty-four. The broth is the fluid stem cells grow in, rich in healing signals. Fifty female rats were split into five groups: healthy, arthritic, gel alone, broth alone, and both together. Arthritis was sparked by two shots of an irritant into the jaw joint.

After four weeks, joints that got both treatments looked best on every measure. The joint disc thinned toward normal and the cartilage layer widened. Collagen rose and a key inflammation switch fell. Each single treatment helped less than the pair. The team says the combo merits study as a joint repair route.
pmc-11545143:
Recovering from COVID-19 can leave lasting strain on mental health. Ting-Fai Man and co-authors surveyed adults in Macau in 2024 who had recovered from the infection, using a twelve-question general health screen. Of nearly five hundred responses, four hundred twenty-six were complete enough to analyze.

About seventy-two percent screened as having poor mental health. Lingering symptoms after the illness were the strongest risk factor, raising the odds nearly sixfold. Adults aged twenty-six to forty-five and those over sixty faced higher risk, as did married respondents and people unhappy with family ties. Men showed lower risk. The authors urge targeted support for recovered patients with lasting symptoms and for the vulnerable groups they name.
pmc-11546743:
Juhong Xie and seven colleagues dissect a devastating fish virus with omics in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Grass carp reovirus causes bleeding disease that heavily damages the grass carp farming industry. The team profiled five tissues, gill, liver, intestine, kidney, and muscle, before and after infection, finding over ten thousand proteins and four thousand metabolites. Analysis of the changes then mapped how the virus rewires each tissue.

Across tissues, the changed proteins and metabolites centered on carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, with fatty acids, glycerophospholipids, and steroids prominent among the metabolites. Joint pathway analysis flagged glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway as clearly enriched, and blocker tests showed both pathways matter for viral copying, making them candidate drug targets. The kidney suffered most; its butanoate metabolism changes were studied in depth. The study supplies a tissue-by-tissue molecular map for designing treatments against the virus.
pmc-11548143:
Sara Khurizadeh and co-authors test leaf sprays to help guar under drought in 2024. Guar is a summer legume prized for its gum and thickening power. Dry spells threaten its yield and seed quality, so protective sprays are worth testing.

Two sprays, a plant hormone and a shell-derived polymer, were tried alone and together in a greenhouse. Two guar varieties grew under full, medium, and low watering. Sprays improved height, pods, seed yield, and roots across the board. The combined dose lifted gum share and thickness most, and one variety held up best under water stress.
pmc-11565443:
Nathan Davies and co-authors describe building a self-management toolkit with people who live with Parkinson's, in a 2024 paper. Parkinson's is progressive and complex, and day-to-day coping falls mostly on patients and families. Self-management programs help in other long-term conditions, but Parkinson's needed its own version, shaped by its own community.

The Live Well with Parkinson's toolkit grew through rounds of co-design. Patients, family carers, and health and social care experts formed a group that drafted and refined the online tools, informed by reviews and theory. A facilitator helps users get started rather than leaving them alone with a website. The paper shares the process and core parts so other teams can adapt the approach.
pmc-11567843:
Ilaria Catanzaro, Anna Gorbushina, Silvano Onofri, and Julia Schumacher tested in 2024 whether dark pigment shields two black fungi from ultraviolet light. Black fungi live on rock faces under harsh sun, and their dark walls are thought to protect them. Past results on that shield role were mixed, so the team compared two species directly.

They exposed normal fungi and mutants that cannot make the pigment to varied doses of UV-B light. After exposure, fungi rested in darkness or in light-dark cycles that let them repair DNA with light. One species took higher doses but was hurt by white light, while the other behaved in a different pattern. The pigment thus helped one species more than the other. Readers learn that a shared trait can serve uneven roles across close species.
pmc-11569143:
Asphalt makes a cheap, sticky coat that guards steel, but on its own it lets rust creep in too fast for harsh settings. Abdalrahman Al-Gamal and co-authors boost it in a 2024 study with a blend of a branching polymer and zinc oxide specks. The blend was stirred into asphalt at several loadings and painted on carbon steel for testing.

One loading stood out: a small share of the blend blocked nearly all the corrosion in lab tests. The polymer spreads the zinc specks evenly and glues them down, forming a tight skin over the steel. The zinc also plays a sacrificial role, reacting with attacking ions before the steel does. The two effects stack, the authors argue, into a coat far tougher than plain asphalt at low added cost.
pmc-11574143:
Diata Traore and co-authors offer a shortcut to chemical accuracy on today's small quantum computers. Precise molecular results normally demand huge basis sets and hundreds of clean qubits, far beyond current hardware. Their trick folds a quantum computing ansatz into density-functional theory, then adds a correction drawn from the electron density itself.

The correction pushes results toward the complete basis set limit without more qubits. Basis sets are crafted on the fly to fit each molecule and a set qubit budget. Ground-state energies, electron densities, and traits such as dipole moments all improve in their tests, run on GPU emulators. The same fix can polish results computed on real quantum hardware later. Drug design and materials science stand to gain.
pmc-11576743:
Shuaijie Zhang and co-authors report a model from two thousand twenty-four for early lung cancer screening in Chinese populations. Many health records have missing fields, which can break standard prediction tools. The team built a model that can still judge risk when data are incomplete, without using radiation-based scans.

The model, called BOUND, uses a Bayesian network and was trained on records from more than nine hundred thousand people. It kept strong accuracy in checks split by time and by place, and it held up when large shares of data were removed on purpose. A simple risk scorecard built from the model raised detection rates several-fold. The authors offer the tool free online for use in basic care settings.
pmc-11576843:
Leyi Loh and co-authors published a study in 2024 on single-photon sources in a sheet material. Crystals one atom thick can host lone defects that act as tiny quantum light sources. The team seeded a tungsten-sulfur sheet with niobium atoms spaced far apart.

At that spacing, each dopant could be studied on its own. The lone dopants gave narrow light lines, tight in space, with the stop-start pattern that proves single photons. The lines sat in a narrow color band across many samples, unlike the wide spread seen in kindred materials. Magnetic splits in the lines pointed to a bound complex of a dark particle pair and the charged dopant. The authors say such dopants are steady, uniform quantum emitters.
pmc-11577643:
Quratulain Ahsan and co-authors explore what drives depression in pregnant women in Lahore, Pakistan, and what helps them cope. The study wraps around a talking therapy program called the Thinking Healthy Programme, adapted for local use. It follows women from screening through therapy to a final review.

Women aged eighteen to forty-five were first screened with a standard mood questionnaire. Those flagged were interviewed in depth about the roots of their low mood. Three themes stood out: hard life events, strain inside marriage, and stress from joint family living. After the therapy course, the same women spoke again about change. Their accounts show which supports eased distress and which pressures stayed. Clinics in like settings can use the themes to target aid before and after birth.
pmc-11577843:
Sara Casey and thirteen co-authors studied the sexual and reproductive health of Sudanese refugee girls in Chad, in a 2024 paper. The girls, aged twelve to nineteen, fled Darfur and live in two camps. The team surveyed the girls, ran group activities with them, and spoke with parents and health workers. They asked what the girls know about bodies and contraception, what they believe, and what they do.

Knowledge was mixed, with older girls knowing more. Despite strong community stigma around sex before marriage, about one in five girls had already had sex. Most girls believed health workers would keep their visits private. Among those who had had sex, under one in five used a modern contraceptive, none of them a long-acting kind. Parents and workers described stigma as the main barrier, though midwives quietly helped girls reach services. The authors call for programs shaped to this setting.
pmc-11577943:
Benjamin R Stultz, Thomas J Beckman, and their co-authors asked what sets apart medical residents who go on to train in lung and critical care medicine. Their 2024 study covers twelve classes of internal medicine residents at one institution, finishing between 2010 and 2021. Fellowship choice is a hard step for many residents, and the paths into this field were unclear.

Of 522 residents, about one in ten matched into a lung and critical care fellowship within a year. Taking a lung elective during residency raised the odds nearly eight fold. A stated plan to enter the field also raised the odds. Curiously, residents with fewer than three publications matched more often than those with three or more. The findings can guide advising and elective planning.
pmc-11580243:
Bahram Sheikhi and Hadi Akbari set out a 2024 plan to adapt a tendon health form for Persian athletes. The form asks athletes with Achilles tendon pain to rate pain, signs, and body function. No sound Persian form yet exists for this ill, which is common in sport.

Their plan follows world rules for picking health forms. One hundred athletes with the tendon ill will fill the form twice to test its steadiness. The team will also check how well it hangs together and how it stacks up against other health scores. A sound form would help clinics in Iran judge care.
pmc-11580443:
Namyoung Park and co-authors weigh ways to count spread to lymph nodes in a rare gut cancer in a 2024 study. The cancer grows where the bile duct meets the gut. Node spread is a top sign of how a patient will fare, but teams count it in unlike ways and had not set them side by side.

The study held 86 patients who had surgery and then drug care, with a median follow-up near 69 months. Each count method was tested alone and with other facts weighed. Two or more sick nodes stood out as a firm risk mark for life span and for return of the illness. The share of sick nodes among those cut also held up for return risk.
pmc-11583643:
Shumpei Tsukamoto and eight co-authors compare a gut drug's effects in male and female rats in a 2024 study. The drug copies ghrelin, a hormone that can drive colon movement through a spinal center. Such drugs might one day ease constipation, so sex differences matter for dosing.

Given through a vein, the drug boosted colon movement in female rats. Females needed about ten times the dose that worked in males for the same effect. The gap held when the drug went straight into the lower spinal cord. Gene tests showed females carry fewer ghrelin receptors in that cord region. Lower receptor counts may explain much of the sex gap.
pmc-11584843:
Ardvin Ong, Gerlyn Altes, and Josephine German study what drives people in the Philippines to actually use cloud storage, not just mean to. Their 2024 paper notes that the country has taken to free tiers of such services, while paid space lags. Proof on real use, as opposed to plans, was thin.

A survey drew 616 valid replies, which the team fed to a blend of learning methods. The blend scored about nine in ten calls right. Five factors kept surfacing as drivers of real use. They were how free the choice felt, what peers do, and the gain users see. How useful the service feels, and how near at hand it seems, counted too. The authors pitch the findings to firms that want paid uptake to grow.
pmc-11584943:
Xuxiao Gong, Hyuk Choi, Yaqi Zhao, Qinchun Rao, and Leqi Cui chemically bond a plant acid to pea protein in a paper from 2024. Pea protein is popular but limited by modest solubility and emulsifying power. Covalent binding with p-coumaric acid reshaped the protein's structure. Helix and coil shares rose while turns fell, and particle size shrank. Soluble clumps formed through water-shy interactions as more acid attached.

The modified protein dissolved and emulsified better across acidity levels. Foaming, however, weakened, and foam lasted less long. Heat behavior shifted too, suggesting unfolding and new bonds. The authors see food uses where emulsions matter more than foams. The trade-offs are mapped for product designers.
pmc-11585143:
Eman Fouad and co-authors test light therapies to help young teeth regrow inner tissue, in a 2024 study. The work used dog teeth whose roots had not finished forming. Standard regenerative care often fails to show true regrowth under the microscope. Disinfection by light-activated drugs was part of the protocol.

Seventy-two root canals were split into groups and controls. One group got the regenerative care plus low-level light sessions. The light was a diode laser given seven times. The other group got the care without extra light. Tissue was checked at one, two, and three months. Microscope evidence can tell real regrowth from mere repair, a bar this field has struggled to clear.
pmc-11585243:
Fangfang Zhou and colleagues build a nanoparticle that mops up the chemical shrapnel of a brain bleed and delivers a protective drug on cue, in this study from twenty twenty-four. After intracerebral hemorrhage, oxidative stress and inflammation drive the second wave of injury. Their particle is a porous silica sphere stitched with selenium bonds, loaded with an anti-inflammatory plant compound, and sealed with a polydopamine coat.

The design is reactive in both senses: the particle itself scavenges reactive oxygen species. Those same species break its selenium stitches, opening the pores to release the drug where damage is worst. In dishes and in mice, it calmed the brain's immune cells, shifting them from attack to repair mode. Injected into veins, it gathered at the bleed's rim and protected the brain, with good safety. The authors pitch it as a two-in-one platform for hemorrhage care.
pmc-11585543:
Zhenpeng Shen leads a team that creates glycoside diversity from glycals. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with sugar building blocks. Tweaking glycosides can change or boost drug traits.

Blocks with many changeable spots were hard to make. A nickel driven reaction adds carbon and boron at set spots. The boron group at one spot can be swapped later. That yields rare sugars with changes at that same spot. Many groups and complex drug shapes were tolerated. Analogs of natural products and drugs were made. The route speeds access to varied sugars.
pmc-11585943:
Lin-Lin Tao and co-authors published this fertility study in 2024. In IVF, clinics choosing an embryo for a day-four single transfer can look back at how many cells it had on day three. The team asked whether that cell count predicts pregnancy and newborn outcomes. They reviewed 431 fresh single transfers, sorting them into three groups by day-three cell number: seven to nine cells, ten to thirteen, and more than thirteen.

Embryos from the middle group did best. Their pregnancy and live birth rates beat the seven-to-nine group across age bands and in the standard IVF subgroup, and after statistical adjustment the gap held. The newborn outcomes, by contrast, did not differ between groups. The authors recommend preferring embryos that held ten to thirteen cells on day three when a day-four transfer is planned. They note the fastest group was small, with only 34 cycles.
pmc-11586443:
I-Chien Wu, Yung-Yi Lu, Wei-Ting Tseng, and Pei-Fen Chen report a 2024 study of nerve balance and body strength change in older adults. Strength in daily acts, like rising from a chair, rests on the body's steady-state control, which the autonomic nerves run. The team tracked 542 adults with an average age near seventy.

Heart rhythm swings marked nerve health, and chair rise time marked strength, both read more than once. Weak low-band rhythm power at the start tied to faster strength loss each year. Shifts in the rhythm bands over time tied to rise time change as well.
pmc-11589143:
Lixiao Zhou, Xingsen Zhao, Jie Sun, and a team of co-authors identify a protein that erases a chemical tag from the packaging of DNA in brain stem cells. Cells mark their histone proteins with small tags to switch genes on and off, and while the writers and readers of one such tag were known, its eraser had stayed mysterious.

The team caught the protein, called Mina53, holding onto the tagged histone, then proved in test tubes and in living cells that it strips the tag away. Computer simulations backed the finding at the atomic level. In mice lacking the protein only in their neural stem cells, key developmental genes fell out of tune and memory suffered. The work completes a missing piece of the gene-control machinery.
pmc-11589843:
Yassine Bouteraa and Mohammad Khishe improve a nature-inspired optimizer for solar models in a 2024 paper. Fitting the parameters of solar cell models is a slippery optimization problem with many local traps. A recent algorithm mimics marine predators switching between two search gaits, a wandering Brownian walk and long Lévy flights, but its switching was unpredictable.

Their fix is a dynamic shift function that eases the transition between gaits continuously, the way a real predator's hunt phases blend. A constraint handler keeps candidate parameters inside physical bounds. Across single, double, and triple-diode solar models, the improved algorithm reached the lowest average error among eleven methods compared, with statistical significance. Accurate solar parameters underpin panel design and monitoring, so better fitting is quiet but useful progress. The paper is a method contribution aimed at the optimization community.
pmc-11590243:
Bone stays strong through a balance of cells that chew it down and cells that build it up. Yonghwan Shin and co-authors study a protein that tips the chewing side in a 2024 paper on bone cell growth.

The protein, VprBP, is known as a kinase that helps silence genes. The team found it pushes precursor cells to mature into bone-eating cells when a key signal arrives. It works by adding a phosphate mark to a histone protein, which shuts off genes that would block the change. Blocking that kinase power revived the blocking genes and stalled cell growth. Animal work tied the mark to low bone mass, pointing to a new drug angle for osteoporosis.
pmc-11590443:
Priyanka Patil and co-authors published a case report in 2024 on a rare skin tumor pattern in a man in his late fifties. The tumors grow from tiny smooth muscles in the skin, most often those that raise hairs. His had spread in a belt-like pattern across several body segments on both sides, a form very few reports describe.

For ten years, dark raised lumps on his upper back and belly had grown in size and number, with pain and itching that wore down his daily life. A skin biopsy confirmed the diagnosis. Options include cutting the growths out, freezing them, or burning them off. The authors share photos so other doctors can spot the pattern sooner.
pmc-11590943:
Reham Kaki, Amjad Taj, and Sultan Bagaaifar assess a new antibiotic at a hospital in Jeddah in this 2024 study. Cefiderocol treats Gram-negative infections that resist many other drugs. Global health groups warn that too few strong options exist for these germs.

The team reviewed care from January 2021 to February 2023. Thirteen patient groups got cefiderocol and twenty got other antibiotics. Death rates, intensive care stays, and illness scores did not differ by a firm margin. Cure rates for cefiderocol were high despite severe illness. Two treated patients caught a second gut infection, so close watch for side effects is needed.
pmc-11592443:
A team of pathologists reviews how bile duct cancers get their blood supply, in a 2024 article. Tumors can grow fresh vessels or hijack ones already nearby. The bile ducts and gallbladder sit in richly vascular tissue, which makes the hijack route, called vessel co-option, worth close study.

Early growths on the duct lining often fed from the existing capillary web beneath them. Full cancers of the ducts and gallbladder, by contrast, mostly grew their own vessels within scar-like tissue. Some growths with complex shapes showed a third pattern: sparse capillaries with no scar tissue. Liver cancers of the small-duct type sometimes spread by replacing liver cell rows and borrowing the local sinus vessels. Mapping which supply a tumor uses, the authors argue, could become a tool for judging how far it has advanced.
pmc-11595943:
Lu Xia, Thomas Tybell, and Sverre Selbach computed in 2024 how straining a thin film of a magnetic oxide changes the cost of missing bismuth atoms. Strain strongly shapes the properties of oxide films, but its effect on defect counts is less studied, and measuring film composition directly is hard. Computer modeling fills that gap.

Using quantum-mechanical calculations, they found squeezing the film made bismuth vacancies much cheaper to form, while stretching made them costlier. Pairs of bismuth and oxygen vacancies became more stable under both kinds of strain when aligned one way, but not the other. The authors discuss how this affects film growth and the formation of conducting walls inside the material.
pmc-11597443:
Michela Furbatto and co-authors pool studies on whether a Mediterranean diet cuts death and heart risk in older adults, in a meta-analysis from 2024. Past results on long-term outcomes in this age group had conflicted. The diet stresses vegetables, grains, olive oil, and fish over red meat.

The search, run to May 2023, found 28 studies with 679,259 people in all. Most were cohort studies, with just two trials. High adherence to the diet linked to a 23 percent lower risk of death from any cause. Heart deaths fell by 27 percent, and non-fatal heart events by 23 percent. The authors call the diet a promising pattern for healthy aging.
pmc-11597543:
The authors develop a method to measure antibiotics inside mussels in a 2024 paper. Traces of drugs in seafood can reach consumers. Mussels also serve as signs of marine pollution. One-step extraction plus cleanup anchors the method.

Three sulphonamide drugs and a partner compound were the aim. Six breakdown products joined the analyte list. Dispersion extraction with a common solvent did the prep work. Liquid chromatography with tandem mass detection finished the job. Linearity, accuracy, and sensitivity all checked well. Detection limits sat below five nanograms per gram. Mussels put in spiked sea water tested the workflow. Both spiked drugs showed in the tissue. One built up more, matching its fattier chemistry. No metabolites were found in these samples. The species earned its status as a living sign of pollution. Food safety labs gain a protocol for many drugs at once.
pmc-11599043:
Alexander Nico-Katz and co-authors ask whether quantum computers lose information even when they sit idle, doing nothing, in a 2024 paper. Qubits face opposite demands: they must be shielded from each other at rest, yet interact strongly when computing. If idle qubits are not shielded well, information leaks into neighbors and is lost. Fixes exist, but no standard protocol measured the effect itself.

The team build a scalable protocol, not tied to one device, using tools from quantum information theory. They run it in over 3,500 experiments across four months on a full series of IBM processors. After other error sources were accounted for, they detect idle information loss with high statistical confidence. The work gives the protection-versus-operation dilemma a firm quantitative base.
pmc-11599943:
Martin Hanze, Andrew Piper, and Mahiar Max Hamedi sew microfluidic channels into ordinary cloth with a sewing machine. Thread-based channels move liquid by wicking, which suits wearable sensors, but building them by hand is slow. Their 2024 work stitches a high-wicking polyester yarn into water-repelling fabrics, including a stretchable one, using only commercial textiles and machines.

The stitched devices mix and separate fluids in flat and three-dimensional layouts. Sewn into a T-shirt, one device collected sweat from the wearer's skin, carried it along the yarn, and detected its contents. The garments survive machine washing, so they can be reused. Stitched gold-coated yarns double as electrodes for chemical sensing inside the channels. The authors present machine stitching as a cheap, scalable route to diagnostic clothing that factories could adopt as they stand.
pmc-11600743:
Gaohan Yin, Tianhang Zhou, and Qingmei Kong report a rare brain harm case. Their case from twenty twenty-four deals with a girl of thirteen in China. She had five months of anorexia, an eating disorder.

Scans showed the classic marks of central pontine myelinolysis. That harm strips the coat from nerves in the brain stem. It can come from fast fix of low blood salt. Her case had no grave salt shift in the tale. Yet her outlook for both ills proved quite good. Care teams should watch for it in refeeding.
pmc-11600843:
Jingyi Yang, Yating Li, Xiaoyan Li, and Nari Wulan weigh two fixes for broken wrists in older adults in two thousand twenty-four. A distal radius break can be held by a surgically set locking plate or by a cast after the bone is nudged back. Which fix serves patients best over years was unclear.

Four randomized trials with four hundred twenty-three patients aged sixty or more, each followed at least two years, were pooled. The plate group scored better on two wrist rating scales, one patient-rated and one on arm and hand limits. Grip strength also favored the plate. Quality-of-life scores and repeat surgery were also tracked. The authors read the edge as real but modest.
pmc-11600943:
Tesfay and Shibeshi (2024) described the pattern of spheroidal degeneration of the cornea at a referral eye clinic in Ethiopia. The condition grows small globules in the cornea and is tied to sun and outdoor exposure. Over sixteen months at the Menelik II hospital's front-of-eye clinic, 62 cases were enrolled and examined with a structured questionnaire.

About 77 percent of patients were men, and most were in their sixties and seventies. Over 90 percent worked outdoors. The disease stage split fairly evenly, with stage III the largest share at about 40 percent. Other eye problems were common in these patients, including cataract, corneal scars, and glaucoma signs. None of them, though, showed a statistical association with the degeneration itself. The authors conclude the condition concentrates in older men who spend their days outside.
pmc-11602643:
Polish researchers built two mouse models to test whether faulty RNA alone can drive part of Huntington disease. The disease stems from a stretched repeat in one gene, which makes a harmful protein. Whether the gene RNA copy harms cells on its own, apart from the protein, has long been debated. One mouse line made both the RNA and the protein, while a second made the RNA in a form that cells could not turn into protein.

Both lines were tracked for 21 months with tests of movement, thought, and gene activity. Both showed changes in behaviour and in gene use in a key brain area. The line with the protein showed a late, fuller disease pattern. Mice with RNA alone still showed motor flaws in some tests and odd activity at night. The work backs a real, if smaller, role for RNA harm.
pmc-11602743:
Spyridon Papageorgiou and co-authors pool randomized trials to find which braces approaches truly improve the final bite, in a 2024 review. Many appliances are sold on claims of better results, and the authors insist choices should rest on trial evidence, not marketing. Searches across seven databases ran to March 2024.

Trials counted if they scored the bite outcome with one of two standard indexes after fixed-appliance treatment. Twenty small to moderate trials qualified. The team extracted data twice, graded bias risk, and combined results with random-effects models, then rated how strong the advice can be. The review aims to separate the few protocol choices with real support from the rest.
pmc-11603043:
Mohammed Al-Shiekh and co-authors count tooth injuries from breathing tubes in children under anesthesia, in a 2024 study. Sliding a tube past a child's teeth with a laryngoscope is routine and safe overall, but loose mixed dentition is fragile, and dental injury is among its commonest complications.

The prospective study followed 110 children aged six to twelve having surgery at the University Children's Hospital in Damascus during 2022. Each child's mouth was examined before surgery, watched during it, and rechecked within a day after. The team logged who was hurt, which anesthesia steps were involved, and which mouth features raised the risk. Hard local numbers, they argue, are the first step to prevention checklists that fit children's changing teeth.
pmc-11603143:
Drug-resistant staph bacteria shrug off standard antibiotics, so Kun Zhang and co-authors engineer a peptide weapon against them in this 2024 study. Starting from a known peptide, they designed variants and picked one, A24, for its stability and killing power. It punches into the bacterial wall, leaks the membrane, and floods the cell with reactive oxygen until it dies fast.

A24 also broke up young biofilms, erased much of mature ones, and killed 99.9 percent of dormant persister cells. Blood and tissue tests showed low harm at working doses. In mice with belly or womb infections, it cut bacterial loads ten-thousandfold and raised survival to 100 percent in one model. The team aims it first at farm animal infections.
pmc-11603643:
The clear gel inside the eye keeps a chemical diary of retinal disease, and proteomics can read it. Tommaso Brighenti and co-authors compared vitreous samples from diabetic retinopathy, retinal detachment, and control patients. Mass spectrometry measured 988 proteins, and the disease groups clustered apart cleanly.

Each disease carried its own protein signature, with hundreds of proteins changed against controls. Yet one pathway, glucose metabolism, shifted in both diseases despite their different causes. One enzyme in it, AKR1B1, stood out as a shared player. A computer screen then nominated diclofenac, an approved eye anti-inflammatory, as a drug that could hit it. The 2024 study links two blinding diseases to one target.
pmc-11603743:
Isobel Todd and four colleagues pool thirty-one studies on over ten million children to ask whether caesarean birth raises infection risk through childhood. The question matters because caesarean rates are high, and early microbial exposure differs sharply by birth mode.

Children born by caesarean, emergency or elective, went to hospital with infections at somewhat higher rates. That included upper respiratory infections, with hazard ratios around 1.10 to 1.12. Effects on infections outside hospital were judged by direction rather than pooled numbers. The evidence comes all from high-income-country cohorts. The authors weigh bias carefully; the raw increase is small but consistent across very large groups.
pmc-11603843:
Liu and seven colleagues review armored CAR cell therapies for solid tumors in twenty twenty-four. CAR-T therapy engineers T cells to hunt cancer by a surface receptor. It has transformed blood cancer care over the past decade. In solid tumors, poor trafficking and a suppressive environment limit its effect.

Two newer variants aim to fill those gaps. CAR natural killer cells need no tissue matching and show lower toxicity. CAR macrophages can eat tumor cells and present their antigens to other immune cells. The review compares features, advantages, and limits of all three cell types. It also suggests ways to boost their performance in solid tumors. The authors frame the variants as complementary, not rival, strategies.
pmc-11603943:
Li and co-authors report a case where nerve damage in the eye was the first sign of acute retinal necrosis. This fast, severe eye infection is caused here by varicella zoster virus, the chickenpox virus. Starting with optic neuropathy is a rare way for the disease to appear.

A 57-year-old man first lost vision in his right eye, with signs of optic nerve damage. Twenty days later, vision in his left eye also fell. The report follows his treatment and follow-up in detail. It warns eye doctors that early nerve signs can precede the classic retinal picture.
pmc-11604343:
Run-Qi Guo, Jin-Zhao Peng, Jie Sun, and Yuan-Ming Li compare two ways to burn or freeze small kidney tumors away. For early T1a kidney cancer, some patients get ablation instead of full surgery, but guidelines differ on tumors in the three to four centimeter range. Their 2024 study uses a national cancer database to form matched groups. One group had heat-based ablation and the other had freezing, called cryoablation.

Cancer outcomes were compared for tumors up to three centimeters and for the larger band. Real-world records let the team study many more patients than a single hospital could. The authors aim to give doctors firmer ground for the size range where advice conflicts. They note that database studies must be read with care, since treatment choice was not random.
pmc-11604943:
Minyoung Kevin Kim and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study designing broad phage and antibiotic cocktails for resistant infections. Virus-like phages kill bacteria, but each phage targets few strains. Personal therapy dominates because coverage is narrow.

The team grouped phages by which bacterial docking sites they use. Mixing groups with complementary targets blocked resistance from emerging. Certain antibiotic classes paired predictably with certain groups. Their three cocktails each covered nearly all tested Pseudomonas clinical strains, including biofilms. A wound infection animal model matched the lab success. Similar cocktails were built for Staphylococcus as well.
pmc-11605043:
Sang Min Park and co-authors describe heart treatment in a 55-year-old man who had both hemophilia A and a heart attack. Hemophilia makes the blood thinners and anti-clotting drugs of standard heart care risky. The man first came in with chest pain after an overdose of clotting factor. Scans showed a narrowed right heart artery, and medicines calmed the pain at first.

Twenty days later he returned with crushing pain and signs of a heart attack. Doctors opened the blocked artery through his wrist and placed a bare metal stent. He then took two anti-clotting drugs for six months while keeping his usual clotting factor doses. After that, one drug alone carried him five years with no new heart events, until pancreatic cancer took his life. The team reads the case as proof that standard heart intervention can work in hemophilia with careful management.
pmc-11605743:
Sarah Meng and co-authors present a 2024 study on sex differences in artery wall cells. Heart artery disease kills widely, and plaque caps built by smooth muscle cells can hold or fail. Sex shapes risk, but women are scarce in studies. The team grew aortic smooth muscle cells from 118 men and 33 women, donors after transplant or fatal crashes, and read their gene activity.

Eight genes showed sex-skewed activity in the cells. Six of them also appeared in a plaque data set, and five tied to disease traits. A signaling pair, NOTCH4 and DLL4, emerged as a driver of the split. The pathway links to artery function and may steer disease in sex-specific ways. The authors call for sex-aware study of plaque biology.
pmc-11605843:
Conflict between families and staff is common in children's healthcare, where emotions and expectations run high. Training can soften such conflicts, but judging whether training works lacks standard tools. Juliette Phillipson and co-authors ask the people who commission that training: thirteen healthcare decision-makers and stakeholders from hospitals and charities, interviewed about what an evaluation should measure.

Four themes emerged. Evaluations should capture how trainees experience the sessions, and whether staff gain and keep real skill and well-being. They should also capture how patients and families experience conflict afterward, and what conflict costs in staff time and clinical resources. The themes line up with the classic Kirkpatrick training framework while reaching beyond it. Interviewees wanted both numbers and stories, plus follow-up long after the course ends. The authors advise shaping each evaluation to its program rather than copying a generic template.
pmc-11605943:
Mohamad El-Chouli and a large team wrote a 2024 nationwide study on what shapes life satisfaction in young people with heart disease. Teenagers and young adults born with heart defects, or acquiring heart disease early, often report lower life satisfaction. The team asked how physical and cognitive challenges, self-efficacy, and social support combine to drive it.

The survey covered 1,691 patients aged 15 to 25 across Denmark; 72 percent had congenital disease and 69 percent reported high life satisfaction. Modeling the hidden factors behind the answers showed clear patterns. Fewer challenges tracked with higher satisfaction, with a strong negative correlation. Self-efficacy showed an even stronger positive link. Social support played its own role in the model. The results suggest confidence-building and support programs could lift well-being in this group.
pmc-11606143:
Jia-min Yan and co-authors follow in 2024 how green surroundings and dirty air relate to failing eyesight in older Chinese adults. Both factors can be measured for each home area over time. The team drew on a national aging study of adults aged forty-five and over, tracked for seven years.

Among 9,591 people, greener home areas went with a clearly lower risk of both distance and near sight loss. Each step up in a plant cover score cut the risk by about a third. Dirty air pointed the other way, raising risk for both kinds of loss. The study adds eyesight to the list of health gains tied to greener living areas.
pmc-11606843:
Sarah Glewis and co-authors run in 2024 a trial of gene-guided dosing for two common cancer drugs in Australia. Some patients carry gene forms that slow how they clear these drugs, which raises the risk of severe side effects. Testing first lets doctors cut the dose for those patients.

Four hospitals enrolled most patients they screened, and gene results came back in about a week, before the first dose in near all cases. About four percent needed a halved dose for one drug. Those patients suffered far fewer severe side effects than past patients dosed without gene checks. The trial shows gene-guided dosing can work in routine care.
pmc-11606943:
Chen, Karedla, and Enderlein watch how the gap between two membranes changes as E-cadherin, a protein that links cells, forms junctions between them. They use metal-induced energy transfer imaging and spectroscopy, a method that reads that gap with high precision, on model membranes coated with the protein.

By matching the measured gaps to known junction states, they map how the junctions form along different paths. They find a short-lived middle state, the X-dimer, and track its timing. Forming one such dimer shifts the membrane a great deal, and that shift then changes how later dimers form. The results give a direct view of how these junctions assemble, with lessons for how tissues and organs grow and for diseases of weak cell adhesion.
pmc-11607343:
Xinglan Li and four co-authors test a plant compound against glioma, a deadly brain tumor, in a 2024 paper. Standard rays and drugs do little to lift survival, so new options are sought. The compound, triptolide, comes from a vine used in Chinese medicine and is known to calm swelling and slow cell growth. The team asks how it kills glioma cells.

Computer mapping of drug and disease targets pointed to a master switch for swelling, called NF-kB. Lab tests then showed the compound cut cell survival and movement, and pushed cells toward self-destruction. It did so, the team finds, by blocking that switch while raising harsh oxygen by-products inside the cells. Two cell fate markers shifted in line with that story.
pmc-11607443:
Carrie Corkish and co-authors review how to study metabolism in tissue-resident innate lymphocytes one cell at a time in a 2024 paper. These immune cells guard organs in health and disease, but they are rare and hard to harvest.

Most past work used lab-grown cells or bulk samples, both of which can distort the true metabolic state. The review sums up what is known about fuel use in innate lymphoid cells, natural killer cells, and their kin. It flags traps in current methods and makes the case for single-cell metabolic assays run straight on fresh tissue. Such tools could reveal how resident cells power defense without culture artifacts.
pmc-11607943:
Wonbeak Yoo and co-authors report a 2024 study of a binding protein as a possible sign of cancer outcomes. The protein controls a hormone that drives the body's stress response. Little was known about its role in tumors, so the team mapped its levels and effects across many cancer types.

Using large public data sets, they found the protein is turned down in most tumors. Low levels linked to worse outcomes, which marks the protein as a useful sign for prognosis. Lab tests added support for a tumor-slowing role. The authors also traced linked genes, immune cell patterns, and shared pathways across cancers.
pmc-11608243:
Seven authors study tiny packets shed by blood cells in this 2024 paper on artery disease. They looked at exosomes, small bubbles that carry signals between cells, taken from patients with stable coronary artery disease.

The team found that these packets carry a changed set of small RNA signals, many tied to cell joints. In lab and animal tests, the packets weakened two proteins that seal the inner wall of blood vessels, so the wall leaked more. One RNA signal did much of the harm, and its level matched how severe the disease was. Blocking that signal could be a new way to slow plaque growth, the authors suggest.
pmc-11608343:
Yang Chen and co-authors build a prediction chart for gut narrowing after surgery in newborns with a severe intestinal disease in a 2024 study. Necrotizing enterocolitis can force emergency surgery, and a later narrowing of the bowel is a feared sequel. The team gathered records of operated newborns and searched for early warning signs.

A variable-selection method picked seven predictors: admission weight, bloody stool, days of abnormal inflammation marker, lactate level, lost bowel movement, operation type, and surgery length. These feed a nomogram whose accuracy, calibration, and clinical usefulness were checked with bootstrap validation. Babies joined by direct reconnection fared differently from those given a stoma, a contrast the model captures. The authors offer the chart to flag high-risk infants for closer watching and earlier intervention.
pmc-11608543: Amaya Alvarez, Andres Rubiano, and Wellingson Paiva write to a journal about predicting when a brain bleed will grow, in a 2024 letter. A recent study combined inflammation markers in blood, signs on plain CT scans, and a contrast spot sign to forecast expansion of intracerebral haemorrhage. The letter welcomes the approach: expansion drives rapid decline, and over forty percent of patients die within a month. Marrying blood markers to imaging fits the trend toward personalised risk scoring in stroke care, the writers argue.
pmc-11608943:
Gabriele Saretzki edits a research topic on chronic stress, telomeres and aging, and this editorial from 2024 sums up its five papers. The collection appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology, with three guest editors from Greece, the United Kingdom and the United States. Three papers deal with telomeres, and two with inflammation in aging and age-related disease.

One paper links shorter leukocyte telomere length to erectile dysfunction in a large United States survey. A Japanese team reports faster telomere shortening in adrenal disease. The editorial also notes lifestyle factors tied to telomere length, such as smoking, diet and exercise. Readers get a compact guide to the collection and to stress as a thread through aging research.
pmc-11609143:
Olga Andreeva and co-authors traced how breast cancer cells gain resistance to hormone and targeted drugs, in a 2024 study. Such resistance caps how well key treatments work. Past work by the team tied resistance to the silencing of a gene that adds chemical tags to DNA. This study hunted for what drives that silencing. Lab methods ranged from growing resistant cell lines to gene switching and tag mapping.

Resistant cells had shifted their growth signals to a backup route. A control factor and its partner gene were both turned down in the resistant lines, with matching tag changes on DNA. Turning the factor down was enough to drive resistance. A second factor, known for helping cells change form, carried the effect onward. The authors propose the paired silencing as a marker that could help doctors pick the right therapy for each patient.
pmc-11610043:
A brain area's activity sometimes mirrors the behavior it produces and sometimes seems to wander off on its own. Friedrich Schuessler, Francesca Mastrogiuseppe, Srdjan Ostojic, and Omri Barak use trained recurrent neural networks to ask when internal dynamics line up with the outputs they generate. They find two regimes: dynamics aligned with the output directions, or oblique to them, tilted away.

The choice can be dialed before training by the size of the readout weights, and the regimes behave differently. Oblique networks are more varied inside, quieter at the output, and tougher against disturbances along it, and the regime appears only in recurrent networks, forced by stability demands. Tendencies toward each regime can even be told apart in real neural recordings, giving experimenters a geometric lens for data that otherwise looks contradictory.
pmc-11610243:
Fraide Ganotice Jr and co-authors test whether feeling close to peers carries motivation into engagement in mixed profession training, in a 2024 paper. Students from eight health fields in Hong Kong learned together, a setting built to socialize them across professions. Eight hundred forty one students gave data at the start and again four weeks later.

Inner motivation at the start raised later engagement and cut disaffection. Outer motivation did the reverse. Peer closeness sat in the middle of the path, passing much of motivation's effect along. The authors say program designers should treat belonging as a working part of the course, not a side benefit, since it turns drive into real engagement.
pmc-11611743:
Ran Meng and co-authors report a dangerous complication of a support ring used for pelvic prolapse in a 2024 case. After womb removal surgery, the stitched vaginal cuff can tear open, letting bowel slip out, an emergency that can strangle the gut or seed infection.

A fifty year old woman arrived with bowel suddenly protruding from her vagina. She had lived with prolapse for seven years, had repair surgery and a hysterectomy, and used a ring pessary for the prolapse that returned. Surgeons repaired the tear at once, and she went home on the eighth day. Three months later she had a reinforcing operation. The authors warn that pessary use after hysterectomy may raise the rupture risk.
pmc-11612143:
Mohamed Atalla, Ali Shebl, Bojan Ðurin, Nikola Kranjčić, and Wael AlMetwaly map where Kuwait might find groundwater in this two thousand twenty-four study. In semi-arid countries, locating groundwater potential zones is critical water management. The team combined Google Earth Engine with analytic hierarchy process decision-making, joining thirteen criteria from geology, slope, and rainfall to vegetation and water indices, drainage, land cover, and the water table itself.

The resulting map favors Kuwait's north and east. High potential covers about twelve percent of the country and moderate about thirty-seven percent, while extremely high suitability is under one and a half percent. Nearly half the country, over seventy-five hundred square kilometers, rates low potential, with chances better in lower areas. The authors argue that combining many factors in the cloud-based workflow increases precision and stability, offering planners a reusable template for arid-region water exploration.
pmc-11612443:
Yuvraj Maphrio Mao and four co-authors boost a miniature microbial fuel cell's output more than sevenfold by dusting its anode with graphene quantum dots. These tiny fuel cells, which harvest electricity from wastewater microbes, could power sensors and implants but remain too weak. The bottleneck is electron transfer at the electrode.

Electrodes were screen-printed on glass, a durable and fouling-resistant format, then the anode was drop-coated with quantum dots to enlarge its active surface. Fed reverse-osmosis wastewater, the modified cell produced about three hundred thirty-two nanowatts per square centimeter against forty-five for the bare electrode. Output held up over long operation. The authors present glass screen printing plus quantum dots as a practical manufacturing route.
pmc-11612843:
Miguel de Felipe and co-authors show, in a 2024 study, that the fate of one Spanish marsh echoes across an entire migratory flyway. The Guadalquivir marshes host wintering waterfowl from across the East Atlantic Flyway, and the team joined thirty-eight years of local and international counts with data from over four hundred protected wetlands. They asked whether local conditions track the fortunes of whole populations.

Local conditions do track them. The wintering community has shifted over forty years, from herbivores and one set of dabbling ducks toward another group crossing the Sahara. Nine of fifteen species declined in step with the decay of the natural marshes inside Doñana National Park. The other six answered mainly to global forces such as warmer winters elsewhere. The authors draw a double lesson: read local trends with flyway data in hand, and know that one wetland's care registers at continental scale.
pmc-11613343:
Sophie M Ansems and co-authors ask Dutch family doctors how they fare with kids' long belly pain in a 2024 study. Such pain is hard to sort: plain gut ills can mask organ ills with like signs. A stool test plan may help doctors sort the two with more faith.

Doctors who had joined a trial of the stool plan told their tales in talks and a group meet. Four themes rose from the talks: faith in calls, fear of a miss, calm for kin, and day care of plain ills.
pmc-11613543:
Carlos Gómez-Restrepo and eight co-authors test music workshops for teens with depression and anxiety in Bogotá, in this twenty twenty-four study. Teen mental distress is common, yet few community activities have been studied as routes to recovery. Music groups are cheap and social, which makes them worth a look.

Thirty-four teens aged fifteen and sixteen, drawn from a larger teen cohort, joined five weekly sessions of music learning and practice. They rated their anxiety and depression before and after, and shared their experiences in writing. Attendance and feedback were tracked as well. This early trial, run without a control group, maps promise and problems for a fuller test.
pmc-11613643:
Marvin Thepsoparn and co-authors test a toxin injection for severe face pain in a study from 2024. Trigeminal neuralgia causes sharp, shock-like pain in the face. A nerve knot behind the nose, the sphenopalatine ganglion, helps carry that pain and is a known target.

Fourteen patients took part. Each had failed standard drugs or could not bear their side effects. Guided by X-ray imaging, doctors injected forty units of onabotulinum toxin-A into the ganglion. Pain strength and attack counts were tracked over time. Side effects were watched with care. The study asks whether this targeted shot can calm a pain that drugs leave behind.
pmc-11614743:
Oded Wertheimer and Yuval Hart offer a 2024 model of why brain and behavior traits vary in autism. Their idea turns on dynamic range, the span of input levels over which a group of neurons still responds. A wider range means the group reacts in a more gradual way as input grows.

The authors show that a wider range can account for trait gaps across tasks such as finger tapping, angle recall, and motion tasks. They suggest the cause may be more spread in the switch-on points of single neurons. The model yields fresh, testable claims about behavior, brain signals, and cell traits in autism.
pmc-11615043:
Xingjian Zhang, Zhaokai Pan, and Guoding Liu prove a quantum magic edge. Their work from twenty twenty-four deals with shallow quantum circuits. Magic states are the key source of quantum power, theory says.

Yet if magic truly gives an edge was still in doubt. Their proof needs no unproven claims or black box tricks. They link shallow circuits to the strongest form of nonlocal play. In that game, magic is a must for matched scores. They then turn that play into computing tasks. Shallow circuits need magic to meet those targets.
pmc-11615243:
Anupam Prasoon and co-authors fake the surface of water inside soap bubbles in a 2024 chemistry paper. Reactions at a water surface run faster and pickier than in bulk liquid, but they need a broad, stable air-water sheet, which cramps their use. Micelles, the tiny spheres soap forms in water, offer a stand-in.

Charged soap molecules past their threshold dose assemble into spheres with a water-shunning core and a wet skin, mimicking the flat surface in miniature. Porphyrin building blocks lined up on those spheres in set poses. Fourteen reactions, reversible and not, then ran with selectivity at or near total. The trick scaled up to weaving crystalline two-dimensional polymer sheets in water. The authors say the mimic frees surface chemistry from the bench top's edge.
pmc-11616143: Navarro-Aceves and five co-authors present a case report from twenty twenty-four on retrieving a broken surgical tool tip from a spine disc. During disc surgery for a man's leg pain, the tip of a grasping tool snapped off inside the disc space. The team widened the entry path. It used hooks, forceps, and a magnetic probe to free the tip safely. The authors urge teams to weigh magnetic retrieval when instruments break mid-surgery.
pmc-11616243:
Aurelio Bonavia and thirteen co-authors introduce a new antibody aimed at respiratory syncytial virus, a leading cause of lung disease in infants. Their 2024 paper presents RSM01, built to last long in the body and meant above all for poorer countries where the virus hits hardest. The work joins lab characterization with a first trial in humans.

In dishes, the antibody neutralized varied virus strains at very low doses, and it protected cotton rats against both virus subtypes. Fifty-six healthy adults then received one dose, by vein or muscle, across a range of amounts, or a placebo. Side effects were mild, mostly headache and tiredness, with no serious events. The antibody lingered with a half-life of seventy-eight days. Modeling from the adult data predicted how infants would handle it. The authors call the candidate potent and well tolerated.
pmc-11616643: Alexis Barbarin and co-authors report an elderly patient in North Carolina who turned out to have Heartland virus, a tick-borne virus, in a 2024 case report. Doctors first suspected ehrlichiosis, a bacterial tick disease with a similar face. The case was tangled by the patient's earlier infection with that bacterium. At the patient's home, ticks carried a second Ehrlichia species and another tick virus, Bourbon virus. The authors urge clinicians who suspect ehrlichiosis to also test for tick-borne viruses.
pmc-11616743:
Rita Thapa Budhathoki and co-authors evaluate a program that trains medical officers in rural Nepal to perform cesarean sections, published in 2024. Most maternal deaths worldwide come from direct obstetric causes. In Nepal, many deaths of women of childbearing age stem from preventable complications, in part due to a shortage of skilled staff outside cities.

The program, called ASBA, trains officers to do cesareans and manage obstetric emergencies. The evaluation combined a survey of graduates with interviews and group discussions at rural hospitals. Right after training, most graduates were performing cesareans, and a majority still were at the time of the study. The main reason others had stopped was a lack of a working operating theater, a system limit rather than a skill gap.
pmc-11617043:
Yi-Chu Wu and co-authors ask people who took part in gum studies how it felt and whether they would join a study again, in work from 2024. Trials of gum care are common, yet no one had asked the people in them what taking part was like. Four wound-healing studies that had ended gave the data.

Seventy-six people in all filled out the same short form at their last visit. They scored how the study felt and whether they would come back, each on a five-step scale, and could add notes in their own words. Nearly nine in ten said the time in the study felt good. The team checked which study traits went with which answers.
pmc-11617843:
Priyo Sasmito and co-authors explore in 2024 why a one hour sepsis care bundle is hard to deliver at a mid level hospital in Indonesia. Fast bundled care in the first hour is key to surviving sepsis, a body wide infection gone wrong. Knowing the blockers is the first step to clearing them.

The team held deep one to one interviews with 13 doctors and nurses from the intensive care and emergency units. Five themes emerged: the bundle was often left incomplete, staff knowledge of it was thin, costs bit, and support fell short. Their account names fixable faults, from training to stock. Other hospitals in similar settings can check the same list. Better first hour care saves lives at low cost.
pmc-11618343:
Paula Sosa-Guillén and four co-authors publish a fine-grained climate dataset for the Canary Islands, in a 2024 paper. The archipelago packs mountains, coasts, and many endemic species into small areas, so climate change will bite unevenly. Coarse global models smooth away exactly the local detail conservation needs.

The team ran a regional weather model at three-kilometer resolution, steered by three global models. Three time windows, past, mid-century, and late century, were run under two emission paths. From temperature, rain, sun, humidity, and wind they derived fifty-three bioclimatic indicators, the measures species actually respond to. The open dataset gives island planners and ecologists a shared, detailed picture of the climates their species will face.
pmc-11618443:
Anju Toor and co-authors build fully printed sensors that track ammonium in soil for farm use, in a paper from 2024. Ammonium feeds plants but is also a path for nitrogen loss. Its levels swing fast across a field and through a season, so farmers need readings in real time.

Each sensor pairs a printed ammonium-selective electrode with a printed silver-based reference. The team tested them in water and in three soils: sand, peat, and clay. Readings stayed near the ideal slope across the range found in soil. Changing soil moisture, a common field headache, was also tested to check reliability. The printed design is cheap and light, suiting wide deployment across fields.
pmc-11619143:
Margaux Lorillon and seven co-authors published a fertility study in twenty twenty-four comparing two hormone supports for women receiving donated eggs. After embryo transfer, progesterone support comes either as an oral drug or as vaginal capsules, alongside weekly injections. Patients prefer swallowing a pill, but proof of equal results was needed.

The Lille hospital team reviewed three hundred seventy-two donation cycles from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-two. Clinical pregnancy rates were thirty-six point seven percent with vaginal support and thirty point three percent with oral, a difference that vanished after adjustment. Ongoing pregnancy, miscarriage, and live birth rates also matched. The oral route appears a fair substitute in this setting.
pmc-11619643:
Shaobo Zeng and co-authors survey college students in 2024 on whether being raised by grandparents links to later addiction to social networking sites. Such care is common, yet its long term effects on the mind are little studied.

More than four thousand students at a medical school in Jiangxi filled in standard scales for addiction, social anxiety, and loneliness. Students with early grandparent care scored higher on all three. Anxiety carried about a fifth of the link to addiction, and loneliness carried about a sixth. Together, the two formed a chain that carried a further share. The authors note the care itself had no direct effect once those paths were counted.
pmc-11620643:
Chadi Azmeh and Marwan Al-Raeei ask whether financial technology and financial inclusion help or hinder each other in developing countries, in this 2024 Europe PMC study. Panel data cover one hundred eight low- and middle-income countries across four survey years. Two sides of fintech are measured, digital payments and mobile e-commerce, against traditional access measures such as ATMs, branches and accounts.

Fintech variables mostly boosted economic growth, especially digital payments, while traditional inclusion metrics often correlated negatively with growth. Digital payments combined with dense ATM networks helped growth, a synergy. But heavier reliance on mobile technology made traditional infrastructure less relevant, a substitution that could obstruct broader growth.
pmc-11621443:
Marzieh Rashidipour and eight co-authors shared a study in twenty twenty-four on tannic acid packed in chitosan nanoparticles. Tannic acid can fight tumors, but the body takes it up poorly. The team put it in tiny chitosan carriers to help it kill germs and cancer cells.

They made the particles by ionic gelation. They checked them with electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and size and charge tests. The particles killed several strains of bacteria and the fungus Candida albicans in dilution tests. They also harmed HepG2 liver cancer cells. They changed how genes that control DNA methylation act. That points to an epigenetic effect that needs more study.
pmc-11621643:
Seungjin Son and eight co-authors describe patchy hair loss that followed COVID-19 infection or vaccination. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The condition, alopecia areata, is an immune attack on hair follicles, and infections and vaccines are known triggers for such attacks.

The team reviewed patients whose hair loss began or worsened within three months of infection or a vaccine dose, from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-two. Fifty patients qualified: eighteen after infection and thirty-two after vaccination. Hair loss started on average about five weeks after infection and four after vaccination. Fever was the most common sickness sign before the loss. Treatment response was also charted. The study adds clinical shape to scattered case reports.
pmc-11621843:
Ai-Zhi Lin, Xian Fu, Qing Jiang, and a large team trace sugar damage to the gut in this two thousand twenty-four paper. High-sucrose diets injure multiple organs, but mechanisms and treatments were uncharted. Feeding mice a high-sucrose diet for sixteen weeks produced gut barrier dysfunction: colon inflammation and impaired tight junctions between intestinal cells. Metabolomics of colon tissue pointed at one enzyme, soluble epoxide hydrolase, which rose while its protective product, an epoxyeicosatrienoic acid, fell.

Blocking that enzyme chemically, or deleting its gene only in the intestine, significantly reduced the diet's intestinal injuries, easing inflammation and restoring tight junctions. In cell studies, the protective fatty acid itself prevented sucrose-induced inflammation and junction damage, while its breakdown product could not. The authors present the enzyme as both mechanism and therapeutic target: inhibiting it preserves the gut barrier against dietary sugar.
pmc-11621943:
Randy J Chandler comments on a labeling method that tracks where virus carriers end up inside the body. The carriers, built from adeno-associated virus, mostly collect in the liver after injection, which limits treatment of other tissues. New carrier types aim at other organs, and testing them requires knowing whether they sit outside cells or have been taken inside. A single label cannot tell the two cases apart.

The method he describes tags the carrier shell with two radioactive labels at once. One label stays trapped inside cells after the shell breaks down, while the other can leak out and be cleared. Comparing the two signals on scans shows the split between carriers inside cells and carriers still outside. Chandler notes the labeling kept the shells intact and did not block cell entry or gene delivery in the reported tests.
pmc-11623343:
Monireh Moniri, Mojgan Mirghafourvand, Shahla Meedya, and Solmaz Ghanbari-Homaie ask whether how pregnancy feels predicts how birth and the weeks after will go, in a 2024 study. Two hundred twenty-eight pregnant women from health centers in Tabriz, Iran, joined the study. Between weeks twenty-eight and thirty-six, they rated the hassles and uplifts of pregnancy on a standard scale. The team then followed them to four to six weeks after birth.

After delivery, mothers rated their birth experience and completed depression and anxiety screens. Statistical models linked the pregnancy ratings to those later outcomes, and birth experience to mental health. If early feelings forecast later strain, midwives could flag mothers who need extra support long before the baby arrives.
pmc-11623943:
Carl Coyle and eleven co-authors find a killer-cell fingerprint for lasting calm in rheumatoid arthritis, in a 2024 study. Modern drugs can quiet the joint disease fully, and doctors would like to ease off the drugs. Flares punish guesses, though, since no test marks true immune calm. Deep cell profiling of blood from patients in calm phases hunted for such a mark.

One killer-cell subset stood out, tagged by a trio of surface marks. It was richer in patients whose calm held. The cells killed targets as usual but made less of the chemicals that drive inflammation. Joint fluid from active disease lacked the subset's traits, which firms the link. The authors say the fingerprint could one day tell doctors whose drugs can safely taper, and whose cannot.
pmc-11624243:
Altaf Hossain and co-authors compare radiation plans for cancer that has spread to the spine, in this 2024 study from Bangladesh. Ninety patients at the national cancer hospital received one of three plans: a single session, five sessions, or ten sessions. Pain relief after twelve weeks was the main measure, with side effects and survival also tracked.

All three plans relieved pain in about seven of every ten patients, with no clear gap between them. Skin harm was lowest after the single session, and no severe side effects appeared in any group. The authors argue the one-visit plan suits places where money, machines, and travel are scarce.
pmc-11624743:
Susann May, Robert Darkow, and co-authors ask folks with aphasia why they skip the dense speech therapy that guides urge, in a 2024 study. Aphasia clouds speech after brain harm. Dense therapy can help, but many who need it do not get it or turn it down.

Talks with more than twenty folks and one kin found five groups of blocks. Staff gaps and poor rural reach led the list. Long time since onset also cut take up. Folks want kin in some meets, clear facts, and more digital aids. A less speech bound, more whole view of care is urged.
pmc-11624843:
William Lewis, Chloé Nater, and co-authors fuse count pools in one model to read crowd ties in quail counts, in a 2024 study. Quail care needs growth drivers and crowd brake grades in one view. Young bird life odds had no straight data in the long pool used.

A long span pool from south fields feeds the fused model. Counts hold flat for years, then grow past a set year in the pool. Brood yield drives growth most years, more than life odds do. Crowd brakes hit brood yield more hard than life odds as well. Young odds fall out of the fuse with a prior push.
pmc-11625643:
Jiahui Shi and co-authors present a 2024 study on a plant compound that may protect the kidneys. Acute kidney injury means a fast drop in kidney function, with waste products building up in the blood. The compound, levistolide A, comes from a plant used in Chinese medicine and is known for anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects.

The team induced kidney injury in mice with glycerol and then treated them with the compound. Blood markers of kidney strain fell in treated mice, and tissue damage looked milder under the microscope. Stress markers improved and cell death signals eased. Tests tied the benefit to blocking a pathway that drives inflammation, known as TLR-4 and NF-kappaB.
pmc-11626143:
Beatriz Borges and a large team of co-authors present a 2024 study asking whether AI chatbots could pass an engineering degree. Students now use assistants like ChatGPT widely, which raises hard questions for exams and learning goals. The authors frame the issue as vulnerability: how much of a degree could such tools complete unaided?

They gathered text exam questions from 50 courses at a Swiss technical university, EPFL. Two assistants, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, answered under eight prompting strategies. Graders then judged whether the answers would pass. The study measures the scale of the risk across science and engineering courses. Its results give universities hard numbers for rethinking take-home assessment in the AI era.
pmc-11626943:
Wenfang He and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on a nano-sized scavenger that mops up harmful oxygen species to treat kidney injury after blood flow returns. The injury spins in a cycle: chemical stress fans swelling, and swelling fans more stress. Their particle mimics enzymes and was designed to break that cycle.

Lab and animal tests showed the particle clearing reactive oxygen, lowering inflammatory signals, and shifting immune cells toward calm. Deep profiling pointed to one blocked enzyme as the lever behind the benefit. The particle also lights up on two kinds of scans, so doctors could watch it reach the kidney. The team frames it as therapy and imaging in one.
pmc-11627043:
Aneta Bednarek, Agnieszka Kabut, Maria Rapala-Kozik, and Dorota Satala watch fungal weapon genes answer to growth conditions in a 2024 study. The yeast, kin to baker's yeast, can invade the whole body, and a family of protease genes may help it adapt to host niches.

Cells grew in fake saliva, a vaginal mimic, and two standard broths, with gene reads across growth phases. Most family genes surged early in growth. Two stayed high into the still phase in select broths, and one led in the acid mimic where the yeast survives without thriving. Conditions clearly retune the arsenal.
pmc-11628343:
Yang-Hsiang Lin and co-authors identify a long non coding RNA that drives liver cancer growth in 2024. Such RNAs come from gene like regions that make no protein. A known signal factor is a key driver of this cancer. The team hunts for the RNA that keeps that factor active. One RNA stood out as far higher in tumor tissue.

High levels of the RNA linked to worse survival and more return of the cancer. Lab tests show it boosts cell movement and invasion. A variant form has an even stronger effect. The RNA binds the active signal factor and shields it from a brake enzyme. A growth gene below that factor also rises. Blocking this axis may offer a new treatment path.
pmc-11629143:
Sienna Butterfield, Rebecca Sizer, Fay Saunders, and Robert White wrote this 2024 paper on raising output from hamster ovary cells used in drug making. Such CHO cells host most industrial production of biologic drugs. A gene placed in the cell must be switched on hard, and chemical marks on its DNA and histones set how hard it runs.

The team found that the CMV promoter, the standard driver, carries histones with too little acetylation in these cells. They used a CRISPR-based tool to guide an acetyl-adding enzyme part right to that promoter. Antibody message levels rose up to twelvefold. The gain far beat a twin tool that removed methyl marks from the promoter instead. The study shows how targeted epigenetic tweaks, rather than new genes, can lift factory cell output.
pmc-11629443:
Bernd Fritzsch and co-authors study two genes, Irx3 and Irx5, that help shape the inner ear in mice. A set of genes normally guides the ear to build the cochlea, which carries a map of sound pitch, plus five balance organs. The team deleted both genes and watched what went wrong. In these mice the saccule, a balance organ, fused with the base of the cochlea, and the membranes that sit over the sensory cells were missing.

Hearing neurons also sent fibers to both the saccule and the cochlea. Their paths into the brain no longer split into the neat streams that form the pitch map. A hidden link between the cochlear tip and the balance system stood out more clearly than in normal mice. The authors argue that these two genes act as a branch point in evolution, keeping hearing and balance apart.
pmc-11630043:
Jasmeet Reyat and a large team of co-authors study how a lack of the PITX2 gene harms mitochondria in atrial heart cells. Their 2024 paper deals with atrial cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation, conditions linked to reduced PITX2 in the left atrium.

PITX2 is found only in left atrial cardiomyocytes in the adult heart, but its links to disease were not fully clear. The team made PITX2-deficient human atrial cells from induced pluripotent stem cells, with matched controls. The deficient cells showed shorter, disorganized sarcomeres and more mononucleation. Electron microscopy and other tests pointed to mitochondrial dysfunction as a core part of the defect.
pmc-11630243:
Hetong Ma and co-authors build a cross-lingual ontology for atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, a vessel illness that kills and disables many people. The disease has drawn less attention than its toll warrants, and no shared concept set existed to fix its scope for clinicians and researchers. The team set out to supply that missing frame.

Their 2024 paper follows nine steps that blend a standard ontology method with expert views. The result holds ten top-level classes, from clinical signs to diagnosis, plus a brand-new branch for rehabilitation. The team tests the frame on a literature sorting task and shows where it can serve in real clinics. The ontology aims to make records clearer and easier to use across languages.
pmc-11630343:
Seda Tekneci, Aylin Ustundag, and Yalcin Duydu tune a standard DNA damage test in a 2024 methods paper. The comet assay measures DNA damage in single cells and is used in human monitoring, lesion detection, and repair studies. Results vary between labs, often because protocols and test controls are not shared.

Positive controls, samples with known damage, are essential for comparing runs. The authors optimized the concentrations and exposure times of commonly used positive controls for the alkaline version of the assay. Clearer standard settings should make comet results more comparable across laboratories.
pmc-11630743:
Rebekah Kaufman and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on a topic often left out of cancer care for women. Treatment side effects that affect sexual health are very common and can change a woman's life. Yet most women get no guidance from their care teams on what to expect or what help exists.

National guidelines do tell doctors what to ask and what care to offer. In practice, few women are asked about such concerns. The authors list blocks, such as low training and no place to refer patients. They also note that social media, where many seek health advice, could carry sound guidance to more women.
pmc-11630843:
A research team applies a repeat map tool to chromosome heart zones in a 2024 genome study. Tandem units stack into higher-order arrays that guard chromosome splits and gene use. The tool, GRMhor, reads those arrays in three human genomes and in three higher primate kin.

All three human genomes held six clear arrays at the chromosome 20 heart zone. Copy counts and build shapes split far more than the near-full gene match would hint. Primate arrays split off in full, which points to a wide gulf at these zones. The tool is shared free.
pmc-11631743:
Subuhi Sherwani and co-authors present a 2024 study on a possible early warning sign for breast cancer. Estrogen can attach to blood proteins and change their shape. The immune system may then make antibodies against the altered protein, and those antibodies could flag the disease before symptoms appear.

The team bonded a form of estrogen to human serum albumin in the lab. Tests measured how strongly patients' antibodies gripped the altered protein.
