The group covered 85 breast cancer patients and 45 healthy controls. Patients carried high-affinity antibodies against the estrogen-bound protein. Binding tests also showed the altered protein behaved differently with its usual partners. The authors propose the antibody as a candidate marker for early detection.
pmc-11632443:
Dongfeng Sun and co-authors built a risk model for non-small cell lung cancer in this 2024 paper, using genes linked to oxidative stress. Lung cancer is a major health concern, yet the role of these genes in outlook was unclear. The team drew on large public data sets from cancer genome projects.

They found seventy-four stress-linked genes that differed between tumor and normal samples. Three genes stood out as key markers in the final model. The model sorted patients into risk groups and was checked in two data sets. Tests showed the score could help predict survival and response to treatment. Clinicians may one day use such scores to plan care.
pmc-11633743:
Lite Yang and co-authors map, in a 2024 study, the cell types of a small brain region that drives motivation, reading gene activity cell by cell. The ventral pallidum steers wanting and reward. Its neurons vary functionally, but the molecular catalog behind that variety was incomplete.

The team sequenced single nuclei from mice, macaques, and baboons, then checked locations with tissue staining. Broad cell classes matched across all three species. Two subtypes, one receiving dopamine and one using a classic transmitter, appeared in primates only. A shared atlas across species helps researchers translate animal findings to humans. It also flags which cell types animal models simply lack.
pmc-11633943:
Eric Cucchi and co-authors test a software watchdog in 2024 that scans intensive care charts for missed daily care steps. ICU patients need a long list of checks each day, from blood sugar to tube removal, and steps slip. Their tool reads each patient's traits and orders, then flags gaps against guideline care across twenty-two measures in seven groups.

The study graded the tool like a test: sensitivity, specificity, and hit rates overall and per measure, at a large teaching hospital and a partner site. A prompt lands in front of the rounding team for each gap found. Software that watches the checklist can free nurses to watch the patient, if its flags prove true often enough.
pmc-11634843:
José Santos and co-authors report an unusual genetic case in a 2024 paper on partial lipodystrophy, a disease where body fat vanishes from some regions. Their patient, an adult woman with no family history, had lost fat from her limbs while keeping it on her face, neck, and trunk, alongside high triglycerides and insulin resistance.

Whole-exome analysis under several inheritance models found the cause: two brand-new harmful changes sitting side by side in the same copy of the LMNA gene, a known lipodystrophy gene. Body scans confirmed the lopsided fat pattern quantitatively. The paired-variant mechanism is a novel route to the sporadic disease.
pmc-11635443:
Sun, Tang, Li, Wang, Yang, and Shen build in twenty twenty-four a rapid test kit for Epstein-Barr virus, a widespread virus that can quietly contaminate lab cell lines. One infected line can spoil others in the same lab, and standard checks are slow or costly. The team built three systems of rising convenience: a classic DNA test, a fast enzyme-copy method, and that method married to a paper strip readout.

The two fast systems spotted tenfold fewer virus copies than the classic one. On nearly two hundred cell lines, results matched industry-standard assays, turning up ten positive lines. The strip version shows results by eye in about fifteen minutes. The authors pitch daily strip checks for labs and cell banks.
pmc-11635643:
Maren Christiane Wichert and co-authors test a drug that blocks two cell-survival proteins in a childhood blood cancer. The cancer, B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia, often resists treatment when its cell-death pathways fail. Drugs that mimic a natural death signal can restart cell death, but cancer cells lean on different survival proteins, so blocking one often falls short.

The drug AZD4320 blocks both BCL-2 and BCL-XL. An earlier such drug harmed platelets, and AZD4320 was dropped over heart side effects, though a slow-release form is in development. The team compared several blockers across leukemia cell lines and patient-derived samples grown in mice, and studied how the dual blocker kills cells. They found it acts on its targets and works better when paired with a blocker of a third survival protein, MCL-1. The results map which leukemias depend on which survival proteins.
pmc-11635943:
Jon Mills, Janusz Jaworski, and Tamir Hargittai review the results of a plastic implant that keeps cats' kneecaps from slipping out of their groove, in this 2024 study. Patellar luxation, where the kneecap rides out of its channel, lames many cats. One repair, trochlear ridge augmentation, glues a polyethylene ridge beside the groove to deepen the channel's wall and hold the kneecap in.

Records from two referral hospitals yielded forty-four knees in thirty-nine cats, most with moderate or severe disease. Complications followed the usual pattern of promise: minor problems like fluid pockets and surface infections in twenty percent of cases, major ones in seven percent. The paper sifts which grades of disease and which ages did well, refining the selection criteria so surgeons offer the implant to the cats likeliest to benefit. Follow-up beyond two years gives the technique a rarer commodity than enthusiasm: a track record.
pmc-11636243:
Aldahan and AlHilali report an implantable lens placed in an eye with both keratoconus and an early cataract, in a 2024 case report. Cataracts usually count against using such lenses, but this patient's splinter cataract spared the visual axis, the center of sight.

The thirty-six-year-old woman wanted freedom from glasses in her right eye. Surgery went smoothly, and she reached 20/30 vision without glasses, matching her best corrected sight before. Over eighteen months the cataract did not progress. The authors argue that a stable splinter cataract away from the visual axis should not bar this lens for keratoconus patients.
pmc-11636443:
Kevin Matlock and five co-authors study stress, mood, and diabetes in Latinx adults in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Latinx people in the United States face higher risk of type 2 diabetes and depression. The team asked whether the strains of city life change how depression links to insulin resistance. They recruited one hundred twenty-one adults with type 2 diabetes in Hartford, Connecticut. Each person reported depressive symptoms and daily urban hassles.

Fasting blood tests gave insulin and glucose levels, from which the team computed insulin resistance. They then tested whether exposure to urban threat strengthened or weakened the mood link. Their framing treats unsafe or wearing city conditions as toxic stress. The results speak to community health work. Tackling neighborhood stress may be part of treating diabetes in this population.
pmc-11637343:
Hiroko Kobayashi and six co-authors show that a brain protein borrowed from ancient retroviruses helps herpesviruses infect nerve cells, in a 2024 paper. The protein, Arc, normally supports learning and memory flexibility. Herpes simplex and its pig cousin pseudorabies both raise Arc levels in infected cells. The team traced that rise to viral switch genes, ICP0 and its pseudorabies counterpart, which turn on early in infection.

They found Arc binds VP5, the main shell protein of both viruses. When Arc was knocked down, infection slowed in its early stages, though viruses still attached and entered cells normally. The authors read this as the virus recruiting a host protein for its own early steps after entry. The work links a domesticated retroviral gene to viral disease in the nervous system, a connection with few precedents.
pmc-11637843:
Neem leaves have long been used in folk remedies, and their extract can also brew useful particles. Laila Al-Harbi and co-authors used neem extract in 2024 to grow magnesium oxide nanoparticles by a green route, then tested what the particles can do. Standard instruments confirmed round particles about twenty-three nanometers wide, stable in heat and in biological fluids.

The plant-made particles beat both plain extract and chemically made particles at quenching free radicals. They killed liver cancer cells at modest doses while sparing normal vessel cells, and they hindered bacteria of both major classes. They also blocked two sugar-splitting enzymes tied to diabetes and eased a protein damage test tied to inflammation. The authors call for animal studies next.
pmc-11638043:
Dagnachew Hailemariam and Elda Dervishi wrote a 2024 editorial that opens a research topic on metabolomics in animal science. That field studies the small molecules found in the body. The topic gathers work on dairy cows, goats, pigs, bats, silkworms, and parasitic worms. Each study uses molecule profiles to answer a question about how animals live and grow.

The editorial sums up studies on feed use and breeding in dairy cows. It also covers the small molecules in the inner ear of two bat species, and how diet changes cocoon yield in silkworms. Other work looks at how parasitic worms survive at each life stage. Together the studies aim at farm gains in health, welfare, and lower drug use.
pmc-11638243:
Marwa Abd El-Hamid and co-authors present a 2024 study of a smart gel for skin wounds infected with the yeast Candida albicans. Open wounds invite the yeast, which stalls healing and breeds complications. The team built a hydrogel loaded with silver nanoparticles, pomegranate peel extract, and hyaluronic acid. Silver fights germs, the peel brings plant actives, and the acid keeps the wound moist and skin-friendly.

One hundred rats with infected wounds were split into five groups, among them an untreated set and a shop cream set. Healing was tracked against the treated groups. A carrier that fights the yeast while it feeds repair answers two needs in one dressing. Plant-plus-metal gels could serve clinics where drug proofing grows.
pmc-11638343:
The Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine issues an expression of concern about a 2020 study of bone-forming stem cells, in a 2024 notice. The original paper claimed a long non-coding RNA called H19 pushes bone marrow stem cells toward bone through a microRNA pathway. A third party later questioned the paper's figures.

The concerns name errors in the regression lines of two figures and apparent faults in flow cytometry graphs in a third. The publisher asked the authors repeatedly for the original data; the authors never replied. Because the journal cannot verify the data, the editors, the foundation, and the publisher agreed to flag the article. Readers are warned the results should be treated as unverified.
pmc-11639843:
Luciano Mariano and co-authors profile a rare diabetes-linked breast disease in a 2024 study. Diabetic mastopathy hardens breast tissue in long-standing diabetes, mostly type one. It looks and scans like cancer, so diagnosis is tricky. One Milan center tracked its cases for a decade.

Twenty-eight women form the series. Most had type one diabetes and were under forty at diagnosis. Eye and nerve damage were common companions. Scans often suggested cancer, forcing needle biopsies to settle the matter. Over half had surgery, and about a third of those saw the lump return. One breast cancer appeared. Careful follow-up, not alarm, is the recommended stance.
pmc-11639943:
Stefan Tatalovic and co-authors track tumour DNA in blood as a call on cure reply in spread gut cancer in a 2024 study. Such spread cases live a few months on the norm, which makes early calls dear. Blood tumour DNA may flag early lapse, yet its step-by-step worth was thin.

Blood was drawn at cure start and each two weeks till re-scan in a matched set. Drop-probe tests read the DNA at each draw in depth. Calls are set next to scan reply and life spans in the checks.
pmc-11640043:
Lisa Abdank and co-authors hunt, in a 2024 Austrian study, for drug-resistant bacteria in cattle: staph germs that shrug off methicillin and gut bacteria resistant to key cephalosporin drugs. Such organisms threaten both animal treatment and, through food and contact, human health.

Milk, nose, and fecal samples came from cows and calves treated for udder infections, pneumonia, and diarrhea on farm visits. Isolates were typed with layered methods, from drug testing to gene chips. Resistant staph of the headline type stayed absent, while the resistant gut bacteria and their gene patterns were mapped in detail. The survey gives Austria a baseline for farm resistance watch.
pmc-11640143:
Zivkovic and co-authors examine whether markers of oxidative stress and inflammation predict how patients fare after surgery for laryngeal cancer. Surgery for this cancer disrupts tissue and can stir up reactive oxygen species, which damage cells and may slow recovery. The study followed 56 patients who had conservative or radical operations. Blood samples were taken before surgery and on the first and seventh days after, and quality of life was scored with a standard questionnaire.

Tumor stage, pain intensity, and the extent of surgery emerged as the main predictors of quality of life. Some marker levels measured before surgery and on day seven also predicted whether complications occurred. The authors argue that these blood markers could help flag patients at higher risk of a rough recovery. For surgical teams, the work links routine lab values to outcomes that patients feel directly.
pmc-11640743:
Wenhua Qiao and co-authors review a new way to make cancer-fighting immune cells in the lab, in work published in 2024. The cells are natural killer cells, a type that can kill virus-infected and cancer cells. Instead of taking them from donors, labs can grow them from induced pluripotent stem cells, which are adult cells reset to a flexible state.

The review covers the steps used to turn those stem cells into killer cells at a scale fit for clinics. It also covers gene edits that help the cells find tumors, grow well, and last longer in the body. The authors weigh the limits of older cell sources, such as donor cells that grow poorly. They close with the problems still to solve before such therapy is routine.
pmc-11640843:
Byoung-Hyoun Moon and Ji-Won Kim test a tight elastic band as therapy for stroke patients' ankles, in this 2024 trial. After stroke, stiff ankles shrink walking range and upset balance. A floss band, wrapped firmly around the joint, is used by therapists to loosen tissue and restore motion. The team compared a real wrap against a sham wrap in forty chronic stroke patients.

Right after treatment, the floss group beat the sham group on ankle bending range, a leaning reach test of balance, steady standing balance, and how the foot struck the ground in walking. All gaps cleared the standard significance bar. The authors call the band a practical way to improve ankle motion, balance, and gait in this group, while noting the study measured only the immediate effects.
pmc-11641043:
Tingting Liu and co-authors review the two-way links between bone and brain in Parkinson disease, in work from two thousand twenty-four. The disease wears down movement control, causing tremor, stiffness, and balance trouble. A bone-brain axis, where skeleton and brain signal each other, has become a hot research theme.

The review covers bone metabolism ties to the disease, plus messenger and hormone roles on the axis. Swelling, immunity, and tiny RNA regulators get their own sections. Treatment ideas that use the axis close the survey. The authors aim to ground fresh care paths in this cross-talk.
pmc-11641443:
Carolina González-Cardona, Walter López, Juan Jovel, Mauricio Soto-Suárez, and Nelson Ceballos-Aguirre study how a helpful bacterium primes tomato plants against root worms. Their 2024 paper tackles root-knot disease, caused by tiny nematode worms that wreck tomatoes and other cash crops worldwide.

Plants got the bacterium alone, the worms alone, or both in sequence. Gene activity scans found over two thousand new transcripts in the plant response. Upregulated genes far outnumbered those turned down in all groups. Defense genes, switch factors, and signal enzymes stood out in the response. Pre-treatment with the bacterium made the defense response stronger still. Lipid and sugar pathways, membrane change, and signaling all play a part.
pmc-11641643:
Tamas Palla and co-authors compare two ways to measure acid strength constants in a 2024 study. These constants shape how drugs are absorbed and act in the body. The classic method tracks pH as base is added. A newer spectroscopic method watches NMR signals shift with pH and also shows where protons bind.

The team ran a meta-analysis of constants in the literature from both methods. Conditions such as temperature and salt strength were weighed in the comparison. The aim is a verdict on when the NMR route can stand in for the classic one. Drug designers get guidance on picking a method that fits their molecule and lab.
pmc-11641743:
Seyed Hesamoddin Bidooki and co-authors test a plant oil compound, packed in nanoparticles, against colon cancer cells. Their 2024 paper studies squalene, found in olive oil, which has shown promise against diseases tied to oxidative stress. On its own it mixes poorly with water and breaks down, which limits its use.

Packed in biodegradable particles, the compound left mature gut cells alone but slowed the growth of immature cancer cells. It pushed those cells into programmed death and halted their cycle early. The effect ran through a rise in reactive oxygen and the release of a key cell protein. Gene tests fit that picture. The work supports particle delivery as a way to give a food compound drug-like reach.
pmc-11641943:
Guilherme Trigo and co-authors test plant compounds from cannabis in skin care formulas. Their 2024 study looks at how these compounds act on the body's own cannabis-linked signaling system in skin. Lab work uses human skin cells of two kinds, stressed in set ways to mimic harm. The team checks markers tied to swelling, healing, and skin strength in both pre-care and care settings.

The formulas cut swelling markers and support repair and skin structure in the lab tests. Live tests then confirm the formulas are well tolerated. Skin health improves in visible ways, including a stronger outer barrier. The authors frame the results as support for careful cosmetic use of these compounds. Readers get both cell-level pathways and whole-skin outcomes in one account, a pairing that helps judge real promise.
pmc-11642043:
Yuqing Cai and co-authors study what controls tannin levels in acorns of an oak found in China, in a 2024 paper. Tannins give the fruit its bitter taste and shape its quality as food. Gene switches are strong levers on tannin output, since each switch can move several genes at once. The team looked for new switches in this oak.

They used gene activity data from acorns known to differ in tannin levels. Two switches stood out, one from each of two families. The two pushed tannin output in opposite ways. Tests on the switches' control regions backed up the split. Knowing which switches raise or lower tannins could help breed or pick oaks for a desired taste.
pmc-11642143:
Abdulkadir Kamal and co-authors measure how steady a pupil timing mark is in healthy adults, in work from 2024. Handheld pupil meters time each phase of the pupil's light reflex. One phase runs from light onset to peak squeeze. That phase shifts in brain injury, but its normal range was not known.

Fifty healthy adults gave paired readings in both eyes across four rounds over two days. Mean time to peak squeeze sat near one second in each eye. Spread within a person ran high, and match scores across rounds were low. The authors say the mark varies a lot even in health, which shapes its use in care.
pmc-11642343:
Rinat Miftakhov and co-authors present a 2024 study of protein chips that catch allergy markers in blood. Fast tests for the antibody tied to inhaled allergens are in demand. The team built two chip types that hold proteins in three dimensional gels or brush layers rather than flat spots.

On the gel chip, allergen and antibody binding reached 60 percent of its cap in six hours. The brush chip did better, reaching full binding in three hours with signals two to three times higher. Proteins were fixed by light on the gel chip and by ring opening chemistry on the brush chip. The work weighs speed and signal for a rapid serum test format.
pmc-11642443:
Felix Mathias Wagner and co-authors compare two surgery styles for childhood glaucoma at a Mainz eye hospital, in a 2024 paper. Both styles cut a drain path in the eye, one with a stiff probe and one with a tube that rings the full circle. Early surgery is key in this illness.

More than one hundred fifty eyes from over one hundred children treated from 2015 to 2021 were reviewed. Eye pressure fell hard in both groups. The full-circle group saw a slightly larger drop and needed fewer redo surgeries. The gap in pressure drop, though, fell short of firm proof. The authors say both styles work, with the full-circle path hinting at better long-term ends.
pmc-11642643:
Amadeo Touet and co-authors link hip shape to fracture shape in a 2024 study. Breaks of the hip socket trouble trauma care, and an aging population brings more of them. Force direction is a known driver of fracture form, but the role of a patient's own joint geometry stayed murky. The team read CT scans from 226 patients, comparing the hurt side with the sound side.

Each fracture was sorted by two standard systems while joint measures were taken from the scans. Median patient age was 58 years. Matching shape measures against break patterns hunts for built in risk traits. If certain socket shapes invite certain breaks, surgeons could plan fixes with the patient's anatomy in mind from the first scan.
pmc-11642843:
Silvia Cimino and colleagues followed fathers of toddlers in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Father involvement in feeding and care supports early learning and feelings, yet fathers with mental health symptoms may struggle, and programs for fathers are rare. Their program used online video feedback sessions held twice a week.

Fathers and children were checked twice, four weeks apart, for symptoms and behavior. The sessions aimed to improve feeding interactions and lower distress in both fathers and young children. Families and therapists gain early evidence that remote, father-focused help is workable during the toddler years, when habits form fast.
pmc-11642943:
Youngmin Lee and Sejoon Lee build a memristive synapse from lithium niobate in this 2024 Europe PMC paper. Neuromorphic computing needs devices that mimic synapses. Their device stacks aluminum, lithium niobate and platinum, and works through oxygen vacancy movement that changes valence charge inside the material.

That movement produces space-charge-limited conduction and a self-rectifying response. By tuning voltage pulses in polarity, size, width and spacing, the device showed many memory states. It reproduced short-term memory, adjustable long-term memory and spike timing-dependent plasticity, a core learning rule. Simulations of handwritten digit recognition reached accuracy above ninety-five percent, supporting its promise for brain-inspired hardware.
pmc-11643443:
Shing-Hwa Liu and three co-authors swap fiber and fat kinds in a fat-rich rat diet to ease fat burn harm. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Thirty-five young male rats sat in five packs for fifteen weeks: plain, fat-rich, fat-rich low-carb, the same with shell fiber, and the same with shell fiber plus fish oil.

The plain fat pack bore the most liver weight; the low-carb pack the most fat cloth. The shell-plus-oil pack cut body, liver, and fat weights, blood harm marks, and fat size, and set fat build and burn in line. The team back the swap.
pmc-11643643: Boris Mahltig and Andrea Ehrmann introduce the topic of nanomaterials in textiles, a field where the words nano and nanomaterials have become buzzwords for decades of rapid research and development advances. Both authors work in textile and materials research, and the piece frames the meeting point of nanotechnology and fabric science. The surviving text is brief, offering the framing rather than detailed findings.
pmc-11643843:
Katarzyna Dylag and co-authors reviewed anorexia cases in Polish children and teens across the COVID-19 pandemic in a 2024 study. Reports had hinted the pandemic years brought more and sicker young patients. Records at a regional referral hospital covered 228 girls aged ten to eighteen, hospitalized between 2013 and 2023.

Stays ran longer during and after the pandemic, and girls admitted afterward arrived thinner than before it. Feeding treatment grew more common over time. Blood markers of strain, from low blood counts to low phosphate and thyroid shifts, appeared more often after the pandemic began. The authors read the pattern as a real pandemic imprint on the disease's course. Services, they imply, should plan for the heavier caseload to stay.
pmc-11643943:
Min Liu and co-authors report in 2024 the long-term results of a large salt-cutting campaign in China, where salt intake ran high. The trial began as a one-year randomized study in six provinces, with about 2,700 adults split between intervention and control, then widened for two more years so both groups received the program.

Urine tests showed salt excretion fell in both groups by the final check, by about 352 milligrams a day in the former control group and 193 in the intervention group. Knowledge and habits around salt improved steadily in both. Few other measures split the groups firmly, a result the team weighs for national scale-up.
pmc-11644243:
Chiara Botta, Corinna Grottola, Davide Amato, and Maria Acocella wrote, in two thousand twenty-four, on how to keep used plastic strong. The plastic is polylactic acid, or PLA. It is made from plants, not oil, so it is sold as a green choice. Yet it breaks down slowly in the open air.

Used PLA can be remade, but the new goods are most often weaker. The team shows, for the first time, that a fill of biochar can fix that flaw. Biochar is a char made by heat from plant waste with no air. At fills of 1, 2.5, and 5 per cent by weight, the mix stayed easy to shape. Its stiffness rose by up to 20 per cent, and it held up far better under UV light. The char seeds crystals too: a near glass-like PLA grew to 30 per cent crystal.
pmc-11644343:
Yousra Bouramdane and co-authors studied cedar wood from Moroccan sites of the ninth and twelfth centuries in 2024. Knowing how the plant fibers in old wood break down helps protect wooden artifacts. Samples from those eras were compared with recent cedar.

Infrared spectra and X-ray diffraction showed cellulose crystals falling sharply from recent to aged wood. Bands tied to firm cell wall parts shrank, while new compound bands appeared in the lignin part. Microscope images of the old samples showed empty voids where whole wall parts had been eaten away, a sign of white rot fungi. Fine horizontal scratches were also noted. The work maps how age and fungi reshape old cedar fibers.
pmc-11644543:
Gabriel Heghedűş-Mîndru and co-authors wrote a 2024 study on Romanian propolis as a farm tool. Propolis is the resin honeybees gather to seal their hives. Farmers in organic systems use it to protect plants and spur growth, in place of synthetic chemicals. The team measured its makeup and tested its effects.

Lab assays found rich levels of phenols and flavonoids, the compounds behind much of its power. It strongly inhibited five fungal strains that attack crops and stored grain. The team also tested how it affects sprouting when applied over or under seed layers. Wheat, maize, oats, and barley were dosed at three levels and watched for 13 days. Effects varied by dose and crop. The study supports propolis as a candidate for sustainable agriculture.
pmc-11644643:
Bernhard Goll, Mehran Saadi Nejad, Kerstin Schneider-Hornstein, and Horst Zimmermann show how putting a single-photon avalanche diode and its gating circuit on one chip cuts avalanche build-up time. Their 2024 paper deals with a parasitic capacitance problem in separate chips.

When the diode and gating circuit sit on two chips, bond pads and wires add capacitance that slows the avalanche. Integration removes those pads. The team measured gating voltage transients with an integrated mini-pad and a picoprobe. They compared CMOS and BiCMOS gating circuits for the same diode. Build-up time fell to about half the wire-bonded value with integration, a gain for fast photon timing.
pmc-11644743:
Bilquees Gul and co-authors study how a desert shrub from southern Pakistan copes with salty soil, in a paper from 2024. The plant grows in dry saline ground and is used as a herbal remedy. Knowing how it handles salt can teach lessons for crops grown on land that is turning salty.

Plants were grown at five salt levels, from none to very high. The team tracked growth, leaf size, water content, salt buildup in roots and shoots, and the plant's defense chemistry. Fresh weight fell as salt rose, and leaves grew smaller and less juicy. Salt levels inside the plant rose in step with the dose. Light capture and defense responses shifted as well, giving a full picture of how this hardy plant adjusts.
pmc-11645743:
Giovanni Montesano and co-authors reply to a peer's qualms on their eye-loss sums in a 2024 letter. The sums in view sort how fast sight fails in the creep ill of the eye, and one step drew fire: it barred true gains in sight.

Sight can not come back in this ill, the team holds, so a true gain must be a gauge flaw. One gauge bends its marks by age, and an old eye that fades more slow than its years can fake a gain. To test the qualm the team re-ran the sums on the raw gauge, with no age bend. The true pace of loss stood near the same. The fake-gain share shrank to what first-use learn can tell. The authors stand by their sums.
pmc-11646443:
Dan Wang, Hailan Chen, and Yunhao Luo review stomach acid drugs as a possible aid in heart failure, in work from 2024. Heart failure still kills many patients despite better care in recent decades. Any added tool that eases strain on the heart draws interest.

The drug class blocks a histamine receptor tied to acid output. Studies link it to better urine flow, wider vessels, and stronger heart output. Lower swelling signals and less adverse heart remodeling are also reported. The class may even cut the risk factors that lead to failure. For patients who also need acid control, the drugs offer a two-purpose option. The review gathers the supporting evidence in one place.
pmc-11646843:
Marta Alvarez De Linera-Alperi and co-authors question an ear scan claim in a 2024 study of Meniere's disease. The illness is marked by fluid swelling inside the inner ear, and scans are said to show the swelling worst in the hearing coil first.

Records from a large center over four years cover patients with the illness in one ear. Fine scans graded the swelling in both the coil and the balance part of each ear, with volume measures to back the grades. The team test whether the coil truly always leads. Their check matters for how scans are read and how the illness is staged.
pmc-11647343:
Rou Yu and Xuemei Lin published the protocol for a trial seeking the best epidural morphine dose after cesarean delivery. Spinal morphine is the gold standard for post-cesarean pain, but newer multimodal strategies, mixing regional blocks and patient-controlled analgesia, aim to cut opioid side effects and monitoring burdens. The single-center, double-blind randomized trial plans to enroll 310 healthy women scheduled for cesarean under combined spinal-epidural anesthesia. Different morphine doses will be layered onto multimodal regimens.

Recruitment was planned at a Sichuan university hospital across twenty twenty-four. Publishing the protocol in advance locks the design, outcomes, and analysis plan against later drift. Pain after cesarean competes with a newborn's needs: mothers must move, feed, and bond. Finding the lowest morphine dose that still controls moderate-to-severe pain would ease both recovery and the respiratory monitoring such doses demand.
pmc-11648643:
Martin Rejhon and co-authors found, in a 2024 study, that three-layer graphene grown on silicon carbide sorts itself into striped domains with unlike stacking, no twisting required. Fancy electronic behavior in layered materials usually comes from expert hands stacking and twisting flakes, a slow and unscalable craft.

Scanning probe maps of the untwisted grown material showed stripes of ABA and ABC stacking, told apart by their conductance. The pattern matched what twisted flakes and theory predict for those stackings. Stripe size and shape arise from strain and soliton crossings as the third layer grows. Because the stripes self-organize during growth, they could be made at scale. The authors see a factory-friendly route to quantum devices built on stacking domains.
pmc-11649643: Zihao Zhang and co-authors report a rare vein flaw on the forehead of a young man in 2024. The flaw links veins inside the skull with veins under the scalp bone. It arose from a head injury in early childhood, on the left side of the forehead. Such trauma caused cases are rarer still. The team removed the flaw through a cut hidden in the hairline. Bone wax sealed the site with care. The report details diagnosis and surgical technique for this rare condition.
pmc-11649843:
Two African caterpillars, mopane worms and their Gynanisa cousins, are eaten across the continent, and Chrysantus Tanga and co-authors put their nutrition under the microscope. Their 2024 study profiles the protein, fats, minerals, and plant compounds in Gonimbrasia belina and Gynanisa maja. The question is whether these insects deserve a bigger place in fighting food insecurity.

Both species concentrate their host plant's protein more than threefold, reaching 73 and 61 percent. They carry strong amounts of key amino acids, omega-3 fats, iron, zinc, and calcium, plus helpful plant chemicals such as rutin and quercetin. The authors argue the caterpillars pack enough nutrition and therapeutic compounds to matter, whether eaten whole or worked into processed foods, and could lift both diets and incomes.
pmc-11650243:
Lei Wang, Wang-Shan Zhang, and Guo-Jin Huang study leaks at the join after rectal cancer surgery. Such leaks are a feared setback, and risk runs higher in patients who had drug and radiation treatment before surgery. Their 2024 study reviewed records from one hospital for patients treated from January 2020 to January 2023. All had the combined therapy, then radical surgery. The team tracked who leaked, when, and how those patients fared over time.

Sixty-three patients with leaks entered the study at first, though two were later lost to follow-up. The authors weigh which factors raise leak risk and which shape recovery. Their goal is better care after surgery: watching the right patients closely and acting early when a leak starts.
pmc-11650343:
Haofeng Pang and co-authors use genetics to test whether immune cells, inflammation signals, and blood chemicals truly cause erectile dysfunction, or merely travel with it. Standard studies cannot easily untangle cause from chance links. The team used a method that treats gene variants as natural experiments, comparing large genetic data sets on both sides.

From hundreds of immune traits, dozens of inflammation signals, and over a thousand blood chemicals, the team found twelve factors tied to risk. Some immune cell patterns raised risk, while one inflammation signal lowered it. Six chemical measures also linked to risk, in both directions. Checks found no sign of bias in the results. The authors say the findings hint at new paths for treatment and prevention.
pmc-11651143:
Yi Shen and co-authors built AthRiboNC in 2024, a database of plant RNAs that may secretly code for proteins. Non-coding RNAs were long held to make no proteins, but short reading frames inside them can yield small working peptides. In plants, a full sweep of such hidden coders was missing.

The team mined ribosome profiling data from 226 samples of Arabidopsis, the model plant. Ribosomes caught in the act mark which RNAs are truly being translated. The database gathers those candidates with their evidence for free search. It gives plant science a map of a dark layer of its genome.
pmc-11651443:
Zhao-Jun Zou and co-authors test a wearable nerve stimulator meant to keep leg blood moving, in a 2024 study. Stagnant deep veins invite clots, and squeezing devices help but are bulky. Their small stimulator zaps the common peroneal nerve to flex the calf. Thirty healthy volunteers tried both the stimulator and a standard compression device in random order, with ultrasound measuring vein and artery flow.

Both tools raised vein peak speed and average flow over rest, by similar amounts. Neither changed artery flow. Results matched across the two order groups. No safety problems appeared. The authors conclude the pocket stimulator rivals the bulky standard for boosting deep vein flow, at least in healthy legs.
pmc-11651743:
Yulian Tang and co-authors mine public data on a growth factor in head and neck cancer in a 2024 study. This cancer type is often caught late and fares poorly. The factor, VEGFC, drives blood and lymph vessel growth and may help tumors spread. Using three large cancer databases, the team compared its gene activity in tumors against normal tissue and against patient outcomes.

They also weighed how the factor's level tracks with immune cells inside the tumor. A factor that flags both outcome and immune mix could guide prognosis and therapy picks. Database studies like this cost little and can point lab work at the most promising leads. The findings set VEGFC up as a candidate marker worth wet lab testing.
pmc-11652743:
Alessandra Mancini and nine co-workers wrote a 2024 case series on insulin eye drops for a stubborn corneal disease where surface nerves fail. Standard care had already failed these patients. Nine eyes from eight patients joined across centers. All got insulin drops four times daily.

Some also wore a special contact lens that stores and releases the drug. Every corneal defect closed fully, in about twenty-six days on average. Healing speed was like in both arms of care. The drops alone closed defects slightly faster per day, without a firm gap. The authors present insulin as a workable rescue option.
pmc-11652843:
Riccardo Scalenghe asks whether plastic buried in soil is a resource in waiting or plain waste, in a 2024 review. Plastics beat older materials on cost and durability, but they persist in soil for very long times. The narrative review builds on the author's earlier work and analyzes over three hundred studies, with weight on work since 2019. Plastics are sorted by resin type, and their breakdown under different soil conditions is traced for both conventional and biodegradable kinds.

Polyethylene is the most studied polymer, while interest grows in plant-based and compostable alternatives. Microplastic research gets special attention, including how the particles interact with soil life. End-of-life options, from reuse to controlled degradation, frame the practical question: what should farming and industry actually do with all this material?
pmc-11653143:
Ya-Wen Zhang and co-authors introduce, in a 2024 genetics paper, a software tool that finds genes whose effects change with the environment. Such gene-by-environment links matter for traits like flowering time, but past tools were not both flexible and accurate. The new tool builds on a mixed-model method for genome-wide association studies.

Simulations showed the new fixed-effect form had more power than two older methods. In a fresh look at flowering time in a small model plant across three heat levels, the tool found more known links than older methods. All of its top finds were backed by checks on gene variants and by past work linking them to heat.
pmc-11653543:
Mahjubi and co-authors study in 2024 whether body size measures link to intelligence scores in young school children in Iran. Growth in the first three years is well tied to brain development, but later links are less clear. They recruited 160 healthy children aged seven to eight from four Tehran primary schools.

Weight, height, body mass index, and arm, waist, and hip sizes were measured. Intelligence was scored with a standard pattern test, normed by age. Single factor and adjusted models tested each body measure against the score, with sex, age, and parent schooling held in check. The study adds data from a region underrepresented in this debate.
pmc-11653843:
Fei Lin and co-authors study in 2024 whether COVID-19 worsens chronic hepatitis B and how often long COVID follows in those patients. Care took place at hepatitis and fever clinics in Beijing. The team gathered symptoms during infection and, for hepatitis B patients, liver, kidney, and virus measures from months before and after COVID-19.

Nearly a thousand COVID-19 patients entered the study, about a fifth of them carrying hepatitis B. Matched groups were then compared trait by trait. Neither the treated nor untreated hepatitis B subgroup saw a clear rise in virus DNA after COVID-19. Body weight index and a few symptoms, such as sore throat, smell loss, and blocked nose, differed between groups. Long COVID symptoms came up more often in the hepatitis B group in the part of the results shown, a point the authors develop for clinic follow up.
pmc-11653943:
Sarah Waliany and six colleagues measured how patients with a rare HER2-mutant lung cancer were treated before any targeted drug existed for them. The retrospective study used a nationwide American clinico-genomic database. Among 9,206 patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, 164 carried HER2 mutations without accompanying EGFR mutations. Their average age was sixty-seven, and most were women; about half had smoked.

Treatment patterns and survival were reconstructed from records spanning twenty fourteen to twenty twenty-one. Chemotherapy-era outcomes in this subgroup become the benchmark every new targeted therapy must beat. Eighty percent of eligible patients received first-line systemic treatment, detailed in the analysis. Rare-mutation cancers are invisible in aggregate trial data. Real-world cohorts like this twenty twenty-four one give drug developers and regulators the historical control arm they otherwise lack.
pmc-11654143:
Meysam Fallahnezhad, Mostafa Langarizadeh, and Afshin Vahabzadeh put out a full review in 2024 on tracking hospital supply chain results. Hospitals need indicators to track how supplies move and serve care. Choosing the right measures is hard without a ready evidence base. Supply chains had got less focus than care readings.

The team searched seven research data banks for matching studies. Thousands of papers were screened down step by step. A few dozen studies made it through the full screening. Back lists of those studies were checked as well. The team pulled and sorted the measures those papers used. The result is a map hospitals can use when building their own score cards.
pmc-11654843:
Wei Zhang, Yan Li, and Ji-Guang Wang reviewed blood pressure effects in 2024 of a new anaemia drug class for kidney disease. These oral drugs raise the body's own blood-forming hormone and improve iron use, unlike injected standard agents. Whether they also raise blood pressure was the safety question.

Twenty-six randomised trials of six drugs were pooled. Against placebo, the class carried a higher hypertension risk. Against the injected standard, risk was slightly lower, especially in patients not on dialysis. The authors stress careful blood pressure watching during treatment, favouring out-of-office readings that catch rises clinic visits miss. The balance differs by comparison group, they note.
pmc-11654943:
Andrea Graham and Roland Regoes model why a middling dose of parasites can produce the longest infections, in a 2024 paper. Host defense comes in tiers: barriers first, then fast innate responses, then tailored adaptive ones. Each tier wakes depending on how many parasites arrive.

Simulating replicating and non-replicating parasites across doses spanning orders of magnitude, the authors find a pattern. Tiny doses die at the barrier. Huge doses trigger every tier and get cleared. Intermediate doses slip past the barrier yet stay too quiet to rouse the next tiers, so they linger longest, in what the authors call wormholes in defense. Two such peaks appear, one at each tier boundary. The model breaks the classic assumption that each parasite acts independently. It also explains why exposure size can scramble infection outcomes, and suggests experiments need finer dose ladders to see the effect.
pmc-11655043:
Empathy in a clinic visit is usually scored by questionnaire, after the fact. Yuyi Park and co-authors asked whether the eyes tell the same story, in a 2024 proof-of-concept study using eye-tracking glasses. One practitioner saw six patients while cameras logged where each side looked.

The team set gaze data beside two standard empathy scores, one self-rated by the practitioner and one rated by the patient, and interviewed patients afterward. Patients felt more empathy when the practitioner's gaze rested on the patient's mouth area, within an overall face-focused pattern. New patients and returning patients drew different gaze habits from the practitioner. The authors present the work as a first sketch of how looking behavior carries the felt sense of being heard, and where training might aim.
pmc-11655143:
Yanjun Wang, Pengli Luo, and Tana Wuren review mesenchymal stem cell therapy for kidney disease in two thousand twenty-four. Acute kidney injury kills a large share of patients worldwide, and chronic kidney disease is set to grow into a top global burden. Dialysis and transplant, the current mainstays, have limited reach and real drawbacks.

Stem cells from connective tissue can calm immune reactions and support tissue repair, which suits damaged kidneys. The review gathers lab findings and clinical trial results on how the cells work and where they help. It weighs safety data and the hurdles still blocking routine use. New tools such as single-cell sequencing and gene editing may enable combined and personalized treatments with fewer side effects.
pmc-11655343:
Jingjing Zhang and co-authors design a universal vaccine candidate against borna virus in a 2024 paper. This emerging zoonotic virus causes severe, often fatal brain inflammation. No effective countermeasures exist against it today. A future outbreak risk demands advance preparation.

The full virus genome guided a computational vaccine hunt. Screening kept only strongly antigenic, safe-looking peptide pieces. Pieces recognized by both antibody and killer cell arms were prized. Overlapping candidates above a strict threshold advanced. Linkers joined them into one engineered protein. Immune-boosting and solubility tags capped the ends. Predicted shape, stability, and receptor docking were simulated. The construct was cloned in silico for lab expression. Five of six virus proteins showed high antigenic value. The design aims at broad population coverage. Wet-lab validation is the necessary next step. Preparedness, not deployment, is the paper's framing.
pmc-11655543:
Maximilian Prochnow and co-authors reconstruct summer water conditions in Central Europe at the last ice age's end in a study from 2024. The Younger Dryas cold snap is blamed on a weakened Atlantic circulation. Most records blend the whole year, hiding season splits. Lake biomarkers can read summer alone.

Leaf-wax isotopes from Bergsee in southern Germany supplied the record. A deuterium excess measure tracked evaporation from the Bølling-Allerød into the Preboreal. Other Central European lake records agreed: no strong isotope dip in the cold snap. Warm summers explain the silence — the proxies simply never felt the winter chill. Annual records may have overstated year-round cold. Season-aware history rewrites how the snap struck daily life.
pmc-11655643:
Bridget Thrasher, Sepideh Khajehei, John Kim, and Ian Brosnan describe a 2024 NASA climate data archive. The archive holds fine scale climate projections for the United States, built from global climate models. Planners and researchers need local detail, since global models are too coarse for many decisions.

The team used a daily form of a bias correction and spatial breakdown method to sharpen model output. The archive covers the years 1950 to 2100 at a fine grid scale. It gives daily high and low temperature, rain, and vapor pressure from thirty global models. Five experiment paths are included, from past runs to four future paths with varied emissions. The data span the mainland United States.
pmc-11655743:
Nader Elmelegy reports long-term results for his own surgical method of rebuilding large lip defects, in a 2024 paper. Surgeons have described over two hundred ways to repair lips since ancient times, and none is ideal. Skin flaps can leave extra scars, and very large defects may lack spare tissue nearby. His method moves local muscle into place, backed by fatty and inner-cheek flaps, to restore both look and movement.

The study covered 128 patients treated for cancerous tumours of the lips. The defects left after tumour removal measured four to six centimetres across. No flap failed, giving a survival rate of one hundred percent for the moved tissue. The author reports that patients regained desirable lip function with acceptable appearance. The paper offers the method as an option when standard flaps fall short for near-total lip loss.
pmc-11655843:
Jenny Lamb and co-authors present a 2024 analysis of handwashing programs in crisis settings during the covid pandemic. A rapid process called Wash'Em was built to design such programs from local evidence. It was used widely in the pandemic. The team pooled data from 38 uses of the process across countries to hunt for common patterns.

Most uses took a small team under a week, as intended. Most groups used the advice given, but within short, poorly funded programs. Answers across settings varied a great deal, with low sameness. That means handwashing drivers were shaped more by prior local factors than by the threat itself. The authors warn against copying programs between settings. Context checks should come first.
pmc-11655943:
Giovanna Talarico and co-authors search for gene markers that can tell apart patients with large granular lymphocytic leukemia who feel ill from those who do not. Published in 2024, the study covers a blood cancer whose course varies a lot: some patients have low white cell counts with no symptoms, while others face grave infections. Tools to predict outcome are lacking.

The team tested gene activity in 27 patients and in healthy controls. Two heat shock genes and the CD279 gene ran higher in the white cells of symptomatic patients. Their monocytes also showed a pro-inflammatory profile, with high levels of several signaling molecules. The authors propose these genes as candidate biomarkers and a base for targeted therapy work.
pmc-11656043:
Composite panels are light and strong, but their layers can peel apart. Gilles Lubineau and co-authors review a strategy for tougher joints and laminates. The classic fix trades strength against toughness inside the material. The newer route spreads damage out: long-range bridging, crack splitting, and ligament formation away from the crack tip. Energy is spent across a wide zone, not just at the tip. The review focuses on fiber-reinforced polymers.

Strategies range from basic principles to working prototypes. Additive manufacturing makes the designs easier to build. Modeling the spread-out damage at structural scale remains hard. The authors highlight the newest predictive tools for that gap.
pmc-11656543:
Congying Zou, Luming Tao, Lei Zang, and Yong Hai study balance problems after scoliosis surgery in adults with severe, rigid curves, in a 2024 paper. Coronal imbalance means the trunk leans to one side after the spine is straightened. Its causes in this hard group were little studied.

The team reviewed ninety patients who had a one-stage back operation. The main curve improved by more than half on average, yet imbalance persisted at follow-up in about a quarter of patients. Three factors predicted it: imbalance before surgery, a very stiff main curve, and imbalance right after surgery. Their prediction chart performed well in checks.
pmc-11656943:
İdil Alpat Yavaş and four co-authors study food knowledge among office workers in Türkiye in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Nutrition literacy means knowing enough about food to eat well. The team asked whether that knowledge tracks with diet quality and quality of life. They surveyed more than three thousand white-collar workers aged eighteen to sixty-five. Standard scales measured their nutrition literacy and their match to the Mediterranean diet.

The survey also captured body measures, eating habits, and activity levels. Workers with stronger food knowledge tended to eat closer to the Mediterranean pattern. Links with body measures and life quality were also tested. Employers run wellness programs for such staff, and this study shows where knowledge gaps sit. Dietitians and workplace health planners are the readers.
pmc-11657143:
Sulaiman Salim Al Mashrafi, Laleh Tafakori, and Mali Abdollahian predict pregnancy risk levels with machine learning on national data from Oman, in a 2024 study. Maternal deaths remain a global concern. Spotting high-risk pregnancies early guides care. The dataset holds four hundred two maternal deaths from 1991 to 2023. It is the first such modeling on Omani data. Ten algorithms were trained and compared. A dimension reduction step was tested on and off.

A random forest model won the comparison. With the reduction step applied, it reached about seventy-five percent accuracy. Its precision ran higher, near eighty-six percent. Tree, neighbor, and boosting methods trailed it. The authors present the model as a decision aid. It classifies risk as low or high for follow-up. They caution that more data would sharpen it further. The study shows national records can feed practical tools. Similar efforts could serve other countries.
pmc-11657243:
Rong Ren and co-authors describe four children with Kleefstra syndrome, a rare cause of intellectual disability and autism traits. Their 2024 case series pairs careful clinical notes with exome sequencing to pin down each child's genetic cause.

Two children carried changes in EHMT1, one a brand-new splice variant and one a known missense change, and a chromosome deletion case was also found. The fourth child, with the less-studied type 2 form, carried a new stop variant in KMT2C. Lab tests showed the variant genuinely lowers that gene's message and protein, the first such proof. The authors widen the known variant list for both forms and urge early genetic testing for children with the syndrome's developmental pattern.
pmc-11657343:
Yousef Alsaafin and co-authors pool studies on schistosomiasis in Sudan, in work from 2024. The waterborne parasite disease is among the most widespread on Earth. Two parasite species occur in Sudan, both tied to contact with fresh water.

The review, run in late 2022 under standard rules, gathered sixty-seven studies. Over eight hundred thousand participants fed the pooled rates. One species showed a pooled rate near twenty-five percent. The other pooled near nineteen percent across a like huge sample. School-age children carried a heavy share of cases. Social and cultural risk factors are mapped for control programs.
pmc-11657743:
A virus type drives benign nose tumors by hijacking a host gene, Zheng and co-authors show in a 2024 study. The tumors grow inward in the nose and often return after surgery. The virus type in view is the most common one found in these tumors, and it slips its DNA into host cells.

Sequencing pinned the landing site to a gene that edits other genes. Cell models with viral genes added, and with the host gene removed, show how growth, movement, and immune cell shaping change. Tumor tests in mice check the pathway in living tissue. The work names a gene hub that future drugs might block to slow these tumors.
pmc-11657843:
Five geneticists chart the oil-making genes of camelina, a resurgent oilseed crop valued for biofuel and as a lab model. The crop carries six sets of chromosomes, so most of its genes exist in several near-identical copies, which complicates editing. The team catalogued the copies of three gene families, FAD2, FAD3, and FAE1, that shape which fatty acids end up in the seed oil, across five camelina species.

Copies inside the six-set crop proved strikingly similar to each other despite their separate origins. Their differences in activity, not in code, seem to divide the labor among them, a pattern called subfunctionalization through expression balance. Seed oil blends also differed among the species, hinting at varied pathway activity. The authors offer the map as groundwork for precise editing aimed at better oil yield and quality.
pmc-11657943:
Malaria mosquitoes in West Africa are shrugging off the pyrethroid sprays meant to kill them, and Nelly Tatchou-Nebangwa and co-authors find two mutations behind the shrug, in a 2024 study. The mutations sit in a duplicated pair of detox genes, CYP6P4a and CYP6P4b, in the major vector Anopheles funestus.

Surveys across the continent show both genes under fierce selection between 2014 and 2021. In the lab, enzymes built from the mutant genes chewed through insecticide faster than the normal versions. Fruit flies engineered to overproduce the mutants survived pyrethroid doses that killed ordinary flies. Computer models show the mutations reshaping the enzyme's active site to grip the poison better. The authors designed DNA markers to track the resistance, tools for control programs deciding where sprays still work.
pmc-11658043:
Hironori Fujii presents a 2024 review of how pharmacists improve cancer chemotherapy by taming side effects. Chemo's adverse events erode both comfort and the treatment's punch. Pharmacist-led fixes to preventive prescribing, covering nausea and a skin rash from targeted antibodies, raised guideline adherence and cut both problems in the author's studies, with a hint of longer treatment success.

The review then flips the lens: some side effects predict benefit. Low magnesium on one drug class and low white cells on another tracked better outcomes, while pre-treatment wasting blunted immunotherapy. Fujii argues side-effect care is both shield and signal in modern chemotherapy.
pmc-11658143:
Tianyu Chu and six colleagues survey nursing students on their willingness to delay career gratification, and what shapes it, in a 2024 paper. The trait, putting long-term professional growth ahead of quick rewards, affects how interns plan and how well they practice. Nursing faces workforce shortages, so retaining motivated students matters.

The study covered 250 students practicing in three Anhui hospitals in early 2024. Average scores sat at a moderate-to-high level. Willingness to pursue further education, intending to stay in nursing, having a relative in medicine, communication skill with patients, and job involvement all predicted stronger delay of gratification. The authors suggest training that builds communication and engagement could deepen students' patience for long-term goals. They caution that one province's hospitals may not represent all settings. Even so, the factors named are levers educators can actually pull.
pmc-11658243:
Ziyan Nie and five co-authors study whether gene variants tied to vitamin D relate to gum disease, in a 2024 paper. Periodontitis is a long-term gum infection that can loosen teeth. Reports on the vitamin D receptor gene and its binding protein gene have disagreed, so the team combined gene testing with gene activity data. They checked eight small gene variants in a large group of people.

The group held six hundred people, split between patients with chronic gum disease and healthy controls. Blood DNA was tested with a mass-based system for the chosen variants. The team also mined gene activity data to see how these genes behave in diseased tissue. The combined approach aims to settle whether vitamin D pathways truly play a role in gum disease.
pmc-11659243:
Zbigniew Wochyński and co-authors track blood markers in cadet pilots during training on special aerial gymnastics equipment, in a 2024 paper. The equipment spins and swings trainees to build the fitness military flying demands. Hard training strains muscles, and blood enzymes can show how the body adapts. The team focused on one enzyme pattern, the lactate dehydrogenase index, and what it can tell trainers.

Fifty-five cadets, all about twenty years old, took part in the study. Forty-one trained on the special equipment with a focus on endurance and strength, while fourteen did general fitness work as a comparison. Blood was drawn before and after each of three training rounds. The lab measured enzyme activity, inflammation markers, and a protein that falls when blood breaks down. Fitness tests ran alongside, letting the team judge the index as a training guide.
pmc-11659943:
Immunoglobulin A, short for IgA, is the antibody the human body makes in the largest amount, and it guards the wet surfaces of the gut, mouth, and airways. Patrick J Gleeson and four co-authors review what is known about this antibody in a 2024 paper. Their theme is double-edged: the same antibody that protects can also do harm.

At body surfaces, IgA keeps a stable barrier by holding off harmful microbes while letting helpful ones settle, and much of the gut's microbe mix wears an IgA coat. In the blood, idle IgA helps calm inflammation. The review gives special weight to the gut, the kidneys, and autoimmune disease, where IgA can turn against the body. It closes with new treatment ideas that aim to use or correct IgA rather than simply block it.
pmc-11660043:
Stefano Menasce and co-authors print silicone parts that are both strong and reprocessable in a 2024 study. Silicones serve everywhere from sealants to implants, but molding limits their shapes and cured silicone cannot be reshaped. A class of materials called vitrimers can flow under stress while keeping their network whole, which opens the door to recycling.

The team writes the silicone vitrimer directly with a printer, laying down ink in complex shapes. Tests of flow and strength show the inks can be tuned so parts resist creep yet can still be reprocessed at room temperature. Those two traits usually fight each other. Printed parts kept high strength after shaping. The work points to silicone goods that can be printed to order and later reworked instead of thrown away.
pmc-11660143:
Arianna Menichetti and six co-authors clean unwanted paint off artworks with a green mat that turns light into heat. Their 2024 study addresses a hard restoration problem: vandal and street-art paints use varnishes that resist normal removal. The team spun nonwoven fibers from a natural polymer dissolved in water.

Cuttlefish ink supplied melanin particles, nature's dark pigment, which drinks in light and warms fast. Laid on a paint layer with a green solvent, the mat lifted alkyd paint quickly and with tight spatial control. The material held up under repeated light exposure. Everything in the system, fiber, pigment, and solvent, comes from benign sources. The authors offer restorers a fast, precise, and low-toxicity cleaning option.
pmc-11662643:
Huaying Wu and six co-authors wrote this 2024 rat study on healing a damaged womb lining. A thin or scarred lining can block pregnancy, so repair methods are in demand. The team paired a platelet extract, rich in healing signals, with a sheet made from amniotic membrane stripped of cells, hoping the sheet would hold the extract in place longer.

Injured rats got the extract alone, the sheet alone, both together, or nothing. The combined treatment rebuilt the lining best, thickening it, restoring glands, and cutting scarring at both check points. It also grew new blood vessels, calmed inflammation, and led to better pregnancy outcomes. The extract alone helped early but faded; the sheet alone did little. The authors read the sheet as a carrier that stretches the extract's working time.
pmc-11663243:
Arpit Singh and co-authors check in 2024 whether the tilt of the shin bone top after knee replacement shapes how well the new knee works. Surgeons set that tilt, called the posterior tibial slope, to steady the joint and guide its motion. Whether the tilt affects bending range over time was less clear.

The study followed forty knees in thirty patients for at least three months. Pain and function scores and bending range all improved a lot after surgery, while the measured slope fell. Patients with a larger slope scored a bit higher on average, but the link was too weak to trust. In the early months, the authors conclude, slope does not drive outcomes.
pmc-11663643:
Mohamed El Ouardi and colleagues analysed wormwood essential oils from Morocco in 2024. Morocco hosts rich Artemisia plant diversity. Two species supplied the oils here. Chemical makeup was profiled in full. Germ killing and antioxidant power were tested. Computer docking added a third angle.

Key compounds bound target proteins strongly. One compound, davanone, stood out especially. Simulated complexes stayed stable over time. Target enzymes included defence-related proteins. Oils showed clear biological potential overall. Traditional plant uses gain scientific support. Further product testing is still needed. Natural antimicrobials remain in demand.
pmc-11663743:
Hao Yuan and nine colleagues published a 2024 study of tinnitus patients treated with transient compound sound therapy. Tinnitus is the perception of ringing or noise without an external source. Sound therapy, which plays tailored sounds to the patient, helps some sufferers but not others, and doctors cannot easily predict who will benefit.

The team reviewed 991 patients with subjective tinnitus treated at their hospital's ear department between November 2019 and January 2022. Patients who responded to therapy differed significantly from those who did not on several clinical characteristics. From these differences the authors built a predictive model. Such a model could spare unlikely responders a long course of therapy and direct them to other options sooner.
pmc-11664043:
Shuying Xu and five colleagues study a blood ratio as a risk sign for stroke, using a large United States survey, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The ratio joins the share of neutrophils, a white cell type, with albumin, a blood protein. The team drew on survey data from 1999 to twenty twenty covering more than fifty-six thousand people. They modeled stroke odds across ratio levels and hunted for bend points.

Higher ratios linked to higher stroke risk, even after other factors were counted. The tie was not a straight line: past a bend point, the rise in risk slowed. The pattern held as curves in men but ran straight in women. The authors offer the cheap ratio as a prevention aid.
pmc-11664643:
Mahato Maeda, Dai Taguchi, and Takaaki Manaka report a 2024 study of small power devices that make charge when rubbed. The devices use a plastic film, and rubbing lines up its molecules in a set way. The team watched that lining-up as it happened, using a laser light method.

Light signals showed that order in the film grew while rubbing went on, then faded in a few seconds once rubbing stopped. The molecules leaned at a set angle and pointed along the rub path. From those measures, the team worked out the top power the device could give. Only part of that power reached the outer load in tests.
pmc-11665343:
Nicola Colatorti and co-authors test whether farm leftovers can soak up long-lived toxins from water, in this 2024 study. Crop sprays and factory leftovers can linger in soil and water for years, threatening soil health and food safety. Orange peel, olive stones, and pistachio shells, all common farm wastes in the region, were tried raw as sponges. Three crop chemicals and one plastic-linked compound were the targets.

The team first profiled each waste's makeup and fine structure with lab tools. Then came soaking tests in water. Raw waste that works as-is skips the cost of chemical treatment, which is where many such sponges price themselves out. Turning local waste streams into cleanup material is the reuse pitch in miniature.
pmc-11665443:
Hugo Felix Perini and co-authors review biomimetic nanocarriers in this 2024 paper. These tiny drug carriers are built to copy traits of natural cells. Borrowing cell features can help a carrier blend in with the body and reach its target more precisely.

The review covers how such carriers improve drug delivery for hard diseases. Cancer, Alzheimer disease, autoimmune disease, and viral infections such as COVID-19 all feature as test cases. Natural cell parts lend the carriers better compatibility with tissue. They also sharpen targeting, so more drug lands where it is needed. The authors frame the approach as a path toward personalized medicine.
pmc-11665643:
Lixuan Chen and four co-authors study housing tastes across generations in China in a 2024 paper. Do children inherit their parents' views on owning a home? National family panel data from three survey years let the team test that idea. Housing is a huge share of household wealth in China.

The team found a clear pass down of housing preference. The link ran stronger for children under forty five and for daughters. Plans for more children diluted the transfer of taste. Families that tie a child's success to family wealth passed weaker housing tastes. Parents also shaped how children feel about borrowing to buy. The authors say these patterns can guide policy on household assets.
pmc-11666943:
Hamilton and co-authors measure what is in coconut water from two towns in Cameroon, Edea and Bafia. They test nuts at two stages of ripeness and track how the drink changes as it is stored. Their 2024 study aims to help add coconut water to a national food table.

As nuts ripened, sugar fell while fat, protein, and some other parts rose. Water volume per nut fell, and the drink grew less sour. Mineral content rose with ripeness, while strength against cell damage fell. Stored water broke down faster at room heat than in a fridge, so cold storage kept it better. Samples were tested with standard lab methods for each trait the team reported here.
pmc-11667043:
Mart Kals and co-authors test gene risk scores after mild brain injury in 2024. Stress disorder and depression are common after such injuries, but their biology is murky. Scores built from many small gene effects may flag who is most at risk.

Data came from two large cohorts in Europe and the United States. Probable stress disorder and depression were judged six months after injury by standard checklists. About one in nine patients met the stress mark, and about one in fifteen met the depression mark. The team also checked whether findings carried over to a cohort of African American patients.
pmc-11667143:
AboArab and co-authors present a software study, published in 2024, on viewing medical scans through a web app that behaves like installed software. Three-dimensional views help doctors read scans of organs. A standard technique rebuilds those views from stacked slices of CT or MRI data. Hospital systems already serve scans over the web, but full viewing tools usually need heavy installed programs. Progressive web apps promise the same reach from a browser, with no install.

The team built a viewer for the standard medical image format with the multiplanar rebuilding built in. They then validated it against the tasks radiologists actually perform. A working browser viewer could put advanced imaging on any screen in a hospital, clinic, or home office. It could also help sites that cannot maintain heavy software. The study checks speed and image quality to prove the concept.
pmc-11667443:
Maeva Zysman and co-authors size the real-world audience for biologic drugs in lung disease in a 2024 paper. Biologics cut flare-ups in asthma, and trials hint they may help a slice of COPD patients too. But trial entry rules are strict, and nobody knew how many real patients fit them. The team checked a long-running French cohort of over four hundred COPD patients, plus asthma patients with COPD-like features.

Only about one COPD patient in five met the entry rules for at least one biologic on trial. Among asthma patients with COPD features, the eligible share was smaller still, and they were mostly women with worse lung function. Depending on the drug, the true target group ran from about one to eight percent of the whole airway population. The authors temper expectations for these awaited drugs.
pmc-11667643:
Deepshikha Verma and co-authors ask whether old-fashioned microscope reading of bone marrow still earns its place in diagnosing low platelets. Their 2024 study reviews one hundred marrow aspirations done for thrombocytopenia at a central Indian hospital over one year. The most common cause was immune thrombocytopenia, where the body destroys its own platelets.

The team catalogued the shapes of megakaryocytes, the marrow cells that make platelets, and checked how consistently observers read them. Marrow from immune cases showed clear morphological changes in those cells. Such changes can mislead, since they may mimic a more sinister marrow disorder. The authors note that guidelines often make routine marrow checks unnecessary when the rest of the picture is clean. Their point is narrower: when a marrow is taken, megakaryocyte form still carries diagnostic weight worth reading well.
pmc-11667743:
Salim Abduljawad and co-authors compare surgery with non-surgical care for torn Achilles tendons in a 2024 cohort study. The Achilles is the tendon humans rupture most. Recent trials find long-term function similar either way. Surgery risks infection and nerve harm, while rest risks re-tear.

Records from a major teaching hospital fed the comparison. Patients fell into surgical or conservative groups by the care they got. A standard rupture score was taken at least a year after injury. Scores are compared across age, sex, side, and tendon gap. No clear score gap separates the routes overall. Notably, every woman in the set was treated without surgery, limiting sex comparisons.
pmc-11668143:
Jeong Jaeuk and co-authors compare gym class feelings among early teens in Korea and China in a 2024 study. Drive, peer bonds, and a sense of being shut out shape how teens take to physical education. School culture may tilt each of those in unlike ways across borders.

About four hundred students aged near fourteen took tested surveys. Chinese students scored higher on self-drive for both sexes. Korean boys reported stronger peer bonds than Chinese boys. Korean girls felt more shut out than Korean boys did. The authors say gym reforms should fit local culture and gender patterns, not copy one model.
pmc-11668243:
Xiangyu Wu and co-authors identify a sugar marker on blood T cells as a possible sign of effector activity in bladder cancer patients, published in 2024. Cancer is a body-wide disease that the immune system constantly watches. Sugars attached to proteins shape how immune cells recognize and respond, and one such sugar pattern, LacNAc, steers immune cell activity.

Their single-cell platform tags the sugar with DNA barcodes, reading it alongside gene activity and receptor sequences without disturbing the cells. Patients at lower cancer stages carried higher levels of the marker on their circulating T cells. Cells rich in the marker showed stronger killing capacity and more receptor clonal expansion. The authors propose this surface sugar as a candidate marker of active, tumor-fighting T cells in the blood.
pmc-11670743:
Shuai Zhang, Chengyue Li, Almujiang-Yimitri Tarken, and Weiming Li tracked motor fitness in Xinjiang youth from nineteen eighty-five to two thousand nineteen. Data came from national student fitness surveys run in eight years across that span. The group covered ages seven to eighteen.

Tests covered speed, heart-lung fitness, strength, power, and flexibility. Overall fitness fell over the whole period. Speed, power, and heart-lung fitness improved in the first decade, then worsened sharply in the next. Decline slowed after two thousand five, and some parts improved, but most kept falling in the last years. The authors say trends differ by sex and age, which policy should reflect.
pmc-11671243:
Brooks Hibner and colleagues measured exercise responses in multiple sclerosis in two thousand twenty-four. Aerobic capacity drops in this chronic nerve disease. Blood flow responses at peak effort were unknown. Fitness itself might explain any differences found. Patients and controls had similar peak oxygen uptake. All pedaled through a maximal cycling test.

Heart and blood measures rose similarly in both groups. Heart rate patterns differed before age adjustment, though. That difference vanished once age was considered. Stroke volume, output, and pressure showed no group gaps. Fitness, not disease, seems to drive responses here. Keeping fit may normalize exercise circulation in MS. Training programs gain a reassuring evidence base.
pmc-11672243:
A journal cover feature from 2024 presents work by Gang Shao, Caiyun Fu, and co-authors on acute myeloid leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer. The cover image shows a leukemia cell and explains, in picture form, how a protein called ANXA1 grips a second protein, Notch1, inside the cell. That grip leads to Notch1 being broken down.

The feature explains that short peptide blockers can compete for ANXA1 and free Notch1. Once freed, part of Notch1 is cut loose and can switch genes back on, restoring a tumor-blocking role in the cancer. Readers get the core idea of the study as told through its cover art.
pmc-11672343:
Mak and co-authors test group therapy for stressed parents during the COVID-19 years. The therapy, called ACT, teaches parents to accept hard thoughts and act on their values. The study ran at a Hong Kong family service center. Parents joined five weekly group sessions. Sessions ran in person or online based on rules and choice.

The study enrolled 250 parents of school-age children. Most were mothers, with a mean age near 41. Stress scores fell after the program, with a small to mid gain. Gains showed in parent stress and general stress alike. The flexible mix of online and in-person groups still worked in real-world use.
pmc-11672843:
Cezary Osiak-Wicha and co-authors compare in this 2024 study the muscle fibers of working dogs against companion breeds. Twelve dogs, split evenly, gave samples from an arm and a thigh muscle. Stains sorted fibers by their myosin type: slow, fast-enduring, and fast-burst forms.
