Working dogs carried larger fibers, more of the slow and fast-enduring types, and more nuclei in each fiber, a build for strength held over time. Companion dogs leaned on burst fibers, packed tighter but with fewer nuclei, hinting at slower repair. The authors tie the contrast to selective breeding for jobs, and urge vets to weigh breed build in care and rehab. Training plans can build on the fiber map.
pmc-11672943:
Wanyu Tang and co-authors present a 2024 system that reads the actions of children with ADHD from video. The children take a standard attention test while a camera watches. Sudden, uneven moves are a hallmark of the condition, and set video tools often miss them. The team's system tracks body and face points instead of raw pixels, which cuts background noise.

One branch reads body points with a graph network tuned for jerky motion. A second branch turns face points into images and reads head and face moves with a phone-grade vision model. A fusion step joins both branches for the final call on each act. The calls map to the symptom traits in the standard diagnostic guide. Such tools could make attention tests more fair and less reliant on a watcher's eye.
pmc-11673043:
Ianis Boboc and colleagues test a diabetes drug in a mouse model of Alzheimer disease. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses semaglutide over four weeks. Alzheimer disease brings memory loss and anxious behaviour. The drug mimics a gut hormone that also acts in the brain.

Twenty mice split into healthy and disease groups, treated or not. Blood sugar and weight were tracked through the treatment. Behaviour tests measured exploration, recognition, social response, and anxiety. Semaglutide brought disease-group blood sugar down to healthy levels. Memory test results improved after treatment in the disease mice. Anxiety-related behaviour was also part of the outcome set. Early animal results justify deeper study, not clinical claims.
pmc-11673243:
Yiying Wang, Abhirup Banerjee, and Vicente Grau rebuild coronary artery trees in 3D from just two flat X-ray views. Heart doctors read vessel shape from angiograms during live procedures. Radiation limits scans to about two angles, so depth must be inferred. Their NeCA method learns a neural field of the vessel tree without any 3D training truth.

A hash-based encoder and a cone-beam projector make the learning self-taught. Test trees came from CT scans of two major heart arteries. Six scores judged shape and branch linking against known truth. NeCA matched a supervised rival on tree shape and branch joins. The result hints at safer, fuller guidance during heart procedures.
pmc-11673543:
A newborn arrived with seizures no drug could stop, a gut that would not work, and a brain scan showing two different injury patterns. Francesco Dellepiane and eight co-authors report the case in a 2024 paper and trace it to a rare gene defect. The boy carried two different faulty copies of PIGO, a gene in the pathway that builds the anchors fastening proteins to cell surfaces.

Only nineteen confirmed cases of PIGO deficiency had been published before, marked by developmental delay, epilepsy, gut malformation, and other birth defects. Scans here first showed restricted diffusion deep in the brainstem and midbrain, a pattern the authors set against the wider injury also present. They argue the double pattern widens what doctors should expect from this disorder, and that early genetic testing belongs in unexplained newborn encephalopathy with resistant epilepsy.
pmc-11673743:
Kevin Wu and co-authors (2024) review how 3D bioprinting might rebuild the retina, the eye's light-sensing lining, for people whose own is failing. The retina is a hard target: a layered sheet of cell types, threaded with blood vessels, with exact wiring between layers. Bioprinting lays down living cells in precise patterns — extrusion, droplets, or laser — building tissue layer by layer. The review walks through each printing method's strengths.

Much of the progress sits in the bioinks, the gels that carry the cells. Formulations aim to copy the retina's softness and chemistry, keep cells alive through printing, and hold shape afterward. The authors survey scaffold materials and attempts at its vascular and layered structure. Their verdict is measured: printing a working retina remains distant, but each piece, inks, cells, architecture, is advancing, and the review maps what a real attempt will require.
pmc-11674343:
Triantafyllou and co-authors teach a classifier to sex skulls from eye socket measures in a 2024 study. Forensic work starts with sex estimation, and the skull carries strong landmarks. Ninety two dried skulls, thirty five male and fifty seven female, supplied orbital measurements: the optic foramen and canal sizes, plus distances within and between the orbits.

A machine learning classifier trained on those numbers sorted the skulls by sex. Eye sockets survive burial and damage better than many bones, so a reliable orbital method fills a real gap. The study frames the classifier as a tool for casework, where partial remains are the norm rather than the exception.
pmc-11674443:
Zhenhe Huang and co-authors build in 2024 a smart fabric that can flag sarcopenia, the age-linked loss of muscle and strength. Clinic tests for the condition need bulky gear and trained staff. Their fabric pairs conductive cloth with a flexible sensor array that reads pressure with high sensitivity and holds up over repeated use.

Worn against the body, the fabric tracks pulse, finger motion, speech, and walking. Built into a shoe sole, it follows walking speed and gait, two telling signs in sarcopenia. Clinic checks showed the system catches the shifts that mark the condition, offering a simple route to screening and follow-up.
pmc-11674643:
Precise radiation may help some lung cancer patients whose disease has spread to just a few spots, and a 2024 review by Benson Wan and Magali Lecavalier-Barsoum weighs the evidence. This in-between state, called oligometastatic, might still be curable with aggressive local treatment added to standard drugs.

The treatment, stereotactic body radiotherapy, delivers a high dose in one or a few sessions and can reach lesions almost anywhere. Trials reviewed show it can delay the next drug switch, cut costs, and improve quality-adjusted survival. The largest trial yet is still running. The authors stress that picking the right patients is what makes the benefit outweigh the harm, and they map the trials that will sharpen that choice.
pmc-11674843:
Josep Maria Cantons, Akash Bachhuka, and Lluis F Marsal build a sensor platform to detect preeclampsia early in pregnancy. Published in 2024, the paper targets a pregnancy specific high blood pressure syndrome that is a leading cause of harm to mothers and babies worldwide. A protein called endoglin is a candidate marker for the condition.

The platform joins nanoporous anodic alumina, whose surface area is huge, with gold nanoclusters that give off light. Antibodies on the surface make it selective for endoglin. Light readings tracked the marker across a set range, with a low detection limit. The authors present the device as a proof of concept for a portable, low cost test.
pmc-11675043:
Osama Mohamed Elsayed Ramadan and co-authors test a training model in a 2024 randomized controlled trial on pediatric orthopedic nursing. Care around children's bone surgery calls for special skills, and the Pediatric Nursing Excellence Model aims to raise nurses' knowledge and daily practice in that setting.

One hundred nurses at two tertiary hospitals in Tanta, Egypt, were split between model training and routine care. The trained group improved far more in knowledge and practice scores right after training, and the gains held over six months of follow-up checks. Path analysis linked the model to better nursing performance through stronger knowledge and adherence.
pmc-11675143:
Cathy O'Callaghan and co-authors evaluate a virtual health hub for people experiencing homelessness in a 2024 Sydney study. Residents of a crisis accommodation service face heavy chronic illness and steep barriers to seeing a doctor. The hub brought video GP and psychology visits to them, with nursing help on site.

Attendance data, patient surveys, staff interviews, and case studies fed the evaluation. About forty percent of clients used the hub, and users praised the care quality, privacy, and clinicians' understanding. A third said they would simply have gone without treatment otherwise. Technical problems were rare. The authors judge the model feasible and valued.
pmc-11675243:
Grace Aldridge and co-authors plan the rollout of a parenting program in a 2024 paper. The program, designed with families and delivered with digital tools, aims to soften the effects of hard childhood experiences. Good programs often fail to reach families, though, because services struggle to adopt them.

The team interviewed 14 staff at a community health service, from managers to front-line workers. Using two standard frameworks, they sorted what would help or hinder adoption. Fourteen factors helped and eleven hindered. A matching tool then paired each barrier with a proven change strategy, giving eleven concrete steps. Most steps involved testing and refining the rollout and building ties among stakeholders. The authors say co-design itself eased the path.
pmc-11675443:
Grazyna Cacak-Pietrzak and co-authors test what happens when cereal coffee replaces part of the flour in wheat bread, in work from 2024. They used levels from two to ten percent. The team checked dough traits, bread size and texture, and the nutrients in the finished loaf.

Dough with cereal coffee took up less water, stayed stable longer, and stretched less. Bread volume fell and the crumb grew harder and denser, more so above six percent. Fiber, ash, fat, and plant compounds rose with more cereal coffee. The study shows a trade off between added nutrients and loaf quality.
pmc-11675743:
Nazira Bekenova and six co-workers looked at heart rate change as a sign of nerve harm to the heart in Kazakhstan. This nerve harm, often tied to diabetes, is not often checked with heart rate tests in day to day care. Their 2024 study took in 5,707 adults from a city clinic group in the capital. Checks mixed forms that patients filled in, health records, and heart traces kept for a full day.

Nerve harm showed up in near 17 percent of those checked. Diabetes was found in near 31 percent of those cases. Rates rose with age. They tracked the same shape as diabetes rates by sex and by age. Two heart rate scores from the day long traces are put forth as handy signs. The team says such tests could flag this harm at an early stage in plain clinic care.
pmc-11676243:
Niyaz Ali and co-authors review integrons, gene-swapping parts in bacteria that spread drug resistance, in a 2024 article. Integrons can capture loose gene cassettes and slot them into their own structure. That trick builds variety and new traits fast. In the age of antibiotics, it has become a key route for resistance genes to spread.

The review traces the structure and history of integrons. It shows how antibiotic use has favored them in many settings. It also tracks their current role in resistance and their spread through farms, clinics, and the environment. Knowing the routes of spread is a first step to slowing a global threat to medicine.
pmc-11676643:
Thararat Phurahong and co-authors compared genomes of a fish-killing bacterium in a 2024 study. The bacterium causes vibriosis, a major disease in farmed fish such as groupers. Strains of one type fall into three subgroups by their virulence genes, and the subgroups differ in growth and harm.

The team sequenced and compared one strain from each subgroup. The genome sits on two circular chromosomes, with about thirty-nine hundred shared genes and thirteen hundred extra ones varying by strain. The most harmful strain carries unique enzymes tied to its outer coating, a part that interacts with the host immune system. Those differences may explain its extra virulence. Knowing which genes track with harm can guide vaccines and tests for fish farms. The study adds a genetic map of a costly disease for aquaculture.
pmc-11676943:
Ángel Sanz-Felipe and Juan Vallés map the design and run settings that let an active waveguide Bragg grating lase. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The structure pairs the sharp bounce of a Bragg grating with the gain of rare earths, a mix that could yield a one-piece laser. Its response swings hard with design, so a model is a must first.

They trace light power through a grating doped with erbium and ytterbium by a numerical method. A full data base of responses is built across the key settings. From it, the critical value of each design and run trait for laser action is pinned down. The map guides later builds and tuning of such photonic parts.
pmc-11677143:
Liang Tang and eight co-authors study a silkworm gene, BmMCP12, and its role in defence against viral infection, in work from 2024. The virus BmNPV causes nuclear polyhedrosis, a disease with heavy losses for silk farming. The gene belongs to the carboxypeptidase family, which has known links to insect immunity, and it is most active in the silkworm midgut.

Gene levels rose after infection in cultured cells. Raising gene activity slowed virus replication, while knocking the gene out had the opposite effect. Transgenic silkworms without the gene resisted the virus less well. The findings name a new target for disease prevention in sericulture, the authors say.
pmc-11677443:
Laura Figueira Garcia and co-authors test whether making microalgae clump before spinning can cut the cost of harvesting them. Separating algae from their water eats roughly thirty percent of production cost at scale, a bottleneck for the whole industry. The Canary Islands team worked outdoors at pilot scale with three native species.

One freshwater and two marine species received three candidate flocculants: the natural polymer chitosan, made from crustacean shells, and two metal salts. Lab screening picked the best doses, then pilot trials used clumping as a first step before centrifugation finished the job. Cheaper pre-concentration decides whether algae farms can sell fuel and feed at sane prices.
pmc-11677643:
Letícia Harumi Oshiquiri and nine co-authors disabled four calcium pumps of the storage vacuole in the fungus Trichoderma reesei to see what they control, in this 2024 study. The fungus is a workhorse for making cellulase enzymes, and calcium signals seem to steer their production. Mutant strains missing each pump were grown on varied sugars and stress agents.

The mutants grew faster on several plant sugars yet wilted under manganese, showing the pumps guard against that metal. The expected calcium-triggered jump in cellulase output vanished in the mutants, and the matching genes stayed quiet. Genes for other natural products shifted too. The authors conclude the pumps sit near the top of the fungus's calcium command chain.
pmc-11677743:
Hamza Alsayouf and co-authors asked whether children starting ADHD medicines need a routine heart tracing first, in a 2024 study from child neurology clinics in Jordan. The worry is that these medicines might stretch a heart signal called the QTc interval. The team reviewed records of children aged two to eighteen who had a baseline tracing and at least six months of follow-up.

Of four hundred and fifty-eight children with tracings, three hundred and sixty-two met the study rules. The average QTc sat at a healthy four hundred milliseconds. One child with a long interval was kept off the medicines. During follow-up, no child showed signs of heart trouble. Most children in the group also had autism. The authors judge routine screening unnecessary for healthy children with no family history of heart disease, pending longer studies.
pmc-11677943:
Xinyue Ren and five colleagues published a cell study in two thousand twenty-four on making the brain's insulation cells. Oligodendrocytes wrap nerve fibres in myelin, and their parent cells often stall before maturing. Vitamin C and a signalling drug were each known to push maturation; together they work even better.

The team traced the effect to DNA demethylation, the removal of chemical tags that silence genes. The pair raised levels of an intermediate tag that marks active tag removal. Blocking that intermediate almost fully stopped maturation. One expected enzyme family member, TET1, proved uninvolved. The authors propose the combination as a future therapy lead for diseases where myelin is lost.
pmc-11678243:
Mateusz Urbaniak and co-authors test a bacterial pigment, pyomelanin, as a spur for bone growth. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The pigment comes from Pseudomonas aeruginosa and mimics deposits seen in a rare genetic disease where cartilage turns to bone. That likeness hints it could wake bone cells on purpose.

Two forms, one that melts in water and one that does not, both lift bone marks in human bone cell cultures. Signal proteins tied to bone growth rise, and the cells move more and shrug off a drug that would kill them. Both forms also fight staph germs from infected bones. The team sees a path to new bone repair mixes built with the pigment.
pmc-11678443:
Rahul Raghav and co-authors boost a gene therapy for Barth syndrome with a cell-entering helper, in this 2024 study. The syndrome is a lethal inherited disorder of boys, caused by a faulty tafazzin gene that weakens heart and muscle. Gene therapy in development needs very high delivery rates to work.

The team attached penetratin, a peptide that ferries cargo into cells, to the therapy gene. In mice, the boosted version guarded the heart against swelling and failure better than the plain gene. The authors suggest such helpers could lower the dose gene therapy needs.
pmc-11678543:
Ibrahim Alkatout and a large group of surgeon authors share guidance on preventing internal scar tissue after gynecologic surgery in a 2024 paper. Such adhesions are a major medical problem with serious health and cost effects. The paper centers on a starch based product that can stop bleeding and prevent adhesions. It can be dusted on as a powder or turned into a gel on the spot or beforehand.

Drawing on wide clinical experience and published data, the authors report less adhesion formation, better recovery, less pain, and improved fertility in their patients. They give practical tips on application and dosing across conditions such as endometriosis. Case studies show the strengths of each form. The authors note evidence gaps remain, but their experience favors the product for large wounds at high risk of repeat surgery, especially when pregnancy is hoped for.
pmc-11678643:
Samira Hosseini and co-authors study how oxidative stress changes the way gum ligament cells answer pressure. Their 2024 work models orthodontic tooth movement in a dish: human ligament cells, the cells that anchor teeth, are pressed with a steady force like the one braces apply.

First the team dosed the cells with hydrogen peroxide to mimic the chemical strain of inflamed tissue, picking levels that barely hurt survival. Pressed cells that had been pre-stressed behaved unlike fresh ones in survival, growth, and death signals. Gene readouts covered bone reshaping, inflammation, cell death, and self-cleaning pathways. The authors read the shift as altered force sensing after stress, and they call for deeper work on the mechanism.
pmc-11678943:
Olamide Ogundare and co-authors study how metal exposure and daily habits jointly weigh on women's mood. Lead, cadmium, and mercury ride along in food, smoke, and workplaces, and each has been tied to depression on its own. Using national survey data from 2017 to 2018, the team modeled the mixture alongside drinking and smoking, letting the statistics sort out combined effects.

Average symptom scores sat in the mild range. Lead and cadmium each tracked with worse symptoms, while mercury pointed the other way in the same models. Alcohol use and smoking also came with heavier symptom loads. The mixture-aware analysis ranked which exposures mattered most inside the blend. The authors argue depression prevention in women should count body burden and behavior together, not one at a time.
pmc-11679043:
Arul Elango and René Landry teach satellite navigation receivers to explain themselves when their signals are attacked, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Jamming, spoofing, and multipath reflections all corrupt GPS-class signals. Operators need to know which one they face. The team recorded signals under seven disruption types, and mined their time and frequency features.

Tools for explainable AI, SHAP and LIME, ranked which features truly drove the model's verdicts. Training on only those top features beat standard feature selection at spotting unknown disruptions. The tools also narrate each event: this signal looks spoofed because these features moved. For ground stations guarding navigation safety, that openness turns a black box alarm into a diagnosis engineers can act on.
pmc-11679143:
Yajun Gong and co-authors link blood lead with high blood pressure in exposed workers in a 2024 study. Lead work is known to harm health, yet large studies in such workers stay few. Workplace heat, dust, and dirty air may sharpen or soften the lead effect.

More than twenty thousand workers fed the models. Higher blood lead went with notably higher pressure and more hypertension cases. Fine dust in the air raised risk further, and hot workplaces widened pressure gains. Oddly, workers without dust exposure showed larger lead-linked gains than dusty trades. The team urges tighter lead and dust control at work.
pmc-11679443:
Andrea Michielon and thirteen co-authors present an artificial intelligence platform that watches farm animals and scores their welfare, in a 2024 journal article. Staff on big farms cannot check each animal by eye each day. The system aims to do that watch by camera and code.

The platform is built in modules, each a deep learning model drawn from factory vision and human conduct study. One module names each animal with no tags. Others score how an animal walks and its body shape, both signs of health. Conduct modules read how feed and housing shape daily acts. The team shows two cases: health watch for dairy cows and conduct study for piglets. They argue such tools let farms act fast on hard data.
pmc-11679743:
Yuntao Duan and colleagues propose a key-point method for watching turbofan engine health, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Turbofans are complex, failure-prone machines where safety counts most. Safe running demands anomaly detection and life prediction. The method pulls two lifecycle key points from engine feature data.

Convolution steps, feature fusion, and derivative analysis produce those points. Counts-based analysis then builds health plans and remaining-life estimates around them. Test-set checks supported the approach. The authors argue key points simplify a messy watch problem. Engine sensor streams are long and tangled. Tying analysis to two key moments could focus upkeep decisions. They present the method as promising for secure engine health care.
pmc-11679843:
Lee leads a large team comparing immune tests after COVID vaccination, in work from twenty twenty-four. Both T cells and antibodies fight the virus, but the many lab tests for each are hard to compare. Agreement across tests over time was largely unknown.

Forty-six health workers with no prior infection were followed. One small group got three doses of the same mRNA vaccine. A larger group got two doses of a viral vector vaccine plus an mRNA booster. Blood at five time points was run on three T cell tests and three antibody tests. The side by side data show which tests track together.
pmc-11680043:
Chao Wang and co-authors speed up coverage planning for cleaning robots in a 2024 paper. Big public halls are messy, obstacle strewn spaces where a robot must still sweep every reachable patch. Their method grows from a spanning tree coverage scheme, with the backtracking step rebuilt around chosen return points.

Trading memory for time, the planners cut solution time sharply. The team proves backtracking cannot be avoided in such spaces, which supports the method's generality. A second encoding turns the plan into one smooth, cuttable path, so several robots can share the floor without path clashes and with balanced loads. In simulations and one real site, computing time fell by about eighty two percent.
pmc-11680143:
Sajid Umar and co-authors report in a 2024 paper the first find of influenza D virus in dairy cattle in Pakistan. The virus is a fresh zoonotic agent with cattle as its main reservoir. It feeds into the cattle respiratory disease complex that costs farms dearly.

Nose swabs from cattle were screened with a sensitive gene test across herds. Nine of 376 samples, 2.4%, came back positive for the virus. Four dairy farms held positive animals, most with breathing signs showing. Two positive animals showed no signs at all, a silent spread warning. Gene reads place all strains in the D/OK lineage, near kin to European and US strains.
pmc-11680343:
Maryame Lamsisi and a large team of co-authors published this 2024 review on bringing cervical cancer screening to the clinic doorstep. The test that matters detects human papillomavirus, but lab-based assays are slow, distant, and staff-hungry, exactly wrong for low-resource regions. Isothermal amplification, which copies DNA at one steady temperature, promises a simpler machine.

The review surveys recent point-of-care HPV tests built on that trick and grades their accuracy against conventional laboratory assays. Sensitivity, specificity, and real-world usability in primary care all come under the lens. The authors see genuine potential to widen screening where centralized labs are scarce. Their closing call is for work on cost, robustness, and collaboration so the devices reach the women who need them.
pmc-11680443:
Carol Maswanganye, Pamela Mkhize, and Nontokozo Matume pool the evidence on human papillomavirus in South African women, where cervical cancer is the second most common cancer. Their review screened nearly twenty thousand records and included 120 studies with over eighty-three thousand participants. They analyzed how common the virus is, its types, vaginal microbe groups, and immune signals together.

Pooled prevalence was fifty-eight percent. Rates were higher in cervical samples and in HIV-positive women. High-risk types 16, 35, and 18 led the spread of types. The weight of type 35 argues for wider vaccine coverage. Infected women had fewer protective Lactobacillus bacteria and more species tied to bacterial vaginosis, which may help the virus persist. The authors call for prevention plans shaped to regional types and HIV status.
pmc-11680643:
Gianicolo and co-authors present a 2024 study re-examining raised childhood leukemia rates near the Krümmel nuclear plant in Germany. Reports of a local excess have persisted for years. The team took registry data for 2004 to 2019 across 321 towns within fifty kilometers of the plant. Three hundred fifty-six cases in children under fifteen were counted.

Rates were computed against both national and regional baselines, which barely differed. Smoothed town-level rates were mapped to hunt for wind-shaped patterns, since plumes follow prevailing winds. Raised ratios did appear near a town named in earlier reports. The authors stress the traps of such area-level work: wobbly small numbers and the choice of comparison population.
pmc-11682543:
Reshmi Mishra, Amit Rup, Bharti Aggarwal, and Jyoti Behera trace in 2024 how scoring systems for child sepsis grew up. Sepsis still sickens and kills many children, and cases in intensive care are rising. Scores that sort risk fast can speed choices and cut deaths, the authors argue.

Scores split into two kinds: those that forecast outcomes, and those that describe a child's state. Each was built for a set place and age, so picking one that fits the ward matters. The review walks from early scores to current ones, with notes on real use. The authors urge tools that also forecast long-term harm, not just death. A ward that picks its score with care gains earlier warning on the children most at risk.
pmc-11682743:
Emina Dervišević and co-authors test lab marks that may prove drowning in a 2024 study. No set test can prove a death was by drowning, since the lung signs look much like those of other deaths. One old lead is to hunt tiny shell algae in body organs, which should reach them only via breathed water.

Their rat work splits beasts by how death came and how long the body lay in water. They set the algae hunt next to standard tissue reads for truth. The study is a first for its land. Crime labs gain a check on which test tells drowning from a body placed in water.
pmc-11682843:
Ashish Munoli, Prakash Mantur, and Vishwanath Jalawadi test whether vitamin D levels track the severity of liver cirrhosis, in a study from 2024. The liver turns vitamin D from food and skin into its main circulating form. Chronic liver disease disrupts that step, so levels may fall as damage grows.

The team studied 89 patients at a hospital in Vijayapura, India, sorting them by Child-Pugh class from mild to advanced. Vitamin D fell as the score rose, with a clear negative link between the two. The authors argue that low vitamin D marks worse disease and higher risk. They propose it as a simple added tool for judging how a cirrhosis patient will fare.
pmc-11683643:
Al Azzi, El Kurdi, and Patra trap curcumin inside a metal-organic framework made with aluminum fumarate, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Curcumin can fight cell damage, but it does not dissolve well and it breaks down fast. Frames of metal and organic parts, called MOFs, can be tuned to hold drugs. The team loaded the frame by wet impregnation, a soak in liquid, and the load took hold well.

Free curcumin loses more than half of its stock in just three days. The trapped form loses far less, and that is over a span of ten days. Its power to fight cell damage also jumps when trapped, well past the free form. The frame guards it, helps it dissolve, and keeps it stable, all at once. The team says the pairing calls for deep study as a way to carry drugs.
pmc-11685543:
Kritin Verma and co-authors present a 2024 case of biparietal osteodystrophy, a rare illness that thins both parietal bones of the skull in a matching pattern. It most often affects women in their sixties and seventies. Their patient was a 73-year-old woman with weak bones and joint disease who came to a skin clinic with a bulging mass near the top of her head.

She also reported spells of dizziness and blurred vision, and she had a past head injury, though the skull change came first. Scans showed loss of bone on both sides with no brain abnormality, and lab tests were mostly normal apart from high vitamin D. She was sent to a nerve specialist for more checks. The case reminds skin doctors to keep this rare condition in mind.
pmc-11686943:
Nicholas Graham and co-authors track coral reefs in the inner Seychelles across twenty-eight years and two mass bleaching events. Reefs have often shifted away from coral after heat stress, yet long records of repeat events are rare. The team compared recovery and community change after the 1998 and 2016 marine heatwaves.

Coral recovered faster after 2016 than after 1998. Seabed and fish communities also changed less the second time, having settled into an altered state with more grazing after the first event. One reef that had flipped to macroalgae after 1998 is now moving back toward coral. Repeat heat stress, the authors argue, can meet with more resilience than expected.
pmc-11687243:
Javiera Martinez-Gutierrez and co-authors scope the evidence on unexpected weight loss as a cancer warning in primary care, in a review from two thousand twenty-four. Weight loss with no clear cause often brings patients to their doctor, and it can hide an undiagnosed cancer. Guidance on how to work it up varies widely.

Twenty-five studies covering over nine hundred thousand patients were included. Nearly all strongly linked the symptom to undiagnosed cancer. Shared advice covered weight tracking, family history, risk checks, and a full exam. Blood tests and simple imaging recurred across guidelines. The review feeds a decision support tool for clinics.
pmc-11688343:
Olubodun Lateef and five co-authors review LIM kinases in cardiovascular health and disease. This kinase pair controls the cell skeleton by promoting actin assembly and loosening the microtubule network. Those actions shape cell division, movement, and differentiation, all vital for heart and vessel function.

The review covers how the kinases switch on and off and their roles in vessel growth, new vessel formation, and sensing of mechanical force. Disease links include high blood pressure, aneurysm, atrial fibrillation, and valve disease. Effects in lining cells, vessel muscle cells, and heart muscle cells are detailed. Early animal studies hint that blocking these kinases could treat disease, but human relevance needs more work.
pmc-11688843:
Ruthann Froberg and Randi Campetti describe how a local group sought older adults' views on elder abuse. Their twenty twenty-four talk notes that abuse is hard to raise, due to shame and a sense that nothing helps. A town coalition still asked older adults and service staff for frank views. Their aim was to guide the coalition's own work.

Three groups of adults aged sixty and older met for an hour each, plus one group of service staff. People stressed social contact, help with online skills, and easier access to aid. Staff stressed joint work, and gaps in staff and funds. The coalition used the points to set clear next steps.
pmc-11688943:
Davis and co-authors study in 2024 whether strong lifestyle help in midlife cuts the load of living with many long term illnesses later. They draw on the Look AHEAD trial, which placed 5,145 adults with diabetes and excess weight into strong help or standard support from 2001 to 2004. The strong plan had cut weight and eased diabetes strain during the trial.

For this study, 2,940 members let their trial records link to Medicare data for the years 2013 to 2019. The team counted long term illnesses from a standard federal list for each year of cover. Their checks test whether early lifestyle help still pays off in fewer illnesses as people age.
pmc-11689043:
Lena Thompson, Steffi Kim, and Jordan Lewis describe a 2024 symposium on aging research led with Indigenous peoples. Standard research has often left Indigenous elders out of study design, and findings then reach programs slowly. Worse, outside groups have at times gained more from such studies than the communities themselves.

The session, backed by groups on Indigenous aging and rural aging, shared projects built with communities rather than on them. Methods included joint program design, storytelling, and talk-based data work. The aim was stronger ties between elders and research, and results that fit local values. The authors argue that strengths-based, community-led work brings fairer gains and programs that last. The piece sums up the session's goals and approach.
pmc-11689143:
W Quin Yow frames a set of talks on easing social cutoff and loneliness in older adults in a 2024 summary. About one in four older adults in the United States face such cutoff, tied to stroke and mind decline. Work at the town level on checks and cures is still thin, the talks note.

One talk maps what makes health staff at ease with screening. One rates a town project in Japan that links older neighbours, and one weighs online ties for easing lone feels. A last talk tests chat agents that nudge older adults to talk and meet more.
pmc-11689243:
Michael Lepore, Tara McMullen, and Karon Phillips introduce a symposium on aging and public policy, in a 2024 paper. Public health gains have let more people live longer, healthier lives. Those gains are not shared equally, the authors note. Policies built for younger, less diverse populations may deepen gaps for today's older adults.

The session draws on a policy journal's past work on hard political questions in aging. Topics include voting patterns among older Americans and support for programs they rely on. State and local efforts to aid low-income older adults are covered. Property tax funded care services in several states get attention. Voting access amid aging, disability, and memory problems is also on the agenda. Discussion looks past a recent election to the future of aging policy.
pmc-11689343:
Hyosin Kim and co-authors set in 2024 end of life care for Asian and isle folk in the United States with brain fade next to white peers. This group bears the ill at high rates and has deep care needs at life end. Race gaps in their last care were scarce known.

Care files for folk who died in one year form the base: near twenty thou sand in the group, over seven hundred thou sand peers. Group folk held dual care cover more yet used home help, care homes, and rest care less. Death in a ward ran high. Gaps grew with ill load.
pmc-11689443:
Laura Xicota, Rong Cheng, Sandra Barral Rodriguez, Lawrence Honig, and Joseph Lee test gene risk scores for dementia in long lived families in a 2024 study. Scores built from many small gene risks flag high risk people in the broad public. Families with extreme long life run low dementia risk, which makes a sharp test case.

Scores built from two large public gene hunts did not predict dementia in the US arm of the family study. Risk gene forms were just as common there, but they lacked their usual effect. Just 6.7% and 7.7% of the gene spots tied to disease in that group. Blood markers of brain harm also failed to rise with the scores. The work warns that public risk scores may not travel to such groups.
pmc-11689843:
Courtney Millar and seven co-authors asked whether an inflammation-raising diet speeds the onset of frailty, and whether depression sharpens that link, in a 2024 study. Diet-driven inflammation is tied to frailty, and people with depressive symptoms tend to carry more inflammation. The team followed adults who were not yet frail.

The study covered 1,701 adults with diet reports from 1998 to 2001 and frailty checks about a decade later. A dietary inflammation score was built from food questionnaires, and depressive symptoms were scored on a standard scale. Each extra unit of diet inflammation raised frailty odds by 14 percent in people without strong symptoms. In people with strong symptoms, the same unit raised odds by 55 percent. The authors say diet advice may matter most for adults with low mood.
pmc-11690243:
Walter Boot and co-authors introduce a conference session on the digital divide in old age. Older adults still trail younger people in owning, using, and mastering technology, and the session's talks probe causes and fixes. One talk proposes coaching tailored to each person's values, aimed at access gaps in communities of color.

Other talks cover feelings toward smart home devices, matching tech information to what older adults find meaningful, and a peer-led exercise program that uses feedback tech to prevent falls. A final talk questions whether cognitive decline truly drives the divide. A discussant closes the session.
pmc-11690443:
Deanna Dragan, Lauren Hagemann, and Cynthia Jarmul report a program review from twenty twenty-four. They study a Veterans Health project that links VA care with local hospice groups. Veterans at the end of life may need care for trauma, moral pain, or suicide risk. Local hospice staff need to know those needs and the benefits that can help.

The team spoke with staff at many levels and with eight local hospice groups. They also made site visits to four groups. Talks surfaced themes such as who to contact, timing of care, and help for families. The groups and the VA then planned joint work they could keep up over time.
pmc-11690543:
Christopher Fagundes presents smartphone data on loneliness in dementia spousal caregivers, in a 2024 paper. Spouses who care for a partner with dementia report more loneliness than peers. Their loneliness ties to worse mood and life satisfaction for both partners, while the ill spouse's loneliness does not seem to flow back. Yet the daily patterns of caregiver loneliness were largely unknown, which blocks well-timed help.

Phones pinged caregivers across a fourteen-day protocol to catch mood and contact as they happened. A caregiver's sense of safety in the relationship decided whether shared care tasks left them lonelier or less lonely afterward. Fagundes argues such momentary maps can guide phone-based support that arrives at the right moment. The work aims to lift life quality for both members of the pair.
pmc-11690643:
Carolyn Adams-Price and Justine McGovern frame a symposium on creative programs for older adults in a 2024 paper. Making art, music, and dance is often urged for healthy aging, for both sharp and impaired minds, but the proof and the best forms vary by group. The session sorts gains by program kind and by the elders served.

One paper lays out theory and the social frame for late life creativity, weighing gains through lifespan and dementia lenses. A dance program for Parkinson's patients reports body and mood gains. A music program with Down syndrome elders shares its own lessons. The discussant ties the three threads into one account of who gains what from making things in old age.
pmc-11690743:
Soomi Lee introduces a 2024 symposium that looks back at the history of gerontology as its main society nears eighty years. The field began in the early nineteen hundreds, when old age was often seen only as decline. Understanding has grown since, but knowledge still passes poorly between generations of scholars, the abstract notes.

Three honored panelists share their experience. One traces how the field evolved, one tells mentorship stories, and one addresses core values and challenges. Lee moderates the talks and the audience discussion. The session aims to help the aging research community reflect on its past and shape a shared vision for what comes next.
pmc-11690943:
Laila Scroggins and four co-authors argue that a fat called ceramide should count as a hallmark of aging, in a 2024 paper. Aging is the top risk factor for chronic disease, and lipids act as both cell parts and signals. The first longevity gene found in yeast makes an enzyme that builds ceramides.

The team gathers data from several animal models. Ceramides build up with age in blood and organs across mouse strains and in marmosets. Long lived mutant mice carry far less of the fat in blood. An established anti aging drug lowers liver ceramides in old marmosets. Low doses of a drug that blocks ceramide making improved blood sugar control and grip strength in mice on a rich diet. The authors place ceramides among the drivers of aging.
pmc-11691043:
Hsin-Ying Tsou, Yu-Ten Pan, and Tsuann Kuo guide healthy Taiwanese elders through talking about their own deaths, in a 2024 study. Death talk is delicate in Eastern cultures, tangled with inheritance and filial duty, and silence leaves families guessing. Eleven older adults met for ten weekly two-hour life review sessions. Observers tracked the talk, the shifts, and the reflections.

Four stages unfolded. Resistance came first: nobody knew how to start. Sharing funeral stories for relatives loosened tongues, teaching that respect, not a standard script, is the answer. Then participants began arranging their own property, medical wishes, and funerals. A closing performance sealed the sharing. The authors say guided life review can open the hardest conversation gently.
pmc-11691143:
Anum Zafar and co-authors explain how they stitched a single life story of memory loss out of scattered Medicare records. Claims forms and care assessments each hold pieces of a person's cognitive path, in different codes and settings. The team harmonized those pieces for beneficiaries who died in 2019, tracking the last five years of life in quarterly steps.

Nearly two million people were included, sorted at each step into no impairment, memory loss, mild impairment, or dementia. Five years before death, about eight percent had dementia or severe impairment; by death, the share passed half. Records added fresh information in only about seven of twenty quarters on average. The authors offer the harmonized file as a tool for tracking decline and hunting its risk factors across the whole Medicare population.
pmc-11691243:
EunKyo Kim and co-authors surveyed nurses and nurse aides in long-term care homes about what drives hand washing. Clean hands are the cheapest infection shield in care settings, yet compliance varies. The study covered 78 registered nurses and 50 aides in late 2020, using World Health Organization tools to score knowledge, attitudes, and workplace facilities. Staff also reported how often they cleaned their hands at the five key moments.

Average compliance came out near 79 percent. Knowledge scores were middling, while facility scores ran high. Compliance rose with better attitudes and, more strongly, with better infrastructure like sinks and supplies. Working in a specialized unit with set nurse staffing levels also predicted cleaner hands. The authors argue that managers should fix the physical setup and unit staffing rather than only lecturing staff about germs.
pmc-11691443:
Duo Wei and co-authors mapped how generative AI entered dementia research after ChatGPT arrived, in a 2024 review. The scoping review covered Alzheimer disease and related dementias in older adults. PubMed searches pulled papers from the first two years of the boom. Nearly two hundred articles were screened for fit.

One hundred forty-five papers passed into the final map. Uses split into themes across care, detection, and support. The review shows where large language models already help. Gaps and hype zones stand out beside the real use cases. The map guides labs planning their next AI study.
pmc-11691543:
About one in six middle-aged and older Americans struggles with a basic daily activity, and their working relatives must trade wages against caregiving. Yuting Qian and Xi Chen study in 2024 what paid family leave does to the care such adults receive. They use Health and Retirement Study data from 1998 to 2018 and the staggered arrival of leave programs in California, New Jersey, and New York.

Among disabled adults who had both a spouse and children, access to paid leave raised the chance of receiving informal care from their children by 8 percentage points. For those with a spouse, leave also raised formal care, home care, and nursing home use. Effects were weaker for some vulnerable groups, such as those with children only. The authors read paid leave as supporting healthy aging, with uneven reach.
pmc-11691943:
Hyunjin Noh and three co-authors present this 2024 conference abstract on a delicate conversation: asking older adults whether they would take fewer pain medicines. Deprescribing, the planned trimming of drugs that may harm more than help, is gaining ground as polypharmacy's dangers sink in. How the patients themselves feel about it, especially for pain, was largely unasked.

The team interviewed thirty Alabama adults aged sixty-five and over, each living outside nursing homes with several chronic illnesses, chronic pain, and a medicine list to match. Three themes emerged. Helpful winds: interest in holistic pain care, worry about long-term side effects, and hope for a better quality of life. Headwinds: fear the pain will surge back, reluctance to disturb a working routine, and too little backing from their own providers. The stated need was simple, trustworthy information from their clinicians about what stopping would actually involve.
pmc-11692043:
Nathan Lewis and co-authors link life purpose to mental exercise in a 2024 study. A strong sense of purpose tracks with better memory, sharper executive function, and lower dementia risk. Why remained open. One candidate path runs through activity: purposeful people may read, puzzle, and learn more, building cognitive reserve that buffers the aging brain.

The study tests whether purpose predicts engagement in stimulating activities, and for whom the link runs strongest. If activity is the bridge, programs might build reserve by feeding purpose rather than drilling cognition. That would be a kinder and possibly stronger intervention for brain aging, aimed at meaning first.
pmc-11692143:
Esther Shin and co-authors chart long-term mixes of family and paid care for older adults. Care studies often split family and formal care, or ask if one swaps for the other. This study joins care type and care source in one view. Data came from a national aging study that ran from 2011 to 2022.

Four care mix paths emerged from the group models. Most people, about seventy-two percent, stayed on a low care path. Others gained informal help with daily tasks, gained formal care, or swapped formal for paid family care. Married women filled the informal growth group most. Those gaining formal care more often lived alone or had dementia.
pmc-11692243:
Boah Kim and four co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, what helps or blocks family care partners of older adults as they seek help from health and town services. Care partners fill key roles, yet they can find the system hard to use. The team used a named model of health access to frame the work.

They drew on a large survey of care and care receipt from two thousand eighteen. More than two thousand care partners of adults aged sixty-five or more were in the study. Those with strong social ties had less trouble finding help. Those whose family used more formal care had more trouble. The authors call for joined up plans and clear rules to close these gaps.
pmc-11692343:
Adil Supiyev, Angela Gutierrez, and Graciela Muniz Terrera assess thinking skills and their drivers in older adults in Kazakhstan in 2024. Proof from Central Asia on this topic is scarce. Near one thousand adults aged fifty to seventy four took part. Four mind tests covered memory, word flow, and focus. Blood samples and body checks added context.

Place of living, ethnic group, and schooling all tied to scores. Income linked factors mattered as well. A famous risk gene variant tied strongly to decline, matching world data. Men, rural residents, and the less schooled scored worse. High deprivation also hurt. The authors urge aimed steps for at risk groups. Local context, they stress, shapes aging minds.
pmc-11692443:
Inhye Jung, Miseon Kang, Seolah Lee, and Hyo Jung Lee published this study in 2024. It asks whether age-friendly surroundings protect life satisfaction in frail older adults. Frailty makes daily tasks hard, and unmet care needs can drag down a person's view of life.

The team used a 2020 national survey of older Koreans and picked out 1,435 frail respondents. They sorted surroundings into three kinds: physical layout, services, and social climate. As expected, heavier care needs went with lower life satisfaction. But good services and a warm social climate softened that drop in a measurable way. Physical layout alone did not show the same buffer. The authors argue that building service-rich, welcoming neighborhoods is a direct way to support aging at home.
pmc-11692543:
Ku and co-authors listen in on how medicines get talked about in nursing home care conferences in a 2024 study. These meetings gather staff, residents, and families to plan care, and medication choices are core to safety, yet the talk itself was unmapped.

Fifteen meetings in a small Midwestern home were taped and themed. Fourteen held medication talk, led mostly by social workers and nurses, with no pharmacist present. Residents and families mostly listened. Talk served three ends: sharing information, deciding changes, and planning discharge supplies. The map shows where family voices could be drawn in.
pmc-11692643:
Pamela Nadash, Marc Cohen, Edward Miller, and four co-authors published a 2024 study inside one nonprofit plan that cares for Massachusetts' most vulnerable older adults. People eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid often get fragmented, costly care with poor results. Commonwealth Care Alliance insures about thirty five thousand of them, including a Senior Care Options program for those over sixty five running since 2003.

Drawing on interviews with key informants and other data, the study asks how the plan actually works from inside. It identifies the challenges of securing both medical care and the wider health related services members need, from transport to housing support. It also traces the mechanisms the plan built over time to meet those challenges, and how its care model evolved.
pmc-11692743:
Jingxuan Wu and Huamao Peng present a 2024 survey study of older adults who use short-form video apps such as TikTok. Many older users do more than watch; they like, comment, share, and send gifts. The team asked whether such active use helps older adults fit into social life, and what inner steps carry the effect.

Two thousand adults aged 55 to 85 filled in four standard scales. The scales covered social fit, video use, basic inner needs, and views on one's own aging. Active use linked directly to better social fit. It also helped through a chain: met needs fed a warmer view of one's own aging, which fed social fit in turn. The results suggest that guided, active app use could support older adults, not just passive viewing.
pmc-11692943:
Low-dose lung scans can cut lung cancer deaths, yet few smokers who qualify get scanned in the United States. Tung-Sung Tseng and co-authors dug into that gap with national survey data in work from twenty twenty-four. Their set held more than fifteen thousand replies from twenty-nine states, plus state facts such as scan site counts.

Fewer than one in five who qualify had been scanned, and state rates split widely. States with more scan sites per smoker had higher uptake. Workers, the never-married, and people with no regular doctor or checkups scanned less. So did people who felt well or lacked some long-term ills. The authors call for wider access and outreach aimed at the groups left behind.
pmc-11693143:
Chakurian and Popejoy review what helps family caregivers of autistic adults stay resilient, in a 2024 paper. These caregivers give lifelong care and face chronic stress, stigma, and isolation, yet most past work studied caregivers of children. The review searched ten databases and kept nineteen studies for close reading.

Caregivers fared better when they used problem-focused and meaning-focused coping, had social support, planned for the future, and felt less burden and stigma. The authors argue that support and coping skills are levers that clinics and policy can actually move. They call for sharper definitions and measures so future reviews can compare studies more cleanly.
pmc-11693243:
Alaa Albashayreh, Nahid Zeinali, and Stephanie White trained a language model to find care priorities hidden in hospital notes. Their 2024 study addresses a gap in end of life care. Older adults with heart failure hold preferences about comfort and life sustaining treatment. Records document them unevenly, though, so they often go unused.

The team retrained a clinical language model on records from a Midwestern hospital, creating Care-BERT. A gold standard set of 1,068 notes, hand labeled for care priorities, was split into training and test parts. Care-BERT beat three rival models, including its own base versions, at predicting the priorities in fresh notes. Reliable detection could help teams honor what patients actually want, the authors argue.
pmc-11693343:
Zhang Zhang, writing alone, studies telehealth payment rules in this 2024 paper. Payment parity means insurers pay the same rate for telehealth as for in-person care. Zhang asks if parity raised use of advised care among workers at high risk of dementia.

The study used a large claims database from 2019 to 2021 and a difference-in-differences design. It focused on workers with mental health disorders or heart and metabolic risks. Parity raised psychotherapy visits, and tele-psychotherapy visits rose even more. Emergency visits among those with mental health disorders fell by a quarter in relative terms. Preventive counseling for metabolic risks did not rise by a clear margin.
pmc-11694043:
Luis Carlos Rodríguez Timaná and co-authors reviewed studies of serious games for children, in a 2024 paper. Serious games are games built to train or treat, not just to entertain. The review asks whether such games can strengthen executive functions in neurodiverse children. Those functions include attention, working memory, flexible thinking, and self-control.

The team searched three databases and kept sixteen studies that fit their rules. Most of the studies worked with children who had attention, autism, or Down syndrome traits. Many reported clear gains in attention, memory, and flexible thinking after game-based training. The authors also weigh study quality and gaps, so readers can judge how firm the gains are and where more trials are needed.
pmc-11697343:
Zachary Cohen and Ryan M Williams review carbon nanotubes as light based sensors inside living bodies in 2024. These tiny tubes glow in ways that shift when target molecules bind. Some sensors are tuned to one target at a time. Others have been placed in live animals and plants. Such tools could watch drugs, disease, and toxins without blood draws.

The review surveys which targets have been sensed inside living tissue. It also covers how sensors are built and placed. Uses range from clinic care to field ecology. The authors stress that much lab work remains. Better materials and design must come first. The prize is steady, implant grade sensing.
pmc-11697543:
Felichi Arines and co-authors set out a lab protocol for studying a cell's internal transport pumps in a 2024 paper. Their subject is Ypq1, a transporter in the membrane of the vacuole, the cell's storage and recycling sac.

The protocol covers making extra copies of the pump, pulling it out clean, and seating it in artificial fat bubbles called proteoliposomes. With the pump in place, radioactive tracer cargo can time its crossings and reveal how it works. Membrane transporters are hard to study in living cells, so this bench setup isolates one pump at a time. The steps adapt to other vacuole and lysosome transporters, giving cell biologists a shared playbook.
pmc-11699243:
Bokhtiar Hasan and co-authors test whether ethical investments shelter wealth when uncertainty strikes. They study seven asset classes, both ethical and standard, against three kinds of shock: geopolitical risk, policy uncertainty, and market volatility. Data run from 2011 to 2021, a span with several global crises. Their 2024 study uses two wave-based tools that track links across time and market mood.

Most assets moved with or stayed neutral to geopolitical risk, a sign they can shelter funds then. Links to policy uncertainty were positive in down markets on a monthly view. Only green bonds and a clean energy index guarded against policy shocks during COVID-19. Volatility shocks hurt every asset except green bonds. The authors suggest ethical portfolios can be tuned to blunt extreme, lasting shocks.
pmc-11700243:
Quang Thieu and co-authors make a battery material from palm shells in a 2024 study. Lithium-ion batteries need better anode materials than graphite. The team turned cellulose from the shells of the nypa palm into a carbon base, then grew zinc oxide particles on it with a water based heating method.

They baked the composite in nitrogen gas for varied times and checked how the bake changed its mix of carbon and zinc oxide. Images showed zinc oxide particles spread on the carbon surface, with a like shape across samples. As a battery anode, the best sample kept a strong charge capacity after one hundred cycles. The authors credit the cellulose based carbon, the right mix of phases, and the structure of the composite.
pmc-11701843:
Jake Crawford, Maria Chikina, and Casey Greene tested in 2024 a piece of modeling folklore: that simpler gene signatures travel better to new data. They trained mutation-predicting models on cancer cell lines and on tumors, then swapped the test sets, and also held out whole cancer types.

Choosing models by their score on a held-out set alone picked winners as reliably as rules favoring simpler models. Heavy shrinkage did not generalize better for either plain or neural models. The practical moral: trust a clean holdout score, and do not pay for simplicity that buys no reach.
pmc-11701943:
Anjali Goel, Matuli Das, and Saswati Sen compared, in a 2024 study, how patients themselves rate two cataract operations for hard brown cataracts. One route uses ultrasound to break the lens; the other removes it through a small hand-made incision. Machines differ in cost, so patient experience matters.

Eighty-one patients aged 40 and up answered a vision questionnaire before surgery and six weeks after. One surgeon did all cases, 41 by the manual route and 40 by ultrasound. Both groups gained sharp sight, with average acuity improving a great deal in each eye. Nearly every patient read near print well afterward. In a few daily-life areas the ratings parted slightly. The study helps clinics weigh patient-reported gains beside price and gear.
pmc-11708943:
George Hafzalla, Hyein Ji, and Niranjan Jeganathan compared in 2024 the death risk COVID-19 posed to Americans with two kinds of chronic lung disease. Earlier studies disagreed on how common lung disease was among the infected. Using national death records, the team focused on people who died and asked which lung condition they carried.

One group had scarring lung disease; the other had common chronic airway diseases. Comparing their COVID death patterns clarifies which patients most need shielding and early treatment. The letter format suits a fast answer to a focused public health question.
pmc-11709043:
India gives out low-cost health goods, from soap to sanitary items, through clinics, but many rural families use them less than hoped. Aditi Sur and co-authors ask why in a 2024 study of villages served by a rural health unit in Hooghly District, West Bengal. They measured how happy users were with the goods and what held others back.

The team interviewed 150 households face to face and spoke in depth with four health workers. Supply gaps, quality worries, and weak promotion all came up as barriers. The mixed approach paired satisfaction scores with staff views on what blocks use. Findings like these can help programs stock goods steadily and explain them better to rural families.
pmc-11709343:
Ana Abril Vidal Escobedo, Facundo Peralta, Paula Cecilia Reggiani, and Joaquín Pardo present a 2025 rat study of a protective gene therapy for Alzheimer’s disease. They aimed a virus at astrocytes, the brain’s support cells, to raise levels of GDNF, a factor that helps neurons survive. The disease state was created with a drug that harms brain insulin signalling.

Rats received the virus into the hippocampus, a memory region, before the disease drug was given. Untreated and control-virus rats later failed behaviour and memory tests. Rats with raised GDNF performed like healthy controls. Their astrocytes also grew longer, more branched arms. The work suggests that strengthening support cells can protect memory, a different target from most Alzheimer’s treatments.
pmc-11709543:
Rafaella Ferreira and co-authors examine in this 2025 study how the brain's support cells fan the inflammation behind Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid oligomers, the toxic clusters at the disease's core, injure synapses and power plants. The team asked what microglia and astrocytes do in reply, in dishes and in mice given the clusters into brain fluid.

A week after infusion, activation markers and complement signals rose in the animals' brains, while one classic cytokine stayed flat. In dishes, the clusters pushed a master inflammation switch into microglia nuclei within hours. Staying switched on for years, the authors argue, may feed the very amyloid cycle that lit them. Calming glia early may slow the slide.
pmc-11709843:
Casey Vanderlip, Michael Lee, and Craig Stark test whether a memory task, read through a cognitive model, can flag the hidden markers of Alzheimer's disease in healthy older adults. Their 2025 study starts from timing: the disease's proteins build up decades before memory slips. The task used probes how well a person tells near-twin items apart, a hippocampus-linked skill.

Data came from 133 unimpaired older adults who took the task and gave spinal fluid for the marker assays. All scored normal on standard tests. The team compared plain task scores with model-based reads of the same answers. Their aim was to see which read better predicts the fluid markers, and so who sits in the silent phase where early action could help.
pmc-11709943:
Ortega, Aslanyan, and Pa study whether telomere length links physical activity to cognition differently by sex in a 2025 paper. Telomeres mark cellular aging in white blood cells. Activity is known to affect both telomeres and thinking skills.

Data came from hundreds of thousands of UK Biobank adults. In men, more weekly activity mostly tracked with shorter telomeres, oddly enough. In women, vigorous activity instead tracked with longer telomeres. Mediation tests also split by sex and by activity intensity. Telomeres carried part of the activity-cognition link for moderate activity in men, and for walking in women. Reaction time links ran through telomeres only in men. The authors say sex and intensity both shape the pathway.
pmc-11710143:
Cherie A Stringer and co-authors share a 2025 conference abstract on a water channel protein in Down syndrome brains. People with Down syndrome build up amyloid early and often develop Alzheimer's disease. The protein, aquaporin-4, sits in support cells called astrocytes and may help clear amyloid, but it can shift out of place as amyloid grows.

The team studied post-mortem brain samples from controls and from people with Down syndrome, with and without Alzheimer's changes. In Down syndrome with Alzheimer's, the protein sat away from its normal spot and was present at higher levels. Support cells also showed shapes tied to reactive, inflamed states.
pmc-11710343:
Sunny Kumar and seven co-authors ask why some brains bear Alzheimer's damage yet keep clear minds. Plaques and tangles can sit in a brain with no dementia at all. Their 2025 study reads post-mortem brains from 103 people in two long aging cohorts, split by damage and by mind fate.

Demented and resilient brains held like counts of tangles, but demented ones bore more tau threads and more loose tau at the synapses. Cleaner cells loaded with waste marks ran high in demented and frail brains, not in resilient ones. Synapse loss tracked the same split. Gene reads showed resilient brains kept down genes for cell death and swelling. The team ties mind fate to tau at synapses plus swelling.
pmc-11710443:
Hirra Arain and co-authors ask whether the APOE4 gene variant changes how tau protein spreads through the brain, in a 2025 paper. Carrying APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk for the common form of Alzheimer's disease. Research long tied it to amyloid plaques, but its grip on the second hallmark, tau tangles, was unclear.

The team built a humanized mouse whose misfolded human tau starts in the entorhinal cortex, the region where tau trouble begins in patients. Crossing it with mice carrying different human APOE versions let them watch spread across the brain up to old age. Their measurements trace how APOE4 reshapes tau's path through regions tied to early disease.
pmc-11710543:
Tomoki Mitani and co-authors set out a 2025 method for mapping very early brain decay across a whole mouse brain at single cell scale. Diseases such as Alzheimer disease are often found only after heavy harm is done. A full organ view could reveal spots and times that normal sampling would miss.

The method, called a cellome-wide association study, merges cell data over space and time into a three dimensional atlas built with tissue clearing images. In disease models the team found decay at spots and times not reported before. In an Alzheimer model, amyloid build up and cell decay seemed to start at the same time, which questions the usual order. They also mapped clusters of inflamed cells around damaged spots.
pmc-11710643:
Holly Cukier and co-authors describe a 2025 study of a rare gene change tied to late onset Alzheimer disease. The change sits in a gene called TTC3 and was found in one family. The team asked what the change does inside young brain cells grown in the lab.

They used gene editing to place the change in stem cells, then grew forebrain nerve cells from them. Cells with the change moved faster and grew longer branches than normal cells. Signs at cell contacts also shifted, and many genes changed in level. Small drugs that act on cell fibers could undo the branch change. The authors link the loss to weak cell contacts.
pmc-11710743:
Sarah Tavares Araújo Santos and co-authors test a drug in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. The drug, FK506, blocks calcineurin, a protein tied to how nerve cells connect and survive. The team asked whether blocking it could protect memory and brain tissue.

They gave the drug to mice harmed by toxins in the hippocampus, to gene-altered mice bred for the disease, and to brain slice cultures. Treated mice kept better memory and social behavior. The drug cut cell death and lowered microglia buildup in the hippocampus. Brain slices also kept more mature nerve cells. The authors see FK506 as a candidate worth more study.
pmc-11710943:
Nisha Ahuja and co-authors detailed in 2024 two eye surgeries that rebuilt vision after blunt trauma. Both patients had traumatic cataracts with widening pupils and torn lens supports, and both were losing sight progressively. The operation removed the clouded lens and part of the front gel of the eye. A fine stitch then cinched the iris smaller, and a claw lens was fixed behind it.

After surgery, both patients reached corrected vision of 6/12. The authors call the paired technique safe, fast, and effective for this injury pattern. Traumatic cataract care is tricky because the normal lens support is gone. Anchoring the new lens to the iris itself sidesteps that problem. The report offers the combination as a rehabilitation route with few complications.
pmc-11712143:
Daniel Arnold and co-authors build a model that predicts Alzheimer's-related brain changes from routine clinical data in a 2025 paper. Trials of anti-amyloid drugs lose many volunteers at screening because their brains lack amyloid. A cheap way to pre-select likely candidates would save time and cost.

Data from three large cohorts covered 1,694 people with known amyloid and tau status from scans or spinal fluid. The model used age, memory test scores, diagnosis, sex, schooling, body mass, and common health conditions. It separated people with both markers from those with neither with strong accuracy. Most participants had no impairment, and about one in five carried both markers. The authors offer the model as a screening aid for trials and clinics.
pmc-11712243:
Greg Windle, writing alone, describes a dementia-friendly communities programme in the east of England in this 2025 paper. Such programmes help towns support people who live with dementia. Forms vary widely, and a national scheme in England ended in 2023.

County councils in the region agreed to keep a scheme going in 2024 under their dementia strategy. A task force of officials, health staff, and charity leaders is building the new version. It sets county-wide levels for what counts as dementia-friendly service. Each local council can then shape those levels to its own population. The paper tracks how this shared model is being put in place.
pmc-11712443:
Isaac Akinkunmi Adedeji and five co-authors published a study in 2025 on training dementia caregivers in Ibadan, Nigeria, in ways that fit local culture. Little is known about how African families handle the difficult behaviors that come with dementia. Training imported from elsewhere may miss the values that shape care at home, so the team listened first.

They interviewed twenty-three caregivers, most of them women, about daily life with a relative with dementia. Five cultural themes emerged from the accounts. Respect for elders and duty to parents anchored care, alongside reading unspoken cues. Families also shared the work through communal living and rotating duties. A training framework built on these themes is the study's goal.
pmc-11712543:
Wooseok Jung and co-authors test how the choice of head-size correction changes judgments of brain shrinkage in Alzheimer's disease. Doctors grade atrophy by comparing a patient's brain regions with healthy peers of the same age and sex. But a big head naturally holds a bigger brain, so the skull volume must be factored out. Three corrections compete: raw volume, proportion, and residual. Their 2025 study runs all three on over fifteen hundred memory clinic and research scans.

Both corrections removed the head-size link about equally well. Yet they disagreed per patient: the proportion method rates more tissue preserved in small-headed patients than the residual method does. Plotting scores against skull size suggested raw volumes detect trouble best in small heads, while proportion wins in large ones. The authors warn that the right correction depends on the head in front of you.
pmc-11712743:
Mario Torso and co-authors ask whether a second protein fault, called TDP-43, leaves its own mark on the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease. The fault often rides along with Alzheimer's, and spotting its mark in life could sharpen care. The team used scans taken during life from people whose disease was later confirmed at autopsy.

Fifty-four such cases came from two United States data banks. In the limbic zone, a memory-linked set of regions, one scan measure of tissue order ran higher in cases with the second fault than in pure Alzheimer's cases. The result hints that diffusion scans can flag this added fault before death, a step toward finer sorting of patients.
pmc-11712843:
Brain scans with the tracer MK-6240 light up tau tangles in Alzheimer's disease. Tobey Betthauser and co-authors ask what the signal actually binds. They studied four people who had scans in life and donated brain tissue after death. Tissue came from ten regions per case, matched to the scan regions. Lab assays measured total tau and four phosphorylated forms. Death came about 32 months after imaging, on average.

Higher scan signal tracked higher levels of every measured phospho-tau form. The pattern held across regions and cases. Two cases with full Alzheimer's pathology showed the same links in detail. The study ties the tracer's glow to real tau chemistry.
pmc-11712943:
Blood tests for Alzheimer's markers are racing toward clinics, and a Lancet Commission summary weighs what they can and cannot promise. Lon Schneider reports the expert group's evidence review. Amyloid, the classic marker, grows common with age: over a fifth of seventy-year-olds test positive, yet most positive, healthy-minded people never develop dementia.

Signs of neurodegeneration track decline far more closely than amyloid or tau alone. Plasma versions of tau markers match or beat the amyloid ratio at spotting brain amyloid. Adding blood markers to prediction barely moved accuracy in one large study. The 2025 recommendations see the tests' best use in ruling Alzheimer's out, not ruling it in.
pmc-11713043:
Ryn Flaherty and co-authors search for a brain imaging signature of subjective cognitive decline. Their 2025 paper studies people who feel their memory slipping while tests still score them as normal. Such complaints can precede Alzheimer's disease, and fluid markers have proven weaker than imaging at forecasting decline.

The team scanned three hundred sixteen cognitively normal adults over fifty-five, one hundred twenty-three of them with memory complaints. Several diffusion models were fit to white and gray matter, alongside measures of volume and cortical thickness. Gray matter diffusion has been little studied in this group, so the work tests whether it carries its own signal. Regional averages were compared between groups to find where the signature lives.
pmc-11713143:
Joshua Harper, Tavia Evans, Johnes Obungoloch and Hieab Adams report building low-field MRI scanners where they are scarce, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. At least two-thirds of the world lacks access to neuroimaging, biasing brain research toward wealthy populations. Low-field MRI is cheaper and portable, and one open-source design can be reproduced mostly with local resources.

Pilot builds in Uganda and Paraguay took different paths. Uganda imported all parts and built in eleven days with expert help. Paraguay sourced locally and built over six months with local staff alone. Quality was maintained in both. The authors argue such locally sustained scanners can widen Alzheimer's and brain research access.
pmc-11713243:
Paul Aisen argues for a fresh role for BACE inhibitor drugs in Alzheimer's trials, in this 2025 paper. These drugs slow the making of amyloid, the protein that builds up in the brain. New antibody drugs can clear amyloid, but keeping levels low afterward may need a different tool.

Aisen notes that clearing amyloid early seems to help most, and treatment before plaques form may help even more. He reviews past trials of both drug types plus new blood markers that track the disease. His case is that a tuned dose of a BACE drug, alone or joined with antibody treatment, deserves testing in the next round of trials.
pmc-11713343:
Howard Feldman and co-authors compare in a 2025 paper who got into four large Alzheimer's drug trials. Two trials test a diabetes drug as a brain therapy, and two past trials tested plaque clearing antibodies. If their entry rules differ, their results may not line up head to head.

Entry rules and entry traits are set side by side for all four trial groups. The four trials randomized 7,337 people in all across their arms. Age bands split from 50 to 90 at the widest to 60 to 85 at the tightest. The diabetes drug trials held the most non White participants, at 741 people. Hispanic share in the US also led in those trials, at 23.6%.
pmc-11713443:
Hill and co-authors model how people recall object locations, in this 2025 paper. Memory for past events fades with healthy aging and is often an early sign of Alzheimer's disease. Standard tests score recall as all or nothing, which can miss small changes in how exact a memory is.

Thirty-five healthy older adults and nine with mild impairment did five rounds of a place-recall task. They studied objects set around a hidden circle, then pointed to where each one had been. A math model split their errors into distinct parts, such as true recall and guessing. Some players also did the task during brain scans, tying the model to brain activity.
pmc-11713543:
