Corvalan and co-authors share first results from a Latin American lifestyle trial cohort, in this 2025 paper. The trial, LatAm-FINGERS, is the first of its kind in the region. It offers a chance to study dementia risk in a mixed group with many heart risk factors.

The team scored twelve hundred people with a risk index built from twelve changeable factors, such as exercise, diet, and blood pressure. Scores ranged widely, and men scored higher risk than women on average. Thinking was tested with a regional test battery. The authors then link risk scores to test results, with country taken into account, to guide the trial's next steps.
pmc-11713643:
Boxin Sun and co-authors map how signals flow between brain regions in people with mild memory trouble. Their 2025 study scans 44 older adults, 19 healthy and 25 with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, as they learn 90 object-location pairs. Memory was tested again after a one-hour delay.

A causal mapping method measured the strength and direction of flow between every pair of regions. The memory-impaired group showed weaker flow along some paths but stronger flow along others. The authors read that pattern as detours: when direct routes fade, the brain reroutes information through spare paths. Such compensation may help explain how people keep functioning early in the disease, even as the usual wiring thins.
pmc-11713743:
Ziwei Zhang, Micaela Chan, Ezra Winter-Nelson, and Gagan Wig ask why some people stay sharp despite Alzheimer's damage in a 2025 paper. Scans can show plaques and shrinkage in people whose thinking still works well. The team tests whether the way brain networks are organized explains the gap. They focus on how separate or mixed the brain's systems look at rest.

Patients came from a national Alzheimer's imaging project. The team measured plaque load, brain shrinkage, and network layout for each person. People whose networks stayed well sorted kept better thinking scores at the same level of damage. Network layout, the study argues, belongs in models of the disease next to plaques and shrinkage.
pmc-11713843:
Sarah Therrien, Oceanna Yueran Li, and Feng Vankee Lin study money skills in older adults in this 2025 paper. Financial capacity, the ability to grasp and complete money tasks, supports independent living, but past studies often drew on narrow samples. The team asked whether this capacity differs by racial and ethnic group, and whether health factors play unlike roles in each group.

They used data from nine hundred adults with normal thinking, mild problems, or dementia. Black and African-American adults scored lower on money skills than non-Hispanic white adults, while the Hispanic and Latino group did not differ clearly. Memory and thinking scores helped explain part of the gap. Mood and behavior symptoms, though, weighed less heavily on money skills in the Black group than in the white group.
pmc-11714043:
Naresh Damuka and co-authors report a first test in people of a new brain scan tracer in a 2025 conference paper. The tracer targets microtubules, the tiny tubes that help hold brain cells in shape. The team wanted to know if damage to these tubes shows up early in Alzheimer's disease, before the well known amyloid and tau clumps build up.

The team scanned five adults with weak thinking skills and five healthy adults of like age with the new tracer. Uptake was higher in the weak group in the front of the brain and in deep areas tied to memory. The scan values also tracked with blood and spinal fluid signs of the disease. Tests on donated brain tissue backed up the scan results, and the team calls the method safe and worth wider study.
pmc-11714143:
Losing the ability to identify smells is one of the earliest signs of Alzheimer's disease, but what drives the loss is unsettled: memory failure, brain shrinkage, or both. Benoît Jobin and co-authors report early results from a Quebec cohort of older adults at risk. They compared 16 people with subjective cognitive decline and 17 with mild cognitive impairment on smell identification, memory tests, and brain scans.

The two groups scored the same on smell identification. Within the impairment group, better smell scores tracked better immediate memory recall, a link absent in the subjective group. Smell scores also tracked the volume of two brain areas, the middle cingulate cortex and the caudate, in the scanned subgroup. The authors caution that the sample is small and the findings preliminary, but they point to memory systems and specific structures as partners in early olfactory decline.
pmc-11714443:
A gene variant that raises Alzheimer's risk does not act the same in every group of people. Jose Javier Sanchez and co-authors studied that variant in Cuban Americans in this 2025 paper. The group mixes European, African, and Native American roots, and it has been left out of most gene studies. Past small studies of this gene in Cuban Americans gave conflicting answers.

The variant in focus is one form of the APOE gene, known as epsilon 4. The team used full genome reads and chip data from 141 people. The set held 40 people with Alzheimer's, 50 with mild memory loss, and 51 with normal thinking. They checked the APOE form and other genes that might cause the disease. The results, per the title, confirm that the variant raises risk in this group too.
pmc-11714543:
Ya-nan Ou, Lan Tan, and Jin-Tai Yu link facts from early life to the risk of dementia decades later, in a 2025 conference paper. Most work on prevention looks at midlife and old age. The team argues that the first years of life may hold missed chances to cut risk.

They used a British health bank with 247,841 adults and eight early life facts, from a mother's smoking near birth to height at age ten and harm in childhood. Over about nine years, 3,661 people developed dementia. A mother's smoking and short height at ten each raised the risk. Birth weight showed a safer mid range for one dementia type. Neglect in childhood more than doubled the risk across types.
pmc-11714643:
Kiana Angela Macharia and co-authors, working with the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network, test whether brain connectivity can estimate brain age in families fated to develop Alzheimer's. Some families carry mutations that make the disease nearly certain, so its course can be studied apart from normal aging. Brain-age models guess a person's age from scans; a brain that looks older than its years signals trouble. Their 2025 study builds the estimate from functional connectivity, the pattern of regions rising and falling together, rather than from structure alone.

An earlier structural study already found raised brain age in this population. A connectivity version could catch change sooner or track it differently. The authors aim at a marker that moves before symptoms, when trials need it most. Their inherited-disease cohort offers a clean clock for testing.
pmc-11714843:
Shenda Orrego and co-authors review a 2025 set of clinic cases from a hospital in Madrid, Spain. Their topic is what two kinds of brain scan add to care for memory and conduct complaints. One scan checks for amyloid, a protein linked to Alzheimer's disease. The other shows how the brain uses sugar. The team looked back at fifty-one patients seen over close to five years.

About two in five amyloid scans came back positive for the protein. Among patients with a negative scan, only about one in four got a firm diagnosis from other means. The sugar scan showed weak use in close to three in four patients, yet many of those patterns were not clear. Mood problems were common and did not predict scan results. The review shows that even strong scans often leave hard cases open.
pmc-11714943:
Augusto Mendes and co-authors test blood marks for early Alzheimer disease in people without dementia. Their paper from 2025 draws on a Geneva memory clinic group. Blood tests could ease world screening, since brain scans are costly and scarce.

A total of one hundred people took part, thirty three with clear minds and sixty seven with mild decline. Blood marks covered three forms of one protein, plus marks of nerve swelling and nerve harm. Brain scans marked who held amyloid and tau, the two disease proteins. One blood mark, p-tau217, stood out as the best single judge of disease state among the set, matching the level once held by scan based proof.
pmc-11715043:
Amalia Jo Peterson and co-authors study white matter change with aging in a 2025 paper across several long-term cohorts. White matter carries signals between brain areas, and its fine structure weakens in Alzheimer disease. The team asked whether that change over time differs by sex, by racial or ethnic group, and by carrying a gene variant tied to Alzheimer risk.

Data covered 2,619 participants aged fifty and older, with 6,837 imaging sessions in all. Diffusion scans were cleaned, corrected for free water, and harmonized across cohorts before modeling. The team tracked 48 white matter tracts and adjusted for age, education, thinking status, and other factors. The study gives a broad base for comparing how brain wiring ages across groups.
pmc-11715243:
Jesús Silva-Rodríguez and co-authors sort memory patients whose scans say their trouble is not Alzheimer's tau. A fifth to a third of people diagnosed with Alzheimer's dementia lack its pathology, and an age-related condition called LATE is a leading stand-in. LATE leaves a telltale pattern of low metabolism on FDG-PET scans, which the team hunted in study data.

They screened 360 impaired volunteers who had both tau and FDG scans, and 185 read as tau-negative. Among those with any low-metabolism patch, about four in ten matched the LATE pattern drawn from autopsy-proven cases. The rest fell into three further clusters with their own shapes. Age, hippocampus size, and thinking scores separated the groups, aiding diagnosis.
pmc-11715343:
Qu Tian and co-authors tied the count of cell power-plant gene copies in blood to one kind of thought skill. Power plants, called mitochondria, hold their own small ring of genes. The count of those rings in blood has been tied to dementia risk in past work. Which thought skills it tracks, and whether frailty bends the link, stayed unclear.

The team read gene data from the UK Biobank, a huge health bank. Thought tests came about nine years after the blood was drawn, in more than thirteen thousand adults. More gene copies went with a higher score on a fast symbol-swap test of speed. The count showed no clear link to the other tests of mind skills. The team also split the group by frailty and by load of gene flaws to test if those states shift the link.
pmc-11715643:
Alina Liaskovik and co-authors test a scan score for the glymphatic system, the brain's waste clearance system, in patients with neurodegenerative diseases. The system was found only recently, and weak flow is blamed in part for each disease studied. The DTI-ALPS score reads water motion along the spaces around blood vessels. The groups held patients with Alzheimer's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson's disease, and normal pressure hydrocephalus, plus healthy controls.

The full set held 116 adults, each scanned on the same class of machine. Scores ran far lower on both sides of the brain in three patient groups than in healthy peers. The Parkinson's group was the exception, with no clear gap. Higher scores went with higher scores on a standard cognitive test across all patients. The team ties weak glymphatic flow to Alzheimer's, the Lewy body form, and the fluid disease, but not to Parkinson's.
pmc-11715743:
Zhibo Wang, Yuhan Chen, and Jianping Jia searched spinal fluid proteins for markers that stage Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. Brain scans stage the disease well but are costly and scarce. Fluid tests exist, yet they track late stages poorly.

The team studied 115 people with both spinal fluid protein reads, covering some six thousand proteins, and two kinds of brain scan. Protein sets tied to the plaque stage and to the tangle stage surfaced, mostly around sugar use and nerve support. Machine learning then picked a seventeen-protein panel that split the scan stages cleanly. Small subsets of two to thirteen proteins already separated key stages with high accuracy. The panel beat the standard fluid markers the team compared against.
pmc-11715843:
Sokratis Charisis and a large team model cerebral small vessel disease using regional MRI markers, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Small vessel disease damages the brain's tiny blood vessels and contributes to cognitive decline. The authors ask whether the location of its MRI markers changes what those markers mean.

Working with 891 participants from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, they segmented enlarged perivascular spaces, white matter hyperintensities, and microbleeds. Deep learning algorithms did the segmentation automatically. They also measured white matter microstructure from diffusion imaging. The team then tested links between marker patterns and cognition. They further examined whether these markers carry the effects of age and cardiovascular risk.
pmc-11715943:
Yanan Zhang and three co-authors trace how the link between exercise and dementia changes as people age, in a 2025 study from the Health and Retirement Study. Many past studies tie activity to lower dementia risk, but most take a single snapshot in time. This team followed the same adults from their mid fifties onward for more than two decades.

The study included 7,001 adults first surveyed in 1996, and 736 developed dementia during follow up. Being active in midlife came with a lower risk of dementia later on. That protective link grew weaker as participants aged, rather than staying fixed. The authors checked the pattern under a second definition of active and found it held. Staying active early in later life may matter most.
pmc-11716143:
Sunu Mathew and co-authors test whether blood vessels in the retina mirror Alzheimer's disease changes in the brain. The eye is the one place vessels and nerves can be photographed directly, and a cheap eye marker for brain amyloid and tau would transform screening. Their tool is a scan that maps retinal blood flow without dye.

Twenty-five older adults across the Alzheimer's spectrum, from normal cognition to impairment, had retinal vessel measures compared with brain scans and tissue markers. The small sample came from an Indiana memory study. Even a modest correlation would justify larger trials. The retina may offer a window where the skull blocks the view.
pmc-11716643:
Dylan Guan and four co-authors studied later-life effects of mild brain injury in older adults, in a 2025 paper. Brain injury is a risk factor for dementia. Their sample held just over twelve hundred community-dwelling older people with no dementia or mild impairment. A screening survey identified suspected mild injury earlier in life.

People with such injury history reported worse everyday thinking and behavior changes. Scores on both survey scales ran higher in that group. Behavior change fully explained the link between injury and daily function in their model. Thinking decline explained just under half of it. The authors suggest early dementia risk checks for older people with injury history. Help for declining thinking and behavior may ease function loss in this group, they argue. The study relied on self-reported injury, a limit they note in design.
pmc-11716743:
Avnish Bhattrai and four co-authors published a mouse study in 2025 on how the human APOE gene shapes the aging brain. Most mouse models copy rare inherited forms of Alzheimer's disease, which affect few patients. This model instead carries human versions of the main risk gene for the common late-onset form.

Forty-three aged mice with different gene pairings had high-detail scans after death. Mice without the risky form kept larger smell and side-brain regions and healthier white matter wiring. Female mice had larger cortex areas in some regions regardless of gene form. The work gives labs a baseline for testing treatments in a model closer to typical patients.
pmc-11716843:
Margherita Squillario, Francesco Reggiani, Matteo Pardini, and Michele Piana set out a 2025 plan for joining many data types to study Alzheimer's disease. Gene roots play a large part in the illness, yet genes alone do not start the slow brain loss. Public sets now hold scans, gene data, fluid proteins, and thinking tests side by side.

The plan first merges a clean multi-type dataset from public sources. It then builds a friendly tool that runs deep and multi-kernel methods on the joined data. Last, it tests known gene panels for how well they predict shrinkage in the hardest-hit brain zones.
pmc-11716943:
Sithara Dissanayaka, Stephanie Rainey-Smith, Ralph Martins and W. Fernando wrote a 2025 view piece on gut microbes and Alzheimer's disease. Gut and brain are linked, so microbes in the gut may shape how the disease grows. Food may also play a part through the gut. The authors set out a study plan and sum up past work.

Past studies found that stool from people with the disease holds fewer kinds of microbes. Some gut shifts tracked with markers of disease in spinal fluid and blood. But results across studies clash often. The authors argue for tests of stool microbes early, before clear symptoms, to aid early checks.
pmc-11717443:
José Araújo, Nuno Pais, and António Andrade report a surprise found during ankle surgery: their patient had the plantaris tendon twice. The plantaris is a small, variable tendon near the Achilles; some people lack it entirely. The thirty-eight-year-old man was being operated on for a ruptured Achilles tendon when the second plantaris tendon turned up.

A doubled plantaris had been described once before, in a cadaver study, where the spare tendon attached to fascia above the heel rather than to the heel bone itself. Whether such variants help cause Achilles trouble, or merely complicate its repair, is unsettled. The authors do not claim their patient's variant caused his rupture. They publish the case so other surgeons keep the possibility in mind when the anatomy in front of them does not match the textbook.
pmc-11724743:
A Samee and co-authors report a rare repeat case of gallstone bowel blockage in 2024. A gallstone can slip from the gall bladder into the gut through an abnormal channel and lodge in the bowel. The patient was a man aged 89 years whose scan showed a stone stuck in the mid small bowel.

Surgeons opened the abdomen and removed the stone, feeling no other stones nearby. Five days later, the blockage returned, and a new scan confirmed a second stone event. A second operation cleared it. The authors weigh care options, from simple stone removal to fuller repair of the abnormal channel, and note the high risk in older patients.
pmc-11725043:
Turki Alanzi and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, whether a two-week break from digital devices eases anxiety and depression in young adults. Device use has soared, and worries about its mental toll have grown with it. The team ran surveys before and after the break on 467 adults aged 18 to 30, with a near even split by sex.

After the break, anxiety and depression scores fell by clear margins in every demographic group. Men's anxiety scores fell by about half, and women's fell by a similar share. Depression slid from moderate to mild bands for staff, job seekers, and students alike. Near half of the group found daily tasks somewhat hard while symptomatic. The authors back scheduled device breaks in schools and workplaces as a low-cost mental health tool.
pmc-11726543:
Christopher S. Semancik and others put out a 2024 review of hidden exposure to Ebola-like viruses. These filoviruses cause deadly hemorrhagic fever outbreaks. Many cases may pass with no name put on them. Blood antibody surveys reveal past contact. The team looked at studies across sub-Saharan Africa.

Eighty-five studies met their bar. Most checked Ebola group markers. A smaller set covered Marburg group viruses. Large antibody rates showed in some groups. Such silent contact changes outbreak planning. Vaccine trials need real background numbers. Rollout plans also depend on who is already immune. The review gathers scattered survey evidence into one map.
pmc-11726743:
Hiba Wanis and co-authors profiled brain tumors across a diverse region in two thousand twenty-four. The tumors, called gliomas, vary in gene traits that guide care. Two traits matter most: a gene change and a gene silencing mark. The study covered adults treated in southeast London and Kent. That area holds about three million people of many backgrounds.

Hospital records covered more than seven hundred patients. Cases spanned five years of diagnoses. The team linked gene traits to age, sex, and ethnic background. Tumor type, site, and surgery extent were also factored in. Rates of each trait were compared across groups. Such profiles help labs plan testing for all patients fairly. They also reveal whether access to new targeted drugs is even.
pmc-11727043:
Behjat Mudassir and co-authors report genetic findings in four unrelated Pakistani families in a 2024 paper. Each family had a child with a neurodevelopmental disorder that standard clinical checks could not explain. Such disorders arise when brain development is disrupted, and their genetic causes are highly varied.

Whole exome sequencing pointed to four different genes across the four children, named HGSNAT, KDM6B, LMNA, and WFS1. The children showed a mix of facial, eye, hearing, speech, and skeletal features. The cases show how broad genetic testing can end a long search for a diagnosis in such families.
pmc-11727343:
Aristides Machado-Rodrigues and nine co-authors examine links among low birth weight, metabolic risk, fitness, and activity in adolescents. Whether low birth weight clusters with metabolic risk factors in youth stays ambiguous in past work. The cross sectional sample covers 491 adolescents aged 14 to 17 years, with body measures, a running fitness test, and a three day activity diary.

A metabolic risk score combines standardized values for lipids, blood pressure, insulin, and glucose. Boys show higher activity and fitness scores, while girls show higher levels of one lipid and insulin. Body mass index predicts clustered metabolic risk in both sexes. More active girls show notably lower metabolic risk. The authors stress weight control and activity promotion in teen health.
pmc-11727543:
Shaheenur Islam Sumon and co-authors stack several machine learning models to tell small cell lung cancer from its non-small cell cousin using blood chemistry profiles, in a study from 2024. Small cell cancer spreads fast and kills quickly, yet diagnosis still leans on invasive tests. The team profiled metabolites from 191 small cell patients, 173 non-small cell patients, and 97 healthy controls.

A stacked ensemble, where one model learns from the others' outputs, sorted all three groups with 85 percent accuracy. Head-to-head between the two cancers, a tree ensemble reached 88 percent. An explanation method flagged benzoic acid, lactate, and the amino acid arginine as the strongest signals. The authors pitch the blood test as a gentler path to early subtyping.
pmc-11727643:
Christian Niederau and co-authors tested xanthohumol, a plant compound from hops, on the ligament stem cells that sit between tooth and bone. During orthodontic treatment, pressure on these cells triggers a controlled inflammation that lets teeth move. The team compressed the cells in a dish to mimic that pressure and measured inflammatory markers with and without the compound.

Dose mattered sharply. Low doses left the cells healthy or helped them, while a high dose cut viability within a day. Pressure alone raised inflammatory signals, including the messenger IL-6. The compound pulled those signals back down and returned two key internal switches to their resting levels. The authors call the effect selective and modest, a starting point for research into gentler orthodontic care and treatment of gum inflammation.
pmc-11727843:
The authors review a class of diabetes drugs, the DPP-4 inhibitors, and their safety for patients who also have heart failure. The drugs lower blood sugar well and are usually well tolerated, but trials disagree about the heart. One large trial found more heart-failure hospital stays with one drug of the class, while other trials found neutral effects. The review walks through how the drugs work, how they might touch inflammation, oxidative stress, and scarring in the heart muscle, and what the major trials showed.

Differences between patients, such as heart failure type and other illnesses, may explain part of the conflict. The review also compares rival drug classes that protect the heart more clearly. The authors conclude the drugs remain a valid option for diabetes, but care is needed in advanced heart failure. They call for research that sorts out which patients each drug in the class suits.
pmc-11728043:
Inês Caetano Santos and co-authors compare two ways of teaching older adults to care for their teeth and gums, in a 2024 trial. Barriers such as poor information, low hand strength, and weak vision can hold back oral health at older ages. Fifty-four adults aged sixty-five and up were split at random: one group got general instruction, the other a technique fitted to each person. Checks ran again after two months.

Both methods boosted use of between-teeth cleaning tools and improved hygiene scores. Self-rated oral health barely moved in either group. The fitted method won on the calculus part of the index. The authors say teaching helps, with personal fitting adding a clinical edge.
pmc-11728143:
Krzysztof Śledziewski, Marcin Górecki, Jakub Gajewski, and Michał Rogala published a structural engineering study in twenty twenty-four on steel girders whose webs ripple like a sine wave. Corrugated webs are gaining on flat ones for resisting shear. This second part of their research varied the wave's geometry in validated computer models.

Longer wavelengths cut the girder's ultimate shear capacity and changed how it failed. Wave height mattered little for peak strength but raised post-failure load and spread the yielded zones. Thicker webs helped a great deal; taller webs barely mattered. The simulations also showed current Eurocode formulas estimate shear buckling very cautiously. The results help designers tune corrugation geometry with confidence.
pmc-11728243:
Adriana Vella and Noel Vella read the genes of loggerhead turtles found in Maltese waters, at the crossroads of the Mediterranean. Knowing where foraging turtles were born guides protection across the whole basin. The team sampled sixty-three turtles from strandings and in-water work, plus Malta's two nests of 2023.

Mitochondrial DNA revealed ten lineages. Most turtles traced to Mediterranean nesting beaches, above all Libya's, with others from Lebanon, Israel, and Turkey. A few carried Atlantic lineages, one linking Malta's feeding grounds to Cape Verde rookeries. Nest samples matched the local picture. Genetics here acts as a passport office for a migratory species.
pmc-11728343:
Pauwels and co-authors compare dizzy elders with healthy peers in a 2024 study. The condition is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, crystals loose in the inner ear that spin the world on head moves. It appears in nearly half of older adults who complain of dizziness. Thirty seven patients, average age about 73, faced 22 matched controls.

Motion sensors and questionnaires measured daily activity. Frailty followed a standard modified scale, and mood, falls fear, and dizziness handicap were scored too. Activity and frailty both proved worse in the vertigo group. A treatable ear fault may quietly shrink an older person's world, and the numbers here show by how much.
pmc-11728543:
Giuliano Sico and his three co-authors, publishing in 2024, test a cheap way to reshape printed zinc oxide films after they are made. The films are printed like ink onto flexible supports that cannot take heat, so the team exposes the printed layer of tiny particles to acid vapor at low temperatures instead. Left in the vapor, the particles rearrange to lower their surface energy, and the team tracks how the film's structure and light behavior change.

Depending on the vapor mix and warmth, the films come out dense or porous, as particles dissolve and regrow, slide past each other, or fuse. The treatment also improves how the particles connect, making the films stronger and more stable. The authors present the method as a low-cost, pressure-free route to films ready for flexible devices, with uses checked by X-ray and light measurements.
pmc-11728643:
Svetlana Nalimova leads a nine-author team building air-pollution sniffers from zinc stannate nanoparticles, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Volatile organic compounds take in explosive and toxic gases. Sensors for them are on hand, but most run hot, and that heat degrades their stability over time.

Zinc stannate particles were precipitated and annealed at unlike temperatures, which changed the phase composition of the stock. Decorating them with silver nanoparticles was put forth to sharpen how they sense. Diffraction analysis tracked what each annealing temperature gave rise to. The goal is keen detection at lower heat than old tools need. Cheap, durable gas sensors count for a lot in factories, mines, and homes, and both crystal phase and surface decoration play their part.
pmc-11728843:
Zhentao Yao and co-authors demonstrate a tiny optical switch carved in silica that reroutes light modes with a whisper of heat. Mode switches are traffic police for photonic chips that multiplex data across light's spatial modes. Their design cascades an interference coupler with small-radius bimodal S-bends, selecting which of two modes exits.

Fabricated with standard chip processes and tuned by simulation, the device was characterized across the telecom C-band. It switched cleanly at under three hundred milliwatts of drive power, with strong extinction and low crosstalk for both input modes. Glass waveguides are the quiet workhorses of photonics; a compact, low-power mode switch strengthens the case for all-optical routing.
pmc-11731443:
Reza Zadehparizi and Amir Sam Kianimoghadam compare thought habits in medical students with and without a past of self-harm in a 2024 study. The harm in view is self-injury with no wish to die, a pattern that runs high among medical students.

The team surveyed four hundred five students in Tehran, of whom sixty-eight told of past self-injury. A web-style map of nine thought habits showed the self-harm group felt weaker at two skills: putting things in a wider view and seeing the good in a hard event. Links between habits also ran the other way in this group, as when a calm focus tied to more dread of the worst. The authors say the gaps can guide help that cuts such acts.
pmc-11734143: Maria Belen Solis Chavez and four co-authors report a heart tumor case from 2024 in a 75-year-old patient. The patient had both mitral and aortic valves replaced seven years earlier and came in with worsening breathlessness. An ultrasound through the food pipe showed a mass resembling a clot on the artificial mitral valve. Imaging, surgery, nuclear scans, and tissue tests pointed instead to a cardiac angiosarcoma, a rare cancer of the heart. The case shows how a clot look-alike can hide a far rarer cause.
pmc-11734943:
Seven authors report a rare case in two thousand twenty-four of shingles in the ear that spread across many nerves. A woman of seventy-four came to a hospital in Patras, Greece, with ten days of ear pain and discharge. She also had weakness of the face on the same side and a blistering rash in the ear canal, the marks of Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

A scan showed inflammation of the facial and hearing nerves, and a lab test confirmed the chickenpox virus. pmc-11736343:
Jiangjiang Zheng and co-authors studied lymphoid structures inside colorectal tumors in a 2024 paper. Tertiary lymphoid structures are immune cell clusters that form near tumors. Their maturity may shape how patients fare. The team asked whether mature clusters link to better outcomes.

They gathered 230 tumor samples with follow-up data from a Yinzhou hospital. Staining split patients into mature and immature cluster groups. Traits like tumor size, spread to nodes, and key gene markers were compared. Survival curves and risk models tested the link. Mature clusters were the larger group by far. If the link holds, cluster maturity could join routine prognosis checks.
pmc-11743443:
Mohammadreza Edraki and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, extra arteries that grow in children with a heart defect called tetralogy of Fallot. In that defect, blood flow to the lungs is too low. The body may grow major collateral arteries from the aorta to the lungs to compensate. Those vessels can interfere with surgical repair. Patients were split into three groups: no collaterals, collaterals closed before surgery, and small collaterals left open. The groups were compared on surgery data, blood transfusion, breathing tube time, intensive care stay, and death rates.
pmc-11757143:
Ayaka Sato and co-authors engineered a soluble protein that switches on a T cell growth signal, in a study published in 2024. The signal comes from OX40, a receptor that appears on active T cells and boosts their growth and survival. Its natural partner sits fixed on cell surfaces, which makes it hard to copy as a drug. Their proteins bound the receptor, fired its internal pathway, and made T cells release signaling molecules in dishes. In mice, one design strongly expanded the T cells matched to a test antigen. Sister designs carrying partners for three other receptors worked in the same way. The authors say tuned clustering may yield stronger immune therapy agents.
pmc-11769943:
Li He and co-authors report a heart study, published in 2025, on simple blood ratios that may flag future danger in older patients with coronary heart disease. One ratio, monocytes over HDL, independently predicted both having the disease and suffering a major cardiovascular event during follow up. It also tracked the severity score of vessel narrowing and beat its two sibling ratios at telling groups apart. The authors propose watching changes in this ratio to catch rising risk early.
pmc-11772343:
Marina Carbone and colleagues pit a wearable augmented-reality guide against the standard brain navigation system, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Brain surgeons use navigation to aim at deep targets. The standard system shows the map on a side screen, forcing the surgeon to look away from the patient. In nine volunteers who had had brain tumor surgery, the headset again won on brow and forehead points, and trended better on the nose point. pmc-11782043:
Fengjuan Lin and co-authors review research on tiny parcels released by immune cells called macrophages, in a paper published in 2024. These parcels, known as extracellular vesicles, carry RNA and proteins from one cell to another. The review covers their role in long-term diseases that are not spread by infection.

The authors gather work on heart and blood vessel disease, metabolic disease, cancer, inflammation, and bone disease. They explain how the parcels change the behavior of the cells that receive them. They also weigh the promise of the parcels as markers of disease, as treatments in their own right, and as a way to carry drugs to target cells.
pmc-11782143:
Wang and co-authors map gut microbes along the donkey digestive tract, in this 2024 paper. Donkeys are single-stomach herbivores whose gut communities support digestion and health. How microbes settle in each gut section of adult donkeys had been little studied.

Samples came from five gut sections and feces of healthy Dezhou males. Gene sequencing catalogued the communities, and software predicted what the microbes do. Diversity was rich everywhere, with each section holding thousands of unique microbial types plus a small shared core. Community makeup differed sharply by section, while overall diversity did not. The map helps explain donkey digestion and feed design.
pmc-11782243:
Jian-Quan Yang and co-authors ask when living with a healthy cage mate can ease autism-like behavior in mice, in this study published in 2024. Their mice were exposed before birth to a drug that models autism, and they grew up with weak sociability, anxiety, and repeated actions. Early social experience is a hopeful, drug-free lever.

The authors read the result as a critical window in which social environment can reset development, a hint for timing help in children.
pmc-11788143:
Lilya Dzhemileva and co-authors wrote a review of a young onset form of diabetes driven by single genes. The head of the text dates the work to 2024. This form, called MODY, passes down in families and starts in teens or young adults. It makes up a small share of diabetes and is often misread as type one or type two.

The most common forms stem from faults in three genes, and rarer forms have grown clear with new gene reading tools. One gene's faults give mild, stable high sugar that needs no drug care. Faults in the other two harm the sugar sensing cells and take standard drugs well. Gene therapy stays a lab idea for now.
pmc-11790443:
Iryna Kril and co-authors probed gene trims in 2024 for ties to rheumatoid arthritis in Ukraine. The disease is a long immune attack on joints. Some variants of each gene tied to who gets the disease. Others tied to how fierce it runs and to which antibody marks a patient holds. Patients let out more of the one enzyme than controls did. pmc-11798943:
Xiaoyin Wu and co-authors hunt gene signs that can flag diabetic kidney disease early. Their paper, listed as twenty twenty-five, centers on glycolysis, the cell sugar-burning path. Faulty glycolysis may drive the kidney damage that diabetes brings.

A learning framework fused many methods into one score, called GScore. Charts checked how well the score sorts cases from controls. Single-cell data then showed which kidney cells carry the signature. A blood or biopsy test on this base could speed personal care.
pmc-11799243:
Joanna Lane and a large team of co-authors set out a 2024 protocol for a European project on paying for better health. The protocol lays out eight work packages, from shaping the finance models to testing them in four test sites. Those sites sit in Sweden, Germany, Spain, and Wales. pmc-11802343:
Xueying Zhang, Feiyan Liu, and Yu Zhou review how two steps in RNA processing affect each other. Their 2024 review covers splicing, which cuts and rejoins RNA pieces, and polyadenylation, which adds a tail that ends the RNA. Both steps shape which proteins a cell can make.

pmc-11813943:
Di Cong and co-authors study a flower gene in sea buckthorn in 2024. The catalog year says 2025, but the head shows 2024. A gene family called MADS-box steers flower organ growth, and one member, a SEPALLATA-like gene, was cloned from this shrub.

The authors frame the work as groundwork for deeper study of this gene family in the shrub.
pmc-11821643:

The authors hope the map of changes will point to new ways to spot and treat flu in children early.
pmc-11830743:
Jui-Kai Wang and co-authors teach a model to map optic nerve damage in a study published in 2024. It also sorted the three diseases well, and the booster codes sharpened the sorting further.
pmc-11862843:

Noise, signal, and contrast measures were logged in lung, aorta, and back muscle, and readers graded the images on a five-point scale. Noise fell as the iterative share rose, with the strongest settings cutting it most in each tissue. The paper weighs how far the new method can be pushed before images suffer.
pmc-11863743:
Tianze Li and co-authors use gene data to test links between dementia and liver cancer in a 2024 study. Surveys have hinted that brain diseases and cancer may pull in opposite ways, but the liver case was little studied.

They ran the gene-based test in both directions, using large public gene studies. Gene signs of dementia tied to a lower risk of two liver cancer types. Alzheimer's disease alone also tied to lower risk across three forms. In reverse, one liver cancer type tied to slightly higher dementia risk. The authors stress that gene-based links are not proof of direct cause, but they mark a pattern worth probing.
pmc-11877143:

The review covers what the loops do inside cells, both as regulators and, for a small share, as templates for making proteins. It then turns to lab methods for building the loops from scratch. pmc-11881643:
Canada's health libraries are shrinking, and their national association is fighting back in public. A petition backed the library, and a second followed when a British Columbia medical library faced closure after a century. pmc-11888643:
Annette M Bhambal and five co-authors survey the mouth symptoms that linger after Covid. pmc-11888743: Sriram Chandra Mallick and co-authors compare two scan types for bone density in women after menopause in a 2024 paper. One scan is cone-beam CT of the jaw, common in dental care. Jaw scan measures alone did not replace the standard test in their data.
pmc-11931343:
Chiran Bhakta Bista and co-authors count haemorrhoid cases among surgery patients at a military hospital in Nepal. Their 2024 study reviews months of visits to one surgery department. About one in seven patients in the sample has haemorrhoids. Inner cases form the largest share, and the mildest grade is the most common grade. Bleeding is the top symptom, with pain and itching close behind. The rate runs higher than in like studies from the region and closer to rates seen elsewhere. pmc-11935543:
Jeonggyu Kang and four co-authors follow a very large Korean cohort in a 2024 study. Higher stiffness also tracked the development of insulin resistance. The authors stress that risk rises even within the range usually called normal.
pmc-11970143:

pmc-12056443:
Lucy Grace Luna Munoz and her team find risk traits for a stay in a sick bay for asthma in kids at a sick bay in Trujillo. Their 2024 study looks back at past files in a case-and-check way. It sifts files of kids aged five to fourteen from twenty fifteen to twenty nineteen.

One hundred twenty-nine kids in the sick bay for asthma were set next to the same count in the bay for the rest of the causes. A math check found birth by knife cut, feed not just by breast, fat build, and mum age firm in the joined model. A past bout of bronchiolitis helped the full guess but was not firm when all traits acted as one. As one, the trait set guessed most asthma cases in their check. The study shows which early-life and clan traits care staff might watch.
pmc-12269743:

Shared themes stress mixed-expert teams, patient co-design, clear methods that others can repeat, and guards against common biases in food trials. The panel also urges trials in less studied conditions. The aim is more rigorous, more useful trials in this young field.
pmc-12285343:

pmc-12490443:

A microscope count that sorts patients by likely course could help teams choose how hard to push after surgery, in a cancer where every edge counts.
pmc-12661843:
Zhishuai Jin and co-authors study what music feels like when pitch will not resolve. Their 2025 paper examines congenital amusia, a lifelong failure of fine pitch discrimination, through the lens of musical reward, the pleasure system that sound learning normally engages.

Forty-four amusic adults and matched controls rated their musical enjoyment and their feelings toward major- and minor-key excerpts. The amusia group scored lower on every reward scale, from social bonding to mood repair. For major-key music both groups felt much the same. For minor-key music the amusic listeners heard it as less tragic and oddly brighter, and their reward scores linked to emotions in the opposite direction from controls. The authors blame altered use of pitch cues in judging musical feeling.
pmc-12663143:
Naifu Zhou, Mingding Chai, and Niankai Fu add a prized two-fluorine group to ring-shaped molecules using electricity and two metals, in a 2025 chemistry paper. The group, CF2H, shows up in many drugs and farm chemicals, yet clean ways to attach it are scarce. Their reagent is a simple salt that is the cheapest, most plentiful source of the group.

An iron and nickel pair, driven by electric current, moves the group onto a wide range of ring compounds, including ones with handy chemical handles left intact. The method scales up well and was used to build and tweak known bioactive molecules at a late stage. That late-stage power matters, since it lets chemists test fluorine variants of a drug without rebuilding it from scratch.
pmc-12663243:
Walden Bjørn-Yoshimoto and co-authors mine, in a 2025 study, cone snail venom for a new drug lead against persistent pain. Persistent pain affects one in five people worldwide, and current drugs fail many patients with moderate to severe pain. A receptor on peripheral pain nerves, called SSTR4, has emerged as a promising non-opioid target. Its close relatives look much alike, which makes a selective hit hard.

The team found a snail venom peptide that binds that receptor with potency and selectivity. It mimics the body's own hormone for the receptor but with a trimmed core that sharpens the selectivity. Injected into the body wall, the made peptide eased pain in mouse models of post-surgical and nerve pain. The team then tuned related forms for more potency and selectivity. They offer venom peptides as a fresh path to pain drugs.
pmc-12663443:
Xiao and co-authors build in 2025 a scoring model to pick the best path for an oil or gas well before drilling starts. A good path serves geology goals and keeps site work safe. Past picks weighed ease of drilling and target safety, but missed cost, drill string stress, hole cleaning, and cycle length.

The new model scores five signs, and adds a fresh score for path difficulty. Each sign is given a clear numeric form, so options can be ranked in a shared way. In a test field, one scheme scored best with the lowest path difficulty. The method gives fields a firmer base for path and wellhead layout choices.
pmc-12663543:
Lei Guan and co-authors examine the cell-cycle protein SKP2 as a warning sign and driver in glioma, in a 2025 study. The team compared SKP2 levels with patient features and survival in their datasets, mined the genes that differ between high and low SKP2 tumors, and built a prediction model. Lab tests then silenced the gene in two glioma cell lines.

High SKP2 tracked with worse tumor features and shorter survival, and the differing genes clustered around cell division. Silencing SKP2 froze the cells in the G1 phase, stalling the cycle. The authors propose SKP2 as both a prognostic marker and a possible drug target, while asking for prospective validation before clinical use.
pmc-12664243:
Merve Ece Erdem and co-authors reviewed a decade of jaw surgery cases in 2025. Orthognathic surgery fixes skeletal jaw and face deformities. The team read records of 1,095 patients treated from 2014 to 2024, aged sixteen to sixty-five years.

Class III deformity, where the lower jaw juts ahead, dominated at about seventy-one percent of cases. Class II made up about eighteen percent. A narrow upper jaw appeared in about nine percent and got a widening procedure. Asymmetry, open bite, and chin reshaping each marked smaller shares. Procedure mixes and treatment orders, like surgery-first plans, round out the census for planners.
pmc-12666043:
Five researchers in China survey pregnant women on thyroid knowledge in a 2025 paper. An underactive thyroid in pregnancy can harm both mother and child, and hormone pills are the standard fix. The survey ran at one university hospital in Sichuan in spring 2024.

More than four hundred valid surveys came back, from women with a mean age near thirty-one. Knowledge, attitude, and practice scores all sat in the fair to good range. Fewer than half knew that hormone pills are safe in pregnancy or that low thyroid can affect a newborn's intellect. Higher knowledge and warmer attitudes each predicted better practice, and the path from knowledge to practice ran partly through attitude.
pmc-12680943:
Siti-Munirah and colleagues describe a new fairy lantern plant, Thismia selangorensis, found in a tree hole on a riverbank in a forest park in Selangor, Malaysia. These plants feed on fungi rather than sunlight, and this one bears cap-shaped flowers. It looks much like relatives in one section of the genus, sharing root clusters like coral and inner petals joined into a cap with three points.

The new species still stands apart in its flower color and the shape of the cap. It differs too in the shape of the petal lobes that form the cap, and in a fine net-like pattern on the inside of the flower tube. Because it is known from so little ground, the authors judge it critically endangered for now, the most at-risk class on the standard red list.
pmc-12690943:
Jianhui Bai and co-authors review how oxidative stress and inflammation conspire to grow calcium oxalate kidney stones. Stones form when crystals seed and stick in the kidney. Reactive oxygen species are harsh by-products of normal breathing chemistry. In excess they wound cells, and wounds call inflammation. Their 2025 review traces where the reactive species come from in stone disease. It then maps how they spark and feed the inflammatory side.

The two forces loop: damage breeds inflammation, and inflammation breeds more damage. Crystal growth rides that loop. The team gathers the chain into one picture. Blocking a link could slow stone birth or regrowth. The review sets a base for such drug work.
pmc-12691143:
Taewoo Yi and a team of co-authors track mammal communities across South Korea over three national surveys, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. The surveys spanned twenty oh six to twenty twenty-three and used one standard method. The team compared sighting rates, dominance order, and diversity by phase.

Dominance reshuffled hard between the first two surveys, then settled. Water deer stayed on top throughout, while wild boar climbed steadily. The Korean hare and other specialists fell back. Forest recovery plus missing top predators favor adaptable generalists, the authors argue, even as balance thins.
pmc-12691443:
Charbel Nassif and co-authors report a 2025 study on breeding Sarda sheep without hormones. Farmers often use hormone drugs to bring ewes into heat at the same time, so lambs can be planned through artificial insemination. The team tested a natural method instead, using cryptorchid rams. These males cannot father lambs, since their testes never dropped, yet they still act like normal rams around ewes.

The ewes were kept away from rams for six weeks, then spent two weeks with the sterile males. In the first trial, most ewes came into heat and were bred, and about half lambed afterward. A second trial compared the method with ewes that had no male contact at all. Far more of the exposed ewes came into heat, and their lambing results matched what hormone programs had achieved for this breed.
pmc-12693543:
Wijaya and co-authors ask a practical question about genes that jump between bacteria. Does the way a genome is written down as numbers change how well a learning model can find those transfers? Such jumps spread drug resistance between species, so detection quality matters.

The team tested 44 genome encodings with five model types across four datasets. The winner paired short word counts of length seven, in a strand-aware form, with a support vector machine, scoring an F1 of 0.959. Models trained on mixed-species data also carried over better to new cases. Their tuned models can flag the island-like regions where foreign genes land.
pmc-12693943:
Adrianna Szalonka and co-authors present a 2025 study of energy drink use in Polish adults and the habits that cluster with it. Energy drinks are under scrutiny for heart and sleep effects. The team asked whether their use travels with smoking, poor diet, and burnout.

They mined a national web survey of 120,000 adults from 2024. About 16.9 percent had ever drunk energy drinks, while weekly use was rare at 2.8 percent. Adjusted models sorted the strongest links among many factors. The authors stress the design shows links, not causes. An age cut off for likely use was also drawn from the data.
pmc-12694343:
Roberto Benocci and five co-authors use wavelet based tools to read soundscape shifts in a river side woodland park near Milan, Italy. Passive sound recording aids ecology, but common sound indices link to wildlife counts in shaky ways. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Audio came from three sites at varied distance from a major highway. The team tracked sound energy by frequency band, peak gaps, and fractal time patterns. The far site held more high frequency energy and longer time memory, a sign of richer bird and insect sound. The near site showed flatter spectra and faster decay, shaped by traffic. Expert notes on birds and traffic backed the gauges.
pmc-12694543:
Xudong Zhang and co-authors build, in a 2025 study, a stretchable heart sound sensor cut in a kirigami pattern. Heart sounds carry information about valve activity and blood flow, but rigid sensors slip on the chest as it moves, which distorts the trace. Their sensor is a five-layer sandwich with a piezoelectric film at its heart. Periodic kirigami cuts let it stretch while it still converts sound into signal efficiently.

Simulations showed the stretch behavior is set most by hinge length and thickness. Bench tests showed a linear response to sound pressure across a wide span, with output rising as sound grew louder. Stretching to thirty percent shifted the output signal by only about a tenth. A week of wear testing showed the two main heart sounds in step with wired heart traces and a commercial sensor. The authors back it for long-wear monitoring and early heart screening.
pmc-12694943:
Javiera Martinez-Gutierrez and co-authors test a cancer-risk alert tool inside a simulated clinic before trusting it in real ones, in a 2025 study. Unexplained weight loss can be cancer's first whisper, yet busy family doctors must weigh it against a hundred innocent causes. Software that flags risky patients inside the medical record could help — but such tools often go unused.

The team embedded the decision support in practice software and watched clinicians use it in simulation, studying workarounds, dismissals, and friction. Observing failure safely, without patients attached, lets designers fix the tool's manners and logic first. Adoption, not accuracy alone, decides whether alerts ever save anyone.
pmc-12695143:
Ha Anh Nguyen and co-authors published this review in 2025. It surveys SERS, a laser sensing method, as a tool for precision farming. The method reads molecular fingerprints off surfaces that amplify the signal hugely. Standard lab tests for plant stress, residues, and germs are slow and centralized. SERS promises fast, sensitive checks right in the field, across leaves, soil, and water.

The review covers how the sensors are built, from hot-spot layouts to flexible patches, and what performance they reach. Reported uses span the whole crop cycle: stress markers, quality compounds, contaminants, and pathogens. Stubborn problems get a frank airing, including sensor repeatability and messy field samples. Fixes like ratio-based readouts and sturdier large-area sensors are weighed. The authors close with cost and durability needs for true field readiness.
pmc-12695943:
Lichen Cao and co-authors pin a mitochondrial protein, BNIP3, as a driver of breast cancer growth. The protein sat at abnormally high levels in tumor tissue and cell lines, and patients with more of it fared worse. Mixing data mining with lab and animal tests, the team traced how the protein feeds the cancer.

Silencing BNIP3 cut the tumor's sugar burning, lowering both glucose uptake and lactate output, and slowed growth. Tumors rich in BNIP3 also hid from the immune system: killer T cells thinned out, suppressive macrophages multiplied, and mutation counts dropped. Drug tests split by BNIP3 level too, with high tumors answering one drug family and low tumors another. The authors pitch BNIP3 as both a warning marker and a target.
pmc-12696943:
Amal Khanolkar and Laia Becares study how past homelessness, mental health, and risky health habits differ among young people in the United Kingdom by sexual identity. Earlier work shows higher risk for sexual minority teens, but no study had used national data in the UK. The authors draw on the age 17 sweep of the Millennium Cohort Study, which covers more than ten thousand young people.

About one in five of the group identified as a sexual minority. Bisexual teens had close to three times the odds of past homelessness compared with heterosexual peers, and gay or lesbian teens also showed higher odds. The team then tests whether poor mental health and habits such as regular smoking or antisocial behavior differ by identity and by past homelessness together. The models account for sex, family income, and ethnic background.
pmc-12699143:
Shan Xu and co-authors read the full mitochondrial genome of a beetle that plagues stored grain. The pest's family placement and mitochondrial traits were murky until now. Its circular genome runs 15,798 letters and holds the standard 37 genes, with a strong tilt toward A and T letters.

Family trees built from thirteen protein genes place the beetle as the sister group of the Tribolium flour beetles. Gene activity peaked in larvae and in the fat body, matching a life spent growing in rich food stores. The genome gives pest science a base for tracking the species and designing controls.
pmc-12699843:
Betül Kurucu Karadeniz, writing alone, tests how three bleaching methods affect single-shade tooth filling resins, in a twenty twenty-five lab study. Two hundred discs from five resins were stained in coffee for twelve days. Groups then got home bleach, office bleach, laser bleach, or none. Color, roughness, and hardness were tracked for a month after.

All bleaching changed the surfaces. Laser bleaching roughened most and softened most, while home bleaching was gentlest. One universal resin resisted best; two single-shade resins stained and weakened more. Hardness partly recovered over time, but color and roughness shifts stayed. The author says dentists should match bleach and resin with care.
pmc-12700143:
Eight researchers map a city country gap in heart device use in Australia in a 2025 paper. The devices include pacemakers and shock units placed in the chest for rhythm faults. The team read ten years of hospital records for the state of New South Wales.

More than a million heart admissions were split into city, regional, and rural groups. Regional and rural patients got pacemakers and resync devices at lower rates than city patients. Shock devices also ran lower for regional patients in most fault groups. The gaps held across sub types like complete heart block. Five year death rates after a pacemaker ran higher for rural patients.
pmc-12700443:
Xiyuan He and co-authors study a plant remedy for psoriasis in mice, in a paper from 2025. Psoriasis is a skin disease marked by red, scaly patches, and it has no cure at present. The plant, a member of the pea family, is used in clinics for throat and gut infections, and past work hinted it could calm psoriasis like skin change.

The team put a cream that triggers psoriasis on the backs of male mice, then treated them with the plant extract. They read the gene activity in skin tissue to see which genes rose or fell. Further checks with gene grouping tools and a second lab test helped confirm the pattern. The aim was to map how the plant works at the gene level.
pmc-12701643:
Yi Feng and co-authors build a model that predicts when induced labor in obese women at term will end in a cesarean delivery, in a study from 2025. Obesity raises both the use of induction and its failure rate. A forecast could guide counseling and planning for mother and staff.

Records came from a Beijing maternity hospital, with a discovery group from earlier years and a validation group from a later one. Three factors raised the risk of failure: higher pre-pregnancy body mass, more weight gained in pregnancy, and a heavier newborn. Having been pregnant or given birth before lowered it, as did greater height. The model's accuracy was scored with a standard curve method and held up in the validation group.
pmc-12703043:
Mei Cha and a large team of co-authors surveyed health workers in Chengdu, China, about the DeepSeek language model in a 2025 study. DeepSeek can read text, work with data, and help review medical images. The team wanted to know how much frontline staff knew about the tool, how they used it, and what shaped their choices.

The survey went to doctors, nurses, technicians, and office staff at two large hospitals for mothers and children, and 788 valid replies came back. Most staff had heard of DeepSeek, mainly through the news and from coworkers, and about three quarters had used it. Nearly nine in ten wanted training, above all hands-on practice. Higher degrees were linked with more use, while staff over fifty used the tool less.
pmc-12703543:
Nobrega, Schiltz, Mathis, and Eggemann report in twenty twenty-five a case where fixing only the front part of a prolapse led to a blocked bowel hernia. A sixty-year-old woman had robot-assisted mesh repair for front and top vaginal prolapse, leaving the back compartment alone. Six weeks later she could not empty her bowel fully and felt pelvic pressure with a new bulge.

Scans showed small bowel sagging into the back compartment, with related rectal faults. A second robot operation added back mesh and rectal support, and her symptoms cleared within months. The authors urge tailored planning and close watch for bowel symptoms after front-only repair. Back support should be weighed when weakness already shows.
pmc-12704443:
Kazushi Shinagawa and his team watch brain and body signs as folk drift from mind drift to a point where they note that their mind has drifted. Their 2025 study tracks brain waves, heart work, and breath while folk do tasks that call for heed.

Folk kept heed on tones or on their own breath while the team tracked the span just prior to when folk knew of the drift. The shift came with drops in alpha and beta brain wave strength and a drop in a brain sign tied to heart beats. That drop marked a rise in how strongly the brain dealt with body signs. Heed on breath changed when breath steps fell at the shift, with a tilt toward breath out. Heart work and heart-beat signs shifted with breath. The team says work on body signs helps spark that note point.
pmc-12705743:
Tao Zhang and co-authors used computer simulation to tune a farm machine that tills sticky soil in layers and raises planting ridges, in a study published in 2025. In southwest China, sticky soil breaks poorly and resists tilling, raising fuel use. Their machine pairs a deep turning shaft with a crushing shaft and a ridging part.

Using a grain-by-grain soil simulation, the team varied the two shaft speeds and their spacing to find the best mix. The crushing shaft's speed mattered most, then spacing, then the deep shaft's speed. At the best settings, the two-shaft design broke about twelve percent more topsoil bonds than a single shaft. Deeper tilling, though, cost more energy and pull, a trade-off farmers must weigh.
pmc-12705843:
Agnes Byström and colleagues compare keyhole surgery results for undescended testes in syndromic and other boys. Their cohort study from twenty twenty-five spans a decade of cases. Boys with genetic syndromes carry higher risk of this condition. Two-stage operations bring abdominal testes down in steps.

Syndrome cases were bilateral and abdominal more often. Those children were also older at surgery. Shrinkage after the staged repair hit about one in five. Syndrome status shapes planning and expectations for families.
pmc-12706043:
Sabine Le Roux and co-authors study how printing settings scar the surface of titanium parts built by laser, in a 2025 paper. Laser powder bed fusion melts metal powder layer by layer, and parts in the workhorse alloy Ti-6Al-4V often emerge with weld traces, stray particles, and pores. Higher energy steadied the melt pool and smoothed the surface, while rough layers propagated their bumps upward for dozens of layers. Measured stresses matched simulations except where porosity was heavy. The work tells manufacturers which dial settings buy smooth, low-stress parts.
pmc-12706243:

Their 2025 protocol paper notes that physicians worldwide report poor sleep at rates near forty-four percent, above the general population, and Bangladeshi estimates run from thirty-two to fifty-eight percent. Pooled prevalence and the risk factors traveling with poor sleep are the targets. The authors frame the synthesis as input for workforce policy, turning fragments into numbers a health ministry can use.
pmc-12706743:
Carlos Diaz-Ufano and co-authors test coatings that keep tiny iron particles active for cleaning polluted water, in work published in 2025. The particles can create reactive oxygen forms that break down pollutants. Their flaw is that they rust fast and lose power within days.

A patchy polymer coat lost most output within a day, while a full coat kept power for at least a day. A manganese hydroxide coat held steady output for the full week, while a nickel coat faded after a day. The results give design rules for longer-lived cleaning particles.
pmc-12706843:

Small wiring choices can tune color without new parts.
pmc-12707243:

The team read microRNAs in ovarian cells from healthy women with a neutral type, healthy women with the phlegm-damp type, and patients. Markers were rechecked in larger groups and mapped into gene networks. Early signs like these could flag women for prevention long before symptoms appear.
pmc-12709743:
MingBin Xu and co-authors build a score to tell if a kidney tube stone will pass on its own. Their paper from 2025 joins sound scans with CT scans and clinical facts. Knowing the odds helps doctors choose between watchful care and a procedure.

Records covered 303 patients with one stone of ten millimeters or less, followed for a month. In all, 191 stones passed and 112 did not. Stones lower in the tube, stones of smaller width, thinner tube walls, and stronger urine jets from the stone side each raised the odds of passing. The joined score beat either scan type alone, and checks showed it fit the real outcomes well.
pmc-12710943:
Wiem Mnafgui and co-authors test how alfalfa copes when salt and a fungal infection strike together, in this 2025 study. In real fields, plants rarely face one stress at a time. The team chose two alfalfa varieties with opposed reputations: one tolerant, one sensitive. Each was exposed to salt, to the fungus, or to both at once, and the responses were compared.

Both varieties shrank in growth, leaf water, and green pigment under stress, with the sensitive one hurt more. A protein scan found a dozen proteins that shifted in telling ways. Those proteins mark the molecular routes each variety uses to adapt. Knowing which routes the tolerant variety leans on can guide breeding of alfalfa for salty, disease-prone land.
pmc-12711043:
Hoque and co-authors map in 2025 the electrical traits of healthy cervix cells against a cervical cancer cell line. Cell electric traits shape normal control and go awry in cancer, but they are usually measured one by one with split tools. The team joined five measures into one fingerprint.

Two methods gave most of the data, with membrane voltage worked out from them. Cancer and healthy cells split clearly on conductance, capacitance, voltage, surface charge, and inner conductivity. A potassium blocker changed the two cell types in unlike ways. The low cost fingerprint could help tell cancer cells from healthy ones in lab work.
pmc-12712543:

Since spearmint already flavors food, no fresh proof of effect was asked.
pmc-12712643:
David Houghton asks whether one caddisfly measure can predict stream health in a 2025 paper. His team identified over half a million specimens, hundreds of species, from more than nine hundred stream sites across the north central United States. Simple richness counts won: family level richness explained the most, beating genus and species counts and a classic tolerance index. Combining all metrics helped only modestly. A three metric mix nearly matched the full model. The author concludes that plain family richness is an efficient stand in for stream condition.
pmc-12714243:
Su Wei, Lixi Zhang, Cuiping Liu, and Xu Qi mine in 2025 a United States database of drug harm reports for the real world safety of tepotinib, a lung cancer drug. The drug targets tumors with a skipped gene segment. Trial data cannot show every harm that appears once a drug meets the wider public.

Reports filed from 2021 to 2024 gave over five hundred cases and close to fourteen hundred events. Most came from older patients. Known harms such as swelling, loose stools, and kidney strain showed up as expected. Fresh signals, including hearing loss and taste changes, also surfaced for study.
pmc-12715343:
Xuefang Shi and co-authors test a skin serum for age signs in Chinese adults with tender skin. The trial appeared in 2025. Asian skin can flare with classic age creams, so soft acts are in need. The serum pairs a plant act with a fruit peel extract in a wrapped form.

Thirty-four adults used the serum twice a day for four weeks. Checks ran at the start, at eight hours, and at two set days. Water loss through skin fell by near a fourth by the end. Red tint and sting scores fell by clear shares too. Wrinkle and spring scores moved in the right way as well.
pmc-12717043:

pmc-12717143:

The team removed the tall plant in some plots and cut insect numbers in others. Plant mass and plant variety rose where the tall plant was removed and where insects were cut. Soil matter broke down fastest in those same plots. Yet plant mass grew less steady over time under both changes, and insects slowed the field's bounce back.
pmc-12717243:
François Mitterand Tsombou and five co-authors study how elevation and plant part shape the chemistry of Senna italica in Fujairah's arid climate in this 2025 paper. Harsh dry regions stress plant metabolism, but data from such places is thin. Young and mature leaves, branches, seeds, and fruits were analyzed.

Plants from the highest sites carried the most pigments, and leaves beat branches, with mature leaves richest. Leaves also led in several minerals and vitamins, seeds in protein and other nutrients, and branches in fiber-related measures. Fruit extracts fought microbes best, with clear inhibition zones. The authors read pigment shifts as an adaptation to aridity. They suggest the plant's chemistry could yield compounds against drug-resistant microbes.
pmc-12717743:
Haojun Huang, Defeng Dong, and Yi Ding link Americans' social risk load to a metabolic syndrome and to death itself, in a 2025 paper. Higher social risk came with higher odds of circadian syndrome and higher mortality, in straight-line fashion. The ties ran stronger in women and in people who drink alcohol. Hardship, the results say, gets under the skin and into the body clock.
pmc-12720443:
Verena Mutzel and co-authors studied how genes that are read in reverse can leave a lasting off state in a cell, in work published in 2025. Cells remember past signals, and one route to memory is two genes that repress each other, like a toggle switch.

The team blended math models, genome scans, and a built test locus in mouse stem cells. Models showed stable memory arises when both genes in a reverse pair are read through a shared start site and set a lasting repressive mark. Genome data fit that picture. The built locus showed reverse reading can indeed lock a gene off, and the lock grew stronger as the cells matured.
pmc-12721543:

Its accuracy was set against the leading rapid test, smear, and culture methods. A test that works at the clinic door could close much of the diagnosis gap. Field proof from a high-burden region carries real weight.
pmc-12722243:

Forty-five healthy people were tested lying down, standing on firm and soft floors, and in heel-to-toe stance. Both sound and touch warnings were tried, with eyes open and shut.
