Taking vision away trimmed the effect slightly without changing the pattern. Sound and touch behaved alike. The authors suggest gating flexes with postural demand, and might one day mark balance control health.
pmc-12722343:
Mingyou Wang and colleagues report early results for a robot-assisted hip replacement system. Their study from twenty twenty-five covers the ARTHROBOT under a fast recovery protocol. Robotic help promises more precise placement of hip components. Hospitals also need to know the learning curve for surgical teams.

Just over one hundred patients had either robotic or conventional surgery. Robotic cases took longer and used slightly longer incisions. Component placement accuracy was clearly better with the robot. Safe zone rates and leg length control both improved. Pain ran higher on the third day after robotic surgery. That gap closed by one month after surgery. Early walking and hospital stay matched between groups.
pmc-12722743:
Yijie Xu and seven co-authors boost ammonia production in plasma with a ferroelectric barrier discharge, in a study from 2025. Plasma can make ammonia without the heat and pressure of classic plants, but yields stay low. A ferroelectric layer may energize the gas more strongly.

Fast laser diagnostics tracked hydrogen and nitrogen radicals, excited molecules, ions, and ammonia as they formed. The ferroelectric discharge quadrupled ammonia yield in their setup. It also raised ion and radical counts and heated molecular vibration. Modeling tied those rises to coupled reactions that build ammonia step by step, which clarifies how the layer helps.
pmc-12722843:
Xuexue Cui and co-authors report a 2025 mouse study with a surprise: germs live inside the healthy eye. The team sampled the retina and the layer beneath it under strict sterile care and read the germ DNA. They then burned the retina lightly with a laser and sampled again an hour and a day later, to see how the inner germ mix answers injury.

Both eye layers held varied germ mixes in health, mostly shared between them, with the retina richer. Injury cut variety in the retina but left the mix shape steady. A few genera rose or fell by site, and two that rose link to immune paths tied to healing. The authors see the eye germ mix as a player in repair.
pmc-12723143:
Juan Yu and co-authors compare doses of the blood thinner rivaroxaban in older patients in this 2025 paper. The patients had non valvular atrial fibrillation, a heart rhythm problem that raises stroke risk. Doctors often lower the dose in older patients out of caution. Whether that helps or harms was the question.

Records covered 214 patients aged 65 and older treated at one hospital in Zhengzhou in 2022. Patients were split into a standard dose group and a low dose group. Outcomes were tracked for twelve months after discharge by records and phone calls. The low dose group was older on average. Stroke risk and bleeding risk scores were much the same in both groups at baseline.
pmc-12723443:
Jiaxu Fan and co-authors map waterbird habitat across southern China in 2025. Climate shifts and human pressure have shrunk waterbird habitat worldwide. Knowing where good habitat remains, and where reserves miss it, guides protection.

Forty-seven species were modeled with a distribution tool fed by climate, land, and human data. Good habitat hugged the coast and reached inland along big rivers. Plant cover and elevation drove suitability for gulls and shorebirds, while herons favored denser growth. Overlay with reserves exposed gaps, above all in the south and southwest, where coverage lags the habitat map.
pmc-12723843:
Xiaona Zhang and eleven co-authors review the gene-silencing RNA called Xist and its disease links in a 2025 paper. Female mammals switch off one X chromosome in each cell to balance gene dose with males. A long non-coding RNA performs that shutdown by coating the chromosome.

The review traces how the RNA recruits protein complexes that remodel packaging and silence genes. Beyond its normal role, this machinery turns up in inflammation of the nervous system, autoimmune disease, and cancers. Mis-set silencing can ripple into those illnesses. The authors weigh the RNA as a possible drug target. Understanding a master switch of gene dose may open therapies that retune it rather than chasing single downstream genes.
pmc-12723943:
Hongying Zhang and a large team of co-authors study a gene-linked kidney disease in Chinese children in a 2025 paper. Changes in the HNF1B gene are a major inherited cause of malformed kidneys and urinary tracts. The same gene can affect other organs too. How the kidney disease unfolds over time matters most for a child's future.

Using a national database of genetic kidney disease in children, the team analyzed 26 cases from 2017 to 2024. Every child showed kidney signs at diagnosis, most often cysts or a malformed kidney. About three in five children lacked a whole stretch of chromosome that holds the gene. Those children showed signs earlier, while children with small gene changes lost kidney function faster. Three children reached kidney failure and had transplants before age fifteen.
pmc-12725543:
The authors explore how severe mental illness strains marriages in Karachi, Pakistan. Marriage carries deep social and moral weight in South Asia, while both psychiatric illness and divorce draw heavy stigma, so the clash between them is rarely studied. The team interviewed more than 40 people linked to a large hospital, sampling across six situations that varied in when the illness was disclosed and whether the marriage survived. Themes were read through family systems theory.

Three forces kept marriages intact: the presence of children, knowing about the illness before the wedding, and the stigma attached to divorce. Spouses described heavy caregiving strain, with roles reversing, emotions wearing thin, and their own health slipping. The authors call for mental health strategies fitted to the culture, above all ones that encourage early disclosure before marriage.
pmc-12727943:
Xu Wang, Qi Feng, and Dawei Cao study how speed skating coaches' leadership shapes athlete engagement, in a 2025 survey paper. More than four hundred skaters from three provinces in northeast China completed scales on leadership, engagement, and mental fatigue. The authors tested whether fatigue carries the effect of leadership onto engagement.

Authoritarian coaching linked to lower engagement and higher fatigue on every measure. Training guidance, democratic style, social support, and positive feedback showed the reverse pattern. Fatigue itself tracked with lower engagement. Regression and mediation tests confirmed that all leadership styles influenced both fatigue and engagement. The authors advise coaches to favor supportive, guiding styles over command-based ones.
pmc-12729143:
Fanxing Du and co-authors ask whether a popular diabetes drug class raises heart rhythm risk in older patients on thyroid medicine, in a 2025 study. The drugs can lower the needed thyroid dose, and too much thyroid hormone can trigger irregular heartbeat and stroke.

Using a method that mimics a clinical trial in real records, the team matched new users of the diabetes drugs against users of a rival class. All were Medicare patients over sixty five, on a stable thyroid dose for at least six months, with no cancer or palliative care in the prior year. Outcomes were new atrial fibrillation or flutter, and stroke. The design aims at a fair head to head safety comparison.
pmc-12729243:
Heart attacks strike some people who eat the same diet as others who stay well, so genes may tilt the odds. Haozhang Huang and co-authors ask how gene variants tied to omega-3 fatty acids shape the link between those fats and a first heart attack. Their 2025 study mixes gene-based tests with a large British health cohort.

First, the team used a method that treats genes as a natural test to find spots that move fat levels and, in turn, heart risk. Next, they hunted for gene spots shared by both traits. Last, they checked in the cohort whether a person's gene pattern changed the link between fat levels and heart attacks. The goal is a clearer view of who gains from these fats.
pmc-12729443:
Chunyan Zhang and co-authors test a Chinese form of a scale on feeling like a burden, in a research paper from 2025. Many older adults in China feel they weigh on others, which can harm health and mood. No scale made for this group in China was ready for wide use.

The team translated the scale with a back-and-forth method and gave it to five hundred older adults. They checked the form with factor tests and with checks of score steadiness over time. They also looked at what traits link to high scores. The paper gives clinics a tested tool for screening and care planning.
pmc-12729543:
Geng Chen and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how alkaline water harms a freshwater fish, the European perch. Around the world, some lakes and rivers are turning more alkaline, which stresses fish. The team exposed perch to strong alkaline water and tracked the damage organ by organ over ninety-six hours.

The gills failed first, with their fine blades fusing and dying, which hurt the fish's salt balance. The liver followed, with rising oxidative damage and widespread cell death. Gene readings showed thousands of changed genes in the liver and hundreds in the kidney. The time-ordered pattern, gills then liver then kidney, helps explain how this stress kills and may guide fishery warnings.
pmc-12729743:
Jianxu Xiao and co-authors tested taurine against uterus inflammation in mice, in a 2025 paper. Endometritis cuts fertility and milk yield in cattle. Taurine, a cell-protecting compound, fights inflammation and oxidation. Mice received a bacterial toxin in the uterus to mimic the disease.

Three taurine doses followed the insult. Tissue damage eased and cytokine levels fell with treatment. Oxidation markers dropped while antioxidant defenses recovered. Cell death eased and gut-like womb microbes rebalanced. Blocked signaling pathways explain much of the effect. Taurine may become a livestock fertility aid. The mouse model now needs testing in cattle themselves.
pmc-12729943:
Thi Hiep Dao and Amy Moss weigh canola meal as a replacement for soybean meal in chicken feed. Soy dominates poultry rations but carries cost, environmental, and social baggage. Canola meal, the pressed leftover of canola seed, is cheaper and can be grown locally. The review gathers feeding trials and judges the swap on nutrition, price, and planet. The meal feeds growth well, though its fiber and bitter compounds trim the energy birds can extract.

Laying hens handled the swap best, tolerating up to a fifth of the ration without losing eggs or quality in the limited data. Broiler results swung more at high shares. Processing, added enzymes, fermentation, and newer plant varieties all raised the meal's value. Local canola also cuts shipping emissions and feeds pollinators, at the price of more land. The authors urge rations tuned by species and region.
pmc-12730243:
Keran Chen and co-authors review how reading single cells one by one is exposing the inner variety of pancreatic cancer, in a 2025 paper. This cancer is famously lethal and famously mixed: its tumours blend many cell types that help it grow and resist drugs. Single-cell sequencing profiles each cell's active genes, revealing who is who inside the tumour. The review tours the cast: cancer cells that shift shape and state, and support cells of several kinds.

Immune cells, scar-forming cells, and even nerve cells each play distinct parts, trading signals that drive spread, immune escape, and drug resistance. The authors also survey technical advances from 2023 to 2025, from sample handling to combined methods that add location and other layers. Their aim is practical: turn the cellular map into treatment strategies aimed at the tumour's weakest neighbourhoods.
pmc-12730743:
Beatriz Marín-García and co-authors test an add-on drug for active lupus in a 2025 study of 106 cases from a Spanish cohort. All patients took hydroxychloroquine plus prednisone, yet their disease stayed active. The team added mepacrine and checked who reached remission after six months.

Remission by the strict DORIS standard came for 71 percent of the whole group. Those on simple therapy hit 79 percent, against 62 percent for those also on stronger immune drugs. Disease activity scores fell by about the same amount in both groups. Steroid doses also tapered alike. The most common reason for stopping the add-on was lack of effect or side effects. The results support mepacrine as a useful extra step when base therapy falls short.
pmc-12731643:
Mohammed Hawash and co-authors review a new generation of cancer drugs that block histone deacetylases, enzymes that help switch genes on and off, in a 2025 paper. Several such drugs are already approved, but most grip the enzyme through zinc-binding parts that cause problems: they break down fast, can damage DNA, and clear from the body poorly.

The review surveys recent designs that swap in alternative zinc-binding groups, comparing how each change affects strength and selectivity across cancer cell lines and enzyme subtypes. It also covers hybrids that hit two targets at once, pairing the HDAC block with attacks on other cancer pathways. The authors aim to guide safer, better drugs.
pmc-12731843:
Liqin Xu and co-authors report early results for a robotic method of burning away lung nodules, in a 2025 paper. The method guides a thin scope through the airways with shape sensing, then applies microwave heat to the spot. It suits patients who cannot have surgery or radiation. The team reviewed cases treated at one center over about a year, for both first lung cancers and cancers spread from elsewhere.

Nine patients with eleven nodules were treated, and every procedure reached its target. Sessions took about ten minutes per nodule. One patient developed pneumonia needing hospital care, but there were no collapsed lungs, major bleeding, or airway injury. Treated spots first swelled, then shrank or held steady. Scans showed the first cancers quieting, and one patient later had surgery that found no living cancer. The authors call the method feasible and safe, with larger studies still needed.
pmc-12732243:
Park and co-authors build working monkey versions of two reproductive hormones and probe how a partner protein steers their signals, in a 2025 study. Gene sequences for the hormone subunits were compared between cynomolgus and rhesus monkeys and found nearly identical. Fused single-chain versions were then produced in cells and shown to carry the expected sugar decorations. The monkey follicle-stimulating hormone switched on its human receptor as it should.

The partner protein, beta-arrestin 1, pulled two ways: it damped the hormone's main cAMP signal yet was required for the second, ERK signal. Human and rat receptors also differed in timing. The system now exists for primate fertility research.
pmc-12732643:
Rui Zhang and Aixia Ma weigh the cost and value of a biotech drug for rheumatoid arthritis in China, in a 2025 study. The drug copies a natural trap for a signal that drives joint inflammation. The question was whether using it first, ahead of the standard cheap drug methotrexate, is worth its higher price over a patient's lifetime.

The authors built a model that steps patients through health states in six-month cycles, fed by results from a Chinese head-to-head trial. The fusion protein gave patients more years in good health, at a cost per extra healthy year far below China's per-person economic output, a common yardstick for value. Checks from the views of patients and insurers told the same story. The authors conclude first-line use of the drug is good value in the Chinese setting.
pmc-12733043:
Alejandra Navarro-Martínez and six colleagues test active paper sheets for keeping cherry tomatoes and kale fresh in storage. The kraft sheets carry thymol and eugenol, plant oils that fight microbes, sealed inside a sugar ring carrier. Spoilage germs and color loss are the enemies.

Produce sat at several temperatures for one to three weeks. The sheets cut microbe growth, above all gut bacteria and moulds on tomatoes and cold-loving germs on kale. Basic quality traits held steady. In kale, greenness faded half as fast at room temperature, and tomatoes kept firmness and color. A growth model captured how the sheets slow microbes across temperatures.
pmc-12733243:
Iuliia Baikova and a large team of co-authors build a mouse model to test how a blood protein affects gut inflammation in two thousand twenty-five. The protein, cyclophilin A, drives inflammation through several signal paths. Mouse immune systems differ from human ones, which makes such models hard to trust.

Their mice were bred to release the human form of the protein into the blood from vessel walls when switched on. At rest the mice seemed well, but a chemical in their drinking water brought on gut inflammation that closely matched ulcerative colitis. The colon lining broke down while the upper gut stayed near normal. The protein thus worsens inflammation once it starts, without starting it alone.
pmc-12733443: Agnieszka Ścibior and co-authors introduce the second edition of a special issue on metal complexes and their drug-like activity. The collection updates work on magnesium and its links to neurodegeneration. It also gathers reports on varied metal-containing complexes and their possible uses as therapies. As editors, they frame the issue as a progress report. Metals were long treated as mere toxins or nutrients. Now they are being tested as designed medicines in their own right.
pmc-12733543:
Irina Engalycheva and co-authors identify the fungi behind melon wilt in Russia, in work from 2025. Fusarium wilt cuts melon harvests worldwide and can ruin a field's value. Which species drive the disease in Russia had not been mapped before this study.

From 2022 to 2025, the team gathered nineteen fungal samples from two southern regions. Gene analysis of two loci, plus shape study, sorted the samples into four species. One species made up over a third of samples, and the other three split the rest evenly. All four appeared in one region, while two appeared in the other. Harm tests on melon and kin plants confirmed each species can cause the wilt.
pmc-12733843:
Qiwei Yang and co-authors studied a family of proteins that read gene marks, in work on uterine fibroids published in 2025. Fibroids are the most common non-cancer growths in women of child-bearing age. The proteins in focus help switch genes on, but their role in fibroids was largely unknown.

Levels of two of these proteins differed in fibroid tissue when set against matched normal tissue from the same women. Drugs that block the proteins slowed fibroid cells more than normal cells and halted their growth cycle. Blocking also changed many gene pathways and lowered genes that build the stiff matrix around fibroid cells. The authors see the proteins as a possible new drug target.
pmc-12733943:
Ulrich Graf and co-authors measure in 2025 how dry-eye drops flow under the shear of a blink. Seven commercial lubricants built on hyaluronic acid were run through a light-based rheometer at eye temperature, across shear rates matching blinking. Natural tears were measured for comparison.

Tears barely changed thickness across the range. The products spread widely, from about two and a half to nearly eight units of viscosity at the low end of shear, and each thinned to its own degree as shear rose. Such shear-thinning shapes how a drop spreads and lingers on the eye, so the ranking gives clinicians a physical basis for matching products to patients.
pmc-12734143:
Mustafa Cem Türkmen and co-authors compare balance and muscle response in people with below-knee and above-knee amputations, in this 2025 paper. Standing steady after a sudden floor shift demands fast leg work. How the two amputation levels differ was not settled.

Ten people per group, plus ten healthy controls, stood on a force plate while surface sensors read leg muscles. Surprise shifts were delivered in several directions. The above-knee group swayed most, especially on soft ground with eyes closed. During forward shifts, front thigh and shin muscles fired harder than back muscles. The results guide balance training by amputation level.
pmc-12734343:
Martino, Szmulewicz, and Birmaher ask in twenty twenty-five whether today's concept of bipolar disorder rests on valid ground. They reviewed a century of texts and studies on the criteria for manic and depressive episodes, judging both whether the illness is a real entity and whether the rules describe it well.

Mania holds up as a genuine construct, though its diagnostic rules need more testing. Evidence for splitting milder hypomania from mania as separate episodes is thin and contested. The modern idea of bipolar depression lumps together unlike episode types, with weak proof all belong to the one illness. The authors call the current definition's validity limited. Sharper definitions, they argue, would speed biology research and tailored treatment.
pmc-12734743:
Hyun Soo Kim and co-authors put a full-size aluminum electric vehicle battery case through punishing tests, in the lab and in simulation. Their study appeared in 2025. The case must survive bottom impacts, crushing, and constant vibration without endangering passengers. The team ran a bottom impact test, a 200 kilonewton compression test, and a random vibration test, then mirrored each in a finite element model with the same supports and loads.

Predicted stresses and bending matched the real measurements closely. Hot spots sat at corners and frame joints, and peak compression bent the case by less than a millimeter. Vibration shook hardest vertically but loosened no bolts and broke nothing. The authors say the design is verified, and the matched model can drive lighter future cases.
pmc-12735143:
Yizhou Hu, Leheng Zhang, Sirui Gong, and Zhenlong Wang polish titanium composite surfaces with an electrochemical finish after spark machining, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The mesh-structured composite suits aerospace work but its uneven makeup makes smooth micro-surfaces hard. Spark machining leaves pits ringed by raised rims.

Standalone electrochemical machining failed first: the fiber reinforcement and the metal base dissolved at wildly differing rates, chewing the surface unevenly. Applied after spark machining instead, the method under tuned settings (salt solution, modest voltage, fast pulses) erased the pit rims. Surface roughness halved, and the finish grew even. The authors present the two-step route as a practical way to machine this tough material cleanly.
pmc-12735243:
Yaoyao Liu leads a team that coats sea sensors with a hard film. Their work from twenty twenty-five uses a film of alumina laid by a strong sputter tool. Sea water wears and rusts sensors, which cuts their life.

Film tests in a sea like setting showed strong wear proof. Surface scans traced how the film changed with rubbing. With the film, a pressure sensor caught tiny forces under water. Mounted on a robot gripper, it sensed fine moves of held things. The coat could extend sea sensor life and skill both.
pmc-12735443:
A radioactive metal's ring-shaped compounds get a full survey in a 2025 review by Ulrich Abram and Maximilian Roca Jungfer. The metal is technetium, and the rings are cyclopentadienyl ligands, a classic scaffold in organometallic chemistry.

Far fewer such compounds are known for technetium than for its heavier cousin rhenium, partly because every isotope is radioactive, but partly from real chemical differences. The review covers compounds with the metal in charge states from +1 to +7, dominated by carbonyl and nitrosyl forms at the lowest state. Those same forms matter for medical imaging agents, where the ring is a handy anchor for attaching marker molecules. Recent labeling work is reviewed alongside the basic chemistry.
pmc-12735543:
Babies born very early often grow poorly in intensive care, and gut bacteria may play a part. Stumpf and co-authors followed infants born before 29 weeks and sorted them into normal, poor, and very poor growth groups. Weekly stool samples, once the babies were on full feeds, were read with gene sequencing under blinded conditions.

Among 263 samples, the very poor growth group carried more Veillonella, Bifidobacterium, and Clostridium than the normal group. The mix of bacteria also shifted with age in ways that depended on how badly growth lagged. The authors see the gut mix as a possible future target for treating poor growth.
pmc-12736243:
Nagihan Sahin and five co-authors study links among sense profiles, blood marks, and eating styles in teens with and without obesity. Teens in the same food rich world vary wide in weight, so inner traits may matter. Near one hundred teens gave blood and spit and filled sense and eating forms.

Sense zone scores did not split by weight group. Yet higher sense sensitivity went with more emotional eating, a mid strength link. Blood hunger marks and a stress mark showed no tie to eating styles after checks. Sense care may matter for mood eating, pending long studies.
pmc-12736343:
Lynette Cusack and co-authors follow newly graduated nurses through their first year in a 2025 Australian study. The step from student to registered nurse brings strain, unclear roles, and a jolt known as transition shock.

A seventy five item questionnaire, built on a staged theory of that transition, was given at three points across the year inside one large health service. Four areas were tracked: responsibilities, role orientation, relationships, and knowledge with confidence. The four areas held together as clean factors. Scores rose by stage in decision making, handling pressure, seeing oneself as a leader, and keeping emotions steady. The authors also model which traits predict reaching each stage.
pmc-12736543:
Arjina Akter and co-authors review disease proofing in Brassica greens in a 2025 paper. Cabbage kin lose much yield to germs and viruses each year. Proof genes in the plants beat sprays that harm soil and water.

Known proof genes for eight major diseases are charted with their markers. Breeders have moved club root proof genes between cabbage kinds by marked crosses. Gene edit tools can now place proof with pin point care. Marks above the gene layer, like DNA tags, add a second tune path. The review maps a green path to hardier greens.
pmc-12736743:
Trey Coughlin, Koki Weng, Maria Laura Salum, Pablo Froimowicz, Chris Scott, and Hatsuo Ishida make heat-stable, flame-resistant resins from a plant compound in two thousand twenty-five. The starting compound, umbelliferone, comes from natural sources and carries a phenol group. Four resin building blocks were made from it, two of them new.

The new blocks use distinct amine partners, which lets the team test how the amine's ring and chain length shape the final plastic. Heat tests showed high char left after burning, a sign of strong heat stability. None of the four plastics could be ignited in flame tests, and their heat release rates were low. The results guide design of safer resins for hot settings.
pmc-12736843:
A drug used for psychosis may also fight a fungal infection of the eye, if it can be delivered well. Rofida Albash and co-authors report a 2025 effort to package that drug, aripiprazole, into tiny carriers placed in the eye.

The team loaded the drug into small fatty bubbles coated for longer action, then set them into printed inserts made of a plant-based plastic. Tests showed the bubbles were tiny, stable, and stuck well to the eye surface. In rabbits with a fungal cornea infection, the insert gave a strong healing effect, and tissue checks showed no harm. The work pairs drug reuse with printed delivery in a fresh way.
pmc-12736943:
Magdalena Gaca and Magdalena Lipińska study rubber composites. In these mixes, an ionic liquid is used to improve the bond between polymer and carbon filler. Their base is a styrene-butadiene rubber, a type in wide use in rubber processing. It is cured with a standard sulfur system. Two fillers were tested, furnace carbon black and graphene nanoplatelets. Each filler was changed during mixing with a pyridinium-based ionic liquid. That liquid can stack onto the filler surfaces.

The study measures curing behavior, crosslink density, and mechanical properties. It then looks at rheology and damping at service temperatures, across a range of deformations. Fillers of distinct shapes and sizes interacted with the polymer in distinct ways. The ionic liquid also shaped contacts between filler particles. The authors map how a small additive reshapes viscoelastic performance in filled rubber.
pmc-12737243:
Anastasia Giannakoula and co-authors study how a salt-loving medicinal plant handles salt stress, and whether biostimulants help, in a 2025 paper. The plant, Crithmum maritimum, grows in harsh coastal settings. At moderate salt levels, growth and photosynthesis rose in their tests.

At high salt levels, biomass, photosynthetic efficiency, and water use all fell significantly. Stress was confirmed by raised markers of oxidative damage in upper tissues. Two bioactive foliar products partly eased the harm of high salt. Treated plants kept higher photosynthesis and a better antioxidant profile than untreated controls. The results inform growing this species on salty land.
pmc-12737343:
Peihua Niu and co-authors chart in 2025 the gene spread of two gut germ kinds in one China port town across a year. Both kinds drive loose gut ills, most in kids. Their split ways bear on health plans and shot work.

Twelve hundred stool takes from sick folk yield near fifty of the germ group. Full gene reads sort the kinds and their change marks. One kind stays near still, with change heaped in a tail gene. Its mate splits wide, with change heaped in a shell gene and clear mix cross lines in that zone. Shape models show the shell shifts may aid shield dodge.
pmc-12737543:
Chaowu Fu and co-authors report a parasite outbreak in captive ring-tailed lemurs, in a paper published in 2025. In September 2024, lemurs at a site in Henan Province, China, fell ill with bloody diarrhea, and three young females died. Their housing sat next to squirrel monkeys. Post-mortem checks found severe bleeding and tissue death in the large gut.

Microscope work and gene tests named the culprit as Tritrichomonas mobilensis, a parasite found in the dead lemurs' gut contents. The same parasite turned up in four of ten squirrel monkeys tested, which points to spread between the enclosures, likely on keepers' tools or footwear. A common anti-parasite drug plus supportive care saved the surviving lemurs, and later tests were clear. The report is the first of this infection in ring-tailed lemurs.
pmc-12738543:
Naseem Akhtar and three co-authors compared in 2025 the full life-cycle footprint of two electrode types used to pull thorium from radioactive waste by electrosorption. Earlier work had reached high recovery with the method but never counted its environmental cost. The team tallied inputs from raw materials to energy using a standard database. Both systems were judged per kilogram of thorium recovered.

Activated carbon electrodes scored far worse than graphene-based ones on human toxicity and harm to fresh and sea water life. End-point tallies for health, ecosystems, and resources also favored graphene. The authors credit heavier chemical use and emissions in the carbon route. They conclude graphene electrodes are both more effective and gentler for managing radioactive waste.
pmc-12738643:
Walaa El-Masry, Samar Monem, Nagy Darwish, and Aboul Ella Hassanein build an AI model to predict drug potency against the p53 protein, in a 2025 paper. P53 controls the cell cycle and suppresses tumors, and it was long thought undruggable. New interest in targeting it needs better prediction tools.

Their hybrid model stacks two kinds of graph neural networks, one that captures local structure and one that attends to long-range links. A pooling step then combines the strongest and average signals. Unlike older tools based on flat descriptors, the model reads the molecular graph directly. It is tailored to p53 inhibitors and aims at a unified prediction framework.
pmc-12738843:
A 2025 correction repairs a reversed claim in a review of autoimmune disease mechanisms and treatments, by Yi Song and two co-authors. The original text placed the signaling protein CD40 on T cells and its partner CD40L on B cells. In fact the placement runs the other way, and the passage has been rewritten to match.

Two figures were fixed as well: one dropped a misleading cell label, and the other's color key for natural versus altered amino acids was swapped back. The authors state that no other findings in the review are affected. The correction keeps the review's account of immune signaling accurate for readers who build on it.
pmc-12739143:
Katarzyna Brzezewska and co-authors study body image in 2025 among bone surgery patients in a Polish hospital. Surgery breaks body wholeness and can bring pain, stiffness, and lost independence, which may stir distress and a changed view of one's body. The team asks whether harmful personality traits shape that view in the first days after surgery.

They assessed fifty-three adults within three days of surgery using two standard questionnaires. One trait, a disregard for others, went with kinder ratings of looks and fitness. A tendency to negative feelings went with poorer health ratings but fuller weight concern. A rigid, order-loving trait went with stronger focus on health and illness. Early screening could flag patients who need support.
pmc-12739843:
Ida Elisabeth Bang and co-authors hunt risk factors for tearing during birth in Norway, in work from 2025. Such tears hit the anal sphincter and can cause lasting harm. The team used a regional birth registry with over twenty-six thousand single births from 2012 to 2022. They tested known risk traits plus a new suspect: breaking the water sac by hand.

The hand-breaking step showed no added risk in this fresh group. Tool-aided birth stood out as the top fixable risk, with vacuum and forceps both raising odds a lot. A cut to ease birth and pain relief through the back each cut risk for first-time mothers. Tear rates held near two percent.
pmc-12739943:
Fangshuo Cheng, Jinghua Wang, and Fen Sun review tiny drug carriers cloaked in real cell membranes for treating ischemic stroke. Their review was published in twenty twenty-five. Stroke drugs struggle to cross the blood-brain barrier, and the treatment window is short.

The carriers pair a synthetic core with a natural membrane coat, gaining targeting and the ability to slip past immune patrols. The review weighs benefit against safety, a balance past work had left incomplete. Size and surface features steer where the particles end up and how long they circulate. Membrane proteins, natural or engineered, add homing power. The authors map which designs look safest inside the stroke-damaged brain.
pmc-12740743:
Veronica Abate and co-authors check how well the rules for bone scans in Italy pick out people with thin bones, in a study from 2025. Thin bones raise the risk of breaks, and a scan is the best test for the state. The rules set who should get a scan, for bone loss from age or from other illness and drugs.

The team used health records for more than twenty four thousand adults sent for a scan. The scan backed the doubt in about eight in ten women and in a lower share of men for age linked loss. For loss from other causes, the scan backed the doubt in about eight in ten of both sexes. The authors call the rules a useful tool, with a clear gap by sex for age linked loss.
pmc-12741143:
Vincent Friedrich and a team of co-authors compare immune responses in monkeys and humans at the level of single cells. Their study is from two thousand twenty-five. Monkeys closely related to humans are often used to test new immune drugs. Yet no one knew in fine detail where their responses match ours and where they part ways.

Blood immune cells from both species were stirred into action in the lab. Cells were read at rest, and at six and twenty-four hours after the stimulus. A deep learning method helped align the two species' data for a fair comparison. Both species shifted from early defense cells toward T cells in the same way. Other gene and pathway patterns were shared too, while some differed. The pipeline can guide future cross-species drug work.
pmc-12741443:
Vinod Xavier and co-authors report a healthcare worker whose tuberculosis nearly killed her in late pregnancy. The 42-year-old woman arrived with long fever and failing breath in her third trimester. First tests found little. Her lungs worsened into severe ARDS, forcing an emergency cesarean and a ventilator.

Two unlikely clues cracked the case. The placenta showed granulomas under the microscope, and an eye exam found tubercles in the retina. Washings from her lungs later grew the TB bacterium. Drugs plus steroids turned her around, and she came off the ventilator. The baby stayed well. The authors stress creative diagnostics when standard tools stall in pregnancy.
pmc-12742143:
Christoph Klivinyi and co-authors lay out a study plan on blood pressure during heart surgery, in this 2025 protocol paper. During operations that use a heart-lung machine, blood pressure targets remain unsettled, with harm reported at both low and high levels. The team will study past operations at one Austrian center from 2014 to 2023.

They will extract pressure and pump flow records and weigh how long each patient spent below set thresholds. Brain outcomes, namely strokes found on scans and delirium in intensive care, are the focus. With hundreds of cases per year expected, the study aims to sharpen guidance for pressure care during bypass.
pmc-12742443:
Renée Firman and Francisco Garcia-Gonzalez ask whether a father's social world echoes in his sons in a 2025 mouse study. Earlier work showed that male mice raised among many males make fewer Y-bearing sperm, which tilts litters toward daughters.

The team raised father mice in mostly male or mostly female groups, then checked the sperm of their sons, who grew up under matched, shared conditions. Sons of fathers from male-heavy groups made more daughter-producing sperm than sons of the other group. Since genes and upbringing were controlled, the shift points to nongenetic, epigenetic inheritance. The effect was small, and the authors call for sharper sperm-counting methods to test it further.
pmc-12743243:
Marzena Zygis and co-authors study the sound of cheering in a 2025 paper, a topic phonetics had not mapped in a planned way. Their case is fans calling a runner's name to urge them on in long races. Thirty native German speakers cheered in a lab while a race video played.

The same names were also read plainly and inside full sentences, for contrast. Four cheer styles showed up, from names split into beats to a sung style. Cheering ran higher in pitch, wider in range, longer, and louder than plain speech, the team found. Names of one to five beats were used. A first map of how cheers are voiced helps speech science treat crowd calls as real speech, not just noise.
pmc-12743843:
Caifeng Gong and co-authors report in 2025 a small trial of a drug pair for advanced liver cancer, and find a blood marker that flags who benefits. Pairing an immune checkpoint drug with a vessel starving pill is now standard care for hepatocellular carcinoma, yet doctors lack good tests for likely winners. The trial gave all patients both drugs on a three week cycle.

After long follow up, survival times landed in the modest range expected for this disease stage. Side effects touched most patients, and about half the group had severe ones. The telling split came from a baseline blood sample: patients who gained clinical benefit started with higher levels of BDNF, a nerve growth factor. Above a cut line, high BDNF tracked with better outcomes. A cheap blood test of this kind could steer the pair toward patients likeliest to gain.
pmc-12744243:
Zamanali Khakhar and co-authors report the case of a 45-year-old woman whose liver pain came from a benign growth, not cancer. The growth type, called focal nodular hyperplasia, is most often found by chance on scans and usually causes no symptoms. It can look like a cancerous liver tumor on images, which can push patients toward needless invasive steps.

Doctors placed the woman on routine scan watch and treated her without surgery. The case stresses how much rides on telling this harmless growth apart from true liver cancers. It also shows the hard calls doctors face when images alone cannot settle what a liver spot is.
pmc-12745443:
Youjin Kong and co-authors test a traditional granule against atrial fibrillation in a 2025 paper. Early clinical work hints that Shenlian Fumai Granule cuts rhythm problems after ablation and eases symptoms. The team probed how it may prevent the condition.

They combined network analysis, chemical profiling, and docking studies to find targets. In rats, fibrillation was induced with two drugs over five weeks. The granule was given daily at two doses, with a standard drug as a comparator. Heart tracings, ultrasound, and tissue checks tracked the effects. The work links the granule to changes in the atrium's electrical and structural remodeling.
pmc-12745843:
Mutaz Mohammed Abdallah and co-authors used computing tools to guess the jobs of mystery proteins in a freshwater bacterium, in a 2025 study. The bacterium, Listeria aquatica, carries a genome rich in proteins with no known role. Though not a known pathogen, its water habitat raises questions about spreading drug resistance genes.

From 2,789 predicted proteins, the team screened for stable, well-placed candidates and kept 919 for a closer look. Two cytoplasm proteins got the full treatment: shape models, family matching, docking tests, and danger screens. One matched immunity proteins that shield bacteria from toxins. The other matched a detox protein family. Both came out helix-rich and water-loving, with high-confidence shapes. The authors offer the pair as leads for lab follow-up.
pmc-12746043:
Aya Barseem, Reem H Obaydo, and Samar H Elagamy present a 2025 paper on a cheap, green way to measure a diabetes drug called imeglimin in its tablets. Their method pairs the drug with a dye in acid, forming an orange pair whose colour strength tracks the drug amount. A phone camera then reads the colour.

Two phone apps were tested for reading the colour, and results were checked against a standard light-based instrument. Both phone routes gave straight-line readings across the tested range with good accuracy. The authors present the setup as a portable, low-cost option for routine quality checks in drug making, with less chemical waste than older methods.
pmc-12746843:
Atopic dermatitis, the itchy skin disease also called eczema, is driven by a tangled loop between nerves and the immune system. Zhongsong Zhang led a team reviewing how that loop works and how new treatments aim at it. Signals such as IL-31 and IL-4 talk both ways between skin, nerves, and brain, feeding the itch-scratch cycle that keeps the disease alive.

Fresh tools, from single-cell mapping to brain imaging and gut microbe profiling, are redrawing the map of these nerve-immune neighborhoods. The review gathers markers that could sort patients and track treatment, then surveys drugs old and new, from pathway blockers to microbe-based care. The authors argue that aiming at the nerve-immune axis could bring steadier, better-matched therapy.
pmc-12747543:
Shinhye Chung and co-authors hunt, in a 2025 study, the chemical fingerprints of prediabetes in Mexican Americans, and the genes and foods behind them. Prediabetes is a major public health concern, fed by many causes. Blood chemistry may reveal its approach earlier than glucose alone.

The team profiled small molecules in 482 adults from Starr County, Texas. Diet records covered six nutrient groups from a long food questionnaire. Statistical models tied each molecule to genes, then tested whether diet changed those links. Molecules tied to prediabetes emerged from the screen. The work aims at risk markers shaped by both inheritance and eating, in a community carrying heavy diabetes burden.
pmc-12748243:
Long Ma and co-authors report a rare spinal tumor case in a 2025 paper on a child with Ewing sarcoma, also called primitive neuroectodermal tumor. These fast-growing cancers of small round cells seldom appear in the spine, and their early signs can point doctors the wrong way.

The eleven-year-old boy arrived with an unsteady gait, growing back pain, weak legs, and trouble passing urine. Scans showed an extradural mass beside the upper thoracic spine that pushed the cord aside, first suggesting lymphoma. Only tissue examination after surgery confirmed the true diagnosis. The tumor later spread into the cord itself, underlining how much early recognition matters.
pmc-12748443:
Rhian Graham and five co-authors published a 2025 interview study with neurodivergent women who also carry a personality disorder diagnosis. Autism and ADHD are common in this group, yet mental health services rarely offer a clear care path for them. The team asked ten women about their experiences of those services.

Five themes emerged, covering staff skills and attitudes, access barriers, feeling involved, the support offered, and the impact of diagnosis. Women described misdiagnosis and services that did not adapt to their needs. The study sketches a better pathway: person-centred assessment, peer-led support, adapted talking therapies, and patients helping to design services. It also sets priorities for clinical practice and future research.
pmc-12748543:
Rajan Kumar and co-authors chart cerebral palsy in children in eastern India in a 2025 paper. Cerebral palsy is a leading cause of childhood disability, with varied forms and added conditions. The team studied children aged four to fourteen at a tertiary center over one year.

Among 127 children, the spastic form dominated at about three quarters of cases. Severe motor limits were present in nearly two thirds. Hand ability worsened in step with motor severity. Factors tied to severe cases included no cry at birth, newborn seizures, and jaundice. Added conditions were common, marking where early help is most needed.
pmc-12748843:
Meng, Hu, and Li build a system that writes Yongju opera text in its own style. Yongju is a regional opera form from Ningbo. The team first built a data set of 100 old scripts and 50 new scripts. They added 500 lyric audio clips from local sources. Two models then split the work of writing and styling.

One model drafts text that fits Yongju grammar from modern Chinese input. A second model adds dialect words and rhythm through style controls. Drafting took 33.32 minutes, about 57 percent faster than a standard baseline. Human raters gave high marks for dialect truth and art quality. Style transfer hit 97 percent accuracy in their tests.
pmc-12749343:
Xuyan Li and co-authors build in 2025 a terahertz sensor that sniffs ethanol in liquid without any labels or reagents. The detector is a patterned metamaterial: interlaced copper wires and nested double letter rings of a phase change oxide on a plastic film over a copper plate. A liquid drop on its surface shifts the device's absorption peak, and the shift's size reports what is in the drop.

A deep neural network tuned the structure's dimensions, reaching high absorption and strong shifts across working conditions. Simulations showed the peak sliding one way as drop volume grows, the other way as ethanol strength rises, and narrowing its spacing as temperature climbs. Field and current maps revealed the mechanism, including the oxide waking up when hot and steadying the read. The authors pitch the design for food safety checks, environmental monitoring, and biomedical sensing.
pmc-12749843:
Yao Xue, Chee Keong Tan, and Wai Peng Wong published this 2025 study on teaching rescue robots to cover unknown, wrecked terrain without running dry. After disasters, coverage path planning decides where a robot sweeps for survivors, and classic algorithms balk at rubble and surprise. Their learner, PERM-QN, wraps Q-learning with three upgrades.

A dynamic reward keeps coverage, path length, and energy use in shifting balance as the mission evolves. Prioritized replay rehearses the most instructive past moves, speeding convergence. A memory network recognizes familiar terrain shapes and reuses routes, cutting redundant wandering. In simulated disaster zones of rising complexity the system covered more ground, more completely, than traditional planners. The authors pitch it for real search-and-rescue fleets.
pmc-12749943:
Hongli Wang, Xiangyao Li, and Bosi Zhang build a safety method for chemical plants, where tangled processes can turn small faults into major accidents. Their 2025 paper merges two tools. The first, a systems-based process analysis, lists risk factors such as gear failure, operator error, and bad links between parts. The second tool weighs how those factors drive each other.

Joined together, the method ranks the factors and maps the paths along which trouble spreads. In a test case on ammonia production, sensor failure for heat readings and errors in the control software stood out as root causes. Failure of the actuators that carry out commands was the key end point. The mapped paths matched how the plant truly runs. Plants and regulators could use the ranking to spend safety funds where they count most.
pmc-12750843:
Gong and co-authors show a Schwann cell gene loss that sparks face pain in mice. Face pain hits 10 to 15 percent of grown hosts in life. It stays a hard ward case with dim root paths. Schwann cells wrap nerves, yet their role here was blurred. The gene in view, Lrp1, sits in those wrap cells. Mice with that gene cut from wrap cells grew sharp pain sense. Both push and heat tests showed the spike in their faces.

Gene reads from nerve hubs showed wide shifts in those mice. Paths for cell power, rust signs, and lime hold all shifted. Flux tests and chem checks backed the power shift in the hubs. Two pain gates, TRPV1 and TRPA1, ran high in the hubs. Those gates were primed past stock in the gene-cut mice.
pmc-12751243:
Lian Zhou and co-authors build a blood-test model to catch a spinal complication of brucellosis early, in a study published in 2025. Brucellosis spondylitis is usually confirmed by imaging, which can delay antibiotics. The team studied seventy-eight brucellosis patients in northwest China. Some had spinal involvement and some did not. Blood tests measured bone-turnover and inflammatory markers in both groups.

Patients with spondylitis showed higher PINP, a marker of bone formation, and lower IL-1beta than the others. A model combining age, back pain, standard inflammation tests, PINP, and IL-1beta separated the groups strongly in the first cohort. It held up respectably in a prospective check. When negative, it ruled out the complication with about ninety percent reliability. The authors offer it as a triage aid where imaging is slow.
pmc-12751343:
Tao Chen and co-authors package a plant compound for depression treatment in this 2025 study. Quercetin, found in many foods, shows antidepressant promise but reaches the brain poorly. The team wrapped it in tiny fat bubbles guided by borneol, a compound that helps cargo cross into the brain. They built and tested the loaded particles step by step.

The particles were round, stable, and released their cargo slowly. Cells took them up at nearly twice the rate of free quercetin. They shielded stressed nerve cells and calmed inflammatory signals in immune cells. In depressed mice, they eased behavior more than a standard drug in the reported tests. Safety checks looked clean.
pmc-12751443:
Jie Liao and co-authors connect blood inflammation ratios to how long a woman's reproductive life runs. Their 2025 analysis of nearly five thousand postmenopausal American women computes four indices that divide immune cell counts by protective HDL cholesterol. It sets them against reproductive lifespan, the years from first period to menopause.

All four indices pointed the same way: higher inflammation relative to HDL tracked a shorter reproductive span, in a straight-line dose pattern. Women in the highest third of the indices had spans shorter by roughly one to two years than the lowest third. The links ran stronger in women without diabetes or hypertension. Cross-sectional data cannot prove inflammation shortens ovarian life, and the authors say so. But the indices are cheap blood arithmetic. If they flag reproductive aging, they could focus monitoring where it matters most.
pmc-12752243:
Julia Koerber and co-authors map cannabis use among primary care patients with depression and anxiety in a 2025 Los Angeles study. The three conditions tangle together, yet few health systems ask about cannabis in a systematic way, so the links stay murky. This system screens routinely with a validated survey built into the medical record.

The team analyzed more than one hundred seventy thousand adult patients. They compared recent use, reasons for use, and risk of cannabis use disorder across patients with and without depression or anxiety diagnoses and related prescriptions. Systematic screening turns a hidden habit into chart data. The results can help primary care doctors counsel patients whose mental health and cannabis use may feed each other.
pmc-12752843:
Mahmud Mohammed, Tulio Fernandez-Medina, Manjunath Rajashekhar, Stephanie Baker, and Ernest Jennings review how well computers can outline jawbone in dental scans, in a 2025 paper. Dentists rebuilding lost gum bone need exact maps of the bone from cone-beam CT scans, and drawing those maps by hand is slow. The review gathered studies from the last five years that use machine learning for this outlining task, called segmentation.

From 834 papers found, 23 met the bar for inclusion. Deep learning methods, above all a design called U-Net, were the most common, and their accuracy scores ranged widely, from 76 to 98 percent overlap with hand-drawn maps. Only four studies used semi-automated methods. Bone with defects proved harder to outline than healthy bone. The authors call for better deep learning tools tuned to damaged bone, since exact maps guide regenerative treatment.
pmc-12753643:
Jae Hyung Woo and five co-authors probe how the brain picks between ways of learning in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Rewards can be learned by linking them to sights or to actions. Under uncertainty, the brain seems to run both systems at once. Some referee must weight them moment by moment. The team had monkeys play tasks with shifting uncertainty while models tracked their choices.

Monkeys with amygdala damage were compared with intact ones and with damage to a reward hub nearby. The amygdala set the starting balance between the two systems. It also proved key to adjusting that balance on the fly. The findings give the amygdala a managerial role in learning. Neuroscientists of decision making are the audience.
pmc-12753843:
Asia's summer monsoon is really two systems, and cave stones in Sichuan record how differently they behaved as the last-but-one ice age ended. Jingyao Zhao and seven co-authors read three finely dated stalagmite records spanning about one hundred and twenty-six to one hundred and thirty-nine thousand years ago, in this 2025 paper. Oxygen isotopes in the stone track the rains above.

Three contrasts separate the southern system from the eastern one. The south ran stronger in the warm age that followed than it does today, while the east stayed steady. The size of the isotope swing across the transition differed too. And during a cold snap, the south's signal drifted steadily while the east's held flat. The southern monsoon, the authors conclude, answers more sharply to heat gradients across the equator.
pmc-12755143:
Triyana Harlia Putri and co-authors present a 2025 scoping review of nursing care that can cut self-injurious behavior. Such behavior harms mental health and can raise the risk of suicide later. Nurses care for many people who self-injure, yet no review had gathered the nursing side of the evidence. The team searched five databases in June 2025, in English and Indonesian.

From a huge first pool, only four studies met the review's rules, covering work from 2015 to 2025. Four kinds of therapy stood out. Group psychological nursing fit group settings best, while a therapy called DBT fit hospitals. Teaching plus mindfulness-based therapy suited community care. A prayer practice called Dhikr was advised where it fits local culture. The authors say these options can guide mental health nursing.
pmc-12755243:
Ling-Li Gao and co-authors review how the gut and muscle talk to each other in sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with age. The illness lowers the quality of life for older adults and costs health systems a great deal.

Bacteria in the gut make products that help keep muscle in balance, while muscle sends out its own signals that shape the gut. In people with the illness, those muscle signals fall, gut variety drops, and harmful types grow, in a loop that feeds itself. The review covers ways to tune the gut that have raised muscle mass and function, and targets for new care.
pmc-12756443:
A staph germ that floods a dog's body can damage many organs at once, driven by its toxins and by stress on cells. Hanem El-Gendy and seven co-authors test whether a mucus-thinning drug can boost a standard antibiotic against that germ. Their 2025 study works in dogs with a lab-raised infection.

Five groups split the dogs: healthy, infected and untreated, and three treated sets. One set got the antibiotic alone, one got the thinner alone, and one got both. The team reads stress markers in blood, germ counts in tissue, and gene marks tied to the germ's attack and to the heart. Tissue slices show the harm or its repair. The pair's joint score is the heart of the test.
pmc-12757443:
Dorota Korsak and co-authors hunt for Cronobacter germs in Polish foods in a 2025 study. These germs live wide in nature and can sicken all ages, with babies and the old at most risk. The team tested 251 food samples: raw milk, milk powder, baby formula, dried herbs and spices, teas, and raw vegetables. They sorted finds by gene marks and by lab traits.

Germs turned up in 26 samples, about one in ten. Five species shared the finds, with Cronobacter sakazakii the most common. The team read the full genome of one strain from dried oregano, the first such food strain read in full in Poland. Set next to a strain from a fatal baby case, it held the same core harm genes. It also bore extra rings of DNA, one of a known harm class. The work warns that dry foods can carry risky strains.
pmc-12757943:
Akihiro Nishi and Jon Stone write in twenty twenty-five about functional neurological disorder, known as FND. People with FND may have seizures, weakness, tremor, or loss of sight. It is one of the most common conditions seen in nerve clinics. For a long time it was called hysteria and was often dismissed or shamed.

The authors take a view based on evolution. They note that brain scans for structure are most often normal in FND. Studies of brain function, though, point to changes in brain networks. There is now broad agreement that FND has clear signs that let doctors rule it in. Readers get a fresh frame for a condition that sits between nerve care and mental health care.
pmc-12764243:
Ming Wei and co-authors report a 2025 case where tissue growing outside the uterus turned cancerous in the abdominal wall. Endometriosis is a common chronic condition in which womb lining tissue grows where it does not belong. Though classed as benign, it can invade, spread, and return much like a tumor.

The case concerns a cancer of the endometrial type arising in abdominal wall endometriosis. The authors pair the case with a review of earlier reports. Their account warns doctors that a lump in a surgical scar can, rarely, hold cancer and needs careful checking.
pmc-12765943:
Imran Ibrahim Shaikh and eight co-authors review, in 2025 work, signal paths as drug marks for a bulge of the belly aorta. Such bulges can burst and kill, and surgery is near the sole fix, since birth paths stay half-known. Flare sits at the core: wall rework, guard cell rush, and muscle cell flaw.

Some paths fan the ill — four named chains — while three shield it. Two more play both sides by scene. Fresh arms eyed span gene-good drugs, grain-borne drug runs, and stem cell care. The team frames a path from cut-only care to drug-first guard.
pmc-12766843:
Courtney Kennedy and co-authors validate a phone app for frailty assessment in older adults in a 2025 study. The guided app scores frailty and muscle weakness across medical history, strength, thinking, nutrition, daily function, and social domains. It returns a total score plus risk flags to guide care, and it is freely available.

Community dwelling adults over sixty five used the app during geriatric clinic visits, helped by a nurse. Clinicians completed a paper frailty index from a full assessment at the same visit. Agreement between the app score and the clinic standard was the main validation test, alongside usability checks.
pmc-12767143:
Marina Senchukova, Evgeniya Zubareva, Natalia Saidler, and Lyubov Krivolapova published a study in 2025 on a new marker of the immune checkpoint protein PD-L1 in breast cancer cells. Earlier work suggested this marker may reveal how tumors progress and resist chemotherapy. The team stained tumors from one hundred and forty-eight newly diagnosed patients and compared marker patterns across cancer types and grades.

Missing marker inside tumor cells, paired with strong marker presence in immune cells, tracked aggressive features like high grade and hormone-negative status. One pattern marked chemo-resistant slow-type tumors, while its opposite predicted high chemo sensitivity. The authors say the combined readout could guide prognosis and drug choice.
pmc-12767243:
Mouth cancer is often caught late, and doctors lack good markers for how a given tumor will behave. Kurundhalingam Chinniah Pradheep Kumar and co-authors test an enzyme called PPT1 in tumor samples from 43 patients in this 2025 study, scoring how strongly the cancer cells produce it.

Stronger enzyme staining tracked closely with higher tumor grade, a sign of more aggressive disease. Links with age were weak, and sex and stage showed no clear ties. Given the small group, the authors call the results early. Still, the enzyme may become a useful warning marker if larger studies across more hospitals confirm the pattern.
pmc-12767443:
Meiying Zhu and a team of co-authors traced how a long noncoding RNA feeds a bile duct cancer's sugar burn and immune hide. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, deals with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, a fierce cancer with a poor outlook. The RNA, NKILA, was read in tumor samples by data scans. Its ties to two mito genes were set out. Cell lines and a mouse tumor graft then test its role in the flesh.

NKILA lifts the Warburg effect, the tumor's fast sugar burn, through that gene axis. It helps the tumor slip immune watch at the same time. Readers in liver cancer get a two front mark that could be hit by one drug aim.
pmc-12768643:
Shan Jiang, Bonny Parkinson, and Yuanyuan Gu weigh cost and fairness of wide gene screening for breast cancer risk in 2025. Inherited mutations drive a share of breast and ovarian cancers. The study compares screening all women with testing by family history alone. A lifetime model tracked costs and quality adjusted years. Income area groups framed the fairness side.

Screening at thirty saved money per health year gained. Screening at thirty five and forty still passed value tests. Later starts failed on cost and widened gaps. Early screening lifted average health and narrowed group gaps. The authors urge policy to favor the young start. Prevention gains and equity gains point the same way here.
pmc-12768743:
Daniela Gorski and co-authors pool observational evidence on long-acting dual therapy for HIV, where two-drug regimens replace daily handfuls of pills. Daily multi-pill schedules strain adherence, and long-acting injections promise relief. The open question is whether the simpler plans hold the virus down as safely over time.

Their 2025 network meta-analysis gathers longitudinal studies of dual regimens built on long-acting agents such as cabotegravir, rilpivirine, and lenacapavir. Virologic failure is compared across the network, while dropouts from side effects are pooled head by head. The synthesis is meant to rank the options on real-world evidence, giving clinics a map of which pairs keep working outside the polish of trials.
pmc-12768843:
Rodolfo Hernández and co-authors weighed in 2025 the costs and benefits of three treatments for lower pole kidney stones. Kidney stones are common in working-age adults. The options compared were keyhole surgery through the back, a flexible scope passed up the urinary tract, and shockwave treatment from outside the body. Data came from the UK PUrE randomized trials.

For stones of ten millimeters or less, the scope cost more and gained few quality-adjusted life years. Shockwave treatment had a ninety-nine percent chance of being cost effective at standard thresholds. For larger stones the scope again cost more on average and fared no better. The analysis helps funders judge which approach earns its price for each stone size.
pmc-12769543:
Xiaoyu Cui and Lu Liu model how weather moves reservoir water levels in a 2025 study. Hydropower depends on steady reservoirs, and climate change brings more extreme weather to unsettle them. The pair used daily water level records from seventeen reservoirs in China's Sichuan Province. They improved a benchmark model by letting temperature and rain act in curved, squared terms rather than straight lines.

Both weather factors drove level changes strongly, and in bent, nonlinear ways. The team then traced the trade-off rate between warmth and rain: how much extra rain equals a degree of heat. That rate itself shifts with conditions. A turning point appeared near seventeen centimeters of rain and thirteen and a half degrees. The authors flag that point for reservoir managers to watch. They offer the model as a tool for tougher, climate-ready water planning.
pmc-12770343:
Benson Thomas M and co-authors study in 2025 whether cash paid to mothers in India helps newborns. The scheme, named Janani Suraksha Yojana, pays women who give birth in health sites. The team used a large health survey from 2019 to 2021, covering 62,415 women in the less developed states grouped as EAG states.

About 54 percent of the women got the cash help. Those who did showed better care for their babies on most checks, such as early feeding and check-ups after birth. The authors used a matching method to compare like with like. Their results suggest the scheme lifts some early care, though some gains were small.
pmc-12770543:
Seven authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five on screening for thinking problems through speech. Fast, accurate checks for cognitive impairment are a major unmet need. Speech offers a cheap, non-invasive signal that software could screen at scale, but models must be explainable and must work on real-world recordings.

The team trained a random forest on features of speech from a standard benchmark set of two hundred ninety-one people. It caught about sixty-nine percent of cases while clearing about eighty-three percent of healthy speakers. They then checked the model on speech recorded in people's homes. Risk levels were split into bands to guide next steps.
pmc-12771143:
Zhang, He, Huang, and Zhong build a risk prediction model for autism spectrum disorder in a 2025 paper. Early identification of high-risk children can improve support and outcomes. The model aims to combine biological, psychological, and social factors.

The team screened many reviews and found a set of candidate risk factors. Four factors held up as independent predictors: adverse childhood experiences, preterm birth, antidepressant exposure in pregnancy, and antibiotic exposure around birth. A simple weighted formula was built from these factors. Testing in a Chinese hospital cohort gave good discrimination. Decision analysis also showed clinical benefit. The authors present the model as an evidence-based tool for early screening.
pmc-12771843:
Maryam Koopaie, Mahnaz Fatahzadeh, and Sajad Kolahdooz combined studies on using saliva chemicals to diagnose pancreatic cancer. The cancer is usually found late and current tests can be invasive or inaccurate early on. Saliva is easy to collect and carries many small molecules that might betray disease. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team searched many databases without language limits and kept the few diagnostic studies that met their rules. Quality was rated with a standard tool, and results were pooled across thousands of patients and controls.

Pooled accuracy was moderate to good, with sensitivity and specificity each near four fifths and an overall ranking score in a useful range. Panels that combined several saliva chemicals beat single markers by a clear margin. The authors present saliva testing as a promising, painless aid, while the small number of studies argues for larger confirmatory work.
pmc-12771943:
A 13-year-old boy with well-controlled asthma collapsed after playing soccer, with breathing failure, widespread hives, and blue skin. Five clinicians in Iran report the case in 2025. The picture suggested anaphylaxis tied to exercise, possibly with food as a partner trigger. At the hospital his coma score was the lowest possible, his pupils were wide, and his reflexes were gone. Scans showed brain swelling and oxygen starvation. Blood tests showed deep metabolic disturbance and high lactate.

Doctors gave fluids, brain protection, antibiotics, and seizure drugs, with full intensive support. The damage still advanced, and signs of brain death appeared three days after admission. The authors stress how hard such reactions are to reverse and call for research on prevention.
pmc-12772543:
Guillaume Roger and five co-authors wrote this review, published in 2025. It explains the case for high-dose eicosapentaenoic acid, a purified omega-3 fat from fish oil, in preventing heart and vessel disease. The target patients carry high triglycerides, a blood fat that keeps risk up even when cholesterol is treated.

Gene and population studies mark fat-rich particles as a true cause of artery disease, not a bystander. Trials show the high-dose fat cuts events in patients already on statins. The review sets out how the treatment fits beside strong cholesterol lowering, with a practical chart for combining therapies after a heart attack or syndrome. The authors present this pairing as the way to attack the leftover risk that statins leave behind.
pmc-12774343:
Paul Alumbugu Tsaku and a large team of co-authors published this clinical trial in 2025. pmc-12775543:
Vortex pumps are small and lift water high, but they waste more energy than most pump types. Computer flow tests showed a flawed twin swirl inside the pump at all flow rates.

A built test model gained height and output under standard load, while drawing less power. The study shows that case shape alone can trim losses that builders once took for granted. It also gives pump makers a clear shape rule to test on other sizes.
pmc-12775843:
Palak Gupta and co-authors reported a surgical study in 2025 from a large hospital in western India. Their subject is holes or gaps in the skull base, the bony floor under the brain. Such gaps can arise by accident or be made on purpose while removing a tumor. A poor repair can let fluid leak from around the brain or let infection in.

All repairs used several layers, mixing the patient's own tissue, graft material, and flaps of living tissue. Every repair held, with no repeat failures. Two serious problems did occur: one case of air trapped inside the skull and one case of vision loss. No patient got meningitis or a new leak after surgery.
pmc-12776243:
Yuting Luo and co-authors ask whether chemotherapy after surgery helps a rare bowel cancer, in a study published in 2025. The cancer grows in the duodenum, the first part of the small bowel, and is the commonest small bowel cancer subtype. Its rarity has left the value of post-surgery chemotherapy in dispute.

The gain was strongest in patients aged sixty-five or over and in those whose cancer had spread to lymph nodes or grown deep. The authors say these groups should be first in line for the added treatment.
pmc-12779443:
Ke Zhong and co-authors review how ageing blood vessels quietly undermine erections, and what might be done beyond today's pills. Standard drugs give relief but do not reverse the vessel ageing itself. pmc-12780243:

pmc-12780443:
Fatima Wilder, Miles McAllister, and six peers use maps to find the state zones where lung lump checks would do the most good. The work came out in 2025. The state is Massachusetts, in the far north-east of the land. Lung lump ends split hard by stock and by funds. To catch lumps young, when cuts and aimed drugs work, is the best lever. But take-up of checks is not the same in all zones.

pmc-12782343:
Nadia Sharif and co-authors screened in 2025 natural compounds by computer for multi-target drugs against Alzheimer's disease. pmc-12784143:
Jia Ying Jennell Koh and co-authors review just-in-time support for weight management in a 2025 scoping review. These phone-based interventions watch for the moment a person is most likely to slip, a craving, a skipped walk, and deliver help right then rather than on a fixed schedule.

The review maps a young field's habits and gaps for the next designers.
pmc-12784743:
Six authors, led by Yunfei Diao, test in 2025 two additives that may help pig egg cells grow in the lab. Growing eggs outside the body is key for breeding science, but the method still needs polish. A growth factor known to aid egg sac growth and fluid drawn from egg sacs were both candidates.

pmc-12785043:

The other tests whether the curve holds real thermal features worth reading. Both ship in ThermogramForge, a free web app that takes uploads and returns reports. pmc-12785843:
Ashokkumar Thirunavukkarasu and Ebtehal Mobarak Zawawi published a health study in 2025 on families caring for people with schizophrenia. The study ran in Jeddah, in western Saudi Arabia. Emotional strain scored highest among the five areas. Adult children caring for parents carried heavier burdens. Government workers reported lower burdens than others. The authors recommend workplace flexibility and financial help for caregivers.
pmc-12786243:

pmc-12786543:
Timur Buniatov and co-authors build a simple risk score for when a blocked small bowel needs surgery, in a study from 2025. The block is a common emergency, and the call between surgery and watchful care is often hard.

Five pre care facts split the groups: few past belly operations, low blood protein, free fluid on scans, air fluid lines on plain films, and a pinch point on CT. The weighted score split risk bands cleanly, from a fifth in the low band to near all in the high.
pmc-12786943:
Irina Zvereva and colleagues studied iron-loaded zeolite crystals in 2025. Zeolites have tiny ordered pores inside. Alkali etching can add larger pores too. Extra pores may help iron enter channels. Optical and surface changes were then measured.

Such changes suit light-driven catalysis. Pre-etching created a useful hierarchy of pores. The authors propose photocatalyst uses next. Cleaner chemical production could benefit. Iron placement inside pores was the core question.
pmc-12787043:
Jürgen Konradi and six co-authors report a team project that shortened intensive care stays for patients with breathing tubes in the neck, in a 2025 paper. A tracheal tube slows recovery and invites swallowing problems. Speech and language therapy led the swallowing and tube work.

New shared procedures were set up in one surgical intensive care unit, with more therapy staff added. The project group of 54 patients was compared with 58 earlier patients. Time with the tube fell from about 43 days to about 24 among those freed of it. Overall stay dropped from about 33 days to about 24. Team based therapy proved practical and effective.
pmc-12787943:
Alexander Gnutikov and co-authors unpick the parentage of a man-made wheat relative bred for hardiness. Their study appeared in 2025. The hybrid, Trititrigia cziczinii, came from crossing bread wheat with a wild wheatgrass, then crossing back to wheat. One outer marker region, though, leaned toward the wheatgrass parent, hinting at reshuffling or mixed sequences in the hybrid. Deep sequencing confirmed wheat-type copies dominate, with a small wheatgrass-like minority. The authors say knowing the true genomic mix guides using this hybrid in breeding.
pmc-12789543:
Michael Bekken and a large team track carbon flows when a drained peatland in Norway is flooded again. Their 2025 study runs two side-by-side sites in the boreal zone. Towers at both sites log carbon dioxide and methane flows from 2019 on. One site is rewetted in 2021 while the other stays drained. Statistical models fill gaps and build yearly balances for both gases at both sites.

Before rewetting, the two sites trade carbon at like, modest rates. In the first year after rewetting, both gas flows at the wet site jump. The second year stays high, though a bit lower. Model comparisons that mimic no rewetting credit the change to the water, not the weather. Two years on, added flows total a clear rise. Rewetting thus trades one climate gain for nearer-term gas costs that planners must count.
pmc-12791043:
Abhishek Walia and co-authors give a genome-level look at Jeevamrit, a fermented biofertilizer used across South Asia, as a tool to restore soil. They join shotgun metagenomics and genome assembly with two seasons of field trials. The test soil was badly degraded Himalayan rice soil.

Thirty good genomes carried genes for nitrogen fixation, phosphate release, potassium transport and plant hormone making. pmc-12796443:
Javad Aminian-Dehkordi, Mohammad Parsa, Andrew Dickson, and Mohammad Mofrad predict gut microbe communities with a graph model, in a paper published in 2025. Which microbes thrive together depends on how they feed and compete, not just on which are present. Models that only learn correlations miss those mechanisms. pmc-12797043:
Sri Nuryati and three co-authors wrote a 2026 study on protecting farmed shrimp from a harmful germ. Pacific white shrimp are a major farmed seafood, and the germ can kill stock fast. Farms often turn to antibiotics, but overuse of those drugs brings its own risks. The team tested leaf powder from the moringa tree as a natural option.
