Shrimp on the powder lived at higher rates and showed stronger immune responses than the control group. The lowest dose, half a gram per kilogram of feed, worked best and also aided growth. Gene tests showed that key defense genes switched on more strongly. The results back moringa as a low-cost shield for shrimp.
pmc-12797743:
Gang Xue and co-authors test whether teaching trauma orthopedics through real problems, aided by three-dimensional reconstructions of fractures, beats lectures. Visualization let students rotate the fracture in their minds before planning treatment. If the pairing wins, surgical teaching gains a tested template.
pmc-12800143:
Weihong Wu and colleagues report a 2025 study of roadbed filler made from coal gangue, a waste rock from mining. Roads need fill that survives endless wheel loads without sinking or cracking. pmc-12801543:
Sabri Kurtay, Mehlika Kuşvuran Kurtay, and Cuma Taşın compared childbirth care for Turkish and Syrian refugee teenagers in Türkiye. The paper calls for care pathways that close them.
pmc-12804943:
Rajini Srinivasan and co-authors build tighter switches for gene editing in cells in a 2025 paper. pmc-12808143:

pmc-12808243:

Tests on a four-rotor drone showed the system can spot faults well, a step toward safer automatic fleets.
pmc-12808643:

pmc-12809343:

pmc-12811243:

pmc-12811643:

pmc-12812043:

pmc-12812243:

pmc-12812443:

pmc-12812643:

pmc-12812743:

pmc-12812943:

pmc-12813043:

pmc-12813943:

pmc-12815743:

pmc-12815843:

pmc-12816743:

pmc-12817443:

pmc-12817543:

pmc-12818943:

pmc-12819743:

pmc-12821143:
Ersoy Oksuz and Bilgehan Demir, two authors writing in 2025, review drug overdose cases at their emergency unit. Overdose by accident or intent carries high death and harm rates. Emergency units see these patients first and bear the highest risk period.

pmc-12821243:
Shima Soleimani Sardou and co-authors compare in 2025 how well AI models and a human specialist sort mouth lesions from photos, aiming at earlier oral cancer detection. The cancer is a global burden, and its varied look makes early spotting hard. Photos taken inside the mouth offer a cheap screening route.

The data set held 518 clinic images gathered over 2009 to 2023 at a dental faculty in Kerman. Of these, 104 showed malignant lesions and 414 benign or normal tissue, all confirmed by a pathology specialist. Three pretrained deep networks were tested on the set. A model that matches the specialist could triage photos in clinics with no specialist nearby. The authors report how close each model came.
pmc-12821443:
Toshiaki Tanaka, Shunichi Sugihara, and Takahiro Miura compared two robot exoskeletons on knee motion after stroke, in this 2025 pilot study. Two patients walked on a treadmill with no aid and with each device. Sensors on body and robot recorded joint angles at the weak knee.

Both devices improved knee motion. Angle error roughly halved for each patient under aid. One device, which syncs to the walker's own rhythm, gave smoother timing than the other, which keys off muscle signals. The authors stress the gap reflects control style, not rank. They offer sensor-based sync checks as a fair way to compare aids.
pmc-12821543:
Aronis and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on shoulder strength in standing men. Overhead reaching strength matters for work design, rehab, and wearable support gear. Fourteen healthy men pushed with greatest effort at eight arm angles. A force sensor read shoulder torque at each angle. Wires on the skin tracked four shoulder and arm muscles. Torque fell steadily as the arm rose higher. One side shoulder muscle fired harder at higher angles.

A chest muscle's activity fell sharply as the arm rose. Two other muscles held high, steady activity across angles. The data set gives reference values for healthy male shoulders. The authors say the values can guide ergonomic checks and support gear design. They caution the sample is small and male only.
pmc-12821843:
Darci Phillips and co-authors explore, in twenty twenty-five, how parents view cardiovascular health for their families. Parents' views shape children's lifelong heart health, yet they are rarely studied. The team ran semi-structured interviews with twenty-one parents of children under eighteen, plus four children. Answers were coded thematically with a constant comparison method until no new themes appeared. Child interviews were analyzed separately, for context on how youth see heart health and how families talk about it.

Eight themes emerged, covering definitions of heart health, information sources, family and community roles, experiences, resources, and emotional links. Parents named real barriers, including limited access to fitness options, the head text notes. The findings aim to guide intergenerational heart health programs.
pmc-12821943:
Aishwarya Guha and co-authors show, in a 2025 study, how platelets educated by a breast tumor can feed the tumor's stem cells. Platelets are blood components that seal wounds. Tumors educate them, and educated platelets help cancers spread. Their grip on breast cancer stem cells, the seed cells that regrow tumors, was not mapped.

The team drew platelets and tumor cells from patients with two breast cancer types, plus mouse models and cell lines. Educated platelets bore more of an adhesion protein, P-selectin, and clung to the stem cells through its partner PSGL1. Under their influence, stem cells grew more aggressive: they seeded tumors, resisted drugs, and invaded. Aspirin calmed the platelets and cut that influence. The adhesion fires a signaling chain involving WNT and beta-catenin that steadies stemness. Blocking parts of the chain by gene silencing confirmed its role.
pmc-12822043:
Nine authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five that shortens a quality-of-life questionnaire. The full measure has sixty-nine items and covers well-being across four elements and eighteen domains. A shorter form would be quicker for patients and clinics to use, if it stayed just as sound.

The new form, called SigQOLM-36, keeps thirty-six items and the same structure as the original. The authors report that its scores hang together very well overall and acceptably in every domain. Checks on how the items group and how the model fits also came out strong. They conclude the short form can stand in for the long one.
pmc-12822143:
Han Liang and co-authors show a tiny RNA dial worsening fatty liver disease in cells and patients in a 2025 study. The microRNA miR-199b-5p ran high in blood from ninety fatty liver patients versus one hundred ten controls. Its level tracked body mass and blood fat measures closely enough to flag the disease.

In liver cells fat-loaded with oleic acid, blocking the microRNA restored viability, calmed inflammation, and cut oxidative stress. Its target is SIRT1, a protective enzyme that ran low in patients and moved opposite the microRNA. The pair forms a candidate axis for diagnosis and therapy.
pmc-12822343:
Yuyang Gao and Char Leung test a COVID vaccine's benefit in patients with schizophrenia in a 2025 study. This group carries weaker immune defenses and faced heavy risk during the pandemic. Whether the Sinovac vaccine cut hospital deaths for infected patients with schizophrenia was not established.

A Brazilian national flu surveillance database supplied the patient records. The retrospective study compared vaccinated and unvaccinated patients admitted with COVID-19. Adjusted models weighed death in hospital against background traits and illness severity. Standard checks graded the model's fit and discrimination. Results speak to a group often left out of vaccine trials. Clear evidence can guide targeted vaccination drives for psychiatric inpatients and outpatients alike.
pmc-12822843:
A blood clot in the lung usually causes breathlessness or chest pain, but it can look like a brain problem instead. Tarun Rana and co-authors reported such a case in 2025. A healthy 41-year-old man came to emergency care after five days of fainting, giddiness, and brief blurring of vision, while brain and eye exams showed nothing wrong.

A bedside heart scan showed a strained right side of the heart, and a chest scan confirmed clots in both lungs. Blood tests pointed to an inherited lack of protein C, a natural brake on clotting. The man was treated with blood thinners and recovered fully. The authors urge suspicion of lung clots in unexplained fainting.
pmc-12824143:
Fentaye Kassawmar and three co-authors surveyed the use of medicinal plants in Meketewa District, in northwestern Ethiopia, in a 2025 ethnobotanical study. Traditional medicinal plants remain an important source of health care for rural communities there, where access to modern medical services is limited. The team collected information from 360 informants across five kebeles, or sub-districts, in different agroecological zones.

The study documented 76 medicinal plant species in 46 families. Fabaceae was the largest family, and herbs were the most common growth form. Most species were used to treat human ailments, while others treated livestock or both. Most plants came from natural forests. Crushing was the most common preparation method, and oral administration was the most common route. The authors call for conservation of these plants and for further laboratory testing of their effects.
pmc-12824243:
Taya Lee and five colleagues published a device study in two thousand twenty-five on treating neck-of-womb cell changes by injection. The therapy injects an alcohol-based gel into the cervix to kill abnormal cells. It is aimed at poorer countries where surgery is scarce.

First the team checked that pig cervix tissue behaves like human tissue; stiffness tests matched. Then they compared two injectors that work with a standard examination tool. Shots placed at least ten millimetres deep, with under two millilitres of gel, leaked less and cracked the tissue less. An extender injector caused fewer cracks than a plain needle one. The findings set practical rules for future clinical use.
pmc-12825943:
Munawar, Zhu, Machado, and Zhou review the many side effects of plant scents in farm fields, in an article published in 2023. Plants release volatile chemicals that do far more than perfume the air. Farmers already exploit them in push-pull systems, where one crop's scent repels pests and another's lures them away. But these chemicals ripple through the whole ecosystem. They can summon pest predators, warn neighboring plants, or shift soil life.

The authors read this through pleiotropy, one trait with many effects. Optimizing a scent strategy for the pest alone may backfire through its other effects. Mapping the ripples could make scent-based farming stronger and safer. The review argues for ecology-wide accounting before scaling these methods. Chemical-free pest control needs such honesty to last.
pmc-12827143:
Preeya Achari and co-authors test a sound-based treatment for bone cancer on limbs taken from dogs, in work whose head dates it to 2025. The treatment, histotripsy, uses focused ultrasound pulses to break up tumor tissue without heat or cuts. The team asked whether the pulses weaken the bone around a tumor, which would limit its use.

Limbs from ten dogs with osteosarcoma, an aggressive bone cancer, supplied tumor and healthy bone samples. Some samples were treated and some left alone, then all were pressed and bent until they failed. Scans mapped the inner structure of the tumors. Treated bone held up as well as untreated bone in both groups, while tumor bone varied a lot from sample to sample. The authors say the method spares bone strength.
pmc-12827343:
Siyuan Liu, Hongkun Zhao, Yang Chen, Fanmin Kong, and Kang Li build a network for reading emotion across text, audio, and video in a paper from 2025. Older methods use fixed windows, which miss feelings that play out at different scales. Signals from voice and face can also clash with the words. Their network lets text guide the other channels. A transformer block scans features at several patch sizes and routes them adaptively.

A second module uses text-based memory to filter out conflicting audio and video signals. A channel fusion step then merges the streams for a final language model. On two standard data sets, the system beat most prior methods. The authors highlight its handling of mixed signals.
pmc-12827643:
Trung-Loc Ho and co-authors find a call sign that brakes bone-eat cells in a 2025 study. Those cells chew old bone so new bone can grow, a fair trade that turns to loss in joint ills, thin bone, and spread cancer.

The sign in view is famed for herding guard cells, but its part in bone craft was not known. In dish tests it curbed the birth of bone-eat cells from their seed stock. It dulled their ring of grip, sped the death of ripe cells, and cooled two fire paths in the cell. Dock sums and pull tests show why: the sign jams the lock where the growth call meets its dock, so the call can't land. The authors name the sign a fresh brake on bone loss.
pmc-12827743:
Nahida Akhter and co-authors test a training and mentoring plan meant to help nurses prevent lung infection in intensive care, published in the head as 2025. The infection, tied to breathing machines, is a known risk for very ill patients. Nurses play a central role in the daily care steps that lower that risk.

The study ran in the intensive care unit of a large hospital in Bangladesh, before and after the plan. Nurses got skill-based training in proven care for this infection, plus support from trained mentors. A structured survey tracked skill, knowledge, practice, drive, and work engagement. The design lets the team judge whether the plan raised nurse competence and, with it, the quality of patient care.
pmc-12829043:
Miaoxin Liu and co-authors present a 2025 study on extreme temperatures and heart hospitalizations in Lanzhou, China. Heat and cold both strain the cardiovascular system, often with delayed effects. The team modeled daily admissions against temperature with a method that handles lags and curved responses. Subgroups by age and sex were checked for sensitivity.

Extreme cold raised admission risk by about 16 percent. Moderate cold, moderate heat, and extreme heat each raised it too, by smaller margins. Cold bit harder than heat overall. Women and under-65s were most sensitive to deep cold. Men and under-65s led the sensitivity to extreme heat. The authors urge weather-aware hospital planning and warnings pitched to the sensitive groups.
pmc-12829143:
Katelyn Brehon and co-authors explore telerehabilitation for public safety personnel with posttraumatic stress injuries, in this 2025 Europe PMC study. Firefighters, paramedics and police face regular trauma exposure that can leave them unable to work. The pandemic pushed their rehabilitation online, mostly to video calls, raising questions about access, safety and quality.

The team interviewed thirty-four people: personnel, clinicians and decision-makers. Three themes emerged: care must respond to each person's context, safety priorities shift over time, and certain facets of care make treatment feel credible. Remote care offers flexibility, but clinicians may miss subtle cues and build alliance more slowly. A person-centered approach is urged.
pmc-12829243:
Artur Plonka and co-authors track blood markers in pro volleyball players before a season in a 2025 study. The final pre-competition block loads athletes hard. Blood chemistry can show how bodies absorb that load. Twelve female players from a top Polish league took part.

Blood was drawn four times across eight weeks of mixed technical and strength work. Muscle enzymes, vitamins, and hormones were assayed by standard lab methods. Muscle stress enzymes shifted clearly across the block. Folate and vitamin D forms also moved with training. Cortisol swings hinted at stress balance shifts. The panel may help coaches tune load and supplements before league play starts.
pmc-12830743:
Artem Oganov and Maksim Kostenko present a simple chemistry model in 2025 for predicting which pairs of elements form stable compounds. Since the time of Linus Pauling, scientists have used a trait called electronegativity to guess such behavior. Prior models worked only for narrow classes of compounds or grew complex when stretched further.

Their model gives each element just two numbers, one for electronegativity and one for chemical mismatch. Values fitted from many computed formation energies follow clear patterns across the periodic table. The model explains several odd cases, such as why reactive alkali metals form few compounds with most elements. Noble metals, by contrast, form stable compounds with most elements in this picture.
pmc-12830943:
Junhao Han and a large team show how one central light source can feed fast data links at the edge of a network. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Small sites such as edge computing rooms need high capacity but have little space, and adding more light channels runs into noise and weak signal quality.

The team used a tiny chip device that makes a comb of laser lines from one source. With it they sent data at very high rates on a single line and core. A wider setup with sixteen comb lines pushed the total far higher. Adding shaping chips and amplifiers shrank the whole system to about a hundredth of its size while still delivering strong rates. The work points to compact light gear for modular data centers.
pmc-12831243:
Eugenia Barone and nine co-authors explore why sexual functioning varies so widely among women with eating disorders. Body trusting and need for approval are core traits in eating disorder psychology, yet their links to sexual desire were poorly studied. The cross sectional study covers 348 women with anorexia, bulimia, or binge eating disorder.

Participants complete measures of sexual function, body awareness, and attachment style. Mixture regression finds two clusters with opposite patterns. In one cluster, higher body trusting and need for approval link to lower sexual desire. In the other cluster, both traits link to higher desire. Structural modeling confirms the split pathways. The authors argue that treatment should account for subgroup profiles, not averages.
pmc-12831343:
Jessica L Kulberg and three co-authors report the first detection of alphacoronaviruses in the small Indian mongoose, in this 2025 study. Relatives of these viruses infect dogs and cats and have jumped between species before. Mongooses scavenge widely and could carry pathogens, yet no one had checked what coronaviruses circulate in them.

The team screened droppings from fifty-three mongooses on the Caribbean island of Saint Kitts. Sixteen samples, about thirty percent, tested positive. Reading three viral genes showed wide variety among the mongoose viruses, signs of at least two past reshuffling events, and a family placement inside the dog virus lineage. Key grip features for entering host cells were preserved. The authors urge wider wildlife checks of this kind.
pmc-12831443:
Tayseer Afifi and seven co-authors review who received a camera exam of the upper gut in Gaza Strip hospitals, and what those exams found. Their 2025 study reads records for 1,159 patients scoped between 2017 and 2022. The exam, called EGD, threads a camera through the mouth to view the food pipe, stomach, and upper bowel.

Belly pain high in the abdomen was the top reason for the exam, given by over half the patients. Most exams ran with local numbing and a calming drug. The most common finding was widespread stomach inflammation, in about twenty-nine percent of cases. Growths appeared in just over two percent. Reflux-linked changes were also common. The authors say the data map the local burden of gut disease in a setting with scarce resources.
pmc-12834943:
Elizabeth Batsel and co-authors show in 2025 that a single growth gene can wake up the growth program in adult nerve cells. Young nerve cells grow their long fibers well, but mature cells lose that power, which blocks repair after spinal injury. The gene, Sox11, fades as cells mature.

Forcing the gene back on in mature mouse tract cells reshaped their gene activity on a large scale. The new pattern closely matched that of young, pre-connection cells and stayed stable over time. The switch worked just as well in cells hurt long before. The work names a potent lever for future repair research.
pmc-12835143:
Kannaiyan Neelavannan and eight co-authors measure microplastic pollution in three high-altitude lakes of the central Himalayas, and tie it to how the surrounding land is used. The lakes, Nainital, Bhimtal, and Garudtal in the Kumaun region, range from busy and urban to remote. The team sampled surface water at twenty-four points in all.

Microplastics turned up in every sample, even in isolated Garudtal. Counts were highest in Nainital, the most urban lake, at about 813 particles per cubic meter, and lowest in Garudtal at about 175. Most particles were fibers, and most were polyester, followed by polypropylene. Blue and pink particles dominated the colors. Larger particles, one to five millimeters, made up about half the catch. Pollution scores marked the lakes as lightly contaminated overall, but abundance rose with local development, waste handling, transport, and fishing. The authors call for tighter local waste control.
pmc-12835443:
Eleanor Stevenson, Jill Sergison, Kevin McEleny, and Eilis Moody argue that female partners carry a hidden load in male factor infertility in a 2025 perspective. Male factors drive about 30 to 50 percent of infertility cases worldwide. Men are now more often included in research and counseling, yet their partners' experience stays little examined.

Women often face both the treatment procedures and the emotional weight of the man's diagnosis. Men may read the diagnosis as a threat to manhood, feel shame, and stay silent. Partners then disclose less to family and friends, partly to shield the man from stigma. The authors propose ways to support both partners' emotional needs.
pmc-12836943:
Nevra Karamüftüoğlu and co-authors test whether parents who understand oral health raise children with healthier mouths, in a 2025 study. Tooth decay in children tracks family habits closely. Parents control brushing, snacks, and dental visits. Their own oral health literacy may set the ceiling for care. A validated scale measured that literacy in this study.

More than two hundred parent-child pairs at a dental clinic took part. Children's hygiene status was compared with parent traits. Parental education and employment linked clearly to cleaner child mouths. Literacy scores added their own signal beyond schooling. Dental teams gain a case for teaching parents, not just children. Simple chair-side lessons could pay off across the family.
pmc-12837043:
Wan and co-authors test whether poor sleep carries the effect of childhood trauma into depression in teens with bipolar disorder. Trauma in childhood worsens bipolar disorder in adolescence, above all by deepening depressive symptoms. The steps between early trauma and later depression, though, were still unclear to clinicians.

Sleep disturbance is a strong candidate for the middle step. The study enrolled 426 adolescents with bipolar disorder and measured trauma history, sleep quality, and depression severity. Statistical mediation tests checked if sleep problems explained the trauma link. A confirmed path would make sleep care a clear target for these teens.
pmc-12837343:
Takahiro Sanada and eleven co-authors hunt for image clues that reveal hidden tumor in treated brain cancer. Glioblastoma often returns after treatment, and one drug used against it makes tumors stop lighting up on scans even where cancer persists. Those dark regions are hard to judge. The team mined hundreds of numerical features from scans of twenty-four patients whose tumors changed under the drug, looking for features that mark the hidden cancer.

Dozens of features stood out. One texture feature from standard scans carried the model: it predicted the hidden tumor with high accuracy in the drug-treated group. Checked against a second group scanned with a special tracer, the same model did moderately well. Rebuilt images using the features also showed the hidden regions in newly diagnosed patients. The authors say such scan mining could help doctors judge treatment response where the eye cannot.
pmc-12837543:
David Mantle, Neve Cufflin, Mollie Dewsbury, and Iain Hargreaves review blood-brain barrier and neuronal model systems for studying coenzyme Q10, a compound that helps cells make energy. Supplements of the compound have been tried in neurological disorders with mixed results. One snag is that the barrier between blood and brain lets the compound through far more readily in rodents than in humans. That gap may explain why animal wins fade in clinical tests.

The review weighs cell culture and 3D cellular models as closer stand-ins for the human barrier. It covers models of the barrier itself and of neurons, and how the compound acts on mitochondria and lysosomes. Interactions with vitamin E and selenium get a look too. A final part shows a neuronal model used to test supplement effects in a deficiency state. The authors back such models for the next round of work.
pmc-12839243:
Lusine Harutyunyan and co-authors gather the scattered record of a rare gene syndrome in a 2025 review. Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome stems from faults in the ADNP gene and affects development across many body systems. A landmark 2019 paper described seventy-eight patients, and case reports have piled up since without a synthesis. The team reviewed them all under standard guidelines.

They found 105 people across thirty-four papers. Sixty-six had both clinical and genetic workups in the reports. The pooled picture sharpens known features like developmental delay, eye problems, and heart defects. Eye findings in particular gain detail from the added cases. The review gives clinicians a fuller checklist of what this syndrome can include.
pmc-12839843:
Mihaela Cozma and six co-authors study how pituitary tumors and their blood vessels grow in step, in a 2025 paper. Whether tumor cells and vessel lining cells divide together was in dispute. The team stained 109 tumors for vessel and growth markers and read them with a digital image tool. A growth signal gene and protein were also gauged.

Growth rates in tumor and vessel cells tracked each other closely. Two tumor types, one that makes prolactin and one that makes no hormone, showed high vessel growth. The growth signal's gene and protein levels tied to the tumor growth rate. Hormone type shaped the pattern in mixed ways. The authors back digital reads for risk sorting.
pmc-12841843:
Nada Abdennour and co-authors tested how trap choice and crop stage shape insect catches in 2025 in Tunisian tomato fields. Knowing which insects are present, and when, underpins pest control and pollination services. Four trap types were run across four growth stages of the crop.

About seventeen hundred seventy insects from seven orders and thirty-one families were caught, with wasps and bees the largest group. Yellow pan traps caught the most diverse sets, while Malaise traps caught the least. Diversity peaked at planting and fell sharply by harvest. Pollinator families dominated at flowering, and parasitoid wasps during fruit growth. Trap type and crop stage together explained a clear share of community change.
pmc-12844843:
The authors hunt gene variants in Chinese Holstein cattle that change the odds of catching a leukemia virus and the amount of virus carried. Their 2025 study types one immune gene in two hundred eighty-nine cattle from Shandong Province. The virus is the top tumor disease of cattle worldwide.

Twenty-eight known variants of the gene turned up. One variant tracked with higher infection risk. Another tracked with low virus load, and farms richer in that variant showed lower average loads. Virus load serves as a gauge of disease advance and spread risk. The authors say breeding choices could exploit these variants. They frame the work as a first for this gene in Chinese Holsteins.
pmc-12845443:
Takafumi Tanei and co-authors follow migraine patients who chose their own course of drug treatment in 2025. The drugs are monthly shots that block a peptide linked to migraine pain. The study asks how many people stay on them, stop, or start again when free to choose.

Of more than a thousand patients screened, 146 met the rules and were tracked. About half were still on treatment after two years. Of those who stopped, most chose to start again. Scores for head pain impact and life quality fell at each check. The team found no clear trait that split those who resumed from those who quit.
pmc-12847843:
Yong-Woo Jun and co-authors trace in a 2025 study a DNA damage loop that drives nerve death in ALS and related dementia. Most cases share TDP-43 clumps, but other shared drivers stay murky. Lab grown neurons from patients offer a window on those shared paths.

Patient neurons showed low SIRT1 and high modified p53, alongside raised DNA damage. Adding SIRT1 back rescued the neurons and cut the modified p53 signal. Damage also lifted p53 marking and levels of the repair protein Ku80. Silencing p53 or Ku80 rescued neurons and restored SIRT1 in turn. Fruit fly eyes confirmed the loop's power in a living model as well.
pmc-12848043:
Ranran Fang and co-authors built a cooler that works even at water's boiling point, in a 2025 paper. Their trick rests on a surface that holds a thin water film in tiny structures. On that surface, water turns to steam at the surface without forming bubbles, even at full boil. The team used this effect to drive a dew point cooler, a design that chills air by evaporation.

The cooler cut a hot air stream from well over four hundred degrees down to below room temperature. It also worked at milder heats, taking air from warm to cool in one pass. Such range is rare for evaporation coolers, which usually fade as heat climbs. The authors point to uses in power plants, engines, and the vast computer halls that run AI systems. All of those sites throw off heat that is now mostly wasted.
pmc-12849143:
Zunqi Hu and co-authors explain in 2025 one way stomach cancer learns to resist the drug cisplatin. Immune cells called M2 macrophages sit near tumors and shed tiny parcels. Those parcels carry a small RNA, miR-668-3p, which the team found raised in drug-resistant tumor tissue.

Cancer cells take in the parcels and the RNA with them. The RNA silences a gene called ETS1, which lowers a growth receptor, EGFR. That drop switches on autophagy, the cell's self-eating cleanup, which helps the cells survive the drug. The chain held in cell tests and in mouse tumors. Blocking the small RNA is the authors' proposed route to restore drug sensitivity.
pmc-12849343:
Hyunjung Lee and co-authors ask how few blood samples can still pin down a tuberculosis patient's exposure to the drug moxifloxacin. Full drug-level curves burden patients, so clinics use limited sampling guided by population pharmacokinetic models. The catch: a model built elsewhere may not hold up in a new group of patients.

The team gathered seven published models and tested them against drug readings from more than a hundred patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. They scored each model's prediction errors, then used the best performers to design a lean sampling plan. Careful validation first, they show, keeps drug monitoring both light and trustworthy.
pmc-12849443:
Mohammad Aadil and colleagues report a malignant neck artery-body tumour in a young woman, with a literature review. Their 2025 case report covers a rare growth that is usually benign and slow-growing.

An eighteen-year-old from a non-mountainous region presented with a painless neck swelling growing gradually for two and a half years. The firm, pulsing lump sat in the front triangle of her neck with a palpable vibration. Imaging established the diagnosis, and complete surgical removal followed. Tissue examination confirmed the tumour type with spread to nearby lymph nodes, which established malignancy. The authors note the rarity of malignant change and its occurrence in so young a patient.
pmc-12852743:
Sathya R and A Valaramathi build an agent-based system to spot diabetic retinopathy in eye scans. The disease is a leading cause of vision loss, and early catches save sight. Standard learning systems classify well but explain little and adapt poorly across patients. Their framework, AADR-AI, gives the analysis to a team of cooperating agents that blend convolutional and transformer networks under a decision fusion layer.

The agents act with autonomy, reacting to each image and adjusting their feature learning to the patient's own pattern. In tests on standard datasets, the system reached accuracy up to 96.7 percent with lower computing cost than rivals. The authors credit the agent design for real-time handling of varied image quality and disease stages. They present it as a step toward decision support that doctors can question and trust.
pmc-12852843:
Igor Karnaukhov and E. Krasovskii study the ground state of electrons confined to a one-dimensional chain where the particles interact. Working from an exact solution of their model, they map the full phase diagram and compute special zero-energy states, called Majorana functions, that sit at the ends of a finite chain.

A winding number marks the liquid's topological character. The diagram holds two topological phases with different winding values, a plain insulating phase, and three sharp transition points, and computer calculations back the algebra. Edge states of this kind draw interest because protected boundary modes are a route toward fault-tolerant quantum devices.
pmc-12853843:
Ipek Bulut and co-authors find a lever against drug-proof prostate cancer in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Once the cancer stops answering hormone therapy, taxane drugs are a mainstay, but resistance grows. The team built resistant cell models and screened epigenetic drugs.

Blockers of the Menin protein restored taxane power, halting cells at a division checkpoint and triggering death. Removing Menin hurt only resistant cells and stopped resistance from forming in fresh ones. Gene and binding studies tied Menin to the mTOR growth pathway. Pairing an mTOR blocker with the taxane worked even better together. Animal tests backed the idea. The authors propose the combo for refractory cases.
pmc-12854343:
Rafat Sultana and co-authors assess mouth health in pregnancy and test a short screening tool in this 2025 study. Hormone shifts during pregnancy can harm teeth and gums, yet oral checks are often skipped in prenatal care. The team used a fourteen-item screening tool alongside a standard oral-health questionnaire and a clinical exam.

One hundred pregnant women took part at several centers. About a third were flagged as at risk of poor oral health, and just over half had seen a dentist in the past year. The screening tool caught most women who truly had problems, though it also flagged many who did not. The authors conclude the tool works well for a first check in pregnancy. They also stress that oral care should stay part of routine care before birth.
pmc-12855843:
Qing Zhao and co-authors speed up precise satellite positioning in a 2025 paper. The BeiDou service PPP-B2b gives sharp fixes but settles slowly, which limits live use. Their fix joins wide lane ambiguity resolution with help from low orbit satellite fleets.

First they pull bias terms for GPS and BeiDou from an uncombined model that heeds clock quirks. Then they fake data for two low orbit fleets of about a hundred craft each. Four test tiers show each trick helps alone, and both together help most. Start fixes jump to fine scale at once, and settle time falls from about twenty minutes to a minute or two.
pmc-12855943:
A poultry germ that drains farm profits may yield to a new vaccine target, in a 2025 study by Luru Zhao and co-authors. Mycoplasma synoviae, listed by the world animal health body, spreads among flocks and resists cheap fixes: flock cleanup is slow, and antibiotics meet growing resistance.

The team screened the whole pangenome with reverse vaccinology, a computational hunt for proteins the immune system can see. Three candidates were chosen and tested as subunit vaccines. A foot pad challenge model scored lesions to judge protection. One protein, VY930, stood out, triggering strong antibody and cellular responses in immunized birds and beating the other candidates. The work offers a concrete candidate for a vaccine industry badly in need of one.
pmc-12859143:
Xu Han and a large team use inverse design to pack light circuits far more densely on lithium niobate chips. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The base film is prized for light work but hard to shrink to silicon-like density. The team used math search to shape tiny parts that split, cross, and bend light in many modes at once.

Built parts took just a small chip area yet held more than ten light path parts. A test chip sent data in many modes and, with built-in speed shifters, hit fast rates per lane. The team claims a ten-fold jump in part density for this film. Wide use in data links is the aim.
pmc-12859843:
Fernando and co-authors reviewed what helps and what hinders family doctors giving end-of-life care in poorer countries, in a paper published in 2025. In such countries, specialists in comfort care are scarce, so primary care doctors carry much of that work. The review gathered studies that asked those doctors about their experience. It followed a standard method for systematic reviews and searched seven databases. Both number-based and story-based studies were included and merged.

The synthesis sorts the findings into supports and barriers. Supports include training, teamwork, and community trust. Barriers run from drug access and time pressure to unclear rules and emotional strain. Knowing the pattern lets health systems fix the worst blocks first. The authors aim their summary at planners who must build palliative care on a thin specialist base.
pmc-12859943:
Yanan Niu and ten co-authors study the genes behind flag leaf thickness in wheat and how that trait links to yield. Leaf size traits get much past study, but leaf thickness has had far less. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team measured thickness directly in a large set of wheat lines bred from two parents. Leaf traits rose along with spike length, grain count per spike, and grain weight and size. The authors map gene spots tied to thickness and to yield parts, with one main spot for thickness found near spots for other traits. The results can guide breeding for higher yield.
pmc-12860143:
Sichao Ma and six co-authors review how fat and immunity conspire in a kidney disease in a 2025 paper. In membranous nephropathy, misdirected antibodies coat the kidney's filters and summon attack proteins that wound the filter cells. It is a top cause of heavy protein loss in adults.

The review argues the immune assault and the body's fat handling feed each other. Fat rafts in the filter cell's skin may stage the antibody attack. Burned fat particles from the blood fan the inflammation. Fat-clogged immune cells, meanwhile, keep making antibodies. Fat levels track disease severity in the clinic, and fat-lowering drugs show early promise, making the crosstalk a treatment target.
pmc-12860443:
Jing Zhang and Haitao Fan use graph neural networks to map how older adults with long-term illness use health care in rural northwest Yunnan. Their 2025 study covers ethnic minority areas where demand is rising but use is uneven. Past work looked at disease mixes and missed how care paths shift over place and time.

The team built a graph linking patients, clinics, and land units, then let attention-based models learn from care paths. The gaps were stark: one prefecture averaged 68 minutes to reach care against 29 in another, and one mountain unit scored 0.31 on coverage. The model beat a strong standard tool at flagging high-risk patients. The authors propose mobile care points and shared nodes across regions to close the gaps.
pmc-12860543:
Zitong Yu and co-authors present CTLESS in 2024, a way to correct heart scans without a separate CT scan. Heart perfusion scans need a correction for tissue that dims the signal. That fix usually needs CT, which adds dose, cost, and a risk of misaligned images.

CTLESS learns the needed map from scattered photons in the scan itself, using a deep network trained on CT data. The map is split into regions, each given a fixed dimming value. The method was tested on past patient scans without names attached. If it holds up, clinics could correct scans with less dose and simpler gear.
pmc-12861643:
Helen Robinson tells her story of living with fibromyalgia in this 2025 first-person account. Her illness began in late 2013 with chronic pain in her neck and shoulders and a general feeling of being unwell. Scans and blood tests came back normal, and physiotherapy made the pain worse rather than better.

Robinson describes returning to her doctor again and again, convinced something was wrong, and once being told the doctor did not know what more she wanted. Pain and fatigue spread, depression and anxiety followed, and she eventually had to give up a job she loved, spending most days in bed yet unable to sleep. A later doctor listened, tried medicines in turn, and first raised the name fibromyalgia. Referral to a specialist pain centre changed her course: there she felt understood and taken seriously. Her account traces the long road from not being believed to being heard.
pmc-12865943:
Eddah Sure and co-authors teach a neural network to see crystals the way crystals are built: parts inside wholes. Graph networks predict material properties well but explain little and ignore the hierarchy from atoms to polyhedra to extended motifs. Their capsule graph network, equipped with symmetry-respecting message passing, organizes what it learns into capsules that stand for local environments.

On standard data sets the model beat a leading crystal graph network at formation energy and matched another at band gap. The capsules themselves became readable: routing by agreement gathers environments like titanium-oxygen octahedra into higher-level units tied to the property. The authors present the design as prediction with a built-in explanation, an unsupervised route to discovering the motifs that matter.
pmc-12866343:
Huiwen Xie and three colleagues ask whether a previous keyhole hernia repair blocks doing the same operation on the other side later, in a cohort study published in two thousand twenty-five. Totally extraperitoneal repair works behind the abdominal wall. Scarring from the first operation might obstruct a second.

Thirty-eight patients who developed a hernia on the opposite side after a first repair were reviewed. The average gap between operations was about four years. The second repair succeeded in thirty-seven cases. Surgeons found that identifying key vessels and dissecting the lateral space first made the reoperative field manageable. Recurrence and complication outcomes were tracked. Patients can be reassured that choosing this repair once does not burn the bridge for the other groin.
pmc-12875943:
Jose Luis Eduardo Doval-Caballero and co-authors review how a gut hormone may shape taste in this 2025 paper. Taste does far more than detect flavor: it links food sensing with metabolism and feeding behavior through a gut, brain, and taste axis.

The hormone glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1, is one of several signals, alongside leptin, ghrelin, and others, that adjust how taste receptors in the tongue and gut are expressed and how they respond. Brain chemicals such as dopamine and serotonin tune taste at the bud and in reward circuits. The review explains how obesity and diabetes disturb these signals, bending taste preferences and driving compulsive eating, and it weighs the possible role of GLP-1 in that system.
pmc-12882443:
Bovine viral diarrhea quietly drains dairy farming worldwide, and Ethiopia lacked the numbers to fight it. Melkamsew, Tessema, Garoma, and Paeshuyse test 1,634 cattle in 180 urban and peri-urban herds across three regions of the country. Blood tests measured past exposure and current infection, and a special search hunted persistently infected animals, the silent shedders born infected for life.

About twenty-eight percent of cattle carried antibodies, and herd-level exposure ran far higher. Persistently infected animals were uncommon, under one percent of cattle but present in about six percent of herds. Risk clustered with location, body condition, herd size, animal origin, and signs like diarrhea and calf deformities. The authors conclude the virus is well established in commercial dairy herds. They urge planned prevention and control, plus studies of the virus strains circulating in Ethiopia.
pmc-12883743:
Dan Li and co-authors present a case report of calcium hardening inside the heart muscle of a young dialysis patient. The twenty-four year old had been on dialysis for about eight years, with badly disturbed mineral balance. His heart tracing showed abnormal Q waves, a sign more often tied to heart attack.

Scans found a calcified mass at the heart's tip and flecks in a side wall. The heart was enlarged and weak. The authors argue that heavy focal calcium can crush cells and silence electrical signals, forging the attack like pattern. In dialysis patients with odd tracings, they urge doctors to think of calcium, not just blocked arteries.
pmc-12884043:
Yeon Hwa Chang, Kyujin Chang, and Yeong Jun Ju describe Korea's 2024 whooping cough epidemic as it played out in Gyeonggi Province, which logged nearly a third of national cases. They analyzed 14,275 reported cases and compared children with adults, and the vaccinated with the unvaccinated. Almost ninety percent of cases were under twenty, concentrated at ages ten to fourteen.

Children were more often part of clusters and had more traced contacts. Adults, though fewer, were hospitalized and sent to emergency care at much higher rates. Among the young, those unvaccinated or with unknown records were hospitalized about twice as often as the fully vaccinated, and their diagnoses came later. The authors call for stronger vaccination aimed at adolescents, the group where the epidemic clearly centered, and better records so no one's status is unknown.
pmc-12884543:
A single cold night can ruin quinoa sprouting, and a study by Ignacio Delfino Yurin and co-authors, published in 2025, tests when frost hurts most. The crop is spreading into harsh high country in Chile, where early frosts threaten young stands.

Two local cultivars, Roja and Amarilla, faced single frosts at zero, minus two, and minus four degrees at three sprouting stages: drinking in water, steady absorption, and root emergence. Fifty seeds per treatment were tracked for sprouting share and speed, water uptake, and stress chemistry. Frost in the first two stages cut sprouting by over seventy percent, worst at the coldest setting early on. Roots already out proved hardier. Timing, the study shows, matters as much as temperature.
pmc-12902943:
The authors track long-term fate of heart valve patients who also carry severe pressure overload in their lung arteries. Their 2025 study reviews cases from 2008 to 2021 at one center, where a catheter route replaces the aortic valve. Recent reports tie lung pressure to higher early death after the procedure.

Of three thousand six hundred ten patients, four hundred fifty-six had severe lung pressure by ultrasound. That group skewed older and showed weaker heart pumping. Early results were worse, with more bleeding, pacemaker needs, and kidney failure. Death gaps persisted at one year and at five years. The authors flag severe lung pressure as a durable risk mark, not a short-term one.
pmc-12903243:
Xiaoqian Dong and co-authors show how a gut bacterium's product can restart a sluggish bowel. Functional constipation affects millions and current drugs give only brief relief without restoring motion. The team hunted for protective gut microbes using genetics and direct testing.

Mendelian randomization and stool sequencing from patients and healthy controls pointed to Roseburia intestinalis. Its metabolite inosine, fed to constipated mice, improved stool output and gut transit. Tracing the signal, inosine switches on a TGF-β pathway that raises transgelin, a protein of muscle-like gut cells. A microbe-made molecule that repairs motion itself, not just symptoms, is a promising lead.
pmc-12906743:
Sulochana Joshi and co-authors study in 2025 how long psychiatric inpatients stay in a teaching hospital in Nepal. Stay length matters for cost, family support, bed supply, and stigma. The team reviewed records from a tertiary care center over four years, from 2013 to 2017.

Of more than a thousand records, the median stay was eight days. Patients with psychotic disorders stayed about thirty percent longer than others. Those who received shock therapy stayed far longer still. The authors call the overall stay relatively short, but flag those two groups as drivers of prolonged care in their setting.
pmc-12907043:
Jiyeon Han reviews how metal ions work inside proteins and small protein-like chains in living systems. Metals are often framed as poisons, Han notes. Yet cells depend on tiny, tightly held amounts of iron, copper, and zinc. These ions sit in buffered pools, passed hand to hand rather than floating free.

Trouble starts when metals land in the wrong place. Loose iron and copper can spark reactions that damage proteins, fats, and DNA. Such damage is tied to nerve cell death, degenerative disease, and cancer. Foreign heavy metals like lead and cadmium can also push native metals out of their slots. Lead, for one, can take zinc's place in an enzyme and shut it down. The review traces how shape and grip decide whether a metal helps or harms.
pmc-12907443:
Sisi Chen and seven co-authors review how thyroid trouble and female reproduction interact through the immune system, in work published in 2026. Thyroid disease is common in women of childbearing age and shadows fertility and pregnancy. The review traces thyroid hormones through the brain-pituitary-gonad axis, both directly and through metabolic messengers such as prolactin and leptin.

Inflammatory cytokines can jam thyroid hormone production, tying immune flare-ups to reproductive failure. At the placenta, thyroid state shapes immune cell mixes and vessel growth factors, with links to preeclampsia. The authors build a frame for immune-targeted treatment of thyroid-linked reproductive disease.
pmc-12911243:
Nizamuddin Khan and co-authors compare two hands-on therapies in a 2025 trial for neck pain in athletes. Tight, tender knots in the shoulder muscle plague overhead athletes. Both therapies pair with high-power ultrasound: one group gets a release technique, the other gets stretching, each three times a week for two weeks.

Thirty-two amateur athletes with active trigger points enroll, and twenty-six are analyzed. Pain, neck movement, muscle length, and disability are scored at baseline, during treatment, and a week after. The trial asks which add-on works better alongside the same ultrasound base. Results feed choices in sports physiotherapy for this common pain source.
pmc-12924443:
Annerstedt and seven co-authors compare two support bundles to help schools run a healthy habits program faithfully, in a trial report from twenty twenty-five. Childhood overweight has risen sharply in Sweden over recent decades. The program joins school lessons with family talks and checks. The trial tests whether extra support beats basic support.

Forty-five schools in Stockholm took part over two school years. Close to a thousand parents and over six hundred children joined. Schools followed the program at about three-quarter fidelity overall. Extra support did not beat basic support on fidelity scores. Two extra strategies never really happened for lack of time and interest. Fidelity improved over time, so early support matters most.
pmc-12936043:
Hong Chen, Yu Zhang, and Hongwei Han compare two malnutrition screening tools in hospitalized children in a study published in 2025. Underfed children heal slower and catch more infections, so wards need a quick, accurate flag. The team scored three hundred two children with both tools and checked them against world standards.

Half the children counted as malnourished or borderline by the standard measure. Both tools flagged digestive disease patients and infants as highest risk. High-risk children indeed stayed longer, caught more hospital infections, and showed lower blood markers. The modified STRONGkids tool proved more sensitive and accurate than its rival. The authors propose it as the ward's screening-to-action path.
pmc-12951343:
Eva Buschmeyer and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on the mental health needs of refugees in Germany. Refugees face high rates of trauma and stress, yet care is hard for many of them to reach. The team used a visual method called cognitive-affective mapping, in which people draw their thoughts and feelings as a map.

Maps let people share views across language and culture gaps, without long surveys or interviews. The study compared groups from West Africa, the Middle East, and Ukraine. It found strong barriers to care, but also a clear will to look after their own health. Needs and hurdles differed by region of origin. The authors argue for care shaped to each culture, not one plan for all. They also show how the map method can serve other groups.
pmc-12962943:
Ellis Eikenboom and a large team of co-authors tested whether CT scan patterns can flag a rare pancreatic cancer subtype in a paper whose text is dated 2025. Most pancreatic cancers have a grim outlook, but tumors with broken DNA repair respond better to immune therapy. Testing for that subtype is not routine, so a scan-based clue would help.

The pilot study mined 254 measured features from scans of the pancreas and tumor in patients with and without the subtype, including Lynch syndrome cases. Random forest models built from the most telling features were checked by repeated cross-validation. The authors frame the work as a feasibility step toward non-invasive subtyping, not yet a clinical tool.
pmc-12970843:
Coutts and Eckmann explore how health workers decide how to feed very ill adults in public hospital intensive care units in Johannesburg, South Africa. Feeding is tricky because swallowing problems in these patients have many causes, and poor choices can do harm. The pair watched care in two large hospitals and spoke with fifteen team members in groups and one-on-one talks.

Three themes stood out. First, choices rested mostly on clinical factors, with no shared protocol to guide them. Second, ward conditions and tight resources often forced changes to the plan. Third, team members used the word tolerance in different senses, which can cause confusion. Although team work helped when it happened, the authors found it was not routine. They call for a standard feeding protocol and closer joint work in these units.
pmc-12995643:
Joo Young Lee and eight co-authors scanned the thalamus in children with growth hormone deficiency in a study published in 2025. The hormone shortage stunts growth and has been tied to thinking and behavior differences, hinting at brain effects. Fifteen affected children were compared with fifteen short children whose hormone levels are normal. Brain software measured the pituitary gland and split the thalamus into ten nuclei, scoring left-right balance for each.

The deficiency group's pituitary glands were clearly smaller. One thalamic nucleus, the anteroventral, was enlarged, and another leaned more strongly leftward than in the comparison group. The first nucleus's imbalance tracked blood levels of a growth marker. The authors read the pattern as altered relay development in this condition.
pmc-13059843:
Cheek lining cancer in India is blamed on tobacco, yet drink may carry a hefty share too. Grace Sarah George and co-authors weigh that share in a 2025 study. They compare one thousand eight hundred three cases with one thousand nine hundred three hospital visitors. The team asked each man how much he drank, how often, and for how long.

Ever-drinkers faced a risk one point six eight times that of never-drinkers. Local brews ran slightly hotter than known brands, at one point eight seven times the risk. Nine grams a day lifted risk by about half. Drink plus chewing tobacco explained sixty-two percent of cases. The national share tied to drink alone was eleven point three percent. Small daily amounts, they warn, are not safe.
pmc-13059943:
Masaki Kojima and co-authors lay out a plan to catalog the scorecards of joined-up youth mental care, in a 2025 protocol paper. The system-of-care model links psychiatry with schools and social services for young people with severe emotional troubles, and it has spread across nearly every American state.

Studies of whether the model works keep growing, yet nobody has gathered the tools used to judge how faithfully it is put in place. The planned review will search for those instruments, describe them, and compare what each one measures. The protocol follows standard reporting rules for reviews. A clear catalog would help new programs pick fair measures and help funders compare sites honestly.
pmc-13079043:
The authors map how high blood pressure, lung inflammation, and diabetes feed each other through shared body pathways. They reviewed 48 papers from the last decade, hunting for common markers and signals. Chronic inflammation and oxidative stress sit at the center of all three.

High blood sugar stokes stress chemicals that damage vessel linings, while pressure strains lung vessels through the same signals. A hormone system that tightens vessels adds fuel. The review, published in 2025, points to shared targets such as NF-κB and TNF-α. It also notes a diabetes drug class that seems to calm all three systems at once.
pmc-13087043:
Kazuki Kishida and co-authors report in 2026 on antibodies in mice that act like T cell receptors and calm a specific immune response. Keeping such responses in check matters, since an overactive response can harm the body. During helper T cell responses to several test proteins, the team found antibodies that bind the exact protein and display complex the T cells target.

These antibodies block T cells from seeing that target, and they form only when the injected protein includes extra edge parts. In a mouse model of an autoimmune brain disease, treatment with such peptides or antibodies held the disease back. The authors propose this as a way to calm specific harmful responses.
pmc-13087443:
Aroni and five co-authors report a gum surgery case with long follow up, in work from twenty twenty-six. The patient was a healthy man aged thirty-seven with many gum recessions on both sides of the upper jaw. Recession exposes tooth roots and can cause sensitivity.

Surgeons used a flap method with two pig collagen matrices as graft substitutes. One product went on the right side and the other on the left. Full root cover was seen in almost all sites within two months. One side gained more thick tissue. Four year follow up lets readers judge whether the gains lasted, which short reports cannot show.
pmc-13091243:
Shi Chen and co-authors map single cells in stomach cancer that has spread to lymph nodes, and single out a gene steering the spread, in a research paper from 2026. Node spread drives poor outcomes in this cancer, yet the cell networks behind it are murky. The team combined single-cell reading with tissue-location mapping.

Eight core cell types appeared, with growing cells split into six subgroups, including growing B cells. Mapped tissues showed immune clusters inside tumors. The B cells changed jobs across stages, from death control to immune activation. Lab and animal tests confirmed the gene's role. The work names a target for slowing node spread.
pmc-13099243:
Powerful genetic tests can now be run before birth, but Austria's prenatal specialists worried they were being used unevenly, and that missed diagnoses carried legal risk. That group reviewed the literature and settled eight practical questions about when invasive prenatal genetic testing is indicated and which method fits.

The group's central advice is restraint guided by findings. Because test results predict poorly in fetuses that look structurally normal. Broad genomic analysis, from chromosomal microarrays to whole exomes and genomes, should be offered systematically when ultrasound shows actual abnormalities, not as a blanket screen. The paper lays out the phenotype-driven approach as Austria's agreed standard, aiming for consistent, meaningful use of the technology.
pmc-13109343:
Shuai Yang and eight colleagues estimate leaf nitrogen from reflected light by wedding a physics model to a transformer network, in a 2025 paper. Their hybrid, DeepSpecN, trains on simulated spectra from a leaf optics model, so no field labels are needed. A wavelet step trims glare, an improved transformer learns the features, and a similarity screen picks the most realistic simulated samples, fighting domain shift. On over seventeen hundred maize leaves it beat rival methods, and it generalized to four other crops. A side finding: chlorophyll-based formulas predicted nitrogen better than protein-based ones. The authors offer the method for precision farming scouts who need chemistry from a camera.
pmc-13117343:
Abrar Alwaheed and co-authors test a simple blood ratio as a marker of high lung pressure in sickle cell disease in a 2026 study. High pressure in the lung vessels is a major cause of illness and death in this disease, and easy markers for risk are lacking. The marker is the ratio of platelets to neutrophils in the blood.

Records covered 114 patients at a hospital in Saudi Arabia from 2019 to 2025, all with heart ultrasound scans. About 43 percent met the scan based signs for high lung pressure. After adjustment, the ratio was not linked to those signs. Higher fetal hemoglobin, by contrast, tracked with lower odds of high pressure and lower flow speeds.
pmc-13132643:
Korin Tateoka, Naofumi Yamamoto, Akiyo Higashionna, and Kazuto Noguchi report a 2026 study of step watching among older workers in Japan. The group came from silver human resource centers, which help older adults keep working. Of 622 members, about a third checked their step counts near daily, most by phone.

Frequent watchers were far more prone to have workout habits than those who never watched. Sitting time, though, showed no clear tie to how often steps were checked. The team frames the tally as ground work for plans that spread step watching more widely.
pmc-13133243:
Miguel Marquez and colleagues build a microscope that films bubbles dancing at a million cycles a second, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Microbubbles driven by ultrasound are used in therapy, but their frantic motion is hard to catch: cameras must trade speed against sharpness and cost. Their instrument squeezes a whole high-speed movie into a single snapshot.

The method streaks the scene, darkens the background, and lets a neural network rebuild the film from the compressed trace. With it they recorded steady bubbling, wild oscillations, free ringing after the sound stopped, and violent collapse, in bubbles a few micrometers wide. In whole blood they watched, for the first time, vibrating bubbles shoving platelets around and squeezing out of shape against a red blood cell. The authors offer the compact rig for labs studying bubble-based therapies.
pmc-13135443:
Nital Vaghela and five co-authors reported a rare case in two thousand twenty-six of pancreatitis caused by a swallowed foreign body. Unlike common causes, this one gives vague symptoms and no clear history, so diagnosis is tough. Their patient was a man aged seventy with vomiting and belly tenderness.

Scans showed a sharp object, four centimetres long, near the head of the pancreas, with inflammation around it. Scope checks from inside failed to find it. Surgery guided by live ultrasound located and removed the object at the junction of stomach outlet and duodenum. The patient recovered without complications. The team stresses early imaging and cross-specialty teamwork.
pmc-13135543:
Fast, cheap tests for dangerous bacteria remain a clinical need. Gunes Kibar and co-authors build a biosensor for Streptococcus pneumoniae, a major cause of pneumonia. The sensor rests on hybrid nanoparticles made in five minutes by a green light-driven method. Magnetic iron oxide and a sticky bio-inspired coating are added in layers. DNA probes sit on the surface and break only when the target bacterium's nuclease enzyme is present. That break produces an electric signal, and a magnet handles the particles.

The test detected the bacterium down to 100 colony-forming units per milliliter. It ignored non-target bacteria. The authors pitch the platform as a rapid, amplification-free diagnostic.
pmc-13137943:
Lauren Gunderman and co-authors report a new gene-based immune flaw in two brothers in a 2026 paper. Both boys flagged on a newborn screen for weak immunity. They lacked key germ-fighting cells in the blood and had too few of a second cell type that makes antibodies.

The cause was a change in a gene on the X chromosome that helps build the cell frame. Their marrow held stalled cells with doubled gene sets, so mature cells could not reach the blood. A stem cell graft from a matched sibling fixed the flaw with mild side effects. Tests in graft models showed the gene steers early cell growth, which marks a new entry in the immune flaw list.
pmc-13138343:

Genetic methods that mimic experiments tied twenty-eight microbes and eighty-two metabolites to the condition.

One small molecule amplified a bacterium's harmful association. Another microbe blunted a protective metabolite's effect. Four genes emerged as network biomarkers, and a prediction chart built on them separated patients from controls with high accuracy. Tissue data added an immune chapter: more macrophages at the maternal-fetal interface, talking more loudly to their neighbors. The authors frame a gut-metabolite-immune axis behind the losses.
pmc-13139743:
Dan Michael and co-authors report a tiny RNA with an unusual birthplace that calms inflammation under cell stress. Stressed cells in the endoplasmic reticulum drive many severe diseases. Probing fibroblasts under mild and extended stress, the team found a microRNA, miR-4488, that switches off inflammation-linked genes. Unlike most microRNAs, it is not cut by the usual Drosha enzyme.

Instead, the molecule is carved from a piece of ribosomal RNA, the workhorse of protein building, through the cell's autophagy and lysosome recycling route. Blocking that route stops its production. The microRNA targets two inflammation genes and binds them only under stress, a selectivity the authors find promising. The work assigns an anti-inflammatory side job to ribosomal RNA and lysosomes at stress onset.
pmc-13144843:
Inés García Bouyssou and co-authors test a mixed plan for lasting tiredness after stroke, built around mild brain stimulation. Their conference abstract from 2026 notes that such tiredness is common and cuts activity and life quality. Sound drug free treatments are scarce, so new paths are worth a trial.

The study runs at a Barcelona hospital and aims for twenty seven patients in each arm. All get teaching on tiredness and coping, plus aerobic exercise over five weeks. One group gets real stimulation before exercise, and the other gets a sham form. Tiredness is scored three months after care with a standard scale. Relatives may join the teaching part.
pmc-13144943:
Birol Önal maps the young research field of remote checks for stroke survivors in a review of past work. The conference abstract from 2026 covers only first hand studies, not other reviews. It asks which skills are checked from afar, which tools are used, and how often the tools are tested for sound results.

Twenty one studies were found through structured database searches. Most appeared in the last few years, with fifteen dated from 2023 to 2025. Leg and arm motor checks were the most common topic, then thinking tests, then balance and walking. Most work tried to prove that known bedside scales still work when used at a distance.
pmc-13145443:
Some stroke patients worsen within a day of a successful clot removal, and doctors cannot yet say who. They compare patients who deteriorated early with those who did not.

The backup network was measurably richer in patients who stayed stable. Lower admission severity scores also, counterintuitively, marked the group that worsened. Together the two measures predicted deterioration on their own. The authors say scan based collateral scores could sharpen risk sorting after thrombectomy. They call for larger studies to firm up the cutoffs.
pmc-13145543:
Adi Abdulaziz R Aldubaiyan and six co-authors describe an ongoing study of how cholesterol-lowering drugs reshape lipoprotein particles in people with cerebrovascular disease. A scanning method based on nuclear magnetic resonance can profile those particles in detail, but drug effects on them are little mapped.

The prospective study enrolls adults with stroke-related disease or white matter disease from neurovascular clinics and hospital wards. Fasting particle profiles are taken at the start and again at six months, with an extra scan whenever treatment changes sooner. Drugs in play are statins, ezetimibe, and PCSK9 inhibitors, alone or combined. The abstract reports that the study began a month before writing, with enrollment and data collection under way. Results will come from adjusted comparisons between treatment groups.
pmc-13145643:
Alex Szolics reports a 2026 conference study on how procedure time and reopening quality jointly shape early gains after clot removal. Care teams often treat time as a straight line and full reopening as always better. Swedish registry data let the author test whether the value of a better grade shifts with time.
