At long durations, gains shrank overall even when vessels reopened. Much of the lost gain came from the longest procedures. The author urges cutting the worst time outliers and routing patients straight to full centers.
pmc-13145943:
Sheng-Feng Sung, Cheng-Yang Hsieh, and Chen-Wen Fang compare heart and brain risk after two kinds of sudden vessel blockage. One group had retinal vascular occlusion, a blockage in the eye. The other had a transient ischemic attack, a brief stroke-like event. Their 2026 study uses the TriNetX database and matches patients so the two groups start out alike.

After matching, each group held 90,698 patients. The eye group had a lower one-year risk of major events such as stroke and heart attack. One subtype stood out: central retinal artery occlusion carried a higher risk than the stroke-like group. The paper also lists risk factors, led by prior heart disease and kidney disease.
pmc-13146043:
Dibij Adhikari and co-authors present a 2026 conference case report on a neck artery tear that first looked like a common dizzy spell in a woman aged thirty-eight. A tear in this artery is a top cause of back-brain stroke in young adults. Hers began as brief spins set off by head turns.

Eye and balance exams hinted at a brain source rather than an ear one. Scans showed a fresh small stroke at the back of the brain. Vessel scans then found a small tear flap with clot in the neck artery, narrowing it by about a third. Aspirin and a strong fat-lowering drug cleared her signs within days. No new spells came in the next month, and the authors urge brain checks for odd vertigo.
pmc-13146243:
People whose kidneys have failed often have hearts that beat with atrial fibrillation, and stroke prevention is a hard choice for them. Blood thinners raise bleeding risk, while a plug that seals a small heart pouch may avoid them. Zeyad Bady and four co-authors pooled the evidence in 2026, comparing the plug procedure with blood thinners across studies holding 22,512 patients.

The plug came with a lower risk of stroke and body wide clots, and less major bleeding, above all against the older thinner warfarin. Death rates, overall and from heart causes, did not differ clearly between the paths. The authors call for randomized trials that test the plug head on against each thinner type. Their summary is a conference abstract rather than a full journal report.
pmc-13146343:
Ieva Celpacenko and co-authors report a 2026 conference study testing a reshaped stroke scale item that screens for language loss and spatial neglect at once. The standard scale undercounts right-brain harm, since its neglect item catches only one narrow sign. The new item uses a classic picture scene in place of plain naming.

More than six hundred patients at two centers took the new item within a week of stroke. Against a bedside function scale, the item caught neglect with high marks for both hits and correct clears. It took under thirty seconds to give. Standard pencil tests missed more cases or went unfinished more often. The authors offer the item as a fast, fairer add-on to routine scoring.
pmc-13146443:
Oshi Swarup and seven colleagues tested whether an enzyme used for mucus can boost a clot-busting drug. The enzyme, dornase alfa, chews up DNA webs that white cells cast into stroke clots. Those webs stiffen clots against breakdown. Earlier work paired the enzyme with an older drug. This study pairs it with tenecteplase, the newer standard.

The team worked on forty-two clots pulled from stroke patients during procedures. Clots soaked in buffer with the drug alone shrank to about forty percent of their weight in two hours. Adding a high dose of the enzyme cut them much further. In plasma, the boost faded and lost statistical strength. The results suggest the pairing can work, but blood proteins blunt it. The authors call for care in moving the idea toward patients.
pmc-13146543:
Emily E Farah and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six Australian cohort study of daily functioning in school children with spinal muscular atrophy. New treatments have transformed this once-deadly muscle disease. How independent treated children are in everyday life was unexplored.

Children aged four to twelve were found through newborn screening or later clinical referral. A standard disability inventory measured social, responsibility, daily activity, and mobility skills. Most children scored as expected for their age in social and responsibility areas. Mobility lagged, with fewer than half at expected levels. Screening-found children did better across all areas.
pmc-13146643:
Jozefien Meersschaut and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on immune action in moyamoya, a rare disease where brain arteries narrow and sprout frail side vessels. A gene fault common in East Asia hints that immune faults help drive the disease. The team read genes cell by cell in blood and mapped them in artery tissue.

Blood from four patients and matched peers was pushed with immune triggers and a gut germ. More than one hundred thousand cells fed the reads. Patient cells answered the triggers in altered ways. Artery maps split blocked from open stretches, with growth and immune paths lit in the blocked zones. The authors tie immune action tight to the vessel harm.
pmc-13146743:
Danae Kingma and co-authors report long-term results for people with unruptured brain artery tangles who were managed without surgery, in a 2026 hospital study. Such tangles carry a yearly bleed risk, and a major trial had favoured careful watching over early treatment. The team asked how patients fared over time and which traits raised the risk of a bleed.

The study followed 126 patients for 700 person-years in total. Twelve first bleeds took place, a low rate overall, and most patients stayed stable. Large tangles and linked weak spots on nearby arteries were tied to higher risk. Seven patients died, six of them after a bleed. The findings back careful watching for many patients, with closer care for those with high-risk traits.
pmc-13146843:
Roman Rohner and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on new stroke zones that appear after vessel-opening therapy, away from the treated area. Such new-zone injury struck a notable share of trial patients and may stem from clot bits breaking loose. The team asked whether a clot drug given first cuts the risk.

Patient data from six trials joined more than two thousand patients with readable scans. New-zone injury appeared in about thirteen percent overall. It struck fewer patients who got the drug first than those who went straight to the procedure. Patients with new-zone injury fared worse at ninety days and bled severely more often. The lower injury rate, though, did not turn into better function in the pooled data.
pmc-13147343:
Kadison Michel and co-workers report a rare case of a bad blood infection from a dog scratch. A 52-year-old woman who had been well got sepsis from Capnocytophaga canimorsus after a small scrape on her brow. The 2026 case report tells of a muddled mind, loose stools, and a sick feeling that got worse fast. She went into shock and her kidneys failed, though she had just had a drug from her own doctor to fight germs.

Blood tests then found the germ, and care was changed to match. She needed a breathing tube and a machine to clean her blood day and night. Scans showed dead tissue in both kidneys. That left her tied to dialysis for life. The team notes this is one of very few such kidney cases on record. It is the sole known case where the patient lived.
pmc-13148143:
A European food safety panel updated in 2026 its review of a food enzyme made by a fungus strain. The enzyme breaks down hydrogen peroxide and is made by a company for use in seven food processes. In an earlier review, the panel could not clear the enzyme. Doubts hung over whether living cells of the fungus remained in the product and over lab signs of gene damage.

New data from the maker settled both points, the panel reports. Tests showed no living cells of the production strain in the enzyme. The fresh evidence also removed the gene damage concern. On that basis, the panel concluded the enzyme raises no safety concerns under its planned uses. The opinion closes the earlier open questions.
pmc-13149043:
Hye Jin Jee and co-authors review the chemistry of sleep pressure in a 2026 paper on adenosine receptors. Adenosine builds up in the brain during waking hours as a by-product of energy use and drains away in sleep, which makes it the body's own drowsiness signal.

Two of its receptors do the persuading through opposite wiring. One quiets wake-promoting neurons across the cortex and deep brain, deepening slow-wave sleep. The other acts through reward regions to switch sleep on. The review maps both pathways region by region. It then asks how their malfunction feeds specific sleep disorders and what drugs might correct it.
pmc-13149543:
Luis Rivas and co-authors argue that biodiversity science still drains knowledge from the places richest in species. For centuries, specimens and data from tropical regions ended up in northern museums and papers. Local scientists got little control and few lasting institutions.

The authors call this pattern parachute science and say it weakens global conservation goals. Their answer is a framework of five building blocks for local research infrastructure. Funded steadily, these blocks let regions run their own collections, labs, and training. The model aims at any under-resourced region that wants science rooted at home.
pmc-13149843:
Zahra Batool and co-authors build a library of new compounds that block enzymes which turn a cell fuel into a calming signal, in a 2026 study. Those enzymes shape immune response, swelling, and cancer growth. Blocking the right one, and only that one, is the prize.

Twenty-two compounds in the new family were made and checked. Four stood out, blocking the target at low doses with clear taste for one enzyme form over its kin. Studies of shape showed which parts drove the strength. Computer models placed the winners snugly in the enzyme pocket, and long simulations held them steady. The work names leads for drug design.
pmc-13150343: Sho Okamura and co-authors published a short technique note in 2026 on heart pacing tests. Some hearts have two backward paths for electric signals near the central node, a fast one and a slow one. Standard pacing can miss the slow path because the fast path masks it. The note shows that adding extra timed pulses to the pacing, while varying which tissue is captured, can reveal the hidden slow path. The trick gives doctors a clearer read on the wiring in such cases.
pmc-13151043:
Emma Eisenbraun and six co-authors rebuild bacterial chatter systems inside a safe host in a 2026 paper. Many bacteria coordinate behavior by swapping small peptide signals, a process called quorum sensing. The circuits of dangerous species are hard to study directly in their native hosts.

The team moved the signal machinery of a major pathogen into a harmless soil bacterium. They built sender cells that make the signal, receiver cells that answer it, and full cells with both halves. Checks confirmed each strain played its assigned role. The toolkit lets researchers probe signal parts one at a time without handling the pathogen. That separation speeds work on blocking harmful coordination, a possible route to new anti-infective drugs.
pmc-13154143:
Salma Abbas, Lale Taner, Orhan Özdiler, and Erhan Özdiler study stuck canine teeth and jaw shape in a paper from 2026. An impacted canine never erupts into place. Upper canines are the ones most often stuck, and jaw shape may play a role.

The team reviewed over nine thousand panoramic X-rays of patients aged fourteen and up. About two in a hundred had a stuck upper canine, more often in females. Ninety-four such cases were compared with matched controls on skull measures. Tooth position, depth, and angle were recorded for each case. Links between impaction patterns and skeletal shape emerged. Orthodontists can use the patterns to plan early treatment.
pmc-13155343:
Yongzheng Hu and Wei Jiang argue in a 2026 viewpoint for life cycle governance of AI generated video shown to patients. Such video now mimics real clinicians in teaching and message clips for care. Pre launch checks alone cannot police a system that keeps changing, they argue.

Their matrix crosses leftover clinical risk with an ethics score built from four classic principles. Scores land each use in one of four stances, from encourage to prohibit. Each stance ties to a review dossier, minimum controls, and watch triggers after launch. Triggers track grasp, extra workload from the content, complaints, and equity gaps. Provenance and change logs keep each decision auditable over time.
pmc-13156143:
Giulia Zucchetti and co-authors gauge burnout in child cancer rehabilitation staff in a 2026 paper. Rehab staff in child cancer wards bear heavy emotional loads. Their strain is seldom studied in psycho oncology work.

Eleven Italian centers in one network joined the study. Thirty staff filled set scales on burnout, stress, and resilience. Talks were mapped for shared meaning themes by a text tool. Staff voiced high compassion satisfaction with mid level burnout. Two thirds scored high on depersonalization, a strain flag. Ward level roots of strain get named for leaders to act on.
pmc-13156243:
Zhixing Huang and co-authors present in 2026 a genetic programming method that builds readable formulas from fish biomass spectral data. Spectra carry chemical clues about fish meat, but noise is high and training samples few. Standard machine learning struggles to find full patterns under those limits, so they cast the task as symbolic regression instead of black-box prediction.

Their linear genetic programming evolves compact formulas from building blocks whose inner constants can tune themselves. Across more than ten biomass targets, the tunable version predicted composition better overall. The resulting formulas stay small and interpretable, spotlighting useful wavelength regions. Tests on other data confirmed broad generality.
pmc-13157343:
Housam Nanah, Arjun Chatterjee, Hisham Wehbe, and Miguel Regueiro compare two weight-loss paths for people who also live with bowel disease. Weight surgery had been linked to better bowel results, while new weight drugs offer a gentler route. Their 2026 study is the first head-to-head check, drawn from a huge US health database.

More than seventeen thousand patients with obesity and bowel disease were split by path: drugs or surgery. The drug group started older and sicker, with more diabetes and kidney disease. After matching, drug patients showed far lower odds of leg and lung clots, gut infection, and gut blockage. The authors note the drug group kept a higher body weight and shorter follow-up. Still, the safety edge looks strong.
pmc-13157543:
Emergency care for mothers and newborns can prevent many deaths, yet its quality varies across hospitals in Ethiopia. Tolera Gudissa Damme, Sileshi Garoma Abeya, and Dereje Bayissa Demissie assessed that care in 2026 at four public hospitals in West Shoa Zone. They audited the facilities and studied 348 mothers through observation, exit interviews, and record reviews.

Scores for inputs, care process, and outcomes were all in the acceptable range, near four fifths. Two factors stood out as linked to how satisfied mothers felt: how long they waited for care, and how long they stayed in hospital. Longer waits and stays both lowered satisfaction. The authors urge stronger supplies, facilities, and adherence to care standards.
pmc-13157743:
Shukar and a large team study access to anticancer medicines in South Asia in twenty twenty-six. The region carries a high cancer burden with low health coverage. Patients often pay large sums out of pocket for drugs. The team examined essential medicines lists, registration, and local production in eight countries.

They compared sixty-seven medicines from the World Health Organization list with national lists. Median national lists held only about twenty-four of those medicines. Registration was broader, with a median of forty-five medicines. Local production stayed very limited, with a median of six point five medicines. Interviews with thirty supply chain stakeholders named key barriers. Financial limits, weak regulation, and poor strategic planning stood out. The authors urge better coordination and regional production.
pmc-13157843:
Roy El Darzi and co-authors report a rare liver cancer case in a young adult and review the literature in a 2026 paper. The cancer, fibrolamellar carcinoma, is a distinct subtype that arises in non scarred livers of adolescents and young adults, without viral hepatitis or chronic liver disease. It makes up under one percent of primary liver cancers and carries a characteristic gene fusion.

The patient came in with upper right abdominal pain and anemia, with preserved liver function. Imaging showed a large liver mass with a dead central area, and tissue tests fit the diagnosis, though fusion testing was not done. A combined drug plan was scheduled, but the patient declined fast before therapy could start.
pmc-13159743:
Miao Wang and co-authors test a belief about back surgery in older patients in this 2026 study. Frail patients over 75 often have a narrowed spinal canal that pinches nerves and causes leg pain. Many surgeons avoid a small-scope operation when the narrowing looks severe on scans, fearing pain will linger afterward.

The team reviewed 152 frail patients who had the scope operation at one level of the lower back. About one in five still had leg pain at every check over the next year, and rates were nearly the same for severe and mild narrowing. A higher frailty score, not scan severity, was the strong predictor of lasting pain. The authors urge judging by symptoms and frailty, not by scan looks alone.
pmc-13159943:
Thamer Alhowaish and co-authors measured in 2026 how common disease of the small blood vessels in the brain is in Saudi Arabia. This disease adds to stroke, memory loss, and trouble walking, but data from the region were scarce. The team reviewed brain scans of adults at a large medical center in Riyadh.

More than a third of those scanned showed signs of the disease. The share rose steeply with age, from under a fifth in the youngest group to over half in the oldest. High blood pressure was the strongest linked factor. Among patients with high blood pressure, some drug types were linked to lower odds of the disease than no treatment.
pmc-13162843:
Chenyang Zhan and co-authors track immune cells in blood before and after liver cancer care. Their 2026 study follows 16 patients whose cancer had spread to the liver. Most had a procedure that blocks blood flow to tumors, and three had heat treatment.

Blood tests looked at T cells, a type of immune cell that can attack tumors. Overall cell mix did not change much after care. Still, in about four in ten patients, more than ten cell types grew in number one month later. Most of that growth faded by three months. In three patients, some cell types kept growing past that point.
pmc-13163643:
Ana Leite and co-authors review turning food by-products into useful ingredients in this 2026 paper. Meat demand keeps rising while its footprint draws concern. A circular bioeconomy would turn waste streams into value instead of landfill.

Fruit peels, pomace, blood, and bones all hold compounds with health or tech value. Those compounds can add water holding, texture, and emulsion stability to meats and plant-based analogs. Upcycling cuts disposal and formula costs at once. Barriers include shifting composition, rules, and consumer doubt about waste-derived goods. Enzyme treatment and fermentation are named as key tools to make the shift work.
pmc-13163943:
Jiajun Liang and ten colleagues report early results of a major aortic repair in older patients with acute type A dissection, a tear in the body's main artery. The operation replaces the aortic arch and plants a stented trunk, a demanding fix even for the young. How patients over sixty fare was not well mapped.

The study pooled 1,634 cases from seven centers over eight years. Older patients arrived with more heart disease, diabetes, and high blood fats. After matching, 699 patients allowed a fair comparison. Older patients stayed longer in intensive care and on ventilators, and their thirty-day survival ran lower. Models that adjust step by step test how much age itself drives the gap.
pmc-13164543:
Xin Ge and co-authors report a 2026 vaccine study based on weakening a cattle tuberculosis germ. The germ shares a family with the human form, and a toxin system called VapBC40 helps it cause disease. The team first mapped how that toxin acts, in both cell and mouse tests.

Deleting the toxin gene made the germ less able to live inside host cells and cause lung harm. Shots of the weakened germ in mice raised a strong cell-based immune response. When the mice later met the full-strength germ, the vaccine strain gave strong protection, which backs its use as a live vaccine base.
pmc-13165143:
Hua Liu, Claire Shi, and Jed Fahey review a broccoli compound for skin disease in this 2026 paper. Sulforaphane, found in cruciferous vegetables, calms oxidation and protects cells. Skin conditions from eczema to acne share threads of inflammation, barrier failure, and microbe shifts, though they differ in cause.

The review sorts what is known for each disorder and for sun injury and photoaging. It traces how the compound nudges key cell pathways. Evidence ranges from lab work to early clinical reports. The authors mark where promise outruns proof. Their map helps clinicians judge a supplement patients already ask about.
pmc-13165543:
Bearing faults hide in factory noise, and Xin Zhang and co-authors built a spotter that keeps sharp fault spikes from being smoothed away, in work from twenty twenty-six. Plain pooling, they argue, irons out the brief knocks that mark a crack. Their network pairs two pooling styles along set axes, so spikes survive next to the broad trend.

Mixed-size filters catch both quick knocks and slow repeats. On three public bearing sets, the spotter beat recent rivals, most clearly under heavy noise. Maps of its focus back the claim that it locks onto true fault marks. The design suits plant floors where roar drowns weak signals.
pmc-13166543:
HIV infections among Chinese university students have drawn growing concern, and this study looks at the sexually active share of that population in Zhejiang Province. From a stratified survey, 3,873 students who report sexual activity are analyzed in depth, about one in eight of all students surveyed. The team compares men and women across background traits, knowledge, attitudes, and behavior, using a web questionnaire built for the study. The average age is just over 20.

Gender gaps run through nearly every measure, from household registration and living costs to attitudes toward one-night stands and commercial sex. Students show open attitudes and decent knowledge of HIV testing, yet actual testing, condom use, and confidence in using condoms stay low. Men report more casual sex than women. The authors call for sex-specific health education that also faces the money and background factors behind the gaps.
pmc-13168843:
Pomegranate peel, a kitchen waste, can brew silver nanoparticles, and a 2026 study by Mandy Sibiya and co-authors compares three green ways to do it. The peel's plant chemicals both build the particles and keep them stable, replacing harsher lab reagents.

The three routes were a simple soak, a microwave run, and a heated pressure vessel. Imaging showed round particles that clump into clusters, with the microwave batch the smallest on average. Crystal tests confirmed all three batches were true silver crystals. The microwave particles also fought germs best, with the strongest effect against Staphylococcus aureus among food-borne foes. The study makes a case for fruit waste as a factory input.
pmc-13171843:
Yajie Zhao and co-authors test electrical acupoint stimulation against low body temperature during chest surgery in a 2026 randomized trial. Cooling is common during keyhole lung surgery and raises complication risk. Gentle skin stimulation at acupuncture points might steady body temperature control, but trial evidence was limited.

Adults having elective keyhole surgery were assigned to real or sham stimulation, from before anesthesia to the end of surgery. Ninety two enrolled and eighty eight finished. Low temperature occurred in about sixteen percent of the treated group versus about forty one percent of controls. Treated patients also kept higher temperatures and had fewer complications.
pmc-13172843:
Thakshila Dasanayake and Nikki L. Hill lay out a planned study of education and Alzheimer's disease using the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center dataset. Clinical diagnosis and brain pathology at death do not always agree. The authors ask whether schooling helps explain the mismatch.

Participants will be sorted into four groups, from true Alzheimer's to people with pathology but no symptoms. Regression analysis will test how education relates to each group. The authors expect highly educated people to appear more often among those who stayed sharp despite pathology. Such a result would support the idea of cognitive reserve. It would also argue for including reserve factors in diagnosis and research.
pmc-13173143:
Laura Campbell and three co-authors describe a shared infrastructure for community engaged research in this 2026 conference abstract. At their medical center, three institutes each ran programs linking academics with communities. The programs united into one collaborative system. A single platform collects and tracks requests for technical help from both academic and community partners. Representatives meet weekly under a shared procedure to route each request. Leadership is joint across the institutes, with one center coordinating.

Since 2021 the system has fielded many requests. Academics asked for help weaving community views into study design, recruitment, and grants. Community partners asked for data analysis, program evaluation, and grant support. Projects reached rural and frontier counties far from the center. The authors present backbone coordination, shared leadership, and one data system as what makes the model hold. They plan to measure partner satisfaction and add more institutes.
pmc-13173643:
Hallward-Driemeier and coauthors track methane gas that leaks from a landfill in New Jersey. Landfills give off a large share of methane in the United States. Methane warms the air far more than most gases. Reports may miss much of what landfills truly emit.

The team read air from one tall tower near the site for two and a half years. That long run caught shifts that short plane or car checks miss. Their counts matched plane and ground checks done at the same times. Heat and air pressure drove much of the month-to-month shift. The work gives a new way to check landfill claims.
pmc-13174243:
Thalia Pacheco-Fernandez and a large team tested in 2026 a new freeze-dried, phenol-free form of the leishmanin skin test antigen. The skin test shows past exposure to Leishmania parasites, but it vanished from use for lack of well-made antigen, and older forms need costly cold storage. A dry form could serve field sites.

In mice with past Leishmania exposure, the antigen raised the expected delayed skin response, rich in CD8 and CD4 T cells and macrophages, while control sites did not. Blood from healed and active patients in Brazil also reacted to it in a lab assay. The authors say the dry antigen could aid vaccine trials and surveys in affected areas.
pmc-13175943:
Toru Negishi, Kiyomitsu Shinsho, Shinji Abe, and Izumi Ogura build an adapter that lets engineers measure the X-ray tube voltage in mammography machines directly, through a common high-voltage connector type. Accurate voltage checks are key for quality control and for estimating patient dose. Direct access had been blocked for this connector, leaving only indirect tools.

Their adapter taps the circuit without altering the main conduction path. On three clinical systems, direct and indirect average voltages agreed in a near-linear way. The ripple in the voltage, however, differed sharply under some beam settings, with indirect readings reaching far higher values. The direct method offers a true electrical reference for judging indirect tools and generators.
pmc-13176143:
Saeed, Siepker, Jang, Shahdadian, and Liu measure coupling between brain blood flow and fluid movement in twenty twenty-six. Alzheimer's disease involves vessel damage and poor waste clearance from the brain. Spinal fluid helps wash out toxins, but measuring it is invasive. The team used broadband near infrared light through the forehead instead.

Three groups took part: young adults, healthy older adults, and early Alzheimer's patients. Coupling between blood volume and free water signals was computed across rhythm bands. Coupling was weakest in the young and strongest in Alzheimer's patients. Older healthy adults fell in between. The authors suggest stiffening vessels and compensation for poor clearance explain the pattern. The cheap, non invasive method may mark early disease.
pmc-13176243:
Yafang Li and co-authors review in 2026 how gut microbe byproducts drive colon cancer tied to long gut swelling. That cancer is the worst ill that can grow from bowel swelling disease. It tends to spread fast, come back, and end poorly.

Some byproducts guard the gut: they calm swelling, shield the gut wall, and block cancer paths. Others do harm: they fire up swelling signals, break DNA, and upset immune balance. High blood levels of one bad byproduct track with worse life odds. The review maps where each type comes from and what cure paths it opens.
pmc-13176643:
Osman Karaarslan, Mehmet Yilmaz, and Macit Kalcik write about a heart pause seen after ablation for atrial fibrillation. Their 2026 letter responds to a study by Guo and co-authors. That study found most long pauses eased within one week. It backed a watch and wait plan for many patients.

The letter urges care before that plan is used for all. The study was small, it notes. Heart node function was not checked in a set way before the procedure. A faulty node may stay silent while the rhythm is off. It may show only when normal rhythm returns. So a pause may reflect old disease, not just a short term effect of the procedure itself.
pmc-13177643:
Saira Ahmed and four co-authors present this 2024 conference abstract on taming one of Wales's biggest health data sets for everyday research use. The Welsh Longitudinal General Practice dataset holds over four billion records. Filtering that mountain for ordinary practice interactions was so slow that queries dragged badly.

Their fix is an R package that runs each time the data refreshes. It rebuilds the events table in a leaner shape, cutting fourteen columns to eight key ones. A companion lookup table collects the distinct event codes and spells out each one's description, type, and place in the hierarchy. The two tables join on an event code identifier. Any approved project can then provision the cleaned pair. Researchers, the authors report, now spend far less time wrestling the data into shape.
pmc-13177843:
Vahideh Faghanizadeh and co-authors tested whether two friendly gut bacteria can slow mouth cancer in rats, in a 2026 study. Mouth microbes and the signals they trip in tissue may help oral cancer grow. The team caused tongue cancer in rats with a chemical, then fed groups of them live or killed Lactobacillus plantarum, or live Lactobacillus casei. Thirty-five rats were split into five groups, including healthy and untreated cancer groups.

Both bacteria killed rival germs in dish tests, and tissue checks confirmed the cancer model worked. In cancer rats, four genes tied to inflammation and cell survival ran high. The bacteria feeds pulled all four back down. The treated rats' gene pattern moved toward the healthy one. The authors say such probiotics may one day aid oral cancer care, but dose and timing still need work.
pmc-13177943:
Katherine O'Sullivan and co-authors present a 2024 dashboard that tracks where linked health data came from, inside a trusted research setting. Linking data in such a haven must stay open to audit, so staff can prove each step was sound. The team built a first working form of the tool and tested it in real use.

Design ran in four stages, from joint sketches with users to a refined data model and a semi-automated capture step. Public talks checked that the design kept public trust. The final dashboard runs as an offline desktop app, shaped to haven rules.
pmc-13178143:
Belics leads a team reporting an exceptionally rare cancer case in a 2026 paper. A choriocarcinoma, a fast-growing tumor that makes pregnancy hormone, arose in the lung rather than the womb. It then spread to a kidney.

The patient was a woman in her early forties whose workup began with a suspected pregnancy problem. Lung and kidney surgery supplied tissue that settled the diagnosis, backed by molecular testing. She then received chemotherapy plus immunotherapy. Follow-up tracks imaging and hormone levels. The authors stress how hard such cases are to recognize. Non-pregnancy tumors in odd sites can mislead every early step. Careful pathology made the difference here.
pmc-13178243:
Jinglu Wang and five co-authors build two zinc-based lattice materials that glow, for use in cell imaging and cancer care. Such lattices can be tuned by design, and their glow lets doctors track them. By varying the mix and fill of the reaction vessel, the team grew two forms from the same parts. One stacks in layers; the other weaves through itself in three dimensions.

Both glowed green in pure water, but the woven form glowed more than twice as strongly and held its glow amid the ions found in the body. The layered form killed cervical cancer cells in dishes through several death paths at once. The paper shows how small build choices tune one material family for seeing or for treating.
pmc-13178543:
Nine battery researchers mix two salts to make a water-based sodium battery that works in the cold. Water-based cells are safe and cheap, but water breaks down at modest voltage, and the usual super-concentrated brines freeze near room temperature. One salt alone gave a wide safe voltage range yet crystallized when chilled. The blend solves both problems at once.

Together the salts reach the highest concentration yet reported for a sodium water-in-salt electrolyte. The liquid stays fluid down to minus twenty degrees and widens the safe window to 3.07 volts. One ingredient also shields the electrodes from corrosion by the other. Full cells built with the blend ran more than five hundred cycles across a broad temperature range and kept much of their capacity at minus twenty. The authors offer the recipe as a platform for safe batteries in harsh climates.
pmc-13179043:
Aharon Steffè and co-authors build tunable nanoparticles in a 2026 paper. Smart design of nanomaterials needs exact control of structure and of how surfaces react. The team made block copolymer nanoparticles in water that carry amine groups on their surface.

The amines could be counted and then linked to other molecules with high yield. One link added a dye; another added a heat-responsive polymer that switches at 41 degrees. The particles could also be assembled into hollow crosslinked shells called colloidosomes. The authors present the platform as a modular base for drug delivery, diagnostics, and tiny reactors.
pmc-13179143:
Omer Baker and five co-authors run in 2026 a pilot trial on whether a chat model helps nose patients share in treatment choices. Shared decision-making blends patient values with sound care. Patients with stubborn sinus disease face choices with real trade-offs, and AI tools might ease those talks.

Fifty-seven patients at one specialty clinic split at random between ChatGPT-4 and Google for treatment questions. Both groups feel less conflict about their choice after the session. Knowledge and usability scores are tracked, and chat answers are rated for accuracy. The chat group gains slightly more calm than the search group, though the gap is not firm. Patients unsure at the start stay more conflicted, a group clinics may support more directly.
pmc-13179943:
Cecily Palmer and co-authors study recruitment into a back pain trial in 2026. The RADICAL trial tests a nerve heating treatment for chronic low back pain. Complex trials often struggle to enroll enough patients. The team embedded a fast qualitative study inside the pilot phase to learn why.

They recorded recruitment talks and spoke with patients who had agreed to join. Quick thematic analysis sorted what information landed and what confused people. Staff needed more support to explain the trial clearly and calmly. Specific hurdles in describing procedures were named. Early fixes can raise enrollment before the main trial stalls.
pmc-13180243:
Mahsa Bozorgvar and six co-authors test whether ginger helps children with a form of childhood arthritis that affects few joints. Forty children aged six to sixteen took part in a trial where neither families nor staff knew who got what. Half received ginger capsules twice a day for three months alongside standard care, and half received dummy capsules.

Response was scored on a standard scale for child arthritis, which counts how many children improve by set amounts. Children on ginger scored higher at every level of the scale, from modest gains to near-complete response. The spice is known for calming inflammation and has a good safety record. Still, the authors note the trial was small and short. They call for larger studies to confirm whether ginger truly adds benefit for these children.
pmc-13180543:
Chao Li and six co-authors link broken sleep, swelling, and a sharper sense of pain through one brain zone. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Broken sleep is known to raise swelling signals and lower the point at which pain is felt. How the brain sits in that chain was not clear.

In a lab test, forced waking cuts deep sleep, raises a key swelling signal, and lowers pain thresholds. Brain scans show one zone, the precuneus, fires more when pain is felt after broken sleep. That zone's heat carries the link from the swelling signal to pain sense. In chronic pain patients, the same zone settles as pain and sleep improve.
pmc-13180743:
Arielle Locke and co-authors report three baby cases of a bleeding disorder in a 2026 paper. Hemophilia B, a lack of clotting factor nine, usually shows as joint or tissue bleeds. These infants presented in odd ways: bleeding inside the belly with a liver bruise, a scrotal lump that mimicked a twisted testicle, and bleeding inside the skull.

None of the families had any history of bleeding trouble, so diagnosis came only after the crisis. The authors urge doctors to weigh inherited bleeding disorders when baby boys bleed without clear cause. Early spotting, parent counseling, and tailored prevention can change outcomes. Readers get a alert for front-line clinicians.
pmc-13180943:
Youssef Natij and co-authors build a lean plant disease spotter that runs on weak hardware in a 2026 paper. Field calls are hard: signs are faint, classes look alike, and counts are lopsided. Big nets call well but cost too much for farm gear. The team's frame pulls traits with a mid vision net, then squeezes them to the sharpest few.

Labels were re-cut by cure type, merging over a hundred classes into eleven that matter on the farm. A tuned classic sorter hit the top score, near eighty-eight in a hundred. Training took half a minute on a plain chip, not hours on a graphics card.
pmc-13181143:
Lauren Wells and co-authors present a case report from 2026 on a rare brain infection. The germ Nocardia veterana lives in soil and usually infects people whose immune system is weak. It can spread to the brain and form an abscess, a pocket of infection that often needs long treatment.

Their patient had no known immune weakness, yet scans found a single brain abscess from this germ. An eight-week course of antibiotics cleared the infection. The authors note that a shorter course will not suit every case, so the result should be read with care. Still, the case warns doctors that such infections can occur in healthy hosts, often with mild and slow-moving symptoms.
pmc-13181243:
Wenxi Yu and four co-authors published a lung cancer study in twenty twenty-six on a circular RNA in tumor cells. Circ-FSCN1 helps the cells grow and dodge a fiery form of cell death. It was found at high levels in non-small cell lung cancer tissues and cell lines, and the team mapped its chain of action.

Silencing the circle slowed cell growth and migration and let reactive oxygen pile up, pushing ferroptosis. The circle normally sponges up a small RNA, miR-506-3p, which otherwise restrains a cystine transporter, SLC7A1. Restoring either downstream partner cancelled the silencing effects in two cell lines. Animal assays extended the story. The axis gives drug hunters three connected targets in one pathway.
pmc-13181343:
Min Cao and Glenn Masson review structural insights into the activity and inhibition of HRI kinase, a stress-sensing enzyme. Their 2026 review examines a protein emerging as a drug target in cancers and neurodegenerative disease.

HRI is one of four related kinases that switch off protein production by modifying a translation factor. It senses several proteotoxic stresses and prevents further rounds of protein synthesis. The review covers recent structural and molecular work on how the kinase activates and how inhibitors act. Regulatory interactions with other proteins and cofactors are also examined. Despite identification decades ago, the authors note surprisingly little is known about its regulation.
pmc-13183243:
Martha Thomas and co-authors set out, in a 2026 paper, the protocol for a feasibility trial on keeping frail people active across the whole day. The programme targets people who live with several long term conditions plus frailty. Its aim is to hold up their daily function and their part in life, through movement habits tailored to each person.

The planned intervention is a behaviour change package, built for patients and their carers. It uses several approaches, and adds new technology to support the 24 hour movement pattern. That pattern spans activity, sitting, and sleep. The trial is a randomized feasibility study, a small run to test whether the design works before a full trial. The protocol fixes the recruitment, measures, and checks in advance. It sits inside a larger research programme on this intervention.
pmc-13183643:
Worry that will not switch off defines generalized anxiety disorder, and a therapy built to attack the beliefs behind worry works well in adults. Hanne Undheim Hoff, Odin Hjemdal, and Henrik Nordahl tried it with teenagers in a 2026 trial. Ten Norwegian adolescents with the disorder received metacognitive therapy from trained clinicians.

The therapy targets beliefs such as the idea that worry is uncontrollable, rather than the worried thoughts themselves. By the end of treatment, nine of the ten no longer met the diagnostic criteria, and several also shook off extra disorders. Gains on symptom and belief measures were large and held at three- and six-month check-ins. Session notes showed steady declines in distress across the course. The authors call for a larger controlled trial of the approach in youth care.
pmc-13183943:
Mayu Yoshida and a large team uncover how a bacterial peptide stalls ribosomes. Arrest peptides pause protein synthesis in response to cell conditions, fine-tuning gene expression. The peptide CliM, found in Clostridia, sits upstream of the gene for YidC, a protein that inserts other proteins into membranes, suggesting it monitors YidC activity.

Two versions behave differently. One, from Clostridium kluyveri, halts the building stage at many codons, while the Clostridioides difficile version stops the ending stage instead. Structural work shows the second folds into helices inside the ribosome tunnel and blocks the entry of the next factor. Simulations suggest membrane insertion unwinds the helices and releases the arrest. One framework explains both behaviors.
pmc-13184043:
Joyeeta Bhattacharya and nine co-authors reviewed plant chemicals packed in nano carriers as a breast cancer treatment path, in a paper published in 2026. The cancer is a top killer of women, and standard treatments cut hard at the whole body. Plant compounds are kind to healthy tissue but weak in reach: they dissolve poorly, fade fast, and land widely. Nano packs fix each flaw.

Fat bubbles, plastic beads, metal particles, and carbon dots all serve as packs in the studies. Packs keep the compounds stable, raise their uptake, and steer them to the tumor. Harm to healthy cells falls as tumor kill rises. The team sorts gains by pack kind and compound kind. They call for trials to carry the green path into clinics.
pmc-13185043:
Candice Lemaille and co-authors survey mpox knowledge and sexual habits in high-risk groups in the Congo, in a 2026 study. The nation has borne the world's heaviest mpox load, with tens of thousands of likely cases in a recent span. A new mpox strain spread through close contact and sexual networks, yet community knowledge had barely been measured. Peer educators questioned 2,794 people across three provinces.

Barely six percent had heard of mpox before the survey. Those who had mostly named animal contact as the route and high-risk zones as the danger mark. Sex workers in the group reported the most risk acts, from many partners to paid and anonymous sex. Both sex workers and men who have sex with men sought care for infections at high rates. The authors plead for teaching built with, not just for, these groups.
pmc-13187843:
Joseph A McBride and seven co-authors published a study in 2026 on a gene-based test for bone and joint infections and whether it helps doctors use fewer antibiotics. The test reads a bacterial gene to name the germ when cultures fail. The team reviewed five years of its use at one Midwestern academic hospital before the pandemic.

Across 452 cases the test found bacteria in under ten percent. It rarely missed germs when it did fire, but it caught only a small share of true infections. Antibiotic narrowing did follow testing in the records overall. Still, doctors kept broad drugs in many test-negative cases they judged infectious. The authors conclude the test helps only a minority of patients.
pmc-13188243:
Simon Witzke and co-authors study how to pick synthetic data for learning the behavior of biological systems in a 2026 paper. Predicting how living systems change over time matters for ecology, epidemics, and therapy, but real data sets are often small. Training first on simulated data can help, yet the gain depends heavily on how that synthetic data is designed.

The team suggests checking synthetic data traits such as size, diversity, and noise before use. In a proof of concept on three classic systems and four real data sets, size and diversity effects were strongly linked. Good settings also depended on how well the real data matched the model behind the simulations. Careful choices cut prediction error by up to ninety-five percent compared with plain deep learning.
pmc-13189043:
Giuseppe Tortoriello gives an update on cancer of the larynx, the voice box. His 2026 report aims to give a current, critical view across many fields. Care can no longer sit within one field alone, he argues. Fast change in tech and closer work between fields demand a joint view. The report is framed as an official overview of what is known and how treatment is chosen.

Surgery stays a core pillar, he writes. It works against the cancer and has grown more sparing of function. Yet drug and radiation plans that aim to save the organ now rival it, above all in advanced tumors. Choice should not be a contest, he says. It should fit the tumor and the patient. Space is also given to the molecular roots of the disease.
pmc-13191043:
Renjie Gao and co-authors test in a 2026 study if gene variants shape the risk of a long term lung disease. The disease harms air flow and is shaped by both genes and the world around a person. A gene called PPARA helps the body cope with low oxygen and differs in groups that live at high altitude.

The team ran a case control study with 1,276 people in Gansu, China, split between Tibetan and Han groups. Four gene spots were typed for each person. One spot raised lung disease risk in Tibetan people, while a second spot lowered risk in Han people. A third spot showed a mixed effect in the Han group. The work hints that gene risk for this disease varies by group.
pmc-13192343:
Carmen Stan, Matthew James, and Mark Lowrie describe a rare nerve inflammation in dogs that answers to steroid treatment, in a study from 2026. The condition swells spinal nerves and roots, and its scans can look much like cancer. Telling the two apart decides whether a dog gets medical care or faces a grim cancer outlook.

Fifteen dogs treated at two British referral centers between 2019 and 2025 were reviewed. Most had weeks of lameness and weakness in one leg, and most were male. Scans showed inflammation in set spinal segments, and each dog was followed for at least a year. The paper lays out the signs, scan traits, treatments, and outcomes of the group. That record helps vets spot the condition sooner and treat with more confidence.
pmc-13194143:
Pan Xie and five co-authors review a chemical tag on proteins that may shape cancer immunotherapy, in this 2026 paper. The tag, succinylation, adds a small acid group to lysine building blocks of proteins. It links how tumors burn fuel with how they face the immune system, two fields often studied apart.

The review maps the enzymes that add, remove, and read the tag, and traces its reach into core fuel cycles. It then shows how the tag steadies or breaks a key immune brake, PD-L1, and how it steers macrophages, dendritic cells, and T cells inside tumors. The same tag can help or hinder immune attack, a dual role the authors stress. They survey drugs that target the tag's enzymes and combos meant to break drug resistance, and they flag gaps in the enzyme map as the main barrier ahead.
pmc-13194443:
Poe Eindra Thant and co-authors pool evidence on the harms of antipsychotic drugs for people with dementia in this 2026 review. The drugs are often given for the behavioral symptoms of dementia, despite long-known safety worries. Guidelines urge non-drug care first, yet use stays wide.

The team gathered forty-five studies covering two million people, published between 2010 and 2024. Use of the drugs came with a clearly higher risk of death, about a third higher in pooled terms. Both older and newer drug types carried similar risk, and people living at home fared worse. Evidence on stroke, pneumonia, and fractures was thinner and mixed. The authors urge cautious prescribing, regular review, and close monitoring for anyone with dementia on these drugs.
pmc-13194543:
Van der Kamp and three co-authors reviewed what helps or hinders screening uptake among people in vulnerable situations in a 2026 paper. They searched five databases for studies from 2013 to 2023 on chronic disease screening in high-income countries, and analyzed 96 papers thematically.

Barriers and aids clustered around health literacy, anxiety about results, and doubt toward Western health care. The same factor could cut both ways. Suggested fixes include education, community-based programs, and support from health workers. Most studies focused on ethnic minorities, whose concerns were mainly sociocultural, such as religious beliefs. Other vulnerable groups were thinly covered. The authors call for broader inclusion so screening design hears more of the voices it currently misses.
pmc-13194743:
Feng Zhu leads a 2026 engineering paper on making tiny hemispherical resonator gyroscopes, devices that sense rotation for precision navigation. Their quality factor, a measure of how cleanly the shell vibrates, and its frequency splitting decide performance. Standard coating lays a continuous metal film on the shell, which adds damping and drags quality down.

The team used patterned coating instead, depositing titanium and platinum films only in designed patches on the curved shell through three-dimensional masks. Coated devices lost little quality, reaching a quality factor above eight million, with even performance around the shell and tiny frequency splitting. Cutting film coverage reduces friction damping, the authors show, and a model links pattern to uniformity.
pmc-13196343:
Fangru Li, Xiaolei Liu, Weiguo Hou, and seven colleagues read archaeal communities as vent detectors in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Deep-sea hydrothermal sediments host archaea driving major chemical cycles, but how their communities differ along heat gradients from vents was unclear. The team sequenced archaeal genes in sediment cores from two different sites in the Tianxiu vent field, Northwest Indian Ocean. One site sat near a vent, the other far from it, with metagenomics added at the near-vent site.

The near-vent sediments were enriched in Hydrothermarchaeia, Nanoarchaeia, and Thermoplasmata, and formed a more complex, highly connected community network. Hydrothermarchaeia abundance tracked heat and chemical gradients closely, and its genomes carried the Wood-Ljungdahl carbon fixation pathway, with potential for methane production and hydrogen oxidation. The far site was led by Nitrososphaeria with simpler structure. The authors propose Hydrothermarchaeia as a marker lineage of hydrothermal influence.
pmc-13196943:
Maria Loconsole, Elisa Tedaldi, and Lucia Regolin test two number senses in newborn chicks, in work from 2026. Baby chicks judge amounts from their first days, but not by one single route. Past work shows both sheer size pull and a shape based oddity response at play.

One group bonded on same items, then faced five against nine of those items. Those chicks walked to the larger set, as past imprint work had found. A second group met only even count sets, then faced a prime count set. Those chicks stared longer at the prime set despite its smaller size. Both routes thus run from life's first days, cued by task setup.
pmc-13197243:
Nivetha Shanmuganathan and co-authors compare two related enzymes that trim pterin compounds in this 2026 study. Both enzymes belong to a large hydrolase family found across life. They help run pathways that recycle key vitamin-like molecules.

One enzyme acts broadly on pterins and feeds into purine balance. The other targets one compound on the path to a vital cofactor. The team probe how their structures and mechanisms split apart. Differences in metal use and substrate choice mark the divide. Knowing those details helps predict enzyme roles from genome data. It may also guide work on disorders tied to the cofactor pathway. Genome miners can use the split to sort new enzyme finds.
pmc-13197343:
Naga Pradeep Rayana and co-authors review fatty acid handling in the eye in a 2026 paper on retinal disease. Photoreceptors need polyunsaturated fatty acids to build and run their light-sensing tips, but they cannot make the key intermediates themselves, so the neighboring retinal pigment epithelium must supply them.

That single cell layer takes up, processes, and exports these fats in a coordinated chain. The review gathers evidence from human genetic disorders, mouse models, and cell studies on what happens when any link breaks: lipid balance fails and the retina degenerates. The authors map the open questions that block better treatments.
pmc-13197443:
Ceren Demir and colleagues ran a 2026 trial of home posture exercise for fibromyalgia, a long-term pain condition. Guidelines pair the drug duloxetine with exercise for this condition. The team tested whether a home posture program adds benefit beyond the drug alone.

Fifty-one patients split into an exercise group and a control group, both on the drug. The exercise group trained at home three times a week for four weeks. Both groups improved in pain, mood, sleep, and quality of life. The exercise group gained more in sleep quality, physical quality of life, and trunk bending range. Pain and mood gains did not differ. The trial was short, with no later follow-up.
pmc-13197743:
Breathing that stalls in sleep strains the heart and brain, yet the full night lab test that proves it is slow and scarce. Qian and co-authors build a sieve from a fingertip oxygen clip in 2026. Eight reads off the oxygen trace — dip counts, burden sums, time spent low — feed six learning models.

The build pool held 2,195 lab-tested sleepers, drawn from 4,156 screened. A second pool of 446 home-tested sleepers checks the sieve cold. Scores are read by hit rate first and curve strength second, and split by sex and age to hunt bias. The aim is a cheap first pass that sends the right people to the lab. Which reads drive each call is part of the report.
pmc-13198943:
Food programs often fail when they ignore how a community actually shops, cooks, and eats. Sze Wan Chan and co-authors worked with the Bangladeshi community in Brooklyn, New York, in 2026 to design a program that fits local life. They interviewed twelve Bangladeshi adults in English and Bangla about food habits, program access, and what they would want from a new effort.

Three themes guided the design: programs must fit community habits, social motives can drive uptake, and logistics matter. Gardening stood out as a way to gain fresh produce and strengthen social ties. The result was Harvest Share Seedlings, a home gardening program built with farming and community partners.
pmc-13200043:
Alexey Orlov and co-authors publish a methods guide for magnetic test strips in a 2026 paper. The strips work like home pregnancy tests, but tiny magnetic chains stir the fluid as they spin. Stirring speeds the binding that makes the test read out. A magnetic reader then counts the particles through the whole strip, not just at the surface.

The guide walks through fluid modeling on a computer, microscope checks of the chains, and the design of the spinning-field machine. Each step is spelled out so other labs can copy it. Reader steps for the magnetic signal are included as well. Careful shared methods matter because the spinning chains make each build step easy to get wrong.
pmc-13200443:
Azza M El-Derby and colleagues review cancer-killing viruses for liver cancer in a 2026 article. Oncolytic viruses infect and burst cancer cells while sparing normal ones. Results in solid tumors still lag hopes, and liver cancer's dense, immune-suppressed setting is among the toughest.

Fixes under study include stroma-targeting designs, viruses tuned to low-oxygen zones, and lab-grown tumor models to test delivery. Engineering now arms viruses to wake anti-tumor immunity. The authors map how these strands could yield stronger next-generation viruses.
pmc-13200543:
Dominic Rutland and eight co-authors delete one enzyme only in mouse kidneys to test organ roles in a 2026 paper. The enzyme clears a tyrosine breakdown product in liver and kidney. Its loss causes alkaptonuria, where that product piles up. Which organ makes the pile was the open question.

pmc-13202243:
Alexandra Laurent and Héloïse Haliday question a cheerful workplace program that cut burnout in intensive care units. The program spent four weeks pushing greetings, thanks, and compliments among staff. Burnout fell on paper, and the teams had fun.

The authors grant the result, then press on its blind spots. Positivity rules can become a moral duty, enforced by smiles. They can also shift blame onto staff while leaving staffing and workload untouched. Kind words may mask, rather than build, real collegial trust. The reflection asks what genuine support would look like. Feel-good programs travel fast through hospitals. This piece slows one down for inspection.
pmc-13202443:
Stronger, water-resistant paper made from farm and mining waste is the aim of a 2026 study led by Oumaima Bendalahcen. The research article treats date palm fibers to enrich their cellulose, reinforces the sheets with phosphate waste rock, and coats them with a bio-based terpene phenolic resin.

The mineral additive, rich in calcium and magnesium oxides, bonded with fiber sugars to strengthen cohesion inside the sheet. After resin coating and heat pressing, the paper shed water far better and showed large gains in stiffness and tensile strength over the untreated material. Ductility also improved, and the authors present the recipe as a route to high-performance paper that valorizes two waste streams.
pmc-13203043:
Prescribing guidelines aim to trim opioid use, and a 2026 systematic review by Jihoon Lim measures whether they actually do. The review and meta-analysis gathers studies of opioid prescribing guidelines for adults, focusing on chronic noncancer pain, and pools their effects on use prevalence, dosage, and treatment duration.

From 190 records found in four databases, seventy-one studies entered the meta-analysis. After guidelines took effect, opioid dose per person and prescription duration fell year by year among chronic pain patients in the pooled estimates. Declines also appeared in the general population and in cancer and acute pain groups, showing effects spilling beyond the intended audience.
pmc-13203143:
Dragana Ljubojević Pelić and co-authors present a 2026 food study on folding donkey milk into a traditional Serbian fresh cheese. Podliveni cheese is normally made from cow's milk alone. Donkey milk is prized for nutrition and low allergy risk, but its thin casein makes cheese making tricky, and trials are few.

The team made one batch the classic way and another with 30 percent milk from Balkan and Banat donkeys. The share was raised after smaller trials showed only mild effects. Both batches followed the same process. Lab checks covered microbes, nutrition, and making traits, and tasters judged acceptability. The study asks whether a value-added cheese can carry donkey milk without losing its character. Results may open a market for rare-breed milk.
pmc-13203243:
Na Cheng and six co-authors review in 2026 why cloning pigs by repeated rounds stalls after a few generations. Transferring a body cell's nucleus into an egg can copy a pig, and mice tolerate many copy rounds. Pigs do not: no live births past three rounds are on record, and success rates sag each round.

The review blames creeping epigenetic drift: chemical marks on DNA are reset sloppily, donor cell memory lingers, and gene imprinting frays, eroding the embryo's program. Fixes using mark-editing drugs help early growth but fade across rounds. The authors frame a species-specific reprogramming ceiling and urge work to break it for farming and medicine.
pmc-13203643:
Fuad Alanazi and Basmah Almaarik chart drug resistance in children's urine infections in a 2026 study. Children born with urinary tract defects get infections often. Repeated antibiotics breed resistant germs in them. The team reviewed eleven years of cases at a Riyadh hospital.

Resistance to ampicillin topped eighty percent of isolates. A common drug pair also failed over half the time. Carbapenems and aminoglycosides still worked in over ninety percent. About a third of episodes were multidrug resistant. One Klebsiella species crossed half resistant. The map guides empiric choices while cultures are pending.
pmc-13203943:
Pudthaya Kumnerdsiri and ten co-authors build food wrap from capsule trash and flower extract in a 2026 study. Sound wave extraction drew a phenol rich juice from yellow peacock flowers, which they stirred into the films at rising doses to add guard power.

Dosed films blocked more light, held heat better, and pulled stronger than plain stock. Water vapor slipped through less, and surfaces shed water more. The extract's own antioxidant scores ran fair to good across three tests. All films rotted away in soil within fifteen days. The two percent dose led the pack on strength and heat traits. pmc-13204243:
Dana-Emanuela Pitic and ten co-authors compare two turmeric extracts with an eye to mouth care in a 2026 study. Turmeric's active compounds fight germs and help wounds close, which suits dental uses. The team made one extract with water and one with strong alcohol, then compared their make-up and their action on mouth bacteria and skin cells.

The alcohol extract yielded more material, held more plant compounds, and fought the two tooth-decay bacteria better. The water extract was gentler on yeast and kinder to skin cells, though the alcohol one closed a scratch wound faster at a low dose. The authors say the solvent choice lets makers trade germ power against tissue kindness in future products.
pmc-13204643:
Plant extracts have long been folk remedies for gut inflammation, and Karolina Merecz and six co-authors put six of them to a lab test in a 2026 study. The backdrop is inflammatory bowel disease, a rising global burden with no simple cure. The extracts came from apricot leaves, peach leaves, chokeberry fruit, rosehip seeds, passion fruit seeds, and linden blossom.

The team dosed mouse immune cells stirred into inflammation by a bacterial toxin. A dye test checked which extracts harmed the cells, and a second test measured a key inflammation product. Apricot and peach leaf extracts stood out: gentle on the cells, yet they cut the expression of all four inflammation genes tracked. pmc-13205143:
Craig McPherson and co-authors review ways to make health record systems share data more smoothly, in a 2026 study. In United States care, record systems often cannot talk to each other, which slows referrals and wastes effort. Leaders in clinics and hospitals face this block day to day.

The review screened work from three databases and kept twenty-four papers that fit the topic. Five themes stood out, led by secure shared ledgers and by the value that smooth sharing brings to outcomes. Other themes covered a federal law pushing for sharing, smart software tools, and linked devices. The authors conclude that pairing new tools with policy steps can bring full sharing within reach.
pmc-13205243:
Verifying a quantum machine with hundreds of modes cannot mean reconstructing everything it does. Jose Rosas-Bustos and co-authors propose checking the collective behavior instead. Their effective mode approximation maps a large system's measured motion onto one representative mode. If the summed signals fit a clean harmonic pattern, the collective dynamics pass.

The leftovers hover near zero, as they should. The framework needs only a fixed handful of numbers, however big the machine grows. pmc-13205543:
Fleischer Kotey and co-authors chart in 2026 the state of invasive pneumococcal disease in Ghana after vaccine rollout. The germ Streptococcus pneumoniae causes severe illness in children, and conjugate vaccines now reach most of sub-Saharan Africa. Breakthrough cases still occur, and vaccine pressure can shift which strains dominate, yet follow-up data for the region are scarce.

The cross-sectional study enrolled 14,597 patients across hospitals in several regions. Spinal fluid and blood samples from meningitis and pneumonia cases were cultured for the germ. The survey describes how often the disease appears, which serotypes circulate, and how resistant they are to antibiotics after vaccination.
pmc-13205943:
Panagiota Peleka, Petros Galanis, and five co-authors review what shapes life quality after a heart event. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, covers acute coronary syndromes. Modern care saves far more lives than before. Many survivors, though, live with lasting limits on daily life.

Past exercise habits, a sense of coherence, and coping style help too. Mood, social support, and heart limits weigh in as well. The map can guide rehab that targets what matters most.
pmc-13206443:
Yu Fu and four co-authors built in 2026 a meal recommender that checks its own suggestions against hard nutrition rules. Many diet apps invent meals from shaky data or miss a user's medical limits. Their engine, CARE, grew from a retrieval-based chatbot into a pipeline that polishes the request, consults a structured food knowledge graph, and verifies each dish.

Every recommendation must pass rule checks on nutrients and restrictions before it reaches the user. Version two's design treats a diet plan as a promise that can be audited, dish by dish, against real food composition data.
pmc-13206743:
Sauce-flavor Baijiu, a prized Chinese spirit, gets its layered aroma from a crowd of microbes fermenting grain in open, solid piles. The technique reads a single cell's chemistry from its light scattering, with no labels and no culturing. Variants can map cell activity, link a cell's traits to its genome, or recover rare useful strains alive. The authors lay out how these readouts feed a design-build-test-learn cycle for fermentation. Their goal is brewing guided by data rather than craft habit alone.
pmc-13207443:
Norris and Bloomquist find that pepper extracts make a natural insecticide far deadlier to mosquitoes, in a 2026 study. Extracts of black pepper, cha plu, and Sichuan pepper each boosted natural pyrethrins sprayed on female mosquitoes, with black and Sichuan pepper raising potency more than thirteen-fold.

Two pepper compounds drove the effect, though one failed against a resistant strain's nerves while the other worked. The authors call this target-site synergism, a new lever for fighting resistant mosquito populations.
pmc-13207843:
Ioana Roxana Codru and four colleagues published a study in two thousand twenty-six on a blood ratio that might flag ventilator pneumonia early. Within that group, patients heading for pneumonia showed higher ratios before diagnosis, with a cutoff near eight point three. In standard care the ratio predicted nothing. The authors call its value limited and context-dependent.
pmc-13207943:
Donghwan Choi, Sang-Hyun Lim, and Jonghwan Moon review rare vein injuries at one Korean trauma center in this 2026 study. The vein that drains the liver sits deep, and blunt tears there kill often. Records span a decade of care at the center.

Ten patients were found, with four in ten dying in hospital. Half arrived with very low blood pressure and deep coma scores. Those who died came in with lower pressure, lower alert scores, and worse blood acid marks. Nine patients had surgery, and most also bore heart, liver, or diaphragm wounds. The authors stress that first-hour body state drives outcomes, and they call for multi-center work.
pmc-13208343:
