Better kneecap tracking is suggested, though the motion measure captures it only indirectly.
pmc-13447743:
Amada and Watanabe studied in 2026 why many older patients fail to reach target calories after a feeding tube is placed through the stomach wall. The procedure is called percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. They reviewed fifty-nine patients aged sixty-five and over treated at one hospital between 2022 and 2024, comparing those who met their energy target with those who fell short.

Only fifteen patients were underfed, while forty-four reached the target. Two factors independently predicted success: using a pectin-containing liquid formula, and having low baseline energy needs of about 990 calories a day or less. Final intake clustered near 1,200 calories in both groups, partly because formula comes in fixed-size packets. The authors suggest formula choice is a practical lever for early feeding adequacy.
pmc-13447843:
Tripti Shrivastava and coauthors present a 2026 doubt-aware tool for plant leaf disease sorting that stays reliable when moving from lab to field images. Their layered vision model pairs multi-scale traits with Monte Carlo dropout doubt and heat tuning, tested both ways across lab and field data sets.

Scores reached 97.8 percent on lab data and 93.6 percent on field data, with tuning errors far below base conv and vision models. Domain-shift decay shrank and doubt conduct stayed stable. Farmers gain a field-use-ready spotting aid, though broader crop and region trials remain.
pmc-13448043:
Hwang and colleagues review sacral slanting in 2026 in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis, a spine curve of unknown cause. Sacral slanting means a sideways tilt of the top surface of the sacrum bone. The tilt appears in up to forty percent of these patients and interacts with the lower curve pattern to shape surgical results.

Fusion level choice is the key issue. When the curve and slant lean the same way, stopping fusion one level higher generally prevents the trunk from tipping off balance. Five-year data also show no worsening below that level. Extending fusion lower in high-slant patients caused more imbalance on X-rays, yet function stayed comparable and no repeat surgery was needed. In one common curve type, the slant can invite gradual curve extension that may simply rebalance the shoulders.
pmc-13448243:
Soumik Ray and co-authors study how disease-linked changes alter droplet formation by the Parkinson's protein alpha-synuclein in 2026 work. The protein can gather into liquid condensates that speed formation of amyloid fibres, a suspected disease step. Inherited point changes and cut-down versions both occur in patients, yet their separate effects on droplet behaviour were unclear.

Inherited variants mostly changed little, with one exception whose droplets resisted fibre formation. Cut-down versions gelled rapidly and formed fibres almost at once, exerting the strongest effects on droplet stability and texture. Inside mixed droplets built from DNA and peptides, the protein could dissolve the host droplets or coat their surfaces like particles, steering fusion and DNA sorting. Those mixed-system roles depended on the protein's acidic tail region.
pmc-13449343:
Linda Cucciniello and a large team chart in 2026 how the risk of progression rises and falls over time in hormone receptor positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer. Standard follow-up scans run on fixed schedules, yet the authors argue the hazard of the disease advancing is anything but steady. Their analysis traces time-varying hazard rates across follow-up to find when patients most need watching.

Two danger peaks stood out, one early at two to three months and another around twenty-four months. Patients whose tumors lacked the progesterone receptor faced the highest early hazard, concentrated in the first one to two months. Lobular cancer type and treatment with fulvestrant also marked higher early progression risk. Liver metastases and a heavy overall burden of disease raised progression risk throughout. The authors propose bending monitoring schedules toward these risk windows instead of spacing scans evenly for everyone.
pmc-13449443:
Paolo Cravedi, Umberto Maggiore, and Andrea Angeletti comment in 2026 on antibody-depleting therapy for recurrent focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, a scarring kidney disease that returns in about a third of transplant patients. The editorial, titled Results Before Reasons, weighs why drugs that wipe out antibody-producing cells are being tried before the disease's driver is proven. Fast recurrence after transplant and experiments with patient plasma strongly suggest a circulating factor injures the kidney's filters, yet no candidate has met modern standards of proof.

Antibodies against nephrin and other filter proteins lead the suspect list, though they appear in only a minority of patients. Rituximab and other anti-CD20 drugs help some patients but fail others, and many still depend on plasma exchange. The authors use the new anti-CD20 and anti-CD38 results to argue the field must pin down which patients carry which mechanism before empiric depletion becomes routine.
pmc-13449743:
Kumar, Dobrosotskaya, and Frankel distill lessons from a trial of hepatitis B virus-specific T cell receptor therapy for advanced liver cancer. The disease remains the third leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Hepatocellular carcinoma makes up 75 to 85 percent of liver cancers. Fewer than 20 percent of patients can have surgery when diagnosed.

Standard drug options remain thin. The first approved targeted drug, sorafenib, extended survival by just 3 months over placebo in its landmark trial. Checkpoint immunotherapy leaves many patients without response. Against that backdrop, engineering T cells with receptors that recognize hepatitis B antigens inside tumor cells offers a way to attack virus-driven cancers precisely. The authors review what the Wu study's results imply for patient selection. They also cover safety around healthy liver tissue sharing viral antigens. And they ask where this cell therapy could fit among existing options.
pmc-13450143:
Chen and colleagues present MGCL-ST, a machine learning method that fills in missing gene expression across tissue slices. The slices are measured by spatial transcriptomics. That technology maps which genes are active where, but leaves gaps and coarse spots. Their approach learns from local and global spatial graphs jointly. It is enriched with image features from a pathology foundation model.

Across three different spatial platforms, the method beat state-of-the-art rivals on imputation accuracy and on spatial clustering quality in the benchmark comparisons reported. Sharper reconstructed maps improved biological interpretability. They let the team delineate tumor microenvironment structures that raw spot data blurred together. The authors highlight precise mapping of tumor margins and immune neighborhoods as the practical payoff for cancer research using these platforms. The software is publicly released. They position super-resolution imputation as a general fix for the resolution limits of mainstream spatial assays.
pmc-13450243:
Zakia Batool Turabee and colleagues release in 2026 a privacy-protected dataset meant to help computers recognize emotional dysregulation in autistic children before a meltdown peaks. Research on early warning systems has been starved of shared, standardized data, partly because classroom video of vulnerable children cannot simply be posted. Their ASC-emotion dataset converts video into point-cloud body tracking through the MediaPipe toolkit, stripping identity while keeping the movement signatures of engagement and arousal.

Three different learning architectures, a bidirectional memory network, a graph network, and a point-cloud plus memory hybrid, each tested the data. Together they reached ninety-six percent accuracy at detecting learning-related affective states. The dataset, built under an Erasmus+ funded project, is deposited publicly on Kaggle with an identifier for reuse. The authors frame it as shared infrastructure: a benchmark that lets other teams reproduce results and push early-intervention tools toward the classroom.
pmc-13450443:
Luojia Chen and colleagues build in 2026 a smart wound dressing that treats fungal skin infection and reports on it at the same time. Dermatophytosis, the ringworm family, recurs often and needs long monitoring, which clinic visits handle badly. Their hydrogel embeds laser-written graphene loaded with the antifungal itraconazole. The graphene's positive surface charge, measured at plus 43.1 millivolts, grabs fungal cells on contact, and ordinary sunlight warms it gently to about forty-five degrees, triggering controlled drug release.

Heat plus drug together inflicted several kinds of damage on Trichophyton rubrum, including an iron-driven death program called ferroptosis, and cleared the fungus and its biofilms in mouse models without recurrence. Because the graphene conducts, fungal load shifts its voltage signal, letting a smartphone track infection in real time. The dressing also calmed the local immune environment. The authors present it as a wearable platform joining therapy, sensing, and immune modulation.
pmc-13450543:
Federico Sandoval Morales and co-authors share a 2026 case quiz built around a painful skin patch that turned black after a blood-thinner shot. Their patient, a woman aged 70, was in hospital after a fall broke ribs and caused bleeding in her chest. Her usual blood-thinner pill was paused and swapped for enoxaparin shots under the skin.

Five days later a target-like patch rose at a shot site on her belly and formed a dark scab within a week. Her platelet count fell by about half, yet tests for a known heparin-linked antibody came back clear. Stopping the shots let counts recover, and wound care alone healed the spot over months, leaving a scar.
pmc-13451043:
Koren Hanson and co-authors study in 2026 how a professional youth mentoring program held up during the pandemic crisis. Social distancing broke the in-person model that most mentoring leans on. The program pairs paid trained mentors with youth for long spans, a distinct form from volunteer models.

One hundred twelve youth with an average age near twelve took part in the study. Mentor time and activity types were tracked before, during, and after the crisis peak. Strong infrastructure, special training, supervision, and peer networks helped mentors keep ties alive. The case shows how a professional model can bend without breaking under strain.
pmc-13452143:
Dola and colleagues surveyed university students in Bangladesh in 2026 about caffeine, mood, and sleep. Their one-time snapshot study covered 530 students chosen at random. Students reported how much caffeine they used, why they used it, and their mood and sleep symptoms. 

About 72 in 100 students said they used caffeine, and use rose with smoking and with having a loan. Symptoms of caffeine use disorder, meaning problem use that is hard to control, clustered around poor control, tolerance, and withdrawal. Craving and self-reward motives formed key bridges between use and other symptoms. Problem caffeine use hurt sleep both directly and through worse depressive symptoms. The authors call for teaching on healthy caffeine use and for mood screening in student health services.
pmc-13453043:
Rosa and colleagues present a 2026 personal view arguing that palliative and serious illness care in the United States is under threat and must be safeguarded. More than thirteen million adults and seven hundred thousand children live with serious illness in the country. Specialty palliative care improves their quality of care across the disease course, especially at the end of life, yet its foundations are shifting.

The authors name three threats. Financing changes squeeze the payment models the field runs on. Privatization of services reshapes who provides care and why. And palliative care sits low in policy priorities despite the population it serves. The piece is advocacy from leaders of the field: if these trends continue, the gains of recent decades in comfort, communication, and goal-matched care will erode first for the most vulnerable patients.
pmc-13453443:
Murdande and colleagues present a difficult case of mpox in advanced AIDS in this 2026 report. Their patient, a 42-year-old man whose antiretroviral treatment had been inconsistent, arrived with fever, cough, swollen lymph nodes, and widespread skin spots. Scans showed more swollen nodes and lung nodules, and the possible causes ranged from fungal infection and a specific pneumonia to Kaposi sarcoma and mpox itself.

Advanced DNA testing of blood identified mpox clade II alongside other pathogens. The antiviral tecovirimat was obtained through a special access program. It was given for 14 days. The skin lesions healed over, though one still tested positive for the virus. The team postponed a lymph node biopsy because no guideline, at any level they checked, spells out isolation procedures for operating on mpox patients.
pmc-13453543:
Akira Ehara maps how far families will travel to nurseries that care for mildly ill children in Japan. Regular day care turns away children with even mild illness, so these special nurseries keep care going for working parents. His 2026 study covers 105 major cities and monthly use from April 2018 to March 2023.

For each extra kilometre between a child's home and the nearest such nursery, use fell by a factor of 0.825, about a 17.5 percent drop. At 12 kilometres, use had fallen to one tenth of the level for a nursery in the child's own area. The pattern held both before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. Ehara sets the working service radius at about 12 kilometres, a guide for placing new facilities.
pmc-13453743:
Hongyan Hao and eight co-authors survey what women of childbearing age in Shandong Province, China know about the law backed fertility provision. Knowing the rules shapes whether a policy can work, the authors note, as China faces falling birth rates. Their 2026 study gathered 2,422 valid surveys from women aged 18 to 45 through layered cluster sampling.

Only 43.31 percent of the women showed adequate knowledge of the provision. City women knew more than rural women by a clear margin. Knowledge ran higher in families with mid level monthly spending, in women planning a first birth at ages 28 to 34, and in those wanting three or more children. The authors call for publicity aimed at rural areas and the groups the survey found least informed.
pmc-13453943:
Kim and colleagues map where fluid from the brain and spinal cord drains into the body's lymph system, a set of vessels that carries fluid and immune cells. Their 2026 study gives mice bacterial outer membrane vesicles, tiny sacs shed by bacteria, tagged with a radioactive copper label. A PET scanner, which tracks that label, then follows the sacs from the spinal fluid into lymph nodes along the spine.

More than three quarters of the signal settled in the surface and deep neck nodes, while most of the rest split between nodes in the belly, pelvis, and tail base. The neck share matches the brain's large share of the surface along the cord. The authors propose that each node group acts as a first guard post for its own segment of the brain and cord, sampling fluid for threats.
pmc-13454143:
Rong Li and others traced rotenone nerve harm to a sugar-burn route in 2026, in a Parkinson's model. Rotenone is much used to mimic Parkinson's, but its harm past the cell power-plant block was not fully known. The team found a sugar-burn path that adds lasting cell harm.

In dish cells, rotenone sped sugar burn, which built up methylglyoxal-made cell harms. Shikonin, by blocking PKM2, slowed sugar burn, cut those harms, and cut cell death. In rats, shikonin eased motor ills and spared dopamine nerves in the brain's dark tract. The work finds a new sugar-burn path in rotenone harm and names shikonin as a bright nerve-shield lead.
pmc-13454243:
Guozhi Hu and four co-authors track what years of growing melons on the same land do to soil microbes, even when a helpful bacterial fertilizer is used throughout. Their 2026 study takes 72 soil samples from Hami melon fields at three sites near Turpan, China, spanning one, three, and five year monocropping runs. All fields received the same Bacillus subtilis based bio organic fertilizer.

Longer runs saw fewer of three harmful fungi, among them Fusarium, and more of several helpful bacteria. Yet the whole community grew more alike from field to field, rare species thinned out, and bacterial networks simplified. Fungal networks held steadier. Of the soil jobs tracked, carbon breakdown peaked at the three year mark in a curved pattern, while nutrient cycling and carbon storage held flat. The authors read sameness, not collapse, as the long run cost.
pmc-13455043:
George-Rafael Samantsidis and Nicolas Buchon reframe, in a 2026 review, how mosquito immunity should be read: through the blood meal, not just the pathogen. A female mosquito's body is remodeled after feeding, with hormones, gut microbes, and metabolism all shifting at once. Infections arrive inside that same window, so defenses cannot be judged apart from it.

The review walks through the gut lining, blood cells, and body-wide hormone signals that set immune strength. Classic defense pathways are then sorted by what they truly do: switch on, kill invaders, tolerate damage, or quietly permit infection. Hormones tied to egg making and growth also tune immune readiness. The authors propose that regular feeding builds an anticipatory immune state, primed before pathogens arrive. That lens, they argue, should guide how vector competence is measured.
pmc-13455543:
Delilah Diana Namara and colleagues checked drug resistance in bacteria from tortoises and birds at a Ugandan wildlife education center in two thousand twenty-six. Diseases passing between animals and people are a growing worry, and resistant germs make them harder to treat. Samples were cultured, tested against antibiotics, and screened for resistance genes.

A common gut bacterium appeared in every bird sample and in some tortoise samples, while a salmonella type dominated the rest of the tortoise isolates. Resistance patterns differed by drug, with some medicines failing often and others rarely. Wildlife vets gain first baseline data for this center, useful for treatment choices and visitor safety.
pmc-13455643:
Chiara Amoroso leads a large team reporting, in 2026, a randomized trial of a multi-strain probiotic for the crushing fatigue of long COVID. Gut imbalance and immune disturbance are suspects in why symptoms linger. Patients with long COVID and clear fatigue took the formulation VSL#3 or a placebo for four weeks, with neither side knowing which.

Forty-eight patients finished the trial, 23 on the probiotic and 25 on placebo. Fatigue scores fell about 24 percent on the probiotic against about six percent on placebo. Two thirds of probiotic patients counted as responders, against roughly a third on placebo. Gains held after dosing stopped, and gut and life-quality scores improved in places. Gut profiling showed friendly genera rising, with matching shifts in immune markers. The authors call for larger trials to confirm the benefit.
pmc-13456743:
Zhang and colleagues use genetics to probe how IL-6 receptor blockers affect diabetes and brain chemistry in this 2026 study. These drugs dampen interleukin-6, an inflammation signal, and the team applied Mendelian randomization, a method that uses inherited gene variants as a natural experiment. They examined effects on type 2 diabetes in European and East Asian populations, then asked whether diabetes mediates changes in spinal fluid metabolites.

In Europeans, genetic mimicry of the drugs was linked with about a quarter lower risk of type 2 diabetes. The reported odds ratio sat near 0.75 in that cohort's analysis, a value consistent with that reduction. In East Asians the pattern differed, pointing instead to higher fasting insulin. The drugs also raised a galacto-glycero-lipid in spinal fluid, but only about three percent of that effect ran through diabetes, so the drug action itself dominated.
pmc-13457043:
Rui Quan and five colleagues track, in a 2026 study, how traditional Chinese medicine service capacity grew and spread across China from 2012 to 2023. The team built a province panel from national health yearbooks, scoring all 31 provinces on six service measures, from clinic visits to practitioner counts, plus economic context.

Every service measure roughly doubled or more across the decade. Visits rose about 106 percent, institutions about 135 percent, and beds about 145 percent. Composite scores climbed across all 31 provinces. Beijing and Shanghai held top ranks throughout. Fairness analysis split the gaps into within-region and between-region parts, and spatial tools checked whether strong provinces cluster. The authors offer the maps as evidence for fairer placement of future investment, since growth alone did not erase the map's tilt toward rich coastal hubs.
pmc-13457643:
Tapan Kumar Panda, Irfhan Sheriff, Jyoti Patel G and Krishna Rao Eswar Neerugatti published this 2026 review on light-based therapies as an antibiotic-free way to kill drug-resistant bacteria, the superbugs. Two methods are combined: photothermal therapy, which heats bacteria to death, and photodynamic therapy, which uses light-activated materials to release reactive oxygen that destroys them. Because the attack is physical and chemical at once, bacteria struggle to evolve resistance.

Older photothermal systems needed powerful lasers that risked burning healthy tissue. The review focuses on newer low-power near-infrared light, which new materials convert well enough to match the old results more safely. Using the deeper NIR-II window extends the approach to infections buried in tissue. The authors survey recent materials, from gold nanostructures to metal-organic frameworks, and list the open problems: targeting, safety testing and clinical translation.
pmc-13457943:
Sakalaki and colleagues followed drug treatment after a first heart attack in Sweden in 2026, linking hospital and prescription registers for patients treated between 2006 and 2022. Guideline therapy after a heart attack bundles blood thinners, cholesterol lowering, beta-blockers, and ACE inhibitors or related drugs, but long-term use is rarely reported. The cohort held 96,272 patients, tracked for how use changed and related to death or a second attack.

Use of the full bundle dropped markedly during the first year after the attack. About a third of patients died over a median follow-up of five and a half years. Blood thinners, cholesterol lowering, and ACE inhibitor or related treatment each went with a lower risk of death or repeat attack. Beta-blocker use, by contrast, went with a slightly higher risk, likely reflecting sicker users. The authors say long-term adherence remains suboptimal with room to gain.
pmc-13458143:
Juliane Müller and colleagues uncover a second job for the cancer-linked kinase AURORA A, beyond switching enzymes on and off. Blocking its catalytic activity halts cells at the edge of division. Destroying the protein with PROTAC degraders instead wrecked the DNA-copying S phase, exposing a scaffolding role. Their 2026 study profiles AURORA A's S-phase contacts and finds a crowd of RNA-binding proteins.

Chief among them, the ribonuclease DICER binds AURORA A, forming a nuclear complex governed by RNA. The complex homes to R-loops, snarls where RNA sticks to DNA during transcription, threatening replication. DICER appears to process the loop while AURORA A recruits SETD2, a histone-marking enzyme suppressing spurious transcription and helping resolve the stress. Removing AURORA A disturbed SETD2's grip on chromatin. The dual-output model reframes a mitotic kinase as an S-phase coordinator, with implications for cancer-drug degraders.
pmc-13458243:
Jack Power and co-authors update in 2026 a survey of doctors who practice palliative care in Australia and New Zealand. The survey asks which drugs they see as essential for easing symptoms at the end of life. It follows a similar survey from the year 2000, and also asks whether patients struggle to get these drugs.

Doctors answered in 2022, with replies from about one in seven society members. For most of the nineteen symptoms covered, doctors named large and varied drug lists as essential. A few clear favorites stood out, such as one drug for noisy breathing and morphine for cough. For some symptoms, many doctors said no drug is truly essential. One mouth treatment was flagged as hardest for patients to get in the community. The authors see a need for more research toward shared, evidence-based practice.
pmc-13458843:
Hiroki Eguchi and five colleagues published this 2026 surgical technique case series on vertebral body stenting for very severe osteoporotic spine fractures with an internal cleft. These crushed vertebrae are hard to treat: anatomy is distorted and bone cement can leak. The team describe using live three-dimensional imaging during surgery, on top of X-ray guidance, in three patients.

The imaging let surgeons confirm that balloons and stents sat in remaining solid bone rather than in the cleft cavity. Vertebral height was restored by 9 to 18 percent across the three cases treated. Pain scores fell sharply, from a mean of 8.0 before surgery to 1.0 afterwards on the standard rating scale. Cement leaked into the neighbouring disc in two cases but caused no symptoms, and no cement reached the spinal canal. Scans at three and six months showed the restored height held.
pmc-13459243:
Jiseon Kim and co-authors examined how generalized anxiety disorder relates to quality of life in the general Korean population. Their 2026 study used the 2021 national health and nutrition survey, covering 5,542 adults, with anxiety measured by the standard seven-item GAD-7 scale and quality of life by an eight-item national instrument. The analysis also sorted participants into three illness profiles, healthy, geriatric disease, and cardiometabolic disease, to test whether the anxiety burden falls unevenly.

The weighted prevalence of anxiety disorder was 4.23 percent in this population sample. Higher anxiety scores and having the disorder both tracked with lower quality-of-life scores across physical and mental domains. The strongest link was with the depression domain, at an odds ratio of 34.43, followed by memory and sleep problems. The strength of the link differed by illness profile and household income, showing the burden concentrates in particular social and health contexts.
pmc-13459743:
Xi Tian and co-authors tested whether knowing about nutrition protects older Chinese adults from frailty, and whether eating a varied diet carries that protection. Their 2026 analysis covered 1,187 older adults. It scored nutrition literacy with a standard self assessment, rated dietary diversity, and classified frailty with a modified version of the Fried physical phenotype covering weakness, slowness, and exhaustion. Statistical models estimated each association while the exploratory analysis probed diet as the connecting step.

Frailty affected about 13.7 percent of the sample. Higher nutrition literacy came with lower frailty odds, an odds ratio of 0.98 per point in the model, and with clearly higher dietary diversity scores. The exploratory pathway analysis found the literacy and frailty link ran partly through dietary diversity, with a small negative linking coefficient as reported. Teaching nutrition may pay off twice, the authors suggest.
pmc-13459843:
Yuki Takigawa and colleagues tested in 2026 a shortcut for lung cryobiopsy, pulling the frozen tissue sample straight back through the narrow channel of an ultrathin bronchoscope. Their retrospective review covered eighteen patients with peripheral lung lesions at a Japanese medical center between late 2022 and late 2025. Fifty-three cryobiopsy samples were compared with eighteen samples taken by small forceps in the same patients.

Cryobiopsy pieces were about twice the area of forceps pieces, and the overall diagnostic yield reached 72 percent of patients. Bleeding stayed mild and was managed with suction alone, and no collapsed lung occurred. One caution emerged: a four-second freeze left pinhole damage in the scope's channel, so the authors advise care with freezing time.
pmc-13459943:
Huandi Jin and co-authors derived in 2026 a gene-based score that predicts survival in early lung adenocarcinoma by tracing how tumors become invasive. Single-cell data from tumors at three stages, from in situ to fully invasive, were ordered along a developmental trajectory to find genes switched on during invasion. A 200-gene set was distilled into a score using cancer atlas data from 269 stage one patients.

High scores meant markedly worse survival in the training group and across three outside cohorts totaling over four hundred patients. The score stayed predictive after adjusting for age, sex, and substage. High-scoring tumors showed less immune infiltration and distinctive drug sensitivities. One gene, ARL4C, disturbed immune programs when silenced in computer experiments.
pmc-13460143:
Qiaoyun Zhou, Guangxi Zhu, Peng Zhang, and Baolong Qi followed in 2026 patients discharged after a flare of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to see who returns to hospital within six months. Acid reflux is common in this population, and its predictive role was unclear. The prospective Anhui study enrolled 683 patients, assessed reflux with a standard questionnaire, and built a nomogram, a scoring chart that turns risk factors into a personal estimate.

Nearly thirty percent were readmitted within six months. Reflux more than doubled the odds of readmission, joining a flare in the previous year, worse lung disease stage, and a heart strain marker as independent predictors, while higher body mass protected. The model discriminated moderately and calibrated well in validation.
pmc-13460243:
Yafeng Pan, Xiaojun Cheng, Guillaume Dumas, and Suzanne Dikker propose in 2026 a framework for multi-brain neurofeedback. The technique shows people a live signal of how strongly their brain activity is synchronized with a partner's. Recording two or more brains at once has linked this synchrony to shared attention, learning, and bonding. Feeding the synchrony signal back, through sight, sound, or touch, may let groups steer their own interaction.

The authors sort training targets into three levels: the raw shared signal, the social thinking processes beneath it, and real social outcomes at the top. Matching the target level to the goal matters, they argue, whether the setting is a classroom or a therapy room. Methodological challenges in measuring and feeding back group brain signals are flagged throughout.
pmc-13461043:
Douwes, Dutkiewicz, and Rinke hunted in 2026 for germ genes that could chew plastic, across the world's soils and waters. Plastic waste piles up faster than bins and burns can clear it. Some germs make tools that crack it, but few such tools are known. The team built search keys from the known tools' shapes. The keys swept field gene banks from dumps, farms, rivers, lakes, and seas, plus a vast germ code bank.

Hits turned up near all over, in sea and land sets alike. The densest fields were foul rivers, polar seas, and the deep sea floor. Most hits sat in germ lines long known to chew plastic. A fresh find stood out: kin of the old Archaea branch, not thought to chew plastic at all. The map now points labs to the best grounds and germ lines to test.
pmc-13461343:
Yu Wu and colleagues investigated in 2026 the gene CNTNAP2 as a brake on glioma, the most lethal brain tumor type. A pan-cancer scan of atlas data showed the gene separates glioma from normal tissue with high accuracy, and patients with low levels survived less long. Experiments in a glioblastoma cell line and in mouse tissue then tested cause rather than correlation.

Removing the gene made cancer cells multiply and move faster, while restoring it slowed them down. Its absence overactivated the ERK growth pathway and shut down a downstream gene called Necdin, and blocking ERK reversed the damage. Low CNTNAP2 also matched heavy infiltration by tumor-friendly M2 macrophages and worse predicted response to immunotherapy, giving the gene diagnostic, prognostic, and treatment interest.
pmc-13461443:
Serdar Efe proposes a three-dimensional pyramid model that shows lung mechanics during machine ventilation as one picture instead of scattered numbers. Ventilator data now arrive fragmented, forcing hard mental assembly at the bedside of critically ill patients.

The pyramid's edges carry the three loads on the lung: stretchy, resistive, and obstructive, with flow, pressure, and volume as its axes. Derived measures such as mechanical power, driving pressure, and a new asymmetry index map onto the shape as it changes. Eleven simulated illness scenarios each produced a distinct pyramid pattern matching the condition mimicked. Efe stresses the tool is a concept for teaching and pattern-spotting, needing prospective tests before any treatment use.
pmc-13461543:
Wang and co-authors presented a 2026 case report and literature review of a patient with papillary thyroid cancer alongside a paraganglioma, a rare nerve related tumour in the neck. Thyroid cancer usually spreads to nearby neck lymph nodes, so a neck lump may be misread. A paraganglioma at the carotid fork can look deceptively similar on examination.

The team reviewed their centre's case and searched three databases for reports up to March 2026 on the pairing. Wang concluded the patient had thyroid cancer with a separate carotid body tumour rather than spread to a lymph node. No clear correlation between paragangliomas and thyroid cancer spread emerged from the gathered clinical data. Telling a second tumour apart from metastasis is crucial, the authors stress, because it changes surgery planning and outlook.
pmc-13461843:
Xin Lai and colleagues report, in a 2026 laboratory study, that the protein TRIM47 helps glioma tumors grow and resist cell death. Glioma is among the most aggressive brain tumors, with a poor outlook. The team measured TRIM47 in tumor tissue and glioma cells grown in the lab. They lowered or raised its levels to watch changes in cell growth, energy use, and survival signals.

Tumor tissue and cell lines held more TRIM47 than normal. High levels went with shorter survival in the most severe glioma form. Cutting TRIM47 slowed cell growth, stalled the cycle, raised cell death, and shifted energy use away from sugar burning. Raising it did the reverse. A drug blocking a survival pathway, NF-kappaB, undid those gains, tying the effect to that pathway. In mice, tumors with lowered TRIM47 grew smaller and lighter. The authors name TRIM47 as a drug target for glioma.
pmc-13461943:
Yuanhui Tian and colleagues combine, in a 2026 analysis, two US data sources to describe locally advanced lung cancer and predict survival. The cancer type, non-small cell lung cancer, makes up most lung cancers; stage III disease has spread nearby but not far. Early detection is rare, and patients differ widely. Records came from a national registry, while gene data came from a cancer genome program.

The registry held 16,370 patients with stage III disease diagnosed between 2010 and 2017, split into training and check groups. A chart-style tool built from age, sex, tumor traits, and treatments forecast one-, three-, and five-year survival with stable accuracy. Gene work found 130 genes that changed against normal and early-stage tumors, marking signals tied to progression. Further screening narrowed candidate genes. The authors aim the combined picture at finding markers and drug targets for a hard stage of lung cancer.
pmc-13462143:
Farida Omar ElZawahry and co-authors paired two eye imaging tools to monitor severe corneal infections, asking what each sees that the other misses. Infectious keratitis blinds quickly if treatment misjudges the germ or depth. In their 2026 study, thirty five eyes with bacterial, fungal, amoebic, or mixed cases had slit lamp exams, cultures, and confocal imaging, which pictures living tissue cell by cell. They also had cross sectional OCT scanning during the acute phase, with features compared across modalities and germ groups.

Confocal imaging won on identifying the culprit, visualizing fungal filaments and amoeba cysts with high sensitivity alongside immune cells and nerve fibers. OCT won on architecture, measuring infiltrate depth, corneal thickness, swelling, and new vessel growth precisely. Cell densities differed significantly between germ groups, with some cell types notably depleted in particular cases. Used together, the pair gives both the germ and the damage map.
pmc-13462443:
Ken Sato reviews, in a 2026 article, links between long-term hepatitis C virus infection and cancers outside the liver. The virus is a known cause of liver scarring and cancer. Growing work ties it to cancers elsewhere, above all a blood cancer family, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, where infected people appear more often than in the population.

Beyond lymphoma, the picture turns mixed. A United States study of older adults linked the virus to cancers of the bile ducts, pancreas, and anus, plus skin cancers and a bone marrow condition. It found lower rates for womb and prostate cancers. Other reviews found evidence only for bile duct cancer and a possible pancreas link. Studies in Japan, France, Korea, and Taiwan added different signals, some raised, some lowered. Sato argues the inconsistency is itself a finding, and sets out how designs and virus-clearing data could settle which links are real.
pmc-13462843:
Xiaohong Lin and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a lean prediction model for height gain in children treated for central precocious puberty. In this condition puberty starts too early and can cut final adult height. Hormone-blocking treatment is standard, yet height gains vary widely. The team reviewed 163 children treated with triptorelin at their center. Children were split into favorable and unfavorable height-gain groups, and starting traits compared.

Three starting traits independently flagged a poor height outcome: a higher body mass index score and a higher growth factor score. Above all stood advanced bone age, bones maturing well ahead of the child's years. A spare two-factor model, using only the growth factor score and bone age advance, kept most of that skill with simpler inputs. The authors offer the lean model as a clinic tool for spotting children at risk early and timing extra help.
pmc-13463543:
Valentino and colleagues developed biodegradable wound films in 2026 from chitosan, a shell-derived polymer, blended with whey protein isolate from milk. Both materials aid healing, but how their mixing shapes film performance was unclear. The team used a design-of-experiment plan, a structured way to test recipe factors together, varying chitosan chain length and the blend ratio.

A flow-based measure of how strongly the two materials grip each other guided the choice. The best film, a one-to-three blend with medium-length chitosan, was the strongest, broke down slowest, and killed Staphylococcus aureus bacteria best, a common wound germ. It sped skin cell movement and growth without harming cells, and in mice left only about five percent of the wound open after 18 days. The authors argue the grip measure is a useful dial for designing such dressings.
pmc-13463943:
Xu and colleagues reported in 2026 a first case series of urologic telesurgery performed with Chinese-built robotic systems. In telesurgery, the surgeon operates from a console far from the patient. Between January 2023 and October 2025, six patients underwent remote operations. They included prostate removals and kidney-sparing tumor surgery on one system. Kidney and bladder surgery on another system completed the set. Local da Vinci cases served as rough context.

All six remote operations finished without switching to local control. None had major complications. The network link stayed smooth across striking distances. Average signal round-trip time was about six milliseconds within the same city. It was about 54 milliseconds over 2,200 kilometers between Harbin and Hangzhou, with no lost video frames. Remote prostate cases took longer and bled somewhat more than local comparisons. Cancer margins and early bladder control showed no worrying signal. The authors call the approach feasible under stable connections.
pmc-13464243:
Maria F Osorio and colleagues describe eight 2026 cases of a rare triple immune attack after cancer immunotherapy, striking heart muscle, skeletal muscle, and the nerve-muscle junction at once. The syndrome, called Triple M overlap, is life-threatening and arose a median 14.5 days after checkpoint inhibitor treatment for solid cancers. Median age was 76 years, and every patient had muscle symptoms.

Five patients needed breathing machines and one later needed a tracheostomy, while heart traces showed blocks and dangerous rhythms despite preserved pumping on scans. Steroids alone failed in practice, and all eight needed added immune-calming drugs. Early recognition and fast team escalation are vital, since the triple hit can worsen within days of first symptoms.
pmc-13464743:
Jason Mallonee and seven co-authors pilot Pensamientos y Pláticas, a four-week group program for Hispanic adults in El Paso, Texas. Hispanic adults use mental health care far less than white peers at like need levels, and local focus groups blamed stigma and hard-to-navigate services. The closed group met weekly with culture-aware teaching.

Eighty-two people joined, and thirty-nine who finished at least half the sessions gave full before-and-after data. Stigma around seeking help fell clearly, with a small-to-moderate shift. Emotional well-being, though, showed no firm gain in the short window. Attendance and feedback marked the program feasible and welcome. The authors back it as a promising first step toward care that fits the community.
pmc-13465043:
Cha and co-authors unveiled in 2026 a wheat breeding shortcut that produced South Korea's first officially released cultivar bred largely indoors. Their integrated speed breeding system combines artificial cold treatment with long-day growth rooms. Generations race forward under those conditions. A new bread wheat, named Irum, went from first cross to fifth generation in only 15 months.

The whole breeding cycle shrank from 128 months to 80 months, roughly four years saved. Statistical checks confirmed the fast-tracked population kept the trait variety breeders need. Multi-year trials across several environments then did the slow work of proof. Irum outyielded the standard check cultivar Keumgang by about 15 percent. Its performance stayed consistent from site to site. It also baked better bread than the quality benchmark Baekkang, giving larger loaves with softer crumb. The authors offer the pipeline as a template for answering climate pressure faster.
pmc-13465443:
Sangaran and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how antibody surveillance is used in Southeast Asia's push to eliminate malaria. Standard tests miss hidden pockets of transmission where cases are few. Blood antibodies reveal past and recent exposure instead. The scoping review followed standard guidelines across three databases for studies from 2000 to May 2025. Screening was done by several independent reviewers.

Of 6,849 records, 33 studies across seven countries qualified. Most were cross-sectional snapshots, with a handful of longer designs. The field's focus has shifted over time. Early work measured heavy transmission; recent work hunts the last reservoirs in near-elimination settings. Newer studies test many markers at once. Markers for the animal-borne species Plasmodium knowlesi and for mosquito bites have joined the standard pair. Rate estimates and machine learning pinpointed past declines and leftover hotspots.
pmc-13466043:
Darius Ashrafi and Laurence Klotz review high-resolution micro-ultrasound for prostate cancer care, in a 2026 article. The method uses a 29 megahertz probe to show the gland's duct patterns in fine detail during a live exam. A large randomized trial named OPTIMUM recently found guided biopsy with this tool no worse than MRI-guided biopsy at finding important cancers.

The review covers a scoring protocol for judging risk, how many biopsy cores to take, and how much readers disagree while learning the method. Newer uses include watching low-risk cancers over time, checking the gland after treatment, and judging tumor extent before surgery. Computer assistance for reading the images is a growing theme throughout.
pmc-13466143:
Jacinto and a large veterinary team traced a brain defect in Limousin calves in 2026 to one inherited gene change. The defect, porencephaly, leaves fluid-filled cavities in the brain. Thirty-four affected calves were reported in Great Britain; sixteen were examined in detail. Blind and dull from birth, they could not suckle unaided. Scans and tissue work showed matching cavities on both sides of the cortex. Some also showed dying cerebellum tissue.

Viruses were ruled out first. Pedigrees pointed to recessive inheritance, where two carrier parents pass on the fault. Genome mapping homed in on a small shared stretch of chromosome 2. Inside sat one private change in SLC25A12, a gene building a mitochondrial carrier protein. The change appeared in none of more than 5,000 control genomes. It was nearly absent from French and Swiss Limousins, giving breeders a test and science a large-animal model of a human brain disorder.
pmc-13466643:
Braccili and colleagues put a compliant prosthetic wrist through a full evaluation in 2026 with six men missing a forearm. The wrist bends softly while reaching, then stiffens on its own when the hand grasps. Users completed standard hand tests and six manual tasks under motion capture, each with compliance on and off. Healthy controls gave a comparison. Questionnaires covered workload and usability.

Compliance cost a little speed and score: hand scores dipped about five percent in soft mode, and some items took over a second longer. Reaching phases also lengthened. Yet the trade bought natural movement: where the wrist bent during grasping, shoulder and elbow contortions shrank toward healthy patterns. Users rated workload as moderate and usability above average. The authors frame the device as a balance: slightly slower, but kinder to the rest of the arm. Bigger trials must judge if that trade prevents long-term joint strain.
pmc-13466843:
Mengzhao Han and colleagues review research on whether exercise fights a specific kind of cell death, ferroptosis, in diseases that waste the brain, in a 2026 article. Ferroptosis is driven by iron overload and fat oxidation when a key antioxidant system fails. Exercise is cheap, safe, and broadly protective, yet proof tying it directly to this death pathway is uneven.

The authors sort the literature into three honesty tiers: studies that truly paired exercise with ferroptosis outcomes, nearby supporting work, and mechanism studies with no exercise at all. The firmest findings cluster in aerobic exercise models. They touch brain iron handling and the glutathione defense system. Gaps between animal clues and human practice are named plainly.
pmc-13467543:
Marek Nikodym and Martin Vasina review in 2026 the main math models used to predict how porous materials absorb sound. Engineers rely on these models when designing wall panels, foams, and resonant absorbers, but each model rests on different assumptions about the material frame and the frequency range. The review covers fitted formulas, equivalent-fluid models, poroelastic models, resonant approaches, and full computer simulations.

For each approach, the authors explain the underlying theory, the core equations, and the inputs a user must supply. They then weigh accuracy, computing cost, clarity of meaning, and the experiments needed, and they discuss published tests where models were checked against real materials. The result is a practical guide for picking the right model for a given material and sound range instead of defaulting to habit.
pmc-13467843:
Snowdon and colleagues examine the digital divide among United States hospitals, asking whether hospitals serving highly deprived communities have weaker digital health record systems, in 2026 health data research. Digital maturity was graded with the EMRAM scale, which rates how fully a hospital uses electronic records, from stage 0 to stage 7. Data covered 2,247 acute-care hospitals, linked to cost reports and area deprivation scores for each hospital's patients.

Hospitals whose patients came from the most deprived fifth of communities were more likely to sit at the lowest maturity level and less likely to reach the highest. In the adjusted model, hospitals in that top deprivation category were 5.9 percentage points more likely to have low maturity than similar hospitals. They were also 4.6 percentage points less likely to have high maturity in the same model. Snowdon argues digital investment gaps mirror social disadvantage, leaving the hospitals with the neediest patients the least equipped.
pmc-13469243:
Zihan Wu and colleagues predict a smartphone remaining battery life in 2026 with a physics-based model that listens to the phone own sensors. Instead of a black box, they extend a first-order resistor-capacitor circuit model with six real-world drains: processor load, GPS activity, screen brightness, network connectivity, battery aging, and temperature. Built on the GreenHub usage data set, the model clusters typical usage patterns and integrates the circuit equations forward in time.

The framework predicts state of charge with a mean absolute error of 4.2 percent and root mean square error of 6.8 percent across the tested scenarios. An interpretability layer ranks the six factors by sensitivity and contribution, finding processor workload the dominant drain. Time-to-empty forecasts that explain themselves could help operating systems schedule background work honestly and tell users which habit actually eats their battery.
pmc-13469343:
Maher Boughdiri, Mounira Msahli, and Albert Bifet present AEGIS in 2026, a defense system that spots tampered images fed into camera networks. Attackers can alter pictures in ways people barely notice yet still fool image recognition software. AEGIS first runs each image through a meaning checker that rejects pictures whose content looks inconsistent.

Images that pass are then varied slightly many times, and the system measures how unstable the predictions become. Five such measures feed a classifier that reports both a label and a measure of its own doubt, which the authors call calibrated uncertainty. On the Tiny ImageNet test set, AEGIS reached about 92 percent on a standard detection score across six kinds of input. The authors say it beat older detectors that rely on plain output scores.
pmc-13469443:
Ma and colleagues profile infections that resist drugs in an intensive care unit, in 2026 hospital research on germs that survive at least three classes of antibiotics. The single-center study covered all adult admissions from January to December 2025 who stayed at least 48 hours and had samples taken. The team described which resistant germs showed up and which early factors, present before infection, predicted who would develop one.

Among 986 patients, 103 caught a resistant infection, an incidence of 10.4 percent across the unit that year. Cases began a median of 6 days after admission and were mainly ventilator-linked pneumonia and bloodstream infections. Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, Enterobacterales, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa were the leading resistant types. After matching 309 patients to balance baseline differences, sickness scores and other early factors flagged risk on their own. Ma argues local patterns like this should steer prevention and drug stewardship.
pmc-13469643:
He and colleagues test a combined procedure for stopping acute bleeding from stomach varices, the swollen veins that form in liver disease, in a 2026 case series. These patients also had large natural shunts rerouting blood flow, at least 1.2 centimeters wide, which make standard glue injections risky. The approach first blocks the shunt with a balloon catheter technique, then injects medical glue through an endoscope to seal the bleeding veins under safer conditions.

The series included 12 patients treated between March 2022 and December 2024, with a mean age of 57.8 years and follow-up lasting one year. All cases traced back to liver cirrhosis, most often from hepatitis B. Clinical success reached 91.6 percent, covering 11 of the 12 patients treated in the series. No early rebleeding occurred, and no patient suffered symptomatic embolism. Late rebleeding, though, affected 33.3 percent of patients as varices recurred during follow-up.

The notice gives the correct authorship for the cited paper (DOI 10.1007/s44228-023-00034-w): the first author is Arslan Davulcu E, not Zhu J. It prints the full corrected author list. No other part of the article is affected.
pmc-13470443:
Delilovic and colleagues test whether mental health screening changes care use among refugees in Sweden. Their later mental health care use is compared with refugees and asylum seekers who were not screened.

Age and region of origin were associated with utilisation in both groups, so screening did not erase those background differences. The authors read the fivefold gap as evidence that screening works as a doorway: distress that stays unasked about stays untreated. pmc-13470543:
Kalliopi Skourti and colleagues review in 2026 the two way conversation between gut and brain and what it may mean for depression and Alzheimer disease. Both conditions are common, long lasting, and linked by chronic stress, which raises the risk of each. Signals travel between gut and brain through hormone stress circuits, the gut own nervous system, and chemicals made by gut microbes.

The review gathers evidence tying shifts in gut microbe communities to mood and memory disorders. Lifestyle and nutrition receive close attention, since food and water shape the microbiome daily. Candidate treatments include live and prepared microbial products, plus trace elements such as lithium and silicon. The authors present microbiome centered care as a promising addition to standard treatment, while noting how much mechanism work remains.
pmc-13470943:
Maria Charumbira, Gabriela Prins, and Quinette Louw audit, in 2026 work, the quality of rehabilitation data at a primary care centre in South Africa. Sound data drive planning and policy, yet low-resource sites often keep patchy records. Their centre's reports across ten years gave the test case.

Of nine core signs, none was fully logged; five were partly logged and four were absent. Fullness of key items ranged widely, and forms and labels shifted by year and by therapy type. The team urges shared tools, training, and a place for such signs in digital systems.
pmc-13471043:
Anne-Laure Mallard de La Varende leads a large team linking in 2026 a quiet liver condition to cancer immunotherapy failure through gut microbes. The authors name the pattern subclinical cholestasis, a hallmark of unhealthy gut flora.
pmc-13471343:
Wylde and colleagues describe the MAPLE project, a UK effort to make trial information leaflets easier for everyone to read. Their 2026 report covers co-design workshops where patients and community members reshaped a prototype leaflet and the guidance that goes with it.

Participants reworded text, reordered sections, and advised on images so the leaflet answers what patients actually want to know first. Future work will track how widely the resources are used and what difference they make.
pmc-13471443:
Ul Haq and co-authors surveyed whether key heart and diabetes medicines are stocked and affordable across Pakistan, using the standard WHO and Health Action International method. Their 2026 survey covered 32 essential medicines in six study areas, including Rawalpindi, Gujranwala, and Islamabad, comparing public and private outlets.

Originator brands showed up more in private outlets, at 54.6% of outlets versus 34.9% in public facilities, while lowest-price generics flipped that pattern. Insulin stood out as both scarce and expensive, a combination the authors call especially worrying for long-term diabetes care.
pmc-13471543:
Lu and co-authors studied a triple therapy for liver cancer patients too frail for standard systemic treatment, combining artery-directed chemotherapy with two oral drugs. Their 2026 analysis covered 49 patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma and poor performance status treated between June 2022 and December 2023, 21 receiving the combination and 28 receiving TACE alone.

Median time without progression stretched to 8.6 months on the triple therapy versus 4.1 months on TACE alone, with a hazard ratio of 0.316 favoring the combination. More combination patients also reported meaningful improvement in their physical condition.
pmc-13471643:
Ang and co-authors reviewed what happens when eyes drift back toward nearsightedness after laser vision correction, comparing three rescue procedures. Their 2026 retrospective study covered 158 retreatments: 136 repeat LASIK, 12 PRK surface procedures, and 10 implantable collamer lenses, with outcomes tracked six to twelve months.

LASIK retreatment sharpened uncorrected vision from 0.37 logMAR to 0.04, and pulled the average prescription from −1.28 diopters to −0.12, while lens implants improved vision from 0.68 logMAR to 0.03 in their small group. pmc-13472243:
Kazuya Kozumi, Yusuke Asakura, and Yusuke Yamauchi report in 2026 a templating route to carbon nitride riddled with well defined pores. Carbon nitride is a cheap semiconductor of carbon and nitrogen, and pores should expose more of its active surface. Their molds were perovskite fluoride crystals, which ordinarily would not survive the fierce heat needed to condense the polymer.

A gentle first heating step formed polymer intermediates that armored the mold crystals against clumping and melting. A second, hotter step finished the condensation while the mold held the pore shapes, and washing the mold away left mesoporous or macroporous products as chosen. In a glucose sensing test, the mesoporous version beat both bulk material and the macroporous version on sensitivity and detection limit. Pore architecture, the authors conclude, governs access to active sites.
pmc-13473643:
Cristina Sánchez-Fernández and thirteen colleagues uncovered in 2026 a switch that controls how the heart's outer layer builds it. The epicardium supplies cells and signals for coronary vessels, connective tissue, and repair, but it was unclear why some cells transform into migratory epicardial-derived cells while others stay epithelial. pmc-13474543:
Ye and co-authors describe removing multiple liver tumors from a 22-year-old woman with glycogen storage disease type Ia, an inherited enzyme defect that floods the liver with stored sugar. She recovered excellently with no sign the tumors had turned malignant, a real risk in this population.
pmc-13474743:
Jie Li and Anli Wang pool trial proof in 2026 on pregabalin for pain after wisdom tooth surgery. Six randomized trials with 545 patients met the bar, and four gave data for pooled math. Pain scores were the main outcome, with side effects tracked beside them. Bias risk in each trial was graded with a standard tool.

Side effects were far more likely with the drug, rising steeply as dose climbed. Relief and harm both grow with dose, so dosing choice needs care.
pmc-13475343:
Zijian Xie and co-authors study microbe turnover in 2026 in mud cores from the largest linked lake system in Northeast Asia. Xingkai Lake pairs a big lake with a small one that share water flow. Turnover, not nesting, drove most community change as depth grew in both lakes. Which phosphorus form ruled differed by lake and by microbe kingdom. Organic forms led in one lake for bacteria, while mineral forms led in the other. Phosphorus sorting may steer how lake mud life renews itself.
pmc-13475543:
Nina H Manaseryan and co-authors publish bone measures in 2026 for rodent skeletons held in Armenia. The collection holds 211 animals from twenty-seven species in five families, gathered from 1940 to 1981. Skulls and limb bones were measured by standard zoology rules. The set is the largest rodent bone collection in the region.

Raw measures cover skull, shoulder, arm, pelvis, and leg bones for each animal. Open access lets others compare finds from digs and modern surveys alike. Fragmented remains from ancient sites can be named against these references. Old collections gain new life when their numbers are shared in full.
pmc-13476243:
Yanhong Su and five co-authors find that a long non-coding RNA, DLX6-AS1, promotes necroptosis, a fiery form of cell death, in heart muscle injury after blood flow returns. The injury, myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury, arises when restored flow harms the tissue it rescues. Their 2026 study builds the injury in mice and reads death markers in the heart muscle. Necroptosis rises with reperfusion, and a specific inhibitor drug can stop it.

Forcing the strip up made cells die more by necroptosis, with a growth signaling pathway's markers lit. Silencing the strip reduced necroptosis and harm through that same pathway, PI3K/AKT/mTOR. The strip is a drug target, the authors hold.
pmc-13476343:
Smetana and co-authors find that a helper protein boosts self splicing by sheltering the raw material in a 2026 study. Inteins are protein segments that cut themselves out of host proteins, and some act as environment switches, yet cell factors behind the cutting were unknown.

A bacterial intein in an essential motor protein splices poorly at warm temperatures. Flooding cells with the folding helper GroEL restored cutting under heat. The helper does not speed the splice itself; it shields the unspliced starter from destruction, so more of it survives to splice. The study is the first to tie a chaperone to splicing control.
pmc-13476443:
Nozomi Toide and co-authors solve a hidden gene case in 2026 for two siblings with GNE myopathy, a rare muscle wasting disease. Standard exome reading misses faults deep inside gene spacers, where this family fault sat. Long-range targeted reading of DNA and RNA from muscle and blood found the spacer fault beside a known one. Prediction tools flagged a splicing fault, and RNA reads proved it.

The spacer fault wrecked message splicing, leaving a dead-end transcript in both muscle and blood. Staining showed reduced sugar coating on muscle proteins, backing the fault role. Blood-based RNA checks could spare some patients a muscle biopsy. The known fault list for this disease grows by one.
pmc-13476643:
Xie and colleagues compared in 2026 how two ways of organising ambulance services in China affect survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. One model runs all stations from an independent public agency, while the other attaches stations to hospitals. Using a national registry covering August 2019 to December 2020, the team analysed nearly twenty-five thousand arrest cases from ten service systems.

The independent model did slightly better than the hospital-based model, and the edge held after statistical adjustment. Its crews took longer to arrive, yet gave adrenaline far more often and placed advanced airways at more than double the rate. Because the absolute gap was small, the authors urge hunting for wider system practices that lift outcomes more meaningfully.
pmc-13476743:
Ivano Di Meo and co-authors review four rare inherited diseases that stem from faults in making coenzyme A, in work from two thousand twenty-six. The helper molecule powers energy making, fat burning, and many cell tasks. Faults in four genes of its pathway cause strikingly unlike diseases.

Two gene faults mainly drive brain disorders with iron buildup. The other two mainly cause severe heart muscle disease in infancy. Total helper levels are often normal, so the fault may lie in local handling under load. Care ideas differ by gene, from early supplements to gene-based plans.
pmc-13477543:
Melanie Joshi and co-authors build a workplace frame for facing illness, dying, and grief at work. Last Aid courses teach the public to handle these hard topics with more calm. The courses were not shaped for office life, though. The team ran 102 courses in work settings, then surveyed 611 past attendees and held five focus groups.

About ninety-five percent called the topics and the workplace setting highly relevant. Confidence in handling the subject rose for nearly all who answered. Attendees asked for more on grief at work, hard talks, and labor law. Focus groups split needs into personal, company, and growth levels. The frame names traits and support for workplace last aiders.
pmc-13478343:
Weixiong Xu and two colleagues built in 2026 a neural network model to predict the flow index of pit drip irrigation emitters, a key design parameter. They tested a plant-inspired emitter design, gathering 160 training-testing points and 25 external validation points across pit depth, spacing, channel angle, and aperture.

Among four network variants, the particle-swarm-optimised two-hidden-layer model performed best, beating six rival machine learning methods and holding accuracy above 0.85 on external data. Aperture mattered most for the flow index, followed by angle, spacing, and depth. The model offers designers a reliable shortcut during emitter development.
pmc-13478443:
Alison Bravington and coauthors published a 2026 realist review of shared decision-making in malignant bowel obstruction, a life-threatening blockage caused by advanced cancer. Many teams take part in each choice, results are unsure, and symptoms like pain and vomiting are severe. The review asked what helps or hinders true joint debate among doctors, patients, and families.

Four problem areas emerged: hidden mix-ups between parties, the pressured nature of the decision itself, how people in the room treat each other, and a split culture of care across teams. For each area the authors built cause-and-effect accounts and derived ways to improve talks. The framework aims to make decisions more open and better valued by patients facing very limited time.
pmc-13478843:
Pranoto and colleagues in the Netherlands asked in 2026 how short a protein's exit tag can get before a workhorse bacterium stops shipping its goods. The greasy core shrank from seventeen units to just seven with no drop in shipped yield. Their test good was alpha amylase, a starch cut enzyme. Short tags mean cheaper builds and less drag on the cell. The authors say tag design rules for this germ can be loosened. Long held length needs were more habit than law for this gate.
pmc-13479543:
Sagara and colleagues surveyed young Japanese cancer patients online in March 2025 about their first community pharmacy visit after diagnosis, asking whether already knowing a pharmacist beforehand changed the experience. The nationwide survey analyzed 407 patients diagnosed between ages 15 and 39 who then visited a community pharmacy. Satisfaction was scored with a 21-item medical interview scale, focusing on distress relief and rapport with the pharmacist.

Rapport showed the same pattern, at 5.20 against 4.60, and both gaps were highly significant after adjusting for age, sex, cancer type, and family factors. The differences, about 0.6 points each on the scale, lead the authors to value continuous pharmacist relationships during the raw weeks after a cancer diagnosis.
pmc-13479643:
Lung infections kill millions, drug resistance is climbing, and animal models only partly mimic a human airway. The organoids grow from human cells and keep the airway's cell mix and mucus, which flat cultures lose.

Set beside animal and dish models, the mini-airways win on human relevance while staying flexible to infect, image, and drug. Studies using them have traced how bacteria invade, hide, and stir immune replies, findings the review gathers. The authors weigh the remaining gaps, from missing immune cells to standardization, and project clinical uses, from testing antibiotics on a patient's own tissue to modeling chronic infection. A methods review with a forward lean.
pmc-13480043:
Megan Visser and co-authors present a 2026 study of faith and inner life needs among Latinx teens with type 1 diabetes and their caregivers. Thirteen youth aged 13 to 17 and thirteen caregivers joined focus groups. The team coded what was said and mapped the themes to the kinds of help trained hospital chaplains can offer.

Speakers described loss of hope, shame, grief, and strain over wearing a device that marks them as ill. They also spoke of feeling cut off from community support and of tools that at times made life easier. The authors argue that chaplains on the care team could ease this strain and lift daily self-care. They call the work a first map of these needs and urge more study of how families wish such help to be offered.
pmc-13481143:
Liam Clifford and Tripti Joshi describe a 2026 case where many small causes stacked into severe phosphate loss. Heavy replacement failed to hold levels until the anti-rejection dose fell and acid balance improved, yet relapses followed across repeat admissions. pmc-13481643:
Jonathan Martínez-Líbano and co-authors describe a 2026 study of how four social platforms relate to addiction-like use among university students. The two image-heavy platforms thus feed a loop where strain and compulsive use grow together. Facebook and WhatsApp showed no firm direct or indirect links in the models. Well-being programs for students should treat platform design, not just screen hours, as part of the risk, the authors argue.
pmc-13482543:
Dong and a large team compare blood-and-body risk scores in 2026 for spotting high blood pressure and neck artery plaque across 154,873 Chinese adults who had checkups with carotid ultrasound. The base score, TyG, mixes blood triglycerides and glucose, and the study pits it against versions blended with waist size, waist-to-height ratio, and body mass index. Participants averaged about 46 years old, and 10.5 percent had hypertension while 52.5 percent had carotid plaque.

The waist-to-height blend won overall, with the top quarter of scorers carrying 8.644 times the hypertension odds and 2.173 times the plaque odds of the bottom quarter. Sex split the verdict for plaque, since the waist-to-height blend was strongest in women while in men plain TyG ran inverse and only the body-mass blend held a positive link. Effects ran stronger in adults under 60, and the authors pitch the cheap scores for primary care screening.
pmc-13483043:

A blood test called IGRA flags people whose immune system has met the tuberculosis germ, which can wake up dangerously after transplant drugs weaken immunity. Nearly everyone received the test before listing.

Of those tested, 96 percent completed screening, and 22 people, about 4 percent, tested positive for the infection. Positive results clustered among people with diabetes, people born abroad, and people who used alcohol. Seventeen patients started preventive treatment, with few side effects and no liver damage reported. No one developed active tuberculosis after transplant. pmc-13483243:

pmc-13483443:

pmc-13483543:

pmc-13483643:

Strength tests took peak inhale and exhale pressures, and spirometry checked lung function. Marathon runners showed distinct patterns in the results. Such profiles may guide targeted breathing training. The study maps how race distance sculpts the breathing pump.
pmc-13483743:

pmc-13483843:

pmc-13484643:

pmc-13485643:

pmc-13486043:
Ilaria Milani and co-authors study a blood protein across metabolic diseases in a 2026 paper. Fetuin-A may link obesity, both types of diabetes, and fatty liver disease. The team measured it in patients and checked livers with ultrasound-based scans.

pmc-13486443:

pmc-13486743:

If lab coolants share those brain acts stays an open, pressing point.
pmc-13487243:

Regression models predicted outcomes within about ten percent.
pmc-13487343:

pmc-13487943:

pmc-13488243:
Nazife Nur Ozer Sensoy and Yavuz Ayar report severe adenovirus pneumonia with kidney failure in a healthy young adult in a 2026 case report. Adenovirus usually causes mild illness in people with normal immunity, so severe lung and kidney involvement is unusual. An 18-year-old woman arrived with severe pneumonia, strong inflammation markers, and kidney function already badly reduced before antibiotics began, while cultures stayed negative and a throat test found adenovirus.

A kidney biopsy showed preserved filtering structures, no antibody deposits, and mild tube damage, which fits injury from infection and body-wide inflammation rather than immune attack on the kidney itself. Steroid pulses and broad antibiotics were given, and kidney function recovered fully during the hospital stay.
pmc-13489943: The MULTI Consortium and colleagues published an author correction in 2026 to their Nature article presenting a sleep chart of biological ageing clocks for middle and late life. The notice adds two relevant prior studies that were missing from the original reference list: a 2022 study and a 2025 study, both by Li and coauthors. The authors state their regret for the omission. Nothing else in the article changes: no data, analyses, figures, or conclusions are altered, and the correction concerns citation completeness only.
pmc-13490243:
Zongkuo Li and Jianting Cai show that zinc calms gut inflammation by pushing harmful T cells toward a rust-like death in a 2026 mouse and cell study. Inflammatory bowel disease is driven by overactive helper T cell subsets, and zinc deficiency tracks with worse disease in patients. The team fed zinc to mice with colitis and grew human helper T cells in dishes, then sequenced gene activity to find the mechanism at work.

Zinc sharply reduced gut damage and stopped pathogenic T cells infiltrating the bowel lining in the reported experiments. Rather than merely blocking their development, zinc stripped their defenses against ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, by lowering two protective proteins and raising a driver gene. The mucosal niche cleared as a result.
pmc-13490343:
Xiaowei Hu leads a large team uncovering a three-part growth circuit in bladder cancer in a 2026 study blending tumor databases, patient tissue, cell sorting, and mouse models. Two cell-division proteins, NEK2 and ZWINT, rose together in high-grade tumors and marked a stable, aggressive cell subgroup enriched in invasive lesions. The team then traced how they cooperate with a third protein, NDC80, that helps chromosomes separate during division.

Silencing both lead proteins together crippled growth, spread, and tumor formation, while silencing either one alone helped only partly in the reported experiments. Removing NDC80 also slowed tumors and restored sensitivity to the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine. Tissue from drug-resistant cancers carried more NDC80. The authors propose the circuit as a drug target.
pmc-13491443:
Susan Musau leads an author group reporting a 2026 study of drug-resistant tuberculosis bacteria from western Kenya. Routine testing in the region relies on narrow gene probes and culture methods that can miss resistance. The authors set those results against whole-genome sequencing of stored samples drawn from twelve counties.

Among 1,053 samples, about one in eight stood up to at least one drug. The largest group no longer answered to isoniazid, though rifampicin still worked on it. Sequencing of 290 good-quality genomes tied rifampicin failure mainly to the rpoB change S450L and isoniazid failure to katG and inhA promoter changes. Resistant samples grouped in four counties and in lineages 4 and 3. Routine tests and sequencing differed often enough that the authors urge using both methods.
pmc-13492343:
Que Kong revisits a 1998 Plant Physiology paper that reported wrinkled-seed mutants of Arabidopsis with drastically reduced seed oil, and traces how it reshaped plant oil research. Plant seeds store oil as triacylglycerol to fuel germination, and vegetable oils matter for nutrition and industry. Their 2026 retrospective follows the science that grew from that single mutant phenotype.

Cloning the responsible gene in 2004 identified WRI1, a transcription factor that switches on late sugar-breakdown and fatty-acid-building genes, showing seed oil depends on developmental control of carbon flow. Later work mapped the DNA element it binds, its upstream regulators in seed maturation, its partner proteins, and the modifications governing its stability, plus the structure of its DNA recognition. Recent studies extend WRI1 into non-seed tissues, hormone and nutrient processes, and crop engineering. Kong presents WRI1 as a central node linking seed development, carbon metabolism, and oil accumulation.
pmc-13492843:
Durman and colleagues surveyed in 2026 sports science students in Indonesia on self-efficacy and study burnout. These students face dual study and athletic demands, and confidence in one's ability may buffer stress. The cross-sectional study enrolled 233 junior-year students at the State University of Makassar in 2025. Burnout and self-efficacy were scored with validated Indonesian forms.

Most students reported moderate confidence, at about seventy percent, and about half showed moderate burnout, with no severe cases. Higher confidence was tied to lower burnout, though the link was modest. Each step up in self-efficacy cut the odds of burnout by about half in the full model. The authors conclude that building student confidence is a plausible lever against burnout in dual-demand courses. They suggest schools screen for low confidence early.
pmc-13494543:
Wanyi Wang and others tune DNA copy enzyme theta to improve exact genome editing by tiny-match repair. In 2026, the study builds editors from the copy enzyme part and the unwinder-like part of the enzyme, aiming for thousand-base-scale aimed inserts that match-guided repair handles poorly in non-splitting cells. Short tiny-match strings guide donor entry.

The copy-enzyme-part editor tripled knock-in rates over standard Cas9 editing, while both part editors cut on-target insert-loss rates by about thirty percent and raised precise inserts by up to eighty percent. The copy enzyme part beat other setups and boosting factors. The work moves forward healing gene inserts with fewer stray edits.
pmc-13495143:
Kang An, Marc Gillinov, Lars G Svensson, and Miralem Pasic present a 2026 case report of valve infection after a catheter-based aortic valve replacement, known as TAVR. An 82-year-old woman arrived with fever and weariness, and scans found a large, loose growth of infected tissue swinging on her implanted valve. Such growths often break off and block arteries, with the brain a feared target.

Scans showed clots had struck her spleen, kidneys, and gut arteries, yet the brain stayed clear. At surgery the growth was gone from the valve, proof it had broken away, and the team removed the valve, cleaned the area fully, and sewed in a tissue valve. She recovered well.
