Three varieties lost the least yield. They were BH5211, BH661, and BH547. Their yields also stayed stable across both soils. BHQPY545 lost the most under acid stress.
pmc-13542243:
Danial Fotros and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study linking how strongly a person's diet and lifestyle raise insulin levels to their odds of fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. All participants had type 2 diabetes, a group where this liver condition is especially common. Diet and habits were captured with validated questionnaires and converted into four scores covering eating patterns and wider lifestyle, each scored for both insulin release and insulin resistance.

People in the highest quarter for the insulin-resistance diet score had notably higher odds of the liver condition, with an odds ratio near 7.8 in the fully adjusted analysis. The lifestyle score for high insulin release gave a similar figure near 8, while one diet score showed no clear link. The authors argue that eating patterns chosen to calm insulin demand may help prevent liver complications in diabetes care.
pmc-13542443:
E Sarmikasoglou and colleagues published a 2026 feeding trial on corn silage made from a short-stature corn hybrid carrying the brachytic2 mutation, which makes plants shorter and sturdier than tall conventional corn. Lactating Holstein cows received silage from either the short hybrid or a tall one, at high or low dietary fibre levels. The team tracked feed intake, milk output, how completely nutrients were digested, and greenhouse gas emissions.

Cows on the short-hybrid silage ate more and produced more energy-corrected milk than cows on tall-hybrid silage, with the advantage largest in the high-fibre diet. Low-fibre diets raised intake and milk yield but lowered feed efficiency, and they cut methane output per cow and per unit of feed. Methane did not differ between corn hybrids. The short hybrid therefore improved cow performance without a methane penalty in this trial.
pmc-13542943:
Xi Lin and colleagues published a 2026 animal study testing nanovesicles from honeysuckle, Lonicera japonica, as a treatment for acute lung injury. These tiny plant-derived sacs were isolated and given to mice whose lungs had been injured with a bacterial toxin. Much of the damage in this condition comes from neutrophil extracellular traps, webs of DNA that white blood cells throw out and that can harm lung tissue when produced excessively.

The vesicles gathered in lung neutrophils, and treated mice kept their weight and activity better while lung injury eased. Inflammatory signals fell, fewer neutrophils crowded the lungs, and fewer traps formed. Markers suggested the vesicles calmed a self-digestion process in cells that feeds trap formation. When a drug that forces trap release was added, the benefit vanished, supporting the proposed mechanism. Plant nanovesicles aimed at the lung could become a new treatment direction, though human testing lies ahead.
pmc-13543443:
Brain imaging experts in Japan built a new head coil to scan awake monkeys with fine detail. Awake scans can show how the primate brain wires itself at rest, which bears on human brain maps. Awake monkeys move and sessions stay short, so signal is weak. The team built a 24-channel coil tuned for a standard scan strength and for fast scan tricks that cut time.

Scans used a blood-volume dye that boosts the signal far past the standard oxygen read. A data clean-up path, adapted from a human brain project, handled motion and layout warps. A trained sorter then stripped out structured noise from the time series. Noise still took more of the signal than brain work did, which the team flags as the next bar. The coil and path open the way to longer awake studies.
pmc-13543543:
Tao Luo's team published a 2026 study combining an approved iron medicine, ferumoxytol, with a gene-silencing therapy to kill acute myeloid leukaemia cells by ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death. The gene target, GBA, maintains the chemistry of lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments; blocking it leaks iron that fuels the death process. Their plasmid was designed to switch on mainly where NF-kappaB, a signalling protein overactive in this leukaemia, is already active, sparing normal cells.

In laboratory tests the iron particles amplified the silencing effect greatly, and markers plus microscopy confirmed ferroptosis as the killing route. Mice carrying the leukaemia lived significantly longer on the combination, with no obvious harm to organs, blood counts, or liver and kidney tests. Turning a tumour's own signalling addiction into the trigger for its destruction is the elegant core of the approach.
pmc-13544243:
Eleven researchers design a hybrid battery anode that stores lithium in two ways at once in a paper from 2026. Most anodes use one storage method, which forces a trade between energy and lifespan. Their anode pairs lithium metal with a silicon oxide layer. Lithium first enters the silicon layer, forming a network that guides later deposits. Fresh lithium then plates in a controlled layer beneath it.

Paired with a standard high-energy cathode, full cells stored half again more energy than silicon-based rivals. They kept most of their capacity after nine hundred cycles. A pouch cell also cycled stably hundreds of times. The authors present the dual method as a general design for next-generation batteries.
pmc-13544943: Ozcan Ozeke and co-authors explain how signals recorded inside the heart during a fast ventricular rhythm can guide treatment. The shape of each signal matters. So does its timing within the rhythm cycle. Together they reveal where the scar sits. They show how the scar relates to the circuit driving the rhythm. The point matters most when a circuit has two entrances or two exits. Doctors must then tell the narrow channel that drives the rhythm from a nearby bystander channel. Burning the wrong one wastes the procedure.
pmc-13545043:
Sanjana Parikh and colleagues published a 2026 modelling study of vedolizumab, a gut-selective antibody drug for ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, asking how inflammation severity changes the drug's path through the body. Exposure varies with disease activity because the drug is consumed by binding its target. Their physiologically based model, built in a standard simulation platform, included that target-mediated disposal and was first checked against healthy-volunteer data.

The model reproduced observed blood levels closely across a wide dose range in healthy adults, with predicted-to-observed ratios mostly between eight- and eleven-tenths. For patients, the team let the amount of target rise with inflammation, as the biology dictates, and predictions for mild-to-moderate colitis again landed near the observed values. A verified model of this kind can forecast dosing in sicker patients before trials enrol them, the authors argue.
pmc-13545143:
Patricia Grant led a 2026 evaluation of a self-guided eye movement training program for adults who have lost central vision. Thirty-three people with retinal disease and a documented blind spot in central vision enrolled, training two hours a week for eight weeks. Twenty-five trained in a clinic, while eight used the same platform at home.

Reading speed, measured with standard low vision charts, rose by about 23 words per minute on average, a gain near 55 percent. Home users improved about as much as clinic users, which suggests the program can reach people who cannot travel for rehabilitation. Vision, mood, and self-reported function were also tracked before and after training.
pmc-13545243:
Ella Paasio and co-authors present a study the catalog lists under 2026. Hyperdimensional computing encodes data as very long vectors, a style that suits fast, low-power chips. In-memory computing does math inside memory to dodge data traffic. The team builds that memory from ferroelectric capacitors of a hafnium-zirconium oxide. The material holds a strong polarization charge and fits standard chip back-end steps. Ten-nanometer films form the devices.

The capacitors show 32 clean, evenly programmable charge states. Many stable states are what in-memory elements need for multi-bit work. Fabrication was tuned to avoid vacuum steps where possible. Chip designers get a non-volatile element that computes where data live. Energy and delay savings drive the field, and multi-bit precision has been its weak point. High polarization is the lever this work uses to fix that weakness.
pmc-13545643:
Silvana Duran-Ortiz and co-authors switch off a growth signal in midlife mice in a 2026 study. Blocking growth hormone signals from birth is known to extend life in mammals. Whether the same trick works when started in midlife, and how cells respond, was far less clear.

At twelve months of age, the hormone's receptor was removed in the mice with a drug triggered switch. The change gave the expected signs of hormone resistance, with lower levels of a linked growth factor in blood. Healthy lifespan grew longer. Liver cells were then read one by one, and gene activity shifts differed between males and females.
pmc-13546043:
A stroke gives a victim minutes, not hours, so public knowledge of warnings and first steps decides outcomes. Three researchers survey adults in two large Yemeni cities in 2026 about risk factors, symptoms, prevention, and treatment. Yemen's war-strained health system makes the question sharper. Recognition runs surprisingly high: nearly 88 percent show solid awareness overall. Blood pressure and excess weight are widely named as risks, and dizziness as a warning.

People with chronic disease in the family, or a stroke of their own, score highest. Schooling lifts scores on symptoms, prevention, and management. The authors still find dimmer corners of knowledge and call for targeted campaigns to light them, especially for residents with less schooling.
pmc-13546543:
Qin Deng and colleagues reported in 2026 on adding the targeted drug apatinib to standard chemotherapy after surgery for stage III stomach cancer. The study covered 112 patients whose tumors showed high levels of VEGFR-2, the molecule apatinib blocks, treated at one Chinese hospital between 2015 and 2021. Fifty-seven received apatinib plus the two-drug SOX regimen, while 55 received SOX alone.

Patients on the combined treatment stayed free of disease far longer, with five-year disease-free survival near 63 percent against 32 percent for chemotherapy alone, and overall survival showed a similar gap. Side effects were mostly mild to moderate in both groups. Because treatment was not assigned randomly, the authors call for a large randomized trial to confirm the benefit.
pmc-13546643:
Ezequiel Forte and co-authors studied in 2026 a blood fat particle linked to heart disease in adults in Argentina with overweight or obesity. This particle is a known independent risk factor for clogged arteries. How it relates to body weight, and whether the link to heart disease changes with weight, was not well known in this region.

The team grouped nearly three thousand patients by body mass index. Raw rates of high levels of the particle fell as weight rose, but after adjusting for other factors, higher weight groups showed higher odds of high levels. High levels were linked to heart disease from clogged arteries in every weight group. The link did not differ by weight, the authors found.
pmc-13547243:
Xiaoli Hu, writing alone, offers a 2026 study of why maritime cadets in China stay driven to learn English. Sailors need strong English for safety and for a required global certificate. A known theory of drive says people thrive when needs for skill, choice, and belonging are met, and stall when those needs are blocked.

Hu tested a two-path model among 304 cadets, where a supportive setting feeds outcomes through both met and blocked needs. Twenty follow-up interviews added depth to the numbers. Feeling skilled proved the strongest driver of inner drive to learn. The study shows how the theory works in a high-pressure training setting outside the usual Western samples.
pmc-13547343:
Shion Masuda and colleagues tested in 2026 whether simply limiting how far the shinbone slides forward after a torn knee ligament can protect the joint's sense of position. The torn ligament normally carries tiny sensors that report joint movement, and surgery restores stability better than it restores that sensing. Rats were split into sham surgery, ligament cut, and ligament cut plus an internal suture brace that controlled the sliding.

Braced rats kept better balance beam performance and healthier-looking sensors at the ligament's attachment points, while unbraced injured rats lost coordination and grew more abnormal sensors. Sensor counts tracked behavior closely, supporting their role in recovery. The authors suggest bracing-style control as a foundation for treatments focused on function, not structure alone.
pmc-13547843:
Zang, Vithoulkas, and Zuo ask in 2026 whether surgery hastens Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment, using a national imaging database. Past findings on surgery and these diagnoses conflict, and timing effects were unknown. Their matched cohort study drew records from 2005 to 2025.

The sample held 1,114 people with mild impairment, 760 with Alzheimer's, and 397 with normal cognition. Surgery did not lower the age at impairment diagnosis, and it tied to Alzheimer's presenting 1.7 years later overall. Under age sixty, surgery tied to earlier diagnosis of both states. Past sixty, it tied to later diagnosis by about five years. Incidence itself did not change with surgery.
pmc-13548143:
Nawal Tahir and a large team compare two sedative drugs for older patients who need a gut scope test. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Sedation keeps the patient calm and helps the test go well. Propofol is long in use, while remimazolam is newer and may be safer for the old.

They pool trials that set the two drugs head to head in older adults. Low blood pressure, the main harm checked, came far less often with the new drug. Slow heart rate, low breathing, and pain at the shot site were also less common. Wake-up time and sickness rates were much the same. More strong trials are still called for.
pmc-13548343:
Maria Byrne and Pauline Ross review how shoreline invertebrates face a harsher climate in this 2026 paper. Creatures at the land-sea edge already ride swings of heat and salt with every tide. Heatwaves, floods, fires, and shifting ice now stack on top, sometimes together. The review covers rocky shores, mudflats, mangroves, and saltmarsh.

Bivalves get a case-study focus, since they anchor food webs and fisheries. Heat at low tide proves especially deadly. Species differ widely in tolerance, and shore height changes exposure hour by hour. The authors weigh how acclimation, adaptation, and refuge habitats might build resilience, and which species back up key services if others fail.
pmc-13548543:
Natasha Beer and colleagues review how injury from transvaginal mesh affects women's sexual lives and relationships, in a 2026 systematic review. Mesh once commonly treated pelvic organ prolapse and stress incontinence, yet it left many women with chronic pain and lasting harm. The authors searched five databases plus grey literature and combined findings thematically from nine reports covering roughly fifteen hundred women.

Seven themes emerged, covering pain-driven changes in sexual function, shifts in sexuality and self-image, strained relationship satisfaction, and altered roles between partners. A central theme tied these together as a disrupted sense of the sexual and relational self. Most reports rated high in quality. The authors note that psychological flexibility may soften relationship distress, and they call for research that can shape proper support and therapy for injured women.
pmc-13548643:
Yanting Chen and colleagues hunt for what predicts lingering neck pain after front-of-neck spine fusion surgery, in a 2026 risk factor study. Axial pain is a recognized nuisance after this operation, though it is more often blamed on back-of-neck surgery. The team reviewed patients operated between 2020 and 2023, comparing imaging measurements of neck curve, disc height, and joint spacing between those who developed the pain and those who did not.

About one in six single-level patients and one in five multi-level patients reported the pain. For single-level surgery, how much the facet joint gap changed after surgery predicted trouble, with a clear cutoff value. For multi-level surgery, the size of the change in neck curve was the culprit. The authors advise surgeons to disturb joint spacing less in short fusions and to avoid over-correcting the curve in longer ones.
pmc-13549343:
Nanrui Yang and colleagues propose flipping the polarization of synchrotron light thousands of times per second, in a 2026 accelerator physics paper. Their trick is to wiggle a magnetic field. The work targets the planned Hefei Advanced Light Facility. Experiments that probe magnetism in materials need rapid alternation between polarization states, yet mechanically shifting magnet arrays is slow, and workarounds with twin devices are bulky and costly.

The proposal adds electromagnetic coils to the undulator, the magnet array that makes the beam. Wiggling its field directly switches polarization at kilohertz rates. The paper lays out the design against the landscape of existing strategies, from hybrid magnet devices at other facilities to beamline switching schemes that pick between two beams. The authors argue source-level switching promises cleaner, faster results for magnetic spectroscopy at the new site.
pmc-13549443:
Tomoki Tanabe and co-authors name in 2026 a new species of gut bacterium found in human feces. The genus Anaerostipes is known for making butyrate, a food for the gut lining. The strain came from a healthy adult during a broad effort to culture gut microbes.

Gene comparisons placed the strain inside the genus but well apart from every known species. Its body chemistry, enzyme set, and narrow range of usable sugars also set it apart. The authors name it Anaerostipes stercorihominis and deposit the type strain in two collections. Along the way they found two named species that look identical by gene measures, and propose merging them.
pmc-13550043:
Hermano Zenaide-Neto and nine co-authors map how a protein kinase A pathway reshapes a fungus used to make industrial enzymes. Trichoderma reesei is a major source of enzymes that break down plant biomass. Nutrient sensing through the cyclic AMP and kinase A pathway guides its response to complex carbon sources such as sugarcane bagasse.

The team combines transcript, protein, and phosphorylation data for a normal strain and a strain lacking the kinase gene, grown on glucose or bagasse. Deletion alters growth traits and lowers output of some biomass degrading enzymes. Gene and protein changes hit enzyme sets, transporters, stress proteins, and regulators in a condition dependent way. Docking tests nominate candidate kinase targets for future validation work.
pmc-13550443:
Mohammed Jamal Mohammed, Javad Rahmani-Fard, and Ali Mohammed Ridha design a silent, sensor-free controller for a hybrid electric motor used in vehicles and industry, in a 2026 engineering paper. The machine needs rotor position to run well, but physical sensors add cost and fragility, while the usual signal-injection trick whines and wastes energy. Their scheme estimates position from the motor's own electrical ripple at low speed, using an adaptive flux observer. At higher speed it hands over to an improved model-based estimator through a smooth weighting curve.

On a six hundred watt prototype, low-speed position error stayed under two and a half degrees with no injection noise. The handover bump shrank, torque ripple fell by more than half across the speed range, and speed sag under sudden loads dropped by over sixty percent compared with the conventional hybrid. Stability proofs accompany the experiments.
pmc-13550543:
Victoria Paredes-Orejudo and colleagues read the sugar decorations on antibodies to tell apart critical illnesses and guess their course, in a 2026 biomarker study. Sepsis and severe COVID-19 both fill intensive care units, and who will crash is hard to foresee. The sugars attached to immunoglobulin G steer immune behavior, so the team profiled them in healthy volunteers, sepsis patients, and COVID-19 patients, splitting the last group by whether they survived.

Chromatography and mass spectrometry revealed distinct sugar patterns linked to which disease a patient had. Within the COVID-19 group, particular structures also tracked survival outcome. The authors argue that antibody sugar profiling could help sort intensive care patients by risk of severe or fatal courses, complementing clinical scores. The study is exploratory, pointing toward a blood test built on the immune system's own handwriting.
pmc-13550643:
Roza Szlendak, leading nine colleagues, published a 2026 study tracing how one genetic deletion disrupts a brain receptor in a child with a severe developmental and epileptic disorder. A screening program found a new GRIN2B variant that cuts off the tail end of the GluN2B subunit, part of the NMDA receptor that supports learning and signaling. The patient had intellectual disability, epilepsy, and hyperkinetic behavior.

Cells and patient-derived neurons showed the shortened subunit still joined receptors, yet fewer reached the cell surface and contact with a key partner protein weakened. Currents shrank, magnesium blocked more strongly, and calcium entry fell. The authors argue such step-by-step variant checks are needed to match treatments to each mutation.
pmc-13550943:

pmc-13551043:

pmc-13551143:
Libby Daniells and co-authors design smarter early drug trials in 2026 for spotting patients a drug will truly help. pmc-13551243:

pmc-13551843:

pmc-13551943:

pmc-13552043:

pmc-13552143:

pmc-13552643:

pmc-13553043:

pmc-13553143:

pmc-13554043:

pmc-13554143:

pmc-13554243: Hasegawa and colleagues published an author correction in 2026 to their EMBO Journal article on neuronal aging. Extra text inserted during proofing is removed from the Figure 5 legend. The Figure EV5 legend has its sample-size wording corrected. Figure EV6 is retitled to drop a mention of neuronal viability. pmc-13554543:

pmc-13554643:
Zirvecan Güneş and Esra Kutsal Mergen track in 2026 how much artificial intelligence writing help appears in abstracts of a leading sports medicine journal over time. pmc-13554743:
Cassidy Ball and co-authors report a 2026 study on using viruses that infect bacteria to protect blueberry crops. pmc-13554943:

pmc-13555343:

pmc-13555743:

pmc-13555943:
Narjes Mirabootalebi leads an eight-author team surveying mobile health app use among nurses in Kashan, Iran, in a 2026 study. pmc-13556443:
A Mouri and a large team study immune activation in pregnancy and offspring brain outcomes in 2026. Pregnant mice received a virus-like trigger at mid-pregnancy. Adult offspring were then tested for abnormal behavior.

pmc-13556543:

pmc-13556643:

pmc-13556743:

pmc-13556843:

pmc-13557143:

pmc-13557843:

pmc-13558143:

pmc-13558343:

pmc-13558643:

pmc-13559043:

pmc-13559343:

pmc-13559443:

pmc-13559643:

pmc-13559843:

pmc-13560143:

pmc-13560243:

pmc-13560643:

pmc-13560743:

pmc-13560943:

pmc-13561343:

pmc-13561443:

pmc-13561643:

pmc-13562543:

pmc-13562743:

pmc-13564043:

pmc-13564543:

pmc-13565043:

pmc-13565143:

pmc-13567143:

pmc-13568043:

pmc-13568143:

pmc-13568343:

pmc-13569043:

pmc-13569443:

pmc-13569743:

pmc-13569943:

pmc-13570443:

pmc-13571243:

pmc-13571343:

pmc-13571643:

pmc-13572043:

pmc-13572343:

pmc-13572443:

pmc-13572543:

pmc-13576843:

pmc-13577243:

pmc-13577643:

pmc-13578043:

pmc-13578243:
