The knockout mice lived longer. Their motor neurons and nerve-muscle links survived in far better shape. In sick cords, microglia bellies were stuffed with neuron remains. That load dropped sharply when the switches were gone. The tag on neuron surfaces also ran high in the disease. The team reads the gardeners as eating living neurons alive, and names the switches as drug targets.
pmc-13578343:
Oh-Hyun Lee and colleagues compare two stomach guard drugs for heart attack patients on twin blood thinners, in a 2026 study of Korean records. After a stent opens a blocked artery, patients take two thinners to stop clots, yet the pair raises the risk of stomach bleeding. Acid blockers guard the stomach, and the team weighed a newer drug, tegoprazan, against the standard class.

Records held more than twenty one thousand patients treated from 2019 to 2022. Before matching, the newer drug group bled less in the gut over one year. After careful matching of like patients, the gut bleeding edge held, major bleeding also ran lower, and rates of repeat heart attack or stroke stayed much the same. The authors frame the newer drug as a safe swap for the standard guard.
pmc-13578443:
Prabin Karki and colleagues caught a bacterial light sensor mid-switch, in a mixed state never frozen in such detail before. Phytochromes flip between red-absorbing and far-red-absorbing forms to control bacterial behaviour. An earlier study had found a stable mixed dimer in the sensor SaBphP2. Using the Spotiton method, the team lit particles on a microscope grid. They froze them just 10 milliseconds later, capturing the same mixed dimer in action.

Compared with the uniform dimer, the mixed form showed a 180-degree swing of its kinase domain. That swing was driven by unwinding of the coiled coils that link sensor to enzyme. The authors present this large reorientation as a mechanistic clue to how light flips bacterial signalling. It also showcases time-resolved cryo-electron microscopy.
pmc-13578843:
Megan S Schuler and colleagues sort addiction trial patients by how complex their needs are, in a 2026 reanalysis of a large collaborative care trial. The parent trial enrolled 797 adults with opioid addiction plus depression or trauma stress, across eighteen low resource clinics in New Mexico and California. A class hunting method grouped patients by their starting mix of mental health, drug use, body health, and social strain.

Three groups emerged: a stable low complexity group, a group heavy on mental health strain, and a smaller group high on both fronts. Team based care eased depression more than usual care only in the low complexity group. Trauma outcomes and use of the main addiction drug looked alike across arms in every group. The authors argue care plans should match the complexity mix a patient brings.
pmc-13579043:
Marah Alsayed Hasan and Rahaf Sultan present a case from 2026 of low parathyroid hormone in a young man with a gene variant. The glands set blood calcium, and low hormone most often comes from neck surgery. Their patient, a 25-year-old man deaf from birth, first seized from low calcium at age 15.

Self-attack tests and a scan for the classic gene loss of DiGeorge syndrome both came back clear. A gene panel then found a variant in TBX1, a gene that builds the glands and inner ear in the womb. Labs split on if this variant is harmful or of unknown weight. The team urges heart, kidney, immune, and hearing checks when such a variant is found, plus family tests to settle its class.
pmc-13579243:
Yabing Zhang and co-authors ask whether low blood albumin truly flags eye damage in diabetes in a 2026 study. Albumin tracks general health, and low levels meet retinal disease often. Kidney damage travels with both, clouding the story. A national survey dataset untangles it.

Over eleven hundred adults with diabetes had eye exams and blood work. A third showed retinopathy. Each step up in albumin cut retinopathy odds sharply before adjustment. Once kidney measures entered the model, the link faded to nothing. In poorly controlled patients, mediation analysis assigns much of the albumin signal to the kidney path. Albumin reads as a burden marker, not a cause.
pmc-13580043:
Ayesha Afzal and co-authors report an ear infection that cost a grown man the use of one side of his face, for a time. Ear infections are rife, but face nerve palsy as a side hit is rare in the drug era. Their 2026 case holds a man in his early fifties with no immune flaws. A throat ill on a Hajj trip turns to sharp ear pain, then full face droop on that side, past pill cures.

Back in Pakistan, scans show ear and mastoid ill with fluid, and a hint of wear near the face nerve path. No brain spread shows. Vein drugs, steroids, and face drills form the care, with no cut. Face strength claws back most ground in ten days and all by day twenty-five. The case warns teams to act fast on this rare pair.
pmc-13580443:
Xiyu Zhao and four co-authors watch the back of the eye for aftershocks of eye-muscle surgery, in a 2026 study. Straightening crossed eyes means cutting the horizontal muscles, and the optic nerve fiber layer nearby might react.

Seventy-three patients with comitant strabismus had scans before surgery, a day after, and at two weeks. One group had one muscle operated, the other two. The one-muscle group showed several fiber layer shifts on day one, mostly settling by week two. The two-muscle group changed less in fibers but kept an altered disc-fovea angle at week two. Day-one swings were bigger in the gentler surgery, a counterintuitive wrinkle. The authors track recovery, not harm, in these short-term shifts.
pmc-13580543:
A fluorine tag on a molecule can report distances inside a protein, if its spin song is read right. Sergei Kuzin and three co-authors sharpen that reading in 2026. The method pairs an electron's spin with the tag's nucleus; its reach runs from five to twenty angstroms, but the song fades fast with distance.

Tags with two or three fluorines sing louder, and their song holds extra notes: shared beats between the twin nuclei. The team's new theory covers those notes in full, for the timed form of the test. With it, the extra notes can be made and read on purpose, not just met as noise. Sharper distance reads serve drug and protein work alike.
pmc-13580843:
Chloe Rybicki-Kler and co-authors study in a 2026 mouse work how a memory circuit loses its chemical support in Alzheimer's disease. A set of brain cells sends acetylcholine to a cortex zone that holds working memory, by keeping neurons firing after a cue fades. The team read genes and firing in that zone in a disease model.

Cholinergic inputs had thinned, a key receptor gene had faded, and the after-firing was weak. The paired loss hints that drugs meant to boost that receptor may miss their target cells. Memory aids may need to guard the input cells as well.
pmc-13581143:
Pérez-Manchón and co-authors run a pilot trial of group sleep therapy for first-year nursing students in Madrid. Sleep quality is a public health priority, and nursing students are a high-risk group. The therapy, CBT-I, was taught in a brief group format with active learning.

Forty students aged 18 to 25 were split by chance into two groups of twenty. One group got the sleep therapy, and the other kept its usual routine. Wrist-worn monitors tracked sleep and body rhythms around the clock. A standard survey captured how students rated their own sleep. The trial ran from October 2022 to March 2023.
pmc-13581643:
Ningning Liu and co-authors present a 2026 study of money strain in lung cancer patients half a year after leaving hospital. Over three quarters of 682 patients met the strain line on a known cost survey. Baseline facts on money, home place, care kind, and mind state were logged at intake. A risk model was built from the traits that stood alone, then checked by curve tests and five hundred reshuffled runs.

Household income, long-term home place, and immune drug care stood out on the care side. Self-trust, bounce-back strength, and fear of the disease's return stood out on the mind side. The model called risk with high accuracy. Nurses gain a screen for who needs money counsel early.
pmc-13582143:
Tadashi Murai and colleagues survey tests done inside heart arteries to find small-vessel heart disease. Small-vessel disease has long been hard to test straight, yet it brings chest pain and poor blood flow even when big arteries look clear. Over twenty years, pressure and flow tests done during heart catheter work have opened this hidden zone to tests matched to each patient.

The review sums up the tests now in use, their clinic uses, their strengths, and their limits, from first diagnosis through risk rank to care matched to the cause. It traces the field from early cases of chest pain with clear angiograms to the CorMicA trial, which showed gain from care guided by these tests. Doctors gain a map of tools that can at last match care to the small-vessel fault.
pmc-13582243:
Joanna Kleckowska-Nawrot and eight co-authors describe two tear glands in the great spotted woodpecker, in a 2026 study. The Harderian gland and the tear gland keep the eye surface wet and protected, and they support the bird's third eyelid. These glands are well known in farm birds but poorly described in wild species. The team examined eighteen birds found dead in nature in Poland.

They measured the glands and studied their tissue structure and chemistry in detail. Both glands sat in the usual spots around the eye, and the Harderian gland's secretory units were mostly one cell type. The work gives a baseline map of these glands in a wild woodpecker, useful for vets and for comparing eye anatomy across bird species.
pmc-13582343:
Liqing Zhao and colleagues trial a dissolving plug for holes between the heart's upper chambers, in a 2026 multicenter study. Standard plugs are metal and stay for life, which can bring late trouble. Their plug uses a frame that the body absorbs. One hundred twelve adults and children across seven centers were assigned by chance to the new plug or a metal one.

At six months every hole in both groups had closed fully, with no leak over the set size at any check. One new plug patient had the device removed at ten months for excess tissue growth; lab views showed the frame nearly gone under a smooth lining. At twelve months closure still held at one hundred percent in both groups. The authors call the showing promising while asking for longer watch.
pmc-13582543:
Shanni Wang and co-authors add proteins to rice noodles to stop them turning hard and stale, in a 2026 study. Fresh wet rice noodles spoil in texture within hours because their starch retrogrades, re-crystallizing as it cools. The team stirred wheat gluten or soy protein isolate into indica rice flour at several doses and followed the starch from paste to gel to finished noodle.

Both proteins slowed gelatinization and retrogradation, kept water from migrating, and delayed the gel's hardening in storage. They worked by different routes, though: gluten strengthened the gel network itself, while soy protein blocked the starch rearrangement and water movement behind staling. Soy came out ahead on the measures reported. Longer-lasting fresh noodles would cut waste for producers and keep a beloved staple pleasant beyond the day it is made.
pmc-13582643:
Hongying Bian and co-authors build a new way to grade workplace health risks and try it in shoe factories, in a 2026 study. Footwear plants expose workers to solvents, dust, and noise, and each existing rating method sees only part of that picture. The team combined four established approaches into one method. It blends a risk matrix with weights that shift as conditions change, and scores were normalized so the methods could merge.

Four factories were measured on site for chemicals, dust, and noise, and each was scored by all four methods and by the new combined one. The authors argue the merged grading supports finer, more dynamic control of plant hazards. Validation rests on how well the grades track measured exposures.
pmc-13582943:
Elizabeth MacAfee and co-authors pose ten sharp questions in 2026 on how to scale up building on water. Seas are rising, land is sinking, and storms are growing, most of all in packed river deltas and small island lands. Floating homes and blocks can ride the water, be moved or reused, and leave flow paths near intact.

Old floating towns in poor lands and small test sites in calm waters hold lessons, the team says. Yet the leap from pilots to wide use is steep. Their ten questions probe how large floating growth can stay safe, open to all, green, and sound in cost. Themes span build craft, law, funds, and life on the water. The list sets a research path for the field.
pmc-13583143:
Elham Esmailpourmoghadam and seven co-workers wrote a 2026 plant study on two twin proteins in the chloroplast envelope. One is coded in the plastid genome, the other in the nucleus. Both move protons across the envelope, which affects energy capture. What happens when both are lost at once was unclear.

The team built plants missing one or both proteins. Double mutants turned pale green under steady light, a trait eased by added salt. All mutants showed a stronger safety response that sheds excess light energy. The double mutant beat each single one on that response. Sugar stores and leaf gas flow also fell.
pmc-13583243:
Lvzhou Li and eight co-authors built a gripper that lets go in a flash, inspired by a cucumber plant, in a paper published in 2026. Gripping tools must hold firmly yet release cleanly, but most designs tune grip strength alone, which puts holding and release at odds. Thin, brittle goods like silicon wafers suffer most. Their method tunes time, not strength: a preload sets a poised grip, and a tiny nudge triggers fast, even peeling.

The soft dome gripper releases in 52 milliseconds. After 300,000 cycles it kept most of its release performance. It completed 10,000 clean moves of hair-thin wafers with no damage, even in near vacuum. A four-part mathematical framework ties design and operating factors to the outcome. The authors present time control as the new route for grip design.
pmc-13583443:
Xuanming Hong and a large team study how genes shape chemical marks on DNA in this two thousand twenty-six paper. The marks, called methylation, help switch genes on and off. They may also sit on the path from genes to blood pressure. Twins offer a clean way to sort genetic from shared-life effects. The team ran a genome-wide study in twin pairs, mapping where methylation levels are under genetic control.

They then tested whether those marks carry part of the genetic effect on blood pressure. Such mediation would name concrete molecular steps between DNA and a vital sign. The findings can guide the hunt for new pressure-lowering targets. Genetic epidemiologists are the main audience.
pmc-13583543:
Aaqib Rashid and co-authors present a 2026 study on tuning a triple perovskite with neodymium. Such oxides can act as magnets and as light-driven catalysts, and defects steer both traits. The team baked a barium-iron-tungsten oxide with graded neodymium swaps. Diffraction, microscopy, and surface spectra mapped structure and chemistry at each step.

The main crystal phase held across the series, with a trace side phase only. Neodymium refined the grain structure and stretched the lattice. Surface iron states shifted as oxygen defects rebalanced. Magnetism flipped from a soft ferromagnetic lean to a mostly opposed order. Dye breakdown under visible light beat the parent oxide, best at mid-level swaps. The work shows rare-earth swaps as a knob for defects and function.
pmc-13583843:
Yu Jia, Shaojie Zhang, and Diying Liao review trials of drawing and visual art activities for anxious children aged five to twelve. Art tasks are cheap, gentle tools often used to calm children facing medical procedures. The team searched six databases for randomized trials and pooled their results.

Ten trials with 816 children qualified. Eight, set in hospitals or around procedures, compared art activities with usual care or non-art controls. In those, children who drew or made art showed much lower anxiety right after the activity. Removing any single trial, or dropping weaker studies, did not change the direction of the result, though the trials differed from each other a lot. The authors conclude that art likely eases short-term anxiety in medical settings. They caution that the evidence does not support one blanket effect across all settings where children feel anxious.
pmc-13584543: Sabino and co-authors comment on a study of bloodstream infections across the COVID-19 pandemic in a 2026 letter. It tracked which germs caused infections in an Iranian teaching hospital, before and during the pandemic. The commenters set it beside intensive care data from Brazil. In their units, forty-four point five percent of patients developed confirmed second infections. Gram-negative germs were most common, and drug resistance reached seventy-nine point four percent. The authors urge wiser antibiotic use, backed by shared global tracking of resistant germs.
pmc-13585043:
William H. Eger and thirteen colleagues published this 2026 qualitative study on why people who inject drugs are shifting toward smoking opioids and stimulants in the San Diego-Tijuana border region. Injecting has been falling across North America, but the reasons operate at many levels, from personal habit to drug supply. The team ran interviews in late 2024 with people who had a history of injecting heroin, fentanyl or methamphetamine.

Among 36 participants, half interviewed in San Diego, 81 percent had both injected and smoked in the past month. Few had switched completely: smoking was the main route with occasional injecting alongside. Participants said they smoked to dodge fentanyl injection harms such as vein damage and infection, and because smoking is easier, more discreet and less stigmatised. Injecting habits, the wish for stronger effects, and patchy access to smoking equipment held the shift back. The authors recommend expanding smoking supplies while keeping syringe services.
pmc-13585243:
Alexander Duggan, Matthew Newman, and David McMillen build a text model that writes gene switch zones for odd microbes. To tune how much protein a microbe makes, labs tweak the zone just ahead of a gene, called its UTR. Odd species lack the tested parts and design tools that model species enjoy. Their model learns the letter habits of a species own switch zones from its genome alone, then breeds fresh zones in that style.

Sets of about a thousand fresh zones were made for a lab workhorse germ and for a probiotic species. About a hundred zones per species then went into cells with a glow gene to read their strength. Both sets gave a broad spread of protein levels from few tries. Designers gain a first tuning kit for species with no part lists.
pmc-13585643:
Guilan Ding and co-authors ask in a 2026 cohort study whether an early sedative after brain aneurysm surgery leaves patients more examinable, the key to catching decline. After clipping for a burst aneurysm, sedation must calm without hiding the neurological exam. The drug dexmedetomidine was started within a day and kept for at least two hours in forty-one of one hundred twenty patients.

Over the next two days, the early-drug group spent sixty-eight percent of time in the examinable band against fifty-five percent without it. Adjusted models kept the gap near twelve points. The authors call the estimates exploratory, not proof, and note the endpoint order was set after the analysis.
pmc-13585943:
Florin Iordache, Jessica Lazar, Catalin Baraian, Tiberiu Giumba, and Roberto Bergamaschi track how the pandemic years changed appendicitis care at one big-city emergency hospital. Their 2026 cohort study covers 1,721 adults from 2018 to 2023, split into before, during, and after COVID-19 periods. The hospital's catchment, surgeon count, and scan volume stayed broadly stable across the span.

Fewer patients arrived during the pandemic, and a larger share came with complicated disease. Yet complication and death rates did not differ between periods, and hospital stays held steady even as keyhole surgery rose. Tumor findings in removed appendixes ran near two percent in the later periods. Colonoscopy volume, by contrast, dipped sharply mid-pandemic and recovered after. The authors read the appendix story as strain without collapse.
pmc-13586443:
Meesha Rao and eight colleagues surveyed lifestyle habits among older teens at university in Rawalpindi, Pakistan. Habits set in these years, from food to sleep, shape later health. The team paired a tested questionnaire with height and weight measures. They asked how habits line up with traits like age, home area, and family type.

Two hundred fifteen students took part, most of them young women. Most had a healthy weight and ate three meals a day. Yet fewer than twelve percent were physically active. Over a quarter slept too little, and a similar share reported low mood. Only about one in ten with problems had seen a specialist. Smoking, vaping, and early first use all appeared in the data. The authors call for campus programs that tackle activity, sleep, and mood together.
pmc-13586543:
Vincent Jassey and a large international team survey bacteria across 171 northern peatlands in this 2026 study. Peatlands store vast carbon, and bacteria drive its cycling, yet their diversity at continental scale was murky. The team paired the survey with a transplant experiment moving peat across climates.

Cold, snow cover, and soil wetness structured the communities most, and environment explained about eighty percent of community assembly. A tipping point emerged: below a certain bacterial richness, the enzymes that free nutrients jumped by about sixty percent, as if leaner communities worked harder to extract food. The authors warn diversity loss could speed carbon release from this giant store.
pmc-13586743:
Aimé Sao Cordiez, Benjamin Popoff, Dominique Vodovar, and Gaëtan Beduneau survey in 2026 how French intensive care units use a leak test before pulling breathing tubes. A swollen voice box can block air after tube removal and force a fast re-tube. French guides from 2016 urge the test for patients at risk, with steroid drugs if the test fails.

The team sent a 32-item web survey to units across France, and 114 of 178 signed-up units replied in full. Just 14 percent ran the test on all patients, and habits for when to test varied widely. The survey also tracked how soon steroids were given after a failed test. The map shows a wide gap between the guides and daily practice, a decade on.
pmc-13586843:
Dagyeong Yang and Elissa Lei looked at gene activity and genome folding in 2026. Transcription and three-dimensional genome shape affect each other. Which drives which stayed open for long. Cut-and-change and imaging studies were weighed. Large genome regions form without transcription. Domain shapes also persist without it.

Finer scales show stronger transcription effects. Local folding responds to gene activity. Layout seems broadly stable overall here. Transcription refines that stable frame as context demands. Cause and result stay tangled in tests. Multi-scale cut-and-change studies are needed next. Varied systems must be set side by side in a set way. Joining it all remains the field's central puzzle.
pmc-13586943:
Drug-resistant staph infections leave doctors with few options, so Ying Chen and co-authors built tiny particles from a plant compound and zinc that assemble on their own, with no carrier needed. The particles killed many clinical isolates of the resistant bacteria faster and better than either ingredient alone, and they blocked new biofilms while cutting living bacteria inside mature ones.

Tests pointed to damaged membranes, drained cell energy, and stress from reactive oxygen. In mice with body-wide infection, the treatment lowered bacterial counts and inflammation and improved survival, even when started six hours late. It also spared blood cells in safety tests, which supports pairing natural compounds with metals against hard-to-treat germs.
pmc-13587543:
Emma Veltman and co-authors present proof of concept for a survivor-led healing program in a 2026 paper. Left Write Hook was designed by survivors of child sexual abuse and is led by peers, not clinicians. It combines expressive writing about trauma with non-contact, trauma-informed boxing training.

Standard support for survivors is resource-intensive and professionally led, which limits access. The program aims to build self-empowerment and let survivors rewrite their stories, literally and physically. A proof-of-concept study checks whether the model is feasible and acceptable before larger trials test its mental health effects.
pmc-13587643:
Jörn Bargstedt and colleagues achieved flip-back light control of the 8–17 DNAzyme, an RNA-cutting DNA cutter. Light is an ideal trigger for chem biology, being gentle and precise, but switching enzymes cleanly on and off remains hard. Their 2026 study placed nucleoside-based diarylethene light switches at chosen spots in the DNAzyme, testing three top variants.

One mix, dU-Ph-tBu at spot 2.1, gave strong flip-back control: UV light cut the cutting rate about 11-fold in the mixed state, while alone open and closed forms stood apart about 200-fold. The switch held up through many cycles with little loss and stood heat. Oddly, adding a single methyl group killed control, showing how finely switch shape must match its bio context.
pmc-13587843:
Stefano Dicorato and co-authors grow thin films of gallium sulfide with control over crystal form, in work published in 2026. The material is a layered semiconductor that can stack in more than one form, and each form acts in its own way. They grow the films from a single source gas with pure hydrogen as the carrier.

By tuning pressure, flow, heat, and growth rate, they flip the films between two forms and between island growth and smooth layers. One set of settings gave even, high-grade films over a wide area. Other settings gave rough islands and weaker traits. The work maps how process choices shape the final film.
pmc-13588543:
Robert Thomas, Richard Rucker, Naudia Gray, and Steven Pappas wrote a white paper on the practical difficulties of measuring toxic metals in cannabis vape aerosols. Regulators need exposure numbers, but collecting the aerosol without contaminating it is notoriously hard. Metal levels are low, in the microgram-per-gram range, so stray contamination from collection gear can swamp the signal. Materials used to trap aerosols for organic analysis are unsuitable for metals work.

Some trapping approaches failed for a second reason: they resisted airflow, so devices would not activate and form aerosol properly. The paper reviews a decade of attempted methods, successful and not. It guides analytical chemists toward workable trapping designs. Reliable metal numbers underpin any future safety standards for cannabinoid delivery devices.
pmc-13588843:
Ghaith Abu-Zeinah and a large team of co-authors review molecular response, event-free survival, and treatment-free remission in myeloproliferative neoplasms. Their 2026 review draws on a recent specialist meeting in Seoul and new literature.

Treatment goals for these blood cancers are shifting. Beyond controlling counts, spleen size, and symptoms, doctors now aim at measures of true disease modification anchored in biology. The review covers three diseases: polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and myelofibrosis. It examines how molecular response links to long-term clinical benefit. Such endpoints could change how trials are designed and how patients judge a therapy's worth.
pmc-13588943:
Yulan Qu and six colleagues, writing for a Chinese Thoracic Society task force, publish an expert consensus on exhaled nitric oxide testing. The breath test measures airway inflammation of the allergic type and is spreading across China. Inconsistent technique, quality control, and interpretation, however, have raised doubts about its accuracy in practice.

The consensus walks through instrument principles, the detection method, step-by-step operation, quality control, and clinical significance for airway diseases. It builds on earlier Chinese guidance for adults and children and on worldwide advances. The authors hope standardized protocols will support precise diagnosis and treatment. The document is a practice standard rather than a research study.
pmc-13589243:
Franziska Lieschke and co-authors studied whether the time of day a brain bleed strikes affects how patients fare, in a 2026 paper. Brain bleeds follow daily rhythms, with peaks in the morning and late afternoon. Whether the hour of onset shapes recovery was unclear.

The team used a state registry in Hesse, Germany, covering 2015 to 2023, and kept 5,665 patients after exclusions. Patients were grouped by onset into morning, midday, evening, and night bands. Bleeds were most common near 8:30 in the morning and 5 in the afternoon, and rarest near midnight. Patients whose bleeds began in the evening, and above all at night, left hospital with higher disability.
pmc-13589343:
Likhitha Atada and co-authors segment tiny retinal bleeds in diabetic eye disease with a patch-trained network, in work from twenty twenty-six. Microaneurysms are the earliest, faintest sign of diabetic retinopathy. Their tiny size and low contrast cause frequent misses in manual exams. Two public fundus data sets supply training and test images. Full images are cut into small tiles to enrich lesion pixels.

Tiling lifts lesion density per sample by a huge factor. A compact U-Net tuned for imbalance learns on those tiles. The tile model reaches high overlap and precision scores on held-out images. A full-image twin trained on the same data finds no lesions at all. Class imbalance explains that total collapse to background. Patch training thus rescues screening for the earliest disease sign.
pmc-13591043:
Pediatric specialist Stephanie Merlino Barr comments on how doctors should chart the growth of babies born early, in this 2026 article. Two chart systems are widely used to judge whether a preterm baby's birth size is normal for its age: the Fenton charts and the INTERGROWTH charts. A study in the same journal compared the two and found they mostly agree, except for the smallest and earliest babies, where they can place the same child in different size classes.

That gap matters, because size labels guide feeding plans and flag babies at risk. Barr asks how the newly updated Fenton charts of 2025 compare, and which set a newborn intensive care unit should adopt. With charts that are not interchangeable, she argues, units should choose deliberately and use one standard consistently rather than mixing the two.
pmc-13591143:
Dong Hoon Kang and colleagues propose a new blood marker for unstable plaques in heart attack patients. Current cardiac markers miss activation of vascular smooth muscle cells, a key step in forming vulnerable plaques. The team found that interleukin-12 receptor beta 2 appears selectively on synthetic smooth muscle cells after interferon-gamma stimulation and is released in cell-derived vesicles.

Circulating levels of the receptor were significantly higher in acute myocardial infarction patients and could be detected with a new capture assay. The marker therefore reflects smooth-muscle-driven plaque instability rather than heart muscle damage alone. It may help doctors stratify risk earlier in coronary artery disease, pending validation in larger cohorts.
pmc-13591343:
Fangzhou Xie leads a large team building a threaded microneedle that treats each skin layer with its own medicine. Skin diseases remake the surface, the middle dermis, and the fat below in distinct ways, yet creams and shots rarely aim by layer. Guided by maps of gene activity across skin, the team loaded a fast release gel on the needle surface with a drug that fights cell aging in the dermis. Grooves in the needle carry gene cargo deeper.

Twisting the needle in deposits fat layer cargo, mRNA wrapped in fat bubbles, into the tissue below the skin. In mice with bleomycin driven skin scarring, the system cut aging signs and scar buildup and restored fat shape. Xie and the team call it a precise route for layered skin disease.
pmc-13591543:
Lorenzo Calò, Martina Cacciapuoti, and Paul Davis discuss a puzzle about blood pressure control in this 2026 article. A protein called RGS2 puts a brake on the hormone system that raises blood pressure, and it is found in large amounts in immune cells of the blood vessel wall. A mouse study they review removed that brake from those cells only, yet the mice showed no extra harm when given the hormone.

The authors set the mouse result beside rare human illnesses, Gitelman and Bartter syndromes, where the same hormone system is naturally blunted. In those patients, high levels of the protein go with low pressure and less vessel damage. The contrast suggests that the protein's effect depends on the cell type and the whole body setting, not on immune cells alone.
pmc-13592643:
Ruba Malkawi and Shengqian Sun turn fish waste into a vehicle for a hard to dissolve plant compound. Baicalein, a flavonoid from Chinese skullcap, fights inflammation and oxidation in lab studies, yet water barely dissolves it, so little reaches the body. Their liquisolid tablets use oil pressed from salmon viscera as the liquid carrier, with corn starch holding it and talc coating the mix. Lab tools checked clashes, crystal form, release speed, and antioxidant strength.

No harmful clashes appeared between drug and helpers. The crystal structure largely melted away inside the tablets, a sign the drug spread at near molecular scale. Release into buffer ran far faster than the pure drug or a plain blend. The fish oil version also quenched free radicals more strongly. Malkawi and Sun frame marine waste as a working pharmacy ingredient.
pmc-13592843:
Haojie Du and co-authors build a gel based sensor that spots a toxic mold poison in food by eye. Their paper from 2026 deals with aflatoxin B1, a strong cancer causing poison. Fast on site tests are needed, since lab checks are slow and tied to fixed sites.

The sensor uses a DNA strand that binds the poison, set in a gel that holds gold specks as a color signal. When the poison binds, the gel falls apart and the specks spill out, giving a color change that can be read by eye or by measure. A recycling step with an enzyme boosts the signal. The sensor reads down to a very low level and picks the target over other poisons.
pmc-13593243:
Hui Zhang and four co-authors review in 2026 the evidence tying a master inflammation switch, NF-κB, to preeclampsia, the dangerous blood pressure disorder of pregnancy. The disease involves body-wide inflammation and damaged blood vessel linings, and the switch has long been suspected of helping drive it.

The team gathered fifteen peer-reviewed studies and pooled their results in a meta-analysis. They asked how strongly activation of the pathway tracks with the inflammatory response seen in patients. A firmer answer could point drug hunters toward calming that switch, and could sharpen tests that warn of the disease earlier.
pmc-13593443:
Karla Jimena Basilio-Aguilar and a large team of co-authors separate the immune effects of obesity and COVID-19 severity, in two thousand twenty-six. Obesity raises the risk of severe COVID-19, but how it reshapes the immune response was not well mapped. Sixty patients were split by both severity and obesity status.

Blood measures fell into three patterns. Some fat-linked signals rose mainly with obesity, whatever the severity. Others rose with severity alone, in patients with and without obesity alike. A few cell types shifted most strongly of all with severity. One memory cell type grew only in critically ill patients with obesity, a joint effect the authors flag.
pmc-13593543:
Masatsugu Nozoe led a team that diagnosed and treated a fast, circling atrial rhythm arising where the superior vena cava meets the right atrium. Their 2026 case involved a 72-year-old man whose atrial fibrillation had returned a decade after a cryoballoon procedure, and they worked with a dual-energy lattice-tip catheter that can both map and ablate.

High-density mapping pinpointed the narrow channel of tissue the rhythm needed to keep circling. Mapping while the heart was in its normal rhythm helped the team relate that channel to the site where the sinus node first fires. Pulsed-field energy could then be delivered while sparing the node itself. The treatment caused neither sinus node damage nor weakness of the phrenic nerve in this patient.
pmc-13593643:
Ekin Kırbaş and colleagues measured how often hidden colistin resistance lurks in Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria taken from bloodstream infections. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic for strains that resist carbapenems, and heteroresistance means a small resistant minority hides inside a population that routine testing calls susceptible. Their 2026 study examined seventy such bloodstream isolates.

Using the reference population analysis method, they found heteroresistance in about six of every ten isolates, a strikingly high share. A simpler gradient test missed every single one of those strains. Being sixty or older, having no recent hospital stay, and a particular colistin test value were each linked to higher risk. Hidden resistance did not, however, track with deaths at thirty or ninety days, and the authors say its real clinical weight still needs to be worked out.
pmc-13593843:
Hua Bai and co-authors report two cases where heart failure patients got maintenance fluids rather than the strict fluid restriction that is standard care. Published in 2026, the case reports cover acute flare-ups of heart failure with other conditions in play. The authors warn that strict restriction can harm patients whose bodies are low on fluid from poor intake or infection.

One man with a weakened heart muscle improved as a key blood marker fell sharply. An older woman with sepsis from a pressure sore also improved, with infection cleared and the same marker falling to near normal. Both kept standard heart drugs. The authors present the physiology guided plan as a hypothesis for selected patients, not a new rule.
pmc-13594543:
Yingru Liu and co-authors review light-and-sound imaging of the placenta in pregnancy diabetes, in work from 2026. Rates of the condition keep climbing, and exercise is the first-line therapy. Yet checks rest on sugar and body measures, which miss how the placenta and fetus adapt week by week.

Photoacoustic imaging maps tissue oxygen in place, while ultrasound tracks blood flow and vessel growth. The review weighs two exercise styles against those images: hard interval work may aid vessel function, while strength work may reshape structure, though diabetes-specific proof is thin. The authors propose imaging marks as secondary outcomes in trials, joined with glucose monitors for tailored plans.
pmc-13594643:
Shilat Haim-Nachum and a large team test a short video against self-shame in a 2026 trial. Adults who were harmed as children often blame themselves, and that shame can bar them from seeking help. Short web clips have eased shame about mind ills, but none had been tried for this group across many lands.

The trial ran in six countries with a blind, by-lot design. Members watched a brief clip built on true contact tales, or a control clip. The team tracked self-shame and will to seek help after the view. Readers learn whether one short clip can move shame at world scale.
pmc-13595443:
Andrew M Dickson and co-authors built a simulation of American mass shootings and fitted it to history using Bayesian methods, an approach meant to handle events too rare for ordinary statistics. Their agent-based model treats a shooting as the meeting of three ingredients: a motivated perpetrator emerging, access to firearms, and a suitable target population.

Calibrated against past events, the model estimated hidden societal quantities such as how often potential perpetrators arise. The density of federal firearms licenses emerged as the strongest predictor of risk, while population density raised risk only up to a point. A version allowing high-lethality weapons but random target choice beat both simple statistical baselines and more behavioral variants. The authors argue such calibrated simulations can test policy counterfactuals while honestly stating their uncertainty.
pmc-13595543:
Jan Lause and colleagues fix a statistical gap in single-cell RNA sequencing. The best normalization methods assumed data collected with molecular barcodes. That left richer full-length protocols such as Smart-seq2 without a principled option. Their 2026 paper models what actually happens to barcode-free data, where each captured molecule is amplified into many copies before counting.

Their compound model treats molecule capture as one random process and amplification as a second layered on top, and from it they derive corrected residuals for every gene in every cell. Amplification behavior across several protocols follows a broken power law, a pattern the model captures. The residuals selected meaningful genes and produced sensible cell maps of Smart-seq2 datasets, while explaining the excess scatter and zero counts that simpler models miss. The authors offer the approach as a drop-in normalization step for non-barcoded experiments.
pmc-13595643:
Jia Yi Anna Ne and colleagues compared outcomes by atrial fibrillation status in 28,492 Australians who underwent open-heart valve surgery between 2003 and 2021. Patients were grouped by no fibrillation, new fibrillation, or prior fibrillation at surgery, then followed to March 2022 for a median of 6.58 years. Aortic valve surgery accounted for 18,949 patients and mitral valve surgery for 9,543.

Mortality was highest with prior fibrillation in both groups, reaching 57.9 percent after aortic surgery and 41.0 percent after mitral surgery, against 32.8 percent and 22.4 percent with no fibrillation. New fibrillation independently predicted death after aortic but not mitral surgery. Both the valve operated on and the patient's fibrillation history should shape risk assessment, the authors conclude.
pmc-13595843:
Menglu Guo and co-authors (2026) used grounded theory to map what drives learning motivation at a Chinese application-oriented university in the digital age. As AI reshapes teaching, motivation is shifting with it. The team interviewed 30 undergraduates at one university, then coded the transcripts in three passes to build a theory from the ground up.

Four layers of influence emerged. A core driving layer holds AI-specific factors, career expectations, self-awareness, and inner drive. A guarantee layer covers school resources and grading methods. A relationship layer carries teacher, peer, and family influence, and a constraint layer covers behavior rules and control of free time. Together they form what the authors call a cognition-context dual-drive model. The authors offer practical routes to stronger motivation, from stimulating inner cognition to building better learning settings.
pmc-13597243:
Ale leads a team on drive and activity in a school health program. Their study from twenty twenty-six is set in Quebec, Canada. The Global Health Program runs across many public schools.

Students filled an online form at the program's start term. Drive for activity was scored with a standard exercise form. Activity levels used age fit activity forms as well. The team asked if self drive links to more activity. School leader support and peer ties may shape that link. Time in the program was also a factor.  Most students in the valid age set were boys.
pmc-13598343:
Alexandra Childs and four co-authors present two decades of sea lion data from the Galápagos in a 2026 paper. The endangered species has lost half to three quarters of its numbers in fifty years. Their long-term study of one colony tracks pup births and survival, asking how extreme climate swings shape the decline. The colony has shrunk since monitoring began, faster after a certain breeding season.

The decline is not explained by climate or by falling female fertility. It looks driven by fewer young joining the breeding pool, because juvenile survival dropped. Mothers adjust foraging and birth timing with food supply, which cushions climate shocks but cannot stop the slide.
pmc-13598543:
Zhen Tian and five co-authors published a 2026 study of lip gland biopsy in patients suspected of Neuro-Sjögren, a nerve-involving form of an autoimmune disease. The biopsy is a proven test for the disease in general, but its value when nerves are the main concern was unclear. The team reviewed records from one Beijing hospital covering 2019 to 2023, including 135 patients with suspected nerve involvement.

These patients needed biopsy more often than other suspected cases, and their biopsies came back positive far more often, about 81 percent against 51 percent. Younger onset and early nerve symptoms predicted needing the test. Certain antibody results made it less necessary. The authors say the biopsy earns its place when blood tests are negative or unclear, while cautioning that their pathway is specific to their center.
pmc-13599343:
Caroline Neumann and co-authors review work from two thousand twenty-six on a protein complex that drives inflammation in severe illness. The complex, called the NLRP3 inflammasome, reacts to signs of germs and cell damage. When switched on, it matures signals that inflame tissue and can kill cells in a fiery form of death.

The review explains how a controlled response helps clear germs, while an excessive one can harm blood vessels and organs in sepsis and lung failure. Too weak a response, in turn, can leave patients open to new infections. The authors discuss drugs that block parts of the pathway, such as blockers of one key signal. They stress that sorting patients well is key to using such drugs.
pmc-13599543:
Tian-yu Wan and co-authors sort the jobs of folding helper enzymes in a social bacterium, in work published in 2026. The helpers, called PPIases, speed the rate-limiting twist in protein folding. The bacterium, Myxococcus xanthus, carries seventeen such genes and is known for group hunting and spore making.

One helper in the outer zone proved vital for growth. Losing a membrane-bound helper hurt group motion, hunting, and spore making, but not fruiting body shape. Near all helpers aided stress defense. Gene use levels varied a lot, even among close kin. The authors see a shared web of labor across the set.
pmc-13599743:
Tokoçin and six co-authors compare leech therapy against standard care for a stubborn breast inflammation called idiopathic granulomatous mastitis. The disease often returns and can form draining channels. Some patients choose leeches first and delay proven care by months.

The study followed 298 patients, 41 of whom had started with leech therapy. Their delay to real care averaged 15 months, against six weeks for others. Complete remission came to only 5 percent of the leech group, versus 59 percent under standard care. Recurrence or persistence hit 95 percent of the leech group. The authors warn that starting with leeches invites worse, harder disease.
pmc-13599843:
Tom Nolan and four co-authors introduce a new article series for the journal BMJ Medicine in this 2026 piece. The series will publish profiles of large health studies and data collections, the kind that follow thousands of people over many years. Its aim is to help researchers find data they can trust and actually get permission to use.

Modern health studies have grown huge. One British study from 1946 recorded every birth in a single week, and today's collections are far larger still. With so many sources on offer, choosing a sound one is hard. The series opens with profiles of a British household study, a long-running child cohort, and a major study from Mexico City. Each profile will set out what the data hold, how they were gathered, and how access works.
pmc-13600043:
Manuela Ceccarelli and co-authors report what happened when people with HIV switched to a three-drug single tablet, in a 2026 real-world study. The tablet joins doravirine, lamivudine, and tenofovir, and doctors often choose it to simplify treatment or improve blood fats. Ninety-eight treatment-experienced patients at seven Italian centers were followed for forty-eight weeks after the switch.

Among those with data at the end, about eighty-nine percent had the virus below the strictest detection line, and ninety-six percent below a looser one. Total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides all fell clearly. Kidney function stayed stable, and liver markers shifted only slightly. The authors, writing from a Sardinian and Sicilian cohort network, judge the switch effective and gentle on the body in routine care.
pmc-13600143:
Ribeiro and co-authors probe social gaps in healthy eating among older adults in Roraima, Brazil. Chronic diseases weigh heavily on older adults, and diet helps prevent and manage them. Proof on social traits and food habits in this group was scarce.

The study drew 1,322 older adults from primary care records across the state. All had a prior COVID-19 diagnosis on file. Food intake for the prior day was scored with Brazil's national food marker form. Models adjusted for many social traits at once. Men, for one result, ate fresh fruit less often than women that prior day.
pmc-13600843:
Nachaat Mohamed and Hamed Taherdoost built in 2026 an intrusion detector for internet-of-things networks that reads the shape of network traffic, not just single records. Standard detectors judge each flow alone, throwing away who talks to whom. Their system draws a graph of flows between addresses and extracts 24 topology features per host, computed only from training data to avoid leakage.

On a standard benchmark, the hybrid model edged out a flow-only detector, reaching about 99.1 percent accuracy with fewer false alarms. Graph features alone performed surprisingly well. Community analysis showed one attacker subnet produced over ninety percent of attack flows. The authors argue that network structure is cheap, powerful evidence that conventional detectors waste.
pmc-13601043:
Yuan Chen, Zhiqiang Lin, and Wenquan Yu present a 2026 study on how a pollen donor can sweeten the fruit it fathers. Citrus growers know the xenia effect: pollen genes can reshape the fruit on the mother tree. The team crossed Fuju tangerines with pollen from Murcott tangor and tracked sugars, acids, and phenolic compounds as the fruit grew.

Self-pollinated Fuju fruits served as the control. Late in development, cross-pollinated fruit shifted their sugar build-up, ending with about fifteen percent more sucrose at harvest. Genes of sugar handling switched on in step with the change. Acid and phenolic profiles moved too. The finding suggests orchards can tune flavor partly by choosing pollinizer trees, not just the fruiting variety itself.
pmc-13601143:
Xiaomei Ma and co-authors published this study in 2026. It looks for blood markers of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, an aggressive blood cancer. The markers are RNAs carried in exosomes, tiny parcels cells shed into the blood. Samples came from nine patients and nine healthy people for a first scan. A larger group, forty-one of each, then checked the top finds.

The scan found wide RNA differences: dozens of small RNAs and thousands of long ones shifted in patients. Three markers held up in the check group, two small RNAs down and one long RNA up. Each alone sorted patients from controls fairly well. Pairs did better, the best reaching a strong score. The authors propose these parcel RNAs as diagnostic aids, and one pair as a possible control network in the disease.
pmc-13601343:
Xiaowen Du and Jiangwei Tan report two spine cases with a rare twist, in this 2026 paper. Both patients had a slipped lower-back vertebra and received a fusion operation through one side. Afterward each developed pain and weakness in the leg on the opposite side, a little-reported problem the authors tie to a pre-existing unevenness of the spinal joints.

Scans and reasoning pointed to a bony spur on the untreated side pinching the nerve root once the segment was fully realigned. The first patient improved after a revision operation trimmed the spur. The second improved after a slim endoscopic procedure widened the nerve passage. The authors say the fix, once the cause is spotted, is surgical room to free the nerve.
pmc-13601743:
Xinyu Yang, Jing Yuan, Sen Huang, and Xiaoli Yao hunt modifiable risk factors for ALS in a paper from 2026. The study used a UK Biobank cohort of over three hundred thousand people. An exposome-wide scan tested one hundred eighty-four changeable factors. During follow-up, seven hundred forty-four participants developed the disease. Forty-five factors linked to risk across six life domains.

Examples include a past chickenpox infection, lower education, and weaker lung function. Joint analysis suggested a large share of cases might trace to these factors together. The authors caution that prevention fractions are estimates, not promises. Still, lifestyle and social factors stand out as targets. The scan offers fresh leads for a disease with few known causes.
pmc-13601843:
Shufang Deng and co-authors follow sleep and mood patterns over eight years in older English adults, to see how their joint paths relate to new arthritis. Joint pain is a top cause of disability in later life, and poor sleep and low mood often travel together. Their 2026 study draws on a national aging cohort of more than thirty-six hundred people free of arthritis at the key wave.

Four joint paths emerged, from steady good sleep with no low mood to steady poor sleep with high low mood. Arthritis odds rose step by step across the paths. The worst path carried near triple the odds of the best path, after full adjustment. The authors urge that sleep and mood be treated as a pair in arthritis prevention.
pmc-13602243:
Soukaina Bichichi and co-authors report a rare 2026 case of emphysematous pyelonephritis in a pelvic ectopic kidney. This infection is a severe, tissue-destroying kidney infection marked by gas forming inside the kidney. A kidney sitting in the pelvis instead of its normal place makes the condition exceptionally uncommon.

The patient was a 56-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes who arrived with fever, pelvic pain, and septic shock. CT scans showed the misplaced kidney, several stones, an obstructing stone in the ureter, and gas in the collecting system. Despite emergency care, he developed refractory shock and organ failure and died two days after admission. The case stresses the key role of CT in spotting such hidden anatomy early.
pmc-13602743:
Rongyu Shi and co-authors take a single liver cancer apart cell by cell to inspect its blood vessel lining. Working from a public single-nucleus data set, they kept about sixty-seven thousand cells and reclustered the seven hundred fifty-four vessel cells among them. Two endothelial states emerged.

One state wore the marks of invasive, vessel-growing tumor lining, scoring high on a microvascular invasion gene set. The other ran hotter on hypoxia programs. Iron-handling genes tied to ferroptosis, including a ferritin chain, appeared broadly across the lining. Follow-up tests in tumor cell lines showed low oxygen switching several of these genes on. The authors stress the work is exploratory, from one sample, and awaits replication in more patients.
pmc-13602843:
Ruiyi Shen and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how tiny sacs shed by tumor cells help cancers grow and spread. These extracellular vesicles carry proteins, gene scraps, and fats between cells in the tumor's neighborhood. Cancer-made sacs bear tumor-specific marks, which makes them both a threat and a clue.

The review sorts five ways the sacs push cancer forward. They reshape the tissue mat and seed spread to set organs. They tire out immune cells and help tumors hide. They call in new blood vessels, rewire how nearby cells burn fuel, and blunt drug action. Clinical findings on using the sacs as markers or drug targets are weighed. The field may turn a cancer tool against itself.
pmc-13603043:
Anny Leudjo Taka and co-authors review ring-shaped sugar hosts in a 2026 paper. The rings have a water-shy core and a water-friendly skin, a rare pairing that lets them trap guest bits inside. Chains built from the rings gain fresh power from that trap trick.

The review shows how the chains catch a wide sweep of dirt from water, from metals to germs, by both trapping and surface grip. The same hosts can also lift the work of solar cells of a new kind. Green chemists gain a host that serves clean water and clean power at once. The survey maps a fast field in one read.
pmc-13603243:
Mariateresa Allocca and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, how electric pulses affect two lines of pancreatic cancer cells. Pancreatic cancer resists most drugs, and pulsed electric fields, which poke holes in cell membranes, are a candidate for local control and better drug entry. The team varied pulse number and strength on the PANC-1 and MIA PaCa-2 lines and watched both instant and delayed effects.

Each line had its own death threshold, one far lower than the other. Days later, the lines also diverged in survival and growth, and their cell cycles shifted in opposite directions. Stress and death pathway markers, though, moved alike in both. The authors conclude that pulse recipes must be tuned to the tumor's own sensitivity, not copied from one cell line to another. Fine-tuned protocols are the path they propose.
pmc-13604143:
Liu and co-authors build a risk model for patients whose face spasms linger after decompression surgery. The surgery frees a vessel pressing on the facial nerve and works well for most. Some patients still spasm a day later, then cure slowly or not at all. That split clouds plans for a second surgery. The team reviewed 500 patients treated from 2021 to 2023. The model was built on the 140 with spasms at 24 hours.

Traits included an abnormal muscle signal seen in surgery and a spasm grade at one day. A chart form of the model was checked with resampling. Time-to-cure analysis added the waiting picture. Early sorting can calm or prompt patients sooner.
pmc-13604443: Marco Cavallo introduces a special issue on eye-tracking as a tool to monitor brain and mental conditions across the life span. The short 2026 editorial frames eye movements as a near-paradoxical source of clinical insight. No abstract or findings are given beyond that opening frame, so the piece serves as a brief gateway to the issue's theme rather than a full study.
pmc-13604543:
Christina Papadouli and co-authors feed two crop mold poisons to farmed sea bream to weigh harm at feed grade loads, in a study from 2026. Plant feeds grow in fish fare, and with them come mold poisons that ride the grain. Six feeds at three loads per poison ran for seven weeks in trios.

Top loads cut feed take, weight, length, and bulk in the fish. Feed waste rose and growth pace fell at most loads. Blood marks, guard work, and liver flesh all shifted on the poisons, and gene harm rose with load. Short runs at feed loads harm the fish, the team finds. Feed watch must stiffen, they urge.
pmc-13604743:
Kaixuan Zou and co-authors published this study in 2026. It tests Nei-Xiao-Luo-Li-San, a classic herbal mix once used for lumps and tumor-like masses. The test bed was Toledo cells, a lab line of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. That cancer is the most common form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults. Many patients see it return or stop responding, so new angles are in demand.

The team profiled the mix, then checked cell growth, movement, and spread. The mix cut all three within the doses tried. Gene reads pointed to stress-response and chromatin pathways. One stress gene, ATF5, drew focus: lowering it copied much of the mix's effect. The work hints the herbal mix acts partly through that gene and the chromatin switches near it.
pmc-13604843:
Yew Chung Chan, Darcy Jamih, and Hong Yee Lim present a heart tracing puzzle for clinicians, in this 2026 ECG challenge. Their patient was a sixty-five-year-old man sent for checks after a slow heartbeat was found by chance. He felt mostly well, with only slight loss of exercise stamina. His tracing showed a faulty electrical relay in the heart: only every second signal, roughly, was reaching the lower chambers.

Two bedside tests then behaved in opposite ways. Massaging the neck artery, which usually slows conduction, oddly restored a one-to-one rhythm. Meanwhile atropine, a drug that usually speeds conduction, made the block worse, pushing it toward near-total failure. Such paradoxical answers help locate where in the relay system the fault sits, which decides whether the patient needs a pacemaker and of what kind. The piece walks readers through the tracings before revealing the reasoning.
pmc-13605443:
Charles Thompson and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 comparing brain volumes in Alzheimer's disease and healthy aging across a large imaging cohort. The disease shrinks the brain, especially memory regions, but big studies tying global and local measures to age, sex, and repeat scans are scarce. The team assembled nearly fourteen hundred people and over thirty-five hundred scans.

Volumes were scaled to head size and modeled with methods that handle repeated visits. Older age meant smaller volumes everywhere. Alzheimer's patients had clearly lower volumes, most sharply in the inner temporal memory areas, and gray matter separated the groups better than white matter. The shrinkage pace with age ran faster in the disease group.
pmc-13606243:
Zhi-Jing Ni and co-authors tested, in a 2026 study, light-activated carbon dots as a weapon against a mold that rots grapes and goji berries after harvest. Alternaria alternata also seeds toxins that threaten food safety. Carbon quantum dots can act as tiny light-driven killers, but their power against this mold was unproven.

The treatment's grip tightened with dose, reaching full inhibition within two days. Fungal weight fell by over 94 percent. Microscopy and stains showed torn walls and membranes, with leaking cell contents. Inside, reactive oxygen piled up while the mold's antioxidant defenses first surged, then collapsed. The authors frame the dots as a promising green protectant for stored fruit, pending residue and safety checks.
pmc-13606643:
Nikita Filatov and co-authors compare heart muscle cells of a spiny mouse and a lab mouse at single-cell level, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The spiny mouse heals heart injury better than the lab mouse. Healthy left heart chambers from adult males of both kinds were read gene by gene.

Both hearts held like cell types, yet gene activity differed within each type. Heart muscle cells split into three states, from contractile to matrix-linked. Spiny mouse cells stayed mature but kept growth-linked programs more active. The profile did not match baby mouse hearts. Matrix programs in support cells also split by species.
pmc-13606843:
Nigar Çelik and Özlem Güner survey women in Türkiye in 2026 about health knowledge and hygiene habits. Good genital hygiene guards against infection, and knowing more about health may support better habits. The team recruited 469 adult women through social media for an online survey.

Scores for health knowledge ran high on average, and hygiene scores did too. The two rose together, though the link was small. In a combined model, health knowledge stood out as the strongest factor. Having had hygiene teaching and seeing a doctor when ill also helped. The authors back wider health teaching as a lever for better habits.
pmc-13607043:
Fixing the junction where skull meets spine changes a knot of anatomical distances, and no single measurement captures the result. Nurullah Kösmene and co-authors reviewed 2026 scans from 26 patients stabilized at that junction, measuring eleven parameters before and after surgery, each read twice by two observers working blind.

Standard distances from the odontoid peg to three skull-base lines all shrank after surgery. The team's novel measure — splitting the atlanto-dental interval into cranial and caudal parts — also shrank on both parts, while the gap between the parts did not change. Observer agreement was good to excellent throughout. The authors present the split interval as an exploratory extra lens on surgical change, not yet tied to patient outcomes or thresholds.
pmc-13607343:
Shuyi Li and Xiang Lu review cell-by-cell stress responses inside artery plaques. Their review from twenty twenty-six uses single-cell sequencing evidence. The endoplasmic reticulum stress response was long treated as one uniform signal. New data show each plaque cell type reacts differently.

Monocytes switch the stress response on strongly. Some macrophage and vessel-lining subsets switch it off instead. Muscle cells adjust it dynamically as they change form. Those differences shape plaque growth and rupture risk. Uniform anti-stress drugs could therefore help and harm simultaneously. Targeting specific cell subsets is the smarter path proposed. Plaque therapy may become cell-type personalised.
pmc-13607543:
Danil Kalinin, Ekaterina Schetinina, Alexey Fedorov, and Igor Granovsky retest genetic switches in a yeast in two thousand twenty-six. Internal ribosome entry sites, or IRES elements, are meant to let one RNA make two proteins. Reports of their activity in this yeast conflicted, and no standard test existed.

Their two-gene reporter system lets the first gene report promoter activity while the second should depend on the IRES. Several candidate elements showed no real entry activity above a tiny fraction of normal expression. Leftover signal traced to hidden promoter activity, not to cap-independent translation. The transcript stayed intact for most constructs. The system gives the field a quantitative way to tell true IRES action from stray transcription.
pmc-13607643:
Georgios Aletras and co-authors present a 2026 study asking whether the heart's squeeze fraction still predicts fate in acute heart failure. Doctors split patients by ejection fraction into preserved and reduced groups, but whether those groups truly die at different rates is debated. The team tracked both through hospital stay and after discharge, separately.

The registry held 530 consecutive patients from one center, enrolled from 2023 to 2025 and split almost evenly between the groups. In-hospital deaths were described plainly, while post-discharge risk got full statistical modeling. Events included death, dialysis, and return trips for heart failure. The paper's title hints at the punch line: two phenotypes, one prognosis. Period-specific analysis matters because the drivers of risk change after discharge.
pmc-13607743:
Leonie Keidel and co-authors compared a tiny stent combined with cataract surgery in 2026 across two forms of glaucoma. The Hydrus microstent opens the eye's drainage path while the cloudy lens is replaced. One group had primary open angle glaucoma, the common form, and the other had pseudoexfoliation glaucoma, where flaky material clogs the drain.

The single-center review covered operations from June 2021 to December 2025 at a Munich university eye hospital, with follow-up at eight to fourteen months. Seventy-four eyes were included, forty-nine of the common form and twenty-five of the flaky form. Eye pressure fell clearly in both groups from baseline, in the results reported. Readers get a side-by-side verdict on whether one operation serves both forms equally well.
pmc-13608043:
Building on the Moon means using Moon dirt, but the glue that hardens it must be flown from Earth, and every kilo counts. Zhenyu Wang and co-authors cut that glue bill in this 2026 study of a geopolymer made from simulated lunar soil. Adding a dusting of nano-silica let them trim the alkali activator mix while tuning its three parts.

At the best recipe, total additive mass fell by about 24 percent, yet strength rose: compression strength up 26 percent and bending strength up about 20 percent. Microscopy and heat tests traced the gains to how the activators dissolve and regrow the soil's minerals into gel. The authors present the mix as a step toward lunar construction that ships less from Earth.
pmc-13608143: Aristotle Koutsiaris and Friedrich Jung survey microvascular dynamics, the behavior of the smallest blood vessels, in a 2026 piece. More than three hundred years have passed since Marcello Malpighi first saw capillaries under a microscope in the 1600s. The piece takes that long view as its starting point. It presents the field's insights and where they are applied, as its title states.
pmc-13608243:
Monthon Lertcanawanichakul and co-authors published a review in 2026 on sea bacteria and drug search. A family of soil and sea bacteria makes a vast range of useful compounds. Sea strains live in harsh spots, from deep mud to vents and salty lakes. Those homes drove them to build rich chemical toolkits.

Their products include many classes that kill germs, fungi, and even cancer cells. New gene-reading and data tools now reveal hidden gene clusters that make these compounds. Yet many pathways stay silent in the lab, and known compounds keep turning up again. Yield is often low and unstable. The review maps current search methods and new plans that mix gene, protein, and chemical data. It aims to turn raw promise into real drugs.
pmc-13608343:
Shuang Zhang and co-authors uncover a liver-to-heart signal that drives harmful heart remodeling, the thickening and scarring that leads to heart failure. In mouse models, a sugar-sensing protein in the liver, ChREBP, rose sharply, while heart levels stayed flat. Removing it only from liver cells protected the heart against two standard remodeling triggers.

The chain runs through a blood protein called ApoM. Without liver ChREBP, the liver released more ApoM into the blood by a secretion route, not by making more of its gene message. Extra ApoM, or the lipoprotein particles carrying it, eased remodeling through a known heart receptor path. The authors propose boosting liver ApoM release as a new treatment angle.

pmc-13609543:

pmc-13609843:

pmc-13610243:

pmc-13610343:

pmc-13610743:

pmc-13611343:

On a 109-person public dataset, accuracy reached about ninety-nine percent with full training data. With only ten seconds per person it still topped eighty-three percent. A second dataset tested robustness across recording sessions. The authors aim at practical biometric systems that enroll users quickly.
pmc-13611743:

Builders can plug in either recurrent or transformer blocks at its core. A side channel of plain linear regression runs in parallel, catching sharp local swings that deep models tend to smooth over. Tests on electricity and California speed data cut average error against rivals, the authors report.
pmc-13612043:

pmc-13612843:

pmc-13613343:

pmc-13613443:

Power density was also strong. Results point to efficient storage uses. Flexible electrodes are a further promise. Charge storage gains were the headline result.
pmc-13614643:

That area gives the amount of infectious virus, and samples outside the range are flagged rather than misread. The team also trained an image model to draw the damaged area on its own. pmc-13615343:

pmc-13616543:

pmc-13616743:

pmc-13617543:

pmc-13617643:

The authors also weigh early ideas for blocking the pathway as treatment.
pmc-13618343:

pmc-13619043:

pmc-13619343:

pmc-13619843:

pmc-13619943:

pmc-13620143:

pmc-13620443:

pmc-13621643:

pmc-13621843:

pmc-13623043:

pmc-13623443:

pmc-13623543:

pmc-13623843:

pmc-13623943:

pmc-13624043:

pmc-13624143:

pmc-13624443:

pmc-13624843:

pmc-13625443:

pmc-13625743:

pmc-13626943:

pmc-13627143:

pmc-13627743:

pmc-13628143:

pmc-13628243:

pmc-13628443:

pmc-13629343:

pmc-13629543:

pmc-13629643:

The enzyme sits at the core of a multi-enzyme complex breaking down a metabolic intermediate. Its catalytic units assemble into trimers that expand into a twenty-four-part assembly. The crystals grew in a highly symmetric space group.

Near one lysine residue, the electron density fit a sulfate-like ion. That spot lies at the threefold junction between subunits of the trimer. Comparison with earlier structures marks it as an oxyanion-sensitive hotspot. A nearby helix reaches toward the active site pocket. It sits shifted relative to other crystal forms of the same domain. The authors link the ion density, the junction, and helix positioning within the assembly. The structure frames how local chemistry may tune this enzyme core.
pmc-13630243:
Joshua Vo and six colleagues publish the plan for a worldwide review of telemedicine teaching. The teaching targets medical students and residents. Virtual care is now core practice, sped up by the pandemic. Yet training for it stays patchy and uneven across schools and specialties.

The review follows set scoping methods. Two reviewers will screen six databases plus reference lists, each working alone. They will extract data on course content and teaching methods. Assessment plans count too. So do the barriers and aids programmes report. Results will be charted by learner group, specialty, and region. Tables and narrative will summarise them. The authors aim to give course designers, researchers, and policymakers a first full map. The literature on this teaching is fragmented today.
pmc-13630643:
Fikret Kayhalak and Suat Karaküçük map the research on environmental awareness and green behavior in this 2026 study. They use bibliometric tools to chart the field's shape over time. Records came from two large citation databases to avoid blind spots.

After removing duplicates, more than nine hundred publications remained. Many papers appeared in only one of the two databases. That gap proves that one source alone would miss part of the field. The maps show key themes, authors, and links in the literature. New researchers can see where the field is crowded and where it is thin. Funders can also spot topics that still lack attention.
pmc-13630843:
Ahmed Wael Moftah leads a nine-author team pooling trials of dye-guided thyroid surgery, in a systematic review from two thousand twenty-six. Thyroid removal puts the neighboring parathyroid glands at risk. Temporary parathyroid failure strikes up to half of patients. Permanent failure is rarer, but it means lifelong treatment for those it hits.

Five databases were searched for studies in the field. They had to compare fluorescence guidance against conventional surgery. The technique joins the glands' natural autofluorescence with injected indocyanine green dye. With both, the team can judge the glands' blood supply live. Randomized and observational studies were pooled into one whole. The quality of the evidence was graded in a formal way. The question is a hands-on one. Does the glowing view preserve hormone function more well than a trained eye on its own? Meta-analysis is how scattered surgical trials can answer as one.
pmc-13631243:
Longjiang Qiao and thirteen colleagues built and stress-tested a machine learning pipeline for drug hunting. It targets one specific enzyme, AKR1C3. The enzyme helps cancers grow and resist chemotherapy. Their framework, called TAME-VS, expands sparse activity data using related enzymes. It then trains its classifiers. The study appeared in 2026.

The honest tests came in two waves. Looking back, the model faced inhibitor families it had never seen. It still prioritised well beyond simple similarity searching. Looking forward, its picks beat designer intuition under a tight synthesis budget. Two flagged compounds proved potent and selective. They restored sensitivity to a standard chemotherapy drug in resistant breast cancer cells. A public web server now runs the workflow.
pmc-13631643:
Yunfeng Weng, Xianjiao Cao, Wenyan Song, and Qingqing He study a tiny RNA molecule that slows thyroid cancer, in a research paper from 2026. The cancer is the papillary type, the most common form. The molecule travels in small packets called exosomes, which cells use to send messages.

Data analysis showed a gene called TPM3 is switched up in this cancer and linked to spread and stem-like traits. Loading exosomes with the RNA and feeding them to cancer cells cut their growth, movement, and invasion. Blocking the RNA reversed the effect. The authors say this RNA-and-gene pair could be a target for new therapy.
pmc-13631843:
Chirag Jain proposes a dedicated frame for anxiety in cancer care in a 2026 perspective paper. Anxiety is one of the most common forms of distress in people with cancer, yet care usually treats it inside a broad distress label rather than as its own target. Jain argues it differs from depression, aims at real future threats such as the cancer returning, and follows a patterned course.

The proposed frame, called onco-anxiology, rests on three commitments: target anxiety itself, track it over time, and heed cancer specific causes. Those causes include learned dread of treatment effects and overlap between anxiety signs and side effects. Body measures are cast as a research aid, and a study agenda is set out.
pmc-13632343:
Whether longer exercise habits improve student sleep over time is examined by Zhang and three colleagues. College students often report poor sleep, late bedtimes, and daytime drowsiness, and short studies cannot show how those problems shift as exercise accumulates. The team followed 687 students at the start of an exercise programme and again at four and eight weeks, tracking sleep quality, bedtime delay, insomnia, and daytime sleepiness.

As total exercise time grew, sleep quality scores fell steadily, meaning sleep improved, while bedtime procrastination, daytime sleepiness, and insomnia severity also declined. Students who began with worse sleep or stronger bedtime delay showed distinct later trajectories, which suggests one-size exercise advice may fall short. Zhang and colleagues recommend pairing regular exercise with behavioural support, tailored for students with the most severe sleep problems.
pmc-13632743:
Leandro Soria and a large team of researchers uncover a new control on sugar storage in the liver in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Glycogen, the storage form of sugar, also builds up inside cell nuclei. Its role there stayed murky for nearly a century. The team found such stores in the livers of mice and people with a metabolic disorder called argininosuccinic aciduria. Breaking down this nuclear glycogen, they show, supports chemical marks on histones and keeps the liver healthy.

The breakdown is governed by a small chemical change to the enzyme that frees sugar. Nitric oxide drives that change, which sets how much enzyme reaches the nucleus. In metabolic liver disease, this control is impaired. The finding links a gas signal, sugar stores, and gene regulation in the liver.
pmc-13632943:
Vishal Shete and co-authors describe chikungunya cases during the 2024 upsurge in central India in a 2026 study. The mosquito borne virus keeps returning in India with fever and joint pain. Records covered patients with acute fever who tested positive on an antibody test during 2024.
