Of 943 people tested, 117, or 12.4 percent, were positive. Most were adults aged 19 to 49 and city residents. Joint pain was the top symptom, hitting large joints more than small ones, and rash appeared in about a quarter. Complications arose in 43.6 percent, most often joint pain that lingered past three months.
pmc-13633443:
Elizabeth Hines and co-authors report a public health risk from a cattle vaccine strain found in milk, in this 2026 study. The RB51 vaccine protects cattle against brucellosis, a disease that also infects people. Records from a national veterinary lab before 2021 held cases of the vaccine strain turning up in dairy milk.

The review found six heifer calves, all properly vaccinated, that were still shedding the vaccine strain in their milk years later as adults. Two of those cows were linked to three human cases of the disease. Every human case followed drinking raw, unpasteurized dairy products. The authors say milk from vaccinated cows should never be sold raw. They also urge officials and vets to rethink where and how widely this vaccine is used, especially in herds with no known brucellosis risk.
pmc-13634143:
Salih Kucuk and three co-authors compare two kinds of lung infection in a hospital study from 2026 set in Kocaeli, Turkey. One group of 37 patients had pneumonia caused by a common gut germ caught outside the hospital, which is an uncommon cause. The other group of 31 patients had pneumonia from other germs. The team compared signs, scans, lab tests, and outcomes.

At first the two groups looked much alike in fever, pain scores, and scan patterns. Yet the gut-germ group stayed in hospital longer, about 16 days against about 10. Deaths within 90 days were also far higher in that group, near half against about one in six. The gap held after the team adjusted for age and cancer.
pmc-13634443:
Høgsbjerg and co-authors check whether four quality fixes steadied patients' chest walls during a breath hold radiotherapy technique for breast cancer. Holding a deep breath moves the heart away from the beam, but chest drift during the hold can misplace dose meant for nodes near the breastbone. Their 2026 study measures geometric errors on treatment images after the fixes, including moving the gating marker onto the chest.

Errors over three millimeters fell to 4.7 percent of cases, down from 21.2 percent before the changes, a clear statistical gain. The trade off was skin trouble: about sixty one percent of patients reported mostly mild effects where the marker block overlapped the treatment field. The authors weigh steadier targeting against that irritation.
pmc-13634743:
Greener solvents for enzyme work can be designed with computer help, Hou and co-authors argue in a 2026 review. Deep eutectic solvents are cheap mixtures that can replace harsh chemicals in enzyme reactions. They can also steady enzymes and steer which product forms. But the mix options are vast, so trial and error wastes time.

The review covers how solvent makeup and water content shape the tiny setting around each enzyme. Tough enzymes from extreme habitats are weighed as sturdy candidates for such media. Computer models can screen mixes, forecast traits, and guide joint design of enzyme and solvent. The authors map a path to faster, cleaner enzyme use in industry.
pmc-13636143:
Murat Kaan Erdal led a 2026 engineering study of a self-adjusting drug dosing system that learns each subject's drug handling in real time, rather than relying on population averages. New sensors can report drug levels in tissue every few seconds. That opens the door to closed-loop dosing. Controllers built on average pharmacokinetics must be set cautiously and can still overshoot when a subject differs. The team built an adaptive controller that estimates an individual's kinetics early in infusion and keeps updating that model.

Tested on the anesthetic procaine in the brain ventricles of live rats, the system faced a hard target because drug transport into the brain lags. It reached target levels in twenty to thirty minutes. It held them within roughly five to twelve percent deviation, including sensor noise.
pmc-13636443:
Carria Xie and co-authors test a counterintuitive feed recipe for meat chickens under heat stress, in a study published in 2026. The diets differed in formulated net energy, 2,360 versus 2,260 kilocalories per kilogram, achieved by cutting crude protein and adding millrun and free amino acids. Birds grew from day fourteen to thirty-five, half under daily eight-hour heat at thirty-three degrees.

Heat hurt weight gain, intake, and feed conversion, as expected. Surprisingly, the lower-energy diet improved feed conversion by about two percent and raised breast meat yield by over eleven percent, under both hot and comfortable conditions. The authors caution that the recipe change, not energy alone, may deserve the credit, since ingredients shifted together.
pmc-13636643:
Jakob Heyer-Müller and four colleagues published this 2026 methods study on tracking protein clumping during purification. Clumped protein is a critical flaw in biologic medicines; makers want to spot it mid-process. A light-based probe can watch protein structure during column purification, yet shifting salt levels bend the signal and confuse standard software. The team built a physics-based model of the signal, with a built-in account of the salt-driven background drift.

Applied to nearly three hundred in-line spectra across varied column conditions, the model rebuilt the data faithfully while keeping each component's identity stable. One derived feature, the center of the main structural band, proved a sturdy clumping marker even while concentrations swung hard. The features predicted the share of single proteins well and lumped forms acceptably. The authors offer the approach as an interpretable alternative for real-time quality watching.
pmc-13638043:
Oliver Umney and eleven colleagues map three proteins inside the Z-disc, the narrow boundary structure that links muscle fibers' contractile units. Z-discs in heart muscle hold more than fifty proteins with structural and signaling jobs, yet sit far below the resolution of ordinary microscopes. The team tagged three residents with fluorescent binders in pig heart fibers: an actin crosslinker, a segment of the protein titin, and a width-regulating protein. A super-resolution microscopy method then located each tag within ten nanometers.

Pattern analysis separated the trio. The crosslinker and the width regulator shared a similar repeating arrangement. The titin segment followed a different but equally regular pattern through the disc. Knowing which proteins march together and which keep their own rhythm constrains models of how the disc bears force and signals. The authors also release their analysis approach for groups imaging crowded protein assemblies.
pmc-13638243:
Hyunsuk Peter Suh, writing as editor of a plastic surgery journal, argues that his field leans too little on strict scientific reasoning. Early writing in the field rested on anatomy studies, single case reports, and before-and-after photos. Those pieces had value, but they mostly showed and told rather than tested ideas.

Suh contrasts that habit with the rest of medicine, where claims face set checks for bias and clear reading of data. He notes that in the natural sciences, math can predict how things will behave. In patients, a sound idea can still fail, since human biology is complex. His plea is for surgeons to frame clear questions, name the factors that matter, and read results with care. The piece sets a standard he wants for his journal's pages.
pmc-13639643:
Hidetaka Wakabayashi and four colleagues present a 2026 paper from the Japanese group for rehab nutrition, setting out version 3.0 of their field. Rehab nutrition pairs exercise care with food care. It aims to help people with illness, frailty, or disability live and move better.

Early versions stressed body function, first as an idea and then as a set care routine. The new version adds mind, social life, and spirit to the frame. It also welcomes digital health tools and smart software. The group calls the update full, personal care for patients and the staff who serve them.
pmc-13639743:
Gay and co-authors build a teaching tool that acts as a virtual dose planner for radiation therapy students. Judging plan quality takes practice on many plans, good and bad. Clinic training gives trainees few plans and little chance to improve them hands-on.

Their models take plain language instructions, like a planner would in review talk. Given words, the model reshapes a dose map, making better or worse versions on demand. That yields endless varied examples for study. Trainees can test fixes in real time and see the result. The tool turns plan review into a dialogue rather than a lecture. It may shorten the path to sharp judgment in a field where dose quality is patient safety.
pmc-13641143:
Chirayu Mohindroo and co-authors profile gene faults in a rare group of cancers of the gut and pancreas. Their 2026 study covers one hundred eleven patients treated at Johns Hopkins Hospital between 2020 and 2022. These neuroendocrine neoplasms vary widely, and their response to treatment is hard to predict.

The team read tumor samples with next-generation sequencing and checked faults against three cancer databases. About seventy-nine percent of tumors carried a harmful or likely harmful change. The most common faults hit TP53 and MEN1, with smaller shares in genes that reshape chromatin. The authors also note a small group with faults more often seen in blood cancers, and they link patterns to survival.
pmc-13643143:
Sami S Zoghbi and Robert B Innis wrote a letter questioning how a recent brain inflammation imaging study should be read. Kalita and colleagues had presented a PET tracer aimed at GPR84, a marker on immune cells, using systemic bacterial toxin injection to provoke inflammation.

The letter warns that toxin in the bloodstream also inflames vessel walls, trapping white blood cells inside brain capillaries where the tracer can bind them. That vascular signal could be mistaken for activation of resident microglia. Blood-brain barrier leakage adds further doubt. The authors ask for checks such as direct brain injection models or correcting the vessel contribution.
pmc-13643543:
Muhammad Junaid Mustafa and Sehar Rana wrote a 2026 letter on a case of heart failure caused by a dialysis graft. A long used graft can shunt so much blood that the heart fails from high output. The case they discuss was solved by tying off a graft that had served for 22 years.

The letter praises the test that proved the cause: a balloon briefly blocked the graft during a heart probe. Pressures in the lung vessels fell at once, which showed the graft load in hard numbers. That proof gave the team firm ground before a step that cannot be undone. The writers also weigh how dialysis care should adapt once such a graft is closed.
pmc-13644543:
Reo Ikumi and five colleagues present a 2026 laboratory comparison of four ways to take digital impressions for a full arch of dental implants. Complete-arch scanning is error-prone, and a two-part scan joined at a palate marker might do better.

On an upper jaw model holding six implants, each workflow was repeated ten times and matched against a laboratory reference scan. The segmented scan with the palate marker agreed best, the conventional tray impression worst. A marker alone without segmentation added nothing, and far-back molar sites suffered most in one-piece scans. The authors present segmentation as an accessible accuracy boost.
pmc-13645743:
Hospitals can jointly study survival without pooling patient records, Veeraragavan and two colleagues show. Survival analysis across hospitals usually stalls because privacy rules forbid pooling sensitive health data. Simpler sharing methods can leak single counts by subtraction. The team built a federated Kaplan-Meier framework using threshold homomorphic encryption. This method lets a coordinator add coded tallies from many sites. Only the combined result is decoded, using shares from a group.

In tests with synthetic breast-cancer data spread across five hundred sites, the coded curves matched the pooled gold standard closely. Message sizes grew in a steady way with site and time-point counts. The authors also prove correctness, stability, and efficient packing of the encrypted vectors. Veeraragavan and colleagues present the design as a way to run high-quality multi-institution survival studies with far less privacy risk than plaintext collaboration.
pmc-13646243:
Stem cell care may help two grave harms of early birth: chronic lung disease and brain injury. Felderhoff-Müser and co-authors ask whether one cell recipe can fit both, in a review from twenty twenty-six. Both harms share roots in swelling, oxygen stress, and stalled cell growth in key weeks of life.

The cells act mostly through what they release: tiny packets, growth signals, and calm-down signals for the immune system. Lab and early clinic work shows the care is workable and seems safe. Yet no large trial has yet proved it truly helps either harm. The review walks through shared paths, organ-specific needs, and the steps left before wards can use the care with trust.
pmc-13646343:
Samuels and co-authors present, in a 2026 paper, the rationale and design of a trial testing a GLP-1 drug after weight loss surgery in patients who remain obese. Some patients keep an obese body mass index long after gastric bypass. Whether the new appetite drugs add benefit on top of surgery had never been studied.

The trial randomizes adults aged 25 to 65, a year after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, with a body mass index still at or above 30. Half get 24 weeks of tirzepatide plus standard care; half get standard care alone. The trial is open label and framed as proof of concept. The main outcome is total percent weight change at 24 weeks. Baseline traits of the enrolled group are reported alongside the design. A positive result would give clinics an evidence based next step for the many surgical patients who plateau too high.
pmc-13647043:
Si-Dan Lin, Xiao-Dong Rao, and Wei Liang measure what makes a bird's bite strong. Bite force shapes prey capture, defense, and competition, yet broad cross-species data on birds were scarce. The team measured bite force and related traits in 175 bird species. Beak depth tracked bite force more strongly than the rest of the skull shape did.

Merging new data with published values gave 223 species for evolutionary models. Body mass mattered, as expected from size scaling. Nest structure also stood out: species that build more elaborate nests bite harder. The pattern supports the nest-complexity hypothesis, which links nest building demands to stronger beaks and bites.
pmc-13647243:
Rhyan Ouaddane Alami and six colleagues present a step-by-step dissection guide to the carotid region of the neck, the corridor carrying the brain's main arteries and several key nerves. Safe surgery here demands a true three-dimensional grasp of vessels, nerves, and tissue layers. The team dissected one side of a preserved adult cadaver from surface to deep structures in six stages. Landmarks anchor each stage, from skin marks through muscle release to the artery fork.

The sequence exposes the jugular vein and a named anatomical triangle, manages small vein branches, opens the carotid sheath. It finishes by mapping the hypoglossal and vagus nerves and the small carotid body. Clinical notes tie each landmark to what a surgeon meets in vascular, head and neck, and spine operations. The authors offer the protocol as a teaching scaffold for trainees who must learn this crowded anatomy before operating on it.
pmc-13647643:
Ji Liu and seven colleagues compare two ways of giving a last-resort antibiotic to patients with pneumonia caused by carbapenem-resistant germs, in a 2026 study. The drug, colistimethate sodium, reaches the lungs poorly when injected because of its chemistry, while breathing it in as a mist delivers it straight to the air spaces. Records from several centers covered 209 patients treated between 2021 and 2023, split between injection alone and injection plus inhalation. Response, cure, stay length, death, and harms were compared.

The combined route produced a clearly higher clinical response rate. Cure rates, hospital stay, and twenty-eight-day deaths did not differ significantly between the groups. Side effects, including kidney and nerve toxicity, skin darkening, and airway spasm, appeared at similar rates. The authors conclude that adding the inhaled route improves response without adding measurable harm. The result supports a practical tweak for infections where few drug options remain.
pmc-13649443:
Yangyang Qian and five colleagues report two women whose breast cancer had spread to the lungs, with drug picks guided by a test on tumour cells caught from blood. Spread tumours can drift from the first tumour, and tissue is not always in reach. Both women had the HER2-positive form of the disease.

The test grew the caught cells and tried drugs on them in the lab. Its calls matched the tissue reads and each woman's past drug proof well. Care then bent to those calls. The authors claim the first such report in far-spread breast cancer. They pitch blood cell tests as a way to pick drugs when tissue is out of reach, with more proof still owed.
pmc-13649743:
Jeevan Yoganand and three colleagues upgrade a zero-trust login frame for vehicles that talk to roadside fog computers. Car networks shift fast, so trust checks and handovers between zones must keep up without slowing traffic data. Their upgrade adds three parts to the base frame.

First, fog nodes now train a shared trust model in a split way that keeps raw data local. Second, a cipher design built to resist future quantum attacks guards trust messages in transit. Third, a token lets a car reuse past proof when it crosses into a new zone, which cut login delay by nearly half in tests. Trial runs also showed steadier trust scores and better catches of behaviour-based attacks.
pmc-13650143:
Radka Roubalová and thirteen colleagues, publishing in 2026, test whether gut microbes help drive anorexia nervosa, a severe eating disorder with low recovery rates. They used a mouse model in which animals with access to running wheels and limited food lose dangerous amounts of weight, echoing features of the human illness.

Germ-free mice received stool transplants from healthy donors, from patients with acute anorexia, or from patients with a severe long-lasting form. Mice given acute-phase microbes showed weaker hunger signals in the brain and ate less. Mice given microbes from the long-lasting form ate normally yet ran much more than the other groups. Neither transplant changed whether the full anorexia-like state developed. The authors read this as evidence that the microbiome shapes parts of the illness course, and that restoring a healthy gut community may be needed for complete recovery.
pmc-13650743:
Zhihao Wu and one colleague review ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, as a thread running through osteoporosis, the bone-thinning disease of aging and hormone loss. In ferroptosis, iron fuels the peroxidation of membrane fats while the cell's defenses against that damage fail, and the review asks how this process plays out in each bone cell type.

Bone-forming cells and their stem cell parents suffer: their growth, matrix production, and mineralization falter when ferroptosis strikes. Bone-embedded sensor cells may pass distorted remodeling signals. Bone-eating cells, by contrast, might be usefully killed by ferroptosis when resorption runs too high. Triggers span estrogen loss, sugar and fat toxicity, steroid drugs, aging, and iron overload. Candidate treatments range from iron chelators to targeted delivery of protective vesicles. The authors insist the goal is selective control by cell type, not blanket switching of the pathway.
pmc-13652443:
A mixed tumor first read as plain gland cancer is told by Maho Takuwa and co-authors in work dated 2026. The tumor sat in the duodenum of a fifty-six-year-old man. A scope biopsy called it adenocarcinoma, so drug care for stomach cancer came first. Surgery then took the tumor and near nodes in one R0 sweep. Full tissue reads told the true tale.

Half the tumor was nerve-type cancer, missed by the biopsy. Nodes split by kind, one stash nerve-type and the rest gland-type. Platinum drugs followed surgery. No return showed at sixteen months.
pmc-13655943:
Szimonetta Eitmann, Péter Mátrai, Péter Hegyi, Márta Balaskó, and Erika Pétervári pool evidence on mothers' weight and their adult children's weight in a paper from 2026. Overeating in pregnancy is known to raise childhood fatness. The open question was whether the effect lasts into midlife and differs by sex. The team searched four databases and found twenty-nine studies covering over four hundred thousand mother-child pairs.

Each small rise in a mother's pre-pregnancy body mass index meant measurably higher body mass and fat in adult offspring. Excess pregnancy weight gain raised the odds of offspring overweight by about a third. The links were strongest in early midlife and in daughters. The authors urge nutrition care before and during pregnancy.
pmc-13656043:
Kate Gallagher and Itay Bentov review, in a 2026 paper, a bedside test meant to flag patients at risk of lung complications after surgery under general anesthesia. Such complications are a major burden in care and cost. They lengthen hospital stays and worsen outcomes, and even minor ones raise the risk of death around surgery. Spotting high risk patients early allows steps that cut that burden.

The best established risk score needs many variables, which can slow its use at the bedside. The air test is offered as a simpler option. The review weighs its promise and its measured performance against the established scores, which have been validated in large studies with good, though uneven, accuracy. It also sets out the new test's limits. The authors' aim is a fair account of where a quick bedside test can help, and where the fuller scores remain safer.
pmc-13658643:
Julia de Macedo Robert and co-authors tune fermentation for a medical compound in a 2026 microbiology study. The soil bacterium Streptomyces eurocidicus makes azomycin, a building block for drugs against resistant tuberculosis and Chagas disease and for tumor imaging, yet the best growing conditions for producing it were unexplored.

Batch fermentations tested sugars, starch, soybean oil, and amino acid mixes as feed. The bacterium built body mass on oil but made no product from it, and it only started producing once the main sugar ran low. Free amino acids boosted yields strongly. A tuned glucose and amino acid medium scaled from small flasks to a bench bioreactor.
pmc-13658743:
Millions of pilgrims gather in Mecca each year, and crowds that size can turn a rare meningitis germ into an outbreak. Laurent Coudeville and co-authors modeled meningococcal spread around the Hajj and the year-round Umrah visits in 2026. They divided the world into five linked populations and tested vaccination coverage levels against thirty million expected Umrah pilgrims.

Umrah now supplies about ninety percent of pilgrimage days, most of them by foreign visitors. With only ten percent of pilgrims vaccinated, the chance of a year topping one hundred cases among pilgrims ran above half. At ninety percent coverage that chance collapsed nearly to zero, and cases across the kingdom fell by more than eighty percent.
pmc-13659243:
Noa Erlitzki and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, how the letters round a DNA mark shape the mark's path in the genome. Enzymes called TET strip gene-off tags in steps: a methyl tag is oxidized to a hydroxymethyl form, then to two more forms that can be cut out. The mid form is the fork in the road. It can stand as a mark of its own, or be pushed on to full tag loss. Past work could read just two of the tag forms at once, so the fork stayed blurred. The team built a fast lab method that reads all three forms at base detail, across hundreds of sites.

The letters next to a tag split its odds: some frames favor the mid form's birth, others its death. In lone strands of DNA those leanings vanish, which ties them to a flip act by the enzyme.
pmc-13660643:
Ehsan Mihandoust and co-authors review smart software for cleaning up CT scans in a 2026 paper. Metal dental work scatters CT images, which blurs tumor outlines and skews dose plans. The scans guide radiation care for head and neck cancers. Past reviews stressed older cleanup methods and image scores over care outcomes.

The team searched for studies of learning based cleanup in this care setting. A set of studies met their rules, split between older and learning based methods. Several learning methods kept dose errors small in clinical checks. Some also passed standard dose match tests at high rates. Methods judged only on image scores still lack direct dose proof.
pmc-13665643:
Awo Mohamed Kahie and co-authors study iron pill use in pregnancy in Somaliland in a 2026 paper. Low blood iron in pregnancy is a grave health problem in poorer countries. Iron pills are advised, yet few women in Somaliland take them as directed. The study used a national health survey to find what drives pill use there.

Only about a third of women reported taking iron pills in their last pregnancy. Attending four or more prenatal visits was by far the strongest link to pill use. Richer households, husbands in paid work, and television exposure also raised the odds. Women whose husbands had no schooling had lower odds, and gaps varied by region.
pmc-13668043:
Federico Mercolini and co-authors ask whether scans can replace marrow sampling in a muscle cancer in 2026. Rhabdomyosarcoma staging has long used needle samples from both hip bones to check marrow spread. A whole-body scan that lights up active tumors might do the same job.

Records for three hundred one patients from Europe and North America were reviewed. Scan and sampling agreed on marrow spread in most positive cases. The scan alone caught spread in twenty-four patients, while sampling alone caught it in just one. The authors test whether a negative scan can safely spare children the sampling procedure.
pmc-13668443:
Sanjeev Kumar and co-authors track how right side heart pacing weakens the left ventricle in a 2026 study. Seventy five patients with healthy hearts received dual chamber pacemakers that pace from the right ventricle. Echo measures, including strain imaging and 3D volumes, followed both sides of the heart over time.

Twenty patients lost left ventricle strength; fifteen developed pacing linked dysfunction and five full cardiomyopathy. That worst group showed weaker strain a week after implant, wider electrical waves before implant, and higher pacing shares. Pacing cut left side function early and late, and the right side faded by six months too.
pmc-13669043:
Andrea Della Penna and co-authors report a 2026 case series on liver transplants that are too big for child recipients. A full-size donor liver may not fit a small belly, and splitting may not be an option. Their fix trims the back right part of the graft outside the body before it goes in. Seven young recipients at one center got this treatment over four years. The grafts were judged too big by weight ratio and by fit.

Trimming cut the weight ratio from well over four percent to just over two. All seven grafts could then be placed, and most bellies closed at once. Three patients had major problems, and one died of a cause apart from graft size. Six of the seven were alive at about five years of follow-up. The authors call the method a workable rescue, with safety still to prove.
pmc-13669343:
Jean-Sébastien Hulot and a large team sort heart failure patients with preserved pumping power into two hidden subgroups, in a study from 2026. This form of heart failure makes up over half of all cases, yet its mix of causes keeps it poorly defined. The team used deep profiling of 155 patients in a French cohort.

Blood protein scans, scans of the heart, and clinical data fed an unsupervised clustering method. One group showed inflammation, cell injury, and worse kidney function. The other showed vessel stress and milder changes. Standard tests alone could not split the groups, but a combined classifier did so with high accuracy. In a second cohort of 456 patients, the inflamed group fared worse over time.
pmc-13670643: Safa Özçelik writes a short 2026 letter in reply to a report on the first fully robotic heart bypass done through small cuts in Southeast Asia. The letter praises the feat as a real step forward. It then asks for more detail on the plan for restoring blood flow, the long operating and recovery times, and the lack of a flow check during surgery. Those points, the author argues, are needed before readers can judge what the case truly shows.
pmc-13670943:
An abnormal channel between the rectum and the urethra is among the rarest complications of prostate laser surgery. Yahya Ghazwani and co-authors report such a case in 2026, involving a man in his early eighties. Four days after his prostate procedure, urine was passing through his anus and stool was draining through his urinary catheter.

Scans showed defects in the rectum and the base of the bladder. Emergency surgery closed the bladder, drained the pelvis, and diverted the bowel. The channel persisted, so urine was diverted from the kidneys before a robot-assisted repair closed the fistula, the rectum, and the bladder neck. Later imaging confirmed the closure and the bowel was reconnected, though a drainage tube remained in place.
pmc-13672943:
Hayley Alderson and co-authors report on a police program for first-time domestic abuse suspects. The program, called CARA, settles lower-risk cases out of court with workshops on relationship abuse. It now runs across police forces in England and Wales. The team held interviews and group talks with thirty-one staff, from police to workshop leaders.

Staff across areas backed the program with strong, shared support. They also urged changes to sharpen how it runs. Risk checks should split cases with more care, they said. Training and rollout steps need tweaks to fit local needs. Views from voluntary groups that aid victims should be heard more fully. The authors frame the study as a guide for the next stage of delivery.
pmc-13673243:
The protein ABCA1 pumps cholesterol out of cells, and Chang Liu and co-authors ask in a 2026 study what happens to the gut when that pump is missing. They used Syrian golden hamsters engineered without the gene, fed on a diet rich in cholesterol and fat for twelve weeks.

The knockout hamsters developed marked inflammation of the colon, with damaged surface tissue and immune cells crowding in. Cholesterol built up four-fold in the gut lining, and the proteins that seal the barrier between cells fell. Oxidative stress rose, and the gut microbe community shifted. Tests in a human colon cell line supported the animal findings. The authors make the case that failed cholesterol export can itself drive bowel injury.
pmc-13674043:
A slipped lumbar disc can bend the spine sideways as the body leans away from the leg pain, a curve called sciatic scoliosis. Shicheng Zheng and co-authors compare two keyhole operations for that problem in a 2026 retrospective study. One approach enters between the vertebrae, the other through the side opening where the nerve exits.

The review covered 237 patients treated between 2022 and 2024 and followed for at least a year. Blood loss and hospital stay were similar in both groups. The between-vertebrae route finished faster, about eighty-seven minutes against ninety-six, and needed half as many X-ray checks during surgery. Both groups' spine curves, pain scores, and disability measures were tracked before and after surgery. The paper helps surgeons weigh access routes for this specific deformity.
pmc-13674843:
Dávid Márai and co-authors answer a critique of their pre-eclampsia biomarker review in a 2026 response. Their meta-analysis found microRNA-210 climbs in step with disease severity. A reader raised three points on method that bear on clinic use.

The reply takes up sample type first: serum and plasma may skew microRNA reads. Source studies report sample type in clashing ways, the authors found. That clash, they argue, does not drive the spread in results. Method rules for scaling reads get the same care. Last, telling a forecast mark from a care guide mark matters. The stepwise climb claim stands their ground.
pmc-13675143:
Eldad Keha and co-authors split the Stroop clash into three kinds to see which kind grows with age. In the Stroop task, a word's print hue clashes with its sense, and old minds show a big lag. That lag could mean a broad brake loss or a crack in one clash kind. Their 2026 study uses a low-grip form of the task that swells clash marks. Young and old adults name hues by hand across shapes, plain words, hue-linked words, and clash words in and out of the reply set.

Reply clash runs big in old adults, the sums show. Sense clash swells a touch with age in both its parts. Task clash, the pull of the wrong job, holds flat across ages. Age lag in Stroop thus reads as clash-kind wear, not one broad fall.
pmc-13675443:
Shouqing Hou, Hongru Ma, Xuye Lang, and Yuan Yao reviewed in 2026 how cells end transcription, the copying of a gene into RNA. Ending matters because it sets gene borders, frees the copying enzyme, and stops one gene's activity from spilling into the next. The signals that trigger ending are often confused with each other in the literature.

The review treats termination signals as rule systems that depend on context, order, and timing. It compares the routes used by bacteria, by archaea, and by the several copying enzymes in cell nuclei. Shared timing limits are met by very different molecular tools in each group. Matching each signal to the right kind of evidence, they argue, will improve prediction and design of terminators.
pmc-13675743:
Terlinda da C Barros and co-authors report the first documented case of chromoblastomycosis in Timor-Leste. Published in 2026, the paper covers a long lasting fungal skin disease that enters through wounds, most often in farm workers in poor tropical regions. It can scar and disfigure the legs, and treatment is long and hard.

The patient was a 49-year-old farmer with itchy, painful ulcerated plaques on his right leg and arm, growing for more than thirty years after a thorn injury. Care was hampered by weak diagnostic capacity, few treatment options, low health literacy, and poor adherence. The authors use the case to flag a neglected disease that remote, low resource settings likely underdiagnose.
pmc-13676043:
Gregory Schwartz leads a team of fourteen in a 2027 analysis of three heart risk factors after a heart event. A fatty particle set by genes, smoking, and diabetes each raise the odds of a further attack or stroke. Whether their risks merely add or multiply each other was unknown.

The team re-read data from a large world trial of patients after acute coronary syndrome. Each factor raised risk on its own terms, and the three stacked in a plain additive way, with no extra spark when they met. The authors say the finding shapes how hard and how fast each factor should be tackled.
pmc-13676143:
Jobin Jacob and co-authors sound an alarm on azithromycin, a workhorse antibiotic for gut infections, in a 2026 review. The drug is prescribed widely for diarrhoeal disease in poorer countries, helped by its tissue reach and simple dosing, and it sits on the World Health Organization watch list for resistance risk. Resistance is now rising in the main gut pathogens it treats.

The review tracks the problem across Shigella, typhoid and other Salmonella, and Campylobacter, whose resistance routes and clinical fallout differ. The drug long half-life keeps pressure on gut microbes for days, breeding resistance. The authors argue for three defences: better diagnostics so the drug is aimed rather than sprayed, stewardship tied to pathogen results, and surveillance to catch resistance early. Vaccines can ease the infection load itself. Their aim is to keep a cheap oral option useful where few alternatives exist.
pmc-13676643:
Helena Aineskog and co-authors studied life quality a year after a burst brain aneurysm in a national Swedish group, in work published in 2026. Survivors who score well on function scales may still face hidden strain in daily life. The team drew on 634 patients treated between 2014 and 2018, of whom 471 had good function scores. Their answers were compared with a matched slice of the general public.

Patients with good scores reported fewer mobility problems than their peers, which surprised the team. Yet they reported far more trouble with usual daily activities, at more than twice the rate of the matched group. Extreme anxiety and low mood were also more common among patients. Patients with poor function scores fared worse than peers on every measure. The authors urge care teams to probe daily life, not just function scores.
pmc-13677043:
Mengguang Wang and co-authors demonstrated this 2026 optical computer that does image math with light. Neural networks built from lenses face a trade: deep stacks are bulky, while single layers are too shallow and cannot subtract. Their single-layer metalens imager fakes depth through time and polarization instead. Fixed vortex channels form the first layer, with one channel acting as a built-in shortcut.

A second layer of swirling light spots follows, and liquid crystals replayed over time supply positive and negative weights. That timing trick solves the sign problem and lets training absorb build flaws. Tests lifted full-color image accuracy from about fifty-eight to eighty-seven percent. Nearly all the heavy arithmetic ran in optics, pointing to fast, tiny vision chips.
pmc-13677443:
Maura Haas-Renninger, Michael Haas, and their co-authors present a way to learn what a parasitoid wasp grew up eating, from the adult wasp alone. Their 2026 study notes that these wasps govern many insect hosts, yet host records are scarce, since adults are caught far from any host and rearing them is hard.

Their method, cuticular barcoding, washes trace host DNA off the wasp's outer shell and reads it with standard DNA barcoding. In tests, wasps were reared on two beetle species. The host was found in 35 of 72 samples, a 49 percent hit rate. Pooled wasps worked as well as single ones, so one field caught wasp can suffice. Host traces lasted in wasps long after they emerged.
pmc-13677743:
Pin Lyu and colleagues published a 2026 structural biology study of a protein pump that moves zinc across cell membranes. Zinc is essential in small amounts but poisonous in excess, so cells control it tightly. Using advanced imaging, the team captured the pump's shape at fine detail while it faced inward, ready to collect zinc.

Experiments and computer simulations showed that the pump's tail acts as both a brake and a sensor: it holds the pump still until zinc levels rise, then releases it. A rich supply segment appears to hand zinc ions to the pump's core binding site. The findings revise older models of how cells import zinc.
pmc-13678843:
Zhang and co-authors review the m6A mark and how crops cope with stress. The m6A mark is the most common inner edit on plant RNA. Three protein groups write, erase, and read the mark. Those acts tune RNA life span, splicing, and protein output. New sequencing tools now map the mark across whole crops.

Studies show shared rules plus species-level twists in the network. Proof of function still rests on a few model plants. Field tests in real farm crops lag behind lab work. The review weighs breeding plans that use the mark. It also lists blocks that slow use in stress-proof crop design.
pmc-13679343:
Mahima Jose and co-authors review how artificial intelligence is being used in humanitarian work around the world. Their 2026 scoping review maps what has actually been deployed, how mature the tools are, and how they are governed. The team searched six databases plus reports from major aid organizations, with extra attention to the Middle East and North Africa.

The review covers 57 scholarly papers and 17 gray literature reports. Most uses cluster around sudden disasters such as floods and earthquakes, for tasks like damage mapping, hazard prediction, logistics, and search and rescue. Evidence on evaluation and governance stays patchy across the field. The authors lay out what helps adoption and what blocks it, giving agencies a base for more careful rollouts.
pmc-13680843:
Kathrine Sullivan and a large team described in two thousand twenty-six how they reshaped a trauma-focused parenting program for military-connected mothers of young children. These mothers, including service members, veterans, and partners, face more trauma than civilian mothers. The original program, Parenting-STAIR, targets trauma, emotion control, and parenting skills.

Interviews with clinic staff, clinicians, and mothers pointed to four needs: shorter treatment, more flexibility, less stigma, and respect for military culture. The team cut the program to a shorter modular form with plainer language and wrote a companion guide for clinicians. Health workers gain a version families are more likely to start and finish.
pmc-13684543:
Saeed and co-authors report a study, published in 2026, on shared gene programs that reshape the heart under metabolic stress. Diseases that combine heart and liver strain are common, yet the common cell programs behind them are poorly mapped. The team used three mouse models, each showing a different form of the stress. They measured heart function, liver injury, and gene activity in both organs.

Comparing the models let the team pull out the programs that all three shared. Those shared programs point to the core response, rather than quirks of one model. Some of the genes involved can be targeted by drugs. The authors argue that treating heart failure may work better when the liver is part of the picture. Their map gives drug hunters a shorter list of targets that hold up across models.
pmc-13688343:
Precision medicine builds a prediction model for one patient from a crowd of similar patients, but how large should the crowd be? Tatiana Krikella and Joel Dubin propose a loss function that tunes that choice directly. The user picks which virtues count, discrimination, calibration, or a blend, and the method searches crowd sizes for the best joint score.

Simulations showed the useful search range runs from twenty to seventy percent of the training data. The optimal size moved with the chosen virtues, proving the setting is not one-size-fits-all. Earlier findings about crowd size and accuracy held up under the new method. The authors aim for personal prediction that is both flexible and cheap to compute.
pmc-13690443:
Peng-Hui Wang argues that muscle pain deserves a place among the causes of bladder symptoms. His 2026 editorial reviews lower urinary tract symptoms, from urgency and leakage to night waking, which burden daily life for many men and women.

Standard definitions long described these symptoms without naming causes, and pain was left out entirely. Newer guidance folds pain syndromes in. A Taipei study of over a thousand women with chronic pelvic pain, three hundred seven of them also carrying bladder symptoms, points at the pelvic floor muscle as a link. Wang walks through how pain traits in that muscle were sorted and tied to symptom patterns. The piece urges clinicians to weigh muscular pain when bladder complaints resist the usual explanations.
pmc-13694143:
Tripathi and Cook looked at how AI could speed radiology reporting in India in twenty twenty-six. Radiologists dictate reports, then edit and finish them. That flow is a choke point. It delays care and piles up paperwork. AI dictation systems mix speech recognition, language handling, set templates, and live quality checks.

From current proof, the authors argue, human-in-the-loop systems beat plain speech recognition. They beat fully automated reporting too, on speed, consistency, and quality. India adds its own hard parts. Clinics run in many languages, basic systems vary by place, and a national digital health mission is still taking shape. Wins thus hinge on more than model accuracy. They hinge on fit with daily work, systems that talk to each other, governance, and local checks. The authors frame AI dictation as a move to structured, clinic-linked reporting, not mere speech-to-text.
pmc-1810543:
Shea, Grimshaw, Wells, and co-authors create AMSTAR, a tool for judging the quality of systematic reviews. Reviews that pool many studies guide medical decisions, so weak reviews can mislead care. The team built their measure from earlier tools, hard evidence, and expert agreement.

They merged existing checklists into a long pool of candidate questions, then shaped a final instrument. AMSTAR lets editors, funders, and readers test whether a review searched fairly, weighed bias, and reported methods clearly. A trusted quality score helps separate reviews worth acting on from those needing caution.
pmc-3891543:
Kumar and Pandey give an overview of the chemistry and body actions of flavonoids. Flavonoids are plant compounds found widely in fruits, greens, tea, and other foods. Interest in them grew because large diet studies link flavonoid-rich diets with wide health benefits.

Since flavonoids come straight from human foods and link to health, their effects need careful review. The authors survey flavonoid types, their chemistry, and reported actions in the body. Their overview serves readers weighing claims for supplements against the underlying evidence from diet studies.  Food scientists cite it when setting standards for extracts used in supplements and health foods.
pmc-4015143:
Horvath asked in 2013 whether chemical marks on DNA could tell a person's age. The marks, called DNA methylation, change over life in patterns that vary by tissue. It was not known if one predictor could work across many human tissues and cell types.

Horvath built a predictor that works across a broad range of tissues and cells. The predicted age tracks real age closely and seems to reflect a real biological process, not just noise. Such a clock lets researchers measure how fast a body is aging. It has since been used to study disease, lifestyle, and the effects of aging itself.
pmc-4711343:
Zhang presented Gctf in 2016, a program for cryo electron microscopy, or cryoEM. To rebuild a molecule's structure at near-atomic detail, researchers must estimate the contrast transfer function, which describes how the microscope blurs each image. Errors in that estimate blur the final structure.

Gctf uses graphics processors to determine and correct this function in real time, as images are collected. Speed and robustness are its main aims, since modern sessions gather huge numbers of images. A fast, accurate correction lets labs judge data quality on the spot. That real-time feedback transformed cryoEM workflows during its rise.
pmc-5023043:
Franke and Svergun presented DAMMIF in 2009, a program for small-angle scattering work. Small-angle scattering lets researchers probe the low-resolution shape of a molecule in solution. DAMMIF determines that shape from scratch, a task called ab initio shape determination, using the scattering data alone.

DAMMIF is a much faster, improved version of the earlier program DAMMIN. Speed matters because shape runs are repeated many times to check stability of the result. A faster program lets labs test more models and larger systems in the same time. Structural biologists use such shapes as a first model of proteins and complexes that resist crystallization.
pmc-5956843:
Nicholas Bokulich, Benjamin Kaehler, Jory Rideout, and colleagues described a QIIME 2 plugin for naming microbes in 2018. Marker-gene studies must assign each DNA sequence to a known group. That naming step shapes every later claim about a community.

The plugin offers machine learning and alignment methods and a way to test which works best on known samples. Honest testing matters because accuracy drops on new sample types. The authors show how to tune the classifier rather than trust defaults. Microbiome researchers use the tool to keep species calls as sound as the data allow.
pmc-6202443:
The GBD 2016 Lower Respiratory Infections Collaborators published this global study in 2018. Chest infections such as pneumonia remain a leading cause of sickness and death worldwide. They strike hardest at very young children and older adults.

The analysis gives illness and death figures plus the likely germs behind them for nearly two hundred countries. Streptococcus pneumoniae stands out as the top killer among the causes studied. Trends show progress in child deaths but stubborn totals overall. Vaccine and treatment programs use these estimates to choose where new tools will save the most lives.
pmc-6618143:
Antonella Viola, Fabio Munari, Ricardo Sánchez-Rodríguez, and coauthors reviewed macrophage metabolism in 2019. Macrophages are immune cells with many jobs, from eating germs to healing tissue. Their behavior depends on how they fuel themselves.

Different tasks call for different metabolic settings inside the cell. Inflammatory macrophages lean on fast sugar burning, while healing types favor slower, oxygen-based routes. The review maps these signatures and the signals that flip them. Reprogramming metabolism may one day steer macrophages in diseases from arthritis to cancer. The authors close by naming the metabolic questions that single-cell methods may soon answer.
pmc-7090843:
Jianbo Lai, Simeng Ma, Ying Wang, and coauthors studied mental health in Chinese health care workers during COVID-19 in 2020. Frontline staff faced heavy exposure, long hours, and fear of infecting family. Their psychological state was a pressing concern.

Surveying staff across dozens of hospitals with fever clinics or COVID wards, the team found widespread depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress. Nurses, women, and frontline workers reported the heaviest burden. The authors urge protected rest, clear support channels, and screening for staff. The study became a reference point for workforce care in later outbreaks.
pmc-7094943:
Fan Wu, Su Zhao, Bin Yu, and coauthors reported a new coronavirus tied to human respiratory disease in China in 2020. Emerging infections like SARS and Zika remain a major public health threat. Where and when new ones appear is still hard to foresee.

The team isolated and sequenced the virus from a patient in Wuhan with severe pneumonia. Its genome marked it as a new member of the coronavirus family, related to SARS-like bat viruses. Sharing the sequence let labs worldwide build tests at once. The paper is one of the founding reports of the COVID-19 pandemic.
pmc-7222643:
Laure Wynants, Ben Van Calster, Gary Collins, and coauthors appraised COVID-19 prediction models in 2020. Models to diagnose the disease, forecast patient outcomes, or flag high-risk people appeared at great speed. Decisions based on weak models could do real harm.

Reviewing published and preprint models against reporting and bias standards, the team found all of them at high risk of bias. Small data sets, poor handling of missing values, and rosy validation were common. The authors urged that none be used in practice yet. Their verdict became a widely quoted guardrail for pandemic modeling.
pmc-7692443:
Spase Stojanov, Aleš Berlec, and Borut Štrukelj examined in 2020 whether probiotics can shift a widely watched balance in the gut. The two largest bacterial groups in the intestine, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, draw attention because their ratio is thought to help keep the gut in a healthy state. Changes in that ratio have been linked to obesity and to inflammatory bowel disease.

The authors review studies in which probiotic products were used to treat those two conditions, asking whether the ratio moved and whether patients improved. They weigh the strains and study designs behind the claims. Their account gives readers a sober measure of what friendly bacteria can and cannot yet do for these common conditions.
pmc-7857443:
Hassanain Ali Lafta and three colleagues measure how moving a wheelchair's rear axle changes the strain on the user's arms. Wheelchair setup affects joint motion, muscle effort, and stability, yet many users never have the geometry fitted to them. Ten healthy men with no wheelchair experience propelled chairs in three configurations. With the rear axle at the maker's position or shifted backward by set amounts, while cameras and muscle sensors recorded their upper bodies.

Three-dimensional motion analysis tracked joint angles and shoulder muscle activity for each setup at a university lab in Cardiff. Even small axle shifts changed how far joints moved and how hard muscles worked during each push. For clinicians and suppliers who fit chairs, the results turn a workshop adjustment into a measurable health decision. Since years of daily pushing on a poor setup can wear out shoulders a user depends on.
pope-dunciad-1743:
Alexander Pope first published The Dunciad in 1728 to mock the bad writers and hacks who had attacked him. He kept expanding it for fifteen years. The final four-book version, printed in 1743, replaced his original target with the critic and playwright Colley Cibber as hero of dullness.

The goddess Dulness holds her games for the worst poets, divers, and critics in London. Pope names real rivals and buries them in mock-heroic verse, with learned notes adding fake scholarship. Beneath the jokes lies real anger at a culture of print for profit. The poem ends with Dulness swallowing art, science, and morality in one great yawn of darkness.
prescott-conquest-mexico-1843:
William H. Prescott published History of the Conquest of Mexico in 1843, a classic of American romantic history. Prescott, nearly blind, worked from Spanish archives copied for him. He tells of the Aztec empire under Montezuma and its fall to Hernan Cortes. Battles, marches, and the siege of Tenochtitlan form the climax.

Prescott writes Cortes and Montezuma as epic figures in a vast drama. His scenes of Aztec temples, markets, and sacrifice drew wide wonder. Modern scholars correct many details and stress native sources he lacked. Yet the narrative power remains unmatched in English. The book made Prescott famous on two continents.
prudentius-psychomachia-1743:
Prudentius, a Christian poet of Roman Spain, wrote the Psychomachia around 405 CE: a war for the soul fought by personified Virtues and Vices. The English verse translation here dates to 1743. His short epic was the first full Christian allegory, and the Middle Ages loved it above almost any other poem.

Faith wrestles Idolatry, Chastity meets Lust, and Patience stands unmoved while Wrath breaks itself on her shield. Each duel ends with a moral drawn tight. The poem's scheme shaped medieval art, where the Virtues and Vices still fight on church walls. Prudentius turned Roman epic inward, to the battlefield of the heart.
psychography-or-the-embodiment-of-though:
Robert H. Collyer, a doctor trained in London, published a treatise at Philadelphia in 1843 on the way thought shows itself in the body. He joins three fads of his day: phrenology, animal magnetism, and what he calls neurology.

The book promises rules to govern and produce the magnetic state, an account of mental hallucination, and an experiment with a bowl of molasses. Collyer wrote as a pupil of Dr. Elliotson and a member of a Massachusetts medical society. Readers get a bold sample of early American mind science, before its claims were tested and mostly dropped.
ptolemy-geography-greek-nobbe-1843:
Ptolemy's other great book maps the earth as the Almagest maps the sky. Claudii Ptolemaei Geographia, in Carl Nobbe's Greek edition of 1843 to 1845, prints the Geography in three volumes. The second-century work holds eight books of place lists and map craft.

Ptolemy gives star-based places for some eight thousand towns, with rules for drawing the world on a grid. The maps drawn from his lists taught the late Middle Ages the shape of the earth. Columbus and his age sailed with Ptolemy's world in mind. Nobbe's text gives the work in its own Greek tongue.
ptolemy-geography-nobbe-1843: Ptolemy's Geography, in C. F. A. Nobbe's 1843 Greek edition, mapped the known world with coordinates for thousands of places. Its eight books shaped mapmaking for 1,500 years. This three-volume edition is the public-domain standard text.
rolle-fire-of-love-1343:
Richard Rolle wrote the Incendium Amoris, the Fire of Love, in Latin. Richard Misyn turned it into English in 1435, close to Rolle's own day. Rolle was a hermit in Yorkshire who wrote for nuns and lone souls. The work dates to the last years of his life.

Heat, song, and sweet taste mark God's touch in Rolle's scheme. He tells how the soul burns more hot as it climbs to full love. Warnings to false hermits and cold priests spice the text. The book is the chief work of the great English mystic of his age.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5043:
Richard Nixon gives five yearly addresses, from January 22, 1970, to January 30, 1974, parted by three stars. The first calls the chance to address a joint session of Congress, in the chamber where he once served, an honor for which he is deeply grateful. Such an address is by custom a long and detailed count of past deeds and of bills the president wants next.

Now and then, Nixon says, a time comes when deep and far-reaching events call for a break with that custom, and this is such a time. He says it not only because 1970 opens a new ten years in which America will mark its two-hundredth year. New knowledge and hard lessons argue with force, he holds, that both the nation's programs and its forms of rule stand in need of reform.
stukeley-abury-1743:
William Stukeley surveyed the great stone circles of Avebury in Abury, printed in 1743. The full title calls the place a temple of the British Druids. Stukeley walked the fields, measured the stones, and drew the vast plan. He read the avenues of stones as a serpent formed in the landscape.

Druid priests, in his account, built the temple, with roots he traced toward Phoenicia. His Stonehenge of 1740 is the companion to this survey. Together the two books invented the Druidic reading of Britain's megaliths. Later ages corrected his dates but honored his fieldwork. The Gutenberg text keeps his plates and reasoning. Avebury still bears his stamp.
summer-on-the-lakes-in-1843:
S. M. Fuller's Summer on the Lakes, in 1843, dated MDCCCXLIV, or 1844, records a tour through the Great Lakes country, with an illustration of the arched rock at Mackinaw at its front. Fuller, later famous as Margaret Fuller, travelled as a young woman of letters seeing the new West.

Verse stands at the head of the book. One poem recalls summer days of busy leisure. A gift poem offers a friend small treasures. They are dried grass from the flowery plain and a shell from a lone shore. They are antlers and an eagle's feather. The feather came from a brave nearly the last of his band. The chapters mix travel notes with reflection on settlers, Native peoples, and the wild country then opening to the East.
sunderland-magnet-1843:
In 1843 La Roy Sunderland started The Magnet, a journal for the young American mesmerist movement. He edited its pages himself in the heat of public debate. Readers sent in case reports, claims, and sharp attacks on rival healers.

Month by month, the journal tracked trances, cures, and tests of magnetic sleep. It also printed fierce quarrels among believers who split over method and fame. Few sources show the birth of mesmerism in America so close up. The excitement, hope, and hype of a new mind science fill every issue, just as its first fans lived it.
sunderland-pathetism-1843:
La Roy Sunderland published Pathetism, with Practical Instructions in 1843, at the start of his American career. The short book laid out his core claim in plain terms. He held that one mind can act on another through sympathy alone.

Half the book gives doctrine, and half gives direct how-to steps. Readers learn how to put a subject into magnetic sleep and what to do next. Sunderland wrote with total faith in his method and his gift. His manual lets modern readers see early mesmerism as its founder taught it, step by step, in his own confident voice.
the-merchant-of-venice-pg2243: The trial scene holds the stage in this edition: Shylock whets his knife for the pound of flesh, and Portia's mercy speech turns the law against him. Venice's Christians and Jews clash in Shakespeare's most debated play. Brilliant, troubling, and endlessly discussed.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 369 of the Mirror, dated Saturday, May 9, 1829, illustrates Cornwall Terrace in Regent's Park and continues a serial anatomy of The Times newspaper. The terrace, adjoining York Terrace, ranks among the park's earliest and most admired buildings. It is named for the king's ducal title when he was Regent. Decimus Burton designed it, with a rusticated ground story and Corinthian principal stories of fluted shafts.

The Times feature, concluded from page 292, walks a reader through the paper's departments. After leaders and war news comes the Court Circular, then Money Market and City Intelligence. The capitalist devours that oracle line by line, the article says, weighing phrases like 'risen about a quarter per cent.' Talk to him during any other part and he will join you; during the money article he can spare only occasional words. Readers get two Regency institutions, stucco and newsprint, examined in one number.

Volume 19, No. 545, dated May 5, 1832, returns to the Zoological Gardens in Regent's Park. Three smaller engravings show the emu enclosure, the pelican enclosure, and an aviary for small birds. The magazine reminds readers that it had pictured these gardens before any other journal gave them a connected notice.

Emus reared at the society's farm at Kingston Hill were exhibited in the old garden each year. Pelicans kept a house of imitation rock-work with a large tank of water. British crows and song birds filled the aviary at the garden's north-eastern corner. A further engraving introduces Happy Jerry, a great mandrill baboon from the Gold Coast and Guinea coasts of Africa.

Staines new bridge opens volume 19, No. 548, dated May 26, 1832. The bridge had lately been finished and opened at Easter, when the king and queen crossed it with the court in ceremony. For Staines, the day joined local pride in a useful public work with loyalty to a popular sovereign.

Quoted particulars describe three flat granite arches, the middle one spanning 74 feet and the side arches 66 feet each. Smaller arches serve the towing paths and let flood water pass. A plain granite cornice, lamp pedestals, and a neat toll-house finish the structure. Bridge and approaches cost about 41,000 pounds. Earlier Staines bridges, beginning with a wooden one recorded in 1262, fill the history that follows.

No. 582 of The Mirror, dated December 22, 1832, shows the York Column from St. James's Park in London. Five years of government-ordered improvements to the park frame the piece. Carlton House, the former royal residence on the site, had been marked for demolition and its grounds opened to the public.

Frederic, Prince of Wales, bought the property from the Earl of Burlington in 1732. Carlton House itself was built only from 1788 for the future king, so the palace lasted barely forty years. On its courtyard site rose two club mansions, for the United Service Club, designed by Mr. Nash, and the Athenaeum, designed by Mr. Decimus Burton. Palatial houses now front the park where the gardens stood.
tob-0043:
Five books on CIA programs and mind control are gathered in this collection, assembled in 2020 from the literature of the declassification era. The set mixes documented history with speculation. Its titles range from John Marks's The Search for the Manchurian Candidate to Victor Marchetti's The CIA and the Cult of Intelligence.

Chan Thomas's Adam and Eve Story, Fritz Springmeier's Bloodlines of the Illuminati, and Ron Patton's history of Project Monarch complete the shelf. Together they show the genre that grew from real revelations, above all MKULTRA, into a wide literature of covert plot. Readers can weigh sourced expose against conjecture within one holding, which is the collection's research use.
tob-10043:
Israel Abrahams, a leading scholar of Judaism, gathered essays on Jewish life, history, and literature in The Book of Delight and Other Papers. Subjects range from medieval poetry to the folk customs of ordinary people. The title piece celebrates the delights of learning itself.

Written with wit and deep knowledge, the papers move between scholarship and everyday culture. Abrahams shows how books, festivals, songs, and habits carried Jewish identity across centuries and countries. For general readers, the volume opens a window on a culture often seen only through its major texts, and it does so through small, human details as much as grand events.
tob-10543:
Max Arthur Macauliffe, a British official in India, spent years with Sikh scholars preparing The Religion of the Sikhs. His work grew to six volumes of translation and history. He learned Punjabi and won the trust of Sikh teachers who checked his renderings.

The volumes translate hymns of Guru Nanak and the later Gurus and tell the lives of all ten Gurus. Macauliffe aimed to give Sikhs a faithful record in English and to correct poor accounts then in print. His edition brought Sikh scripture and history to Western readers and is still quoted by students of the faith.
tob-13143:
Swami Vivekananda's lectures on Karma Yoga came out in 1896, drawn from talks he gave in New York. They teach the yoga of action, one of the four paths he set before Western pupils. Of those paths, this is the one aimed at daily work.

The secret, he says, is to work without clinging to results, offering each act rather than grasping its fruit. Duty, charity, and even hard or dull jobs become training for freedom when done in that spirit. Karma Yoga remains the most practical of his books, read by people with no wish to leave the world.
tob-13643:
The 1908 Hermetic primer The Kybalion appears in this edition under the Three Initiates name, an authorship commonly attributed to New Thought writer William Walker Atkinson. Seven rules unfold as laws of mind: mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender. Each is stated as an axiom, then explained and applied.

Atkinson's hand, if the attribution holds, fits the book's practical tone: ancient Egypt and Greece supply the pedigree, but the intended use is modern self-mastery. V1 evidence calls it the occult bestseller that never went away. A century of reprints, study groups, and arguments over its sources supports the claim.
tob-14243:
An early Christian letter found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt, the Treatise on the Resurrection, answers a man named Rheginos who doubted the teaching. Its unknown author writes as a teacher to a pupil. The letter is short, calm, and sure of its case.

Resurrection, the author argues, is not the flesh rising as flesh, but a spiritual reality the believer already shares in Christ. The world is an illusion that death exposes, while the risen life endures. The letter gives a clear, compact case for the Gnostic view of resurrection and shows how early Christians argued over the body's fate.
tob-4043:
Friedrich Schiller, the playwright of German classicism, turned thinker in his aesthetical essays, above all On the Aesthetic Education of Man. Writing in letters to a patron, Schiller asks how human beings divided between sense and reason can become whole, and how whole people might make a free state. His answer runs through beauty.

Play, in Schiller's famous play-drive, reconciles our warring natures: form and feeling meet, and only lovely souls, he argues, make free citizens. Other essays treat the sublime, grace, and tragedy. The collection shaped German classicism and influenced readers from Coleridge to Marcuse, wherever art's power to educate humanity is claimed.
tob-4243:
Lady Charlotte Guest's edition of the Mabinogion in its 1849 to 1877 form presents the complete Welsh tales in the translation that made them English classics. The Four Branches of the Mabinogi, Culhwch and Olwen, and the Arthurian romances are all included, with Guest's notes preserving the Wales of storytellers, scholars, and vanished customs behind the texts.

Guest learned Welsh as an English aristocrat married into Welsh industry, an unlikely path to founding a literature's modern fame. Her Mabinogion is often called the Celtic Twilight's founding text in English. Readers get the tales whole, with the apparatus of the edition that first carried Welsh myth across Europe.
un-ga-res-43:
Long before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights took shape, the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 43 on 11 December 1946. The Economic and Social Council had set up a Commission on Human Rights that year. Its charge was to draft plans for an international bill of rights. A draft Declaration on Fundamental Human Rights and Freedoms was already in hand.

The Assembly sends that draft to the council, for the commission to use as it drafts the bill. It also voices the hope that the question will come back to the Assembly in time for its second regular session. The path from this referral led, two years later, to the famous 1948 declaration.
un-ga-res-a-69-43:
A timed plan to end nuclear arms is urged in Resolution A/69/43, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls a chain of votes since 1994 on the step-by-step cut of the nuclear threat. It holds that the mere life of such arms puts mankind and all life on earth at risk. The sole sure defense, it argues, is their total end, with a pledge they will never be made again.

The pledges of the nuclear states are spelled out: the firm vow of 2000 to wipe out their arsenals in full. Deep concern at the toll of any use of such arms runs through the vote. The Conference on Disarmament is pressed to open talks on a phased plan, with a set frame of time.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 43 was adopted on 11 December 1946, at the fifty-fifth plenary meeting. It fed a draft text into the making of an international bill of rights. The Assembly sent the draft Declaration on Fundamental Human Rights and Freedoms to the Economic and Social Council. It was for passing to the new Commission on Human Rights. The Assembly voiced the hope that the question would come back to it for the second regular session.

General Assembly resolution 69/43 (2014) follows up the International Court of Justice's 1996 advisory opinion on nuclear weapons. The Assembly stresses the Court's unanimous conclusion. States are obliged to pursue negotiations in good faith. They must bring them to an end leading to nuclear disarmament under strict international control. It calls on all states to fulfil that duty at once. They should start multilateral negotiations toward an early nuclear weapons convention. The convention would ban the weapons and provide for their elimination.
un-sc-res-1343:
The Council adopted Resolution 1343 on Liberia on 7 March 2001. United Nations experts had found hard proof of Liberian support for Sierra Leone's rebels, the RUF. Rebel diamonds moved out through Liberia, with top officials involved. That trade paid for guns, fuel, and training across the border.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council first ends the old 1992 arms embargo on Liberia, its war now over. It then sets a fresh arms embargo for fourteen months. Liberia must expel RUF members, halt all money and military help, and stop uncertified diamond imports. A ban on Liberian rough diamonds and a travel ban on senior officials follow in two months unless Liberia complies.
un-sc-res-143:
Days after the Republic of the Congo gained independence, its government asked the United Nations for military help, and Belgium still had troops on Congolese soil. Resolution 143, adopted on 14 July 1960, was the Security Council's first answer to the Congo Crisis. The vote was eight to none, with three abstentions.

The Council calls on Belgium to withdraw its troops from the Congo. It authorizes the Secretary-General, in consultation with the Congolese government, to provide military assistance until Congo's own security forces can fully do their job, with UN technical help. He must report back to the Council. The decision launched one of the UN's largest early peacekeeping efforts.
un-sc-res-1443: The Council spoke on Iraq's oil-for-food program through Resolution 1443, adopted unanimously on 25 November 2002. The program let Iraq sell oil to buy food and medicine under sanctions. Its current phase was about to lapse. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the standing rules for just nine days, until 4 December 2002. The short bridge keeps aid flowing while members finish talks on the next phase. Nothing else in the sanctions setup changes.
un-sc-res-1543:
Timor-Leste's support mission was reshaped by the Security Council on 14 May 2004. The foreign minister of Timor-Leste had asked in February for a one-year extension of UNMISET. The Secretary-General advised a one-year consolidation phase, though with a smaller mission. The country's institutions were still forming, above all in justice, public administration, and policing.

The Council extended UNMISET for six months, with a view to one further final period of six months. The mission would shrink and take on revised tasks drawn from the Secretary-General's April report. Its new shape included up to 58 civilian advisers, with police and military parts scaled to the plan. Human rights principles had to stay at the core of its training work. The Secretary-General would report often and advise on the police and military shape ahead. The Council also restated the need to fight impunity for the crimes of 1999.
un-sc-res-1643:
Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions were renewed and widened on 15 December 2005. The African Union's October decisions and resolution 1633 (2005) had set the road map for the transition's final year. An international working group now watched the process. The arms embargo and targeted measures of resolution 1572 (2004) were nearing their first term. Peacekeepers' freedom of movement still met blocks.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renewed the arms embargo and the travel and asset measures of resolution 1572 to 15 December 2006. Any grave block on UNOCI's movement would itself draw the targeted measures. All states were ordered to bar the import of rough diamonds from Côte d'Ivoire, in line with the Kimberley Process bar on Ivorian stones. States in the region had to report on the steps they took. The Secretary-General and France were to keep reporting on breaches and obstructions.
un-sc-res-1743:
On 15 February 2007, the Council adopted Resolution 1743 on Haiti. Elections in 2006 had restored an elected government after years of turmoil. Armed gangs still ruled parts of Port-au-Prince, the capital. United Nations troops, called MINUSTAH, worked beside the Haitian police.

The text extends the mandate of MINUSTAH until 15 October 2007. The mission must keep up strong operations against armed gangs, above all in the capital. It should shift its disarmament work toward cutting violence in poor districts. The Council also asks for faster police, court, and prison reform, and for job projects that show quick results.
un-sc-res-1843: Resolution 1843, from 2008, is a Security Council decision held in this collection in official-record form. Its source transcription comes from English Wikisource. The document's two registers are easy to hear: the preamble's diplomatic weighing, then the operative part's plain commands and requests. The entry keeps both registers complete and in sequence.
un-sc-res-1943:
The Council's vote on 13 October 2010 produced Resolution 1943 on Afghanistan. The London and Kabul conferences had set a shared plan for the country's future. A joint board would start handing security duties to Afghan forces. The shared aim was Afghan command of most operations by the end of 2014. Civilian deaths stayed high, most caused by insurgent attacks.

The Council extends the International Security Assistance Force until 13 October 2011. States in the force may take all necessary measures for the mission. Members are urged to add troops, gear, and funds. Training Afghan soldiers and police comes first, so the handover can hold. The force must report to the Council every three months.
un-sc-res-243: Under number 243, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 1967 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-343:
Cyprus kept its United Nations peacekeeping force under a Council decision of 14 December 1973. The Secretary-General's report of 1 December held that the force was still needed if peace was to be kept on the island. The Government of Cyprus agreed the force should stay past 15 December 1973. The Council also took note of the conditions then prevailing across the island.

The Council reaffirmed the long line of Cyprus resolutions back to resolution 186 (1964), which created the force. It urged the parties to show the utmost restraint. Both communities were told to press on with joint efforts toward the Council's goals while the climate was favorable. The force's stationing was extended to 15 June 1974. As in each renewal, the Council voiced the hope that progress by then would allow a withdrawal or a large reduction of the force.
un-sc-res-43:
Violence and disorder were rising in Palestine in the spring of 1948. On 1 April 1948 the Security Council said an immediate truce was urgently needed. It acted, the text notes, under its chief duty for world peace. The call went to both national movements. The Jewish Agency and the Arab Higher Committee had to send representatives. Their task was to arrange a truce between the two communities.

Any party that failed to uphold a truce would bear heavy blame. Arab and Jewish armed groups had to stop all acts of violence at once. The resolution came six weeks before the British mandate ended. The truce it sought did not hold.
un-sc-res-443:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force came up for renewal again in December 1978. On 14 December 1978 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 June 1979. The Secretary-General had reported on the operation at the month's start. The parties agreed the force should stay. Cyprus's government said conditions on the island still required it. The Council restated the terms set when the force was created in 1964.
